en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Monks in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
(Second Part) 4.
Catukkanipāta 1.
Commentary on the Verses of Thera Nāgasamāla
The verses beginning with "Alaṅkatā" are the stanzas of the Venerable Elder Nāgasamāla. What is their origin?
He too was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara;
having reached maturity, he saw the Teacher walking on ground heated by the sun's rays during the summer season, and with a mind full of faith, he offered him a parasol. By that meritorious deed...
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha’s appearance within the Sakyan royal family.
Having received the name Nāgasamāla, he attained faith during a gathering of his kinsmen upon reaching maturity; having gone forth, he served as an attendant to the Blessed One for some time.
One day, having entered the city for alms, [he saw] a certain person adorned and arrayed in finery...
Seeing a dancer dancing on the high road while musical instruments were being played, he established the contemplation of decay and fall, thinking:
"This is the turning of the body made of kamma through the expansion of the air-element as a mental activity; oh, how impermanent are conditioned phenomena!
Thus, by intensifying his insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“The earth was ablaze with embers, the world was filled with glowing coals;
yet the Blessed One Padumuttara walked in the open air.
Taking up a white parasol, I set out upon the journey.”
Having seen the Fully Awakened One there, a realization arose within me:
"The earth is covered with mirages; this ground is like glowing embers.
Great winds blow, causing the comfort of my body to vanish."
“Warding off cold and heat, and shielding against wind and sun, accept this parasol; I shall touch upon Nibbāna.
Anukampaka, Kāruṇika, Padumuttara of great renown—”
Knowing my intention, the Victor then accepted it.
"For thirty eons I exercised sovereignty over the gods as Lord of Devas;
and five hundred times I was a wheel-turning monarch."
“I experience my own well-performed karma from the past: a vast regional kingship, beyond counting.
This is my final birth; this is my last existence.”
"Even today, my white parasol is held over me at all times.
Because I gave that parasol back in a hundred thousand aeons, I have never known an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of the gift of the parasol."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she said:
“Adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands, and anointed with sandalwood paste;”
In the middle of the great highway, a female dancer was dancing to the sound of musical instruments.
"Having entered for alms, as I was walking along, I beheld her—
adorned and well-dressed, like the outstretched snare of Death."
“Then right attention arose in me through proper method;
the danger became manifest, and disenchantment took firm root.
Then my mind was liberated; behold the excellence of the Dhamma!”
"The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
With these four verses, he declared his full realization (*aññā*) by way of praising his own practice.
In this context, "adorned" means having limbs adorned with ornaments such as bracelets and the like; "well-clad" means wearing beautiful garments.
She was dressed in beautiful garments. "Mālinī" means wearing a garland, one who has put on a flower wreath. "Candanussadā" means one whose body is smeared with an abundance of sandalwood paste.

"In the middle of the great road, a woman, a dancer, dances to the music"—in the aforementioned place, a certain woman, a dancing girl (*naṭṭakī*), danced in the middle of the city street while five-fold musical instruments were being played.
"He performs the dance exactly as it was rehearsed.
"Piṇḍikā" means almsfood. "Having entered" means having entered the city. "Going along, I looked at her":
while walking through the city streets, looking down the road for the sake of avoiding dangers, I looked at that dancing girl.

What is it like? It is "like the snare of Death set. Just as the snare of Death—the King of Death—consisting of form and so forth, which has been set out and remains wandering through the world, brings about exclusively harm for sentient beings, so too does this [craving] bring about exclusively harm for blind worldlings who abide in a lack of reflection;
thus it is said to be similar to the snare of Death.
"Therefore" means for that reason, because it resembles the snare of Death. "To me" means to myself. "Appropriate attention arose" means:
"This collection of bones, bound together by sinews, unsmeared by flesh, covered by skin, impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive;
subject to the nature of being impermanent, requiring constant covering, rubbing, breaking, and destruction—it displays such a transformation," thus [arose] appropriate attention.

"Attention arose; the danger became manifest. Thus, for one who attends to the rise and fall, as well as the inherent perishability, of the body by way of maintaining its true nature—and of the mind and mental factors dependent upon it—and who perceives them as terrifying, like ghosts or demons, [he reflects]:
"In this regard, there are many kinds of dangers for me."
Fault became manifest. And because it is the opposite of that, there is a benefit in *nibbāna*. "Disenchantment became established":
the meaning is that the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*), accomplished through the power of contemplating the danger (*ādīnava*) [of conditioned things], took its stand in my heart;

for even a moment, the mind had no inclination toward grasping those material and immaterial phenomena, but rather, by way of the desire for liberation and so forth, it became entirely indifferent toward them.

"Beyond that" means after that knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). "My mind was liberated" means that while the supramundane cultivation (*lokuttara-bhāvanā*) was proceeding according to the sequence of the paths, my mind became liberated from all defilements (*kilesa*). By this, he shows the arising of the fruit (*phala*).

For it is said that at the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*), the defilements are being liberated, and at the moment of the fruit (*phalakkhaṇa*), they are liberated. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nāgasamāla is finished.
2. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhagu begins with the verse starting "I [was overcome] by drowsiness. What is his origin? It is said that he [lived during the time] of Padumuttara...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One and having reached maturity, he honored the relics of the Teacher after his final passing away with flowers.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the Nimmānarati devas;

wandering successively through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha’s appearance in the Sakya royal family, where he received the name Bhagu and reached adulthood.
Having gone forth together with Anuruddha and Kimbila, while dwelling in Bālakaloṇakagāma, one day,
in order to dispel the onset of sloth and torpor, he emerged from his dwelling and ascended the walking path;
there, having fallen, he used that very fall as a goad, dispelled his sloth and torpor, increased his insight, and attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the Blessed One Padumuttara of great fame had attained final Nibbāna,
I adorned his body by fashioning a flower-ornament for his head.”
“Having gained confidence in that regard, I attained a state of mastery;
having gone to the world of the devas, I remembered my meritorious deed.
A rain of *ambarā* flowers falls for me at all times.”
If I wander among humans, may I become a king of great renown.
There, a rain of flowers shall fall upon me at all times,
by virtue of that very offering of flowers made to the All-Seeing One.
“This is my final one; my last existence is now unfolding.
Even today, the rain of flowers rains down upon me at all times.
Because of that flower which I offered a hundred thousand aeons ago,”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of honoring the body [of the Buddha].
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as in the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, spending his time in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, [he lived] in a solitary dwelling with the Teacher.”
Having approached to express his appreciation, when asked, "Bhikkhu, do you dwell with diligence?",
he announced his own dwelling in diligence:
"Overcome by drowsiness, I went out from the monastery..."
While ascending the walking path, I fell right there upon the ground.
Having rubbed my limbs and ascended the walking path once more,
I walked back and forth upon that path, well-composed within.
“Then right reflection arose in me, based on fundamental principles;
the danger became manifest, and disenchantment took firm root.
Thereupon my mind was liberated—behold the excellence of the Dhamma!”
“The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”—These four verses he spoke.
Therein, “overcome by sloth” means overcome by sloth characterized by physical lethargy and a nature that obstructs capability.
"From the monastery" means from the dwelling place. "I went out" means I went out for the purpose of walking meditation (*caṅkama*).
"Right there I fell down, alas" means that right there on the steps of the walkway, being overcome by drowsiness, I fell to the ground.
"Having rubbed my limbs" means having rubbed the parts of my own body which were covered in dust due to falling on the ground. "And having climbed up again, I walked."
Without falling into despondency, thinking, "I have fallen away from generosity," he again ascended to the walking path (*caṅkama*). The construction is as follows:

"Being well-composed internally" means that, having become well-composed and one-pointed in mind within the sphere of his meditation subject (*gocarajjhatta*) by suppressing the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), he walked.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. And this itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhagu is finished.
3. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sabhiya begins with the words "Others... What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various states of existence, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher departing for his midday rest, he offered him a pair of sandals with a devout heart.
Through that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained final Nibbāna...
When the Golden Cetiya was completed, he went forth in the Dispensation together with six noble sons, making seven himself.
Having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and dwelling in the forest, being unable to produce any distinction (*visesa*), he said to the others:
"When we go for alms, we are still attached to life; and for one who is attached to life, it is not possible to realize the supramundane Dhamma."

“To attain [this], the death of an ordinary person is painful. Come now, let us build a ladder, climb the mountain, and practice the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) without regard for body or life. They did so.
Then, because the Great Elder was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (upanissaya), he became possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiñña) on that very day; from Uttarakuru...
He brought almsfood [to them]. The others, saying, "Venerable sir, you have fulfilled your task; even a mere conversation with you is an impediment.
We shall attend only to the duties of a recluse; you yourself should devote yourself to dwelling in happiness in this very life," refused the almsfood.
Unable to persuade them to accept it, the elder departed.
Then, after two or three days had passed, one among them realized the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) together with its supernormal powers (abhiññā);

having spoken in that same manner, he departed, being rejected by the others. Among them, the elder whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava) attained final nibbāna (parinibbāyi), while the non-returner was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heavens.
As for the others, having merely passed away as worldlings (puthujjana), they were reborn in the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure (kāmasagga) in both direct and reverse order.
Having experienced celestial prosperity, at the time of our Blessed One, they passed away from the world of the gods and took rebirth:
one in the family of a Malla king, one in the family of a Gandhāra king, one in a foreign kingdom, and one in the womb of a noble maiden in Rājagaha.
The other took rebirth in the womb of a certain female wanderer.
She took hold of it. It is said that she was the daughter of a certain kṣatriya;
her parents, thinking, "Let our daughter learn another doctrine," handed her over to a certain wanderer (paribbājaka). Then one wanderer misconducted himself with her.
She conceived a child by him. Seeing that she was pregnant, the wanderers cast her out.
While she was traveling elsewhere, she gave birth on the road in a rest-house (*sabhā*). Therefore, they gave him the name Sabhiya.
Having grown up and gone forth into the wandering life of a paribbājaka, he mastered various treatises and became a great debater.
Wandering about intent on debate, and finding no one equal to himself, he established a hermitage at the city gate and [instructed] the sons of the khattiyas and others.
While living as one training in a craft, he became disgusted with his own female state;
having developed jhāna and been reborn in the Brahmā world, he took up twenty questions formulated and given [to him], and he questioned various recluses and brahmins about them.
They were unable to explain the meaning of those questions to him. (In the commentary on the Sabhiya Sutta...)
However, it is recorded that "a Brahmā from the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) formulated those questions and gave them [to Sabhiya].

But when the Blessed One, having set the excellent Wheel of Dhamma in motion, arrived in Rājagaha in due course and was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana), Sabhiya went there, approached the Teacher, and asked those same questions. The Teacher [answered] for him...
That he answered those questions should be understood according to the method set forth in the Sabhiya Sutta.
When the Blessed One had answered those questions, Sabhiya gained faith; having gone forth and established insight, he attained Arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“To the sage Kakusandha, the brahmin of established virtue,
as he was departing for his midday rest, I gave him a stepping-stone.
Whatever gift I gave back then in this very eon— ”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of my stepping across [the path].
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so forth]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having become an Arahant, while Devadatta was striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, he gave this exhortation to the monks who sided with Devadatta:
“But others do not understand that we strive for this here;
yet those who do understand therein, their quarrels are thereby stilled.
And when, though lacking understanding, they conduct themselves as if they were immortal,”
And those who understand the Dhamma remain undistressed amidst the distressed.
Whatever action is lax, whatever vow is defiled,
and whatever holy life is dubious— none of that bears great fruit.
“He for whom respect toward his fellow practitioners is not found is far removed from the true Dhamma, just as the sky is from the earth.
Thus he taught the Dhamma with these four verses.

In that context, "others" refers to those other than the wise—those who are prone to dispute by way of illustrating the grounds for division, such as saying "what is not Dhamma is Dhamma" or "what is Dhamma is not Dhamma.
While they engage in dispute there, they do not realize: "We are being restrained, we are ceasing, we are perishing;
we are constantly and continuously going into the presence of Death. And "those who understand therein" refers to those...
In this regard, the wise understand: "We are going into the presence of Death. Then they settle their quarrels;
for knowing thus, they arouse wise attention and proceed toward the pacification of quarrels (*medhaga*).
By that practice, those quarrels of theirs are settled. Or else, "and others" refers to those who [act] according to the Teacher’s instruction and admonition.
Because they have not grasped [the truth] and are outside the teaching, others [do not understand];
as long as they do not realize, "Having taken up a wrong grasp, we are striving and exerting ourselves here in this world to counteract the teaching," so long will disputes not be stilled.
However, when that grasp is relinquished, and regarding those who were previously immersed in dispute concerning what is non-Dhamma and Dhamma therein—
They understand, as it truly is, what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma; then, by relying on those wise men, their quarrels—termed "strife"—are settled.
This is how the meaning here should be understood. "Yadā" means at whatever time.
"Not understanding" refers to not knowing the means for the pacification of quarrels, or [not knowing] the Dhamma and non-Dhamma according to reality.

Not knowing, they behave like immortals; like those who have transcended aging and death, they act, move about, and wander about—haughty, arrogant, fickle, talkative, and loose-lipped. At that time, the dispute is not pacified.
But those who understand the Dhamma, who are undistressed amidst the distressed, [understand] the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma as it truly is.
Those who know [this] dwell free from affliction, free from defilement, and free from distress among beings who are tormented by the disease of the defilements;
it is with reference to them that the dispute is completely and utterly stilled—this is the intended meaning.
Whatever action is slack means: having acted sluggishly, having formed a lax grasp through procrastination, and having performed it with a state of negligence.

Whatever wholesome deed there may be. "Defiled" refers to the undertaking of a vow that has become defiled by wandering in improper resorts such as among prostitutes, or by wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and the like.

"Suspicious" means it should be suspected; having heard something unsuitable occurring in the monastery, others should not suspect—thinking, "Surely this was done by so-and-so"—regarding any particular duty such as the Uposatha ceremony and so forth.
Even upon seeing the Saṅgha assembled, [he thinks], "Surely these people, having learned of my conduct, have assembled desiring to suspend me.
Thus, his own life is accompanied by suspicion, distrust, and apprehension.
"That does not exist" means that for such a person, this holy life—which constitutes the duty of a recluse—does not bear great fruit. Precisely because it does not bear great fruit for him...
Even for those who provide him with requisites, it does not bear great fruit. Therefore, one should live a life of effacement (sallekha).
The intention is that for one living a life of effacement, there is simply no occasion for dispute.
"Respect is not found" refers to [the lack of respect] toward fellow practitioners of the holy life who ought to be honored because they accept instruction respectfully.
In that person for whom respect and veneration do not exist, the true Dhamma is far away.
Such a person is distant from both the true Dhamma of practice and the true Dhamma of realization. For those who are venerable do not train him;
not being trained and not taking it to heart, he does not practice. Not practicing, how could he penetrate the Truths?
Therefore he said: "He is far from the true Dhamma. How so? "As the sky is from the earth.
Just as the sky, that is, space, is distant from the earth, from the earth-element, by its very nature, and never comes into contact with it; for this very reason he said:
"The sky is far and the earth is far; they say the further shore of the ocean is far."
"Therefore, they say that the Dhamma of the virtuous is far more distant than even the king of the unvirtuous.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sabhiya is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nandaka.
The verses beginning with "Dhiratthu" (Woe! belong to the Venerable Thera Nandaka. What is their origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was a very wealthy merchant in the city of Haṃsavatī.

While listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being the foremost among those who instruct the bhikkhunīs. [Seeing this, he aspired to] that same status...
Having made his aspiration and worshipped the Blessed One with a cloth worth a hundred thousand pieces, he offered a lamp-worship at the Teacher’s Bodhi tree.
From that time forth, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he became a *karavika* bird during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha; uttering sweet songs, he circumambulated the Teacher.
He did so. Later on, having become a peacock, he would, with a devout mind, cry out three times a day with a sweet song at the entrance of the cave where a certain Paccekabuddha dwelt.
Having thus performed meritorious deeds here and there, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One; having reached maturity, he received the name Nandaka.
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and by developing insight, attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“At the supreme footstool of the Bodhi tree of Buddha Padumuttara;”
With a clear mind and a joyful heart, I offered three torches.
In a hundred thousand aeons, I have maintained that torch;
I do not recognize a state of misery—this is the fruit of giving a torch.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus become an Arahant and spending his time in the bliss of liberation, he was instructed by the Teacher to give exhortation to the bhikkhunīs;
on a single Uposatha day, he led five hundred bhikkhunīs to Arahantship with a single exhortation. Because of this, the Blessed One [praised him].

He placed [her] in the foremost position among those who exhort the bhikkhunīs. Then one day, while the Elder was walking for alms in Sāvatthī, a certain woman who had formerly been his wife looked at him with a mind defiled by passion and laughed.
Seeing her action, the Elder, while preaching the Dhamma by way of analyzing the repulsiveness of the body, said:
“Shame on you, Pūra, foul-smelling one, who has flowed over toward the side of Māra!
There are nine streams in your body that flow at all times.
Do not think of the past, and do not insult the Tathāgata.”
They do not even lust after heaven, much less after the human world.
But those who are fools, witless, ill-advised, and shrouded by delusion—
such as these lust there for the bondage cast by Māra.
“Those for whom lust, hatred, and ignorance have faded away—such persons do not take delight therein, their cords cut, free from bonds. Thus he spoke this verse.
In that context, *dhī* is a particle used in the sense of loathing; *ratthu* contains the letter *ra* as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*), meaning “let there be loathing for that.”
"I loathe you; let there be a reproach upon you"—this is the meaning. The words beginning with "pūreti" (fills) are vocatives intended to illustrate her state of being censurable.
"Pūreti" means she is filled with various kinds of filth and various impurities that are exceedingly disgusting.
"Duggandhe" (foul-smelling) means she is naturally foul-smelling precisely because she is filled with corpses. "Mārapakkhe" (on Mara's side) is because she is an object discordant [with the path].

Because blind worldlings increase the defilement-māra through their improper mental attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and provide an opening for the son-of-deva-māra (*devaputtamāra*) to enter, they belong to the faction of Māra. Therefore it is said, “in the faction of Māra.
“Lustful” (*avassuta*) means being lustful at all times due to the flowing forth of defilements and the trickling out of impurities here and there.
"Now, there are nine streams in this body that flow constantly"— this shows the place where the impurities flow out, as stated in the passage beginning with "from the eye,
the eye-excrement," and so forth. Thus, knowing the body as it truly is— with its nine openings, constantly leaking, and filled with impurity— one should not [cling to] the old...
“Do not think” (*amāññittha*) means: do not regard with pride the laughing, talking, and playing that occurred in the past when you were ignorant;
do not think, “He will act in this same way even now. “The Tathāgata did not despise them” means:
just as the previous disciples of the Buddhas came through the perfection of their underlying potential (*upanissaya*), or just as they went and practiced by means of right practice, and just as...
The true characteristic (*tathalakkhaṇa*) of both material and immaterial phenomena, as well as the Noble Truths (*ariyasacca*), have been arrived at, attained, and realized;

and since these [beings] are likewise so, he addressed them with contempt—approaching them as if they were ordinary beings through the influence of defilements—on account of their arrival and other such qualities being "thus" (*tathā*).
He stated the reason why they should not be treated with contempt: even in heaven...
"They do not take delight"—how much less in the human realm? Even in the heavens, where even the All-Knowing Buddha could not exhaustively describe the bliss, those disciples do not take delight;
because they have clearly seen the danger in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), they do not generate lust.
How much less so for the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) in the human realm, which are like a heap of filth? Therein they do not take delight.
There is simply nothing that can be said [of them].
But those who are called "fools" (bāla) are so because of their application to foolishness; they are "dull-witted" (dummedha) due to the absence of the wisdom born of the essence of the Dhamma;

they are "bad counselors" (dummanti) because of their ill-considered thinking through the contemplation of the beautiful in the ugly; and they are characterized by a mind entirely shrouded by delusion (moha) and ignorance (aññāṇa).
Such blind worldlings, shrouded by delusion and of such a nature,
take delight— becoming impassioned, greedy, infatuated, intoxicated, and obsessed— in that which is called "woman," within that very bond cast by Māra, in the snare set by Māra.
But those whose taints are destroyed are "dispassionate," for their passion— which, like the stain of oil or collyrium, is by nature difficult to remove— is their enemy.

Just as one who has found an opportunity [to escape], hatred—which is by nature prone to reviling—and ignorance—which is by nature lack of knowledge—have been entirely discolored (virājita), abandoned, and cut off by means of the fading away (*virāga*) of the Noble Path.

Having had the cord of existence (*bhavanetti*) severed by the sword of the supreme path, they are therefore "unbound" (*abandhanā*) due to the absence of any fetter whatsoever; thus, they do not become attached to that aforementioned snare of Māra.
Thus the Elder, having preached the Dhamma to that woman, departed.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nandaka is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Jambuka.
The verses beginning with "Pañcapaññāsa" (Fifty-five) belong to the Venerable Jambuka Thera. What is their origin?

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher’s Perfect Enlightenment; having paid homage to the Bodhi tree, he—
He worshipped with a seed. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.

Upon reaching maturity, he went forth into the teaching and lived as a resident monk in a monastery built by a certain lay devotee, being supported by him. Then, one day, a certain elder whose taints were destroyed—
Wearing coarse robes, he was returning from the forest toward the village to have his hair removed. Seeing him, the lay devotee gained confidence in his deportment;

he had a barber shave his hair and beard, fed him with choice food, gave him beautiful robes, and made him stay, saying, "Venerable sir, please dwell right here. Seeing this, the resident monk became overcome by envy and stinginess.

He said to the Elder Khīṇāsavatthera: "Bhikkhu, it would be better for you to live here being supported by this wicked lay follower, than to live as a naked ascetic with hair plucked out by the fingers, subsisting on excrement and urine.
Having spoken thus, he immediately entered the privy and, as if increasing the milk-rice, increased the excrement with his hand.
Having increased it, he ate as much as he desired and drank urine. Remaining for the full span of his life according to this routine, he died and was boiled in hell;

then, having lived again as one whose food is excrement and urine, and due to the remaining residue of that same karma, even when reborn among humans, he became a Nigaṇṭha who subsisted on excrement for five hundred births.
Furthermore, even though he was reborn in a human womb during this current appearance of a Buddha, by the power of his abuse of the Noble Ones, he was born into a destitute family;
while being nursed with breast milk, curd, or ghee, he would spit that out and drink only urine;
while being fed rice, he would spit that out and eat only excrement—thus he grew up consuming excrement and urine.
Even when he reached adulthood, he continued to consume that very same food. When people were unable to dissuade him from it, they abandoned him.
Having been renounced by his kinsmen, he went forth as a naked ascetic;
he did not bathe, wore dust and dirt, plucked out his hair and beard, rejected all other modes of conduct, stood on one foot, and did not accept invitations.
Having undertaken a month-long fast, he would take food given by those seeking merit once every month with the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass and lick it with the tip of his tongue during the day;
at night, however, not eating "fresh excrement containing living beings," he ate only dried excrement.
While he was acting in this way, fifty-five years passed by, and the great multitude [of people]...
Thinking, “He is one of great asceticism and supreme fewness-of-wishes,” he became inclined toward that and leaning toward that.
Then the Blessed One, seeing within the heart of that man the necessary condition for Arahantship blazing like a lamp inside a jar,
went there himself, taught the Dhamma, established him in the fruit of stream-entry, and [ordained him] by the "Come, monk" admission.
Having received full ordination, he exerted himself in insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and established himself in *arahantship*. This is the summary here.

The detailed account, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the verse in the *Dhammapada* beginning with “Month after month, with the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass...”.

But once established in *arahantship*, at the time of his final passing away (*parinibbāna*), [he said]: “Although I practiced wrongly from the beginning, [I have now reached] the Perfectly Enlightened One...”
Showing that "what must be attained by a disciple has been attained by me," he said:
"For fifty-five years I bore the dust and dirt;
eating a single meal every month, I shaved off my hair and beard."
“I stood on one foot, I avoided sitting down;
I ate dried dung and did not consent to receiving formal instruction.
Having done such things as these, which lead to many miserable rebirths,”
“Being swept away by a great flood, I went for refuge to the Buddha.
Behold this going for refuge! Behold the excellence of the Dhamma!
The three knowledges have been attained; the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.”
He spoke these four verses.
Therein, "for fifty-five years he bore dust and dirt" means that by undertaking the naked renunciation and by the prohibition against bathing, for fifty-five years—
counting the five extra years— he bore the dust known as adventitious soil and the filth known as bodily impurity clinging to his body.
And I bore filth upon my body. While eating, [I would say] "I am eating once a month";

thus, for the sake of deceiving the world, having become known as a "month-faster," I would eat the food given by those seeking merit only once a month, merely by placing it on the tip of my tongue while reciting.
"I am shaving" means that by throwing away such refuse-rags, I made my hair and beard loose at the roots.
I had my fingers plucked out.
"I stood on one foot" means that I completely avoided sitting on a seat;
while standing, I raised both hands and remained standing on one foot alone. "Recitation" refers to an invitation.
"Udissakataṃ" means "prepared for a specific person," according to some. "Na sādiyiṃ" means "I did not accept" or "I rejected"; this is the meaning.
"Having performed such as this, much that leads to an unhappy destination":

having performed and produced such—that is, of such a kind—as much evil karma leading to an unhappy destination which produces such a result, both in previous births and here; [and thus] being swept away by the great flood.
Being dragged toward the ocean of the states of misery by the great flood of sensual desire and so forth— specifically by the flood of views—

one who has attained this human existence through such a rare opening of meritorious karma now takes refuge in the Buddha by the power of merit, with the conviction: "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One."
"I have placed my confidence in the Teacher. Behold the going for refuge;

behold the excellence of the Dhamma."—Behold my going for refuge directed toward the [Three] Bases, and behold the excellence of the Dhamma of the Dispensation, since even though I had previously practiced wrongly, I was brought by the Teacher to such an attainment through a single instruction.
He shows that attainment with the words beginning "the three knowledges," and thus he said:
“Having paid homage to the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Tissa,
I took up a fan there and fanned his lion throne.
Ninety-two aeons ago from now, I fanned the lion throne.”
“I do not recognize a state of misery; this is the fruit of sowing seeds.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Jambuka is finished.
6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Senaka The verses beginning with “Welcome indeed” are the stanzas of the Venerable Elder Senaka. What is his origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Having been reborn and reached the state of discernment, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a mind full of faith, honored the Blessed One with a peacock-feather fan.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family;
he was conceived in the womb of the sister of the Elder Uruvelakassapa, [the son] of Senakoti.
Such was his name. When he reached maturity, having attained proficiency in the sciences and arts of the brahmins, he lived the life of a householder.

At that time, the great multitude, celebrating a festival every year in the month of Phagguna under the constellation of Uttaraphagguṇī, performed ritual ablutions at the ford in Gayā. Therefore, that festival was called "Gayāphaggū."
So they say. Then, out of compassion for those to be converted, the Blessed One stayed near the ford of Gayā on such a festival day;
and the great multitude also approached that place from here and there with the intention of performing ablutions at the ford.
At that moment, Senaka too, having arrived at that place for the purpose of bathing at the ford, saw the Teacher teaching the Dhamma and approached him.
Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and while applying himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long.
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Taking a peacock-feather fan, I approached the Leader of the World;”
With a clear mind and a joyful heart, I gave a peacock-feather fan.
“By means of this peacock-feather fan and through my intentions and aspirations,
the three fires were extinguished, and I obtained vast happiness.”
“Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, our perfection of a Teacher!
Having given this peacock-feather fan, I obtain abundant happiness.
The three fires have been extinguished within me; all states of existence have been utterly uprooted.”
All taints are utterly destroyed; there is now no further becoming.
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of the gift I gave back then, I have not known a miserable rebirth—this is the fruit of that peacock-feather fan."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he became filled with joy and, as an inspired utterance, said:
“Welcome indeed was my arrival at Gayā on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika!”
I saw the Fully Awakened One teaching the supreme Dhamma— the one of great radiance,
teacher of the assembly, the foremost vessel, the leader,
the Victor of the world with its devas, whose vision is incomparable.
“The Great Naga, the Great Hero, of great radiance and free from taints;
the Teacher who has utterly exhausted all taints and is fearless from every quarter.
Alas, for a long time I have been defiled, bound by the fetters of wrong views!”
“The Blessed One has liberated me from all bonds, Senaka,” he said, and uttered these four verses.
Therein, “*Svāgatam vata me āsī*” means: “Truly, it was a most welcome arrival for me; indeed, it was a beautiful thing for me.”
There was an arrival. *Gayāyanti* means near the ford of Gayā (*gayātittha*).

*Gayaphagguyā* refers to the full moon day of Phagguna (Phālguna) when the moon is in conjunction with the constellation Uttaraphalgunī—a designation commonly known as "Gayā-Phaggū. The words beginning with "ya" (*yaṃ*) and so forth show the reason for the state of welcome.
In that context, *yaṃ* means "because"; *addasāsiṃ* means "I saw"; and *sambuddhaṃ* means one who has perfectly and by himself awakened to all phenomena.

"Sambuddha" means one who has awakened to Buddhahood. "Teaching the supreme Dhamma" means speaking the Dhamma that is most excellent, foremost, best of all, leading exclusively to liberation, and suited to the inclinations of those to be trained.
"Possessing great radiance" means being endowed with both the great radiance of his physical body and the radiance of his knowledge. "Teacher of the assembly" means...
He is the teacher of the community (*gaṇācariya*) through his supreme taming of groups such as the assembly of monks by means of training in proper conduct.
He has reached the pinnacle (*aggappatta*) through the attainment of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), which are themselves supreme.

He is the leader (*vināyaka*) because he disciplines gods, humans, and others through his supreme discipline, and because he is himself free from a need for a leader. Having remained unconquered by anyone, he has conquered the entire world.
Because he is steadfast and because he has conquered the five Māras, he is the Conqueror (Jina) of the world including its devas;

and because his physical body is adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, and his Dhamma-body is adorned with qualities such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence,
he is the Supreme Conqueror in the world including its devas, whose vision is immeasurable to the world including its devas.
And because of his incomparable vision, it is "vision beyond measure.
Because of his perfection in gait, strength, prowess, and so forth, he is like a great elephant (*mahānāga*);

and because of his great majesty even among those *nāgas* who have destroyed the taints, he is a "great elephant. Because of his crushing of Māra’s army and his great valor, he is a "great hero" (*mahāvīra*). "Great radiance" means great heat.
The meaning is "of great majesty. It is "untainted" (*anāsava*) because he has no taints (*āsava*) whatsoever.
It is "one by whom all taints are utterly destroyed" (*sabbāsavaparikkhīṇa*) because all taints, together with their underlying tendencies (*savāsana*), have been completely exhausted in him.

Although disciples and *paccekabuddhas* are indeed those whose taints are exhausted, the term "untainted" is stated here in order to show that only the omniscient Buddhas exhaust the taints along with their underlying tendencies.

Furthermore, it is said: "one who has completely destroyed all taints" (*sabbāsavaparikkhīṇa*). By this it is meant: "one whose taints, together with their underlying tendencies (*savāsanā*), have been completely destroyed—thus he is 'one who has completely destroyed all taints'.
He is the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs those to be trained according to their needs through the ultimate truths pertaining to the present life and the future life;
and because, due to his confidence in the four grounds of self-assurance (*vesārajja*), he is free from fear from any quarter whatsoever.
The construction is as follows: "Since I have seen such a Perfectly Enlightened One, who is fearless from any quarter, therefore it was indeed a welcome occurrence for me.
Now, demonstrating the qualities he himself has gained through the sight of the Teacher, he spoke the fourth verse. Its meaning is as follows:
like a gourd filled with sour gruel, like a bowl filled with buttermilk, and like a rag soaked in fat—with these bases of defilement...
In this beginningless saṃsāra, it has been defiled for a long time.
Like a dog tied to a post with a leash, I was bound to the post of the self-body by the tether of views;
and as he was releasing me from that, the Blessed One—by means of the hand of the Noble Path—has indeed liberated me, Senaka, from all the fetters such as covetousness.
"Mayhaṃ satthā" (He is my Teacher) expresses deep confidence in the Blessed One.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Senaka is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sambhūta.
The verses beginning with "In the time of darkness" (*yo daṇḍhakāle*) are those of the Venerable Elder Sambhūta. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, was reborn in the womb of a *kinnara* on the bank of the river Candabhāgā at a time when the world was empty of Buddhas.
One day, upon seeing a certain *paccekabuddha*, his mind became filled with serene faith.
Having paid homage with palms joined, he made an offering of *ajjuna* flowers.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Having attained the name Sambhūta and reached maturity, he heard the Dhamma from the presence of the Dhamma-treasurer (Ānanda) after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna; having gained faith, he—
Having gone forth and practicing the duty of a recluse, he developed insight and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the bank of the Candabhāgā River, I was then a kinnara;
I saw the stainless Buddha, the self-become, the unconquered.”
“With a clear mind and a joyful heart, filled with rapture and palms joined in reverence,
I took an *ajjuna* flower and worshipped the Self-Existent One.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations...”
Having cast off my kinnara body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
For thirty-six times I exercised divine sovereignty as Lord of the Devas;
ten times I exercised great kingship as a Wheel-turning Monarch.
“A vast regional sovereignty, beyond all counting—this seed sown by me in the Excellent Field, the Self-Existent One!
There is merit remaining for me; I have gone forth into the homeless life.”
“Today I am worthy of worship in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, when the Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa for a hundred years, in Vesālī...”
When the Vajjiputtakas had taken up the ten points and remained obstinate, the Elder Yasa, son of Kākaṇḍaka, together with seven hundred arahants who had destroyed the taints,
refuted that view and upheld the true Dhamma. When they had performed the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, the Elder,
moved by a sense of spiritual urgency at the way those Vajjiputtakas were manifesting what was contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, said:
“He who is slow when he ought to hurry, and hurries when he ought to be slow—
by acting without proper method, the fool encounters suffering.
His goals decline, like the moon in the dark fortnight.”
One incurs misfortune and is alienated from friends.
But the wise person who delays when there is time to delay, and hastens when it is time to hasten,
attains happiness through such prudent planning.
“His goals are fulfilled, like the moon in the bright fortnight;
he attains glory and renown, and he is not at odds with his friends.”—
Reciting these verses, he declared his final knowledge (of liberation).
In this context, "one who crosses over at a time of delay" refers to one who,

when some matter to be done arises— such as when a scruple regarding the Vinaya has arisen, wondering, "Is this permissible or not?"— does not dispel that scruple until he has consulted a competent expert in the Vinaya;
thus, while that duty is still at a stage where it ought to be delayed, he "crosses over" by crushing [the scruple] through transgression.
He does so. Furthermore, he causes delay in what ought to be crossed over: for a householder, in the undertaking of the refuges, the precepts, and so forth;
for one who has gone forth, in the performance of the major and minor duties and the application to serenity and insight.
When the time to cross over has arrived, instead of promptly engaging in that task, he delays, thinking, "I will do it in the coming month or fortnight. That task—
One would simply pass away without doing anything. "By way of improper preparation" means that by hesitating where one should act swiftly,
and by being slow where one should cross over, through such lack of skillful means and absence of strategic planning,
the foolish person of dull intellect encounters suffering and misfortune both now and in the future.
"His welfare declines" means that for such a person, the various kinds of welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth decline like the moon in the dark fortnight;
day by day they go toward exhaustion and total depletion.
[This is known] by such statements as, "That person is faithless, lacking confidence, lazy, and of inferior energy," and so on. "Blameworthiness" means being subject to censure by the wise.

*Pappoti* means he attains. *Virujjhati mittehi* (he is at odds with friends) means that by refusing to accept advice from virtuous friends who offer counsel, saying, "We are not to be spoken to," he is said to be in conflict with them by simply not taking their instruction—thinking, "Practice in this way; do not practice in that way.
The meaning of the remaining two stanzas should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. However, some here [interpret] the words *tarati dandhaye*...
They cite [the passage] regarding the exertion and restraint of the developing mind by way of its state of being (*atthabhāva*). This fits with the latter verses.

For the first two verses were spoken by the Elder concerning the Vajjiputtakas who were expelled by the Saṅgha after they had failed to practice the ascetic duty (*samaṇadhamma*) from the time of their ordination and had fallen into remorse, illustrating the ten points (*dasavatthu*); whereas the latter...
But [he is one] who, having practiced rightly toward those similar to himself, stands having accomplished his own welfare.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sambhūta is finished.
8. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Rāhula.
The verses beginning with "By both" are those of the Venerable Elder Rāhula. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having reached maturity, he placed the Teacher at the head of those desiring training, [and] a certain bhikkhu...
Seeing him making [the offering], he himself also aspired to that same position; having performed sublime merit such as cleaning and lighting the lodgings, he made a formal resolve (*paṇidhāna*).
Passing away from there, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current arising of a Buddha in the womb of Queen Yasodharā, dependent upon our Bodhisatta.
Named Rāhula, he grew up surrounded by a great retinue of kṣatriyas; the account of his going forth is found in the Khandhaka itself.
Having gone forth, he received excellent instruction from many sūtra passages in the presence of the Teacher.
With matured knowledge, he intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the seven-storied palace of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the World-Chief, the Neutral One, I spread out a mirror.
Surrounded by thousands of monks whose taints were destroyed, the Great Sage— ”
The Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men, approached the fragrant chamber.
Shining upon the fragrant chamber, the God of gods, the Bull among men,
the Teacher standing before the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, spoke these verses:
“I shall praise that by which this bed is made radiant, like a well-polished mirror; listen as I speak.
It is made of gold, of silver, and likewise of beryl.”
“Palaces will arise for him, whatever is dear to the mind.
Sixty-four times he will exercise sovereignty as Lord of the Devas;
a thousand times he will become a Wheel-turning Monarch without interval.”
“In the twenty-first aeon, a kshatriya named Vimala will become a wheel-turning monarch, a conqueror of the four quarters.
His city, named Reṇuvatī, will be beautifully constructed with bricks.”
In length it was three hundred [yojanas], and it was provided with four equal sides.
"The palace named Sudassana was built by Vissakamma;
it was adorned with excellent gabled chambers and embellished with the seven precious gems."
“Devoid of the ten sounds and crowded with holders of the sciences (vidyādharas),
it will become like the city of Sudassana belonging to the devas.
Its radiance will go forth like the rising sun.”
It will shine constantly for eight yojanas all around.
"In a hundred thousand kappas, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a Teacher in the world."
“Having passed away from Tusita, impelled by the root of his wholesome merit,
he will become the son of the Blessed One Gotama.
If he should dwell in the household life, he would become a wheel-turning monarch.”
"It is impossible that such a one as he should find delight in the household life.
Having gone forth from the home, he will go forth under the rule of the virtuous;
he who is named Rāhula shall become an Arhat."
“As a hen guards her eggs, or as a yak guards its tail,
so did the wise Great Sage, endowed with virtue, protect me.
Having understood his Dhamma, I dwelt delighted in his teaching.”
“Having fully understood all taints, I dwell taintless.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*).
“Endowed with both qualities, the wise call me ‘Blessed Rāhula’:
that I am the son of the Buddha, and that I am one who has eyes regarding the Dhammas.
That my taints are exhausted, and that there is no further becoming.”
“I am an arahant worthy of offerings, one possessed of the three knowledges, a seer of the Deathless.
‘Blinded by sensual desire, shrouded in a net, covered by the veil of craving,
they are bound by their heedless kinsman like fish at the mouth of a trap.’”
“Having abandoned that sensual desire, having severed Māra’s bond,
and having uprooted craving, I have become cooled and attained Nibbāna.”—
Thus he spoke these four verses.
In this context, "endowed with both" means endowed and possessed of both the perfection of birth (*jātisampadā*) and the perfection of practice (*paṭipattisampadā*).
"The wise know me as Rāhulabhadda" means that my fellow celibates recognize me as "Rāhulabhadda.
For when they heard the announcement of his birth, the Bodhisatta spoke these words: "Rāhu is born; a bond is born."
Based on this, the great king Suddhodana gave him the name “Rāhula. In that regard, taking first the very same etymological explanation stated by his father, he said:
“The wise know me as Rāhulabhadda. *Bhadda* is a word of praise.
Now, in order to demonstrate that twofold excellence, he spoke the words beginning with “yañcamhi. In that context, *yaṃ* means “because”; the particle *ca* [is used for conjunction].
This is the sense of the compound. "I am the son of the Buddha" means: I am the legitimate (urasaputta) son of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"In regard to phenomena" (dhammesu) means: in regard to both mundane and supramundane phenomena; the meaning is "in regard to the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. "Possessing vision" (cakkhumā):
one should connect this by saying, "I am also possessed of vision through the eye of the wisdom of the Path."
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate his own twofold perfection through yet other methods, he spoke the verse beginning, “And since my taints are exhausted.
Therein, *dakkhiṇeyyo* means worthy of offerings. *Amataddaso* means one who has seen Nibbāna. The rest is easily understood.
Now, it was due to the absence of this perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā*) and perfection of liberation (*vimutti*) that the multitude of beings were like fish bound in a net.

As he was thus revolving in *saṃsāra*, he spoke these two verses beginning with “Blinded by sensual pleasures” (*kāmandhā*) in order to demonstrate within himself that attainment of both [the mundane and the supramundane].

Therein, they are “blinded by sensual pleasures” (*kāmandhā*) because they are blinded by sensual pleasures (*kāma*) or regarding sensual pleasures. They are blinded by the defilement of sensual pleasures—such as those analyzed as “desire and lust” (*chando rāgo*)—due to their failure to see the danger in the objective sensual pleasures such as forms (*rūpa*).
They are “covered by a net” (*jālapacchannā*) because the entire threefold existence (*bhavattaya*) is covered by the net of craving.
It is covered and enveloped on all sides by the snare of attachment that stands over it, having overspread it.
"Covered by the covering of craving" means that for that very reason it is covered, shrouded, and completely closed off by the covering known as craving.
"Bound by the kinsman of negligence" means bound at the mouth of the net, like fish in the mouth of a fisherman’s fish-trap.
Just as fish are bound by a fisherman with a hook, so too these beings, bound by Māra—the kinsman of negligence—with the bond of sensual desire, do not escape from it;
they remain as if cast into an internal prison.
Having abandoned that such-like sensual desire which has become a bond, and having relinquished it through the practice of the preliminary stage, [one escapes] from the Māra of the defilements.
Having severed the bonds, and having cut them off entirely with the sword of the Noble Path,
and having thereby uprooted craving— beginning with sensual craving— along with its root known as ignorance, he has become cooled due to the absence of the distress and fever of all defilements;
thus, "I am" means he is extinguished by the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Rāhula is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Canda:
"With gold," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Canda. What is his origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...
Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merits in various states of existence, in the thirty-first aeon from now—when the world was devoid of Buddhas—he was reborn as a tree deity.
Seeing the Paccekabuddha named Sudassana dwelling in a mountain glen, he offered worship with *kuṭaja* flowers with a devout mind. By that meritorious deed, among gods and humans...
Wandering through saṃsāra, during this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a family endowed with great wealth.
Having received the name Candana and reached maturity, while living the household life, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and became a stream-enterer.
After obtaining a son, he abandoned the household life, went forth into homelessness, and took up the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā).
While dwelling in the forest, the Elder had come to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher and was staying in the charnel ground.

Having heard that he had arrived, his former wife, having adorned herself and prepared her appearance, went to the Elder’s presence with a large retinue, taking her child with her, thinking, “I will entice him with feminine gestures and the like, and cause him to leave the Order. As she was approaching, the Elder—
Seeing him from afar, [the Elder thought], “Now I shall become beyond her reach,” and by intensifying his insight (vipassanā) as he had begun it, he attained the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Vasala;”
The Buddha named Sudassana dwells within the mountains.
"A golden-hued flower from me flew through the air;
there I beheld the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has crossed the flood and is free from taints."
“Taking a *kuṭaja* flower and placing my hands together in reverence upon my head,
I offered it to the Buddha, the Self-Existent One,
the Great Sage. Thirty-one aeons ago, that flower which I offered in worship— ”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Having said, “The defilements are burnt away by me… [and so on]… the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished,” he became one possessed of the six supernormal powers.
Standing in the air, he taught her the Dhamma and established her in the Refuges and the Precepts.
He went to the very place where he himself had lived before.
When questioned by his companion monks, "Friend, your faculties are serene; have you realized the Truths?", he replied:
"Covered with gold, surrounded by a retinue of female slaves..."
My wife approached me, carrying her son on her hip.
Seeing her coming— her own son’s mother,
adorned and well-dressed, like the noose of Death laid out— I [knew].
“Then right attention arose in me through proper method;
the danger became manifest, and disenchantment took firm root.
Then my mind was liberated—behold the excellence of the Dhamma!”
"The three kinds of higher knowledge have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
By means of these verses, speaking of his own practice, he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*).
In this context, "covered with gold" refers to being adorned with ornaments made of gold, such as head-ornaments and the like, for the purpose of decoration.

"With her body concealed" means adorned with all her ornaments. "Attended by a host of female slaves" means surrounded and preceded by her own group of female slaves, who were appropriately decorated and prepared.
"Taking her son on her hip" means taking her son onto her own lap, thinking, "Perhaps even by seeing my son, she might find some satisfaction in the household life."
"Coming" (*āyanti*) means arriving. "The mother of my own son" means the mother of my legitimate son;
the sense is: my former wife. The Elder says all this while highly esteeming his own eradication of sensual desire.
"It arose through wise reflection" means: "Even such prosperity as this is indeed overcome by old age, sickness, and death."
“Alas! Conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, and unreliable”—thus did appropriate attention arise. The rest is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Candana is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammika.
The verses beginning with "Dhammo have rakkhati" are the stanzas of the Venerable Elder Dhammika. What is their origin?
This venerable one also had performed his duties under previous Buddhas; accumulating merit in various states of existence, he became a deer-hunter during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
One day, while in a forest glade, as the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma to an assembly of deities, [he heard: "This is the Dhamma..."
Having grasped the sign from this teaching, he was reborn among gods and humans as he transmigrated due to that meritorious deed.
In this current arising of a Buddha, he was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kosala and given the name Dhammika.
Upon reaching maturity, having gained faith at the acceptance of the Jeta Grove, he went forth into homelessness and became a resident monk in a certain village monastery.
While living there, he was prone to frequent complaints and lacked patience regarding the proper and improper duties of visiting monks.
Consequently, the monks abandoned that monastery and departed. He remained all alone.
When the lay devotee who owned the monastery heard of this matter, he reported the situation to the Blessed One. The Teacher summoned that monk, questioned him about the matter, and—
When he replied, “So be it, venerable sir,” [the Buddha] said, “It is not only now that this man was intolerant; he was intolerant even in the past.
Having been requested by the monks, he spoke on the nature of trees and then gave him further instruction:
“Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives according to Dhamma; Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.”
This is the benefit when the Dhamma is well-practiced: one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.
For neither the Dhamma nor the non-Dhamma have the same result;
the non-Dhamma leads to hell, while the Dhamma brings about a happy destination.
“Therefore, one should indeed apply zeal toward the teachings,” thus rejoicing with the Tathāgata, the One Thus-Gone;
“the wise disciples of the Excellent Sugata, established in the Dhamma, are led forth as those who go to the supreme, foremost refuge.
“The root of the boil has been burst open; the net of craving has been utterly uprooted.”
Thus he spoke these four verses: "One whose wandering in *saṃsāra* is exhausted has nothing at all, like the moon on the full-moon night when it is complete with its rays.
In this context, "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of good conduct, both mundane and supramundane. "He protects" means he protects one from the suffering of the states of misery (*apāya*).

And it indeed protects one who has become a necessary condition for turning away from the suffering of *saṃsāra*. "One who lives according to the Dhamma" means one who practices and follows that Dhamma.
"Well-practiced" means well-performed, accumulated by having faith in the fruits of kamma and by performing it with care and reverence.
"Happiness" refers to both mundane and supramundane happiness. Among these, mundane happiness is first of all divided into the realms of sense-desire (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.
The Dhamma, according to its respective nature, brings about and accomplishes happiness either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period;

however, it is appropriate to say that when practiced while standing upon the supporting condition for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), it brings results through a succession of births, because such a result does not exist for that which lacks a supporting condition.
This is the benefit when the Dhamma is well-practiced: "One who lives by the Dhamma does not go to a state of woe"—thus is one a "Dhamma-practitioner."
“A person does not go to a state of misery because of well-practiced Dhamma”—this is the benefit and fruit of well-practiced Dhamma; such is the meaning.

Since it is by means of Dhamma alone that one goes to a happy destination, and by means of non-Dhamma alone that one goes to a miserable destination, he spoke the second verse beginning with “For Dhamma [does not lead]” in order to show that these two—Dhamma and non-Dhamma—have results that are not confused with one another.

In this context, "unrighteousness" (*adhamma*) refers to misconduct (*duccarita*), which is the opposite of righteousness (*dhamma*). "With similar ripening" (*samavipāka*) means having a corresponding ripening or identical fruit.

"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because there is this aforementioned distinction in the ripening of both righteousness and unrighteousness; therefore. "Desire" (*chanda*) refers to the desire for the wish to act.

"Thus rejoicing with the Sugata, the Such-like One" (*iti modamāno sugatena tādinā*) means by the Sugata—the one who has gone well—by means of the instruction given in the manner thus described, [and] by the one who has gone rightly.

The construction is as follows: "One who has practiced rightly, rejoicing and attaining satisfaction by means of becoming 'neutral' (*tādi*) toward the desirable and so forth—due to which he is called 'neutral'—should cultivate desire for the Dhammas.
Having thus far shown the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he now says "those established in the Dhamma," etc., in order to show the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*).
Its meaning is: because [he is established] in the Sugata, the excellent one, and among the Sugatas...
The disciples of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, are wise ones established in his Dhamma; they have gone for refuge to that which is exceedingly supreme.
By virtue of being established in that very Dhamma known as "going for refuge," they are led out from and escape even the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
Therefore, it is said: "One should indeed take delight in the Dhammas."

When the Teacher had thus taught the Dhamma with these three verses, he—while remaining seated exactly as he was—developed insight in accordance with the teaching and attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“In former times I was a deer-hunter in the forest wilderness;
there I saw the stainless Buddha, honored by the host of gods.”
“I heard the sweet Dhamma from Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World, as he proclaimed the Four Truths and taught the deathless state.
My heart was gladdened by the voice of that peerless individual.”
Having gladdened my mind therein, regarding existence which is so difficult to transcend:
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of the perception I then obtained, I do not recognize a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of that perception of the sound."
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. Thus he was established in Arahantship.
Having attained Arahantship, however, he declared his full knowledge (*aññā*) with the final verse, announcing to the Teacher the distinction he had realized for himself.

In that context, “shattered” (*vipphoṭita*) means shaken off; the meaning is that they were relinquished by means of the knowledge of the Path. “The root of the tumor” (*gaṇḍamūla*) refers to ignorance (*avijjā*).
For it swells and flows. Regarding the statement by the Teacher, "Monk, 'abscess' is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging," because they are joined with the root of suffering,
because they flow with the filth of the defilements, and because they swell, ripen, and burst through arising, aging, and dissolution,
the root or cause of that pentad of aggregates of clinging which is designated as an "abscess" is [suffering].
"The snare of craving has been eradicated" means that the snare known as craving has been utterly uprooted by the Path.
"I have exhausted saṃsāra; there is nothing whatsoever" means that because craving—the latent tendency—has been abandoned in this way, I have exhausted saṃsāra;
and because the root of existence has been abandoned, there is nothing whatsoever, such as passion and the like, that exists or is perceived. "Like the full moon on the night of the full moon."
"Just as the moon, when free from defects such as clouds and mist, is perfectly full on the night of the full moon, so too have I become one whose store of Dhamma is complete,
having attained Arhatship and being rid of all defilements such as lust.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammika is finished.
11. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sappaka.
The verses beginning with “When the crane... belong to the venerable Elder Sappaka. What is his origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, became one of great power thirty-one aeons ago.

Having been reborn as a Nāga king, he offered worship by taking a great lotus and holding it over the head of the Paccekabuddha named Sambhava while he was seated in meditative attainment in the open air. By virtue of that meritorious deed,
wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha’s appearance into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
Having received the name Sappaka, upon reaching the age of discretion, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.

Having gained faith, he went forth, took up a meditation subject, and while dwelling at the Leṇa Mountain Monastery on the bank of the river named Ajakaraṇī, he attained Arahatship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Not far from the Himālayas is a mountain named Romasa;
at that time, the Buddha named Sambhava was dwelling in the open air.
Having emerged from his dwelling, I held up a lotus flower."
Having worn it for a single day, I returned once more to my abode.
"Because I worshipped the Buddha thirty-one eons ago, I have not known an unfortunate rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he came to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher.

While staying there for a few days, being attended upon by his kinsmen, he taught the Dhamma and established his relatives in the refuges and the precepts. Then he returned to the very place previously mentioned.
He desired to depart. His kinsmen entreated him, saying, "Venerable sir, please stay right here; we shall look after you.
He remained there, making a show of his intention to go, while manifesting his delight in solitude by describing the place where he had lived:
"When the crane, with its pure white wings, is terrified by the fear of the black cloud..."
“When the crane, seeking her home, finds her home, then the Ajakaraṇī River delights me.
When the crane, pure white and stainless, terrified by the fear of the black cloud,
seeks a shelter but finds no shelter, then the Ajakaraṇī River delights me.”
“What indeed does not delight them there, where on both sides are rose-apple trees?
They beautify the bank of the river behind my cave.
Those frogs, having completely abandoned intoxication and pride, croak with dull voices.”
“This is no time for separation from the mountain streams;
Khemā, Ajakaraṇī, Sivā, Surammā”—with these four verses he spoke.
Therein, “yadā” means at which time. “Balākā” means a female crane. “Sucipaṇḍaracchadā” means having pure, bright, and white wings.

"Terrified by the fear of the black cloud": she is frightened and struck with dread by the fear of rain from the thundering, rainy-season cloud that is black like a mountain of collyrium and laden with a weight of water.
"She will flee" means she will fly up and depart from her feeding ground. "Her abode" (*ālaya*) means her dwelling place, her own nest. "Seeking an abode" (*ālayesinī*) means seeking shelter there.

Desiring only to remain hidden, she thought: "At this time of heavy rains, the river named Ajakaraṇī delights me. During that rainy season, the river called Ajakaraṇī was filled with new water and carried away all its adornments;
thus, by means of describing a particular season and location, she manifested her delight in solitude, saying, "The deer-antelope [kulaṅka] delights me; it pleases my heart."
*Suvisuddhapaṇḍarā* means having a very pure, white color; the meaning is that her color is unmixed and entirely white.
*Pariyesati* means she searches for. *Leṇaṃ* means a dwelling place. *Aleṇadassinī* means not seeing a dwelling place.
She is called "not seeing a dwelling place" because of the absence of a fixed dwelling place previously established; now, during the rainy season, due to the thundering of clouds...
"Carrying her womb, she seeks a shelter"—the meaning is that she makes a nest as a fixed place of residence.

"What indeed is there... [etc. "...behind?"—behind, in the rear part of my great dwelling-cave, on the bank of the Āpagā river, on both shores of the Ajakaraṇī stream, here and there, shining in every direction, with branches perpetually bent down by the weight of their fruit.

In that place, who indeed would the Jambu trees—not with their glossy foliage and shade—not delight? They delight everyone. "Those who have well abandoned the assembly of the intoxicants of the deathless":
the "deathless" (amata) refers to the antidote (agada); those who are intoxicated by it are the "intoxicated with the deathless" (amatamada), namely the snakes.
Their "assembly" is the *amatamadasaṅgha*; from that, they are "well abandoned," meaning departed. "Frogs" (*bheka*) means female frogs; "Mandavatī."
The Saravatī rivers resound, making that place echo with their sweet flow.
"Today is not a time of separation from the mountain rivers" means that even now, at this present time, there is no occasion for separation from other mountain streams;
moreover, the Ajakaraṇī River is secure, being free from predatory fish and crocodiles. It is endowed with beautiful plateaus, bathing-ghats, and sandy banks.
"Peaceful. It is exceedingly delightful and charming; therefore, the intention is that "my mind finds delight right there.

Having spoken thus, he dismissed his kinsmen and went back to his own dwelling place. By demonstrating his delight in empty dwellings, this very thing became the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sappaka is finished.
12. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Muditatthera.
The verses beginning with "Pabbajin" (I went forth) belong to the Venerable Muditatthera. What is his origin?

This [Venerable One] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having been reborn and attained the state of discernment, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a mind full of faith, gave him a couch.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha in a household of householders in the kingdom of Kosala;
having received the name Muditā, he reached the state of discernment. At that time, that family [was visited] by the King...
He was detained by some business or other. Fleeing out of fear of the king, he entered the forest and approached the dwelling place of a certain elder whose taints were exhausted.
Knowing his state of fear, the elder comforted him, saying, "Do not be afraid. He asked, "Venerable sir, after how much time will this fear of mine [end]?"
Having asked, "Will it subside? and being told, "After seven or eight months have passed," he said, "I am unable to endure for such a length of time;
Venerable Sir, I shall go forth. Ordain me. For the sake of preserving his life, he requested ordination.
The Elder ordained him. Having gone forth, having gained faith in the Teaching, even though the danger had subsided—
Delighting solely in the ascetic’s duty (samaṇadhamma), he took up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and performed the work of insight (vipassanā).
Making a formal resolve such as, “I shall not go outside this dwelling cell until I have attained Arahantship,” he exerted himself in insight and reached Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“To the Blessed One Vipassī, the World’s Elder, the Neutral One,
I gave a single couch with my own hands, filled with serene faith. Through that,
I attained elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and celestial vehicles.”
"By that gift of a bed, I have attained the destruction of the taints.
Since I gave that bed ninety-one eons ago, I have never known an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of giving a bed."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, when asked by his fellow bhikkhus about what he had achieved, he spoke of his own manner of practice:
“I went forth for the sake of a livelihood; having received full ordination...”
Then I gained faith and strove with firm energy:
"Let this body break asunder, let the mass of flesh be torn apart,
let both my shanks fall away from the joints of the knees."
“I shall not eat, I shall not drink, and I shall not leave my dwelling;
nor shall I lie down to sleep as long as the dart of craving has not been extracted.
Behold the exertion of energy of me who dwells thus!
“The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus he spoke these four verses.
Therein, “seeking a livelihood” means one who desires a livelihood, whose purpose is a livelihood. “Having gone forth here, free from fear...”
