"May I live happily and without weariness"—this is the meaning of "going forth for the sake of a livelihood.

"Having received the full ordination (upasampadā)" means that, having first stood in the novice's going forth (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā), he received the full ordination through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (ñatti-catuttha-kamma).
"Then he acquired faith" means that from the time of his full ordination onwards, while attending upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta), he acquired two... [the text continues].

While learning the *mātikā*, the three types of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*), certain discourses (*sutta*), the meditation subjects for tranquility (*samatha-kammaṭṭhāna*), and the method of insight (*vipassanā-vidhi*), I perceived the great majesty of the Buddha and the other [Three Jewels].
Seeing this, I acquired faith in the Triple Gem, thinking: "The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded;
the Saṅgha has practiced rightly. Thus, having acquired faith, I strove with firm energy.
Having offered [this], while performing the work of insight (*vipassanā*), before long I exerted myself with firm and steady energy for the penetration of the Truths.
I strove rightly for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states.
To show how I exerted myself, it is said, "Sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) and so forth. Therein, "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) means according to one's desire.
Or let it break asunder completely. "This body"—this putrid body of mine—let it break apart through this exertion of energy;

let it be shattered and split. "The masses of flesh shall fall away"—through this firm perseverance, if the masses of flesh fall away from this body, let them fall; let them crumble here and there. From both knee-joints...
"May my shanks fall down"—meaning, may both my shanks, along with both knee-joints, break from the hip-bands and fall to the ground.
There is also the reading "maṃ," which has the same meaning. The rest is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Muditatthera is finished.
The Commentary on the Catukkanipāta is finished.
5. Pañcakanipāta 1.
Commentary on the Verses of Thera Rājadatta.
The verses beginning with "In the Pañcaka-nipāta, a bhikkhu went to a charnel ground" belong to the Venerable Rājadatta Thera.

What is their origin? This venerable one, too, had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; having accumulated merit conducive to the attainment of liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family when the world was devoid of a Buddha fourteen aeons ago, and reached the state of full maturity.
Having attained [the state of a stream-enterer], one day he went to the edge of a forest on some business;
there, seeing a certain Paccekabuddha sitting at the foot of a tree, with a mind full of faith he gave him a very pure *ambāṭaka* fruit.
By that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was born in Sāvatthī into a caravan-leader’s family.
He was reborn. Because he had been obtained by his parents after they had propitiated the Great King Vessavaṇa, they gave him the name Rājadatta.
When he reached maturity, he took merchandise with five hundred carts and went to Rājagaha for the purpose of trade.
At that time, there was a certain courtesan in Rājagaha who was handsome, beautiful to behold, and possessed of the highest degree of loveliness.
Every day he received a thousand [pieces of gold]. Then that caravan leader’s son, giving a thousand to that courtesan every day while living with her, soon exhausted all his wealth.
Having become destitute and unable to obtain even enough food and clothing, he wandered here and there until he was overcome by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). He—
One day he went to Veḷuvana together with lay followers.
At that time, the Teacher was seated teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a great assembly.
Having sat at the edge of the assembly and heard the Dhamma from the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and went forth.
Having undertaken the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), he dwelt in a charnel ground.
At that time, a certain son of a caravan leader was living with that courtesan after giving her a thousand pieces of gold. When that courtesan saw a precious jewel in his hand, greed arose in her;
she had him killed by other rogue men and took that jewel for herself. Then, as for that son of the caravan leader...
When the people heard of this occurrence, they dispatched spies.
Those men entered the house of that courtesan at night and, without even damaging her skin or other parts, killed her and abandoned her corpse in the charnel ground.
While wandering through the cemetery to grasp the sign of the foul (*asubhanimitta*), the Elder Rājadatta brought that courtesan’s carcass to mind as something loathsome.

Having approached several times with the intention of practicing, and having applied his mind methodically (*yoniso manasikāra*), he—due to the short duration of her life, the fact that her skin had not yet been damaged by dogs, jackals, and the like, and because she was an object of a dissimilar nature (*visabhāgavatthu*)—applied his mind improperly (*ayoniso manasikāra*).
Consequently, giving rise to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) toward her, he rebuked his own mind with great agitation.
Then, withdrawing to one side for a moment, he returned once more to the very same sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) that had first appeared to him.
Having taken it up and attending to it thoroughly, he aroused jhāna;
making that jhāna the foundation, he established insight and immediately attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Having seen the Buddha, the Self-Existent One, the Unconquered, in the forest..."
Having taken an ambāṭaka fruit, I gave it to the Self-Existent One.
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of that fruit I gave back then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit."
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he was filled with rapture and joy, and said:
“A bhikkhu went to a charnel ground and saw a woman abandoned there;”
[He saw] one cast away in the charnel ground, bloated and being devoured by worms.
"When some people feel revulsion upon seeing a foul corpse,
sensual lust arises within me, and I become like a blind man wandering about."
“Before the rice was cooked, I departed from that place;
mindful and clearly comprehending, I withdrew to one side.
Then, right reflection arose in me through wise application.”
“Danger has appeared, and disenchantment has become established.
Thereupon my mind was liberated; behold the excellence of the Dhamma!
The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
He spoke these five verses.

Therein, "a bhikkhu having gone to a charnel ground": he is called a *bhikkhu* because he beholds (*ikkhati*) the terror within *saṃsāra*; having approached a raw cemetery for the purpose of the meditation subject on the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).
The Elder speaks of himself here, referring to himself as "a bhikkhu. "A woman" (*itthi*): [etc.]
Because semen and blood coagulate (*thīyati*) here and are consolidated into the state of a living being’s continuity, it is called *thī*; thus, it refers to a woman (*mātugāma*).

And so, by way of its own inherent nature and etymology, she is also called "a woman" (*itthī*). However, in the case of barren women and others, the designation is applied because they resemble her and do not deviate from that essential nature.
The term "woman" (*itthī*) refers to the female corpse. It is called "cast off" (*ujjhita*) because it has been abandoned and is fit to be discarded.
Thus cast away, it is thrown off with a state of indifference. "Being devoured by worms" means being filled with worms and then eaten. Regarding that which some loathe:

having seen a corpse, they call it "wicked"—that carcass which, due to the departure of life-force, heat, and consciousness, is wicked, base, and loathsome, such that some of pure birth loathe it and do not even wish to look upon it.
“Sensual lust appeared” means that due to the power of improper attention toward that corpse, sensual lust appeared and arose within me.

“It flowed like a blind man” means that while impurity was flowing and streaming from the nine apertures of that carcass, I was like a blind man because of my failure to see its impure nature. Therefore he said:
"One who is lustful does not know the goal; one who is lustful does not see the Dhamma.
It is blinding darkness then, when lust overcomes a man. And:
"Sensual desire, brahmin, makes one blind and makes one sightless," and so forth. However, some here [add] the letter *t* [as a euphonic insertion].
Having composed [the verse], they explain the meaning as: "One who is not subject to the influence of the defilements' obsession, or one who is subject to the influence of the defilements.
Others, citing the Pāḷi reading "andhova asati ahu," explain the meaning as: "Being truly blind through sensual lust, he became devoid of mindfulness.
However, neither of these two readings exists in the Pāḷi.

"Before the rice was cooked": before the cooking of the rice; that is, within the time it takes for rice to be cooked from well-washed, soaked grains of rice—within just that much time, dispelling passion even more quickly than that, I departed from that place, I withdrew from that spot where, while standing, passion had arisen in me.

Having departed, mindful and clearly comprehending, and having established the perception of a recluse, I approached one side by means of mindfulness through the mental application of the foundations of mindfulness;
being mindful and clearly comprehending through the correct knowledge of the true nature of phenomena, I sat down, folding my legs crosswise.
And as I was sitting, right reflection arose in me—thus all [that follows].
"According to the method explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Rājadatta is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Subhūta.
The verses beginning with "Ayogeti" are the stanzas of the Venerable Elder Subhūti. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa in a family of great householders in Bārāṇasī.
Having attained maturity, one day he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and, with a mind full of faith, [proceeded further].
Having established himself in the refuges and the precepts, he had the Teacher’s fragrant chamber strewn eight times every month with four kinds of scented flowers.
By that meritorious deed, in each place where he was reborn, he possessed a fragrant body;
and in this current dispensation of a Buddha, having been reborn in a household of lay devotees in the kingdom of Magadha, he received the name Subhūta.
Having reached maturity, with a disposition toward renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth among the heretics;

finding no essence there, and seeing many recluses and brahmins— such as Upatissa, Kolita, Sela, and others— who had gone forth in the presence of the Teacher and were experiencing the bliss of the ascetic life,
he gained faith in the Dispensation, went forth, and [served] his teachers and preceptors.
Having mastered his meditation subject and dwelling in seclusion, he increased his insight and attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In this auspicious aeon, a man of great fame, a kinsman of Brahmā;”
One named Kassapa by clan arose, the best among those who speak.
He was perfected in the secondary marks, endowed with the thirty-two excellent primary characteristics,
surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, and enveloped in a web of rays.
“He is a consoler like the moon, a bringer of light like the sun;
he is a quencher like a cloud, and a mine of virtues like the ocean.
He is like the earth in virtue, and like the Himalayas in meditative concentration.”
Like space, through wisdom, I was unattached like the wind.
At that time, I was reborn in Bārāṇasī in a great family,
possessing abundant wealth and grain, and a collection of various jewels.
“Approaching the Leader of the World as he sat with a great retinue,
I listened to the Dhamma, which was as enchanting as the Deathless.
He bore the thirty-two marks, like the moon amidst the stars.”
Perfect in his secondary characteristics, like a blossomed king of sal trees;
surrounded by a net of rays, like the radiant mountain of gold;
encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, like the sun with its hundred rays.
“The Supreme Victor, with his golden face, was like a mountain of rock and a female ascetic;
his heart was filled with compassion, like the ocean in its virtues.
His fame was renowned throughout the world, like Sineru, the best of mountains.”
The Hero is renowned for his glory, the Sage is like the sky.
With a mind unattached everywhere, the Leader is like the wind;
the Seventh Sage is the support for all beings, like the earth.
“Unstained by the world, like a lotus by water;
A burner of the thickets of false doctrine, he shines like a mass of fire.
Like a medicine everywhere, he is the destroyer of the poison of the defilements.”
Like Mount Gandhamādana, he is adorned with the fragrance of virtues.
The hero is a mine of virtues, like the ocean of jewels;
he is like the Indus River for the rows of forest trees, a remover of the stains of the defilements.
“Like a victorious great warrior, crushing the army of Māra;
like a universal monarch (cakkavattī), he is the master of the jewels of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).
Resembling a great physician, he is the healer of the disease of hatred.”
Like a surgeon skilled in surgery, who lances the tumor of wrong views,
the Conqueror, the Lamp of the World, honored by humans, gods, and Sakka,
that Sun among men, teaches the Dhamma to the assemblies.
“By giving gifts one gains great wealth; by virtue one reaches a happy destination;
and through meditation one attains Nibbāna—thus you should instruct them.
That teaching of yours is greatly delightful, beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end.”
The entire assembly hears it as if it were the great flavor of the Deathless.
Having heard the most sweet Dhamma, with confidence in the Victor’s teaching,
having gone for refuge to the Sugata, I shall pay homage [to him] for as long as life lasts.
“At that time, I cleared the ground around the Perfume Chamber of the Sage with four kinds of fragrant scents for eight days during the month.
Making an aspiration for the state of being sweet-smelling, [I did this] for one whose body was foul-smelling.”
Then the Jina prophesied for the one who had obtained a fragrant body:
“Whoever once scatters fragrance upon the ground of the Perfume Chamber,
by the ripening of that kamma, he will be reborn in various places.”
“This man shall have a fragrant body everywhere;
having become endowed with the fragrance of virtues, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
By that well-performed deed and by his volition and aspiration,”
Having cast off the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
And now, in my final existence, I was born into a brahmin family;
while I dwelt in the womb, my mother’s body became fragrant.
“And when I emerged from my mother’s womb, at that time the city of Sāvatthī blew as if perfumed with all kinds of fragrances.
A rain of flowers fell— sweet-smelling, divine, and delightful.”
And at that time, they burned highly precious incenses.
The gods, with all kinds of perfumes, incense, and flowers,
scented that house with a fragrant aroma— the very house in which I was born.
“When the auspicious one was young, established in the first stage of youth,
he then guided Sela and his assembly, a charioteer of men.
Surrounded by all of them, he arrived at the city of Sāvatthī.”
Then, having seen that power of the Buddha, I went forth.
Having developed these four qualities— virtue, concentration, wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation— I attained the destruction of the taints.
“When I went forth, when I became an Arahant,
and when I was about to attain Parinibbāna— at those times there was a rain of fragrance.
And the scent of my body always surpassed even the most precious sandalwood, campaka, and blue lotus.”
In the same way, having completely overcome all other odors, I strove here and there.
"The defilements have been burnt up by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, he reflected upon the suffering of self-mortification that he had practiced while ordained among the non-Buddhist sects.
Having gone forth in the Dispensation and reflecting upon the bliss of jhāna and other attainments, he declared his own realization by way of reviewing his own practice:
“If a man desiring what ought to be done, while applying himself to what is improper,
should fail to achieve his goal while wandering— this is a mark of ill fortune for me.”
“If one were to abandon even a single [evil deed] that has been committed and has reached its consequence, it would still be like a loss;
if one were to abandon them all, one would be as if blind, because of not seeing the distinction between the even and the uneven.
For what one does, that one should speak; what one does not do, that one should not speak.”
The wise fully understand one who does not act but merely speaks:
"Just as a beautiful flower may be colorful yet scentless,
even so well-spoken words are fruitless for one who does not act."
“Just as a beautiful flower, colorful and fragrant,
so too the well-spoken word bears fruit for one who acts upon it.”—
He spoke these five verses.
In that context, "non-application" (*ayoga*) refers to the two extremes which are not to be applied to or cultivated.
Here, however, the meaning should be understood by way of devotion to self-mortification. "One who applies oneself" (*yuñjanta*) means one who applies, joins, or practices in such a manner.

"Desiring what ought to be done" (*kiccam icchako*) means desiring the task that brings welfare to both [self and others]; if one were to "wander" (*caranto*) while practicing non-application, it would be the opposite of that.
“*Nādhigaccheyya* (he would not attain)” means he would not reach the intended benefit and happiness; this is the logical conclusion (*ñāyo*).

Therefore, that which I—who was deceived by the doctrines of the *tīrthikas*—applied myself to inappropriately, that is my mark of ill fortune (*dubbhagalakkhaṇa*), my nature of demerit (*apuññasabhāva*). By saying, “Deluded by past karma, I applied myself to what was inappropriate,” he shows this.

Regarding the phrase “the evil (*agha*) that had gone forth was uprooted”: because they have the nature of causing affliction, lust and the other defilements are called “evils” (*agha*); it is these very evils...
“*Aghagataṃ vijitan*” refers to the realm of suffering (*aghagata*)—the occurrence of saṃsāra—which has been conquered;
their victory is the overcoming of unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*). It is stated thus without eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) in “*aghagataṃ vijitan*.

By one who has “uprooted that conquered realm of suffering,” meaning by one who has uprooted it without having yet eradicated the defilements (*kilesa*), being thus constituted, [he is called] one who has uprooted the conquered realm of suffering. This is the meaning.

"If he were to abandon even one": if he were to abandon, relinquish, or give up even a single instance of heedfulness or right application—whether due to being alone or due to the intensity of his striving—that person would be like a "Kalī" (an ill-omened person), like a black-eared dog. "And if he were to abandon all":
if he were to abandon all those faculties that bring liberation to maturity—the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
If one were to discard it through non-cultivation, one would be like a blind person, because of not seeing what is even and uneven.
*Yathā* is a particle used for the purpose of introducing a simile. *Ruci* means beautiful. *Vaṇṇavantaṃ* means endowed with color and shape.
*Agandhakaṃ* means devoid of fragrance, such as the varieties of *pālibhaddaka*, *girikaṇṇika*, *jayasumana*, and so forth. Thus [is] well-spoken.
"Speech that is well-spoken" refers to the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka),
which is like a flower endowed with both color and fragrance. For just as the scent does not permeate the body of one who carries a flower that lacks fragrance,
so too this [Dhamma] does not permeate the person who does not practice it with careful listening and the like— namely, whatever ought to be done therein.
For one who does not act upon it, the fragrance of what has been heard does not bring about the fragrance of practice, and thus it becomes fruitless. Therefore it was said:
"Thus well-spoken speech is fruitless for one who does not act.
"Sugandhaka" refers to the various kinds of flowers such as jasmine, campaka, and blue lotus. "Evaṃ" means just as [the fragrance] belongs to one who wears that flower.

Just as fragrance pervades the body, so too the well-spoken words known as the Buddha’s word contained in the Tipiṭaka bear fruit for that person who performs what is to be done therein through careful listening and other such means;

it becomes of great fruit and great benefit because it brings forth the fragrance of learning and the fragrance of practice. Therefore, one should practice according to the teaching; one should be as one speaks.
"And may it be so. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Subhūta is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Girimānanda.
The verses beginning with "Vassati devo" (The god rains) are those of the Venerable Elder Girimānanda. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.
Upon reaching maturity, while living as a householder, he was struck by the arrow of grief when his wife and children passed away.
Having entered the forest, the Teacher went there, preached the Dhamma, and extracted the dart of sorrow.
With a mind full of faith, [the man] honored him with fragrant flowers, paid homage by prostrating at his five limbs, and, placing his palms together in reverence upon his head, praised him.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this present age of a Buddha in Rājagaha as the son of King Bimbisāra.
He was reborn as the son of the royal chaplain; his name was Girimānanda.

Upon reaching maturity, he witnessed the Buddha’s supernatural power during the Teacher’s journey to Rājagaha. Having gained faith and gone forth into homelessness, he practiced the duties of a recluse.
After staying for a few days at a village monastery, he went to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher.
When King Bimbisāra heard of his arrival, he approached him and invited him, saying, "Venerable sir, please stay right here;
I shall attend to you with the four requisites. Having thus offered his hospitality, the king departed, and due to his many duties, he did not remember [to visit].

Thinking, "The Elder is living in the open air," deities, fearing that the Elder would become wet, caused the rain to cease. The king, perceiving the reason for the cessation of the rain, [inquired about it].

He had a small hut built for the elder. While dwelling in that hut, the elder, having attained concentration through the acquisition of a suitable dwelling, applied himself with balanced energy, intensified his insight, and reached Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“My wife has passed away, and my son has gone to the cemetery;”
Mother, father, and brother were carried away upon the same funeral pyre.
Tormented by that grief, I became emaciated and pale;
my mind was distraught, for I was afflicted by that sorrow.
“Overwhelmed by the dart of sorrow, I approached the edge of the forest;
having eaten wild fruits, I dwell at the foot of a tree.
There is a Perfectly Enlightened One named Sumedha, a Conqueror who brings an end to suffering.”
Desiring to lift me up, he came into my presence.
Having heard the sound of the footsteps of the great seer Sumedha,
I raised my head and looked up at the Great Sage.
“When the Great Hero had arrived, joy arose within me;
at that time, my mind was one-pointed upon seeing him, the Leader of the World.
Having regained my mindfulness, I offered a handful of leaves.”
The Blessed One, the one with vision, sat there out of compassion.
Having sat there, the Blessed One, the wise leader of the world,
the Buddha, taught me the Dhamma that dispels the arrow of sorrow.
“Uninvited they came from there; unpermitted they departed from here.
As they came, so they went; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Just as travelers, when the rain is falling...”
“They approach with their belongings for the onset of the rains;
when the rains have passed, they depart as they please.
Such is the way of your mother and father; what cause for lamentation is there in that?”
“Guests and visitors, moved and shaken by the wind—such are your mother and father; what lamentation can there be for them?
Just as a snake, casting off its worn-out skin, goes forth.”
"In this way, mother and father, you have both perished here before me.
Having understood the Buddha’s words, I cast off the dart of sorrow;
having given rise to joy, I paid homage to the Best of Buddhas.
Having paid homage to the Great Naga, I worshipped the mountain-peak,
the one of excellent wisdom, the Leader of the World, who was emitting a divine fragrance.
Having worshipped the Fully Enlightened One, I placed my joined palms upon my head.
Recalling his supreme virtues, I praised the Leader of the World:
“O Great Hero, you have crossed over; O All-Knowing One, Leader of the World!
You lift up all beings by means of your wisdom, O Great Sage.”
“You cut away my doubt and perplexity, O Great Sage;
you have set me upon the path through your wisdom, O Seer of the Eye.
The Arahants who have attained mastery, possessing the six super-knowledges and great psychic power—”
The wise ones who roam the sky then surround you.
"There are disciples who are practicing, those still in training, and those established in the fruits;
like lotuses at sunrise, your disciples are in full bloom."
“Like the great ocean, unagitated, immeasurable, and difficult to cross;
so, endowed with wisdom, you are immeasurable, O Visionary One.
Having paid homage to the Conqueror of the World, the Visionary One of great renown;”
Worshipping the various directions, I came crawling on my belly.
Having fallen from the world of the gods, fully aware and mindful,
I entered my mother’s womb, wandering through existence after existence.
“Having gone forth from the home, I went into homelessness;
ardent, wise, meditative, with seclusion as my domain.
Having exerted myself in striving, I satisfied the Great Sage.”
Freed from the dense clouds of passion, I wander forever.
Devoted to seclusion, peaceful and free from acquisitions,
having fully understood all taints, I dwell without taints.
“In thirty thousand aeons, because I worshipped the Buddha, I have never known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as in the standard formula] ...the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.”

Then, while the rain was falling as if the gods were raining out of joy and satisfaction at the Elder’s attainment of Arahatship, he uttered another verse by way of directing the rain to fall upon him, thus explaining his own realization:
“The god rains according to his well-sung song; my little hut is thatched, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind.
Therein I dwell, calmed; so, O god, rain if you so desire.”
“The god rains as one well-sings; my little hut is thatched, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind.
Therein I dwell with a peaceful mind; so rain on, O god, if you wish.
“The god rains... [as before] ...therein I dwell free from passion...”
“The god is raining... [as before] ...I dwell there free from hatred... [as before]....
“The god is raining... [as before] ...I dwell there free from delusion;
yet if you wish, O god, rain down!”—with these words he spoke these five verses.
In this context, "in accordance with a well-sung song" means conforming to a well-sung song;
the meaning is that it is exactly suitable for his own beautiful cloud-song.

For just as a cloud does not shine when it merely rains without thundering, so too, even though it has arisen with hundreds and thousands of layers [of clouds], thunders, roars, and emits streaks of lightning, it does not shine if it does not rain; such being its nature.
But it is said that "the rain-god shines as he rains" like a well-sung song.
Therefore he said: "O Pajjunna, thunderer," and "both a thunderer and a rainer. "In that [hut] I dwell" means:

in that little hut, I dwell by way of the dwelling in postures, which is the womb of noble dwelling. "With a tranquil mind" means: with a mind perfectly calmed by the concentration of the highest fruit (arahantship).
Thus, accepting with his head the Elder’s repeated exhortations, the deva-son Valāhaka caused a great rain to fall, filling both the lowlands and the highlands.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Girimānanda is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sumanas.
The verse beginning with "Yaṃ patthayāno" is the stanza of the Venerable Thera Sumanas. What is its origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various states of existence, was reborn in a noble family when the world was devoid of a Buddha ninety-five aeons ago.
Having attained maturity, he saw a Paccekabuddha who was afflicted by illness and [gave him] myrobalan fruit.

He gave [the gift]. Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance into a householder family in the kingdom of Kosala. Having received the name Sumanas, he grew up in comfort.

His maternal uncle, however, having gone forth and become an Arahant, was dwelling in the forest; when Sumanas reached maturity, the uncle ordained him and gave him a meditation subject suitable for his temperament.
He gave it. While applying himself there, he realized the four *jhānas* and the five *abhiññās*.
Then the Elder explained the method of insight (*vipassanā*) to him. Before long, having developed insight, he was established in *arahantship*.
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Harītaka, āmalaka, mango, jambu, and vibhītaka;
kola, bhallātaka, and billa—these I gather myself.
Having seen the sage dwelling in a mountain cave, absorbed in meditation and delighting in jhāna,”
To the peerless Great Sage, who was being oppressed by illness,
I took a myrobalan fruit and gave it to the Self-Existent One.
As soon as he had consumed that medicine, the disease was immediately pacified.
“The Buddha, whose distress has been abandoned,
expressed his appreciation for me because of this gift of medicine and the resulting allaying of my illness.
Whether born as a god, a human, or in any other state of existence,”
“May you be happy in every respect, and may no disease come upon you.
Having said this, the Self-Existent One, the Unconquered, the Wise Sambuddha,
rose up into the sky like a king of swans in the air.
“Since the myrobalan fruit was given to the Self-Existent Great Sage,
from this birth onwards, no disease has arisen for me.
This is my last, my final existence.”
The threefold knowledge has been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Ninety-four eons ago, I gave medicinal herbs at that time;
I have never known an unhappy rebirth—this is the fruit of those medicinal herbs.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me… [as before] …the Buddha’s instruction has been accomplished.
Having thus established himself in Arahantship, one day he went to visit his maternal uncle, the Elder. When the Elder questioned him regarding his attainment, he replied while explaining it:
“That which my preceptor supported me in seeking among the teachings…”
For me who longed for the Deathless, what was to be done has been done.
The Dhamma, independent of others, has been reached and realized by me;
with purified knowledge and free from doubt, I declare it in your presence.
“I know my former births; the divine eye has been purified.
My own goal has been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Through diligence, I have well-heard the training in your dispensation.”
“All my taints are exhausted; there is now no further becoming.
You have instructed me in the noble way; out of compassion, you have favored me.
Your instruction was not in vain; I, as your pupil, have been trained.”
Roaring this lion’s roar with these five verses, he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*).
Therein, regarding the phrase "desiring the deathless, longing for which among the states my preceptor supported me":

it means that my preceptor, desiring and longing for which state among the blameless states such as serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), [supported me]—that state being the deathless *nibbāna*.
He favored me, who was yearning [for the goal], by means of giving me instruction. "What was to be done has been done by me":
for the sake of his attainment, the sixteenfold task—beginning with full understanding (*pariññā*)—that was to be performed has been completed and brought to fulfillment by me.
Consequently, the fourfold Dhamma of the Path has been reached, attained, and realized. The Dhamma itself is beyond dispute.
One has personally made for oneself the Dhamma of Nibbāna and the Dhamma of the fruit free from calamity and free from doubt, realized by one’s own direct experience;
thus, while severing the doubt known as *itihasa* (legendary uncertainty) that occurs in the form of “it is thus,” or “it is said to be thus,” the Noble Path proceeds.
Therefore he said, “With purified knowledge, free from doubt,” and so forth. Therein, “with purified knowledge” refers to purification from all defilements.
"Of purified knowledge. "In your presence" means in your vicinity.
"One's own goal" refers to Arahatship. "Trainings" refers to the training in higher virtue and so forth.

"Well-heard" means thoroughly learned by way of the fulfillment of both scriptural learning (*pariyatti-bāhusacca*) and penetrative realization (*paṭivedha-bāhusacca*). "In your teaching" means for one who stands within your instruction and guidance.

"Ariyavata" means by virtue of undertaking the very pure vows of morality and so forth. "Trained as a resident pupil" (*antevāsi*) means: "Because I have lived the life of celibacy in your presence, I am a resident pupil; I am one who has been trained, having completed the training in higher morality and the other trainings.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sumanatthera is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vaḍḍha.
“Excellent indeed! and so forth are the verses of the Venerable Elder Vaḍḍha. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was born into a family of householders in the city of Bhārukaccha during the appearance of this Buddha.
Having received the name Vaḍḍha, he grew up in due course.

Then his mother, having become spiritually stirred by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), entrusted her son to his relatives, went forth in the presence of the bhikkhunīs, and while practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), attained *arahantship*.
At a later time, she also had her son—who had reached the age of discretion—ordain in the presence of the Elder Veḷudanta. Having been ordained, he [studied] the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*).
Having mastered the teachings, become learned, and become a preacher of the Dhamma, he bore the burden of the scriptures.
One day, thinking, "I shall see my mother alone, clad only in my inner and upper robes," he went to the nuns' quarters.

Seeing him, his mother reproached him, saying, "Why have you come here alone, clad only in your inner and upper robes? Being thus reproached by his mother, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency, realizing, "I have acted improperly."

Having gone to the monastery and sat in the daytime resting place, he attained arahantship through insight. Then, declaring his realization by way of demonstrating the success of his mother’s exhortation, he said:
“It was indeed well for me that my mother presented this goad;
having heard her words and being thus instructed by my progenitor.”
“Exerting energy and resolute in purpose, I have attained supreme enlightenment.
I am an arahant worthy of offerings, a possessor of the three knowledges, a seer of the Deathless;
having conquered the army of Namuci, I dwell free from taints.”
“Whatever taints there were within and without me,
all have been eradicated without remainder and shall not arise again.
Confident indeed, sister, you have thus proclaimed this matter.”
“Surely there is no resentment in me either; no forest-thicket of craving exists within you.
Suffering has been brought to its end; this is the final body.
The cycle of birth and death is over; there is now no further becoming.”—with these verses he spoke.
"In that regard, it was indeed good for my mother that she showed me the goad. This means: "It is truly well of my mother that she shows me the goad known as advice;
by means of that, inciting my energy, she pricked me on the head, which is the supreme limb. "Of her" (yassā) refers to my mother.
"Enlightenment" (sambodhiṃ) refers to Arhatship. Herein, this is the construction: "Instructed by my mother, of whom..."
Having heard these words of instruction, I dwelt with energy aroused and resolute;
thus I attained the supreme fruit of enlightenment, which is Arahantship.
Precisely because I have gone far away from the defilements (ārakatta), I am an Arahant; and because I am a field of merit, I am worthy of offerings and deserving of the sacrificial gift.

Because he has attained the threefold higher knowledge beginning with the knowledge of past lives, he is "possessed of the three knowledges" (tevijjo). Because he has realized Nibbāna, he is "a seer of the Deathless.

Having conquered the army of Namuci Māra—the host of defilements—with the army of the factors conducive to enlightenment, and because that army was thus defeated, he dwells happily, free from taints (anāsavo).
Now, in order to make the meaning expressed by the term "taintless" (anāsava) more evident, he spoke this verse beginning with "internally" (ajjhattañca). Its meaning is as follows:

those taints (āsava), whether internal—having their basis within—or external—having their basis without—which existed and were found in me prior to the attainment of the Noble Path, have all been eradicated without remainder;
they have been completely cut off by the Noble Path.
“Now that they have been abandoned, they shall never arise again; they will simply not arise.
Now, taking his mother’s words as a goad because he had himself attained Arahatship, he praised his mother by reciting the verse beginning with “Visāradā.
Therein, “visāradā kho” means one who is entirely free from timidity (or shame). Thus [he spoke] to his mother...
And by attaining the state of an Arahant, proclaiming himself to be a heart-son of the Teacher, he addressed his mother as "sister.
"He spoke this matter" means he uttered this matter which was my instruction. But in instructing me in this way, she was not only confident;
indeed, she must have been free from attachment toward me and likewise free from attachment toward your two sons—she seems to be unattached to them. Why?

Or rather, by this very supposition: "The forest does not exist for you"—meaning that the forest beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*) is simply non-existent within your continuum—refers to her who enjoined me toward the destruction of existence (*bhavakkhaya*).

Now, demonstrating that "I have practiced exactly in the manner enjoined by you," he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "made finite" (*pariyantakata*); its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vaḍḍha is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nadīkassapa:
"Truly, for my benefit... and so forth are the verses of the Venerable Elder Nadīkassapa. What is their origin? This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences,
he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher wandering for alms,
he conceived a mind of serene faith and [offered] the first fruit that had appeared on a mango tree he himself had planted, which was the color of emerald (*manosilā*).

He gave a single mango fruit. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha as the brother of Uruvelakassapa.

Upon reaching maturity, out of a disposition toward renunciation, he did not desire the life of a householder; having gone forth into the ascetic life, together with three hundred ascetics, [he lived] by the Nerañjarā River.
Having established a hermitage on the bank of a river, he dwelt there. Because he lived by the river and belonged to the Kassapa clan, he became known by the name Nadi-Kassapa.
The Blessed One granted him and his retinue the higher ordination through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehi-bhikkhu*).
All of this is recorded in the Khandhaka. Through the Blessed One’s teaching on the "Discourse on the Burning," he attained Arhatship.
It was established. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“For Padumuttara Buddha, the World’s Eldest, the Neutral One, as he wandered for alms, bearing supreme glory.”
“Having taken the finest fruit, with a serene mind,
I gave it to the Teacher, the Hero worthy of offerings.
By that deed, O Lord of bipeds, Foremost in the world, Bull among men...”
I have reached the immovable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.
In a hundred thousand aeons past, the gift that I gave then— I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of that supreme gift.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
Having thus established himself in Arahantship, and later reflecting upon his own practice, he declared his full knowledge (*aññā*) by way of praising the eradication of wrong views:
“Truly for my benefit did the Buddha go to the Nerañjarā River;”
Having heard his Dhamma, I abandoned wrong view.
I performed various sacrifices and offered the fire-oblation,
thinking, "This is purity," while remaining a blind worldling.
“Plunged into the thicket of views, deluded by dogmatic adherence, I imagined impurity to be purity, blind and ignorant.
Wrong view has been abandoned by me; all states of existence have been shattered.”
I sacrifice to the fire of those worthy of offerings; I pay homage to the Tathāgata.
“Delusion has been entirely abandoned by me; the craving for existence is shattered.
The wandering through births is exhausted; now there is no further becoming.”
He spoke these five verses.
Therein, "atthāya vata me" means "truly for my benefit, truly for my welfare. "Buddho" refers to the Omniscient Buddha.
"Nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ agā" means he went to the river known as the Nerañjarā; and on the bank of that river, for me...
The intention is that he has approached the hermitage of Uruvelakassapa.
Now, in order to explain the aforementioned meaning, the passage beginning with "yassāhaṃ" was spoken. "Yassa" means of which Buddha, the Blessed One.
"Sutvāna dhammaṃ" means having heard the Dhamma associated with the Four Noble Truths, following along the path of the sense-door of hearing.
"Having perceived": "Avoiding wrong view" means he abandoned the perverted vision that proceeds in such a manner as "purity comes through sacrifices and the like.
To explain in detail the very meaning already stated—"avoiding wrong view"—he said, "He sacrificed," and so forth.
Therein, "I sacrificed various sacrifices" means that I performed many kinds of manifest sacrifices, such as the Soma sacrifice, the Vājapeyya, and so forth.
"I offered the fire-oblation" means that by way of performing those sacrifices, I maintained the fire while presenting the oblations.
"Thinking, 'This is purity'" means that they thought this performance of sacrifice and service to the fire was purity because it served as a cause for purification. Thus...
"Thinking, 'Purity from saṃsāra will come to me,' the worldling is blinded;
being blinded by the blindness of ignorance due to the deficiency of the eye of wisdom, he becomes a worldling who has entered the thicket of views.

Just as it is difficult to traverse dense forests and mountain thickets, so too, because of its difficulty to transcend, view itself is a thicket; having plunged into that, he has entered the thicket of views."
"By misapprehension" means by way of wrong adherence known as *parāmāsa*, because of grasping [views] beyond the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) with the thought, "This alone is the truth.

"Deluded" means led into a state of confusion. "I imagined impurity to be purity" means I imagined the path that is not pure to be "the pure path"; I so conceived it. He states the reason for this: "Blinded and ignorant."

Because he was blinded by ignorance, and for that very reason was ignorant of what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma, as well as what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, he therefore conceives [them] in such a way— this is the meaning. However,
for one who has heard the discourse on the Dhamma containing the essence of the Four Noble Truths in the presence of the Teacher who has thus abandoned wrong view,
and who practices with wise attention, all wrong views are abandoned through the complete eradication by means of the right view of the Noble Path.

They have been abandoned by me. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to all forms of existence, such as sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth; these have been split open and destroyed by the sword of the Noble Path.

"I sacrifice to the fire worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyaggi*): having discarded the sacrificial fires such as the *āhavanīya*, I sacrifice to and serve the Perfectly Enlightened One, the fire worthy of offerings, because he is the foremost object of offerings for the world including its devas and because he burns away all evil. This, then—
"My service to the fire of those worthy of offerings is not dependent on curd, fresh butter, clarified butter churned from milk, and so forth;
rather, it is the mere act of paying homage to the Teacher," he said, "I pay homage to the Tathāgata.

Alternatively, "I sacrifice to the fire of those worthy of offerings" means that by making the offerings of donors bear great fruit and by burning away evil, I sacrifice to—that is, I serve—myself as having become the fire of those worthy of offerings.
"Having done so, I serve; having done so, I maintain [the practice]. Previously I worshipped the fire-god, but now I worship the Tathāgata.
"All delusions have been abandoned by me": all delusions, consisting of ignorance regarding suffering and so forth, have been abandoned and utterly cut off by me.

Therefore, by supplying the word *me* (by me) and connecting it to the three phrases: "Craving for existence has been shattered; the wandering in birth is exhausted; now there is no further becoming," [the verse is completed].
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nadīkassapa is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gayākassapa The verses beginning with "At dawn, at midday," etc., belong to the venerable elder Gayākassapa. What is his origin?
This [elder] also, having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences...
Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was reborn in a noble family.

Upon reaching maturity, out of a disposition toward renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a forest ascetic. Having established a hermitage in a forest region, he dwelt there subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
At that time, the Blessed One, alone and without a companion, was walking near his hermitage. He [saw] the Blessed One...
Having seen him, with a mind full of faith, he approached, paid homage, and stood to one side. Looking at the time, he offered some charming *kola* fruits to the Teacher.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, due to his inclination toward renunciation, he [left] the household life.
Having abandoned the ascetic life and gone forth, he dwelt at Gayā together with two hundred ascetics.
Because he resided at Gayā and because of his lineage as a Kassapa, he acquired the name Gayākassapa.

When the Blessed One granted him the ordination of "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) along with his retinue, and was instructing him with the discourse on the burning (*ādittapariyāya*), he established himself in Arahatship.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“Clad in an antelope skin and wearing a garment of bark at that time,
having filled a cartload, I brought jujube fruits to my ascetic.”
“At that time, the Buddha Sikhī was alone, without a second;
knowing all things as they truly are, he approached my hermitage.
Having gladdened his own heart and paid homage to me, who was firm in my vows,”
Taking a jujube fruit with both hands, I gave it to the Buddha.
Thirty-one eons ago, because of that fruit I offered then, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of that gift of a jujube.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
Having thus established himself in Arahantship and reviewing his own practice, he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*) by way of praising the removal of evil:
“Morning, midday, and evening—three times a day, I...”
At the ford of Otalī, at Gayā on the full moon of Phagguṇa, I thought:
"Whatever evil was committed by me in former lives in other births, that I now wash away here. Such was my view in the past.
“Having heard well-spoken words, phrases endowed with the meaning of the Dhamma,
I reflected wisely upon that meaning as it truly and exactly is:
‘I am cleansed of all evil, stainless, purified, and pure.’”
"Pure, he is the heir of the pure, the legitimate son of the Buddha.
Having plunged into the stream of the Eightfold Path, I have washed away all evil;
I have attained the three knowledges; the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished."
He spoke these five verses.
Regarding them, the summary meaning of the first verse is as follows:
"In the morning at the time of sunrise, at midday at the time of noon, and in the evening at the time of sunset"—thus three times, or in three sessions, during the day, I [offer] water.
I descended into the water. And as I descended, I did not descend just anywhere or at just any time;

rather, at the ford of Gayā known as Gayātīrtha—which is highly esteemed by the common people as "the removal of evil"—on the full moon day of Phagguṇī at Gayā, under the constellation Uttaraphagguṇī in the month of Phagguṇī, I was devoted to the ritual bathing in water every year.
Now, in order to show the intention with which he was devoted to descending into the water, he spoke this verse beginning with "Whatever by me.

Its meaning is as follows: "Whatever evil karma was accumulated by me in other previous births, that I now wash away, remove, and cleanse here at the ford of Gayā on this Gayā-Full-Moon day by means of this descent into the water."
Before approaching the Teacher’s pure dispensation, I held such views and possessed such a perverted perspective.
The term "word" (*pada*) is an elliptical designation including both the doctrine (*dhamma*) and its meaning (*attha*).

It refers to a section endowed with both doctrine and meaning—one that is connected with the doctrine from the beginning, middle, and end; connected with the meaning; and which is thoroughly and exclusively conducive to liberation.
Having made this speech my own and having heard the words of the Perfectly Enlightened One—

words which are "true" (*tatha*) because they reveal the ultimate reality (*paramattha-bhāva*) in their true nature, and which are "as-it-is" (*yāthāvaka*) because there is no deviation regarding the means for proceeding or ceasing as appropriate—
I have reflected with proper method upon the meaning of suffering and so forth, in terms of their being fully understood and so on: "Suffering is to be fully understood."
“I have contemplated: ‘The origin [of suffering] is to be abandoned, cessation is to be realized, and the path is to be developed’;
I have seen with the eye of knowledge and penetrated it”—this is the meaning.
“I am one who has washed away all evil”: because I have thus penetrated the Truths, I am one whose every evil has been cleansed by the water of the Noble Path.
I am [he]. Precisely because he is stainless due to the absence of the stains of passion and so forth, he is "stainless" (*nimmala*).
Precisely because his bodily conduct is purified, his verbal conduct is purified, and his mental conduct is purified, he is "pure" (*suci*) and "cleansed" (*suddha*).

He is an "heir" (*dāyāda*) because he receives from the Blessed Buddha—the giver of the supramundane Dhamma—who is himself pure through the purification of all stains of the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*). This is due to the nobility produced by the vigorous effort arising from that very Teacher’s knowledge of the teaching.
The construction is: "I am a son born from his heart.

Furthermore, in order to clarify once more his own state of being a *nhātaka* (one who has washed away defilements) in the ultimate sense, he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "having plunged" (*ogayha*).

Therein, "having plunged" (*ogayha*) means having entered or immersed oneself. "The stream of the Eightfold Path" (*aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ sotaṃ*) refers to that which consists of the convergence of the eight factors, beginning with right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).

"The stream of the Path. "I washed away all evil" means I cleansed the impurity of evil without remainder; by the flow of the water of the Noble Path, I became one who has bathed in the ultimate sense.
For that very reason, "I attained the threefold knowledge"—the meaning of this is exactly as stated: "The Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Gayākassapa is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vakkali The verses beginning with "Afflicted by a wind-disease" are the verses of the venerable Elder Vakkali. What is their origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara...
Having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī and having reached maturity, he went to the monastery together with lay followers who were going into the presence of the Teacher.

Standing at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being foremost among those resolved through faith; desiring that same position for himself, [he remained there] for seven days.
Having given a great gift, he made a formal aspiration (paṇidhāna). The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, gave a prediction.
He too, having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn at the time of our Teacher in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī;
they gave him the name Vakkalīti. When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas.
Having attained proficiency in the arts of a brahmin, he saw the Teacher and, being insatiable in beholding the perfection of the physical body, wandered about together with the Teacher.

Thinking, "If I live in the midst of a household, I shall not be able to see the Teacher at all times," he went forth in the presence of the Teacher; except for the time for meals and the time for bodily needs, he remained there.
At all other times, wherever he was able to see the One of Ten Powers, he would stand there, abandoning all other duties, and remain gazing at the Blessed One.
As the Teacher waited for his wisdom to reach maturity, He said nothing while Vakkali spent much time thus occupied with the sight of the physical form.
Then one day, [the Buddha asked], "Vakkali, what is the use of this putrid body to you?"
“By what is seen? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me; he who sees me sees the Dhamma. For, Vakkali, seeing the Dhamma, one sees me; seeing me, one sees the Dhamma.
Even though the Teacher spoke thus, the Elder was unable to leave the sight of the Teacher and go elsewhere.

Then the Teacher, thinking, "This bhikkhu will not attain awakening without experiencing a sense of spiritual urgency," dismissed the elder on the day of the rains-retreat commencement, saying, "Begone, Vakkali!

Having been dismissed by the Teacher, unable to remain in his presence, he thought, "What is the use of my life, since I am not permitted to see the Teacher? and went to a precipice on Mount Gijjhakūṭa.
"Ascend! Knowing his situation, the Teacher thought, "If this bhikkhu does not receive consolation from me, he will destroy the underlying potential for the paths and fruits.
Thus, manifesting himself by emitting a radiance, he said:
"A bhikkhu full of gladness, with confidence in the Buddha’s teaching..."
“May he attain the state of peace, the bliss that is the subsiding of all conditioned formations.
Having spoken this verse, [the Buddha] extended his hand, saying, “Come, Vakkali!

The Elder, thinking, “I have seen the One of Ten Powers, and I have even received his summons, ‘Come’,” gave rise to powerful joy and gladness, and [considering] from where he had come, reflected upon his own journey.
It is recorded in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Dhammapada-vaṇṇanā* that, not knowing [the danger], as he was leaping into the air in the presence of the Teacher,

he recalled the verse spoken by the Teacher while still standing on the mountain with his first foot; thus, even in mid-air, he suppressed his rapture and attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Furthermore, it is said here that after being exhorted by the Teacher with the words, "What to you, Vakkali?
and so forth, he established insight while dwelling on Gijjhakūṭa; however, because his faith was so powerful, the insight did not enter its proper course.
The Blessed One, knowing this, purified the meditation subject and gave it to him. Then, in order to bring insight to its culmination—
He was indeed unable [to do so], and then, due to a deficiency in food, a wind-affliction arose within him.
Knowing that he was being oppressed by that wind-affliction, the Blessed One went there and asked:
"Afflicted by a disease of wind, you dwell in the grove and forest;..."
“How will you fare, O bhikkhu, in this desolate and forsaken range?”—he said.
Having heard that, the elder replied:
“Filling my entire body with abundant rapture and bliss...”
“Enduring even what is coarse, I shall dwell in the forest.
Developing the foundations of mindfulness, the faculties, and the powers;
and developing the factors of enlightenment, I shall dwell in the forest.”
“Seeing those who have aroused energy, who are resolute, and who always possess firm perseverance—
seeing them living in harmony and in unity— I shall dwell in the forest.
Recalling the Fully Awakened One, the foremost, the tamed, and the composed;”
“Unweariedly, day and night, I shall dwell in the forest”—
thus he spoke these four verses.
Therein, “overcome by a wind-disease” means brought to a state of dependency through the affliction of wind, being overcome by the malady of wind.
"Tvanti" addresses the Elder. "Vihāranti" means dwelling while maintaining that particular mode of conduct (*īryāpatha*).

"In the forest" (*kānane vane*) means in a forest that has become a wilderness; the sense is "in a great forest. "In a place where food is abandoned" (*paviddhagocare*) means in a place where food is neglected, where requisites are difficult to obtain.
[It is] "rough" due to the absence of medicines such as ghee which are suitable for wind-diseases, and because of the harshness of the terrain.
"In a place of coarseness. How will you, O bhikkhu, manage?"—thus the Blessed One asked, "How will you dwell?
Having heard this, the Elder, demonstrating his own dwelling in happiness through spiritual joy (*pīti*), gladness (*somanassa*), and so forth, spoke the words beginning with "With joy and happiness.
Therein, "with joy and happiness" refers to the joy characterized by upliftment and the joy characterized by pervasion, together with the happiness associated therewith.
Therefore he said, "By the vast," meaning by the sublime.
"Pervading the entire body" means filling the whole body with the exquisite forms produced by the aforementioned joy and happiness, making it continuously suffused.
"Overcoming even what is coarse" means overcoming and enduring even the difficult-to-bear coarseness of requisites arising from the cause of a life of austerity born of dwelling in the forest.
“I shall dwell in the forest” means: “I shall dwell in the forest region with the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of insight.
Therefore he said: “And he experienced happiness with the body.
“From whatever [aspect] he comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates...”
"One who understands that attains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless.
And: "Developing the foundations of mindfulness" means arising and increasing the four foundations of mindfulness—such as the contemplation of the body—which are included within the path.
"Faculties" refers specifically to the five faculties, beginning with faith, which are included within the path. "Powers" refers to...

Likewise, there are the five powers beginning with faith (*saddhā*). "Factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅgāni*) refers to the seven factors of enlightenment beginning with the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*).

By the word "and" (*ca*), the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), and path-factors (*maggaṅga*) are included; for because they are inseparable from those [previously mentioned], their inclusion occurs simply by mentioning them.
"I shall dwell" means that while cultivating the aforementioned states conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), one dwells in the bliss of the Path (*magga-sukha*).
I shall dwell in the bliss of the fruit and the bliss of Nibbāna established through the realization of that [truth].

"One who has aroused energy" means one whose energy is exerted by way of the fourfold right effort (*sammappadhāna*). "One who has sent forth the self" means one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna.
"Always firm in exertion" means one whose energy is never slack at any time. By way of non-contention...

And by way of giving harmony to the body, he sees those who are harmonious; seeing his fellow practitioners in communion through their commonality of view and virtue, he thereby demonstrates the perfection of having virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitta*).

Recalling "the Fully Awakened One" (*sambuddha*)—meaning the Perfectly Self-Awakened One (*sammāsambuddha*) because of having perfectly and individually awakened to all phenomena, and because of being the most supreme among all beings—

"Being untiring and diligent, I shall dwell constantly, day and night, recollecting: 'Thus indeed is that Blessed One, the Worthy One,' and so forth—recollecting him who is tamed by supreme self-mastery and composed through unsurpassed concentration.
By this demonstration of the manner in which one is engaged in the cultivation of the recollection of the Buddha, he expresses the application to the meditation subject in all respects.
By means of the former [verse], he devoted himself to the practice of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having spoken thus, the Elder intensified his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Leader appeared;”
Of sublime name and immeasurable, known by the name Padumuttara.
With a face like the form of a lotus, with a complexion as pure as a lotus,
he was unsullied by the world, just as a lotus is unsullied by water.
“A hero with eyes like lotus petals, as lovely as a lotus,
and possessing a fragrance like that of the supreme lotus— therefore he is Padumuttara.
He is the foremost in the world, free from pride, like eyes for those who are blind.”
The peaceful one, a treasury of virtues,
an ocean of compassionate wisdom— once that Great Hero,
the supreme Victor, honored by Brahmās, asuras, and gods, stood in the midst of a crowd teeming with devas and humans.
“With his fragrant speech and his sweet voice,
he delighted the entire assembly and conversed with his own disciple: ‘O one of excellent mind,
devoted to faith, longing for a sight of me!’”
"There is no other such as this, as is this monk Vakkali.
At that time, in the city of Haṃsavatī,
having been born into a brahmin family and having heard those words, I delighted in that state."
“Having invited that stainless Tathāgata together with his disciples,
and having fed him for seven days, I then covered him with fine cloths.
Prostrating my head before him, that ocean of infinite virtues...”
Submerged and filled with rapture, I spoke these words: “O Sage,
that monk who was praised by you seven aeons ago—
the foremost among those possessed of faith— may I become just like him, O Sage.”
When this had been said, the Great Hero, the Seer Unobstructed,
the Great Sage, uttered these words to the assembly:
“Behold this young brahmin, wearing a bright yellow robe!”
“With limbs adorned by the merit of past offerings, captivating the eyes of women—
this one will, in a future time, become the foremost disciple of the Great Sage Gotama among those resolved through faith.”
“Whether having become a deva or a human, free from all burning fevers,
and enriched with every enjoyment, he will wander through existence in happiness.
In a hundred thousand aeons, born into the Okkāka clan,”
"One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma,
will be a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Vakkali."
“By that specific deed and through my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Having been happy everywhere, wandering through various states of existence, I transmigrated.”
I was born in the city of Sāvatthī, in a certain family.
Though I was delicate as a non-breast-fed infant, soft as a newly sprouted leaf, slow-moving,
and accustomed to lying on my back, they were terrified by the fear of a *pisāca* demon.
“At the feet of the Great Sage, with dejected minds, we said:
‘We give this to you, O Lord; be our refuge, O Leader.
Then the Sage, the refuge for those who fear, accepted me.”
With his webbed hands, marked with wheels, and soft and tender palms—
"From that time forth, I have been protected by him through that which is not to be guarded;
freed from all enmity, I have grown up in happiness."
“Without the Sugata, I have become distressed even for a moment;
though I was only seven years old when I went forth into homelessness.
[I long for] that excellent one, born of all the perfections, with dark-blue eyes.”
“Form is entirely mixed with impurity, yet I dwell unsatisfied.
Knowing my delight in the form of the Buddha, the Conqueror then exhorted me:
“Enough, Vakkali! Why do you take pleasure in form, that which brings joy only to fools?”
“The wise one who sees the true Dhamma, he sees me;
But not seeing the true Dhamma, even while looking at me, he does not see me.
The body has endless dangers; it is like a poisonous tree.”
“Dwelling is the abode of all diseases, a mere heap of suffering.
Having become disenchanted with form therein, and seeing the arising and passing away of the aggregates,
you will go to the end of defilements with ease.”
“Thus instructed by that Leader who seeks our welfare,
I ascended Vulture Peak and meditate in a mountain cave.
Standing at the foot of the mountain, the Great Sage comforted me.”
Having heard those words from the Victor, "Vakkali," I was filled with joy.
I leapt onto a rocky mountain cliff hundreds of fathoms high;
then, through the power of the Buddha, I descended to the earth as if in ease.
“Once again he taught the Dhamma, the arising and passing away of the aggregates;
having understood that Dhamma, I attained arahantship.
In the midst of that very great assembly, he then led me to the end of the path.”
The Great-Minded One designated me as the foremost among those resolved through faith:
"Because of the deed I performed a hundred thousand aeons ago, I have never known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, the Elder likewise recited these very verses while declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*). Then the Teacher, seated in the midst of the community of monks, established him in the foremost position among those resolved through faith (*saddhādhimutta*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vakkali is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vijitasena The verses beginning with "I shall cling" (*olaggessāmi*) are those of the venerable Elder Vijitasena. What is his origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, [was reborn] during the time of the Buddha Atthadassi...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he reached maturity, abandoned the household life, and went forth as an ascetic.
While dwelling in the forest, seeing the Blessed One traveling through the air, he stood with palms joined in reverence, his heart full of faith and manifesting his devotion.
The Teacher, knowing his inner disposition, descended from the sky. He—
He brought sweet and heart-pleasing fruits to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One accepted them out of compassion.

Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a family of elephant trainers in the kingdom of Kosala;
having attained the name Vijitasena, he reached the age of discretion. His maternal uncles were Sena and Upasena.
Thus, these two elephant trainers, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, acquired faith, went forth, fulfilled their duties as residents,
and attained arahantship. Vijitasena, too, having reached perfection in the art of elephant training,
his mind unattached to the household life due to his inclination toward renunciation, saw the Teacher’s Twin Miracle and, having acquired faith, [approached] the Mātula Theras.
Having gone forth in their presence and performing the work of insight through their instruction and guidance, he leaped across the path of insight and,
admonishing his own mind as it was running outward toward various objects,
said: “I will restrain you, O mind, as one restrains an elephant at the gate with a goad.”
“I will not lead you toward evil—the web of sensual desire born of the body.
You shall not go on clinging, like an elephant that cannot find the opening of a gate;
nor, O wicked mind, shall you proceed again and again, advancing while delighting in evil.”
"Just as a powerful elephant-handler with a goad restrains an untamed young elephant against its will, so shall I restrain you.
Just as a preeminent charioteer, skilled in taming noble steeds, subdues a thoroughbred horse,"
"Established in the five powers, I shall thus tame you.
I will bind you with mindfulness; being devoted to it, I shall tame you.
Held back by the yoke of energy, O mind, you shall not go far from here."
He spoke this verse. In it, "I shall restrain" means I shall guard and ward off. "Them" (*te*) refers to that; for this genitive case is used here in the sense of the accusative.
Or, "them" (*te*) is a remainder of the word "going. And "of the female elephant" (*hatthinam*) means "to the female elephant" (*hatthinim*). "The mind" (*cittam*) refers to one's own mind.
He speaks. To show how he intended to prevent [the elephant], he said, "Like an elephant at the gate-post.

A "gate-post" (āṇidvāra) refers to the small gate of a walled city, which, once the bolt has been inserted into the socket-hole, cannot be opened from the inside even by those standing there, without the use of a mechanical device. By means of this, humans, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth—
It is not possible to go out. Even when an elephant desires to go outside the city, the elephant trainer entices it and prevents its departure.
Alternatively, "āṇidvāra" means a bolted door;

for there, having placed a crossbar (paligha) across, they fasten a pin (āṇi)—known as a wooden peg—over the top of the crossbar. It causes [the arising of] evil states such as covetousness that arise toward forms and so forth.
I will not urge it; I shall not urge it. "The nets of sensual desire" (*kāmajālāni*) means that which has become a net for sensual desire.

For just as a net belonging to fishermen or hunters is a means for them to act according to their will regarding fish and other creatures, so too the mind, fallen under the influence of improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), is a means for Māra to act according to his will.
By means of that, he casts sentient beings into misfortunes. "In bodies" (*sarīrajāti*) means among bodies.
"Arising. For in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), consciousness is called "body-born" because its activity is bound to form.
"You cling and do not go"—O wretched mind, now that you have been restrained by me with the goad and hook of mindfulness and wisdom, you shall no longer go according to your whim;
you shall not be permitted to act as you please under the influence of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).

Like what? Like an elephant that does not find an opening in the gate; just as an elephant, failing to find an opening in the gate for exiting from the city or from the elephant-stable, [remains inside].
"Cittakalī" means one with a black heart (cittakāḷakaṇṇi). "Punappunaṃ" means again and again. "Pasakkā" means by way of seeking refuge and right mindfulness (*saraṇa-sampassāsa-vasena*).
"Pāparato" means one who delights in evil deeds; [the Buddha says: "As before, you shall not now act [in such a way]."
The meaning is: "I will not allow him to act in such a way.
"Untamed" means not yet trained in the art of elephant-training. "Recently captured" means one who has been caught not long ago. "Holder of the goad" refers to the elephant trainer.
"Powerful" means powerful both in physical strength and in the power of knowledge. "He turns back" means he makes [the elephant] turn back even though it is unwilling and does not desire it.

He turns it back by means of restraint. Just as the elephant trainer will turn back the aforementioned elephant, so shall I turn back that mind—the rogue mind—from the commission of misconduct by means of restraint.
"Skilled in taming the best of horses" means being skilled in the training of the most excellent horse-animals. For that very reason, he is the preeminent charioteer.

"Among those who are charioteers of horses to be tamed, he is preeminent; he tames the noble thoroughbred horse, the animal to be tamed, according to the appropriate place and time, taming and training it with both gentle and harsh means, making it free from stubbornness.

'Established in the five powers' means that, having become established in the five powers beginning with faith, he will tame—that is, he intends to tame—it by means of suppressing lack of faith and so forth."

"By mindfulness they will bind you"—not allowing you to go outside the sphere of the meditation object, they will bind you, O wretched mind, to the pillar of the meditation subject by means of the rope of mindfulness;

I shall bind and restrain you. "I will tame you as is fitting"—while binding you there, being appropriately engaged, I will tame you; I will purify you from the stains of defilement. "Restrained by the burden of energy."
Just as a well-trained and skillful charioteer, having yoked a horse to the yoke and restrained it by the yoke, does not allow it to pass beyond the space between the yokes;

even so, O mind, being restrained by me in the burden of energy, and being unable to act otherwise due to your practice of thoroughness and constancy, you shall not go far outside from this sphere of your field of activity. For one devoted to spiritual development...
For even though it was close from the perspective of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), it was indeed distant from the perspective of its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
Thus, while restraining his own mind with these verses, the Elder increased his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Fully Enlightened One, golden-hued, Possessing the thirty-two excellent marks...”
“Like a blossoming king of sal trees moving at the edge of the forest, I prepared a grass mat and entreated the Supreme Buddha:
‘May the Buddha have compassion for me; I wish to give you almsfood.’”
“Compassionate and merciful, the seer of the goal, possessed of great fame;
having understood my intention, he descended into my hermitage.
Having descended, the Fully Awakened One sat down upon the spread of leaves.”
Having taken a bhallātaka fruit, I gave it to the Best of Buddhas.
While I was looking on, the Victor then consumed it;
having gained confidence of heart therein, I then paid homage to the Victor.
“In eighteen hundred kappas, because I gave that fruit back then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [the rest as in the standard formula] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Furthermore, having attained arahantship and declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*), he spoke these verses.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vijitasena is finished.
