10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Yasadatta.
The verses beginning with "Upārambhacitto" are the stanzas of the Venerable Yasadatta Thera. What is their origin? This venerable one also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas;
in various existences, he accumulated wholesome karma conducive to the turning away from worldly existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
Thus, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a brahmin family and attained mastery in the sciences and arts of the brahmins.
Having abandoned sensual pleasures and gone forth into the ascetic life, he dwelt in the forest. One day, upon seeing the Teacher, his mind was filled with serene faith;

raising his joined palms, he offered this praise. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during the present appearance of a Buddha in the kingdom of the Mallas within the royal family of the Mallas, where he received the name Yasadatta and reached maturity.
Having gone to Takkasilā and mastered all the arts, he traveled on tour together with the wanderer Sabhiya.
Eventually arriving at Sāvatthī, he approached the Blessed One.
While Sabhiya was answering the questions he had asked, [Upatissa] sat down to listen, seeking an opportunity to find fault with the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama.
“I shall give it. Then the Blessed One, knowing his state of mind, gave him this exhortation at the conclusion of the teaching of the Sabhiya Sutta:
“The fool who listens to the Conqueror’s dispensation with a mind intent on finding fault is far from the True Dhamma, just as the earth is far from the sky.”
“One of malicious intent and dull-witted, who listens to the teaching of the Conqueror,
falls away from the true Dhamma like the moon in the dark fortnight.
One of malicious intent and dull-witted, who listens to the teaching of the Conqueror...”
One withers away from the true Dhamma, like a fish in waterless places.
With a mind intent on fault-finding, the foolish one listens to the Victor’s teaching;
he does not grow in the true Dhamma, like rotten seed in a field.
“But whoever with a contented mind hears the teaching of the Victor,
having exhausted all taints and realized the unshakable state,
attaining supreme peace, that one whose taints are gone attains final Nibbāna.”
He spoke these five verses.
Therein, "with a mind of reproach" (*upārambhacitta*) means with a contentious mind; the meaning is that his intention is to attribute faults. "Dull-witted" (*dummedha*) means lacking wisdom.
"Far from the true Dhamma" (*ārakā hoti saddhammā*): such a person, like the earth is far from the sky, is distant even from the true Dhamma of practice.

He is far removed from the true Dhamma of realization, let alone from the true Dhamma of penetration. For one who is intent on contentious talk, such as saying, "You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya," how could there be the true Dhamma of practice that is peaceful and subtle?
He falls away from the true Dhamma; that is, from the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, as well as from the true Dhammas of the preliminary stage, such as faith and the rest.

"It diminishes" (*nihīyati*). "It withers away" (*parisussati*) means it dries up due to the absence of wholesome states such as rapture (*pīti*) and gladness (*pāmojja*), which have the function of refreshing body and mind.

"It does not grow" (*na virūhati*) means it does not reach growth or increase. "Putrid" (*pūtikaṃ*) means having reached a state of decay due to the lack of offerings such as the application of cow-dung plaster.
"With a contented mind" (*tuṭṭhena cittena*): this is an instrumental case used to indicate a characteristic state; the meaning is "having become satisfied and joyful."
"Having cast off" means having utterly severed. "The unshakable state" refers to Arahantship. "Having attained" means having reached it.

"Supreme peace" is Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa). To show that his attainment of this was merely the arrival at the proper time and not some kind of calamity, it is said: "the taintless one who has attained final Nibbāna."

Thus exhorted by the Teacher, he was filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Having gone forth and established insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“I beheld the Supreme among Bipeds, shining like a *kaṇikāra* tree, radiant like a lamp-tree, and gleaming like gold.”
“Having set down my water-pot, my bark garment, and my water-strainer,
and having placed my antelope skin over one shoulder, I praised the Supreme Buddha:
‘He dispels that darkness which is entangled in the net of delusion.’”
Having shown the light of knowledge, you have crossed over, O Great Sage.
You have uplifted this entire world, unsurpassed;
there is no comparison for your wisdom as far as the reach of the world extends.
“By that knowledge he is omniscient; thus is the Buddha proclaimed.
I pay homage to that Great Hero, whose omniscience is unobstructed.
A hundred thousand aeons ago, I praised the Best of Buddhas.”
“I do not recognize a state of woe; this is the fruit of the exertion for knowledge.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [etc. ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, the elder likewise spoke these very verses while declaring his final knowledge.”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Yasadatta is finished.
11. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa:
"And ordination was obtained by me," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa. What is their origin? This—
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having been a wealthy merchant in the city of Haṃsavatī and established in great prosperity and power,
he one day saw the Teacher entering the city with a retinue of one hundred thousand arahants,
displaying the great grace of a Buddha and the magnificent majesty of a Buddha; and with a mind full of serene faith, he paid homage to him.

He stood with palms joined in reverence. Later, after his meal, he went to the monastery with the lay followers and, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those of beautiful speech.
He too aspired to that same position, gave a great almsgiving, and made a formal aspiration. The Teacher [responded] to him...
Seeing that there was no obstacle, he prophesied: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, he will become the foremost among those of eloquent speech.
Having performed meritorious deeds there for as long as he lived, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī—
Having gone forth in the Dispensation and fulfilling the major and minor duties, he sewed a robe for a certain bhikkhu and gave it to him.
Later, when the world was empty of a Buddha, while living as a tailor in Bārāṇasī, he joined together a torn edge of a robe for a Paccekabuddha and gave it to him.
Having thus performed meritorious deeds here and there, in this present arising of a Buddha, in the kingdom of Avantī—
He was reborn as the son of a very wealthy merchant in Kuraraghara. They gave him the name Soṇottara.
Because he wore an earring worth a crore, although he should have been called "Koṭikaṇṇa" (Crore-Ear), he became known as "Kuṭikaṇṇa" (Broken-Ear).
As he grew up in due course and established a household, he lived near the venerable Mahākaccāna at his family home.
While dwelling on Mount Pavatta, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of that elder, established himself in the refuges and the precepts, and served him with the four requisites.
Later, having become spiritually stirred by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), he went forth under that elder;
after assembling a Saṅgha of ten members with great difficulty and hardship, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and spent some time there.
Having lived in the presence of the Elder and having taken leave of him, he went to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher.
Having been granted lodging in the same Fragrant Cottage as the Teacher, at the time of dawn, when the sixteen groups of eight were being recited, he gave his approval with a cry of "Excellent!
at the conclusion of the Udāna verse beginning, "Having seen the peril in the world... (Disvā ādīnavaṃ loke).
Having increased his insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the recipient of offerings, entered the city at that time together with one hundred thousand seers.”
“As the Tranquil One, the Tathāgata, was entering the city,
the jewels shone forth and there was a great sound.
By the power of the Buddha, drums resounded even though they were not struck.”
The lutes played of their own accord as the Buddha entered the city.
"I pay homage to the Supreme Buddha, the Great Sage Padumuttara;
having witnessed the miracle there, I brought my mind to serene confidence."
“Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the perfection of our Teacher!
Even these insentient musical instruments resound of their own accord.
“That which I attained as a perception one hundred thousand aeons ago—”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of perceiving [all beings] as Buddhas.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus established himself in Arahantship, according to the method explained by his own preceptor, he [went] to the border regions.”

Having requested five boons—ordination by a community consisting of at least five members including one who is an expert in the Vinaya, permanent bathing facilities, a leather mat, multi-layered sandals, and permission to be apart from his robes—and having obtained them from the Teacher, he returned once more to his own dwelling place and reported the matter to his preceptor.
This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, is in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā.

It should be understood according to the method already stated. However, in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: “Having been fully ordained, he received a meditation subject from his preceptor, and having developed insight, he attained arahantship.
Later, while dwelling in the bliss of liberation, he reflected upon his own practice and, filled with joy, uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*):
“I have received full ordination, and I am liberated and free from taints.
I have seen the Blessed One and dwelt with him in his monastery.
For much of the night, the Blessed One spent it sitting in the open air.”
The Teacher, skilled in abiding, then entered his dwelling.
Having spread out his outer robe, Gotama made his bed,
like a lion in a mountain cave, having abandoned fear and terror.
Then Soṇa, a possessor of beautiful speech, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
proclaimed the True Dhamma in the presence of the Best of Buddhas:
“Having fully understood the five aggregates and having cultivated the straight path...”
"Having attained supreme peace, he will attain final Nibbāna, free from taints."—
These five verses he spoke.
Therein, "And full ordination was obtained by me" refers to that [ordination] which was obtained after having with difficulty assembled a Saṅgha of ten monks.

"Ordination obtained by oneself. Furthermore, there is the ordination authorized by the Teacher in all border regions by a group consisting of a fifth member who is an expert in the Vinaya, granted as a special favor; it is with reference to both of these that he speaks.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction; by it, he includes the other special favors obtained from the Teacher as well. [He is] liberated.
"I am free from taints" (*anāsava*) means that I am liberated through the liberation from the entire basis of defilements by means of the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
For that very reason, the construction is: "I am free from taints such as the taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*).

"And that Blessed One has been seen by me" means that for whatever purpose I went from the kingdom of Avantī to Sāvatthī, that Blessed One—who had never been seen before—has been seen by me. "And he dwells together with me in the monastery" means... [not provided in source].

"I have obtained nothing more than the mere sight of that Blessed One; yet, I dwelt together with the Teacher while he resided in the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi) of the monastery, having perceived a certain purpose. Some say "in the vihāra" means "near the vihāra.
"For much of the night" refers to the first watch [of the night], by way of teaching the Dhamma to the bhikkhus and by way of purifying their meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna).
And during the middle watch of the night, for the purpose of cutting through the doubts of the devas and the brahmās, the Blessed One spent and passed much of the night in the open air.
"Skilled in the dwellings" means skilled in the divine, brahma, imperturbable, and noble dwellings.
"He entered his dwelling" means that he entered the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) in order to dispel the fatigue arising from excessive sitting and walking.
"Having spread out his outer robe, he made his bed"—that is, having prepared his outer robe folded fourfold, he assumed the lion’s posture.
Therefore it was said: "Gotama, like a lion in a rocky cave, has abandoned fear and terror.
In this context, "Gotama" is a designation for the Blessed One by way of his clan. "Like a lion in a rocky cave" means in a cave of a rocky mountain. Just as...
The lion, king of beasts, having abandoned fear and terror due to his majestic splendor, lay down with one leg placed over the other on his right side;

likewise, the Blessed One Gotama, having abandoned fear and terror because the defilements that cause mental panic, horripilation, and trembling have been utterly eradicated, lay down— this is the meaning.
"Then afterwards," means that after he had assumed the lion’s posture and emerged from it, he was requested by the Teacher, "May the Dhamma occur to you, O Bhikkhu;
speak it. "Of beautiful speech" (*kalyāṇavākkaraṇo*) means one whose vocal expression is excellent; the meaning is that his sequence of words is endowed with the [thirty-two] characteristics.
"Soṇa spoke the True Dhamma" means that Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa spoke the sixteen discourses of the Aṭṭhakavagga to the Best of Buddhas.
The Elder spoke thus of himself as if he were another, saying that he had spoken in the very presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One, directly before his eyes.
"Having fully understood the five aggregates" means having thoroughly understood the five aggregates of clinging by means of all three types of full understanding;
while in the very act of such thorough understanding, and having cultivated the noble eightfold path, the straight way, he attained—having reached—the supreme peace, Nibbāna.
He stands free from taints. It is for this very reason that he will now attain final Nibbāna, meaning he will pass away by way of the Nibbāna without residue.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Soṇakuṭikaṇṇa is finished.
12. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kosiya.
The verses beginning with "He who [honors] his elders," etc., belong to the Venerable Kosiyatthera. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having attained maturity, one day, upon seeing the Teacher, he conceived a heart full of faith.

He gave a piece of sugarcane. By that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha; they gave him the name Kosiya after his clan.
Upon reaching maturity, he frequently approached the Venerable Dhammasenāpati and listened to the Dhamma in his presence.
Thus, having gained faith in that teaching, he went forth into homelessness and, by applying himself to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), attained *arahantship* before long.
It is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, I was a gatekeeper;”
I saw the stainless Buddha, who has gone beyond all phenomena.
Taking a piece of sugarcane, with a clear mind and joyful heart, I gave it to Vipassi, the supreme Buddha, the great seer.
“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that sugarcane, I have not known a state of misery.
This is the fruit of that piece of sugarcane.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But having attained Arahantship and reflecting upon his own practice, he praised living with teachers and relying on true friends:
“The wise man who indeed understands the words of his teachers and conceives love for them—such a one is called devoted and is wise;
and having understood the Dhammas, he shall become distinguished.”
“He who, when great calamities arise, does not waver but reflects with discernment—he is called strong and wise;
having understood things as they are, he becomes distinguished among all phenomena.
He who stands unshakable like the ocean, possessing profound wisdom and seeing the subtle meaning—”
He is called a wise man who is unshakable, and having understood things, he becomes distinguished among phenomena.
He is one who is learned and a bearer of the Dhamma, and he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
such a person is indeed called wise, and having understood things, he becomes distinguished among phenomena.
“He who understands the meaning of what is spoken,
and having understood the meaning acts accordingly—
he is a wise man, one who truly grasps the essence.”
"Having understood, he would become distinguished among the teachings"—thus he spoke these five verses.

Therein, "whoever" (*yo*) refers to anyone among the four assemblies, such as the kṣatriyas and so forth. "Vedi" means one who is skilled. "The venerable ones" (*garūnam*) refers to those endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and the like that are worthy of respect.
"Of the wise": one who knows their word of instruction; the meaning is that one who understands the instruction, practices according to what was taught, and, having practiced, knows its fruit.
"The steadfast" (dhīra): one endowed with fortitude. "And dwell in that, generate love for it":
one should abide in those words and counsels of the teachers and practice according to what was instructed.

Having practiced accordingly, one should generate affection and arouse reverence for that [instruction], thinking: "By this very exhortation, I have indeed transcended this suffering of birth and so forth.
For these two points clarify the meaning already expressed by the two phrases, "the wise one who knows the words of his teachers. As for "he" (so):
he who is the wise one knowing the words of his teachers, through practice according to what was instructed, therein...

He is indeed possessed of devotion, because he does not transgress [the Teacher's instructions] even for the sake of his life; and he is indeed wise, because he has distinguished himself among the teachings after having understood them.

And by practicing in such a way so that he may become distinguished among the teachings, through that very practice and by reason of knowing the Four Noble Truths, he becomes—by way of the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*), the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*), the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), and so forth—"one of the three knowledges," "one possessing the six direct knowledges," or "one who has attained the analytical insights" among mundane and supramundane phenomena.
The meaning is: "He becomes distinguished, he is one who possesses distinction.

"Yaṃ" means that person for whom those dangers—both manifest dangers such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and hidden dangers such as lust and so forth—which are designated by the conventional term "calamity" (āpadā) because they create obstacles to spiritual practice, have arisen or have appeared;
and even though these are great and powerful, they do not cause him to falter.
They cannot shake him at all. Why? Because he is "reflecting" (*paṭisaṅkhāyamānaṃ*); the meaning is that he stands firm by the power of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*).
He who cannot be shaken even by more severe calamities is called one who possesses strength, fortitude, and firm exertion.
He is wise because he is endowed with the power of wisdom capable of overcoming the entire side of defilements without exception.
And he indeed becomes such; having become so, and having known, may he excel among the states of existence—this is precisely the meaning already stated.
"Stable like the ocean" means his essential nature is established just like the ocean.
For just as the great ocean near the base of Sineru, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, remains unmoving despite natural winds arising from all eight directions, so too is he stable.
He is unshaken and profound; thus, because he is immovable by the winds of the defilements and the winds of the doctrines of other sects, he stands unshaken (*aneja*).

Because he has penetrated the meaning of dependent origination and so forth—which is profound, subtle, and delicate, and which remains unfathomed by those who have not accumulated the equipment of knowledge—he is one of profound wisdom who sees the subtle meaning. And such a wise man is called "irremovable" (*asaṃhāriya*).
Such a person is called "unshakable" because he cannot be led away by defilements or by anyone among the Devaputta-Māras and so forth;
and in the sense already stated, he is also called "wise. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
"Learned" (bahussuta) means learned by virtue of great learning in the scriptures (pariyatti); that is, much has been heard by him, such as the Suttas, Geyyas, and so forth.

He is one of great learning (*bahussuta*). Because he retains that very same Dhamma without letting it perish, like lion’s milk placed in a golden vessel, he is also a bearer of the Dhamma (*dhammadhara*).

"He lives in accordance with the Dhamma" means that, having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma of the teaching as it was heard and mastered, he practices the Dhamma corresponding to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma—that is, the preliminary practice known as the path of development.

He is a "practitioner of the true Dhamma" (*anudhammacārī*) because he practices and engages in the various divisions such as the fourfold pure virtue, the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and the meditation subjects on the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).
He wanders about desiring penetration [to the truth], thinking, "Today, indeed today.
Such a person is called "wise" (*paṇḍita*), who, relying upon a teacher, becomes one of great learning, a bearer of the Dhamma, and a practitioner of the true Dhamma.
And such a person as that is called wise because he is similar to that teacher due to the similarity of his practice.
Being thus, having understood the teachings, he would become distinguished, in the same way as the meaning already stated.
And as for the one who "knows the meaning of what was spoken," this refers to the person who knows the meaning of the *pariyatti*-dhamma spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

He understands the meaning. Knowing it, he understands the meaning as it was stated in each respective place—“here virtue is taught, here concentration, here wisdom”—and having understood it, he acts accordingly; he practices exactly as instructed by the Teacher.
Such a person is called "one who has reached the goal" (atthantaro), because he is wise and acts for the sake of the goal.
One becomes wise by relying solely on the mere knowledge of the meaning of virtue and so forth. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Herein, in the first verse, the specific quality of the support of faith is stated by the words "He who [serves] his teachers," and so forth;
in the second verse, the support of energy is stated by the words "Whatever [calamity]," and so forth; in the third verse, "He who [is like] the ocean... [and so forth].

It should be understood that by the words beginning with "established" (*ṭhito*), the support for concentration (*samādhi-upanissaya*) is stated; by the fourth verse beginning with "one who is learned" (*bahussuto*), the support for mindfulness (*sati-upanissaya*);
and by the fifth verse beginning with "he who knows the meaning" (*atthañ ca yo jānāti*), the specific nature of the support for wisdom (*paññā-upanissaya*) is expressed.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kosiya is finished.
The commentary on the Pañcaka-nipāta is finished.
6. The Chakka-nipāta: 1.
Commentary on the verses of the Elder Uruvelakassapa.
The verses beginning with "Having seen the miracles" (*disvāna pāṭihīrāni*) in the *Chakkanipāta* belong to the Venerable Elder Uruvelakassapa.

What is their origin? This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; and when he had reached maturity...
While listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of chief among the great assemblies.
Aspiring to that very position himself, he gave a great almsgiving and made a formal resolution. The Blessed One, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, prophesied:
"In the future, within the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, he will become the foremost among the great assemblies."

Thus, having performed meritorious deeds there for as long as he lived, and passing away from there, he wandered among gods and humans until ninety-two aeons ago, when he was reborn as the half-brother and youngest sibling of the Blessed One Phussa. He had two other younger brothers as well.
All three of them, having honored the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with the highest worship, practiced wholesome deeds for as long as they lived.
Having performed [meritorious deeds], while wandering among gods and humans, they were born even before our Blessed One;
having been born in Bārāṇasī as brothers in a brahmin family, they gradually attained maturity and, by virtue of their lineage, all three were named Kassapa.
When they reached adulthood, the three of them mastered the three Vedas. Of these, the eldest brother had five hundred young brahmin students.
The eldest had one hundred followers, the middle one three hundred, and the youngest two hundred.
Examining the essence of their own scriptures, they saw only worldly benefits and thus took pleasure in the life of renunciation. Among them, the eldest brother went with his retinue to Uruvelā;
having gone forth as a seer (*isi*), he became known as Uruvelakassapa, and he was ordained in a bend of the great river Gaṅgā.
One was born as Nadīkassapa, and having gone forth at Gayāsīsa, he was known as Gayākassapa. Thus,
while they were living here and there after having gone forth into the ascetic life, after the lapse of many days, our Bodhisatta,
having made the Great Renunciation and having realized omniscient knowledge, proceeded by stages.

Having set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, having established the five bhikkhus of the group of five in arahantship, and having guided his fifty-five companions headed by Yasa, he dismissed sixty arahants with the words, "Bhikkhus, go forth on tour.
Having then guided the Bhaddavaggiyas, he went to the dwelling place of Uruvelakassapa; entering the fire-hall for the purpose of staying there, he sat down.
Therein, beginning with the subduing of the Nāga, he converted Uruvela Kassapa along with his retinue by means of three hundred and fifty miracles and ordained him.
Knowing that he had gone forth, the other two brothers also came with their own retinues and went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
All of them became "Come, Bhikkhu" disciples, wearing robes and bowls produced through supernormal power.

The Teacher, taking those thousand ascetics with him, went to Gayāsīsa and, sitting upon the flat rock, established them all in Arahatship by means of the discourse on the "Series of Burning. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"The Victor named Padumuttara, the Sage who knows all the world, the Possessor of Eyes, arose one hundred thousand aeons ago from here."
“The Buddha, the instructor, the communicator, the deliverer of all living beings,
skilled in teaching, has ferried across the multitude of people.
Compassionate, merciful, and seeking the welfare of all living beings.”
He established all the Tīrthikas who arrived there in the five precepts.
Thus it was free from disturbance and empty of Tīrthikas,
yet variegated with Arahants who had attained mastery and were "such-like" (tādin).
“That Great Sage has arisen, possessing fifty-eight precious qualities;
he resembles a priceless golden ornament and is endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks.
His lifespan extends for as long as one hundred thousand years.”
Remaining for that long, he delivered many people across.
At that time, in Haṃsavatī, I was a brahmin highly esteemed as virtuous;
having approached the Lamp of the World, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma.
“Then, having heard that he was appointing one with a great assembly and a great assembly of disciples as the foremost among them, I was filled with joy.
Having invited the Great Conqueror along with his vast retinue, I provided him with offerings.”
I gave a gift together with a thousand brahmins.
Having given that great gift and paid homage to the Leader,
I stood to one side, joyful, and spoke these words:
“O Hero, through your faith and through the quality of my service,
may there be a great assembly wherever I am reborn. Then,
with a voice like the trumpeting of an elephant, he spoke to the assembly:
The Teacher, whose voice is like that of the karavīka bird, said: "Behold this brahmin, O brahmin!
He is gold-colored with mighty arms, his face and eyes like lotuses;
his limbs are uplifted, he is joyful, and he has faith in my virtues."
“That bhikkhu Sīhaghosa aspires to this state:
‘In a future time, you shall obtain that heart’s desire.
A hundred thousand aeons hence, born into the Okkāka clan,”
"One named Gotama by clan shall become a teacher in the world.
His heir to the teachings, a legitimate son fashioned from the Dhamma,
shall be a disciple of that Teacher, named Kassapa by clan."
“Ninety-two aeons ago, there was an unsurpassed Teacher,
incomparable and peerless, Phussa, the Leader of the World.
Having destroyed all darkness and unraveled the great tangle, he— ”
It rains the rain of the Deathless, satisfying the world together with its devas.
For at that time, in Bārāṇasī, we were the king’s sons;
we were all three brothers, held in high confidence by the king.
“Men of heroic form and strength, unconquered in battle;
at that time, the border region having become provoked, the lord of the earth said to us:
‘Come, go to the border, and having cleared away the force of the forest-dwellers,’” he said.
“Having ensured a peaceful livelihood, give [it] back,” you said.
Then we replied: “If you would give the Leader to us for our service, we shall then accomplish your purpose.”
“Then, having obtained boons, we were sent by the protector of the earth;
having brought the border region to a state where weapons were laid aside, we returned once more to him.
Having requested the Teacher’s attendance, we [approached] the King, the Leader of the World.”
Having obtained the Hero among Sages, we made offerings to him for as long as we lived—
costly garments, exquisite flavors,
delightful dwellings, and beneficial medicines.
“Having given to the Sage together with the Saṅgha— these things acquired by us through the Dhamma—
we who are virtuous, compassionate, and whose minds are intent on meditation,
having served the Leader with faith and a heart of loving-kindness...”
When that Foremost One in the World had passed away, we performed worship according to our ability.
Then, passing from there, we went to the Santusita heaven, where we all experienced great bliss;
this is the fruit of our worship of the Buddha.
"Just as a magician displays many transformations upon a stage,
so too, wandering through existence, I became the lord of Videha.
By the words of Guṇācela, my heart was set upon wrong views."
I had ascended the path to hell because of my daughter Rucā.
Although I was repeatedly exhorted by Brahmā Nārada,
I did not accept his advice and instead abandoned my evil view.
“Having fulfilled, in particular, these ten paths of kamma here,
I abandoned the body and went to heaven, to my own abode.
When my final existence was reached, I became a kinsman of Brahmā.”
Born in the great Brahmin clan in the prosperous city of Bārāṇasī,
terrified by death, disease, and old age, I entered the great forest and went forth among the matted-hair ascetics, seeking the state of Nibbāna.
“At that time, my two brothers went forth together with me;
having built a hermitage at Uruvelā, I dwelt there.
By clan I was named Kassapa, a resident of Uruvelā.”
Then there arose for me the designation, "Uruvelakassapa.
My brother was in the vicinity of the river, known by the name Nadīkassapa;
at Gayā, he was known by his own name as Gayākassapa.
“Two hundred were the disciples of my youngest brother, three hundred those of my middle brother,
and five hundred less than five hundred were my own disciples— all of them followed me.
Then the Buddha approached me and performed various [miracles] for me.”
The Leader of the World, the Charioteer of Men, tamed [beings] through miracles.
With a retinue of one thousand, I was addressed with "Come, monk";
together with all of them, I attained arahantship.
“Many other disciples as well surrounded me; I was capable of speaking,
and therefore the Seventh Sage [placed me] in that great assembly,
establishing me as the foremost therein.”
"Aho! The service rendered to the Buddha has borne fruit for me.
'The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship and reflecting upon his own practice, he uttered this lion's roar:
“Having seen the miracles of the illustrious Gotama,
I did not yet prostrate myself, being deceived by pride and envy.
But perceiving my intention, the Charioteer of Men urged me on.”
Then a sense of spiritual urgency arose within me, extraordinary and hair-raising:
"Having now cast aside those limited powers of mine that were achieved while I was a matted-hair ascetic,
I have gone forth in the teaching of the Conqueror."
“Formerly satisfied with sacrifice, placing the realm of desire before me,
I later uprooted lust, hatred, and delusion as well.
I know my former births, and the divine eye has been purified.”
“Possessing supernormal power and knowing the minds of others, I have attained the divine ear.
That purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—
that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been reached by me.”
He spoke these six verses.
Therein, "having seen the miracles" means having seen the three thousand five hundred miracles, such as the taming of the Naga King and others.
For "pāṭihīraṃ," "pāṭiheraṃ," and "pāṭihāriyaṃ" are identical in meaning; only the phonetic form differs. "Of the illustrious one."
“‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One’ and so forth refers to the Blessed One whose fame has spread according to reality throughout the world including the devas.
‘I do not yet prostrate myself’ means: as long as the Blessed One has not said to me, ‘Kassapa, you are neither an Arahant nor have you entered the path to Arahantship;
that practice which would make you an Arahant or one who has entered the path to Arahantship does not exist in you.’”
I did not urge him on, nor did I prostrate myself before him. For what reason? Because I was deceived by envy (*issā*).

Thinking, "Now that he has become my disciple, my own gains and honor will diminish, while his alone will increase," I was possessed by envy, which is characterized by an inability to endure the prosperity of others;
and [by pride], thinking, "I am the leader of the group, esteemed by many people."
Thus, he was deceived by conceit characterized by overestimation; the meaning is that he became deluded.
"Having understood my intention" means having known my wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*);

and whatever superhuman feat of psychic power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*) the Blessed One displayed beyond human nature, seeing each of those, [he thought], "The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty."
Even while reflecting, though he knew the wrong thought that had arisen in the form of "But surely an Arahant is not like me," he remained equanimous,
waiting for the ripening of his knowledge; later, having warded off the water on all sides in the middle of the Nerañjarā River and walking upon the dust-covered ground,
even then, as he stood in the boat brought by him, [the thought] "He is one of great psychic power," and so forth, occurred.
The meaning is: having reflected, he then recognized that my wrong intention—which had occurred in the form of the thought, "Arahant indeed I am not as [others] say"—[the Teacher] rebuked me.

"The Charioteer of Men" means that then, knowing the ripening of my wisdom, the Teacher, the Charioteer of those to be tamed by men, rebuked and restrained me with the words, "Indeed, you are not an Arahant," and so forth.
From that, a sense of spiritual urgency arose within me, wonderful and hair-raising.
Then, due to the aforementioned cause of reproach, because it had never occurred before for such a long time, there arose in me a sense of wonder accompanied by horripilation;
a sense of urgency through the occurrence of horripilation; and the arising of knowledge together with self-reproach, thinking: "Though not yet an arahant, I imagined myself to be an arahant.
"Jaṭilabhūtassa" means "of one who has become an ascetic. "Siddhi" means the success of gain and honor. "Parittikā" means "slight."
*Tāhaṃ* means "that I. *Tadā* refers to the time when spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arises through the Blessed One’s exhortation.

*Nirākatvā* means having removed, discarded, or cast aside; the sense is that one has become indifferent to it. Regarding the word "supernormal power" (*iddhi*), they say it is "the supernormal power consisting in development" (*bhāvanāmaya-iddhi*).
That is incorrect, because at that time he was not yet an attainer of jhāna. For it is said: "placed at the head of the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-purakkhato*).

“Content with sacrifice” means one who is satisfied with performing sacrifices, thinking, “Having sacrificed, I shall experience the bliss of heaven; that much will suffice,” and thus perceives his task as completed.

“Placing the realm of sense-desire before him” means having craving arise directed toward a happy rebirth in the sense-sphere, he stands placing the world of sense-desire ahead of him by means of performing sacrifices.
If that sacrifice is associated with the taking of life, [it is not a true sacrifice].
By that [unwholesome action], it is not possible to attain a happy destination (*sugati*). For a desirable or pleasing result does not arise from what is unwholesome.
However, if there is wholesome volition (*cetanā*) such as giving (*dāna*) present there, one might go to a happy destination when the necessary conditions coincide.

"Afterwards" means after renouncing the life of an ascetic, at the time of applying oneself to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of the Four Noble Truths by following the Teacher’s instruction, having abandoned the ascetic’s conceits.
Having brought insight to its peak, they uprooted greed, hatred, and delusion entirely through the successive stages of the Path.

Since this elder attained the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiññā*) precisely while uprooting greed and the other defilements by means of the Noble Path, he spoke the words beginning with "I know my former births" in order to demonstrate his own possession of the six supernormal powers. Therein, "former births" (*pubbenivāsa*)...

"I know": by means of the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), I directly know and awaken to my own and others' past lives—the aggregates (*khandha*) produced in previous births and the things connected to those aggregates—just as one sees a myrobalan fruit on the palm of one's hand.
"The divine eye is purified" means that the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) has been purified; it is the ordinary form that has come within the range of the natural eye.
The meaning is: "I have obtained, through meditation, purified knowledge capable of discerning forms—whether divine or human, distant or situated beyond, and even extremely subtle.

"Possessed of psychic power" (*iddhimā*) means one who possesses psychic powers such as the power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) and the power of transformation (*vikubbanā-iddhi*); the meaning is one who has attained the knowledge of the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*). [He is so called] because he knows the minds of others, categorized by passion and other factors.

"Knower of others' minds" means one who has attained the knowledge of penetration into the minds of others (*cetopariyañāṇa*). "And I have reached the divine ear" means that I have acquired the knowledge of the divine ear (*dibbasotañāṇa*).

"That goal of mine has been attained, the destruction of all fetters" means that this goal of my own and the supreme goal—which consists in the destruction of all fetters, or which is to be obtained through their destruction—has been realized by me through the attainment of the Noble Path.
Thus, it should be understood that by means of this verse, the Elder’s proclamation of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*) occurred.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uruvelakassapa is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Tekicchakārita.
The verses beginning with "Atihitā vīhī" (The rice has been harvested) are those of the Venerable Tekicchakāri Thera. What is their origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī ninety-one aeons ago.
Having reached maturity, he attained mastery in the science of medicine. Of Vipassī...
He restored to health the Elder named Asoka, who was the personal attendant of the Blessed One when he was ill;
out of compassion for other beings overcome by disease, he also provided medicinal remedies.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he became known as Subuddha.
He was reborn as the son of a brahmin. Because he had been protected from dangers during his time in the womb by physicians, they gave him the name Tekicchakārī.
He grew up studying the branches of knowledge and crafts appropriate to his family.
At that time, Cāṇakka [observed] Subuddha’s proficiency in wisdom and his skill in practical actions.
Seeing his skill in means, King Candagutta— motivated by jealousy, thinking, "If he gains a foothold in this royal family,
he will surpass me"— had him cast into prison. Having heard that his father had been imprisoned,
Tekicchakārī fled in fear and went into the presence of the Elder Sāṇavāsī, [where he told] the Elder the cause of his own spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having spoken thus, he went forth, took up a meditation subject, and dwelt as one who lives in the open air and remains in a sitting posture;
disregarding cold and heat, he practiced the duty of a recluse and especially devoted himself to the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Seeing this, Māra the Evil One thought, "I will not allow him to transcend my domain," and desiring to cause distraction, [approached him].
When the rice was ready for harvest, [a man] dressed as a field-guardian went before the Elder and, while prodding him, said:
"The rice is harvested, the paddy is in the barn;
yet I receive no alms—how shall I live? Hearing this, the Elder—
“Recalling the immeasurable Buddha with confidence, you shall have a body suffused with rapture and be constantly uplifted.
‘Recalling the immeasurable Dhamma… constantly uplifted.
‘Recalling the immeasurable Saṅgha… constantly uplifted,’ he said. Having heard this, Māra—
“You dwell in the open air; these winter nights are cold.
Do not be distressed by the cold; enter the monastery, its doors bolted shut,” he said.
Then the Elder—
“I shall touch the four immeasurables and dwell in happiness through them;
dwelling unshakable, I shall not be distressed by cold,” he said.
In that context, "grain brought in" (*atihitā vīhī*) means grain that has been brought into and stored in the granary (*vīhayaḥ*), having been transported from the threshing floor.
The meaning is "brought to the house. Here, by the mention of *vīhi* (rice), other grains are also included;
however, he says this because *sālī* (paddy) generally ripens after *vīhi*.

"Sālī gone to the threshing floor" means they have gone to the threshing floor—the place for processing grain—and are situated there in the form of a heap, by way of being pounded, winnowed, and so forth. And here, it is for the purpose of showing their status as the primary grain that—
The separate mention of "rice" indicates that grain is fully present both within the village and outside the village.
"And I do not obtain even alms-food": thus, at a time when grain is so easily obtained and there is an abundance of food, he said, "I do not receive even a mere portion of alms.
"Now how shall I manage?"—he thus engaged in a playful jest, asking, "How shall I act? How shall I live?"
Having heard this, the Elder thought, "This poor fellow has revealed his own conduct to me; however, I must exhort myself alone, for I have nothing further to say.

Thus, directing himself toward the recollection of the Three Refuges, he spoke three verses beginning with "Recall the Buddha, the immeasurable. Therein, "Recall the Buddha, the immeasurable... refers to the recollection of the Buddha.
"Confident" (*pasanna*) means: because of the absolute departure of the sleep of ignorance along with its latent tendencies, and because of the blossoming of his awakening;

and because the Blessed One is the Buddha, he is "immeasurable" (*appameyya*) due to the absence of defilements such as lust which are taken as standards, due to his possession of immeasurable qualities, and due to his being an immeasurable field of merit.
He is "confident" through a serene confidence characterized by total trust, with a mind full of faith, [thinking]: "Thus indeed is he..."

"Recollect [the Buddha] by way of the formula beginning with 'The Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One,' and so forth; maintain mindfulness directed toward the Buddha as its object, and your body will become suffused with rapture (*pīti*).

Being constantly elated means that while recollecting, your body is at all times continuously suffused by rapture characterized by pervasiveness, your body being overwhelmed by the sublime matter produced by rapture, and by the rapture of uplifting joy."
If you were to become uplifted, having made your body uplifted, and capable of leaping into the sky,

you would experience a sublime joy and gladness with the Buddha as its object through the recollection of the Buddha. The meaning is that from that point on, you would be invincible even by hunger and thirst,
just as one is invincible by cold and heat.
"Dhamma" refers to the noble supramundane Dhamma. "Saṅgha" refers to the noble ultimate Saṅgha. The rest is exactly as previously explained.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one recollects," one should connect it thus: one recollects the Dhamma by means of the formula beginning with "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One," and one recollects the Saṅgha by means of the formula beginning with "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way."

When the Elder had thus exhorted himself by way of directing him toward the recollection of the virtues of the Triple Gem, Māra, desiring once more to separate him from his dwelling in seclusion, spoke the fifth verse, "You dwell in the open," as if showing himself to be a well-wisher.
Its meaning is this: O Bhikkhu, you dwell in the open—uncovered and exposed ground—in the four postures.
He made this arrangement: "These cold nights of the winter season, fallen into the time of snowfall, are passing.
Therefore, being overcome and oppressed by the cold, do not be distressed; do not fall into exhaustion; do not grow weary.
Enter a lodging with its bolts fastened and its doors closed; in this way, your dwelling will be comfortable."
Having heard that, the Elder spoke the sixth verse beginning with “I shall touch,” showing: “I have no need to search for a lodging;
I shall dwell happily right here. In this context, “I shall touch the four immeasurables” (*phusissaṃ catasso appamaññāyo*) means:

because their range of activity is boundless, they are designated by the conventional term “immeasurables” (*appamaññā*); I shall touch—that is, I shall realize—the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
"From time to time I shall attain [these meditative states]. And by means of those immeasurables (appamaññā), being happy and having become one whose happiness is born, I shall dwell;

I shall maintain all four postures. Therefore, for me there is only happiness at all times, not suffering, so that I shall not be distressed by cold even during the intervals between seasons or at the time of the falling snow.

"I shall not be distressed by the cold; therefore, dwelling unshaken, because I have thoroughly abandoned ill-will and other causes for the mind’s wavering, and because there is an absence of any wavering arising from conditions, I shall dwell happy through the very bliss of meditative attainment.
While the Elder was speaking this verse, he thus increased his insight and realized Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, I was a well-trained physician,
bringing great happiness to the people who were afflicted and suffering.
Seeing a sick ascetic, virtuous and of great luster, [I approached him].”
With a serene mind and joyful heart, I then gave that medicine.
Because of that, the ascetic with restrained faculties became free from illness;
he was the attendant of Vipassī, known by the name Assoka.
“Ninety-one eons ago, when I gave away medicinal herbs, I did not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of that medicine.
And eight eons ago from now, I was named Sabbosadha.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, the wheel-turning monarch brings great fruit.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [and so forth] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
And here it should be understood that these verses were recited at the Third Council, because this elder appeared during the time of King Bindusāra.”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Tekicchakāri is finished.
3. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahānāga begins with the verse starting, "In whom [there is no fault] among fellow-celibates. What is his origin? He too—
Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence throughout various births,
he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha. Upon reaching maturity, one day,
having entered deep into the forest, he saw the Blessed One Kakusandha seated at the foot of a certain tree, enjoying the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

With a mind full of faith, he gave him a pomegranate fruit. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha at Sāketa as the son of a brahmin named Madhuvāseṭṭha;
his name was Mahānāga. When he reached the age of discretion, while the Blessed One was staying in the Añjana Grove at Sāketa...
Having seen the miracle of the Venerable Gavampati Thera, he gained faith and went forth in the presence of that very Thera.
Abiding by his instruction, he attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Kakusandha, the Great Hero, who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena;”
Having withdrawn from the community, he went into the depths of the forest.
"Taking some seed-pulp, I strung it upon a creeper;
at that time, the Blessed One was meditating within the mountain range."
“Having seen the God of Gods with a serene mind,
I gave seed and gruel to that Hero worthy of offerings.
Because I gave that gruel back in this very eon, [the result was as follows].”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of the seed of *miñja*.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, the Elder, seeing that the group-of-six monks (*chabbaggiya*) were living without showing respect toward their fellow celibates, spoke these verses as an exhortation to them:
“He in whom no reverence for his fellow-celibates is found Falls away from the true Dhamma, like a fish from a pool that has run dry.
He in whom no reverence for his fellow-celibates is found...”
It does not grow in the true Dhamma, like a rotten seed in a field.
He in whom no reverence for his fellow-celibates is found is far removed from Nibbāna in the teaching of the King of Dhamma.
“He in whom reverence for his fellow-celibates is found does not fall away from the true Dhamma, just as a fish does not leave the water.
He in whom reverence for his fellow-celibates is found...”
Thus one flourishes in the true Dhamma, like a noble seed in a field.
For one in whom reverence for fellow practitioners of the holy life is found,
Nibbāna is near within the teaching of the King of Dhamma.
He spoke these six verses.

Therein, "among fellow-celibates" (*sabrahmacārīsu*) means those who practice the same holy life (*brahma*), such as virtue and other qualities; they are fellow-practitioners (*sahadhammika*) who have attained equality in virtue, view, and so forth—among them.
"Veneration" (*gārava*) means the state of being respected, the act of holding in high esteem on account of qualities such as virtue. "Is not found" (*nūpalabbhati*)...

"It does not exist" means it does not proceed; "it does not stand near" is the meaning. "Nibbāna" means the extinction (*nibbāpana*) of the defilements; thus, the meaning is the destruction of the defilements.

"Of the Dhamma-King" refers to the Teacher. For the Teacher is the Dhamma-King because he delights and satisfies the world, including the devas, with the mundane and supramundane Dhamma as is appropriate. And here, [the phrase] "in the teaching of the Dhamma-King" [is used].
By this it is shown that what is called Nibbāna exists only within the teaching of the Dhamma King and not elsewhere.
In that regard, he shows that the fellow-celibate who is devoid of reverence is as far from Nibbāna as he is from the teaching of the Dhamma King.
"In much water" means in abundant water. "Nibbāna is near" means that Nibbāna is near to him, in his vicinity.
It is exactly so. The rest is precisely as previously stated. These were the very verses by which the Elder proclaimed his full knowledge (*aññā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahānāga is finished.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kulla.
"Kullo sivathikaṃ... and so forth are verses of the Venerable Elder Kulla. What is their origin?

This [Elder] as well, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha into a family of householders in Sāvatthī.
Having attained the age of discretion and received the name Kulla, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
Having heard this, he gained faith and went forth. Because he was of a lustful temperament, he was by nature prone to intense passion;
consequently, the defilements frequently remained, completely overwhelming his mind.

Then the Teacher, knowing the movement of his mind, gave him the meditation subject of the foul (asubha) and said, "Kulla, you must frequently go on alms-rounds in the charnel ground. He entered the charnel ground.
Having seen various foul objects such as a bloated corpse and having momentarily aroused the contemplation of the foul,
he was immediately overcome by sensual lust as soon as he departed from the charnel ground. Again, the Blessed One, knowing his state of mind,
on one occasion when he went to the charnel ground, [saw] the body of a young woman who had recently died and whose skin was not yet decomposed.
Having created it, he showed it to him. As soon as he saw it, lust arose suddenly in him, just as it would toward a living being of the opposite sex.

Then, even as he was looking on, the Teacher made it exceedingly loathsome, foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive, showing it oozing impurities from its nine openings and swarming with hosts of worms. He [the monk]—
Gazing at it, he stood there with a mind free from attachment. Then the Blessed One, pervading him with radiance and arousing mindfulness in him, spoke:
“Behold this heap of bones, Kulla—sickly, impure, and putrid;
Oozing and trickling, it is what fools delight in.”
He said: Having heard that, the Elder correctly contemplated the true nature of the body;
having acquired the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*), he attained the first *jhāna* therein. Taking that as his foundation, he developed insight (*vipassanā*) and reached Arahantship.
Then, reviewing his own progress, he said:
“Having gone to every cemetery, he saw a woman abandoned, cast away in the charnel ground, covered with worms and being devoured. “Afflicted...
[as before] ...delighted by fools.”
“Having taken up the mirror of the Dhamma for the sake of attaining knowledge and vision, I examined this body—empty within and without. ‘As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this.’”
As below, so above; as above, so below.
As by day, so at night; as at night, so by day.
As before, so after; as after, so before.
“There is no such delight from a fivefold musical ensemble as there is for one whose mind is one-pointed and who correctly discerns the Dhamma.”—
He spoke these verses by way of an inspired utterance (udāna).
In this context, the Elder speaks of himself as "a raft," treating himself as if he were another.
"Afflicted" means constantly oppressed by various kinds of suffering. "Impure" means devoid of purity, loathsome, and repulsive.
"Putrid" means foul-smelling. "Behold" means look at it according to its true nature. At the time of giving this exhortation, the Blessed One spoke thus: "O raft! (Kulla).
[The Blessed One] addresses the Elder. But at the time of the *udāna* (inspired utterance), the Elder speaks of himself. "A mass" (*samussaya*) refers to the body.

"Oozing" (*uggharanta*) means flowing with impurity from the openings of the wounds above. "Dripping" (*paggharanta*) means flowing with impurity from the openings of the wounds below and from all sides.
"Delighted in by fools" means [delighted] by foolish worldlings (*puthujjana*), who are blind, through their delight in views and craving.
“Delighted by clinging to ‘I’ and ‘mine. The “mirror of the Dhamma” is a mirror made of the Dhamma.

For just as beings see their own virtues and faults on their faces or bodies by means of a mirror, so too the practitioner of yoga sees the phenomena of defilement and purification within his own personal existence exactly as they are.

That insight-knowledge is here called the "mirror of the Dhamma. Having generated that knowledge within one's own continuum for the sake of attaining the eye of the Dhamma—known as the path-knowledge of vision—one reflects upon this body:
"This physical body is empty, being devoid of any permanent essence, and it is both internal and external, distinguished by its own and others' continua."
I examined and saw with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*).
To show how I examined it, the passage beginning with "Just as this" was spoken. Therein, "just as this, so that" means:
just as this impurity (*asubha*) consisting of my own body remains [as such] because life-force (*āyu*), heat (*usmā*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*) have not departed;
It displays various kinds of activity that are like an illusion; likewise, this dead body previously displayed such activity because those factors had not departed.
Just as this dead body now displays no activity at all because those factors have departed, so too will this body of mine perish when those factors depart. Just as...
And this body of mine, which is currently not dead nor lying in the charnel ground, has not yet reached the state of being bloated and so forth;

likewise, this very body of mine was previously a dead body. And just as this present dead body lies in the charnel ground and reaches the state of being bloated and so forth, so too will this body of mine become. Now...
Or, just as this body of mine is impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, repulsive, impermanent, suffering, and non-self, so too is this dead body.
Or, just as this dead body has the nature of being impure and so forth, and the nature of being impermanent and so forth, so too does this body of mine. As below, so above; as from the navel...
Below, that is, beneath this body, there is impurity, a foul odor, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness; it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Likewise, above the navel, its nature is likewise characterized by impurity and so forth. Just as it is above, so it is below;
and just as its nature is characterized by impurity and so forth above the navel, so it is also below the navel.
“As by day, so by night”: just as this body during the day oozes impurities—such as “eye-dung from the eye” and so forth—so too does it by night.
“As by night, so by day”: and just as this body oozes impurities by night, so too does it by day;
the meaning is that there is no change in its nature due to the division of time. “As before... [and so on].
"Likewise afterwards" means that just as this body was previously, in its youth, impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive, so too is it afterwards in its old age.
And just as its nature is one of impurity and so forth in its later stage of old age, so too was it in its earlier stage of youth.
Or rather, just as in the past, during the time when it possessed consciousness, its nature was one of impurity and so forth, and its nature was one of impermanence and so forth.
And likewise, "afterwards" means in the future time, in the period when consciousness is absent; such is the meaning to be understood here.

"With a fivefold musical ensemble" means with a musical ensemble endowed with five components—namely, *ātata*, *vitata*, *ātata-vitata*, *ghana*, and *susīra*—as he was being entertained by such a fivefold ensemble while possessing sensual pleasure, like a lordly person.
Such a delight and such a relish for pleasure does not exist as that which belongs to one whose mind is one-pointed and who correctly discerns the Dhamma— namely,
the delight in the Dhamma experienced by the practitioner who, having yoked serenity and insight together,
sees the arising and passing away of the aggregates through insight that has entered the path by means of the single flavor of the faculties. Even a fraction of that [delight]...
“He does not attain delight in sensual pleasures. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Whenever one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one finds rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for one who understands.”
These were also the verses by which the Elder proclaimed his realization.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kulla is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Māluṅkyaputta.
The verses beginning with “Of a man” (manujassa) are the stanzas of the Venerable Elder Māluṅkyaputta. What is their origin?

This [Thera] too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit in various states of existence, was reborn at the time of this Buddha’s appearance as the son of the chief courtier of King Kosala in Sāvatthī. His mother was named Māluṅkyā; it was after her that [he was named].
He was known as Māluṅkyaputta. Having reached maturity, out of a desire for renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a wandering ascetic.
While wandering about, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher;

having gained faith in the Dispensation, he went forth and, applying himself to insight meditation, before long became one possessed of the six supernormal powers. Out of compassion for his kinsmen, he...

He went to his family home. His relatives served him with excellent hard and soft foods and, desiring to entice him with wealth, placed a great heap of money before him and pleaded, "This wealth is yours;
leave the monastic order and, supporting your wife and children with this wealth, perform meritorious deeds. The Elder—
Standing in the air, he turned their minds around and said:
“For a person who wanders heedlessly, craving grows like a creeping vine.
He leaps from this world to that, like a monkey in the forest seeking fruit.”
“Whatever this wretched craving, that clings in the world, tolerates,
for that person sorrows increase like grass after rain.
But whoever tolerates this wretched craving, so difficult to overcome in the world— ”
Sorrows fall away from him like drops of water from a lotus leaf.
"I say this to you, may it be well with you, all you who have gathered here:
dig up the root of craving, just as one seeking fragrant usīra root digs up the bīraṇa grass."
“Let not Māra break you again and again, as a river breaks reeds.
Practice the word of the Buddha; let not the opportune moment pass you by.
For those who have let the moment pass grieve when they are consigned to hell.”
“Negligence is dust; negligence brings forth dust. One who has fallen under the sway of negligence [is covered] by dust.
By means of heedfulness and true knowledge, one should pull out the arrow from oneself.
With these six verses, he taught the Dhamma.
In this context, "of a person" means of a being. "One who wanders negligently" refers to one whose conduct is negligent due to negligence characterized by the loss of mindfulness;
for such a person, neither jhāna, nor insight (vipassanā), nor the paths and fruits increase.
Just as the māluvā creeper grows by binding and entwining a tree for its destruction, so too, depending upon his six sense-doors—
Craving, arising again and again toward forms and other objects, increases.

As it increases, just as the māluva creeper, having completely overspread the tree that serves as its support, causes it to fall, so too does craving cast the person who is subservient to it into the states of misery.
"He floats" means that this person, subservient to craving, drifts and runs hither and thither from existence to existence. Just as...
What is it like? It is like a monkey in a forest desiring fruit:

just as a monkey seeking fruit in the forest runs about, grasping one branch of a tree, letting go of that to grasp another, and letting go of that to grasp yet another, never reaching a point where it can be said, "He sits having found no branch";
even so does a person subject to craving run from here to there.
Even though they are running [after objects], one cannot say of them that "they have reached the non-arising of craving because they have not found an object.

"Yaṃ" refers to whichever person. This [craving] has come to be designated as *visattikā*—meaning "that which is attached"—because it is base (*jammī*), because its root is poison (*visamūlatā*), because its fruit is poison (*visaphalatā*), because its enjoyment is poison (*visaparibhogatā*), and because it is attached (*āsattā*) and clings (*visattā*) to forms and so forth; it is the sixfold [craving] pertaining to the six doors.

Craving overcomes and masters that person. Just as *bīraṇa* grass—that is, *bīraṇa* reed—grows and increases when it has been repeatedly rained upon by the rain falling in the forest, even so, sorrows rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) increase and reach growth; this is the meaning.
And as for the one who... [pe] ...is difficult to overcome: but that person who is unable to transcend or abandon such a state as described above.
Because of its difficulty, he endures and overcomes craving, which is hard to transcend; from such a person, the sorrows rooted in the cycle of existence fall away.
The meaning is that they do not take root, just as a drop of water fallen upon a lotus leaf in a pond does not remain.
"I tell you this" means: for that reason, I say this to you. "May it be well for you" means: may it be well for you;
do not, like a person who follows after craving, fall into ruin or misfortune—this is the meaning. "As many as have gathered here" means:
as many as have assembled in this place, so many [are you]. If one asks, "What do you say? [the answer is: "Dig up the root of craving."
Dig up and utterly eradicate the root-cause of this craving with its six doors—the grasping of defilements such as ignorance—with the hoe of the knowledge of the path to Arhatship. How so?
Just as one who needs *usīra* root digs up the grass called *bīraṇa*—which is another name for *usīra*—with a large hoe, so too should you dig up its root.

The meaning is as follows: "Mā vo naḷaṃ va sotova, māro bhañji punappunan" means: "May Māra—the defilement-māra, the death-māra, and the devaputta-māra—not repeatedly break you, just as the river current with its great force breaks the reeds growing on the riverbank.
Therefore, practice the word of the Buddha, which was spoken by the Buddha in such passages as: "Bhikkhus, meditate; do not be negligent."
"Carry out the word of the Blessed One; accomplish the practice as it has been instructed. Do not let the opportune moment pass you by.

For this moment of the arising of a Buddha, the moment of dwelling in a suitable place, the moment of having acquired right view, and the moment of the completeness of the six sense bases—this moment passes for that person who does not act upon the word of the Buddha.

Every moment passes; may that moment not pass you by. Those who have passed that moment—whether they are individuals who have let that moment slip away or those for whom that moment has already elapsed—are cast into hell, reborn there, and grieve for a long time.
Negligence is passion: negligence, characterized by the abandonment of mindfulness regarding sense objects such as forms and so forth, is so called because its intrinsic nature is defilement.

And it is "dust" (*rajo*) because of its association with the dust of passion (*rāga*) and the like. Whatever is called "dust," such as passion and so forth, all that is "overcome by negligence" (*pamādānupatito*);

it arises solely through the power of negligence. "By heedfulness" (*appamādena*) means by non-negligence, by the practice of heedfulness. "By clear knowledge" (*vijjāya*) means by the clear knowledge of the supreme path.
"He shall pull out the dart from himself" (*abbahe sallamattanoti*) means the dart of passion and the like residing in his own heart.
"Should uproot and eradicate.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Māluṅkyaputta is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sappadāsa.
The verses beginning with "Paṇṇavīsati" are those of the Venerable Sappadāsa Thera. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha as the son of the royal chaplain to King Suddhodana in Kapilavatthu; he was named Sappadāsa.
Such was his name. When he reached maturity, having gained faith upon meeting the Teacher’s kinsmen, he went forth into homelessness.
Failing to attain mental concentration due to being overcome by defilements, he lived the holy life;
then, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, he later drew the sword [of renunciation], increased his wise attention, attained arahantship, and declared his realization:
“For twenty-five years since I went forth,
I have not attained even for the duration of a finger-snap the peace of mind.
Not having attained one-pointedness of mind, I was tormented by sensual lust.”
Raising my arms and weeping, I stepped out from the monastery:
"I shall take up a weapon; what is the use of my life?
For how could one like me pass away after having abandoned the training?"
“Then, taking a razor, I sat down upon my bed;
the razor was whetted for the purpose of cutting my own veins.
Thereupon, right reflection arose in me.”
“Danger became manifest, and disenchantment took firm root.
Then my mind was liberated; behold the excellence of the Dhamma!
The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
He spoke these verses.
Regarding them: "Twenty-five years since I went forth"—from the time I first went forth, these have been twenty-five years.
"Not even for the duration of a finger-snap have I attained peace of mind"—I [have not attained it] for all this time.

"Though I lived the holy life for a long time, I did not obtain even for the duration of a finger-snap or a moment's flash of lightning the peace of mind or the composure of mind [that comes from] one-pointedness of consciousness.
And because I did not obtain such one-pointedness of consciousness, he states the reason for that: 'Afflicted by sensual lust. Regarding this:
"Afflicted" (*aṭṭita*) means oppressed; the meaning is "overcome. "Wailing with arms outstretched" means wailing with his face turned upward and his arms outstretched, thinking:
"This is most improper that, having gone forth in the dispensation which leads to liberation, I am unable to extricate myself from the mire of the defilements.
"Departing from the monastery" means having gone outside the dwelling where he lived.
In order to show the intention with which he set out, it was said: "I will take up a weapon," and so forth.
Therein, in the phrase "I will take up a weapon," the word *vā* (or) has the sense of an alternative;
by it, other modes of death such as "I will throw myself from a tree" or "I will die by hanging myself" are included. They train in the training of higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). They renounce...
*Paccācikkhanto*: rejecting or renouncing. There is also a Pāli reading *paccakkhā*, meaning "having rejected. *Kālaṃ*: death. The meaning is:
"How indeed could one like me die by means of the rejection of the training?
For in the Vinaya of the Noble Ones, the rejection of the training is called "death. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, this is indeed death: the rejection of the training..."

“Having renounced [the training], he returns to the lower life. But regarding the reading “having renounced the training” (*sikkhaṃ paccakkhā*), how indeed could one such as I die after having renounced the training? Rather, one should die while still possessing the training.
Therefore, the construction is: “I shall take up a weapon; what is the use of my life?”
"At that time" means when, due to being overcome by defilements and the consequent inability to practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he becomes disenchanted with life.
"A razor" (*khura*) means a sharp-edged razor or a blade similar to a razor.

"He sat upon a couch" means that, out of fear of being restrained by others, he entered a small room and sat down on a couch. "Led away" (*parinīta*) means brought near; it means placed around the neck.
The intention is as follows: "A vein" (*dhamanī*)—some say it refers to the "vein in the throat," the "throat-vein," or the "windpipe.
"To cut" (*chettuṃ*) means to sever.
"Then my attention arose properly" (*tato me manasīkāro yoniso udapajjatha*) means that when [I thought], "I shall die," [the intention] to cut the vein in the throat arose.

I applied the razor; thereafter, as I reflected, "Is my virtue indeed healthy?", I saw that my virtue was unbroken, untorn, and perfectly pure, and joy arose. In one whose mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil;
for one whose body is tranquil and who experiences spiritual happiness, there arises through concentration of mind and by way of insight (vipassanā) wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).

It arose. Or alternatively, "from that" means that as he was applying the lancet to his throat, when a wound had formed, the appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) by way of insight (*vipassanā*) arose, suppressing the pain that had arisen.
Now, in order to show that the knowledge of reviewing the path and fruit (*maggaphala-paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*) arose thereafter, it was said:
"The danger (*ādīnava*) became manifest," and so forth. That has already been explained in meaning above.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sappadāsa is finished.
7. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kātiyāna begins with the words "Arise," etc. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various existences, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin of the Kosiya clan.

However, because of his mother’s clan, he received the name Kātiyāna. Upon reaching maturity, having been a childhood friend of the elder Sāmaññakāni, he saw the elder and went forth into homelessness.
While performing his ascetic duties, he ascended the walking path at night, thinking, "I shall dispel the onset of sleep.
As he was walking, overcome by drowsiness and nodding off, he fell down and lay right there upon the bare ground.
The Teacher, seeing this occurrence, went there himself and, standing in the air, called out, "Kātyāyana! by way of address.
He gave [the gift]. Upon seeing the Teacher, he rose, paid homage, and stood there overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Then the Teacher, teaching him the Dhamma, said:
“Arise, Kātyāyana, sit down; do not be prone to sleep, but be watchful.
Let not King Death, the lord of Māra, conquer you as a rogue defeats one who is lazy and a kinsman to negligence.”
"Just as the surging of the great ocean, so does birth and old age roll on.
Therefore, make yourself an island; for no other refuge exists for you.
The Teacher has indeed conquered this path, having transcended the bonds of fear regarding birth and old age."
“Diligent throughout the first and last watches of the night, apply yourself and make your practice firm. ‘Cast off those former bonds;
wearing the outer robe, with shaven head, and subsisting on alms-food, do not indulge in play or pleasure, nor in sleep—meditate, Kātiyāna!’”
“Meditate, Kātiyāna, and conquer! You are skilled in the paths to security from bondage.
Having attained supreme purity, you will be extinguished like a flame by water.
“The lamp-maker with his meager radiance is bent over by the wind like a creeper.”
