"Even so, you too, not grasping, shake off Māra who is of the same clan as Indra;
being free from passion for sensations, wait for your time right here, having become cooled."—
He spoke these verses.
In this context, "Arise" means: arising from sleep, exert yourself with the energy of effort (*uṭṭhāna-vīriya*). Since lying down belongs to the side of indolence, therefore do not lie down.
"Sit" means: sit having folded your legs crosswise, set your body erect, and established mindfulness before you. "Kātyāyana" is an address by name. "Do not be full of sleep."
"Do not be one who has much sleep, overcome by sloth. Be awake; be devoted to wakefulness.

Let not King Death overcome you—lazy, indolent, and a kinsman of negligence—as a hunter with a deceptive snare might catch a deer or a bird, but rather let him not conquer you through old age and disease.
The meaning is: "May it not overwhelm. *Seyyathāpi* means "just as if. *Mahāsamuddavego* means the surge of waves from the great ocean.
*Evaṃ* means that just as, for example, the surge of waves from the great ocean, rising higher and higher, [overwhelms] a man who is unable to advance against it...
It overcomes; likewise, birth and old age overcome and overwhelm that person who is overcome by laziness, piling one upon another. "Make it for yourself" means:
O Kātyāyana, you must make for yourself a secure island known as the fruit of Arhatship, which cannot be overwhelmed by the four floods;
produce it within your own continuum. For no other refuge exists for you.

*Hi* is a particle used in the sense of a reason (*hetuatthe*). Because no other refuge for you is found here or hereafter than that supreme fruit, therefore make that which is reckoned as *arahatta* a well-established island.
For it was in order to establish that "the Teacher has indeed conquered this path"—which the many heretics, being unable to achieve, were defeated by—that [the verse was spoken].

Therefore, having overcome the sons of the devas, Māra, and others, your Teacher has discovered and accomplished this Noble Path— which is the cause for that excellent island, which consists of five factors,

and which transcends the fears of birth and so forth— for the sake of its attainment, [he applied himself] during the first and last watches of the night. Since that which belongs to the Teacher must be realized by the disciple and not relinquished, therefore, for the sake of its realization, during the first and last watches of the night...
During the first watch and the last watch of the night, being diligent, mindful, and clearly comprehending, apply yourself to practice and make your cultivation firm.
"Release the former bonds" means: release and cast off those former bonds tied during your time as a householder—the bonds of household life and the bonds of the strands of sensual pleasure;
be without regard for them. "Wearing the outer robe, shaven-headed, and subsisting on alms-food" means: one who wears the *saṅghāṭī* robe.
"With a head shorn by a razor, subsisting on alms-food"—these three are statements regarding the cause for release from former bonds and for the pursuit of play, pleasure, and sleep.
Since you, though clad in the outer robe, are shaven-headed and live on alms-food, therefore your pursuit of sensual pleasure and your pursuit of play, pleasure, and sleep are not fitting;
thus, release yourself from those former bonds, [and abandon] play and pleasure.
The construction is: "And do not devote yourself to sleep. "Meditate" (*jhāya*) means: "You should meditate; devote yourself to the contemplation of the object" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).

Furthermore, showing that while devoting oneself to that, one should devote oneself to the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*)—that meditation by which, for one who meditates, the defilements are completely conquered—he said, "Meditate and conquer" (*jhāyāhi jināhi*).
"You are skilled in the paths to security from bondage" refers to the four bonds (*yoga*).
You were skilled and adept in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), which serve as the path to the secure state of *nibbāna*.
Therefore, by exerting yourself in meditation, you shall attain—and having attained—supreme *nibbāna*, which is unsurpassed, purity, and *arahantship*, you will then enter final *parinibbāna*.
Just as a mass of fire is extinguished by water, so too [is the fire of defilements quenched] by the falling of a great downpour of rain.
He will attain final nibbāna through the falling of the rain of the Noble Path, as it were.
"Pajjotakaro" means one who makes light; a lamp. "Parittaraṃsi" means a small flame. "Vinamyate" means it is bent down or removed.
"Latāvā" means like a creeper. This is what is meant: just as [a lamp] through the deficiency of conditions such as the wick...
A small wick, dimly glowing, or a tiny flame will be scattered and extinguished by the wind;
even so it shall be with you. O Indasagotta, because of your lineage of the Kosiya clan, you belong to the same lineage as Indra.
Without turning back under the power of Māra, and without grasping due to non-clinging, shake him off, scatter him, and extinguish him! And being thus extinguished—

"Therefore, having become free from desire and lust for all feelings whatsoever that are experienced, you shall here and now—in this very existence—become cooled and extinguished through the absence of the fever and distress of all defilements; wait for the time of your own final Nibbāna.
Thus, when the Teacher had brought him to the Nibbāna without residue and completed his teaching, at the conclusion of the discourse, the Elder—
Having increased his insight (vipassanā), he attained arahantship. Having reached arahantship, however, he spoke these verses according to the very method taught by the Teacher.
These very verses became the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kātiyāna is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Migajāla.
The verses beginning with "Well-taught" (Sudesito) belong to the venerable elder Migajāla. What is his origin?
This [elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born in Sāvatthī during this appearance of a Buddha.
Having been reborn as the son of the great female lay devotee Visākhā, he was named Migajāla.
Having gone to the monastery and gained faith through frequent hearing of the Dhamma, he went forth into homelessness.
Developing insight and attaining arahantship, he declared his realization:
“Well-taught by the Visionary One, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun;
it transcends all fetters and destroys all rounds of existence.
It leads to liberation, brings across [the flood], and dries up the root of craving.”
Having cut down the execution ground whose root is the uneven, he brings one to Nibbāna.
It is the destroyer of the mechanism of karma for the sake of breaking the root of ignorance;
it is the casting of the thunderbolt of knowledge upon the grasping of consciousnesses.
“An elucidator of feelings, a liberator from clinging;
one who contemplates existence with wisdom as if it were a pit of glowing embers.
Great in flavor, profoundly deep, and a barrier against old age and death.”
The Noble Eightfold Path, which brings the cessation of suffering and is auspicious.
Having understood action as action and its result as a result,
one sees the phenomena arisen through dependent origination exactly as they appear.
“Mahākhemaṅgamo santo, pariyosānabhaddako”—these verses he spoke.

Therein, “well-taught” (sudesita) means well-expounded; the meaning is that it was taught by way of clearly elucidating, according to reality, the matters pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.
Alternatively, “well-taught” means correctly taught, [showing] the process of occurrence and cessation.
The meaning is that it is called "well-expounded" (*svākhyāta*) because it explains both those causes without error.
"By the One with Eyes" (*cakkhumatā*) means by one who possesses these five eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, the Buddha-eye, and the universal eye.
"By the Buddha" (*buddhena*) means by the Omniscient Buddha. "By the Kinsman of the Sun" (*ādiccabandhunā*) means by one of the Solar clan.

For there are two kinds of kṣatriya lineages in the world: the lineage of the Ādityas and the lineage of the Soma. Among these, the lineage of the Ādityas should be understood as the royal lineage of Okkāka.
Because he was born from that [lineage], the Sākyans are of the Ādicca clan; thus the Blessed One is called "Kinsman of the Sun" (Ādiccabandhu).
Alternatively, the Blessed One is the Kinsman of the Sun because he is a relative of the Āditya; this meaning has already been explained above.
Because it transcends all fetters, beginning with the fetter of sensual lust, it has "transcended all fetters" (*sabbasaṃyojanātīta*).

Precisely for that reason, because it destroys and shatters the rounds of defilements, karma, and kamma-results, it is the "destroyer of all rounds" (*sabbavaṭṭavināsana*). Because it leads out from the prison of *saṃsāra*, it is "leading out" (*niyyānika*);
in the sense of crossing over the great flood of *saṃsāra*, it is "crossing over" (*uttaraṇa*). [It is the destruction] of sensual craving and so forth...
It is called "the drying up of the root of craving" because it withers and dries up ignorance and improper attention, which are the roots of all cravings.
It is the "root of poison" because it is the cause of suffering—the very essence of poison—due to its destruction of the penetration of the three Vedas.
Having cut off and utterly severed [this] slaughter-ground, which is the place where the calamities of beings arise, whether it be karma or the defilements;
It brings about extinction, which is Nibbāna.
The root of ignorance is unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) and the taints (*āsava*); for it is said, "With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance.

"For its destruction" means for the purpose of shattering it with knowledge that is like a thunderbolt. Alternatively, because of such statements as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth...

"Rooted in ignorance" (*aññāṇamūla*) means that its root is ignorance; the connection is that [the teaching] was taught for the purpose of shattering the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) with the thunderbolt of knowledge of the path.
"The shatterer of the machine of karma" (*kammayantavighātana*) means the destroyer of the machine of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) constructed by karma.

"In the grasping of consciousnesses" (*viññāṇānaṃ pariggahe*) means it stands as the apprehension of consciousnesses by their respective karmas within the realms of sense-desire existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth.

This is a remainder of the statement. For when rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) has been grasped in this or that state of existence, the consciousnesses dependent on those respective states are also necessarily included.
"The falling of the thunderbolt of knowledge" means the falling of the thunderbolt of knowledge; it is that which, having let fall the thunderbolt of knowledge, shatters them.
For when the supramundane dhamma arises, it [shatters] those consciousnesses that would otherwise have arisen in the seventh existence and so forth.
"It arises precisely as it breaks.

"The manifester of feelings" means one who makes known, according to their respective order, the three feelings—pleasure and so forth—as they truly are, by way of being suffering, a dart, and impermanent.
"The deliverer from clinging" means [one who delivers] the mental continuum from all four types of clinging, beginning with sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*).

The liberator: one who demonstrates through the knowledge of the Path—by means of eleven fires—that the ninefold existence, beginning with sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), is like a pit of glowing embers that is more than a man's height because it is ablaze; [one who shows this] by direct perception through knowledge.

Because of its state of being peaceful and sublime, it is "of great flavor" in the sense of not providing satisfaction; or, because of its great function through the modes of full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth, it is so called by way of the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

It is a great flavor because of its great excellence; it is profoundly deep because it is difficult to fathom and impossible to find a footing in for those who have not accumulated the necessary provisions;
and it wards off old age and death, acting as a preventer of old age and death by turning back the production of future existence.
Now, demonstrating in its true nature the Dhamma endowed with these aforementioned specific qualities:
Having said, “the noble eightfold path,” he further spoke the words beginning with “the auspicious pacifier of suffering” in order to clarify some of its qualities.
The meaning of this is as follows: it is *ariya* (noble) in the sense of being utterly pure; it is *aṭṭhaṅgika* (eightfold) because of the convergence of the eight factors beginning with right view;

it is the *magga* (path) in the sense of seeking Nibbāna; it is the *dukkhūpasamana* (pacifier of suffering) in the sense of pacifying all the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); and it is *siva* (auspicious) in the sense of security.
Just as, in the doctrines of outsiders, there might be a perversion regarding the ripening of kamma because they are not proclaimed by a Fully Enlightened One,
so too— without such perversion— having understood through preliminary knowledge that among dependently arisen phenomena,
kamma is indeed kamma and ripening is indeed ripening, one dispels the graspings at eternalism and annihilationism by means of that very understanding.
It is the vision of light according to reality for one who practices it; it is the vision of the supramundane knowledge-light.
Because it is never, by anyone, at any time, afflicted by anything, it goes to and leads beings to Nibbāna, the great security; thus it is "one whose course is the great security.

It is peaceful because it pacifies all the distress and fever of the defilements; it is auspicious in its consummation because it brings about the unshakable liberation of mind and the Nibbāna-element without residue.
"Proclaimed by the One with Vision"—this is the construction [of the verse].
Thus, the Elder, praising the Noble Dhamma through various methods, revealed that he himself had attained that Dhamma by way of an indirect statement (*aññāpadesena*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Migajāla is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Jenta, the Son of the Family Priest (*Purohitaputtajentattheragāthāvaṇṇanā*).
The verses beginning with "Intoxicated by the pride of birth" (*jātimadena matto*) belong to the Venerable Elder Jenta. What is his origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit in various states of existence, was born in this current dispensation of a Buddha in Sāvatthī.
He was reborn as the son of the royal chaplain of the King of Kosala, and his name was Jenta.

When he reached maturity, intoxicated by the pride of birth and the pride of wealth, sovereignty, and physical beauty, he wandered about haughty with conceit, despising others and failing to show respect even to those worthy of honor.
One day, he saw the Teacher surrounded by a great assembly.
Having seen him teaching the Dhamma, he approached with the thought: "If the ascetic Gotama addresses me first, I will address him;

if not, I will not. Having approached and stood there, when the Blessed One did not address him first, he himself, out of pride, failed to speak and signaled his intention to depart. The Blessed One [perceived this]—
“O Brahmin, pride is not good; for one who has a need here, O Brahmin, he should cultivate that very purpose for which he has come.

With these words, he addressed him in verse. Thinking, “The ascetic Gotama knows my mind,” he was deeply inspired with faith. Bowing his head at the Blessed One’s feet and performing the highest act of prostration, he said:
“Toward whom should one not harbor pride? Toward whom should one be respectful?
Toward whom should one show honor? Who is it that is well-worshipped?”—thus he asked.
To him, the Blessed One said:
“Toward one’s mother and father, as well as toward one’s elder brother,
toward the teacher as the fourth, and toward recluses and brahmins—
one should not harbor pride toward them; one should be respectful toward them.”
They should be honored by you; it would be well for them to be properly worshipped.
“Toward the Arahants, who have become cooled, who have done what was to be done, and are free from taints—bowing down your pride, being humble, worship those who are unsurpassed.”

While answering the question, he taught the Dhamma. Through that teaching, [the king] became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). Having gone forth and applied himself to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*), he attained Arahantship and, declaring his own realization by way of praising his own path of practice, said:
“Intoxicated by the pride of birth, and by wealth and power;
By my stature, complexion, and form, I wandered about maddened with intoxication.
“I did not consider anyone to be my equal or superior;
struck by overweening pride, the fool was stiff and held his banner aloft.
Even toward my mother, my father, and others who were held in high esteem—”
I did not pay homage to anyone, stiff with pride and disrespectful.
Yet I saw the supreme Guide, the most excellent among charioteers,
blazing like the sun, honored by the community of monks.
“Having cast aside pride and intoxication, with a serene mind,
I paid homage with my head to the Supreme among all beings.
Excessive pride and self-deprecation have been abandoned and thoroughly uprooted.”
“Self-conceit is utterly severed; all forms of pride are destroyed.”—These verses he spoke.
Therein, “intoxicated with the pride of birth” means: “I was reborn in a distinguished brahmin family; there is no one like me on both sides... [and so forth].
The construction is: "Intoxicated by family pride (*kulamāna*), stiff with conceit (*mānathaddha*), I did not go out, thinking, 'There is another who is well-born.

And "by wealth and sovereignty" means: intoxicated by the intoxication arisen in dependence upon the perfection of wealth and the perfection of sovereignty—having prosperity and lordship as their causes—I did not go out;
such is the construction. "By configuration, color, and form" means: configuration is the excellence of height and circumference.

*Vaṇṇa* (complexion) is the excellence of the skin’s luster, such as being white or dark; *rūpa* (form) is the beauty of the limbs and members. Here too, the application should be understood according to the method already stated.
"Intoxicated with pride" means intoxicated by some form of pride other than those types already mentioned.
"No one equal to himself" means no one who is his equal or similar in birth and so forth, or even someone superior.
"I did not think of myself, nor did I think [of others as] equal to me, much less superior"—this is the intended meaning. "A fool ruined by overweening pride" means:
I am a fool; because of that state of foolishness, my wholesome conduct has been destroyed and struck down by overweening pride.

For that very reason, he is stiff and his banner is raised; being utterly rigid due to a lack of humility even toward elders, he has become stiff with an unbending nature, his banner of pride uplifted.

In order to make this very matter more evident, the passage beginning with “his mother” was spoken. Therein, “others” refers to his elder brother and so forth, as well as to recluses and brahmins. “Those esteemed as venerable” means those who are recognized as venerable and worthy of respect. “Disrespectful” means devoid of reverence.

Having seen the Leader as supreme—thus wandering about while stiff with pride—he [sees] the Leader because he leads those to be trained by means of the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal, and because of his state of being a leader through his self-enlightenment.
In the world including the devas, by virtue of qualities such as moral conduct...
Because he is the most excellent, he is the foremost. Because he tames those who are to be tamed among men with absolute perfection, he is the best and most supreme among charioteers.

Seeing the Teacher—the most excellent of all beings—shining like the sun with the radiance of his fathom-wide aura and other splendors, illuminating as he taught the Dhamma while being honored by the community of monks, [the king] was struck with awe by the majesty of the Buddha.

The construction is as follows: having cast off and abandoned the intoxication of wealth and so forth—which manifests as the thought, "I alone am the best, others are inferior"—they paid homage with their heads with a mind that was perfectly serene.

But how is it that one who was thus stiff with pride abandoned his pride merely by seeing the Teacher? This should not be viewed in that way; for he did not abandon his pride merely by seeing the Teacher.
However, by means of the teaching beginning with “Pride is not good, brahmin,” he abandoned pride. With reference to this, it is said:
“Having cast aside pride and intoxication, with a serene mind, he paid homage with his head.
In the phrase “with a serene mind,” the instrumental case should be understood as expressing a characteristic state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇe).

“Conceit” (*māna*) that proceeds as “I alone am the best” is “overweening conceit” (*atimāna*). They say that the conceit of one who regards others as inferior, thinking “But these are low,” is “inferiority-conceit” (*omāna*).
Furthermore, “conceit of superiority” (*seyyamāna*) is the conceit that proceeds in one who, surpassing another, regards oneself as superior, thinking “I am better.
“Conceit of inferiority” (*hīnamāna*) is that which proceeds as “I am inferior”; this is “inferiority-conceit” (*omāna*). These have been abandoned and thoroughly uprooted.
Having been abandoned by the lower paths, they are thoroughly eradicated by the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
"The conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)" is that which occurs by way of grasping the aggregates as "I" through the thought "this I am.

"All" means not only the overweening conceit (*atimāna*), the inferiority conceit (*omāna*), and the conceit "I am," but rather all nine types beginning with the conceit of one who is superior regarding those who are superior, along with their many internal subdivisions.
The various kinds of conceit and the constituent parts of conceit have been destroyed; they have been eradicated by the supreme path.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Jenta, son of the family priest, is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sumanas.
The verses beginning with "When he was newly ordained" are those of the Venerable Thera Sumanas. What is their origin?

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi into a family of garland-makers.
Having reached maturity, one day, upon seeing the Blessed One Sikhi, his mind became filled with serene faith, and with *sumana* flowers...

He performed an act of worship. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in this present age of a Buddha in the house of a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*). That lay follower was the attendant of the Venerable Anuruddha Thera.
Previously, every child born to him had died; therefore, he thought: "If now I [should have] one son..."
He conceived the thought: "I shall receive it; I will go forth into homelessness in the presence of the venerable Elder Anuruddha.
When ten months had passed, he was born healthy, and as he grew up in due course, he reached the age of seven.
His father then caused him to go forth in the presence of the Elder. Having gone forth, because his wisdom was fully matured, he [applied himself] to insight meditation.
While performing his duties, he soon became possessed of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Attending upon the Elder, he took a water-jar with the thought, "I shall fetch drinking water," and by means of psychic power (*ṛddhi*), he went to Lake Anotatta. Now, a certain Naga king holding wrong views was covering Lake Anotatta;
having encircled it seven times with his coils and raised a great hood above, he [obstructed] Sumanas.
He did not grant permission for him to take water. Sumana, assuming the form of a garuḍa, overcame that nāga king, took the water, and departed through the air toward the Elder’s dwelling place.
Seeing him traveling in that manner while seated in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher addressed the Dhamma-Senāpati, saying, “Sāriputta, look at this,” and so forth.
He spoke of his virtues with four verses. Then the Elder Sumanatthera said:
“When he had newly gone forth, being only seven years of age, Having surpassed by means of psychic power the Lord of Serpents, who possessed great iddhi.”
“‘I am bringing water for my preceptor from the great lake Anotatta.
Having seen me there, the Teacher said this to me:
‘Sāriputta, look at this young man coming here;’”
Taking a water-pot, well-composed within,
with a pleasing conduct and beautiful deportment,
the novice Anuruddha was confident in his supernormal power.
“A thoroughbred by a thoroughbred, well-trained by one who is good;
disciplined by Anuruddha, he has been trained by one who has accomplished his task.
Having attained supreme peace and realized the unshakable state,”
“The novice Sumana desires that they may not know me”;
thus he spoke six verses by way of declaring his higher knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇa*).
Therein, the first two verses were spoken by the Elder Sumana himself, while the other four were spoken by the Teacher in praise of him.
[These verses] were spoken [by various beings]. The Elder Sumanas, having brought them all together, subsequently spoke them by way of his own declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
In that context, "the lord of serpents" refers to the king of the *nāgas*. "There" means in that situation:

when the newly ordained novice, being seven years of age, having overcome the powerful king of the *nāgas* through the strength of his psychic power (*iddhi*), [fetched] drinking water for his preceptor from Lake Anotatta.
“I bring it,” means “at that time.

Showing that my Teacher said this concerning me, he spoke the words beginning with, “Sāriputta, look at this one. “Well-composed within” means well-composed by means of the concentration of the highest fruit, which has become internal with respect to its objects.
“By means of a pleasing conduct” means by means of a mode of behavior that brings confidence to those who see; this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the agent.
"Of beautiful postures" means possessing perfected postures. "With pleasing conduct" is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*).
The state of being a recluse (*samaṇa*) is *sāmañña*; the meaning is "recluseship.

One who strives (*īrati*) for that purpose and proceeds toward it is a *sāmaṇera*, a novice. "Confident in supernormal power" means skilled and proficient even in supernormal powers (*iddhi*). "By a thoroughbred" [means...]
"By a noble person": by Anuruddha, who has accomplished his task and is virtuous because he achieves both his own welfare and the welfare of others;

or, he is well-trained and tamed like a thoroughbred horse. "Disciplined by the supreme knowledge" means he has been trained and instructed by being brought to the state of one beyond training (*asekkha*).

Thus, having attained supreme peace—Nirvana—by reaching the highest path, having realized it, and having made it manifest to himself, the novice Sumana, because his state of fewness of wishes had reached its ultimate excellence, desired and longed for the unshakable fruit of Arhatship with the thought:
"May no one know me; may no one recognize me as 'this one whose taints are destroyed' or 'one possessed of the six direct knowledges.'"
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sumanatthera is finished.
11. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nhātakamuni “Afflicted by a wind-disease,” etc., are the verses of the venerable Nhātakamuni. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various successive existences, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance into a brahmin family in Rājagaha.
Upon reaching maturity, he attained proficiency in the fields of knowledge and other sciences; because he possessed the characteristics of one who has bathed [in wisdom], he became known as Nhātaka.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life, he dwelt in a forest retreat within a three-league radius of Rājagaha.

He lived subsisting on wild rice while performing fire-worship. The Teacher, seeing that within his heart there was burning like a lamp in a vessel—the necessary condition for attaining Arahatship—went to his hermitage.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, he was joyful and satisfied, and offered food according to his own means of sustenance. The Blessed One partook of it. Thus for three days...
On the fourth day, after he had given [the food], the Blessed One said, "Venerable sir, you are extremely delicate; how can you sustain yourself with this kind of food?
The Teacher taught him the Dhamma, elucidating the virtue of noble contentment.
Having heard it, the ascetic became a stream-enterer, went forth, and attained arahantship. The Blessed One, having established him in arahantship, departed. And he...
While dwelling right there, at a later time, he was afflicted by a wind-disease. The Teacher went there and, inquiring about his dwelling through the manner of friendly greetings, asked:
"Afflicted by a wind-disease, you dwell in the forest grove."
“In a desolate, abandoned place, how will you fare, O bhikkhu?”—thus he spoke this verse. Then the elder said:
“Having pervaded my entire body with abundant rapture and bliss, Enduring even what is coarse, I shall dwell in the forest.”
“Cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, the faculties, and the powers;
endowed with the subtlety of jhāna, I shall dwell free from taints.
My mind, liberated from defilements, pure and untroubled.”
Constantly reflecting thus, I shall dwell free from taints:
"Whatever taints there were within and without me,
they have all been cut off without remainder, and shall not arise again."
“The five aggregates have been fully understood; they remain with their roots cut off.
The destruction of suffering has been attained; there is now no further becoming.
With these remaining verses, he announced his dwelling place to the Teacher.
In this context, "endowed with the subtlety of jhāna" means being possessed of the subtle state of jhāna. The "subtlety of jhāna" refers to the formless jhānas;
therefore, what is meant is that he is one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*). By this, he demonstrates his liberation in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutti*).
Others, however, say: "'Subtle' refers here to the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññāsikkhā*) intended within the supreme path and its fruit."
"Then, by the mention of *jhāna*, he makes manifest his own liberation in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutti*).

"Completely freed from defilements" means liberated from all defilements through the liberation of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhivimutti*); for that very reason it is a "pure mind," and it is "unclouded" due to the state of having unclouded intentions.
By all three terms, he speaks specifically of the mind of the fruit of Arahantship. The rest is according to the method already explained below.
And this indeed was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nhātakamuni is finished.
12. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Brahmadatta.
"Of one free from anger," and so forth, are the verses of the Venerable Elder Brahmadatta. What is their origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various states of existence, was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha as the son of the King of Kosala in Sāvatthī;
his name was Brahmadatta. Upon reaching maturity, at the Great Festival of Jetavana...
Having seen the majesty of the Buddha, he gained faith and went forth into homelessness.

While practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiññā*) together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). One day, as he was walking for alms in the city, a certain brahmin reviled him.
Even upon hearing this, the Elder remained silent and continued his alms-round; the brahmin again—
They continued to revile him. Even as they were thus reviling him, people said, "This elder says nothing at all.
Hearing this, the elder, teaching the Dhamma to those people, said:
"How can there be anger for one who is free from anger, who is self-controlled and lives in equanimity?"
For one who is liberated through perfect knowledge, who is tranquil and steadfast—
worse for him is he who, being provoked, returns the provocation.
He who does not return the provocation of one who is provoked wins a battle that is difficult to win.
“He acts for the benefit of both, himself and the other, who,
knowing the other is provoked, remains composed with mindfulness.
He is the healer of both, himself and the other.”
"Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma think, 'He is a fool.
If anger should arise in you, reflect on the simile of the saw;
if craving for flavors should arise, remember the simile of the son's flesh."
“If your mind runs toward sensual pleasures and states of existence,
restrain it quickly with mindfulness, as one would a difficult-to-catch wild beast that feeds on grain.
Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, "of one who is without anger" means of one who is free from anger, whose anger has been completely eradicated by the Path.
"Whence could anger arise? means: from what cause indeed could anger arise? The meaning is that there is no cause for its arising.

"Of the tamed" means of one who is tamed by the supreme taming, the taming of the highest Path. "Living in harmony" means having entirely abandoned physical impropriety and so forth, [one who lives] in physical propriety and so forth.
For one who lives in accordance with that [practice], proceeding rightly with the sevenfold clear comprehension;
for one liberated through perfect knowledge—that is, liberated from all taints after having correctly known the phenomena to be directly known and so forth;

and for that very reason, for one who is tranquil through the subsiding of the distress and fever of all defilements, having attained the characteristic of equanimity toward the desirable and so forth.
"How can there be anger in one who is such, whose taints are destroyed?"— by means of this indirect statement (*aññāpadesa*), the Elder,

having explained his own absence of anger and its causes, now spoke the verse beginning with "Tassevā" while preaching the Dhamma by showing the danger in anger and the benefit in the absence of anger.
Therein, "he who returns anger for anger" refers to that person who, toward another person who is angry or provoked against him...

He retaliates; by that retaliation—by means of reviling, striking back, and so forth—he becomes worse off, being more unfortunate and more unwholesome both in this world through the censure of the wise and others, and in the next world through the suffering of hell and the like.
However, it cannot even be said that evil accrues to one who is not angry simply because another is angry. Some, however, [say]: "He who [is angry at] one who is not angry..."
They say the meaning is: "one becomes angry with one who is already hostile. But as for "not being angry with one who is angry":

when one knows that a person is angry and overcome by anger, and yet does not retaliate but instead forgives them, such a person is said to conquer the battle against the defilements, which is difficult to win.
Not only does he achieve victory in this battle against the defilements, but he also practices for the welfare of both himself and others.

Showing this, he said: “The welfare of both... [etc. ...is pacified. One who, knowing another person to be agitated, angry, and "overcome by wrath," becomes pacified toward them—whether through loving-kindness (*mettā*) or equanimity (*upekkhā*)—being mindful and clearly comprehending (*sato sampajāno*), forgives and does not resist;
such a person brings about the happiness of both himself and the other, that is, of both, in both worlds.
He practices for the welfare and benefit [of others].
Regarding the one who treats both— meaning the person who treats both himself and another by curing the disease of anger in both—
the fools are those people who are unskilled in the Dhamma, that is, in the Dhamma of noble conduct.
“They think, ‘This man is ignorant because he does nothing at all when one reviles him or strikes him’;
the intention [of the verse] is that this is their improper reflection. Some also read “tikicchana,” meaning “having the nature of healing.
Having heard the Dhamma being spoken thus by the Elder, the reviling brahmin became agitated and his mind was filled with serene faith.
Having asked the elder for forgiveness, he went forth into homelessness in that very elder’s presence.
As the elder was giving him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he thought, "Loving-kindness (*mettā*) is suitable for this man," and so he gave him the meditation subject of loving-kindness.

Then, showing the method of reflection and so forth regarding the obsession of anger and other such states, he said, "If it should arise in you," and so on. In that context, "if it should arise in you" means if it should arise while you are devoted to that meditation subject.
If anger should arise due to long-standing acquaintance with a certain person, then for its subsiding, reflect upon this instruction on the simile of the saw spoken by the Teacher:

"Bhikkhus, even if bandits with saws having teeth on both sides were to hack away at your limbs and members one by one, whoever should allow his mind to become corrupted thereby would not be following my teaching.
And if craving for flavors should arise—if a longing for flavors of various kinds, such as sweet and so forth, should arise in you—for its subsiding—

“Just as the *jāyampatika* birds eat their own offspring’s flesh solely for the purpose of crossing the wilderness, and not out of craving for flavor, so too does a clansman who has gone forth partake of almsfood...
[and so on] ...for the sake of dwelling in comfort.”—Remember, recall this instruction likened to the eating of one’s own son’s flesh.
“If your mind runs away”: your mind, due to improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*), runs toward sensual pleasures, the five strands of sense-pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

If it runs, remembers, or speeds along by way of desire and lust, or by way of longing for existence among the realms of existence such as the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, restrain it quickly with mindfulness.
Just as a man would tie up a difficult-to-control, wicked ox that eats grain— a "grain-eater"— by a rope to a post, so too, do not allow it to run in that manner.
“Bind it with the rope of mindfulness to the firm post of right concentration;
restrain it quickly and swiftly so that, through the departure of the defilements, it becomes free from turbulence; thus tame it. Some, however, say:
“While still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), the Elder endured the abuse, proclaiming the noble qualities (*ariyaguṇa*) to those people and teaching the Dhamma...”

They say that after speaking thus, he spoke these very same verses while instructing himself with two stanzas; then, having increased his insight and attained arahantship, he uttered these verses as his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Brahmadatta is finished.
13. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sirimaṇḍa The verses beginning with “Channam ativassati” belong to the venerable elder Sirimaṇḍa. What is his origin?

This [elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit in various states of existence, was born during the arising of this [present] Buddha on Mount Saṃsumāragiri.
Having been reborn in a brahmin family and received the name Sirimaṇḍa, he reached maturity and approached the Teacher while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Bhesakaḷā Grove.
Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and upon receiving full ordination, practiced the duties of a recluse.
On a certain Uposatha day, while sitting at the place for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, during the recitation of the Nidāna...
At the conclusion [of the discourse], reflecting on the meaning of the passage, “For one who has revealed it, there is ease,” he considered:
“If one conceals an offense committed by failing to reveal it, one incurs further offenses; therefore, for such a person there is no ease.
But for one who reveals it and makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, there is ease. Having brought this matter to mind, he exclaimed: “Oh, Teacher!”...
Having gained confidence that "the Teaching is perfectly pure," he suppressed the rapture thus arisen, increased his insight, and attained Arahantship.
Reflecting upon his own practice with a serene mind, he gave this exhortation to the bhikkhus:
"The covered leaks; the uncovered does not leak."
Therefore, uncover what is covered; thus the rain will not drench you.
"The world is struck down by death, surrounded by old age, pierced by the dart of craving, and constantly smoldering with desire."
“The world is struck down by death and hemmed in by old age;
it is constantly slaughtered, defenseless, like a culprit with a raised staff.
Death, disease, and old age—these three come like a mass of blazing fire.”
There is no strength to go against it, and no speed to flee from it.
One should make that day fruitful, whether by little or by much;
for whatever night one passes, by that much is one's life diminished.
“Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the final night approaches;
it is not the time for you to be negligent.
Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, "covered" (*channa*) means concealed, not disclosed as it truly is, unrevealed, and undisclosed misconduct.
"It rains excessively" (*ativassati*) means that both the rain of offenses and the rain of defilements fall excessively.

For the concealment of an offense through such states as shamelessness is of one kind, whereas through that very concealment, one subsequently commits another offense of the same nature or even one more grave than the former.
"Should enter upon" (*āpajjeyya*) refers to the act of covering as the cause for rain. "Open" (*vivaṭaṃ*) means revealed or uncovered.
"It does not rain excessively" (*nātivassati*): here, *ati-* is merely a prefix; the meaning is "it does not rain.

And "not raining" here should be understood by way of the opposite of what was previously stated, because the continuum of the mind has been purified. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers back to the very meaning already stated, treating it as the reason.

The meaning is: because evil conduct that is concealed is rained upon excessively—by way of offenses, years, and so forth—and because that which is uncovered is not so rained upon. "Uncover what is concealed" means:
even when the intention to conceal arises through the state of being a worldling (*puthujjana*), do not follow it, but uncover it, reveal it, and make amends according to the Dhamma.
"In this way" refers to practicing according to the Dhamma by means of such uncovering.
That concealed misconduct does not rain heavily upon him; neither the rain of offenses nor the rain of defilements falls.
The meaning is that it establishes such a person in the state of purity.
Now, as for the reason why "one must purify oneself resolutely and swiftly, and practice with heedfulness":
Showing the grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he said, "The world is struck down by death," and so forth.

In this context, "the world is struck down by death" means that this entire world of beings is assailed by death—by *maraṇa*, which brings about the fall from all conditioned existence (*vaṭṭa*)—just as a thief is by an executioner;
it does not escape from its grasp. "Encompassed by old age" means that this world, following its arising...
"Enveloped and overwhelmed by old age, which has the nature of bringing about death"—the meaning is that he is liberated from the aggregate of old age.

"Pierced by the dart of craving" means he is pierced and plunged into the interior of the heart by the dart known as craving, which is characterized by clinging, like a poisoned arrow-head sunk within the body. For craving, because it produces affliction, is [like] an internal [dart].
Because it pierces and because it is difficult to extract, it is called a "dart" (salla).
"Smoldering with desire" means being tormented by desire, which has the characteristic of longing for an object.

For a person who desires that object—whether they obtain the desired object or not—becomes scorched and reaches a state of feverish burning by that very desire, which has the characteristic of consuming. Always...
"At all times"; and this phrase is to be joined with every subsequent clause.
"Encircled by old age" means that he is not only struck down by death, but is also encircled by old age.
He is hemmed in by old age, enclosed within the rampart of old age; the meaning is that he does not transcend it. He is slain.
"Always without protection": being without protection and without refuge, one is constantly struck down and oppressed by aging and death.

How so? Like a criminal with a raised staff: just as a thief who has committed an offense and reached the point of execution is without protection and is struck down by the king's command, so too is this world [struck] by aging and death; thus it is shown.

"Great masses of fire coming": when the great forest is burning, death, sickness, and old age—these three, like great masses of fire in their sense of being consuming fires—come overwhelming this world of beings.
Yet, there is no strength or effort capable of going out to meet them, to overcome, or to master them.
For this world, there is no speed to flee when things are rushing upon it and overwhelming it.
Even where they do not yet overcome it, this world lacks the speed of the legs to flee from that point by turning its back.

Thus, being personally incapable of resistance against the three kinds of powerful enemies who stand ever-present—enemies whom one cannot counteract through means such as deception—what is to be done?
How so? One should make the day fruitful, whether by a small amount or by a great amount;

that is, one should make the day not in vain and not barren through the attention of insight (vipassanā-manasikāra), whether practiced for even as little as the time it takes to milk a cow, or practiced for a great amount throughout the entire day and night.
For, as each night passes away, one's life becomes diminished accordingly.
Whatever night this being departs from, destroys, or exhausts, his life becomes diminished by that very amount.
By this, he shows that the "destruction of the night" is indeed the destruction of the life of that being, from which there is no turning back. Therefore he said:
"The youth who dwells for the first time within the womb for a single night;..."
“He goes as if already risen; once gone, he does not turn back.
It is said, beginning with the words “of one who walks,” to show that the exhaustion of life should be observed not only by way of the night, but also by way of the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
“Of one who walks” means of one who is going. “Of one who stands” means of one who maintains the posture of standing. “Of one who is sitting or lying down.”
The meaning is: "it blows while one is sitting, lying down, sitting, or reclining. Some also read it as *āsīdana*;
in that case, the accusative case should be understood in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*). "He approaches the final night" means that the night, together with the final consciousness, arrives;
and here, the mention of "night" is merely for the sake of the teaching's introduction. By whichever posture among walking and so forth—
Since it is precisely at the time of one's final passing that these [conditions] come together, they proceed by exhausting one's life-span moment by moment through the postures;
therefore, there is no time for you to be negligent, nor is this the time for you to fall into heedlessness, because it is unknown [when one will die]:
"Death does not occur at such-and-such a time. For it is said:
“The life of mortals here is signless and unknown,
It is frail, limited, and joined with suffering.
Therefore, having thus exhorted oneself, the intention is that one should apply oneself with heedfulness to the three trainings.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sirimaṇḍa is finished.
14. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sabbakāmi.
The verses beginning with "Dvipādako" (the two-footed one) belong to the Venerable Elder Sabbakāmi. What is his origin? It is said that he [was a disciple] of Padumuttara...
Having seen an elder who, having cleared away a corruption that had arisen in the Blessed One’s dispensation, restored it to its original state, he made this aspiration:
"May I too, in the future, be capable of clearing away a corruption in the dispensation of a Buddha and restoring it to its original state.
Having performed meritorious deeds corresponding to that aspiration, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During this appearance of a Buddha, while the Blessed One had not yet attained final Nibbāna, he was reborn in a khattiya family in Vesālī and received the name Sabbakāma.
Upon reaching maturity, he was made to take a wife by his relatives;

however, out of a disposition toward renunciation, he felt disgust for the household life, went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Dharma-treasurer (Ānanda), and practiced the duties of a recluse.
Having arrived at Vesālī together with his preceptor, he went to the house of his relatives.
There, his former wife—suffering from the pain of separation, emaciated, disfigured, unadorned, and dressed in soiled garments—paid him homage and stood to one side weeping.
Upon seeing her, as the Elder established a mind imbued with loving-kindness preceded by compassion toward that object experienced in the past, [the Elder’s heart was moved].
Due to improper attention, defilement arose in him suddenly.
Struck by that whip, he became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency like a noble steed;
he went immediately to the charnel ground, grasped the sign of the foul, made the jhāna attained therein his foundation, and by developing insight, attained Arahantship.

She attained [the fruit]. Then her father-in-law, taking his daughter who was fully adorned and prepared for marriage, went to the monastery with a great retinue, desiring to cause her to leave the religious life.
The Elder, knowing her intention, proclaimed his own state of detachment from sensual desires and his complete lack of defilement in all things—
“This two-legged impurity is foul-smelling and decaying;
it is filled with various corpses and oozes from every side.
Like a deer hidden by a snare, or a lotus by a fishhook,”
Just as one might afflict a monkey with an ointment, so do they afflict the worldling:
"Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and delightful tangibles—
these five strands of sensual pleasure are seen within the form of a woman."
“Those worldlings of lustful mind who frequent these [pleasures] increase the terrible cremation ground and accumulate renewed existence.
But he who avoids them, as one would avoid the head of a snake with his foot— ”
Mindful, one overcomes the attachment to *soma* in the world.
“Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and having seen renunciation as security,
I have emerged from all sensual desires and attained the destruction of the taints.”—
He spoke these verses.
Regarding the phrase "two-footed": although even the bodies of those without feet and so forth are indeed impure, this was stated either by way of specific context or as a superior limit.
Or rather, because other bodies that have become impure are prepared for humans with salt, sour liquids, and so forth...
Even when brought forward for food, they are not the human body; therefore, showing its nature to be of an impure essence, he said "two-legged.
The word "this" refers to the female form present at that time. "Impure" means simply impure;
the meaning is that there is nothing pure here at all. "The foul-smelling thing is concealed" means that, being foul-smelling, it is mixed with the fragrance of flowers and so forth.
It is being discarded. "Filled with various kinds of filth" means it is packed with many types of corpses, such as hair and so forth.
"Dripping here and there"—even for those striving to conceal its loathesomeness with flower perfumes and the like, that effort is rendered fruitless;
for it continues to flow from the nine orifices, including saliva and snot, and from the pores of the skin, sweat and grime. Thus it is indeed "dripping."
The connection is: "it is being lost.

Thus, showing that although this body is indeed loathsome, it deceives blind worldlings with its own form and so forth—just as a trap and the like deceive deer and other animals—he said "a deer," and so on.
In that context, "a deer hidden by a trap" refers to a snare, a net, and so forth.
"Hidden by a snare" means having concealed [the prey], like a hunter [concealing] a deer. For the word *iva*, which will be explained later, should be brought over and applied here as well.
"Like a fish with a hook" means a fisherman [catching] a fish (*ambuja*) with a baited hook, just as [one catches] a fish.
"Like a monkey with glue" means a monkey [caught] by monkey-glue applied to trees, stones, and so forth.
Like a deer-hunter deceiving and afflicting the blind worldling (*andhaputhujjana*), they "afflict" him.

But what is it that afflicts? He says: "Forms, sounds," and so forth. For the five divisions of sensual desire (*kāma*), such as forms and the rest—specifically those based on objects that are discordant (*visabhāga*)—are surrounded by improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) which serves as a supporting condition for the perversions (*vipallāsa*).
For the minds of blind worldlings, these things cause affliction because they bring about harm by serving as the basis for the defilements.
Therefore it was said: “Forms, sounds... [and so on]... are seen in the form of women.
And here, the mention of “women” should be understood as being made by way of the specific context. For this very reason he said: “Those who attend upon them,” and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: Those worldlings who, with minds colored by passion and overcome by lust, pursue these women based on the perception of them as objects of enjoyment—they increase the terrible cremation ground.
They increase that which is "terrible" (ghora) by way of birth and so forth, and by way of the hells and so forth;

it is fearsome, and because it is to be delighted in by the blind fools, it is the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) designated as a "cremation ground," characterized by repeated rebirth, death, and so on.
They cause [them] to increase. Therefore he said: "They accumulate renewed existence.

As for the person who—by either suppressing or utterly eradicating desire and lust for these women—avoids them as one would avoid the head of a snake with one's own foot, he, because he stands having relinquished the entire world...
Being mindful, he transcends craving, which is known as attachment in the world.

"Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures" means having seen the danger and fault in objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-based sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*) in their many forms and aspects, according to such passages as: "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton; they bring much suffering and much despair. "Having seen renunciation as safety" means...

Having seen renunciation (*nekkhamma*)—which is the state of having departed from sensual pleasures (*kāma*) and states of existence (*bhava*), namely the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and Nibbāna—as secure and free from calamity;
and having become detached and disjoined from all sensual pleasures as well as from the phenomena of the three planes (*tebhūmakadhamma*);

for all phenomena of the three planes are "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) in the sense of being desirable, and the Elder is disjoined from them. Therefore he said: "The destruction of the taints (*āsava*) has been attained by me."
Thus, having preached the Dhamma with the first five verses, the Elder declared his attainment of *aññā* (full knowledge) with the sixth verse.
Upon hearing this, the father-in-law thought, "He is untainted in every respect; it is impossible to lead him astray into sensual pleasures," and departed by the same way he had come.
As for the Elder, one hundred years after the Blessed One had attained *parinibbāna*, he was a centenarian who had received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and had wandered the earth.
Having become an elder, he purified the corruption that had arisen in the Teaching through the Vajjiputtas of Vesālī;
then, having convened the Second Council of the Dhamma, he commanded the Great Brahmā Tissa, saying,
"Purify the corruption that will arise in the future time of King Dhammāsoka," and subsequently passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sabbakāmi is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter of Sixes is finished.
7. The Chapter of Sevens.
1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sundarasamudda The verses beginning with "Adorned" (*alaṅkata*) in the *Sattaka-nipāta* belong to the venerable Elder Sundarasamudda. What is his origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit in various states of existence, in this [present life]...
During the time of a Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn as the son of a certain very wealthy merchant in Rājagaha.
His name was Samudda, but because of his physical beauty, he was known as Sundarasamudda.

While still in his early youth, having witnessed the majesty of the Buddha upon the Blessed One’s entry into Rājagaha, he gained faith; and due to his inclination toward renunciation, [he went forth].
Having gone forth and received full ordination, he adopted the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and traveled from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī.
There, having learned the method of insight meditation (vipassanācāra) from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), he dwelt devotedly applying himself to his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
On a festival day in Rājagaha, his mother saw other sons of merchants, adorned and dressed in their finery, sporting in the festivities together with their wives.
Having seen her, she wept as she remembered her son. Seeing this, a certain courtesan asked the reason for her weeping.
She explained the matter to her. Upon hearing this, the courtesan said, "I will bring him; just see my womanhood!
and added, "If it is so, I shall make him my husband and become the mistress of this family."
Thinking, "I shall do so," she gave her much wealth and was sent away with a large retinue.
Having gone to Sāvatthī, she stayed in a certain house in the area where the Elder went for alms; day after day, she had others respectfully provide alms-food for the Elder.
And having adorned herself and put on golden sandals, she [presented] herself...

She showed herself. Then one day, seeing the Elder as he was passing by the door of her house, she took off her golden sandals, raised her hands in reverential salutation, and walking before him, invited the Elder with various kinds of sensual enticements.
Hearing this, the Elder thought: "The mind of an ordinary person is indeed fickle; what if I were to exert myself right now?"
Remaining right there, he intensified his meditation and became possessed of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). With reference to him, it was said:
“Adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands, and embellished, with feet dyed with red lac, the courtesan mounted her sandals.”
“Having removed her sandals and standing before me with palms joined, she spoke to me gently and softly, as one who had previously been my wife:
‘You are young and have gone forth; stay within my teaching.’”
“Enjoy human pleasures; I shall give you wealth.
I promise you this in truth, or I will carry fire for you.
“When we have grown old, both of us leaning on our staffs...”
"Both of us shall go forth; in both cases, the harvest is won.
Having seen that courtesan with her hands joined in reverence—adorned and well-dressed, yet like the outstretched snare of Death—he spoke thus.
“Then right attention arose in me through proper method;
the danger became manifest, and disenchantment took firm root.
Thereupon my mind was liberated—behold the excellence of the Dhamma!”
“The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

In this context, *māladhārī* means wearing a garland (*mālādhārinī*), one whose body is adorned with flower wreaths. *Vibhūsita* means her limbs are decorated with flowers as well as perfumes, ointments, and so forth, in order to fill out any deficiencies.
By the word *alaṅkata*, [it refers to] being adorned with hand-ornaments, neck-ornaments, and the like.
Adornment with ornaments is what is intended. "With feet dyed with red lac" (*alattakakatapādā*):
her pair of feet was colored with lac juice having the hue of a fully ripened *jaya-sumana* flower. This is a compound word;

although it should have been stated as "alattakakatapādā," it is spoken with a long vowel for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. However, in the absence of the compound, it should be understood that the word "tassā" (of her) is to be supplied.
"A courtesan mounted on sandals" refers to a certain woman who lives by her beauty; having put on golden sandals according to the aforementioned attire, she "stood"—this is the ellipsis of the verb.
"Having descended from the sandals" means having stepped down from the sandals, that is, having taken off the golden sandals. "With palms joined" (paṃjalīkatā).
That courtesan, with her hands joined in *añjali*, spoke to me of her own accord—without words passed through others.
"Gently" means smoothly; "softly" means sweetly. Although the word "with speech" was not explicitly stated, it is understood from the fact that she "spoke.
"You are young, having gone forth"—you went forth while still young; you went forth while being merely a youth, did you not?
This shows that one should go forth when the seventh decade has arrived. "Stay in my teaching" means stay according to my word.

But what is that? He says: "Enjoy human pleasures. For one who wishes to enjoy sensual pleasures, excellence of form, excellence of youth, excellence of retinue, and excellence of wealth are required.
Regarding these, [one might ask]: "Whence shall I have excellence of wealth?"
"She would say" means she says, "I will give you wealth. Thinking, "How is this word to be believed?
she says, in order to make him believe it, "I promise you the truth; we shall even carry fire for you.
"Enjoy human pleasures; I will give you wealth"—this which has been promised by me is absolutely certain.
"I swear by truth itself; if you do not believe me, I shall bring fire for you, and having brought the fire, I will make an oath by means of that fire"—this is the meaning.
"A victory in both cases" (*ubhayattha kaṭaggaho*) means that when we two have grown old and go forth into homelessness, there will be a winning grasp in both instances.
That we enjoy wealth until the time we must lean on staffs—[that is our victory].
The intention is this: "In this world as well, we shall not be overcome by wealth; we will go forth later. In the next world too, we shall not be overcome by wealth.

"Therefore" means for that reason—on account of the words spoken by that courtesan, who was inviting him with sensual pleasures, beginning with "You are young," and so on, and "When we have become old," and so on. For those words were like a goad.
Having done so, the Elder, practicing the duty of a recluse, fulfilled his own goal. The remainder is exactly as described below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sundarasamudda is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya.
"O Ambaṭaka Grove," and so forth, are the verses of the Venerable Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya. What is their origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great wealth.
When he reached maturity, while sitting listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, at that moment the Teacher [proclaimed] one bhikkhu among those with sweet voices...
Seeing him being placed in the foremost position, he himself aspired to that same rank; having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he made this aspiration:
"O, may I too in the future become the foremost among those with melodious voices in the dispensation of a single Buddha, just like this bhikkhu. And the Blessed One [granted] his lack of obstacles.
Having seen him and made his declaration, he departed.
Having performed meritorious deeds there for as long as he lived, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he became a *cittapattaka* cuckoo in the time of the Blessed One Phussa.
While going from the royal park, carrying a sweet mango fruit in his beak, he [encountered] the Teacher.
Seeing this, with a mind full of faith, he resolved, "I shall give.
The Teacher, knowing his thought, took the bowl and sat down. The cuckoo placed a mango fruit into the bowl of the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher consumed it.
With a mind full of faith, that cuckoo spent seven days in that very joy and happiness. And by that meritorious deed—
He possessed a sweet voice. During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, when the construction of a cetiya was begun, they asked, "What size shall we make it?
"Seven yojanas. "That is far too large. "Six yojanas. "That also is far too large.
When they proposed five yojanas, four yojanas, three yojanas, and two yojanas, this man, being the chief architect at that time, said, "Come now," and—
“Friends, it is right to prepare for his future care,” he said;

then, while encircling [the site] with a rope, he stood at a distance of one *gāvuta* and declared, “Let each opening be one *gāvuta*, and the Cetiya shall be one *yojana* in circumference and one *yojana* in height.
They remained by his word. Thus, they measured the Buddha who is immeasurable.
Furthermore, in whatever place he was reborn as a result of that karma, he was shorter in stature than others.
During the time of our Teacher, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a family of great wealth; his name was Bhaddiya.
However, because of his extreme shortness, he was known as Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he...
Having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness; becoming learned and a preacher of the Dhamma, he taught the Dhamma to others with a sweet voice.

Then, on a festival day, a certain courtesan traveling in a chariot with a brahmin saw the Elder and laughed, baring her teeth. The Elder took the sign of her teeth as his object of meditation (*nimitta*).
Having grasped [the object] and attained jhāna, he took that as his foundation, established insight (vipassanā), and became a non-returner (anāgāmī).
Dwelling frequently in mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), one day, while being exhorted by the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, he was established in arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the eye-possessor regarding all phenomena,
arose as a Leader one hundred thousand eons ago from here.
At that time, I was the son of a wealthy merchant in Haṃsavatī.”
While wandering on my journey through the countryside, I went to the monastery.
At that time, the Leader, the Lamp of the World,
was teaching the Dhamma and praised his disciple who possesses the most excellent, melodious voice.
“Having heard that, being joyful, and having performed service for the Great Sage,
I worshipped the Teacher’s feet and aspired for that state.
Then the Buddha, the Guide, gave a prophecy in the midst of the Saṅgha.”
"In a future time, you shall obtain that heart's desire.
One hundred thousand aeons hence, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a Teacher in the world."
“He will be a true heir to the Dhamma, a son born of the Dhamma itself;
known by the name Bhaddiya, he will be a disciple of the Teacher.
By that well-performed deed and by his intentions and aspirations,”
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Ninety-two aeons ago, the Leader Phussa appeared;
the Conqueror was difficult to approach, difficult to overcome, and supreme over the entire world.
“Endowed with conduct, tall, upright, and majestic;
seeking the welfare of all beings, he liberated many from bondage.
In his pleasure grove, I was a *phussa* cuckoo.”
I was dwelling in an ambarama tree near the Fragrant Chamber. Then,
seeing the Supreme Victor, the most worthy of offerings, going for alms,
I gladdened my heart and cooed sweetly.
“Then, having gone to the royal garden, I took a cluster of mangoes that were well-ripened and had golden skins, and offered them to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, knowing my mind, the Victor, the Great Compassionate One, [accepted them].”
The Leader took the bowl from the hand of his attendant.
“With a joyful heart, O Great Sage, I gave you a cluster of mangoes;
having placed them in your bowl, I joined my palms and spoke with sweet words.”
“With a voice that was essential, delightful, and melodious to hear,
I went to my nest and lay down while raining for the sake of worshipping the Buddha.
At that time, my heart was filled with joy, and my mind was inclined toward love for the Buddha.”
A hawk approached and, with a wicked mind, killed me.
Having passed away from there, I experienced great happiness in the Tusita heaven;
by the force of that karma, I have now come to human birth.
“In this auspicious aeon, a man of great renown, a kinsman of Brahmā,
named Kassapa by clan, arose as the best among those who speak.
Having illuminated the teaching and overcome the false teachers,”
Having disciplined those who were to be trained, he, together with his disciples, has attained Nibbāna.
When that Foremost One in the World had attained Nibbāna, many people, full of faith,
built a stupa for the Teacher in order to honor the Buddha.
“We shall build a stupa seven yojanas in height, adorned with the seven precious gems for the Great Sage,” they thus deliberated.
At that time, there was a leader of the army belonging to Kikin, the King of Kāsi.
Having spoken of a measure for the immeasurable at the cetiya,
I said: "Then, by my word, they built for that hero among men a cetiya rising one league high, adorned with various jewels."
“By that well-performed karma and by my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
And now, in this final existence, I am born into a family of merchants.”
In the preeminent city of Sāvatthī, prosperous, flourishing, and possessed of great wealth,
I saw the Sugata entering the city. With a mind filled with wonder,
I went forth into homelessness, and before long, I attained arahantship.
“Because of that deed of making a cetiya according to its proper measure,
I was born with a body like that of a dwarf, deserving of contempt.
But by honoring the Seventh Sage with a sweet voice, [I attained this fruit].”
I attained preeminence among the monks of sweet voice.
“By the gift of fruit to the Buddha and by the recollection of his virtues,
I dwell, having attained the fruits of recluseship, free from taints.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
Later, while declaring his final knowledge (aññā), he said:
“In the Ambāṭakārāma grove, Bhaddiya [dwelt] in the forest thicket...”
Having uprooted craving along with its root, Bhadda meditates there.
“Some delight in mridanga drums, lutes, and cymbals;
but I, at the foot of a tree, take delight in the teaching of the Buddha.”
“If the Buddha would grant me a boon, and if that boon could be obtained by me,
I would choose constant mindfulness directed toward the body for the entire world.
Thus he spoke these three verses.
In this context, *para* means "best" or "superior"; the sense is "distinguished. For this word *para* expresses superiority, as in such phrases as *paraṃ viya mattāya* ("beyond measure," etc.).
*Ambāṭakārāme* refers to a monastery (*ārāma*) of that name. It is said that it was delightful, endowed with shade and water, and adorned with groves of trees;
therefore, he specified it as "the *para*" (the superior one). [It was] in the Ambāṭaka Grove, among the *ambāṭaka* trees...
And they say, “In the Abhilakkhita forest. “In the forest thicket” (*vanasaṇḍamhi*) means in a dense mass of trees, shrubs, creepers, and vines;
this is the meaning of “forest. “Bhaddiya” is his name; the Elder speaks of himself as if he were another.
“Having uprooted craving with its root”: the root of craving is ignorance (*avijjā*). Therefore, it means having eradicated craving together with its ignorance by means of the supreme path.

The meaning is as follows: "Therein, the auspicious one alone meditates" means that he, being auspicious and beautiful by virtue of supramundane virtue and so forth, meditates with the meditation of the highest fruit (*aggaphala-jhāna*) through dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*), owing to having accomplished his task in that very forest grove.
And "he passes the time with the bliss of the fruit and with the attainments of meditation" shows his own delight in solitude; thus [the verse says], "some find delight."
The verse also demonstrates this same point by way of contrast. In that context: "With mudiṅgas" means with muraja drums such as the aṅgika and others.

"With vīṇās" means with lutes such as the nandinī and others. "With paṇavas" means with musical instruments; some enjoyers of sensual pleasures take delight in these, but that delight of theirs is ignoble and not conducive to welfare.
"And I" (ahañca) means, however, I alone [rejoice] in the Blessed Buddha.
"Delighting in the Teaching"—the meaning is that for that very reason, I dwell delighting and taking pleasure in the foot of a tree.

Having thus extolled his own delight in seclusion, he now spoke the verse beginning with "If the Buddha were mine" in order to praise the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati-kammaṭṭhāna*) by cultivating which he attained *arahantship*. Its meaning is: if the Blessed Buddha...
“Venerable sir, I ask a boon of the Blessed One for one day.

When I had thus requested it, [the Buddha] would grant me the boon exactly as requested, without refusing it by saying, “Monk, the Tathāgatas have transcended boons,” provided that the boon obtained fulfilled my intention and brought my heart’s desire to its ultimate fulfillment—thus the Elder speaks by way of supposition. “Venerable sir...”

Thinking, "Let the whole world at all times develop the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body," and intending to show that he would choose the boon, saying, "Mindfulness directed to the body should be developed constantly by the whole world," he said: "I choose for the whole world constant mindfulness directed to the body.
Now, by way of censuring non-examination, he praises examination:
“Those who have perceived me by my form, and those who have followed after my voice—
those people, possessed as they are by desire and lust,
do not know me. He who does not know within, and does not see without...”
The fool, completely shrouded, is indeed carried away by sound.
He does not know within, yet he looks outward;
seeing only the external fruit, he too is carried away by sound.
“He understands within and sees without;
seeing with unobstructed vision, he is not carried away by mere sound.”—
Thus he spoke these four verses.

In this context, "those who judged me by my form" means those ignorant people who, because of my unattractive and inferior physical appearance, thought, "Wisdom corresponds to one's outward form," and thus judged me to be inferior in terms of the body of Dhamma;
the meaning is that they despised me as "inferior" and conceived of me through the process of delimitation. And "those who followed after my voice" refers to those beings who [judged] by my voice...
Because they followed me with gentle esteem, they thought much of me; that was their mistake.
For I am not to be despised on account of my mere physical form, nor am I to be highly esteemed on account of my mere reputation.
Therefore, those people—both types of people who are possessed by desire and lust—do not know me; they have fallen under the sway of desire and lust, and have not abandoned desire and lust.
“They do not know me as one who has entirely abandoned desire and lust.
To show that such a person like him is beyond their reach because they have not fully understood the internal and external bases, the words beginning with “internally” were spoken.
“Internally” refers to the phenomena such as the aggregates and sense-bases within one’s own continuum; “externally” refers to those in the continua of others.
Alternatively, "internally" (*ajjhatta*) refers to the aggregates of the virtue of one beyond training (*asekkha-sīlakkhandha*) and so forth within myself.

"Externally" (*bahiddhā*) refers to the occurrence of external material phenomena associated with my own excellence of appearance and so forth, as well as the occurrence of eye-consciousness and the rest.

"One who is completely obstructed" (*samantāvaraṇo*) means one who, through such non-knowing both internally and externally, is possessed of a total obstruction and follows a course of knowledge that is blocked. Such a person is indeed carried away by mere report (*ghosa*).
Thus, the fool whose intellect is led by others is carried away, led, and dragged along by the sound of others' words.
And he "inspects externally" means that one who, according to the method already described, does not know within himself,
