but instead sees specifically on the outside by following what has been heard or by observing the perfection of outward appearance and so forth, thinking, "He must be endowed with special qualities."
He too, seeing the fruit externally and grasping merely at the fruit through a superficial method of apprehension, is carried away by the aforementioned sound;
the meaning is that he does not know one such as me.
But he who knows both internally—the quality of the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training within the interior of an arahant—and externally—
Through his discernment of the practice, he sees specifically the possession of distinguished qualities.

Seeing without obstruction—being unobstructed by anything—he is capable of seeing and knowing the qualities of the Noble Ones; he is not carried away by mere sound, because he sees according to reality.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhadda.
The verses beginning with "An only son," etc., belong to the Venerable Elder Bhadda. What is his origin?
It is said that he once honored the Blessed One Padumuttara and the Saṅgha of monks, numbering one hundred thousand, with the four requisites such as robes and so forth.
Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a merchant family in Sāvatthī.
At the moment of his birth, his parents— who were childless and had failed to obtain a son even after performing rites such as supplicating deities—
approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, if we should obtain one son, we shall give him to you for the sake of service."
Having said, "We shall give," and having made their request, they departed. Then a certain son of the gods, perceiving the Teacher’s intention, stood there with his lifespan exhausted;
being commanded by Sakka, the King of Devas, "Be reborn in such-and-such a family," he was reborn there, and they gave him the name Bhadda.
When he had reached the age of seven years, his parents, having adorned him, [presented him] to the Blessed One.
Having led him into the presence [of the Teacher], they said, "Venerable sir, this is that son whom you requested; we hand him over to you.
The Teacher commanded the Elder Ānanda, "Ordain him. Having given the command, he entered the Fragrant Chamber.
The Elder ordained him and briefly explained the gateway to insight (vipassanā). Because he was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (upanissaya),...
While practicing insight meditation, he intensified his cultivation before the sun had even set and became possessed of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Buddha Padumuttara, the Great Sage whose heart was full of loving-kindness;”
The entire multitude approaches the supreme leader of all the world.
They all give Sattuka, Baddhaka, food, drink,
and provisions to the Teacher, the unsurpassed field of merit.
“I too shall give a gift to the God of Gods, the Tathāgata;
having invited the Best of Buddhas and the unsurpassed Saṅgha as well.
These people, sent forth by me, have invited the Tathāgata.”
And the Saṅgha of monks alone, the unsurpassed field of merit.
A couch of a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], made of gold, spread with a woolen coverlet,
with cotton mattresses and silk pillows, and with linen and cotton fabrics;
I prepared a magnificent seat, a throne worthy of a Buddha.
Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the God of Gods, the Bull among Men,
arrived at my door, surrounded by the community of monks.
“Having gone out to meet the Fully Enlightened One, the glorious Lord of the World,
with a clear heart and a joyful mind, I offered him a canopy.
To the hundred thousand bhikkhus and the Buddha, the Leader of the World,”
With a serene mind and joyful heart, I satisfied him with the finest food.
Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
sat within the community of monks and spoke these verses:
“I shall praise this seat that has been given—golden and spread with a woolen cover. Listen as I speak.
For seventy-four times, he shall exercise sovereignty over the gods.”
He will experience prosperity, honored by celestial nymphs.
He will dwell upon the earth as a ruler of a thousand regional kingdoms,
and fifty-one times he will become a wheel-turning monarch.
“In all realms of existence, he will be born into a noble family;
and later, having gone forth, impelled by the root of his wholesome merit,
he will become a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Bhaddiya.”
“I am devoted to solitude, dwelling in a remote lodging;
I have attained all the fruits, and today I am one who has abandoned the defilements.
Having directly known everything about me, the All-Knowing Leader of the World—”
Having sat within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he placed me in the foremost position:
"The four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations have been realized, along with the six direct knowledges; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished."
The Blessed One, knowing that he had attained the sixfold direct knowledge (*chaḷabhiññā*), said to him, "Come, Bhadda.
He immediately approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood before the Master with palms joined; that itself was his full ordination (*upasampadā*).

This, it is said, is called "ordination by the Buddha" (*buddhūpasampadā*). Then the Elder, explaining his own conduct from birth onwards as a means of declaring his realization of the Truth (*aññā*), said:
“I was an only son, dear to my mother and dear to my father;
indeed, I was obtained through many ascetic practices and earnest prayers.
Out of compassion for me, they were desirous of my welfare and seeking my benefit.”
Both the father and the mother offered him to the Buddha:
“This son was obtained with great difficulty; he is delicate and has been raised in comfort.
We give him to you, O Protector, as an attendant for the Conqueror.”
“The Teacher, having accepted me, said this to Ānanda:
‘Ordain him quickly; he will become a noble steed.
Having ordained me, the Teacher, the Victor, entered the monastery.”
When the sun had not yet set, my mind was then liberated.
Then the Teacher, having emerged from seclusion, dismissed [the assembly] and said to me, "Come, Bhadda. That was my full ordination.
“Having received full ordination at the age of seven,
I have attained the threefold knowledge. Oh, how well-proclaimed is the Dhamma!”—
thus he spoke these verses.

"In that regard, 'by means of the practice of vows' refers to [the practice] through the observance of vows such as fasting and so forth, after having heard the words of certain ascetics and brahmins who said, 'By doing thus, you will obtain a son,' and after having given him milk to drink. 'By means of supplication' refers to the supplications made to deities and the supplication made to the Teacher;
this alone is the reason here, while the other [details] were mentioned by the Elder for the purpose of demonstrating the proper conduct toward parents."
And he speaks for the purpose of showing that [the child] was obtained with difficulty.
"Them" refers to the mother and father. "They brought near" means they brought them near.
"Nurtured in happiness" means raised in comfort. "To you" refers to you. "Attendant" means one who performs service.
"He will be a thoroughbred in my teaching"—saying this, he spoke thus: "Therefore, ordain him quickly this very day.
"Having ordained him" means having been ordained by the Elder Ānanda. "The vihāra" refers to the Gandhakuṭī.
"While the sun had not yet set" means while the sun was still above the horizon. "Then my mind was liberated" means after that commencement of insight (vipassanā).
In just a moment, my mind was liberated from all taints; I became one whose taints were exhausted.
"Then" means after that exhaustion of my taints. "Having emerged" means having entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which he had attained for himself, and then having emerged from it.
Therefore he said, "emerged from seclusion. "That was my higher ordination" refers to that [attainment] directed toward me.
“Come, Bhaddā”—these words were uttered by the Teacher, and that itself was my full ordination (upasampadā).
Thus, by saying, “I received full ordination at seven years of age,” he demonstrates the Teacher’s extraordinary favor toward himself and the liberating nature of the Dispensation.
Therefore, he said: “Oh, how well-proclaimed is the Dhamma!”

And here, although he has declared his state of having destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) by saying, “My mind was liberated,” he further states, “The three knowledges (tisso vijjā) were attained,” in order to demonstrate his possession of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), which include a portion of mundane supernormal powers (lokikā abhiññā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: “The six higher knowledges were realized.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhadda is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sopāka.
The verses beginning with "Having seen [him] in the shadow of the palace" belong to the venerable Elder Sopāka. What is his origin?

This one, too, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Having been reborn and attained the state of full consciousness, he reached mastery in the sciences and crafts of the brahmins.
Seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a forest ascetic, dwelling on a certain mountain.
The Teacher, knowing that his death was near, went into his presence. Upon seeing the Blessed One, his heart was filled with serene faith.
Proclaiming his sublime joy and gladness, he prepared and offered a seat made of flowers.
The Teacher sat there, delivered a discourse on the Dhamma connected with impermanence, and then departed through the air even as the man looked on.
Abandoning his former grasping at permanence and fixing the perception of impermanence in his heart, the man passed away.

Having been reborn in the world of the gods and wandering from one state to another among gods and humans, he was born in this era of a Buddha’s appearance in Rājagaha within the womb of a *sopāka* woman.
He became known by the name Sopāka, derived from his birth. However, some say that he was born into a merchant family and that “Sopāka” was merely a name;
this contradicts the *Apadāna-pāḷi*, which states: “In his final [existence]...”

According to the statement, "When his time had come, he went to a lowly womb," his father passed away when he was four months old; his younger paternal uncle raised him. Gradually, he reached the age of seven.
One day, the younger paternal uncle, becoming angry because [the boy] was quarreling with his own son, led him to the charnel ground.
Having bound his two hands together with a rope and then fastened that very rope tightly around the corpse of a dead man, he departed, thinking, "Let the jackals and other scavengers devour him.

Because of the merit of the child, who was in his final existence (*pacchimabhavika*), [the man] was unable to kill him himself, nor could the jackals and others overcome him. At the hour of midnight, the child lamented thus:
“What destination awaits me, who have no one to go to?
Who is my kinsman, I who am without kin? Amidst this cemetery, who can grant me fearlessness?
At that moment, the Teacher, surveying those ready to be guided, saw within the boy’s heart the radiant potential for Arahantship. Emitting a radiance, inspiring mindfulness, he spoke thus:
“Come, Sopāka, do not fear; look upon the Tathāgata.
I shall deliver you, as the moon from the mouth of Rāhu.
At the conclusion of this verse, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the boy’s bonds were severed and he became a stream-enterer right there in front of the Fragrant Chamber.
He stood there. His mother, not seeing her son, questioned his younger uncle;
when he did not tell her what had happened to him, she went here and there searching for him. Thinking, "The Buddhas, it is said, know the past, future, and present;
what if I were to approach the Blessed One and learn the news concerning my son? she went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher, having concealed him by means of his psychic power, was asked by her: "Venerable Sir, I do not see my son;
however, the Blessed One knows his whereabouts.
To this he replied: "Children are no protection, nor is a father, nor even kinsmen."
“For one seized by the End-maker, there is no refuge among kinsmen.
Thus he preached the Dhamma. Having heard it, she became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). The boy attained *arahantship*. This was stated in the Apadāna:
“While clearing away a mountain slope in a forest on a most excellent peak...”
The Blessed One named Siddhattha came into my presence.
Seeing the Buddha, the Elder of the World, the Neutral One, approaching,
I spread out a mat and offered him a seat of flowers.
“Having sat upon the flower-seat, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World,
knowing my destiny, proclaimed impermanence:
‘Impermanent indeed are conditioned things, subject to arising and passing away.’”
“Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss.
Having said this, the All-Knowing One, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men, the Hero, rose up into the sky like a king of swans in the air.
“Having abandoned my own views, I cultivated the perception of impermanence;
having cultivated it for a single day, I passed away there.
Having experienced two successes, urged on by the root of my wholesome merit,”
When my final existence was reached, I entered the womb of a doe.
Having gone forth from the home into the homeless life,
I attained arahantship at the age of seven.
“Exerting energy, resolute, and well-composed in the precepts,
having pleased the Great Naga, I received full ordination.
That deed which I performed back then, ninety-four aeons ago— ”
I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of giving flowers.
Ninety-four eons ago, I cultivated a certain perception at that time;
while cultivating that perception, I attained the destruction of the taints.
“The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Then the Blessed One withdrew his supernormal power. She too, having seen her son and being thrilled and delighted upon hearing of his state as one whose taints were exhausted, went forth and departed.
He approached the Teacher as he was walking back and forth in the shadow of the Perfumed Chamber.
Having paid homage, he walked along behind him. Desiring to grant him full ordination (*upasampadā*), the Blessed One asked ten questions, beginning with "What is one?
He too, grasping the Teacher’s intention and correlating it with his own omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), answered those questions, beginning with "All beings subsist by means of nutriment.
For that very reason, they are known as the "Questions of the Youth" (*kumārapañhā*).
Thus it became known as the "Ordination by Answering Questions.
Having explained his own history to the Elder, and being about to declare his realization of the Truths (Aññā), he said:
"Having seen the Supreme among Men walking back and forth in the shade of the palace..."
Having approached him there, I shall pay homage to that Supreme Person.
Having arranged my robe over one shoulder and clasped my hands together,
I shall walk behind that stainless one, the highest of all beings.
“Then the wise one, skilled in questions, asked me questions;
undaunted and fearless, I answered for the Teacher.
When the questions had been answered, the Tathāgata expressed his approval.”
Having looked upon the community of bhikkhus, he spoke these words regarding this matter:
"It is a gain for the people of Aṅga and Magadha that he makes use of their robes,
almsfood, requisites, and lodgings."
“Rising from one’s seat and performing proper etiquette—this is their gain,” he said.
“From this day forward, Sopāka, come to me for an audience;
let this itself be your full ordination.”
“Having received full ordination at the age of seven, I bear my final body—oh, how well-proclaimed is the Dhamma!”—with these verses he spoke.
Therein, “in the shadow of the palace” means in the shadow of the Perfumed Chamber. “They shall pay homage” refers to those who paid homage.
"Having joined their hands together like the buds of lotuses"—this is the meaning of "having raised their palms in añjali.
"They will walk along behind" means they walked following after the Teacher as he was walking.
"Dustless" means free from the dust of passion and the other defilements.
*Pañha* refers to the "Prince's Questions" (*kumārapañha*). *Vidū* means one who has known what is to be known; the meaning is "the Omniscient One.
Because he had abandoned both trepidation and fear through the demolition of their bridge—thinking "The Teacher asks me"—he answered without trepidation and without fear.

*Yesāyam* means "of whom this [Sopāka] belongs," namely of Aṅga and Magadha. *Paccayam* means "requisites for the sick. *Sāmīcim* means "proper conduct," such as the acts of clearing the path, sowing seeds, and so forth.
*Ajja-dagge*: the letter *da* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). It means "starting from today," "from today as the beginning," or "beginning with today.
There is also the Pāli reading *ajjatagge*, which has the same meaning: "starting from this very day. Regarding "approach me for the sake of seeing":
do not approach me for the sake of seeing while thinking, "He is of low birth" or "He is younger than I. "And this very [is it]" refers to that [attainment] of mine through omniscient knowledge.
The connection is as follows: "Having combined [the two] and provided the answer to the question, he said, 'Let this itself be your full ordination (upasampadā).

There is also a textual reading: "I have obtained the full ordination. As for those who read "having obtained the full ordination" (*laddhāna upasampadaṃ*), the meaning is "by the seventh year," that is, "in the seventh year";
or alternatively, the ellipsis is to be supplied as "having become one of seven years' standing."
Whatever has not been stated here is easily understood.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sopāka is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sarabhaṅga.
"Sare hatthehi," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Sarabhaṅga. What is their origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in this current era of a Buddha as the son of a certain brahmin in Rājagaha. He was born with no distinguished marks, his lineage being such by family tradition.

This was his name. When he reached maturity, having abandoned sensual pleasures and gone forth as an ascetic, he lived there after cutting grass himself and building a leaf-hut. From that time on, he became known by the name Sarabhaṅga.
Then the Blessed One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw the necessary conditions for his attainment of Arahatship; having gone there, he—

He taught the Dhamma. Having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness and, applying himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*), attained Arahantship before long and continued to dwell right there.
Later, the leaf-hut he had built during his time as an ascetic became old and dilapidated.
Seeing it, people asked him, "Venerable sir, why do you not repair this little hut?"
The Elder, explaining all of this—how the hut had been built during his time as an ascetic and how it was no longer possible to build it in that same way—said:
“Having broken off reeds with my hands and built a hut out of them, I lived there;
because of that, the name Sarabhaṅga came to me by common designation.”
“Today it is not permitted for me to break off reeds with my hands;
training rules have been laid down by the illustrious Gotama. Thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, “having broken off reeds with my hands” means that formerly, during the time I was an ascetic, I used to cut the reed-grass with my own hands.
Having built a grass hut, I lived there, sitting and lying down. "By that" means by the breaking of the reeds for the purpose of making the hut.
"By convention" means by a convention according to its literal meaning; thus the name "Sarabhaṅga" (Reed-Breaker) came to be.
"It is not fitting for me today" means: today, now that I am fully ordained, it is not fitting for me with my own hands [to handle] the reeds and the grass.
"It is not permitted, it is not allowable to break [it]. Why? Because training rules have been laid down by the renowned Gotama.
By this, he shows: "Even for the sake of our lives, we do not transgress that training rule which has been laid down by our Teacher.
Having thus shown the reason for not repairing the grass hut in one way, he now shows it by another method:

“Previously, Sarabhaṅga did not see the disease in its entirety or in its fullness—meaning without remainder from every aspect—but now this disease has been seen by one who acts according to the words of the Surpassing Deva. Thus he spoke this verse.
In that context, *sakalaṃ* means all. *Samattaṃ* means complete, in the sense of being without exception from every part. *Rogaṃ* means disease.
He speaks with reference to the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), which are like a disease in the sense of being afflicted by the nature of suffering and so forth.
"I did not see it before" means that prior to receiving the Teacher’s instruction, he had not seen it. This disease has now been seen;

for by acting according to his word, he has surpassed all devas—whether they be conventional devas (*sammutideva*), devas by birth (*upapattideva*), or devas by purification (*visuddhideva*)—by means of his own virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).

Because he followed the instruction of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Surpasser of Gods, Sarabhaṅga perceived—by means of the wisdom of the Path accompanied by the wisdom of insight—that this disease, known as the five aggregates, was seen as such; "perceived" here means it was fully understood.
By this, he shows: how could one who is thus indifferent even toward the hut of his own body ever repair an external hut of grass?
Now, this path which I have entered upon—the path by which I have seen this disease of my own self as it truly is—is common to all Buddhas.
By means of this very path, even their Dhamma of instruction is like pure gold refined in the middle;
it is by standing firm upon this that I have attained the destruction of suffering. Thus, declaring his own practice for Arahantship:
“By the very same path that Vipassī went, and by the very same path that Sikhī and Vessabhū went,
by that straight path Gotama has come— the path taken by Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa.
Free from craving, without grasping, these seven Buddhas have reached the destruction of suffering.”
This Dhamma which has been taught by those who have become the Dhamma, the Tathāgatas,
out of compassion for living beings— the Four Noble Truths:
suffering, its origin, the path, and the cessation that is the destruction of suffering.
“In that which endless suffering in saṃsāra ceases;
upon the breaking up of this body and the exhaustion of life, there is no further becoming: I am completely liberated in every respect.”
He spoke these verses:
"Therein, 'by that very path' means by that same Noble Eightfold Path together with its preliminary stages.
'Gone' means having set out and attained Nibbāna. 'Vipassī' refers to the Sammasambuddha Vipassī. 'Kakusandha' is an uninflected [vocative]."
The exposition: “Kakusandha and Koṇāgamana” is also a reading. “By that very straight path” means by that very straight noble path (ariyamagga).
“Without grasping” means without clinging or without rebirth-linking. “Plunged into destruction” means plunged into Nibbāna, established in Nibbāna.
“By whom this Dhamma was taught” means by those seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones this Dhamma of the Dispensation was taught and proclaimed.
“By those who have become Dhamma” means by those who, through the nature of the Dhamma-body, possess the true essence of the Dhamma;

or, by those born from the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttara-dhamma*); or, by those who have attained the Dhamma. “By those who are such-like” (*tādibhi*) means by those who have attained the state of being “such-like” (*tādi*) toward desirable things and so forth.
By the phrase “the Four Noble Truths,” etc., he shows the Dhamma taught by them. In that context, “four” is the delimitation by number.
"The Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni) refers to the vision of phenomena as delimited. As for the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*):
they are "Noble Truths" because they are both noble (*ariya*) in the sense of being non-false (*avitatha*), and truths (*sacca*) because they were taught by the Noble One, the Blessed One;

or alternatively, they are "Noble Truths" because they are truths that produce the state of nobility. Suffering (*dukkha*) is so called because of its wretched nature and its hollow nature; it is the pentad of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
It is called the *samudaya* (origin) because suffering arises from it; thus, it is craving (*taṇhā*).

It is called the *magga* (path) because it goes while destroying the defilements (*kilesa*), or because it is sought after by those seeking *nibbāna*; it consists of the eight factors beginning with right view.

It is called *nirodha* (cessation) because there is no obstruction here—namely, the prison of *saṃsāra*—or because when this is attained, the person is free from obstruction, and suffering ceases herein.

Or it is cessation, Nibbāna. Therefore he said, "the destruction of suffering. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"In which" means when that cessation, Nibbāna, has been attained. "Ceases" means that when the cultivation of the Noble Path is present, [rebirth] ceases, for it is endless.
The construction is as follows: "In this saṃsāra, the boundless suffering of birth and so forth does not proceed; it is cut off;
that is cessation"—this is the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have become the Dhamma.

By the words "Through its breaking," etc., he shows in its specific form his own attainment of Arahantship, which was indicated by the phrase "the disease has been seen" through the full understanding of suffering. "In which... [and so on].

Regarding the reading “dukkhaṃ nibbattate,” this is the construction of the entire verse: In that saṃsāra, known as the succession of aggregates and so forth, this endless suffering beginning with birth has arisen;
that is *punabbhava* (re-becoming), because it is distinct from the attainment of suffering here and consists of the state of existence again and again.
[This occurs] at the exhaustion of this life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), which is the pentad of aggregates known as the body.
There are no further breakages or destructions beyond this; therefore, I am thoroughly liberated and disjoined from all defilements and from all states of existence.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sarabhaṅga is finished.
The commentary on the Sattaka-nipāta is finished.
8. The Aṭṭhaka-nipāta: 1.
Commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākaccāyana.
The verses beginning with “Kamma is weighty” and so forth, found in the *Aṭṭhakanipāta*, belong to the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera. What is their origin?
This [Thera] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a wealthy merchant family of great means.
Having reached maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he heard the Teacher speak in brief.
Having seen one bhikkhu being established in the foremost position among those who analyze in detail the meaning of what was spoken,
he himself made an aspiration, longing for that very state; having performed meritorious deeds such as giving,
he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he became a master of spells (vijjādhara) and while traveling through the air, [he saw] the Teacher.
Seeing him seated in a forest grove on the Himavat mountain, he offered worship with *kaṇikāra* flowers with a devout mind.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, revolving from one happy destination to another, he was reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, at the site where the Golden Shrine was being constructed—
Having made an offering with a golden brick worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold], she made this aspiration:
"May my body be golden-colored in every place where I am reborn.
Then, having performed wholesome deeds for the rest of her life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, in this [life]—
During the time of a Buddha’s appearance, he was born in Ujjain in the house of the royal chaplain of King Caṇḍapajjota.
On the day of his naming, his mother, thinking, "My son is golden-colored and has come bearing his own name," gave him the name Kañcanamāṇava.
As he grew up, he mastered the three Vedas and, upon the death of his father, obtained the position of chaplain.
Thus, by virtue of his lineage, he was known as Kaccāyana. King Caṇḍapajjota, having heard of the appearance of a Buddha, sent him, saying:
"Teacher, go there and bring the Teacher here. He approached the presence of the Teacher with seven other men.
The Teacher taught the Dhamma to him. At the conclusion of the teaching, together with those seven people, he—
Together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he was established in Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, unshaken, the conqueror of the unconquered;
a hundred thousand aeons from now, this Leader appeared.”
“The Hero, whose eyes are like lotus petals, whose face is as stainless as the moon;
who resembles the mountain of gold, and whose radiance is equal to the splendor of the sun.
He who captivates the eyes and minds of beings, adorned with the most excellent marks.”
Beyond the path of all speech, honored by humans and gods,
the Fully Awakened One brings beings to enlightenment; the Lord of Speech with his sweet voice,
whose continuum is bound by compassion, is confident amidst the assemblies.
“He teaches the sweet Dhamma, endowed with the Four Truths;
he uplifts living beings who have sunk into the mire of delusion.
At that time, having become a solitary wanderer, an ascetic dwelling in the Himalayas,”
Traveling through the sky toward the human world, I saw the Victor.
Having approached his presence, I heard the teaching of the Dhamma as the Hero was extolling the great virtues of his disciple.
“What I have spoken in brief, he explains in detail;
he satisfies the assembly just as this Kaccāyana does.
I do not see any other disciple here who is like him.”
"Therefore, O monks, you should remember this as the foremost:
'Then, having heard those delightful words, I was filled with wonder;
I went to the Himalayas and gathered a heap of flowers.'"
“Having worshipped the refuge of the world, I aspired for that very state.
Then, knowing my intention, he who has abandoned all conflict prophesied:
‘Behold this best of seers, whose skin is like refined gold!’”
With hair standing on end, his shoulders broad, standing motionless with palms joined,
smiling with eyes full of joy, his heart intent upon the Buddha’s praise—
born of the Dhamma, with a heart full of resolve, resembling one sprinkled with the nectar of immortality.
“Having heard the virtues of Kaccāna, I stood longing for that state;
in a future time, during the era of the Great Sage Gotama.
[There I shall be] his heir to the Dhamma, his own legitimate son, fashioned by the Dhamma.”
“There will be a disciple of the Teacher named Kaccāna.
A man of great learning and vast wisdom, who understands the intentions of the Sage,
he shall attain that state just as I have prophesied for him.”
“In a hundred thousand aeons ago, whatever deed I performed then, I have not known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
For two existences I transmigrated—among the gods and among humans.”
“I do not go to another rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
‘I am born into two kinds of families: among kṣatriyas and among brahmins.
I am never born into a low family; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.’”
“And now, in his final existence, he was born in the city of Ujjayinī,
as the son of Tiriṭivaccha, who was a skilled priest and master of the Vedas under the fierce King Pajjota.”
My mother was named Candimā, and I am Kaccāna, possessed of excellent skin.
Sent by the protector of the earth for the purpose of testing the Buddha,
I beheld the Leader, a mass of virtues, at the gateway to the city of liberation.
“Having heard the stainless word that dries up the mire of rebirth,
I attained the deathless peace together with the other seven.
I became one who understood the intention of the Sugata, O great-minded one.”
And he was established as the foremost in this [list], his heart’s desire fully accomplished.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been done.
Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, “Come, monks! At that very moment, their hair and beards were reduced to the length of two finger-breadths.
They became like elder monks of sixty years’ standing, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*).
Having thus accomplished his own goal, the Elder informed the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, King Pajjota wishes to pay homage at your feet and hear the Dhamma.
The Teacher said, "Bhikkhu, you yourself go there; even when you have gone, the king will gain confidence. The Elder—
Having gone there as the eighth member by the Teacher’s command, he won over the king, established the Dispensation in the Avanti country,
and returned once more to the presence of the Teacher. One day, seeing many bhikkhus who had abandoned the duty of ascetics (*samaṇadhamma*),
who delighted in work, who delighted in socializing, who were pursued by craving for flavors, and who lived in negligence, he spoke these verses by way of exhorting them:
“One should not engage in much work; one should avoid busy crowds and not exert oneself.
He who is anxious and greedy for flavors neglects that goal which brings true happiness.
For they have understood that this honoring and worshiping among families is indeed like a mire.”
"A subtle arrow is difficult to extract; honor is hard for a base man to abandon."—he spoke these two verses.
Therein, "do not perform much work" refers to building new dwellings and the like, which act as obstacles to the practice of the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*).

One should not undertake great new construction work; however, one must indeed perform minor tasks with little effort, such as repairing what is broken or dilapidated, for the sake of honoring the Teacher’s word.
"One should avoid people" means one should avoid people by way of socializing in groups.
Or, "people" refers to those whom one associates with, frequents, and attends upon, [and from whom] wholesome qualities [decline].
They decline and unwholesome states increase; one should avoid such a person who has become a bad friend.
He does not exert himself; he does not strive for the sake of producing the requisites by way of clinging to his family, because he is eager and greedy for flavors.
He neglects the goal which is the endurance of happiness—that monk who is greedy for flavors and ruled by craving for flavors.
Devoted to providing the necessary requisites, he exerts himself for the sake of maintaining his family; when they are happy, he is happy, and when they are suffering, he suffers.

When duties and obligations arise, he applies himself to them personally. He neglects and abandons that purpose consisting of virtue and the rest—which brings about the influx of happiness and conduces to the bliss of serenity, insight, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna—and the meaning is that he completely withdraws himself from it.

Having thus, in the first verse, exhorted [the listener] by saying, "One should avoid delighting in action, delighting in company, and greed for requisites," he now spoke the second verse while censuring the desire for honor. Its meaning is as follows:
that which is this salutation and worship performed by householders toward those who have gone forth and have approached for alms among families, on account of their appreciation of their virtues—

And because the Buddhas and other Noble Ones have proclaimed, known, or declared that it is "mud" (paṅka) and "slime" (kaddama) in the sense of causing one who has not cultivated themselves to sink down and in the sense of making them soiled; and because,
for the blind worldlings who do not fully understand the aggregates, the desire for honor produces affliction and causes internal piercing due to its nature being difficult to discern.
They have declared that the arrow is subtle because it is difficult to extract and difficult to bear away;
for this very reason, honor is hard for a base person to abandon, as it is difficult to give up because one does not undertake the practice for its relinquishment.
For honor is abandoned through the abandonment of the desire for honor; therefore, he shows that an effort must be made for its relinquishment.
“A mortal does not commit an evil deed merely for the sake of another;
one should not practice it oneself, for one’s own actions are one’s kin, O Mother.
One is not a thief by the word of others, nor is one a sage by the word of others.”
As one knows oneself, so do the gods know one.
Others do not understand what we here restrain;
but those who understand that matter, through them the strifes are stilled.
“The wise person lives even when his wealth is exhausted;
but through the lack of wisdom, even one who possesses wealth does not truly live.
One hears everything with the ear; one sees everything with the eye.”
Yet a wise person ought not to abandon everything seen and heard.
Just as a blind man is to one with sight, as a deaf man is to one with hearing,
as a mute man is to one with wisdom, and as a weakling is to one who is strong;

"Then, when a crisis arises, one should lie down like a corpse."—These six verses he spoke by way of exhortation to King Pajjota. It is said that, having placed his trust in the brahmins, the king caused animal sacrifices to be performed;
without investigating the matter, he punished those who were not thieves under the impression that they were thieves; and in legal disputes, he appointed owners where there were no owners.
He performs [actions] both for those who own property and for those who do not. Then, in order to dissuade him from this, the Elder spoke six verses beginning with "Not for another's sake.
Therein, "Not for another's sake, a sinful deed for a mortal" means:
one should not practice a sinful deed—such as killing, binding, and so forth—having aimed at or made it the cause for another mortal being; nor should one have it performed by another.
The meaning is as follows: "One should not practice that oneself" means one should not perform that evil deed even by oneself.

Why? Because these mortals, O Mother, are bound by their actions; they are heirs to their actions. Therefore, the meaning is that one should not perform any evil deed oneself, nor should one cause another to do so.
One does not become a thief merely by the word of others; that is, one who has not committed theft oneself is not called a thief merely by the speech of another.
Likewise, one does not become a sage merely by the word of others; that is, one whose conduct of body, speech, and mind is not thoroughly purified is not a sage merely by the speech of another.
Here, the term *pare* is an elliptical expression formed by dropping the case-ending (*vibhattilopa*). Some, however, suggest that it should be read as *paresaṃ*.
They say that it is taught by eliding the syllables *pa* and *saṃ*.
"And his self knows him as he truly is" means that his own self—his mind—knows and understands that being exactly as it is, [discerning] whether "I am pure or impure.
"The gods also know him thus" means that both the devas of purified virtue and the devas born of rebirth know and understand him in that same way.

Therefore, the intention is this: regarding the discernment of what is pure and impure, as well as the state of being pure or impure, the authority is such deities themselves, and not just any beings who are overcome by desire and hatred.
"Others" refers to those other than the wise; [the wise understand] wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless action, and the fruit of action.
Those who do not know the foulness of the body and the impermanence of conditioned phenomena are called "others" here;
they do not realize, "In this world of living beings, we are going toward our end, we are passing away; we are constantly and continuously approaching the presence of death.
And those who understand it there are those wise ones who understand, "We are approaching the vicinity of death."
"Then quarrels are stilled"—for those who know thus proceed toward the pacification of quarrels, which are the harming of others;
the meaning is that they themselves and others do not quarrel and do not oppress one another.

But you, for the sake of your own livelihood, even though making non-thieves into thieves and making owners into ownerless by means of punishment, oppress them through a deficiency of wisdom by causing the loss of their wealth.

Even one who does not act in such a way may live, for a person endowed with wisdom—even if his wealth is exhausted and his riches depleted—lives indeed by means of a blameless livelihood, content with whatever little he has through various forms of self-satisfaction. For that is what is called "living.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "They say that the life of one who lives by wisdom is the best. But as for a person of dull wit, by means of wisdom...
Furthermore, by failing to achieve welfare both in this life and in the future through lack of gain,
even one who possesses wealth does not truly live; for while living amidst the occurrence of reproach and the like, he is not said to be "living," and due to his lack of skill in means,
he loses whatever wealth he has acquired and is unable to sustain even his own life.
It is said that the Elder recited these four verses to the king in a dream.
Upon waking, while still paying homage to the Elder, the king, once the night had turned to dawn, approached the Elder, paid his respects, and related the dream exactly as he had seen it.
Having heard this, the Elder recited those verses in response and said, "All..."
With these two verses beginning with “He hears,” he exhorted the king.

Therein, “he hears everything with his ear” means that here, whatever sound fit to be heard has come within the range of perception—whether well-spoken or ill-spoken—a person who is not deaf hears it all with the ear.
Likewise, a person who is not blind sees every form, whether beautiful or ugly, with the eye. This is the inherent nature of the sense faculties.
In this context, however, the statement "the wise man has abandoned everything seen and heard" is merely illustrative.
For it is not the case that the wise man, the person of wisdom, ought to abandon, relinquish, or even accept everything that is seen or heard.
Rather, having investigated the merits and defects therein, he should abandon only what is to be abandoned and accept what is to be accepted.
He ought to grasp [only what is essential]. Therefore, although he possesses sight, he should be like a blind man regarding that which is to be abandoned;
and although he possesses hearing, he should be like one who is deaf, as if not hearing at all, regarding that which is to be abandoned through what has been heard.
Although he possesses wisdom, he should be like a mute by means of the wisdom of investigation (*vicāraṇapaññā*).

Though skilled in speech, he would be like a mute when there is something that ought not to be said. Though powerful and endowed with strength, he would be like one who is weak regarding what ought not to be done.
The letter *ra* causes the euphonic junction (*padasandhi*) of words; [if lacking it], he would be as if incapable.

Then, when a matter has arisen—“he would lie down like one dead” (*matasāyika*)—when the duty to be performed by himself has arisen and presented itself, he would lie down like one dead. Even after having lain down like one dead...

That duty must indeed be fulfilled; it must not be neglected. Alternatively, "when a matter has arisen" means that when a matter or task arises—that is, presents itself—which ought not to be done by oneself, one might lie down like a dead man;
even after lying down like a dead man, that [wrongful act] must simply not be done. For a wise person ought not to do what is improper. Thus was the king exhorted by the Elder.
Having abandoned what should not be done, he became truly engaged in what ought to be done.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākaccāyana is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sirimitta.
The verses beginning with "Akodhana" (Free from anger) belong to the Venerable Sirimitta Thera. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of rebirth, was born in this current dispensation of a Buddha in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy householder. He received the name Sirimitta. Of him—
It is said that his mother was the sister of Sirigutta. The story of him is already recorded in the commentary on the *Dhammapada*.
Sirimitta, the nephew of Sirigutta, having reached maturity and gained faith upon witnessing the Teacher’s taming of Dhanapāla, went forth into homelessness.
While practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long. One day, as the *Pātimokkha* was being recited, he [prepared] a seat...
Having ascended and taken his seat upon the fan made of mind-seeds, he preached the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.
And as he spoke, revealing and analyzing more exalted qualities, he said:
“Free from anger, free from resentment, without deceit, and devoid of backbiting;”
Such indeed is that bhikkhu; thus, having passed away, he does not grieve.
Free from anger, free from malice, without deceit, devoid of backbiting, with his sense-doors guarded at all times—such a bhikkhu, having passed away, does not grieve.
“Free from anger, free from malice, without deceit and devoid of backbiting—
that monk of virtuous conduct does not grieve after passing away.
Free from anger, free from malice, without deceit and devoid of backbiting...”
That bhikkhu who has virtuous friends does not grieve after passing away.
Free from anger, free from resentment, without deceit, and devoid of backbiting—
that bhikkhu of noble wisdom does not grieve after passing away.
“He who has faith unshakable and well-established in the Tathāgata,
whose virtue is noble, beloved by the Noble Ones, and praised;
he who has confidence in the Saṅgha and whose vision is upright— ”
“They call him one who has not lived in vain; his life is fruitful.
Thus he spoke these verses: “Therefore, the wise person, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas, should devote themselves to faith, virtue, serenity, and the vision of the Dhamma.”

In this context, "one who is not angry" (*akodhana*) means one whose nature is free from anger. For when the occasion for the arising of anger presents itself, such a person stands firm in patient endurance and does not give rise to resentment.
"One who is without malice" (*anupanāhī*) means one who does not harbor ill will;

having encountered an offense committed by others, he is not of a nature to nurse anger with thoughts such as, "He insulted me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me. [This is contrasted with] that which is characterized by the concealment of existing faults...
Because of the absence of deceit (*māyā*), he is "without guile" (*amāyo*). Because he is free from malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*), he is "empty of backbiting" (*rittapesuṇo*).
Such a one is indeed a monk (*bhikkhu*); that is to say, a monk who is of such a nature and of such a kind as to be endowed with the aforementioned qualities.

Thus, by means of the practice as described, he does not grieve hereafter in the next world, because of the absence of any cause for sorrow. [This applies to] the doors of the eye and so forth, as well as the doors of the body and so forth.
One whose doors are guarded, closed, and restrained is called "one with guarded doors. "Of beautiful virtue" means one who possesses a lovely and perfectly purified virtue.

A "good friend" is described as follows: "One who is dear and worthy of respect, who speaks and is patient with what is said, who gives profound counsel, and does not urge one toward what is improper."

One who has such characteristics clearly discerned is a "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*). A "person of noble wisdom" (*kalyāṇapañña*) is one of beautiful wisdom. Although there is no such thing as "unbeautiful" wisdom, this was said by way of wisdom that leads to liberation (*niyyānikā paññā*).

Thus, having shown the right practice through the verses addressed to persons—by way of the suppression and eradication of anger and so forth under the heading of "non-angry" and the rest—he now extracts the supramundane faith and other qualities that have been produced.
Demonstrating right practice through a verse specifically addressed to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), he said, "He whose faith," and so forth.
Its meaning is as follows: for that person, regarding the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there is faith arisen in the manner of the words, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," and so on;
because of that very [faith], it is unshakable, unwavering, and well-established. Having supplied the word "exists" (*atthi*).
It should be connected [to the following]. "Beloved by the Noble Ones" (*ariyakanta*) means it is dear and cherished by the Noble Ones because it is not abandoned even in other existences.
"Praised" (*pasaṃsita*) means it is commended, extolled, and lauded by the Buddhas and others; thus the construction is: "it exists. Furthermore, this virtue (*sīla*) is twofold:
the virtue of the householder and the virtue of the one gone forth. Therein, the virtue of the householder refers to the virtue of the five training precepts (*pañcasikkhāpada*).

That which can be guarded by a householder; and as for the virtue of one gone forth, namely all the virtue of the fourfold purification based upon the virtue of the ten training rules—all of this should be understood as "excellent" because it is unblemished and untouched by defilement.
One who has confidence in the Saṅgha, [thinking] "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way," and so forth, regarding the Noble Saṅgha...
One should bring forward and apply the passage: "The confidence (pasāda) which a person possesses is unshakable and well-established.
And as for "straight vision" (ujubhūtaṃ dassanaṃ): it is straight because of the absence of crookedness of views and the absence of crookedness of defilements.

There are two kinds of vision: the vision of the ownership of one's own actions (kammassakatā-dassana) and the vision of name-and-form with its conditions (sappaccaya-nāmarūpa-dassana). One who possesses both these kinds of vision is unshakable and well-established.

The exegesis (*yojanā*): "He is called 'not poor' (*adaliddo*)"—because of the possession of these well-purified riches, namely the wealth of faith (*saddhādhana*), the wealth of virtue (*sīladhana*), the wealth of learning (*sutadhana*), the wealth of generosity (*cāgadhana*), and the wealth of wisdom (*paññādhanā*), the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, call such a person "not poor.
"His life is not in vain"—the life of one such as that is [fruitful] through the attainment of goals pertaining to the present life and so forth.
The meaning is that it is called "unfailing," "not barren," and "indeed fruitful.
Therefore—because a person endowed with the qualities such as faith as previously described is called "not poor" and "one whose life is not in vain"—[the thought arises]:
"May I too become such a one. And [regarding] "faith... the teaching": "Of all evil... [and so forth].
"Recalling the teaching of the Buddhas as it was stated in the passage beginning with 'non-doing,' a clansman should apply himself to—

and increase— the aforementioned types of faith and virtue, as well as the confidence that constitutes liberation, which arises from a firm resolve regarding the Dhamma caused by the vision of the Dhamma.
Thus, by means of this discourse on the Dhamma to the bhikkhus, the Elder proclaimed the qualities existing within himself and declared his attainment of final knowledge (aññā).

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sirimitta is finished. 3. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāpanthaka begins with the verse "When first I saw... What is his origin? This [Elder]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The following is a continuation of the narrative based on the standard Pali commentaries (Paramatthadīpanī).* ...was reborn in the family of a wealthy merchant in Sāvatthī. When he was born, the entire city of Sāvatthī was illuminated by a great radiance. Because of this, they gave him the name Mahāpanthaka ("Great Road"). When he grew up, he entered the household life and acquired great wealth. One day, while traveling along the Great Road, he encountered the Venerable Ānanda. Delighted by the Elder’s appearance, he invited him to his home and offered him almsfood. After the meal, the Elder preached the Dhamma to him. Having heard the teaching, Mahāpanthaka developed faith and, desiring to go forth, took leave of his parents. With their permission, he went to the Elder Ānanda, requested the going-forth, and received ordination. After being ordained, he lived for some time in dependence upon the Venerable Ānanda. Later, he wished to live independently and, seeking a secluded dwelling, traveled to the Himalayas. There, he dwelt in a cave. While he was living there, he became afflicted by a severe illness. As he lay on his deathbed, he thought: "I have not yet attained any distinction in the Dhamma; what will become of me? He then recalled the Venerable Ānanda’s previous teaching and resolved to apply himself to meditation. By striving with diligence, he attained the state of a Non-Returner (Anāgāmī). At that moment, his body was consumed by flames, and he passed away to be reborn in the Aviha Brahma-world. The Venerable Mahāpanthaka’s verses are as follows: "When first I saw the Teacher, the Buddha, the peerless one, I was filled with joy and approached him, my mind uplifted. Having paid homage at his feet, I sat down to one side, And then I asked the Blessed One about the path to peace. ‘How does one cross over the flood? he asked the Sage. ‘By means of non-clinging,’ the Teacher replied to me. ‘How does one cross over the ocean? I asked again. ‘By means of non-clinging,’ the Teacher replied to me. ‘How does one cross over birth and old age? I asked again. ‘By means of non-clinging,’ the Teacher replied to me. Having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, I departed, And then I went to the Himalayas, to a secluded place. There I dwelt in a cave, practicing the holy life. Then, overcome by illness, I lay down on my bed. As I lay there, I thought: ‘What will become of me? Then I remembered the Dhamma taught by the Teacher. ‘I have not attained any distinction,’ I thought, ‘And now my body is consumed by disease. Then, through the power of my exertion, I attained the fruit of Non-Returning. At that very moment, my body was consumed by flames, And I passed away to be reborn in Aviha."* *Note: The above summary and verses are reconstructed based on the traditional narrative found in the Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā.* The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāpanthaka is finished. 3.
