It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, while living as a wealthy householder in the city of Haṃsavatī,
he one day heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.

Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those skilled in the turning away through perception, he himself also aspired to that same status and offered alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having performed a great almsgiving for seven days, he said: "Venerable Sir,
that bhikkhu whom you placed at the very head of the 'foremost in skill in turning away from perceptions' in my teaching seven days ago—
by the power of this meritorious deed, may I too become foremost in the teaching of a future Buddha, just like that bhikkhu."

He made his aspiration. His younger brother, however, having likewise performed meritorious service toward the Blessed One, made a resolution according to the method already described, based on two factors: the manifestation of a mind-made body and skill in the turning away of the mind.
The Blessed One, seeing that the aspirations of both would be fulfilled without obstacle, [prophesied]: "In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons..."
"Your aspiration shall be fulfilled under the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama," he prophesied.
Both of those individuals performed meritorious deeds there for as long as they lived, and passing away from there, they were reborn in the world of the gods.
There, the noble Dhamma that had been interrupted was not recited to Mahāpanthaka; however, Cūḷapanthaka [recited it] under Kassapa.
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and performed the meditation on the white kasiṇa for twenty thousand years, he was reborn in the city of the gods.
However, in the *Apadāna*, it is recorded: "In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, Cūḷapanthaka was a forest ascetic living in the Himālayas;
there, having seen the Blessed One, he made an offering with a flower parasol. Among those [who attained such states] among gods and humans—
While they were thus wandering in saṃsāra, one hundred thousand eons passed by.
Then our Teacher, having attained full enlightenment and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, was dwelling at the Great Monastery in the Veḷuvana near Rājagaha.
At that time, the daughter of the merchant Dhana in Rājagaha had formed an intimate relationship with her own slave.
Fearing her relatives, she took his essential belongings and fled with him, living elsewhere.
Having conceived a child because of him, when her pregnancy was mature, she set out thinking, "I will go to my relatives' home and give birth. While still on the way, she gave birth to a son;
then, turned back by her husband, she lived at the place where they had previously stayed. Because the son was born on the road, he was named Panthaka.
He gave him the name Paṇṭhaka. While he was running about and wandering here and there, she conceived a second pregnancy on account of him.
When her pregnancy had matured, she gave birth to a son along the way, just as previously described;
she was then turned back by her husband, who named the elder son Mahāpaṇṭhaka and the younger Cūḷapaṇṭhaka.
Having given them names, they continued to live in the very place where they had resided.
As the children gradually grew up, they began to press her, saying, "Mother, show us our grandfather’s family. Being thus importuned, she sent the children to their parents.
From that time on, the children grew up in the house of Dhanaseṭṭhi. Among them, Cūḷapanthaka was very young; Mahāpanthaka—
However, having gone into the presence of the Blessed One together with his grandfather, he saw the Teacher; upon that very sight, faith was born in him.
Having heard the Dhamma, and because he was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he desired to go forth.
He asked his grandfather for permission, who informed the Teacher of the matter and ordained him. Having gone forth and mastered much of the Buddha’s word, and being of full seniority—

Having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he applied himself with wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and, specifically becoming an attainer of the four formless meditative absorptions (*arūpajjhāna*), emerged from them and, having intensified his insight (*vipassanā*), reached Arahantship.
Thus, he became the foremost among those skilled in the turning away from perception (*saññāvivaṭṭa*).
Passing his time in the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhānasukha*) and the bliss of the fruit (*phalasukha*), one day he [reflected] upon his own practice.
Reflecting upon the success he had attained and feeling joy born thereof, he uttered this lion’s roar:
“When I first beheld the Teacher, who is fearless from every side,
Then a sense of spiritual urgency arose in me upon seeing the Supreme Person.”
“He who would strike with his hands and feet one who has come to him for glory—
such a person, having propitiated a Teacher like this,
would only fail him. At that time, I abandoned my children, my wife, and my wealth and grain.”
Having shaved off my hair and beard, I went forth into the homeless life.
Endowed with the training and the livelihood, well-restrained in my sense faculties,
I dwelt undefeated, paying homage to the Fully Awakened One.
“Then this was my aspiration, the longing of my heart:
‘I shall not sit down for even a moment as long as the arrow of craving has not been extracted.
Behold the exertion of energy as I dwelt in this way!”
The three types of higher knowledge have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
“I know my former births; the divine eye has been purified.
I am an arahant worthy of offerings, completely liberated and free from acquisitions.”
Then, at the end of the night, toward the rising of the sun, having dried up all craving, he sat down cross-legged—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, *yadā* means at which time. *Paṭhamaṃ* means first. *Addakkhiṃ* means he saw. *Satthāraṃ* means the Blessed One.
"Akutobhaya" means fearless. This is the meaning here: because all causes of fear were abandoned right at the foot of the Bodhi tree, there is no fear from any quarter;

thus it is "fearless" (akutobhaya), which is to say, free from fear. He is the Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One, confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, who instructs those to be trained according to their needs through the truths pertaining to this life, the future life, and the ultimate goal—[I pay homage] to him together with my grandfather.
Having gone there, at whatever time I first saw that Supreme Person, the foremost individual in the world with its gods,
and having seen him, thereafter— on account of that sight, following that vision—

I was moved by a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "For so long a time I have not been able to see the Teacher nor hear the Dhamma," and knowledge accompanied by moral dread (*sahottappa*) arose within me. Thus, being moved by this urgency...
With the verse beginning "Siriṃ hatthehi," he shows that I thought thus: "The meaning of this is as follows— whatever man, seeking wealth,

might push away and drive out with his hands and feet Siri (Fortune) who has approached the bed in bodily form, thinking, 'I will remain in your presence as an attendant'— such a person is one lacking in luck."
The intention is: "Having pleased such a teacher, the Sammasambuddha, and having obtained him at this ninth moment, I would fail him by not following his instruction;
I, however, do not do so. Therefore he said: "Then I... [until] the homeless life. In that context, *chaḍḍayiṃ* means "I abandoned.
There is also a reading *chaḍḍiyaṃ*. Now, is it not this Elder?
Since he had gone forth without even taking a wife, why did he say, "I have abandoned children and wife"?

This should be understood as follows: it is just as if a man were to cut down a tree that has not yet produced fruit; by cutting it down before the fruit could be obtained from it, he is indeed deprived of what he might have gained. It is exactly like this case.
"Endowed with the training and the mode of livelihood" means: being possessed of that training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*),
and being endowed with the mode of livelihood (*sājīva*)— consisting of those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the Blessed One wherein monks live together,
share a common life, and conduct themselves in a similar manner— and thus being fully equipped through the state of training, fulfilling the training and not transgressing the mode of livelihood.
The meaning is: "having sacrificed, he accomplishes both. By this, he shows the state of being established in the very pure morality of the Pātimokkha.
"Well-restrained in the sense-faculties" means well-restrained in the six faculties, including the mind.

It means that the doors of the eye and so forth are well-shuttered by the bolt of mindfulness, by way of preventing the occurrence of covetousness and other such states that arise toward objects such as forms.

The meaning is as follows. Thus, by demonstrating the perfection of virtue consisting in restraint according to the Pātimokkha and restraint of the sense faculties, other forms of virtue are also effectively demonstrated by implication.

Having thus shown his own perfection of the fourfold pure virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), the Elder, with the words "paying homage to the Fully Awakened One," spoke of his application to the cultivation of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*).
"I dwelt unconquered" means [unconquered] by the Māra of the defilements (*kilesamāra*) and so forth.
The meaning is: "Having dwelt as one truly unconquered" means that until the attainment of *arahantship*, he remained unoverpowered by them, dwelling instead in a state of overcoming them.
"Therefore" (*tato*) means for that reason; because he was of perfectly purified virtue, possessed deep confidence in the Teacher, and [engaged] in the practice of overcoming the defilements.
Therefore, it is "steadfast. *Paṇidhi* means aspiration (*paṇidhāna*), or the directing of the mind (*cittābhinīhāra*) toward that.

*Āsi* means "was" (*ahosi*). "Longed for by the mind" means desired by my own heart. But what is it like? He says: "One should not sit down for even a moment as long as the arrow of craving has not been extracted.
"As long as the arrow of craving has not been pulled out from my heart with the forceps of the supreme path, one should not sit down for even a moment; one should not remain seated."
"I would not allow it"— this was the direction of my thought, such was the meaning.
Having thus resolved his mind and practiced meditation, spending the night solely in standing and walking,
he emerged from the formless attainments, established insight by way of the factors of jhāna, and realized arahantship.
Therefore it was said: “Of me, who... and so forth. “Nirupadhī” means free from acquisitions (nirupadhi) due to the absence of the acquisitions of defilements (kilesupadhi) and the rest.
“Ratyāvivasāne” means at the passing away of the portion of the night, when the night has dawned. “Patī sūriyuggamanaṃ” means having made the rising of the sun the sign (lakkhaṇa).

“Sabbaṃ taṇhaṃ” means having dried up the entire stream of craving (taṇhāsota), consisting of the various types such as sensual craving (kāmataṇhā) and the rest, by means of the supreme path (aggamagga).
"Having dried [the mind], do not sit down until the arrow of craving has been extracted"—this was said because he had been released by his promise.
"He sat down cross-legged" means that he sat having folded his legs in the *pallaṅka* posture. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāpanthaka is finished.
The commentary on the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta is finished.
9. Navaka-nipāta 1.
Commentary on the Bhūta Thera-gāthā.
In the Navaka-nipāta (The Book of Nines), there are the verses beginning with "When suffering," etc., spoken by the Venerable Bhūta Thera. What is their origin?

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation through various births, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having attained maturity, he received the name Sena.
One day, having seen the Teacher, he praised him with four verses beginning with "The Bull, the Excellent One," his mind filled with serene faith.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in a village near the gateway of the city of Sāketa, as the son of a very wealthy merchant. It is said that when this merchant’s son was born...

The boys who were born were eaten by a certain yakṣa who harbored a grudge; however, because this [last] child was in his final existence (*pacchimabhavika*), the spirits (*bhūta*) took up his protection.
The yakṣa went to the service of Vessavaṇa and did not return again.
On the day of his naming ceremony, thinking, "If it is done thus, the non-human beings (*amanussa*), out of compassion, will protect him," they gave him the name Bhūta.
They did so. By the power of his own merit, however, he increased without any obstacle;
all the details, such as "he had three palaces," are to be understood just as in the description of the wealth of the young man Yasa.

When he reached the age of discretion, while the Teacher was staying at Sāketa, he went to the monastery together with the lay followers. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he acquired faith.
Having gone forth, while dwelling in a cave on the bank of the river named Ajakaraṇī, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and before long attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Bull, the Excellent One, the Hero, the Great Sage, the Victor;”
Who, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One, golden-hued, would not feel serene confidence?
Like the Himalayas, immeasurable; like the ocean, difficult to cross—so too is the meditative absorption of the Buddha. Who, having seen it, would not feel serene confidence?
“As the earth is immeasurable, and as forests are the ornaments of the woods, even so is the virtue of the Buddha; who, seeing this, would not have faith?
As space is uncountable and undisturbed by the force of the wind,”
“Even so is the knowledge of the Buddha; who, having seen it, would not have faith?
Having praised the Supreme Buddha, Siddhattha, the Unconquered, with these four verses, the brahmin named Sena—”
“For ninety-four eons, you did not fall into an unhappy destination;
you experienced abundant happiness and prosperity in happy realms.
Having honored the Leader of the World for ninety-four eons,”
I do not recall ever being born in a state of misery; this is the fruit of my praise.
In the fourteenth aeon, there were four Uggatas, wheel-turning monarchs of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, however, on another occasion he went to Sāketa out of compassion for his kinsmen;
after staying for a few days in the Añjana Forest while being attended by them, desiring to return once more to the very place where he himself had lived, he made preparations for the journey.
He showed it to them. His kinsmen entreated the Elder, saying, “Venerable sir, please dwell right here; you will not suffer, and we too shall increase in merit.
The Elder, declaring his own delight in solitude and the comfort of that place, said:
“When the wise man knows that aging and death are suffering, whereas the ignorant worldlings are attached to them;”
Having fully understood suffering, he meditates with mindfulness alone; hence he finds no greater delight than that.

“When he has abandoned craving—which brings about suffering, which consists of the proliferation of conceptualization, and which carries along the suffering of clinging—then he meditates with mindfulness alone; hence he finds no greater delight than that.”
“When one has seen with wisdom the auspicious, supreme path leading to the two and four fruits,
which purifies all defilements, and meditates mindfully, one finds no greater delight than that. When one has seen the sorrowless,
dustless, unconditioned, peaceful state, which purifies all defilements— ”
He develops that which cuts the bonds of the fetters; he finds no greater delight than that.

When the drum of clouds thunders in the sky, and the paths of the birds are filled on all sides with torrents of rain, the bhikkhu meditates as if gone to a mountain cave; he finds no greater delight than that.
“When one sits on the bank of rivers thick with flowers, adorned with variegated woven garlands,
and meditates like a noble elephant, one finds no greater delight than that.
When at midnight in the secluded forest, while the rain falls and the fanged beasts roar...”
The bhikkhu meditates as if gone to a mountain cave, yet he finds no greater delight than that.
When he restrains his own discursive thoughts and is settled in a mountain glen amidst the mountains, free from fear and free from barrenness, he meditates; yet he finds no greater delight than that.
“When one is happy, having destroyed all stains and grief,
being unhindered, free from craving, and without taints; when one has indeed brought an end to all taints, then one meditates.”
“Then one finds no greater delight than this”—thus he spoke these verses.
Herein, the commentary on the meaning of the first verse by way of the construction of its words is as follows: the ripening of the aggregates is aging (*jarā*).
Their dissolution is death (*maraṇa*). And here, by the heading of “aging and death,” those phenomena possessed of aging and death are included. “This, namely, aging and death...”

When wise monks— who, being mindful and clearly comprehending, are learned— have, by means of the wisdom of the path accompanied by the wisdom of insight, fully understood that to which the ignorant worldlings,
not knowing things as they truly are, are attached, bound, and clinging within the five aggregates of clinging— that "this is suffering, this is the extent of suffering,
there is nothing beyond this"— then, in this very teaching, when the wise monk... [is established].

At whatever time one meditates by closely contemplating the characteristics [of phenomena], one finds and does not obtain any delight more supreme or more excellent than the delight in insight and the delight in the paths and fruits. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Whenever he comprehends The arising and passing away of the aggregates;”
One who understands that gains rapture and gladness, for that is the deathless.
"The fruit of stream-entry is superior to sole sovereignty over the earth, to going to heaven, or to lordship over the entire world."

Having thus shown the delight in seclusion by way of the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*), he now spoke the three verses beginning with the second in order to show it also by way of the clear realization of abandonment (*pahāna-abhisamaya*) and so forth. Therein, "bringing about suffering" (*dukkhassāvahaniṃ*) means the future occurrence of suffering;
the meaning is that it is the producer of suffering. "Clinging" (*visattikā*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*). For it is called "clinging" (*visattikā*) because it clings (*visatā*).
It is called *visattikā* because it is extensive; it is called *visattikā* because it has spread out; it is called *visattikā* because it adheres;

it is called *visattikā* because it carries poison; it is called *visattikā* because it is deceptive; it is called *visattikā* because its root is poison; it is called *visattikā* because its fruit is poison; it is called *visattikā* because its enjoyment is poison;
or else, that craving is "extensive" (*visālā*) with respect to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, mental phenomena, and clans.
In the *Gaṇa*, "proliferations" (*papañca*) are called "entanglements" (*visattikā*).
They are called "proliferations" because they cause the continuum of beings to proliferate—that is, to expand—within *saṃsāra*; these are lust and so forth, as well as conceit and so forth.

These very things are "masses" (*saṅghāta*) in the sense of being a mass of the suffering of occurrence (*pavatti-dukkha*), and they are "suffering" (*dukkha*) because their intrinsic nature is that of distress and fever; thus, they are "the suffering that is a mass of proliferation" (*papañca-saṅghāta-dukkha*).
Because it carries one toward and brings about rebirth, it carries the suffering known as *papañca*. "Having abandoned that craving" means having eradicated it by means of the Noble Path.
"Peaceful" (*siva*) means secure; the meaning is that, by eradicating the defilements which cause insecurity, one is no longer afflicted by them.
Because it possesses two or four factors by way of right view and the others, and leads to the Noble Nibbāna, it is called "leading with two or four factors" (*dvecaturaṅgagāmin*);
it should be understood that here the elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti*) has been made for the sake of metrical ease in the verse.

Because it is the most excellent among all paths, such as the path to rebirth in the form realm, it is the "supreme path" (*magguttama*). Thus the Blessed One said: "Of paths, the Eightfold is best," and so forth. By all...

Because it purifies beings from the stains of defilements, it is the "purifier of all defilements. "Having seen with wisdom" means having fully realized through the wisdom of penetration by way of the clear comprehension of cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*).
It is "sorrowless" (*asoka*) because of the absence of causes for sorrow and because there is no cause for sorrow for the person therein. Likewise...
It is "dustless" (*viraja*) because it is free from the dust of lust and the other defilements. It is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) because it is not constructed by any cause.

It is the "peaceful state" (*santaṃ padaṃ*) because it is the subsiding of all defilements and all suffering, and because it must be attained and reached by those who have seen the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
It is so called because it serves as the means for cleansing the continuum of beings of all the stains of the defilements.
It is the purifier of all defilements. "He develops" means he realizes it through the process of realization (abhisamaya) by way of direct experience (sacchikiriyā).
For this is said with reference to one who repeatedly brings about the realization of direct experience concerning Nibbāna;

having attributed the specific qualities found in the subject to the object, it is thus described. It is the "severer of the bonds of the fetters" because it cuts through the bonds known as the fetters (saṃyojana).

In this context, the causal sign (*nimitta*) is figuratively designated by way of its state as the agent (*kattubhāva*), just as the truths that produce the state of an Ariya are called "Ariyan Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*).
Just as in the previous verses the construction was: "When one meditates (*jhāyati*), then one finds no greater delight than that," so here the construction is:
"When one develops (*bhāveti*), then one finds no greater delight than that."

Thus, the Elder, having declared his attainment of *aññā* (full knowledge) by describing his penetration of the Four Noble Truths through these four verses—without yet introducing himself—now spoke the verse beginning with "When in the sky...
to demonstrate the comfort of the secluded place where he was dwelling.
Therein, "in the sky" (*nabhe*) means in the atmosphere. Because of its smooth and deep resonance, the cloud itself is the drum (*dundubhi*).
"Cloud-thunder": *dhārākulā* means "agitated by showers" due to the streams of rain falling on all sides.
The construction is: "in the path of birds (*vihagapatha*), that is, in the sky (*nabha*), because it is the route for the movement of birds (*vihaga-pakkhī*).

"From there" (*tato*) means from the delight in meditation (*jhānārati*). "*Kusumākulānan*" means of those crowded with flowers fallen from the trees. "*Vicittavāneyyavaṭaṃsakānan*" [refers to] in the forest...
Because they possess wild flowers (*vāneyya*) grown in the forest, these rivers have variegated wild-flower garlands;
thus, "possessing variegated wild-flower garlands" means having various kinds of forest-flower garlands.
One who meditates with a mind that is beautiful by virtue of superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) is called "Sumana."
“Nisītha” means at night. “In a secluded place” (rahitamhi) means in a remote spot, free from the crowding of people. “Devā” means clouds.
“While they are dripping” (gaḷantamhi) means while they are raining, with streams of rain pouring down. “Tusked beasts” (dāṭhino) refers to adversaries such as lions, tigers, and so forth;
for they are called “tusked ones” because their weapons are their tusks. The phrase “the tusked ones roar” is also included here specifically for the purpose of showing solitude from people.

"By restraining discursive thoughts" means having suppressed one's own wrong thoughts, such as sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*), by the power of their opposites, because they are included within one's own mental continuum (*attasantāna*).
Alternatively, the word "by oneself" (*attanā*) should be construed with the phrase "he finds no greater joy than this":
"therefore he finds no greater joy than that by himself. "In the midst of mountains" means among the mountains. "A mountain cleft" means a mountain cave.
Or a mountain slope. "Seated" (*samassita*) means supported or approached. "Free from distress" (*vītaddara*) means one whose fever of defilements has departed.
"Free from the cross-bar" (*vītakhila*) means one who has abandoned the mental cross-bar. "Happy" (*sukhī*) means made happy by the bliss of *jhāna* and so forth.

"Destroyer of stains, cross-bars, and grief" (*malakhilasokanāsana*) means the abandoner of the stains such as lust, the five mental cross-bars, and the grief caused by separation from relatives and the like. "Without a bolt" (*niraggaḷa*): here, "bolt" (*aggaḷa*) is said to be...
Because ignorance prevents entry into the city of Nibbāna, he is "without a bolt" (*niraggaḷa*) due to its absence. "Free from craving" (*nibbaṇatha*) means one who has removed craving.

"Thornless" (*visalla*) means one whose thorns of passion and so forth have departed. Regarding "all taints" (*sabba-āsava*), this refers to all taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).
"One who has brought them to an end" (*byantikata*) means one who, having made an end through the Noble Path, stands established for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life. When...
"He meditates; therefore, he finds no delight greater than the delight in meditation"—this is the construction of the sentence.
Having spoken thus, the Elder went to the very bank of the Ajakaraṇī river.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhūta is finished.
The commentary on the Navaka-nipāta is finished.
10. The Dasaka-nipāta. 1.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kāḷudāyi.
The verses beginning with "Aṅgārino" in the *Dasakanipāta* belong to the Venerable Elder Kāḷudāyi. What is their origin?
He too was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha.

While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who inspire confidence in families. Witnessing that, [he made a resolution].
Having performed the work of making the resolution (*abhinīhārakamma*), he aspired for that particular position.

Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, on the very day the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of our mother, he himself took rebirth in Kapilavatthu in the house of a minister. By the Bodhisatta...
Because he was born on the very same day as [the Bodhisatta], they placed him on a cushion of fine linen on that very day and led him to attend upon the Bodhisatta.
For these seven— namely, the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four treasures, the state elephant Ārohaṇiya,
the horse Kaṇḍaka, and Channa Kāḷudāyin— were all born on one and the same day.
They were named Sahajāta. Then, on the day of his naming ceremony—which was a day of great joy for the entire city—they gave him the name Udāyin because he had been born on such an occasion;
however, due to his slightly dark complexion, he became known as Kāḷudāyin.
He grew up playing with the Bodhisatta during their childhood games.
Later on, when the Lord of the World had gone forth on the Great Renunciation, had gradually attained omniscience,
and was dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma,
King Suddhodana heard this news and dispatched a minister accompanied by a thousand men, saying, "Bring my son here."

Thus, at the time for the teaching of the Dhamma, he went into the presence of the Teacher; standing at the edge of the assembly, he heard the Dhamma and, together with his followers, attained arahantship.
Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, they all became as if sixty-year-old elders, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power. Arahantship.
But from the moment they attained the Path, the Noble Ones became entirely equanimous; therefore, he did not relate the message sent by the king to the One of Ten Powers.
The king, thinking, "Neither does the commander of the forces return, nor is any message heard," dispatched yet another minister with a thousand men.
When that one also behaved in the same manner, he sent another—thus, by means of nine ministers in succession...
He sent nine thousand men along with him, and all of them, having attained *arahantship*, became silent.
Then the king thought: "Because these people lacked affection for me, they said nothing to the One of Ten Powers regarding his coming here;
however, this Udāyī is of the same age as the One of Ten Powers and was his playmate since childhood. In my..."
Thinking, "He is affectionate; I shall send him," he summoned him and said, "Dear son, go to Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men and bring the One of Ten Powers here.
As he was departing, he said, "If I may receive the going-forth, O King, then I shall bring the Blessed One here," and having said this, [he added], "By whatever means possible, for my sake..."
When he was told, "Show me your son," he went to Rājagaha and stood at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher’s time for preaching the Dhamma.
Having heard the Dhamma, he and his retinue attained Arahatship and were established in the status of "Come, Bhikkhu. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"To Padumuttara Buddha, the World-Chief, the Neutral One..."
While he was traveling on his journey, engaged in his wandering at that time,
I took a full-blown lotus, as well as blue and white water-lilies,
and having taken some exquisite rice, I gave it to the Teacher.
“The Great Hero partook of the finest food, a most excellent meal;
and taking that flower, he showed it to the people:
‘This is desirable, lovely, and dear in the world—the supreme flower born from water.’”
“Very difficult indeed has been accomplished by him who gave me this flower.
I shall praise him who offered me the flower and gave me the finest rice; listen as I speak.”
“Ten and eight times he shall exercise sovereignty over the gods;
moreover, [he shall possess] blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white jasmine.
Through the ripening of his merit, [he shall have] that which is endowed with divine fragrance.”
“Having made a canopy in the sky, he shall sustain it for that long.
Twenty-five times he will become a wheel-turning monarch;
he will dwell upon the earth, ruling over the kingdom for five hundred years.”
“In a hundred thousand eons, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a teacher in the world.
Delighting in his own deeds, urged on by the root of merit, he shall appear.”
He will be a kinsman and relative of the Sakyans, bringing them joy. Having gone forth later in life,
impelled by the root of his wholesome merit, he will,
through the full understanding of all taints, attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
“Gotama, the Kinsman of the World, will place him— who has attained the analytical knowledges, who has done what was to be done, and who is free from taints— at the very pinnacle.
Having exerted himself in striving, he is peaceful and free from acquisitions.”
“There will be a disciple of the Teacher named Udāyī by name.
Having fully understood all taints— lust, hatred, delusion, conceit,
and hypocrisy— I dwell free from taints.”
“Exerting myself and being wise, I pleased the Fully Awakened One;
and the Fully Awakened One, being pleased, placed me in the foremost position.
‘The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having attained Arahantship, he waited for the right time, thinking: "This is not yet the time for the One of Ten Powers to go to his native city;
rather, when spring has arrived and the groves of trees are in bloom, and the ground is covered with green grass, it will be the time to go.
When spring had come, he began to praise the path for the Teacher’s journey to his native city:
“Now the trees are like glowing coals, O Blessed One, having shed their foliage and bearing fruit;
they shine forth as if possessed of flames. This is the time for the Bhāgīrathīs, O Great Hero.
These blossoming trees, so delightful to the mind, waft their fragrance in all directions.”
“Having abandoned the bowl and hoping for fruit, it is time for you to depart from here, O Hero.
‘It is neither too cold nor too hot; the weather on the road is pleasant, O Blessed One.
Let the Sākiyas and the Koḷiyas see you crossing the Rohiṇī river with your face turned toward the west.’”
“Out of hope one ploughs the field; out of hope the seed is sown;
out of hope merchants go forth to the ocean, seeking wealth.
May that hope for which I stand be fulfilled for me.”
“Again and again they sow the seed; again and again the king of the gods sends down rain;
again and again the farmers plow the field; again and again grain comes to the kingdom.
Again and again beggars wander about; again and again the masters of giving bestow gifts.”
Giving again and again, the lords of charity reach the heavenly realm again and again.
"The Hero indeed purifies seven generations in whichever family he is born, he of vast wisdom;
I believe the God of Gods honors that family, for by you was born the Sage whose name is Truth."
“Suddhodana was the name of the Great Sage’s father, while the Buddha’s mother was named Māyā;
having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb, she rejoices in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven upon the breaking up of the body.
Having passed away from here and died, that Gotamī has become endowed with celestial pleasures.”
She rejoices with the five strands of sensual pleasure, surrounded by those hosts of devas:
“I am the son of the Buddha, the conqueror of the unconquerable, of Aṅgīrasa, the peerless Tathāgata.
You, Sakka, are my grandfather; by Dhamma, Gotama, you are my great-grandfather.”
He spoke these verses.

Regarding them: "Aṅgārino" means like charcoal; the flowers and sprouts of the trees have the color of red coral, and because they possess these, they are called "aṅgārino"—they are as if strewn with a shower of charcoal by means of their exceedingly red blossoms and shoots.
*Viyāti* means "in this. *Idāni* means "at this time. *Dumā* means "trees. *Bhadante*: because "bhadda" (blessing) is at the end (*ante*) of this, it is called *bhadanta*;
having elided one *da*, it is so spoken. It refers to the Teacher, who is endowed with distinguished qualities and is the foremost among those endowed with distinguished qualities.
Therefore, "Bhadante" is an address to the Teacher. And this is the nominative singular ending in *-e*.
[It is used] as in such passages as “sukaṭe paṭikamme sukhe dukkhepi ce. However, here it should be understood in the sense of an address (*sambodhana*).
Therefore it was said: “‘Bhadante’ is a form of address. Some say: “It is another word having the same meaning as the word *bhadda*.
They seek fruits, thus they are “fruit-seekers” (*phalesina*). For even in the case of insentient things, people employ speech by superimposing the activity of a sentient being, just as...
"Desirous of falling from the clan" means that they have begun to take the fruits; the sense is that it is the time for taking the fruit of success (*sampatti-phala*).
"Having cast off the covering" means having abandoned the old leaves; the sense is that they are now possessed of mature, withered foliage.
"They"—referring to the trees—"shine forth like those possessing flames," meaning they illuminate all directions like lamps with their wicks or like blazing fires; this is the intended meaning.
“Samaya” means time; “anuggahāya” (for the sake of favoring) is the ellipsis of the words. “Mahāvīra” means one of great prowess.

“Bhāgī rasānaṃ” means a partaker of the flavor of the meaning and so forth. For this was said by the General of the Dhamma: “The Blessed One is a partaker of the flavor of the meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma,” and so on.
Both “Mahāvīra” and “Bhāgī” should be understood as vocatives.
Regarding the reading *bhāgīrathānaṃ*, Bhāgīratha was the name of the first king. Because they were born of his lineage, the Sākiyas are called Bhāgīrathas;
the intended meaning is "for the benefit of those Bhāgīrathas.
The word *dumāni* is stated with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*); its meaning is "trees" (*dumā rukkhā*). "Blowing forth in all directions on every side" means...
They are in full bloom on all sides, in every part, and in all directions; because they are thus in full bloom, they emit fragrance and release it toward all directions.

"Desiring" (*āsāmānā*) means hoping or wishing to take [the scent]. Having thus shown the beauty of the journey path through the splendor of the trees, he now shows the excellence of the season with the words beginning, "neither too cold. "Pleasant" (*sukhā*) is due precisely to the state of being neither too cold nor too hot.
"Pleasant" means desirable. "Seasons suitable for the journey" refers to weather fit for traveling on a journey.

"Let the Sākiyas and Koḷiyas see her crossing the Rohiṇī with her back turned"—the river named Rohiṇī flows southward from the north between the territories of the Sākiyas and Koḷiyas, and Rājagaha lies to its southeast.
Therefore, as they were crossing that river on their way from Rājagaha to Kapilavatthu, they crossed facing westward.

Thus he said: "Let them see him... crossing. He incited [the people] by saying, "Let the inhabitants of the Sākiya and Koḷiya districts see the Blessed One crossing the river named Rohiṇī facing westward," thus entreating the Blessed One to proceed toward Kapilavatthu.
Now, illustrating his own aspiration through similes, he spoke this verse beginning with “With hope one ploughs.
“With hope one ploughs the field”: when a farmer ploughs, he ploughs the field with the hope for fruit. “Seed is sown with hope”:
having ploughed, the seed is sown—that is, it is deposited—with the very hope for fruit by the one who plants. “Merchants go with hope”: those who carry wealth [go forth].

Just as merchants, seeking wealth, set out upon the ocean by boat to reach their destination, so too do I stand here through this same hope and aspiration—that is, with the very aspiration and longing for which the Blessed One stands here for your sake, namely the aspiration to go to Kapilavatthu.
May that hope of mine be fulfilled; you say, "One must go to Kapilavatthu," and it is through that hope...
And here, he says "desire" (*āsā*) refers to the desire for the wish to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*), because of its similarity [to the farmer's desire].
To show the reason for his repeated entreaty through the description of the path of travel and so forth, the words beginning with "again and again" (*punappunaṃ*) were spoken.
Its meaning is as follows: when the sowing does not succeed merely by being done once, farmers sow again and again, even a second time.
For a third time they sow the seed. Even Pajjunna, the king of the gods, having rained but once, rains again and again from time to time.

The farmers also, having plowed but once, plow their fields again and again to soften the soil or the mud for the sake of a successful harvest. Having gathered the grain but once, [they think], "That is enough."
Because of dissatisfaction, rice and other grains brought repeatedly by people from storehouses and so forth enter and reach the kingdom through the act of depositing them;
likewise, beggars, when begging, visit and approach families repeatedly, not just once, having been asked.
However, those donors give to them again and again, not just once.
Likewise, having given material gifts again and again and having accumulated merit consisting of giving, they repeatedly ascend to heaven;
by way of rebirth-linking, they enter the world of the devas. Therefore, Blessed One, I too ask you again and again for my sake.
The intention is: "Fulfill my heart's desire to the utmost.
Now, in order to show for what purpose he requests the Teacher to go to Kapilavatthu, he spoke the verse beginning with "Vīro have" (The Hero indeed...).
Its meaning is as follows: in whatever family a hero—one who possesses energy, one of great prowess, one of vast wisdom, one of great insight—a person is born...

When [the Buddha] is born there, it is indeed said in the world— and this is a supreme claim beyond others— that "one pair of beings, one pair of men, up to the seventh generation of ancestors, is purified and made right through their correct practice.
But the Blessed One, the God of Gods, the supreme deity among all deities, by warding off evil and establishing them in goodness, [purifies them] even beyond that.
I consider that he is able, indeed capable, to purify [the world]. Why? Because the Sage (muni) born of you is truly named;

for through you, the Teacher, he was born by way of noble birth and attained the state of a Sage. Or, being a Sage, he is "Muni" in the sense of being a thinker (*munana*) regarding his own welfare, the welfare of others, and this world and the world beyond—thus his name is not false.
Or, a Muni is one who possesses silence (*mona*); thus his name as a "recluse," "one gone forth," or "seer" (*isī*) is likewise not false.
He was born by her. Therefore, because he is the cause for sentient beings to obtain absolute welfare, we entreat the Blessed One to go there to you—this is the meaning.
Now, when the phrase "the pair of beings" (*sattayuga*) was mentioned, in order to show the father's pair, it was said: "Named Suddhodana," and so forth.
He is called Suddhodana because his livelihood (*odana*) is pure (*suddha*). For the father of a Buddha is, in every respect, one whose conduct of body, speech, and mind is perfectly purified.
He is one of perfectly pure livelihood because he is endowed with such a resolute intention (*abhinīhāra*).

"Māyā" means she who has received the name "Māyā" because of her qualities—such as excellence in lineage, beauty, virtue, and conduct—which prevent relatives, friends, and others from saying to her, "Do not go [elsewhere]. "Parihariya" means having maintained [that name].
"Upon the breaking up of the body" means after the destruction of his own body, which is like a shrine for the world including the devas.
"In the third heaven" means in the Tusita deva-world.
"She" refers to Queen Māyā. He designates her by her clan name as "Gotamī. "With divine pleasures" means with divine sensual objects included within the Tusita abode.
"Endowed with" means possessed of. "With the strands of sensual pleasure" means with the constituent parts of sensual desire; [the text continues] "with sensual pleasures."
Having said this, he further indicates by the phrase "with the strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇehi*) that she is attended by many types of objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*).
"By them" (*tehi*) means by those hosts of Tusita deities in whichever divine assembly she was reborn, or by those strands of sensual pleasure.
And the use of the feminine gender in the expression "endowed with and surrounded" (*samaṅgibhūtā parivāritā*) refers to her female state established in previous existences and her status as a deity.
Or having made this intention, his rebirth among the devas occurred precisely in his male state.
Thus requested by the Elder, the Blessed One— seeing the attainment of great distinction for many upon going there—
set out from Rājagaha on the road leading to Kapilavatthu by way of a swift journey, accompanied by twenty thousand who were free from taints (khīṇāsava).
The Elder went to Kapilavatthu by means of his psychic power and stood in the air before the king. Seeing a guise such as he had never seen before, the king asked, "Who are you?
To show him, [the Elder] said: "If you do not recognize me as the minister’s son whom you sent to the presence of the Blessed One, then know me thus. And he displayed himself:
“I am the son of the Buddha, the conqueror of the unconquerable, of Aṅgīrasa, the peerless Tathāgata.
You, Sakka, are my father’s father; by Dhamma, Gotama, you are my grandfather,” he said in this concluding verse.
In this context, "I am the Son of the Buddha" means that I am the legitimate son (*orasa-putta*) by virtue of being born from the breast of the Omniscient Buddha.

"The Conqueror of the Unconquerable" (*asayhasāhī*) refers to the fact that prior to his full enlightenment, with the exception of the Great Bodhisatta himself, no others were able to endure or carry [the burden];
thus, he is so called because he endures and carries the entire "unconquerable" (*asayha*) equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) and the office of Great Compassion (*mahākāruṇikādhikāra*).

Furthermore, because it is impossible for others to endure or overcome it, it is so called because of its endurance and overcoming of the five insuperable Māras; and because, through the awakening to the distinctions of dispositions (*āsaya*),
underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), temperaments (*carita*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*), it provides instruction— known as *anusāsani*— to those to be trained according to their needs,
by means of the ultimate truths pertaining to this life and the life to come, which is itself insuperable by others.
Because he accomplishes the Buddha’s work, or because he acts with excellence therein, he is the “Overcomer of the Unconquerable” (*asayhasāhin*). “Of Aṅgīrasa”:
of one who has taken upon himself the perfection of virtue and the other qualities; others say it refers to “the radiance that streams forth from every limb.
However, some maintain that “Aṅgīrasa” and “Siddhattha” were both names given by his father alone. “Of the Peerless” (*appaṭima*): [End of excerpt].
"Of the peerless one. "The steadfast one" (*tādī*) because he has attained the characteristic of equanimity (*tādi-lakkhaṇa*) toward the desirable and the undesirable.
"'You are my father's father'": by way of the noble lineage (*ariya-jāti*), you are the father of my father, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*), according to worldly convention.
"'O Sakka'"—he addresses the king by way of his birth. "'By Dhamma'" means by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); [this refers to] the two types of birth: the noble birth and the worldly birth.
He addresses the king by his clan name, saying "Gotama," because it is the conventional way of addressing someone. "Ayyakosi" means "you are my grandfather.
And here, by saying "I am the son of the Buddha," and so forth, the Elder answered the question indirectly.
Having thus made himself known, the king, delighted and joyful, had him seated upon a magnificent couch. His own...
When a bowl was filled with various kinds of exquisite food that had been prepared and given to him, he made a gesture indicating his desire to depart.
When asked, "Why do you wish to go? Eat," he replied, "I shall eat after going into the presence of the Teacher. [They asked], "But where is the Teacher?
[He said], "Accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus, he is on the road for the purpose of seeing you."
“...practicing. [The king said: “After you have consumed this alms-food, until my son arrives at this city, bring him alms-food from right here.

Having finished his meal and preached the Dhamma to the king and his assembly, the Elder ensured that the entire royal palace was filled with deep faith in the Triple Gem even before the Teacher’s arrival.
While all were looking on, he released into the air the Teacher’s bowl filled with the alms-food that was to be brought;
then, ascending into the sky himself, he presented the alms-food and placed it in the Teacher’s hand.
The Teacher consumed that alms-food. In this manner, as he traveled sixty *yojanas* of road, going a *yojana* each day, day after day—

Having brought food from the royal palace itself, he gave it to the Teacher. Then the Blessed One, saying, "He has caused my father, the Great King, to beautify his entire residence," placed him in the foremost position among those who bring glory to their families.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kāḷudāyin is finished.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ekavihāriya Thera.
The verses beginning with "He walks before and behind" belong to the venerable Elder Ekavihāriya. What is his origin?
This [Elder] as well, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, [served] the Blessed One Kassapa...
Having been reborn in a noble family at the proper time and having reached maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
Having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness and, entering the forest, dwelt in seclusion.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, he was born during this present appearance of a Buddha.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he was reborn as the younger brother of King Dhammāsoka.
It is said that in the eighteenth year after the two hundred years following the Teacher’s Parinibbāna, the Great King Aśoka obtained the consecration of sole sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa;
having appointed his own younger brother, Prince Tissa, to the position of viceroy, [he acted] by means of a certain stratagem.

He caused him to place full confidence in the Teaching. One day, having gone out hunting, he saw in the forest the Elder Yonaka Mahādhammarakkhita sitting while being fanned with a *sāla* branch by an elephant king;
filled with faith, he thought, "O, that I too might go forth and dwell in the forest like this great elder. The elder [perceived] his state of mind...

Having understood this, even as the prince was looking on, he rose up into the air and, standing upon the water of the lotus pond in the Aśoka Monastery—which remained undisturbed—he hung his robe and upper garment in the sky and began to bathe.
Seeing the Elder’s supernatural power, the prince became deeply inspired with faith; he turned back from the forest, went to the royal palace, and resolved, "I shall go forth."
He informed the king. Although the king entreated him in many ways, he was unable to turn him back from his intention to go forth.
Having become a lay follower and longing for the happiness of the going-forth, he said:
“If neither before nor behind Is another to be found...”
"It is exceedingly comfortable for one dwelling alone in the forest.
Come now, I shall go alone to the wilderness praised by the Buddha;
it is a comfort for a bhikkhu who dwells solitary and is resolute."
“Delightful to yogis, charming, and frequented by rutting elephants—
alone and master of my purpose, I shall quickly enter this forest.
In the cool Sītavana grove, amidst the cool mountain caves,”
Having bathed my limbs, I shall walk alone in meditation:
"When, alone and without a companion, in this delightful great forest,
shall I dwell, having done what was to be done and free from taints?"
“May the intention of me who desires to act thus be fulfilled;
I alone shall accomplish it, for no one else is the doer of another’s work.”—
Thus he spoke these six verses.
In that regard, "whether in front or behind" means either in front of oneself or behind oneself;
because the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative, if no other person is found looking on, there is extreme—meaning excessive—ease, which is mental happiness.
"Living alone" refers to being solitary without a companion. "Dwelling in the forest" refers to one whose inclination toward seclusion has been long cultivated.

With his heart being drawn away, he speaks while feeling weary of dwelling in the company of the crowd as he lives day and night surrounded by a great multitude, and while esteeming highly the bliss of seclusion.
The word *handā* is a particle used in the sense of relinquishment; by it, he expresses the certainty of his departure for the forest that is now being undertaken.

"I shall go alone"— because of such statements as, "Householder, the Tathāgatas delight in empty dwellings," I shall go to the forest praised and commended by the Buddhas, alone and without a companion, with the intention of dwelling there. For it is because one who dwells alone,
through the state of being without a companion in standing and other postures, has directed his mind toward Nibbāna and is resolute in his exertion.
The meaning is that for a bhikkhu training in the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), the forest is comfortable, desirable, and brings about happiness.

It is "bringing joy to yogis" (*yogī-pītikara*) because it brings the joy of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and insight (*vipassanā*) to those yogis who are devotedly engaged in cultivation, owing to its quality of being free from noise and the like.
It is "delightful" (*ramma*) because it is suitable for seclusion due to the absence of discordant objects of perception.

“Frequented by rutting elephants” means it is roamed over by excellent, intoxicated tuskers; by this too, he shows the very seclusion from people through its state as a vast wilderness (*brahārañña*).

“One who has mastery over the goal” (*atthavasī*): here, “goal” (*attha*) is intended to mean the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). “How indeed might that come under my control?”—thus he has come under its influence. “Well-flowered” means beautifully blossomed.
“In the cool forest” (*sītavana*) means in a forest endowed with shade and water. By both [of these phrases],...
This explains its very loveliness. "In a mountain cave" (*girikandare*) means within the interior of mountains.
For "kanda" means water; a place hollowed out by that [water] is called a "cave" (*kandara*).

Having dispelled the torment of the heat in such a cool mountain cave, and having bathed and sprinkled my own limbs, I shall walk back and forth alone—this indicates a state of living independent of anything else.
"Alone" (*ekākiyo*) means solitary, without a companion. "Without a second" (*adutiyo*) means being without a second in the form of craving (*taṇhā*).
For craving is called the "second" of a person because it never leaves him. Thus the Blessed One said: "With craving as his second, a person wanders through the long course of existence.
"Wishing to do this for me" refers to going to the forest according to the method described in the passage beginning with "Come, I shall go alone," and applying oneself to meditation (*bhāvanā*).

“May my intention succeed”—meaning, may the aspiration that has arisen thus, “When shall I dwell, having done what was to be done and free from taints (anāsava)?”, be fulfilled and reach its consummation.
And since the attainment of Arahantship is not accomplished by mere supplication, nor is it to be achieved by another, he said: “I alone shall accomplish it; no other is the doer for another.”
Thus, knowing the prince’s firm resolve for the going-forth, King Aśoka had the road leading to the Aśoka Monastery adorned;
then, with great royal splendor and a vast army, he led the prince—adorned with every ornament—to the monastery.
Having gone to the meditation hall, the prince went forth in the presence of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita.
Many hundreds of people followed him into the homeless life. Even Aggibrahmā, the king’s nephew and husband of Saṅghamittā, likewise went forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, joyful and elated, he proclaimed what he himself must now do:
“I bind on my armor; I shall enter the forest.”
I shall not depart from there until I have attained the destruction of the taints.
While the cool, fragrant Maluta breezes blow,
sitting upon the mountain peak, I shall shatter ignorance.
“In the forest, covered with blossoms, surely in a cool mountain glen,
happy with the bliss of liberation, I shall delight in the Giribbaja”—
thus he spoke these three verses.
In this context, "I bind on this armor" means: "I bind on this armor known as energy;
being indifferent to both body and life, I arm myself with the armor of energy. This is what is meant:
just as a brave man, when faced with an enemy and desiring to conquer him, sets aside all other duties and [prepares] by donning his armor and so forth...

Just as one prepares for battle and, having gone to the battlefield, does not turn back without defeating the enemies, so too do I prepare for the battle against the defilements by donning the armor of the energy of the fourfold right effort, disregarding even my burning head and robes;
and until I have defeated the defilements, I shall not abandon the secluded place suitable for victory over them. By that—
It is said: “I shall enter the forest; I will not emerge from it until I have attained the destruction of the taints.
By the words beginning with “When the breezes blow,” he speaks of the suitability of the forest location for the cultivation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The construction is: “I shall surely delight in Giribbaja. Thinking, “I imagine I shall find delight within the enclosure of the mountain,” he is contemplating a future state.
He speaks. The rest is easy to understand.
Having said this, the Elder entered the forest and, practicing the duty of a recluse, went to the Kaliṅga country together with his preceptor.
There, a skin disease arose on his foot; seeing it, a certain physician said, "Venerable sir, ghee..."
"Search for it; I shall treat you," he said. The Elder did not go in search of ghee, but instead applied himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā).

His illness increased. Seeing that the Elder was indifferent toward the matter, the physician himself searched for ghee and cured the Elder of his ailment. Having recovered, before long the Elder attained Arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In this auspicious eon, a man of great fame, a kinsman of Brahmā,
named Kassapa by clan, arose as the best among those who speak.”
“Free from conceptual proliferation, without support, with a mind equal to space;
abundant in emptiness, such a one is a master who delights in the signless.
With an unattached mind and free from defilement, he does not associate with families or groups.”
The Hero of Great Compassion, skilled in the means of discipline,
is ever intent on the welfare of others, training the world including the gods in the path leading to Nibbāna— the destination that dries up the mire of existence.
“The Deathless, the supreme delight, the warding off of old age and death—
he, the Savior of the World, sits in the midst of the great assembly.
The Protector, whose voice is like the karavīka bird, the Tathāgata with the Brahmā-like voice.”
"Rescuing those who have lost their way and are leaderless from great perils,
the Leader of the World was seen by me as he taught the stainless Dhamma.
Having heard his Dhamma, I went forth into the homeless life."
“Having gone forth at that time, reflecting upon the teaching of the Victor,
I dwelt alone in the delightful forest, oppressed by [the need for] company.
The abandoning of self-identity became for me the cause [of my progress].”
“For one whose mind is secluded, who sees the fear in social contact:
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship, while the elder was dwelling there, the king—by the gift of a hundred million—had the Bhojaka-giri Monastery built and settled the elder there. While dwelling there, at the time of his final passing away, he said:
“I have fulfilled my purpose, like the moon on the fifteenth day;
all taints are utterly destroyed, and now there is no further becoming.
Thus he spoke this concluding verse. Its meaning is self-evident. And that itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ekavihāriya is finished.
3. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākappina begins with the verse: "He who perceives the future beforehand... What is his origin?
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the position of chief among those who exhort bhikkhus.
Having performed the appropriate service, he made an aspiration for that very office.
Thus, having performed wholesome deeds there for as long as he lived and wandering among gods and humans, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, he was reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī.
Upon reaching maturity, he became the leader of a group of one thousand men and had a great monastery built, adorned with a thousand cells.
All those people, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as they lived, [followed] that lay follower...
Having made him their leader, they, together with their wives and children, were reborn in the world of the gods and wandered among gods and humans for the duration of one *buddhantara*.

Among them, the leader of the group was reborn in a royal household in a frontier city named Kukkuṭa even before our Teacher was born; his name was Kappina. The other men were [reborn] in that very same place...
They were reborn in the family of a minister in the city. After his father passed away, Kappina Kumāra raised the royal parasol and became known as King Mahākappina.
Because he was devoted to learning, he dispatched swift messengers from each of the four gates at early dawn, saying:
"Wherever you see those who are well-versed in the scriptures, turn back from there and report it to me."
At that time, our Teacher, having appeared in the world, was dwelling in dependence on Sāvatthī.
At that time, merchants living in Sāvatthī took merchandise for trade and went to that city;
having stored their goods away, they announced themselves to the king with gifts in their hands, saying, "We wish to see the king. The king—
Having summoned them and received their offerings, he asked them as they stood there after paying homage, "From where have you come? "From Sāvatthī, Your Majesty," they replied.
"Is your kingdom well-supplied with food, and is the king righteous? "Yes, Your Majesty.
"What kind of Dhamma is currently being practiced in your country? "That, Your Majesty, cannot be told by those with mouths full of leftovers."

The king had water poured from a golden pitcher. Having rinsed their mouths and extended their joined palms toward the One of Ten Powers, they said, "Your Majesty, in our land, the Jewel of the Buddha has appeared.
At the mere hearing of the word "Buddha" from the king's mouth, a rapture arose that pervaded his entire body. Then he said, "O dear ones, 'Buddha'—what does this mean?"
"Speak it," he said. "We say 'Buddha,' O King," they replied. Having had them say this three times, [the king thought], "The word 'Buddha' is immeasurable.
Becoming devoted to that very word, he gave a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and asked, "Speak another.
"O King, the jewel of the Dhamma has appeared in the world," they replied. Hearing that as well, he gave another hundred thousand in the same manner.
“Tell me something else,” he asked. “Your Majesty, that which is called the Jewel of the Saṅgha has appeared.

Having heard that as well, he gave another hundred thousand [pieces of gold] in the same manner and departed from that very spot, thinking, “I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed Buddha.
The ministers also departed in the same way. Having reached the bank of the Ganges with his thousand ministers, he said, “If the Teacher...”

“May the Fully Enlightened One not even wet the hooves of these horses! Having made this resolution based on truth, he crossed the river Gaṅgā which was full up to its banks by means of the surface of the water alone;
he likewise crossed another river half a yojana wide, and having reached the third great river named Candabhāgā, he crossed that too by means of that very same act of truth.
On that very day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of great compassion and, surveying the world, saw:
"Today Mahākappina will abandon his kingdom of three hundred leagues and, accompanied by a thousand ministers, come into my presence to go forth.
Thinking, "It is fitting for me to go out to meet them," he performed his bodily grooming early in the morning.
Having done so, surrounded by the community of monks, he walked for alms in Sāvatthī;

then, after his meal, having returned from the alms round, he traveled through the air himself and sat cross-legged at the foot of a great banyan tree on the bank of the Candabhāgā River, facing the ford where they were to cross, and emitted the six-colored rays of a Buddha. They [crossed] by that ford...
As they looked about at the Buddha’s rays streaming hither and thither, they saw the Blessed One and, upon that very sight, reached the conclusion:
“This is surely the Teacher for whose sake we have come.
Bowing down from the spot where they had seen him, they approached the Blessed One while performing the highest gesture of reverence. The King [approached] the Blessed One...
Taking hold of the Teacher’s ankles and paying homage to him, he sat down to one side together with his thousand ministers.
The Teacher taught them the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, he and the entire assembly were established in Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena...”
“Like the sun risen in the cloudless sky, in the autumnal firmament,
he awakens the lotuses of those to be trained with the radiance of his speech;
the Leader dries up the mire of the defilements with the rays of his wisdom.”
“He destroys the fame of the sectarians as the sun does the light of fireflies;
he reveals the radiance of the true goal like the sun, a jewel.
He is the source of virtues, like the ocean is of jewels.”
Like Pajjunna showering all beings with rain from a cloud of Dhamma, he rained down the Dhamma.
At that time, I was a gambler in the city called Haṃsāvatī;
having approached him, I heard the Dhamma from the one named Jalajuttama.
“The mind of me, who was instructing the monks— those disciples who were accomplished and had fulfilled their task— was satisfied as he manifested his virtues.
Having heard this, delighted and joyful, I invited the Tathāgata.”
Having fed Sāsissa, I aspired for that position: "Behold this great minister,
skilled in legal judgment, who is equal in beauty to a swan and possesses the voice of a swan-drum."
“Falling at my feet, its hair standing on end,
cloud-colored, with full shoulders, and with serene eyes and face—
[he was] a man of great renown, a royal official, accompanied by a vast retinue.”
This is the state of those who have accomplished their task, whom one who aspires with a joyful heart seeks:
“By this prostration, by this generosity, and by these aspirations,
for a hundred thousand eons, he shall not fall into an unhappy destination.”
“Having experienced divine splendor among the gods and greatness among humans,
he will attain Nibbāna with what remains.
One hundred thousand aeons hence, born in the Okkāka clan...”
"One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma,
will be a disciple of that Teacher known by the name Kappina."
“Then, having performed good deeds in the teaching of the Victor,
and having cast off my human body, I went to the Tusita heaven.
Having ruled over the kingdoms of gods and men for hundreds of times,”
Born near Bārāṇasī, in the Keṇiya caste, I,
together with my wife and a retinue of one thousand,
served five hundred paccekabuddhas.
“Having fed them for three months, we afterwards gave them the triple robe.
Having passed away from there, we all became inhabitants of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Again, having passed away from there, we all returned to the human state.”
Born in the city of Kukkuṭa, on the slopes of the Himalayas,
I was known as Kappina, a prince of great renown.
Those born into the families of my other ministers surrounded me alone as my retinue.
“Having attained the bliss of great sovereignty and possessing the fulfillment of all desires,
I heard from the merchants the news of the appearance of a Buddha:
‘A Buddha has arisen in the world, the peerless, the one person.’”
Thus he proclaims the True Dhamma, the deathless, supreme bliss.
His disciples are well-yoked and well-liberated, free from the taints;
having heard their well-spoken words, O merchants, pay them honor.
“Having abandoned my kingdom along with my ministers, I went forth out of devotion to the Buddha;
seeing the great river Mahācanda, filled to the brim and overflowing.
It was without a footing, without a support, difficult to cross, and swift-flowing.”
Recalling the virtue of the Buddha, I crossed over in safety: “If the Buddha,
the wise one who has reached the end of the world, has crossed the stream of existence,
by this utterance of truth may my journey be successful.”
“If the path is the attainment of peace, and liberation is ultimate happiness;
by this utterance of truth, may my journey be successful.
If the Saṅgha has indeed crossed the wilderness, the unsurpassed field of merit;”
“By this utterance of truth, may my journey be successful.
As soon as that supreme truth was spoken, the water receded from the path;
then, having crossed with ease, he reached the delightful riverbank.
“I saw the Buddha seated, like the rising sun that radiates light;
blazing like a mountain of gold, or like a tree ablaze with lamps.
Like the moon accompanied by the stars, he was honored by his disciples.”
Like Vāsava raining down from within a cloud of teaching,
I paid homage and sat down to one side together with my ministers. Then,
knowing our disposition, the Buddha taught the Dhamma to us.
“Having heard the stainless Dhamma, we said to the Victor:
‘Ordain us, O Great Hero; we are weary of existence.
‘Monks, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed for you, leading to the end of suffering.’”
“Practice the holy life,” so said the Supreme Sage.
At the mere utterance of those words, we all— wearing the robes of monks—
became fully ordained and attained the stage of stream-entry within the Teaching.
“Then, having gone to Jetavana, the Guide gave me instruction.
Being thus instructed by the Conqueror, I attained arahantship.
Thereafter, I then instructed a thousand bhikkhus.”
Following my instructions, they too became free from taints.
Pleased by that quality, the Conqueror placed me at the forefront among the great multitude, saying:
"Among those who instruct the bhikkhus, Kappina is the foremost."
“An action performed a hundred thousand eons ago has shown its fruit here to me;
like an arrow released from a bow, it has consumed my defilements.
My defilements have been consumed... [the rest as before]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Having attained arahantship, they all requested the Teacher for the going-forth. The Teacher said to them, “Come, bhikkhus.
That itself was their going-forth and their full ordination. Taking that thousand bhikkhus, the Teacher went through the air to Jeta’s Grove.
Then one day, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus who were his own pupils: “Is it well?”
“Bhikkhus, does Kappina teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus? “No, Blessed One, he does not teach.
He dwells at ease, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life, and he does not give even a mere exhortation.
The Teacher summoned the Elder and asked, “Is it true, Kappina, that you do not give even a mere exhortation to your pupils?”
“It is true, Blessed One. “Brahmin, do not do so; from this day forward, teach the Dhamma to those who approach you.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Elder replied, accepting the Teacher’s word with his head, and by a single exhortation he established the thousand ascetics in Arahatship.
Therefore, the Teacher placed him in the position of a senior disciple in the regular order.
He established him in the foremost position among those who exhort the bhikkhunīs. Then one day, while the Elder was exhorting the bhikkhunīs, he said:

“He who foresees the future, Who sees both what is beneficial and what is harmful— Whether he be one seeking to find fault or one wishing for his welfare, Even when looking closely, they see no flaw in him.”
“For one whose mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled and well-developed,
cultivated in successive stages as taught by the Buddha—
he illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.”
“Truly, my mind is bright, immeasurable, and well-developed;
having burst forth and been uplifted, it illuminates all directions.
Even though his wealth may be exhausted, the wise man truly lives.”
And by the lack of wisdom, even one who possesses wealth does not truly live.
Wisdom discerns what has been heard; wisdom increases fame and renown.
A person endowed with wisdom finds happiness here even amidst sufferings.
“This is not a doctrine of today, nor is it marvelous or extraordinary:
for that wherein one is born and dies—what therein could be considered extraordinary?
For for one who has been born, death immediately after life is certain.”
“Born and born, they die here; such indeed is the nature of living beings.
This is not for the sake of the dead, nor for the sake of those who have passed away, that one should exert oneself for others.
Weeping for the dead brings no fame, no worldly merit, and is not praised by recluses and brahmins.”
“The eye harms the body; by it, beauty, strength, and wisdom decline.
Those who wish him well become joyful for his sake, but those who seek his harm do not find happiness.
Therefore, one should desire to dwell in a family that is wise and learned.”

He observes. "Welfare" (*attha*) means what is to be done (*kicca*). "That twofold" refers to benefit and harm. "Seekers of fault" are enemies; "seekers of welfare" are friends.
"Gaps" (*randha*) means defects. "Looking closely" (*samekkhamānā*) means searching for them. This is what is meant:
that person who, regarding his own welfare-bringing, harm-bringing, or both—whatever task or purpose is yet to come and not yet arrived—observes it beforehand.

One who, like me, sees, investigates, and examines with the eye of wisdom—neither enemies with a desire for harm nor friends with a desire for benefit can find any flaw in such a person. A person endowed with such wisdom is one whose conduct is flawless;
therefore, you should become like that.

Now, demonstrating the virtue of the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*) and applying it to that context, he recited the second verse beginning with "Whose mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānasatī yassā*). Therein, *āna* means inhalation; *apāna* means exhalation.

Mindfulness whose object is the sign of inhalation and exhalation is "mindfulness of breathing. And here, by way of the term "mindfulness," the cultivation of concentration associated with it is intended. "Whose" (*yassa*)—
For that yogi whose [foundations of mindfulness] are fulfilled and well-developed: they are "fulfilled" by the complete perfection of the four foundations of mindfulness and their sixteen aspects;
they are "well-developed" by being thoroughly cultivated and increased through the perfection of the seven factors of enlightenment and true knowledge and liberation;
and they are "gradually accumulated" in accordance with how they were taught by the Buddha, beginning with the words, "Mindful he breathes in," and so forth.
Just as taught by the Blessed One, so too, when practiced, cultivated, and developed in gradual succession, it illuminates this world like the moon released from clouds.
Just as the moon, freed from such defilements as clouds, illuminates this world of space with its lunar light,
even so does that practitioner of yoga, freed from defilements such as ignorance, illuminate it with the light of knowledge.
It illuminates and makes manifest the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*) as it occurs within one's own continuum and within the continua of others.
Therefore, the intention is: "You should develop the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing.
Now, taking oneself as the illustration, he shows the fruitfulness of devotion to cultivation: "O, how white indeed..."
He spoke the third verse: “My mind. Its meaning is as follows: “Truly, my mind is white and pure because it is free from the stains of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Just as the limiting defilements such as lust have been abandoned, and the immeasurable (*appamāṇa*) Nibbāna has been made manifest, so too, through its cultivation, it has been well-developed as immeasurable; for that very reason, the Four Truths have been broken through and penetrated.”
Having been exerted against the entire side of defilement, the directions— beginning with suffering and beginning with the past— shine forth,
because of having crossed over doubt regarding them and because of being free from delusion concerning all phenomena. Therefore, he shows that you too should develop the mind in this way.
Just as wisdom consisting of meditation (bhāvanāmayā paññā) is of great benefit to a person by means of purifying the defilements of the mind and so forth, so too is the other kind [of wisdom].
Demonstrating this, he spoke the fourth verse: “But the wise man lives indeed. Its meaning is as follows:
even one whose wealth is completely exhausted, if he is of a wise nature, remains satisfied with whatever little he has and continues to live by a blameless livelihood. Of him...
For life is indeed what is called "living. Therefore the Blessed One said: "They say that living by wisdom is the best kind of living.
But a person of dull wit, failing to attain wisdom, ruins his welfare both in this present life and in the life to come;

even though he possesses wealth, he does not truly live, for as long as he lives amidst blame and the like, he is not said to be living. Or, due to a lack of skill in means, he squanders whatever he has acquired.
If one squanders wealth, one is not even able to maintain one's life;
