therefore, the intention is that you too, being heedful, must accomplish practical wisdom (*pārihāriyapaññā*).
Now, in order to show the benefits of wisdom, he spoke the fifth verse: "Wisdom discerns what has been heard. Therein:
"Wisdom that discriminates what has been heard": this wisdom is indeed the discriminator of what has been heard;

it generates discrimination regarding the meaning that has entered the range of hearing as it was heard, such as "this is unwholesome, this is wholesome, this is blameworthy, this is blameless," and so forth.
"Increasing fame and renown": it increases fame (*kitti*), which is praise in one's presence, and renown (*siloka*), which is the spreading of one's own nature.

For it is only through wisdom that fame and other such qualities are praised by the wise. "Endowed with wisdom" means being possessed of both the wisdom of comprehension (*pārihāriya-paññā*) and the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).

"He finds happiness even amidst sufferings" means that through right practice toward the aggregates, bases, and so forth—which are by nature exclusively suffering—he attains non-sensual forms of happiness by means of awakening to their true nature as it really is.

Now, while preaching to those bhikkhunīs the Dhamma connected with impermanence which brings about a state of steadfastness, he spoke the remaining verses beginning with “This Dhamma is not of today. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:
This nature of beings—namely, their being born and passing away—is not a Dhamma that has come into existence only today (ajjatana), because it has been occurring continuously.
It is not wonderful, because it lacks the quality of being unprecedented; nor is it marvelous.
Therefore, where one is born and dies—in whatever world a sentient being might be born—one would inevitably die there. What, then, would be marvelous about that? What indeed could be called a marvel?
Because death is natural—for there is no cause for momentary death. For immediately after [birth]...
For one who is born, death from life is certain;
for one who is born, death immediately following birth is inevitable, because the aggregates that have arisen must necessarily perish.
However, the worldly convention that "he lives" here is not certain, because that which is grasped depends upon many conditions. Since this is so, therefore those born here die; such is their nature.
"Indeed, for living beings, this is the nature of things: that what is born must die. By this, he spoke of the fact that birth is followed by death.
Now, because among those bhikkhunīs there were some whose minds were still bound by grief, he said, "This is not for the sake of that," and so forth, in order to dispel their sorrow.
In that context, "this is not for the sake of the dead" refers to that which [is done] for the one who has died.
The weeping for other people and other individuals for the sake of life and on account of life—
let alone for the sake of the life of that deceased being, it serves no purpose whatsoever; and as for those who weep,
their weeping is merely on account of the deceased person, and it brings neither fame, nor worldly merit, nor renown, nor purity.
"It is not praised by recluses and brahmins" means that it is not even commended by the wise; rather, the sense is that it is indeed censured by the wise.

Not only are there these disadvantages for one who weeps, but showing that "these [others] also exist," he spoke the verse beginning with "The eye afflicts the body," and thereafter, for the purpose of warding off misfortunes such as sorrow and so forth, [he spoke on] attending upon spiritual friends.
Enjoining these [points], he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmā*). Therein, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means:
because weeping harms and afflicts the eyes and body of the person who weeps; by that weeping, one's complexion, strength, and intelligence diminish and decline;
and for that weeping person, the quarters become filled with enemies, full of joy and exultation.
They become full of joy. Friends who wish for one's welfare become sorrowful when one is sorrowful;

therefore, because they are endowed with the wisdom of the essence of the Dhamma, the wise person—possessing great learning that is grounded in the welfare pertaining to this very life and so forth—should desire and expect those who dwell in his own family, and he should make them his spiritual associates (*kulūpaka*). "Of whom" means of those...

Just as those who are intelligent, learned, and wise cross a river full of a great flood by means of a boat through the excellence of their wisdom and the power of their wisdom, so too do sons of noble family cross over their own purposeful tasks and reach the further shore.
The construction of the sentence is: "They would desire to dwell in a family."

Thus the Elder, having preached the Dhamma to those bhikkhunīs, dismissed them. Abiding by the Elder’s instruction, they dispelled their sorrow and, practicing with wise application, fulfilled their own goal.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākappina is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka.
The verses beginning with "Slow is my progress" belong to the Venerable Elder Cūḷapanthaka. What is their origin?
Whatever needs to be said here by way of the occasion for the story has already been told in the context of the Mahāpanthaka episode in the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta.
This, however, is the distinction: after the Elder Mahāpanthaka had attained Arahatship and was spending his time in the bliss of the supreme fruit, [Cūḷapanthaka...]
He thought, "How indeed might it be possible to establish Cūḷapanthaka in this happiness as well?
He approached his own grandfather, the merchant Dhanaseṭṭhi, and said, "If you permit me, Great Merchant, I would have Cūḷapanthaka go forth.
"Go forth, venerable sir," he replied. The Elder ordained him. He [was ordained] in ten...
Established in the precepts, he stood before his brother and said:
“Just as a fragrant red lotus might bloom at dawn with its scent unabated,
behold Aṅgīrasa shining brightly, blazing like the sun in the sky.”
While learning a verse, he was unable to master it in four months; each word he learned did not remain in his heart.
Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, "Panthaka, you are incapable in this dispensation; you cannot even learn a single verse in four months.
How then will you bring your purpose in going forth to its ultimate fulfillment?"
"Go forth from here! Thus dismissed by the Elder, he stood weeping near the gateway.

At that time, the Teacher was dwelling in Jīvakambavana. Then Jīvaka sent a man with the instruction, "Invite the Teacher together with five hundred bhikkhus. At that same time, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka—

He was the distributor of alms-food. When he was told, "Venerable sir, please accept alms for five hundred bhikkhus," he replied, "I shall accept it for all except Cūḷapanthaka. Upon hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka became even more deeply distressed.
The Teacher, perceiving his mental anguish, [thought], "Cūḷapanthaka has been treated by me..."
“He will awaken by means of a skillful method. Having thus spoken, he showed himself in a place not far from him and asked, “Why are you weeping, Panthaka?
“Venerable sir, my brother has sent me away,” he replied. “Do not worry, Panthaka; you shall go forth in my teaching.
Come, take this and attend to it, thinking, ‘The dust-remover, the dust-remover. By means of his psychic power, [he gave him]—
Having prepared a pure piece of cloth, he gave it to him.
The man sat down, rubbing with his hand the piece of cloth given by the Teacher, saying, "Dust-remover! Dust-remover! As he rubbed it, it became soiled;
as he rubbed it again, it became like the residue from a mortar. Because his knowledge had reached maturity, he [realized its nature].
He thought thus: "This piece of cloth is naturally pure, yet by depending on this appropriated body it has become defiled and changed;

therefore, just as this is impermanent, so too is the mind. Having established the contemplation of destruction and fall, he produced the jhānas upon that very sign, and having established insight based on those jhānas, [he attained the fruits] together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
He attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the recipient of offerings, was then dwelling in the Himalayas, having withdrawn from the company of the multitude.”
“At that time, I too was dwelling in a hermitage in the Himalayas;
I approached the Great Hero, the Leader of the World, who had recently arrived.
Taking a flower parasol, I went before that Bull among Men.”
As he was entering into meditative absorption, I created an obstacle for him.
Grasping it with both hands, I offered a flower-parasol;
the Blessed One, the Great Sage Padumuttara, accepted it.
“All the gods, their hearts filled with joy, approached the Himālayas;
they uttered cries of ‘Excellent! for the One with Vision will give his approval.
Having said this, those gods drew near to the Supreme among Men.
To one who held an exquisite lotus-parasol aloft in the sky, an ascetic gave me a hundred-petaled parasol.
I shall praise that gift; listen as I speak.
“For twenty-five eons he will exercise divine sovereignty;
and thirty-four times he will become a wheel-turning monarch.
Whatever womb he transmigrates into—whether among the gods or among humans—”
He will hold a lotus that has appeared in the open air:
"In a hundred thousand eons, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a Teacher in the world."
“When my teaching has been proclaimed, he will obtain human birth;
in a mind-made body, he will become supreme.
There will be two brothers, both called Panthaka.”
Having realized the supreme goal, they will illuminate the Teaching.
“At eighteen years of age, I went forth into the homeless life;
yet I found no distinction within the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans.”
“My progress was slow, and formerly I was held in contempt;
even my brother sent me away, saying, ‘Go now to your own home.
Having been thus sent away, I stood at the gateway of the monastery.”
Dejected, I remained there, longing for the state of a recluse.
Then the Blessed One came there and stroked my head;
taking me by the arm, he led me into the monastery.
“Out of compassion for me, the Teacher gave me a foot-wiping cloth;
resolve upon it as pure, resolving upon it as one.
Taking it in my hands, I [prepared] that *kokanada* lake.”
Therein my mind was liberated, and I attained arahantship.
Having reached perfection in all things regarding mind-made bodies,
and having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
“The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Through the path of arahantship itself, the three Piṭakas and the five higher knowledges came to him.
The Teacher went with four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus and sat down on a seat prepared in Jīvaka’s residence. Cūḷapanthaka—
However, because he had not accepted alms for himself, he did not go. When Jīvaka began to offer rice-gruel, the Teacher covered his bowl with his hand.
When asked, "Why do you not take it, venerable sir? he replied, "Jīvaka, there is a certain monk in the monastery.
He then sent a man, saying, "Go, my man, and bring the noble one who is sitting in the monastery."
"Come! Thus the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, having manifested a thousand monks each of whom was unlike any other in appearance and action, sat down.
When that man saw the great number of monks in the monastery, he went and told Jīvaka:
"The community of monks in this monastery is more numerous than the community of monks here; the noble sir who was to be summoned—"
“I do not know. Jīvaka questioned the Teacher: “Venerable sir, what is the name of the bhikkhu sitting in the vihāra?
“He is named Cūḷapanthaka, Jīvaka. “Go, my man, ask ‘Which one is named Cūḷapanthaka? and bring him here.
He went to the vihāra and asked, “Venerable sir, which one is named Cūḷapanthaka? “I am,” [he replied].
"Cūḷapanthaka," "I am Cūḷapanthaka"—in a single utterance, he spoke thus even to a thousand bhikkhus.

He returned again and reported this occurrence to Jīvaka. Jīvaka, because he had penetrated the Truths, thought, "The noble sir must surely possess supernormal power," and having understood it through inference, said, "Go, my man, and first say to the noble sir who is speaking, 'The Teacher summons you.'"
Having said, “Take hold of the corner of my robe,” he spoke. He went to the monastery and did exactly so;
at that very moment, the created monks vanished. Taking the Elder with him, he departed.
At that instant, the Teacher accepted rice gruel and various kinds of solid food. The Blessed One had finished his meal.
When they had finished building the monastery and departed, a discussion arose in the Hall of Dharma: "Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas!
For even one who was unable to memorize a single verse in four months, they have made so mighty in such a short moment.
The Teacher, having heard the conversation of those bhikkhus, came and sat upon the Buddha’s seat.

Having asked, "What do you say, monks? and being told, "This very thing, venerable sir," he said, "Monks, by means of Cūḷapanthaka, my worldly inheritance was obtained in the past, but now, by abiding in my instruction, the supramundane inheritance has been obtained.
When they requested it, he related the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka. Later on, the Teacher, surrounded by a company of noble ones—
Seated on the Dhamma-seat, he placed himself in the foremost position among those bhikkhus who were capable of creating mind-made bodies and those skilled in the turning away of the mind.

On another occasion, when questioned by the bhikkhus, "How did you penetrate the Truths with such sluggish faculties?", he explained his own practice, beginning from the time of his brother's dismissal:
“Slow was my progress, and formerly I was treated with contempt;
even my brother sent me away, saying, ‘Go now, you, to your own home.
Thus, having been sent away, I stood at the gateway of the monastery.”
Dejected, I remained there, longing for the Teaching.
The Blessed One came there and touched my head;
taking me by the arm, he led me into the monastery.
“Out of compassion for me, the Teacher gave me a foot-wiping cloth.
Resolve upon this as pure, well-resolved on one side.
Having heard his words, I dwelt delighting in the Teaching.
I practiced for concentration in order to attain the supreme goal.
I know my former births, and the divine eye has been purified;
the three types of higher knowledge have been realized, and the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
“Having manifested himself a thousandfold,
Panthaka sat in the delightful mango grove until the announcement of the time was made.
Then my Teacher sent me a messenger to announce the time.”
When the time had been announced, I approached from the air.
Having paid homage at the feet of the Teacher, I sat down to one side.
Seeing that I was seated, the Teacher accepted my purpose.
“He is the sacrifice for the entire world, the recipient of offerings;
he is the field of merit for human beings—may he accept this gift.
Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context: *dandhā* means dull; it refers to those who are weak because they are incapable of learning even a four-line verse within four months.
*Gati* means the course of knowledge (*ñāṇagati*). *Āsi* means "was. *Paribhūto* means despised for that very reason, being reproached as "one of confused mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension.

*Pure* means formerly, during the time of being a worldling (*puthujjana*). The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), meaning "and," indicating that it was not only [the teacher] but also his brother.
As if despised, my brother then dismissed me, saying: "Paṇṭhaka, you are dull-witted and seem to lack the necessary cause;
therefore, you are incapable of bringing the purpose of going forth to its fulfillment. You are not fit for this teaching.
Go now to your grandfather's house. Thus he cast me out. "Brother" means by his brother.

"At the gatehouse" means near the gate-tower. "Dejected" means filled with mental distress (*domanassa*). "Having regard for the teaching" means having regard for the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, desiring not to depart from it.
"The Blessed One came there" means that the Blessed One, his mind impelled by great compassion and wishing to favor me, came to the very place where I was standing.
And having arrived, he said: "Paṇṭhaka, I am your teacher, not Mahāpaṇṭhaka; [come to] me..."
"Your renunciation was for my sake," he said, comforting me as he stroked my head with his palm—
a hand adorned with fingers that were webbed, soft, tender, plump, and long, beautiful like a blooming lotus, marked with the wheel-sign—
and thus stroked my head while indicating, "Right now, you shall become my son. Then, taking me by the arm, he said, "Why do you stand here?"
Taking me by the arm with his own hand, which was fragrant with the scent of sandalwood, he led me inside the monastery.
Regarding the phrase "he gave a foot-wiper" (*pādapuñchanī*): having made it a foot-wiper, he gave it;

the meaning is that he gave it while saying, "Consider this a dust-remover" (*rajoharaṇa*). Some read both "he gave" (*adāsī*) and "foot-wiper" (*pādapuñchanī*). However, some [read] "foot-wiper" (*pādapuñchanī*)...
They say, "A piece of cloth for wiping the feet has been placed at your feet. That is incorrect, because it was given as a piece of cloth fashioned through supernormal power (*iddhi*).
Resolve upon this as pure: "It is well-resolved on one side.
Having made this pure piece of cloth well-resolved on one side by means of the mental attention, "It is a dust-remover, a dust-remover," [place it] to one side.
Seated in the secluded Gandhakuṭī, resolve your mind in such a way that it becomes concentrated, and then teach.

Having heard his words—having heard the instruction of that Blessed One—I dwelt delighting in and rejoicing in that teaching and counsel, practicing exactly as directed. And while practicing, [I attained] concentration...
"I practiced for the sake of attaining the supreme goal" means that the "supreme goal" is *arahantship*.

For the attainment of that, one should develop the fine-material jhānas by way of the preliminary work on the *kasiṇas*, establish insight (*vipassanā*) based upon those jhānas, and thus accomplish the concentration of the highest path through the sequence of the paths.
Herein, "concentration" refers to access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).
From the beginning up to the concentration of the fourth path, he is included by way of the commonality of concentration;

however, the concentration of the fruit of Arhatship is included by way of grasping the supreme goal. Moreover, this venerable one was exceedingly skilled in concentration; therefore, it is said that "he established himself in concentration.
Indeed, through his skill in concentration, this venerable one became known as "skilled in the turning away of the mind," as did the Elder Mahāpanthaka.
Furthermore, due to his skill in insight (vipassanā), he is called "skilled in the turning away from perception" (saññāvivaṭṭakusala).
Among them, some describe one as being expert in the characteristic of concentration (samādhi), another in the characteristic of insight; one as being immersed in concentration, another in insight;

one as being expert in the compendium of factors (aṅga), another in the compendium of objects (ārammaṇa); and one as being expert in the defining of factors, another in the defining of objects. Moreover—
The Elder Cūḷapanthaka is described as being especially skilled in the turning away of the mind (*cetovivaṭṭa*) due to his attainment of the four fine-material-sphere jhānas;
the Elder Mahāpanthaka is [described] as being skilled in the turning away of perception (*saññāvivaṭṭa*) due to his attainment of the four immaterial-sphere jhānas.

Alternatively, the first [Cūḷapanthaka] is skilled in the turning away of the mind because, having attained the fine-material-sphere jhānas, he emerged from them with their constituent factors and reached Arahantship.
The other, having attained the formless-sphere jhānas, emerged from the factors of jhāna and reached Arahantship; thus he was skilled in the turning away from perception (*saññāvivaṭṭakusala*).
However, when producing a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), others produce three or four [such bodies], but not many;
they produce them by making them identical to one another, performing only a single kind of kamma. But this Elder—
With a single act of adverting his mind, he created a thousand ascetics; yet he did not make even two of them identical in body, nor did they perform their work in a uniform manner.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who manifest mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
Now, in order to demonstrate the specific excellence he had attained, he said, "I know my past lives," and so forth. And indeed, this—

The Elder possessed the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). However, in order to demonstrate that specific direct knowledge which is of great assistance for the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*), he said, "I know my former births;
the divine eye has been purified," and thus stated, "The three true insights (*tisso vijjā*) have been reached.

For the knowledges of past lives, of the passing away and rebirth according to one's deeds (*yathākammūpaga*), and of the future (*anāgataṃsa*) are of great assistance to the practice of insight (*vipassanācāra*), whereas the other knowledges are not so.
“*Sahassakkhattum*” means a thousand. Some say it means “a thousand times. However, the Elder created a thousand mind-made bodies with a single act of adverting (*ekāvajjana*), not by turns.

Moreover, they were all dissimilar from one another and performed various kinds of work. [Question: “But can such a manifestation of psychic power (*iddhinimmāna*) also occur for disciples? [Answer: It cannot.
However, among all of them, it was this very elder who acted in this way due to the perfection of his resolve;

for he was established in this "foremost position" on account of this specific factor. "Panthaka sat down"—he speaks of himself as if he were another. "In the mango grove" means in the monastery built by Jīvaka in the mango grove.
"Approaching from the air"—*vehāsā* is an ablative used in the sense of an instrumental; thus, *vehāsena*.
*Attha*: the letter *da* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). *Atha* means "after my sitting. *Paṭiggahī* means he accepted the water of donation (*dakkhiṇodaka*).
*Āyāgo sabbalokassa*: because he is the most worthy recipient of offerings for the entire world including the devas, he is the place where one should bring the objects of merit and perform sacrifice.
*Āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho*: because he causes offerings to yield great fruit.
He was the receiver of the sacrificial offerings. He received the offering—consisting of rice gruel, solid food, and so forth—which had been brought by Jīvaka.
Then, having finished his meal, the Blessed One instructed the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka: “Give the blessing of thanksgiving.”

Thus, as if churning the great ocean while grasping Mount Sineru, and as if agitating the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas through his attainment of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā),
he offered an expression of thanks while grasping the Teacher’s intention. Furthermore, although this venerable one was endowed with such a decisive support (upanissaya),
he was constrained by a corresponding fragment of past karma (kammapilotika) and [could not recite] even a four-line verse.

He was unable to grasp it even after months. However, observing his excellence of spiritual potential (*upanissaya-sampatti*), the Teacher directed him toward wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) in accordance with his former conduct.

For at that time, while seated in Jīvaka’s residence, the Blessed One—knowing that Cūḷapanthaka’s mind was concentrated and that insight (*vipassanā*) had entered its course—manifested himself while remaining exactly as he was sitting.
“Panthaka, although this rag may be soiled and covered in dust, there is another kind of defilement and dust in the discipline of the Noble Ones,” he said, showing this:
“Lust is dust, but it is not called ‘dust’ in the sense of fine powder; ‘dust’ is a designation for lust.”
“Having utterly abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust:
‘Hatred is dust… [as before] …in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
‘Delusion is dust… [as before] …in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.’”
He recited these three verses on illumination. At the conclusion of the verses, Cūḷapanthaka attained Arahantship together with the superknowledges and the analytical knowledges.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kappa.
The verses beginning with "Filled with the impurities of various families" are those of the Venerable Elder Kappa. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Upon the passing of his father, he reached the age of discretion and [was adorned] with garments of many kinds, variegated with colors of diverse hues.
Having adorned what is known as a *kappa*-tree with various kinds of ornaments, diverse precious gems, and many sorts of flower garlands and wreaths, he worshipped the Stūpa of the Teacher with it.

Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in the royal family of Maṇḍalika in the kingdom of Magadha; and upon the passing away of his father, he [ascended] to the throne.
Established in sensual pleasures, he dwells exceedingly attached and greedy for them.

When the Teacher, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion, surveyed the world and saw him appearing within the net of his knowledge, he reflected, "What will become of him? and perceived:
"Having heard a discourse on the foul from my presence, this man will become dispassionate toward sensual pleasures, go forth into homelessness, and attain Arahantship."
Knowing that he would reach [that state], he went there through the air and said:
“Filled with various kinds of filth, produced from great excrement,
it is like a ripe cesspool— a great boil, a great ulcer.”
“Filled with blood from the previous [birth], confined within a pit of excrement;
the body is a flow of water, always discharging putridity.
Bound together by sixty sinews, it is smeared with a coating of flesh.”
This useless, putrid body is bound with a leather casing.
"Constructed as an assembly of bones and bound together by cords of sinew,
it performs its postures through the conjunction of many parts."
“Set forth inevitably toward death, in the presence of the King of Death;
having cast off everything right here, a man goes wherever he desires.
The body is shrouded by ignorance and bound by the four ties.”
The body sinks in the flood, ensnared by the net of underlying tendencies.
Engrossed in the five hindrances, possessed by discursive thought,
followed by the root of craving, and covered by the veil of delusion.
“Thus this body proceeds, driven by the machinery of karma;
its success ends in failure, and its various states fall apart.
Those blind fools, mere worldlings, who claim ‘this body is mine’—”
“They increase the terrible cemetery and take up renewed existence.
But those who cast off this body, like a snake sloughing its skin smeared with dung—
having vomited out the root of becoming, they, free from taints, will attain final Nibbāna.”

With these verses, he gave him a discourse on foulness (*asubha*). Having heard from the presence of the Teacher this discourse on foulness—which reveals the true nature of the body in its many aspects and modes—he became terrified, ashamed, and disgusted by his own body.
With a heart moved by spiritual urgency, he paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One."
He requested the going-forth. The Teacher commanded a certain bhikkhu standing nearby:
"Go, bhikkhu, ordain this man and grant him full admission, and then bring him back. He gave him the meditation subject of the fivefold skin and ordained him.
At the very edge of the razor, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the presence of the Blessed One Siddhattha, the most excellent of Stupas,
I hung a variegated cloth and established a wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha).
Whichever womb I was reborn into— whether among the gods or among humans— ”
“Adorning my doorway, the wish-fulfilling tree stands firm.
Both I and my assembly, and whoever else depends upon me—
taking cloth from that tree, we shall always wear it.”
“In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, I planted a tree;
I have never known a miserable rebirth—this is the fruit of that wish-fulfilling tree.
And in the seventh aeon from here, there were eight kṣatriyas named Suceḷa.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, mighty wheel-turning monarchs.

Having attained arahantship and received full ordination, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sitting to one side, spoke these very verses while declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*). For that reason, they became known as the *Theragāthā*.
In this context, "filled with various kinds of filth" means filled with various types of filth from diverse sources;
the meaning is that it is packed with heaps of various impurities such as hair, body hair, and so forth. "The great receptacle for excrement" (*mahāukkāra-sambhava*): *ukkāra* refers to a cesspool.
To whatever extent the mother has aged, for that long a time the mother’s womb is intended here by the term "great receptacle for excrement," because it resembles a cesspool saturated with excrement.
Thus, "born from the belly" means that its place of origin is the belly; hence, "born from a great heap of excrement. "Or like a cesspool" (*candanikam vā*):
a cesspool is a place for discarding used water, womb-impurities, and so forth, which is knee-deep and filled with filth;
such is the meaning. "Ripe" (*paripakka*) means matured or old. By this, it is just as [at] the gate of a village of Caṇḍālas.
In the heat of summer, when the rain falls in large drops, there is a cesspool— filled with various kinds of filth such as urine,
excrement, bones, skin, fragments of sinews, saliva, and mucus, all overflowing with water and churned by mud; which, after a few days have passed, becomes teeming with swarms of worms,
heated by the scorching rays of the sun, emitting foam and bubbles on its surface, dark blue in color, utterly foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.
It stands as something unfit to approach or even to look upon; thus it shows that "this body is of such a nature.

Because it is constantly joined with the root of suffering, because it drips with impurities, and because its inherent nature is to swell, ripen, and break apart through birth, aging, and death, it is like a great boil;
thus it is called a "great boil" (*mahāgaṇḍa*). This is because it is bound by painful sensations at all times, like boils.
Because it must be endured and because it exudes impurity, it is like a great wound; thus it is called a "great wound" (*mahāvaṇa*).

It is "dug out by a cesspool" (*gūthakūpena gāḷito*), meaning it is filled with feces by means of a cesspit or simply by excrement. There is also a textual reading, *gūthakūpanigāḷhito*, which means "emerged from a cesspool.
The body is a flow of water; it always flows with putridity. This body has the nature of constantly oozing due to the water element.
And that which flows out is indeed putrid and impure—bile, phlegm, pus, urine, and so forth; it is never pure; such is the meaning.

"Connected by sixty tendons" means: starting from the upper part of the neck, there are twenty [tendons] binding the body—five each on the front, back, right, and left sides of the body—and those binding the hands and feet...

Having placed five [tendons] on each of their front and back sides, it is "bound and enveloped on all sides by forty-six tendons" (*saṭṭhikaṇḍarasambandho*), meaning by sixty large sinews (*mahānhāru*).
"Smeared with a coating of flesh" (*maṃsalepanalepito*) means anointed with the ointment known as flesh;
the meaning is that it is anointed with nine hundred pieces of flesh. "Encased in a sheath of skin" (*cammakañcukasannaddho*) means [encased] by that which is called skin...
"Completely covered and enveloped by a garment" means it is fully enclosed. "A putrid body" means a body that is entirely foul-smelling.
"Useless" means devoid of purpose; for while the bodies of other living beings might have utility through the application of hides and so forth, the human body is not like that.
"Constructed as an assembly of bones" means by an assembly of more than three hundred bones.
The connection is established. "Bound by cords of sinews" means it is bound by nine hundred sinews that resemble cords.

"Through the coming together of many things" means that through the composite connection of the four great elements, the life-faculty, inhalation and exhalation, consciousness, and so forth—and through the composite union of the tendons—it fashions the postures such as standing and so on, like a machine.
"Set forth for death" means he is going exclusively toward death; it has proceeded from the moment of birth toward death.
For that very reason, he stands in the presence of King Māra, that is, death.
"Having cast off right here" means having abandoned the body in this very world; this being goes to whatever place he desires. Therefore, "having abandoned..."
"This body is subject to going [to its end]"—by this he shows that no attachment should be made.
"Enveloped by ignorance" means covered by the hindrance of ignorance, with its dangers concealed; the intention is: otherwise, who here would produce attachment?
"By the four ties" means by the fourfold tie, beginning with the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhā-kāyagantha*).
"Bound" means tied by way of being a thing to be bound. "Sinking in the flood" means one who sinks in the four floods, such as the flood of sensual desire, by way of being subject to them.
They are called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*) because they lie down (*anu-senti*) repeatedly within the continuum of existence due to their state of not having been abandoned;

these latent tendencies are lust for sensual pleasure and so forth. "Enveloped by the net of those latent tendencies" means overcome by that net. The letter *m* is used here merely to facilitate the euphonic junction (*sandhi*) of words.

It is stated with a long vowel for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukhatthaṃ*). "Intent upon" (*adhimutta*) means being joined with the fivefold hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*);
the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇatthe bhummavacanaṃ*).

"Absorbed in" (*samappita*) means being thoroughly occupied by wrong thoughts (*micchāvitakka*), such as thoughts of sensual pleasure; thus, he is "absorbed in thought. "Followed by the root of craving" (*taṇhāmūlena anugata*) means...
He is bound by the root of existence, which is called craving. "Covered by the veil of delusion" means he is enveloped by the obscuration known as confusion.
All of this is said with reference to the material body possessed of consciousness;
for the conscious personal existence of the Tathāgata remains, O monks, with the cord of existence cut. And this...
In such passages as "the body and externally name-and-form," it is called "body" (kāya). Thus this "body" proceeds;
in this way, by the manner described in such phrases as "filled with various kinds of filth" and "shrouded by ignorance," this body proceeds.

And as it proceeds, it is driven and constructed by the "kamma-machine"—that is, by the machine known as kamma consisting of good and evil deeds. Or, just as [one might proceed] to go to a place of safety...
He is unable [to remain so]; thus, being agitated, he wanders and revolves through happy and miserable destinies.
"Prosperity ends in misfortune": whatever prosperity there is here ends in misfortune.
For all youth ends in old age; all health ends in illness; all life ends in death; every meeting ends in separation.
Therefore he said: “Separation occurs. “Separation” (*nānābhāva*) means being apart (*vinābhāva*), a dissociation;
it is reached or attained in various ways (*vividhaṃ pajjati*), sometimes by way of that which causes the dissociation and sometimes by way of that which is to be dissociated.
“Those who treat this body as ‘mine’” refers to those blind fools, worldlings (*puthujjana*), who [regard] what is thus impure, impermanent, unstable, and suffering...
Those who grasp at this essence-less body, thinking "this is mine," cherish it and give rise to desire and lust.

They repeatedly increase the cycle of existence—which is characterized by birth and so forth, as well as the terrors of hell and other realms, which is dreadful and frightening, and which is called a "mass of filth" because it is to be delighted in only by the foolish—by means of repeated birth, death, and so on.
Therefore, he said: "They take up renewed existence."
"They avoid this body like a snake smeared with dung": just as a person desiring happiness and desiring life,
upon seeing a venomous snake covered in dung, avoids it and does not approach it because of its loathsomeness or its dangerous nature,
even so do those wise sons of noble family [avoid it] because of its loathsomeness due to impurity and its dangerous nature due to impermanence and so forth.
They avoid this body by abandoning desire and lust; they abandon it.

Having vomited up and discarded ignorance—the root of existence—and craving for existence, having abandoned them once and for all, they will, being entirely free from taints, attain final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining and the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kappa is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:
"Secluded, free from noise," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Upasena. What is their origin? It is said that this...
In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī and reaching maturity, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
While listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who are serene in every way.
Having performed a service for the Teacher and made a resolution for that specific status, he practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life.
Having wandered among gods and humans, he was reborn in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance in the womb of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī at Nālakagāma;

his name was Upasena. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas, and having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth, and after one year of full ordination, [entered] the noble womb.
Saying, "I am increasing [the community]," he admitted a certain son of good family into the higher ordination in his own presence and went with him to the Teacher's presence.
When the Teacher heard that this newly ordained bhikkhu had become the resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) of that [elder], he rebuked him, saying:
"O foolish man, you have indeed turned back to abundance far too quickly! [The elder thought: "Now, even though I rely upon this assembly..."
“Though censured by the Teacher, I shall nevertheless gain praise from the Teacher by relying on the assembly itself.
Thus reflecting, he applied himself to the work of insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One Padumuttara, the eldest in the world, the bull among men;”
I approached the Supreme among Men as he was sitting in a mountain cave.
Having seen a *kaṇikāra* flower, I then cut it from its stalk,
adorned it for an umbrella, and offered it to the Buddha.
“I offered almsfood there— excellent food, a most delicious meal—
and on that ninth day, I fed eight ascetics with the Buddha at their head.
The Great Hero, the Self-Existent One, the Supreme Person, expressed his appreciation.”
“By this gift of a parasol, by the offering of excellent food,
and through that clarity of mind, you shall experience prosperity:
thirty-six times as the lord of gods, you will exercise sovereignty over the devas.”
“Twenty-one times he will be a wheel-turning monarch;
his local sovereignty will be vast, beyond all calculation.
One hundred thousand aeons hence, he will be born in the Okkāka clan.”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
In the divine measure of the Dispensation, he will attain human status;
he will be an heir to his teachings, a true-born son fashioned from the Dhamma.”
“One named Upasena will become a disciple of the Teacher;
because of his all-encompassing grace, he shall be established in the foremost position.
My final existence is now unfolding; all states of becoming have been utterly eradicated.”
“I bear my final body, having conquered Māra and his mount.
[He declared: “The four analytical knowledges... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he himself undertook and practiced all the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and for the sake of others as well, he encouraged them to do the same.
He exhorted [the monks], and for that reason the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position among those who are "all-appealing" (*samantapāsādika*).
Later, when a dispute had arisen in Kosambī and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had split into two factions, a certain bhikkhu, wishing to avoid that quarrel, thought:
"Now indeed a quarrel has arisen and the Saṅgha is divided; how now..."
Being asked, "How should I practice? he explained his own practice, beginning with dwelling in seclusion:
"A bhikkhu should frequent a lodging that is secluded, free from noise, and frequented by wild beasts, for the sake of solitary retreat."
“Having gathered [rags] from heaps of refuse, from cemeteries, and from streets;
having then fashioned them into a saṅghāṭi robe, one should wear that coarse garment.
Having humbled the mind, one should go from family to family in regular succession.”
A bhikkhu should wander for alms, guarding his sense-doors and well-restrained.
He should be content even with coarse food and not long for other abundant flavors.
For one who is greedy for flavors, the mind does not delight in meditative absorption (jhāna).
“Let the sage live with few desires, contented, secluded,
and unassociated with both householders and those who have gone forth.
Let him present himself as if he were dull-witted or mute.”
A wise person should not converse excessively in the midst of the Saṅgha.
He should not revile anyone and should avoid causing harm;
he should be restrained according to the Pātimokkha and moderate in his eating.
584. “One who has well grasped the sign, who is skilled in the arising of the mind, should devote himself to serenity at the proper time and to insight at the proper time.
Endowed with persistent energy, one should always be engaged in yoga.”
And a wise person should not place trust until the end of suffering has been reached.
“For a bhikkhu who dwells thus and desires purity,
all taints are exhausted and he attains Nibbāna.”
He spoke these verses.
Therein, "secluded" (*vivitta*) means a forest and so forth, secluded from people, empty. "Quiet" (*appanigghosa*) means soundless, devoid of the clashing of sounds.
"Frequented by wild beasts" (*vāḷamiganisevita*) means inhabited by lions, tigers, leopards, and other wild beasts. By this, too, he demonstrates precisely the seclusion from people.
This is because it illustrates the nature of the robe and the lodging. "Lodging" (*senāsana*) here refers to a dwelling place suitable for lying down and sitting;

this is what is intended by "lodging. "For the sake of seclusion" (*paṭisallānakāraṇā*) means for the purpose of seclusion—that is, for the sake of withdrawing the mind from various objects and causing it to settle properly and repeatedly upon the very subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Having thus pointed out a dwelling place suitable for meditation and demonstrated contentment with regard to lodgings, he now says "heaps of refuse," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that same contentment regarding robes and other requisites.
Therein, "heaps of refuse" (*saṅkārapuñja*) means a heap (*puñja*) of refuse (*saṅkāra*); [it refers to] from such a place of rubbish.
"Having brought" (*āhatvā*) means having carried. "From there" (*tato*) means from those pieces of cloth thus brought.

For in this context, the word "lūkha" (rough) is used in the ablative sense; it is "rough" in the sense of dispraise, such as being rough with a weapon, rough with a hoe, or rough with dust and so forth.
"Dhāreyya" means one should wear it by way of using it as an undergarment and so on; by this, he speaks of contentment with robes.
"Having made the mind humble" means having recollected the advice of the Sugata, beginning with: "Monks, this is the lowest of livelihoods."
Having made the mind free from pride and conceit. "Sapadānaṃ" means without skipping houses; the meaning is "from house to house.

Therefore he said, "from family to family" (*kulā kulaṃ*). "From family to family" (*kulā kulaṃ*) means from one family to another; the meaning is by way of the succession of families, that is, the sequence of houses.
"For alms" (*piṇḍikāya*) means for mixed alms-food; by this he speaks of contentment with alms-food (*piṇḍapātasantosa*). "Guarded in the doors" (*guttadvāro*)...
"With the sense doors of the eye and so forth well-guarded. "Well-restrained" means being thoroughly restrained due to the absence of hand-fidgeting and other such distractions.
Regarding the phrase "even with what is coarse": the word *api* (even) is used in the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*), while the word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*).

By both [phrases], one should be content—equally and rightly satisfied—with whatever is easily obtained, whether it be coarse or fine, or even something very small. Therefore he said: "He does not long for anything else."

"Many flavors. He does not long for another flavor as being many; he should neither long for nor crave any other sweet or refined flavor than what he has obtained himself. By this, contentment even with the requisite of medicine is shown.
Furthermore, stating the reason for restraining greed for flavors: "One who is not free from lust for flavors does not delight in jhāna."
He said, "The mind. The intention is: for one who does not fulfill even the restraint of the faculties, how can there be the concentration of a distracted mind?
Having thus shown the practice of effacement regarding the four requisites, he now said, "And being of few wishes," etc., in order to show the remaining topics of discourse.
Therein, "of few wishes" means having no desire, being free from longing for the four requisites.

By this, he speaks of the suppression of the arising of craving regarding the fourfold requisites. "Contented" means being content with whatever is obtained among the four requisites, such as through contentment with what one has received. For it is said:
"One should not grieve for the past, nor should one long for the future."
"One who should live on what is present is called 'contented.
"Secluded" means having abandoned the company of crowds, secluded in body and withdrawn. For he will speak later of mental seclusion and so forth.
"Should dwell" is to be connected everywhere. A "muni" is one endowed with the qualities of munificence (*moneyya*). "Unmixed" means...
"Unassociated" means devoid of the aforementioned associations, by virtue of the absence of seeing, hearing, conversing, sharing enjoyments, or physical contact.
"With both" means unassociated with both—both householders and those who have gone forth. This is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental.
"He should show himself thus": although he is neither dull-witted nor mute, he should show himself as if he were dull-witted or mute.
"He should show"—by this, he speaks of the abandonment of improper conduct (*pāgabbiya*).

In the phrase "like one dull or mute," the short vowel is used for metrical ease, and the particle *vā* has a conjunctive sense. "He should not converse excessively" means he should not speak beyond measure;
the meaning is that he should be moderate in speech. "In the midst of the Saṅgha" refers to the community of monks or a gathering of people.
"He does not reproach anyone": that bhikkhu who practices according to what has been stated should not reproach anyone in speech, whether they be inferior, middling, or superior.
"He avoids injury": he should avoid physical injury or harassment.
"Restrained by the Pātimokkha": he should be restrained in the Pātimokkha, that is, in the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha.

The meaning is: "One should have body and speech restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint. And regarding "one should be moderate in eating": one should know the proper measure in food with respect to seeking, receiving, consuming, and discarding.
Regarding "one who has well-grasped the sign": [the sign] characterized by the thought, "When I attend to it in this way, my mind became concentrated."
While observing, he should be one who has properly grasped the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*). There is also a reading, “*suggahitanimitto so*,” which means that such a person is a yogi.
Being skilled in the arising of the mind: as he cultivates in this way, he should be proficient in the causes for the arising of a mind that is either sluggish (*līna*) or agitated (*uddhata*).
For when the mind is sluggish, the factors of enlightenment consisting of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*), energy (*vīriya*), and rapture (*pīti*) [should be cultivated].
The enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity are to be developed when the mind is agitated; however, the mindfulness enlightenment factor is required in all cases.

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "But on whatever occasion, bhikkhus, the mind is sluggish, that is the time for the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor," and so forth. One should devote oneself to serenity (*samatha*).

One should develop the cultivation of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*); one should arouse concentration (*samādhi*) that has not yet arisen, and having arisen, one should increase and expand it until mastery is attained—this is the meaning.

And "at the proper time, insight" means that one should not, out of attachment to the concentration already obtained, allow it to become partaking of decline or partaking of stagnation, but rather, by not exhausting that attachment, one should make it partaking of penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*) at the proper time.

And one should devote oneself to insight (vipassanā). Alternatively, "insight at the proper time" means that while practicing serenity (samatha), when it has become stable, one should not fall into contraction but should instead devote oneself to insight for the attainment of the Noble Path. As it is said:
"Or else, by the attainment of concentration, or by a secluded dwelling..."
“A bhikkhu may place his trust [in others], though he has not yet reached the destruction of the taints.
Therefore it is said: “Endowed with persistence and steadfastness,” and so forth. *Sātacca* is the state of being constant; *vīriya-sātacca* is the constancy of energy.
One who is endowed with that, possessed of it, is one whose energy functions continuously, one whose energy is constantly exerted—this is the meaning. One who is engaged in practice (*yuttayoga*).
“Always” means one should always be devoted to meditation. “The end of suffering” refers to the end, the limit, the cessation, and Nibbāna of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*);
until reaching that, one should not go to rest, one should not proceed with confidence.

The meaning is: one should not become complacent, thinking, “I am pure in virtue, an attainer of *jhāna*, an attainer of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and I stand having brought insight (*vipassanā*) to its peak.”
"Of one dwelling thus" means of one dwelling by way of the method culminating in the application of effort through insight, such as resorting to secluded lodgings and so forth.
"Desiring purity" means desiring the purification of knowledge and vision, absolute purity, Nibbāna, and Arahantship.
For the bhikkhu who perceives fear in saṃsāra, all taints—beginning with the taint of sensual desire—are [abandoned].

They waste away and go to destruction; through that very process of going to destruction, one attains and reaches the twofold Nibbāna—distinguished as *sa-upādisesa* (with residue remaining) and *an-upādisesa* (without residue remaining).
Thus, under the pretext of giving advice to that bhikkhu, the Elder declared his own state of *aññā* (final knowledge), illuminating the fact that he himself had practiced in such a manner.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta is finished.
7. The commentary on the verses of the Elder (Apara-)Gotama begins with the verse starting, "One should understand one's own welfare. What is the origin [of these verses]?

This man also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn even before the arising of our Blessed One in a family of northern Brahmins in Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity, he became a master of the three Vedas; having mastered the path of debate, he [stood] above his own doctrine.
Failing to find anyone who could speak superior to him, he wandered about engaged in contentious debate with various people.

Then our Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, gradually guided those to be trained, such as Yasa and others, and eventually arrived at Sāvatthī at the request of Anāthapiṇḍika.
At that time, during the Teacher’s acceptance of the Jetavana...
Having gained faith, he approached the Teacher, and after hearing the Dhamma, he requested the going forth.
The Teacher commanded a certain alms-collecting bhikkhu: "Bhikkhu, give this man the going forth.
While being given the going forth by him, he attained Arahantship at the very edge of the razor; then, having gone to the Kosala country and dwelt there for a long time, he returned once more.
He returned to Sāvatthī. Many of his kinsmen—wealthy brahmins—approached him, paid their respects, and sat down, asking:
"In this world there are many ascetics and brahmins who claim purification within the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
Among them, whose doctrine is truly liberating? How must one practice to be purified from the cycle of existence? The Elder [responded] to them...
To clarify this point, he said:
“One should understand one’s own goal, and one should look to the true teaching;
and whatever therein is appropriate for one who has entered the state of a recluse.”
“A virtuous friend in this world, extensive training and undertaking of vows,
and heeding one’s teachers— this is fitting for a recluse.
Reverence for the Buddhas, and honor toward the Dhamma as it truly is;”
And honoring the Saṅgha— this is fitting for a recluse.
Being intent on proper conduct and range of activity, with livelihood purified and beyond reproach,
and the settling of the mind— this is fitting for a recluse.
“Conduct and restraint, a deportment that inspires confidence,
and application to higher mental states— this is fitting for a recluse.
Dwellings in the forest, remote and free from noise;”
These things should be cultivated by the sage; this is what is fitting for a recluse:
virtue and great learning, the investigation of phenomena as they truly are, and the realization of the truths—this is what is fitting for a recluse.
“One should cultivate the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, and the perception of foulness;
and a lack of delight in the world—this is appropriate for a recluse.
One should also cultivate the factors of awakening, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers.”
“The Noble Eightfold Path—this is what is fitting for a recluse.
‘The sage should abandon craving and shatter the taints along with their roots;
he should dwell liberated—this is what is fitting for a recluse.’”
He spoke these verses.
Therein, "one should understand one's own welfare" means that a person of discerning nature, having investigated his own welfare as it truly is, should come to know it.
And while investigating, he should look to the word here in this world—[the teaching] of the Fully Enlightened One among the many recluses and brahmins.
And the spoken word is the teaching; this is the occasion. In that regard, one should look at and behold with the eye of wisdom that which leads to liberation.

For these various ascetics and brahmins of other sects are wrongly intent upon what is impermanent as "permanent," upon what is not-self as "self," and upon what is not the path of purity as "the path of purity," and they hold mutually contradictory doctrines. Therefore—

Their doctrine is not conducive to liberation. But the Perfectly Enlightened One, having realized through his own independent knowledge exactly as it is that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all phenomena are non-self, Nibbāna is peace," proclaims it;
therefore, one should contemplate the greatness of the Teacher’s dispensation by considering that "his doctrine is conducive to liberation. And whatever is appropriate in this regard—

"Of one who has entered upon the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*)": of that noble son who has approached the state of a recluse (*samaṇabhāva*), the state of renunciation (*pabbajjā*), whatever here in this dispensation is appropriate, fitting, and worthy for the condition of one gone forth—that too he should look for. What, then, is that?
He says: "A friend here who is virtuous," and so forth. A virtuous friend being cultivated in this dispensation...
The construction is: "It is suitable for a recluse. This same method applies to the others as well.
For, by relying on a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta), one abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, and maintains oneself in purity.

"Vast undertaking of the training" (sikkhā vipulaṃ samādānaṃ) means a vast undertaking of the training; the meaning is the performance of the great training in higher virtue and so forth that leads to Nibbāna.

"Service to teachers" means the desire to hear the instruction and the performance of service toward teachers—such as preceptors (upajjhāya) and instructors (ācariya)—who are one's virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta). "This" refers to the cultivation of virtuous friends and so forth.
"Reverence for the Buddhas" means the application of respect and the attitude of honoring the omniscient Buddhas, thinking, "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One."
"Honoring the Dhamma as it truly is" means paying homage to the Noble Dhamma according to its true nature, worshipping it with reverence.
"In the Saṅgha" refers to the Noble Saṅgha. "Esteem" means honor and respect. "This" refers to the honoring of the Triple Gem.
"Engaged in proper conduct and resort" means being free from improper conduct—defined as physical and verbal transgressions—and [properly engaged] for the sake of alms-food and so forth.

Having abandoned improper places to visit, such as the haunts of prostitutes, and being endowed with—meaning possessed of—a proper sphere of activity suitable for visiting for the sake of alms-food and so forth, characterized by conduct consisting of non-transgression in body and speech, he is one whose conduct and sphere of activity are perfected;
this is the meaning. His livelihood is purified, [having abandoned] the giving of bamboo-staves and other things censured by the Buddha.

Having abandoned wrong search, one who makes use of requisites that arise without fault has purified and thoroughly cleansed his livelihood; because it is thus purified, he is beyond reproach by the wise.

And as for "the steadying of the mind": it is the correct settling of the mind upon what is seen, etc., by way of the mere fact of its being seen, etc., so that covetousness and other such states do not arise toward objects such as visible forms through the doors of the eye and so forth.
These three are: perfection in conduct and resort (*ācāra-gocara-sampadā*), purity of livelihood (*ājīva-pārisuddhi*), and guardedness of the sense-faculties (*indriyesu guttadvāratā*).

"Conduct" (*cāritta*) refers to the virtue that must be fulfilled by practicing [the precepts]. "Restraint" (*vāritta*) refers to the virtue that must be fulfilled by abstaining from non-action through renunciation.
"Gracious in the postures" (*iriya-pathiyaṃ pasādanīyaṃ*) means that which brings confidence to others, based on the postures, as a sign of the perfection of deportment.
Full awareness (*sampajañña*). "Application to higher mind" (*adhicitta-āyoga*) means devotion to and cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Forest-dwelling" (*āraññaka*) means those included within the forest. "Remote" (*panta*) means secluded.
"Virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the virtue of the fourfold purification; for while it was explained below by breaking it down [into its components], here he speaks of it without breaking it down.
"Learnedness" (*bāhusacca*) means the state of being well-versed in the teachings. For that is highly conducive to the practice of meditation;

for one who is frequently engaged in correct discernment regarding the skill in the factors of enlightenment, the unsurpassed state of coolness, the application of higher consciousness, and so forth, the practice of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) succeeds.

"Discernment of phenomena as they really are" (*yathābhūtaṃ dhammānaṃ pavicayo*) refers to the thorough investigation of material and immaterial phenomena by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*). By this, he speaks of the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena (*adhipaññā-dhammavipassanā*).

“The realization of the truths” (*saccānaṃ abhisamayo*) means the penetration of the Noble Truths, such as suffering and the rest, by way of the realization of full comprehension (*pariññā-abhisamaya*) and so forth.
To show how this realization of the truths occurs, it is said: “one should cultivate [the perception] that ‘it is impermanent’,” and so on.

Therein, “one should cultivate that it is impermanent” refers to the undifferentiated [view] that “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” and [specifically], “whatever form there is—past, future, or present,” and so forth.
The meaning is that, either by way of analysis or regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), one should develop and both generate and increase the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
Regarding "the perception of non-self" (*anattasaññā*): the construction is that one should develop the perception of non-self as it occurs in the thought, "All phenomena (*dhammā*) are non-self.

The same applies to the remaining [perceptions]. Regarding "the perception of the foul" (*asubhasaññā*): [it refers to] the body born of karma (*karajakāya*) or to all conditioned phenomena of the three planes (*tebhūmakasaṅkhāra*).
"Loathsome" refers to the perception occurring with respect to that which drips with the impurities of the defilements. For this [perception] is accompanied by the perception of suffering;

thus, it should be understood that the perception of suffering is also included herein. "And non-delight in the world" refers to the perception of non-delight in the entire world—that is, in the conditioned phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
By this, he speaks of the contemplation of danger and the contemplation of disenchantment.
However, showing that one who is devoted to the cultivation of insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*) and striving toward it should increase these states, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"And he should develop the factors of enlightenment" (*bhāveyya ca bojjhaṅge*). Its meaning is as follows:

they are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because they are the sevenfold collection of states beginning with mindfulness that constitute enlightenment (*bodhi*), or because they are the limbs (*aṅga*) of enlightenment—that is, of the person endowed with it. These are the states beginning with mindfulness. Regarding those states beginning with mindfulness...

One should develop all the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā), namely: the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgā); the four bases of psychic power beginning with zeal (chanda-iddhipādā);
the five faculties beginning with faith (saddhindriyā); the five powers beginning with faith (saddhabalā); and the noble eightfold path by way of right view and the rest.

By the word "and" (ca), the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānā) and the right endeavors (sammappadhānā) are included. Thus, one should develop all these thirty-seven varieties of factors conducive to enlightenment.

It should both arise and increase. In this context, that which is their arising at the moment of the first path and their increase at the moments of the subsequent paths is what is appropriate for a recluse, a bhikkhu.
Thus, by developing the seventy-three states conducive to enlightenment, one [realizes] the truth of the path through the penetration of development.

He fully realizes [the truths]: he fully realizes the truth of the origin by way of the full realization of abandonment, and he fully realizes the truth of cessation by way of the full realization of actualization.
Demonstrating this, he spoke the concluding verse: “One should abandon craving.

In that context, “one should abandon craving” means that one should completely eradicate all craving—divided into the categories of sensual craving and so forth—without remainder by means of the Noble Path; [this is] *mona*.
It is called "knowledge," and because he is endowed with that, he is a sage (*muni*).

"He would shatter the taints together with their roots" means he would break and utterly eradicate all taints, such as the taint of sensual desire, which have their roots in the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) like sensual lust.

"He would dwell completely liberated": thus, because all defilements have been abandoned in every respect, he is liberated in every way; [he dwells] in the relinquishment of all acquisitions, in cessation, which is Nibbāna.
"Having realized it, he should dwell. "This" refers to this very dwelling; the meaning is that this is fitting and appropriate for a monk, a recluse who has stilled evil.
Thus, by way of praising the practice appropriate for a recluse, the Elder [describes] the liberating nature of the Dispensation and its opposite.

He also clarified the lack of deliverance in the doctrines of the outsiders. Having heard this, those wealthy brahmins gained deep faith in the Teaching and established themselves in the refuges and other precepts.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Apara-Gotama is finished.
The commentary on the Dasaka-nipāta is finished.
11. The Ekādasa-nipāta. 1.
Commentary on the verses of the Elder Saṅkicca.
In the *Ekādasanipāta*, the verses beginning with "What, father, is your purpose in the forest? are the stanzas of the Venerable Saṅkicca Thera.

What is their origin? This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, took rebirth in this current dispensation of the Buddha within a prominent brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
He took her. While the child was still in her womb, the mother fell ill and died. When she had been carried to the charnel ground and was being cremated, the interior of the womb did not burn.
People, piercing her belly with stakes, struck the corner of the infant’s eye.
Having pierced him, they covered him with glowing embers and departed. Even that region of the belly burned.
But upon the charcoal mound, there was a boy resembling a golden image, lying as if within the heart of a lotus.
For a being in his final existence, even if he were to be crushed by Mount Sineru, there is no such thing as the end of life until he has attained Arahantship.
On the following day, people who went to the cremation ground saw the boy lying in that manner and were filled with a sense of wonder and amazement.
Taking the boy, they entered the village and asked the fortune-tellers.
The fortune-tellers said, "If this boy lives as a householder, his family lineage will remain in poverty for seven generations.
But if he goes forth into homelessness, he will wander about surrounded by five hundred ascetics. His kinsmen said, "Let it be so; when he has grown up, we..."
Having said, "We shall cause him to go forth in the presence of the noble Elder Sāriputta," they called him Saṅkicca because the tip of his eye had been cut off by a thorn;

later, he became known by that name. When he was seven years old, having heard of the death of his mother while he was still in her womb and of his own circumstances while in the womb, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and said, "I shall go forth. His kinsmen—
Saying, “Excellent, dear ones,” they led him into the presence of the Dhamma General and handed him over, saying, “Venerable sir, please grant him the going forth.

The Elder gave him the meditation subject of the five aggregates of clinging (*tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*) and ordained him. At the very moment the razor touched his head, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
While dwelling in the forest with about thirty monks, he rescued [a man] from the hands of bandits.
Having tamed those thieves and ordained them, while dwelling together with many bhikkhus in a certain monastery, he saw that they were intent on dispute.
Thinking, "I shall go elsewhere," he took leave of the bhikkhus. This is the summary here;
the detailed account, however, should be understood according to the method found in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*. Then, a certain lay follower...
Desiring to attend upon him, he requested a dwelling in a nearby place, saying:
“What need have you for the forest, dear father, like a peacock during the rains?
To you, the Verambha grove is delightful, for solitude is for one who meditates.”
He spoke the first verse. Having heard it, the Elder said:
"Just as the Veramba wind drives away the clouds in the rainy season, so do perceptions overwhelm me, though they are associated with seclusion."
“Not white, born from an egg, wandering with its dwelling in the charnel ground—
this very thing arouses mindfulness in me, directed toward detachment amidst the corpse.
That which others do not protect, and that which one does not protect others from;”
Truly, that bhikkhu sleeps in happiness, having no longing for sensual pleasures:
“The rocky crags with clear waters, frequented by oxen, ploughs, and deer,
and covered with moss— those mountains delight me.”
“I have mastery in the forests, in the ravines and in the caves;
in secluded lodgings frequented by wild beasts.
‘May these living beings be slain! May they be executed! May they encounter suffering!’”
I do not recall any ignoble intention associated with hatred.
“The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.”
“The purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—
that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life.”
“I await my time, like a servant awaiting his wages.
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life.
I await my time, mindful and clearly comprehending.”—with these verses he spoke.
In this context, what is the meaning of *vaneti*? It is stated with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
The meaning is: "What is the purpose (*kiṃ payojanaṃ*) in the forest? He addresses him as "Tāta" (Son), placing him in the position of a son because he is a young novice (*daharasāmaṇera*).
"Like Ujjhāna pouring rain": there was indeed a mountain named Ujjhāna, which was covered in thickets and possessed many caves and ravines.
With its waters flowing here and there, it is unsuitable during the rainy season; therefore, the meaning is: "What is the purpose of this mountain Ujjuhāna to you now at this time of the rains?
However, some here say: "Ujjuhāna is the name of a certain bird that cannot endure the cold;
during the rainy season, it remains hidden in the forest thickets. According to their opinion, [the question concerns] the Ujjuhāna.
"Who desires what use for you, who are like a bird in the rainy season?"—the construction is: "The Verambha winds are delightful to you";
that is, as the Verambha winds blow, what is delightful to you? Some say, "Verambha is the name of a certain mountain cave, a mountain slope.
And that place is suitable for coming and going, free from the crowding of people, and endowed with shade and water.
Therefore, Verambha is delightful and suitable for dwelling in the forest. Why? Because seclusion is what meditators such as these desire;
since seclusion alone is required by such meditators wherever they may be, he says, "Dear one, live here at Verambha instead of going to some distant wilderness place.
This is the intended meaning here: because [Verambha] is capable of providing seclusion for meditators...
"Meditative absorptions (jhāna) and the like arise only when one has obtained a comfortable dwelling place for living, not when one has not;
therefore, it is not possible to dwell anywhere at random in the forest during such cold weather, whereas it is possible in caves, mountain slopes, and the like.
When the lay follower had spoken thus, the Elder, showing that it was the forests and such that delighted him, said: "Just as from a cloud," and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as in the rainy season the Verambha wind drives away, scatters, and expels the clouds and mists, even so my mind—through perceptions associated with seclusion—draws toward the very place of seclusion. What [is it that draws it]?
A crow: not white, black in color, born from an egg, an oviparous bird, frequenting the charnel ground—that is, the cemetery. It is one who dwells in its own home.
Making that very place his dwelling and wandering about there, it arouses mindfulness in me;

thinking, "In this state of doubt, it is dependent on dispassion," the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), which is associated with dispassion toward the body, indeed arises for me.
It is said that one day, having seen a human corpse being devoured by crows, the Elder attained the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā). That—
Having intended this, he spoke thus. By this, he shows that because there is a complete absence of desire and lust for the body, he wishes to dwell in the forest itself.
And as for the word "yañca" (and which), the particle "ca" has the sense of conjunction; by it, he shows: "Hear also another reason for my dwelling in the forest.
[He speaks of] that which is to be protected by one who has gone forth, due to his abiding in loving-kindness and his possession of requisites that inspire non-greed.

Because others, such as servants and the like, do not exist, they do not protect him. And the one who has gone forth does not protect others from anything that constitutes a burden or an impediment, because such things simply do not exist for him. "That bhikkhu indeed sleeps in peace":

that bhikkhu, through the complete eradication of the desire for defilements, being entirely without regard for and devoid of longing for sense-objects (*vatthukāma*), sleeps happily wherever he may be. For him—
The meaning is that because there is an absence of both suspicion and apprehension, the forest is exactly the same as the village.
Now, in order to show the beauty of mountains, forests, and so forth, as well as the fact that he has previously dwelt there, it is said: "With clear water," and so on.
Therein, "I have dwelt" means it was inhabited by me in the past. "Frequented by wild beasts" refers to a forest frequented by wild beasts such as lions, tigers, and the like.
"I do not recall any intention" refers to any such thought as: "May these living beings be struck with spears, arrows, and other weapons;
may they be killed, beaten with fists and the like, or afflicted; or may they encounter or undergo suffering in any other way whatsoever.
Such an intention is accompanied by hatred, associated with resentment, and for that very reason, it is ignoble, consisting of the various types of ill will, cruelty, and so forth.
“I do not recall giving rise to an evil intention; wrong thought has never arisen before”—this shows his dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*).

Now, with the words “served” (*pariciṇṇo*) and so forth, he shows that his duty has been fulfilled. In this context, “served” means attended upon by way of carrying out instructions and admonitions. “Laid down” (*ohito*) means set down. “The heavy burden” refers to the even more weighty burden of the aggregates (*khandha*).
“I do not rejoice in death” means I do not desire death, thinking, “How might my death come about? I do not rejoice in it.
Regarding "life": even life itself, thinking "How indeed might I live long?", I do not desire.
By this, he shows an equal state of mind toward both death and life. "And I await the time" means I wait for the very time of final Nibbāna.
"Nibbisam" means working for wages; "yathā bhatako" means just as a hired laborer [works] for another.
Just as one performing work, even while not delighting in the completion of that work, merely awaits the end of the day while still working;
so too, I, though not delighting in life and not delighting in death for the sake of maintaining this physical form, await the time of its conclusion.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Saṅkicca is finished.
The commentary on the Eleventh Chapter is finished.
12. The Twelfth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sīlava:
The verses beginning with “Sīlam eva” (Virtue alone) belong to the venerable Elder Sīlava. What is his origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, [attained this state].
