During this dispensation of the Buddha, he was reborn as the son of King Bimbisāra in Rājagaha; his name was Sīlavāti.

When he reached maturity, King Ajātasattu, desiring to have him killed, placed him upon a fierce, rutting elephant and attempted to kill him by various means, yet he was unable to do so, for one destined for his final existence cannot be slain until he has attained Arahantship.
Because there was no obstacle to his life, the Blessed One, seeing his conduct, commanded the Elder Mahāmoggallāna:
"Bring Prince Sīlavat here. By means of his psychic power, the Elder brought him along with the elephant.
The prince, having descended from the elephant, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma in accordance with his disposition.
He taught him. Having heard the Dhamma and gained faith, he went forth into homelessness.
Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon attained Arahantship and lived in the kingdom of Kosala. Then Ajātasattu ordered men, saying, "Kill him!
They went into the presence of the Elder and stood there; having heard the discourse on the Dhamma spoken by the Elder, they were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (sañjātasaṃvega).
With hearts full of faith, they went forth into homelessness. The Elder taught them:
“One should train here in virtue, well-trained in this world;
for virtue, when practiced, brings about every success.”
“A wise person, aspiring after three kinds of happiness—
praise, the acquisition of wealth, and rejoicing in heaven after death—
should guard their virtue. For one who is virtuous attains many friends through self-restraint.”
But the immoral person, practicing evil deeds, is cast down by his friends.
An immoral man gains disrepute and ill-fame;
one who is virtuous always gains renown, fame, and praise.
“Virtue is the beginning, the foundation, and the mother of all that is wholesome;
it is the foremost of all dharmas. Therefore, one should purify virtue.
It is the boundary, the restraint, the virtue, and the delight of the mind.”
This is the bathing place for all Buddhas; therefore, one should purify one’s virtue.
Virtue is an incomparable strength; virtue is the supreme weapon;
virtue is the most excellent ornament; virtue is the marvelous armor.
“Virtue is a bridge of great power; virtue is the unsurpassed fragrance;
virtue is the most excellent ointment, by which one’s scent wafts in every direction.
Virtue is the supreme provision for the journey; virtue is the best travel rations.”
Virtue is the best vehicle by which one travels from place to place.
"Right here the fool incurs blame, and after death he is dejected in the woeful states;
everywhere the fool is dejected, for he is not established in virtue."
“Right here one gains renown, and after passing away, one is joyful in heaven;
everywhere the wise person is joyful, being well-composed in their virtues.
Virtue alone is supreme in this world, but the one possessed of wisdom is the highest.”
"Among humans and among devas, one triumphs through virtue and wisdom"—with these verses he taught the Dhamma.
Therein, "one should train in virtue here in this world": "here" (*idha*) is a mere particle; it means "in this world of beings."
A clansman who desires his own welfare should first train in virtue alone, which is divided into the categories of conduct (*cāritta*) and restraint (*vāritta*).

And while training in it, he should train so as to have trained it well—that is, having made it thoroughly trained, perfectly pure, and complete by bringing it to a state of being unbroken and so forth.
"In this world" means in this world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*), among the things to be trained in, virtue is first...
One should train. Because virtue is also the foundation for the attainment of right view, he said, "Virtue, indeed," and so forth.

In this context, "indeed" (hi) is a word expressing reason. Because virtue—when cultivated, mastered, and guarded—brings about and leads toward all forms of excellence, namely human excellence, divine excellence, and the excellence of Nibbāna, for the being who possesses it.
"Virtue brings about all success"—having stated this meaning in brief, he says "One should guard virtue," and so forth, in order to show that same point in detail.

Therein, "one should guard" means one should protect. For by refraining from killing living beings and so forth, and by fulfilling one's duties and obligations, one guards it by overcoming its opposites.
"The wise one" means the one possessed of wisdom; this is shown as the means for guarding it.
For by means of the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), his undertaking and its non-disturbance come to be. "Patthayāno" means desiring. "Tayo sukhe" means three kinds of happiness;
or rather, that which is the cause of happiness is intended by the term "happiness. "Pasaṃsanti" means fame, or being praised by the wise.
"Vittilābhaṃ" means the attainment of satisfaction; they also read it as "vittalābhaṃ," meaning the attainment of wealth.
The meaning is as follows: For one who is virtuous attains a great mass of wealth through heedfulness. *Peccha* means having passed away.
*Sagge pamodanaṃ* refers to the connection with "rejoicing in the world of the gods through desirable sense-pleasures.
The construction is: desiring praise in this world, the acquisition of wealth, and rejoicing in divine prosperity in the next world, one should guard one's virtue.

"By restraint" means by the restraint of body and so forth. For one who is restrained, not harming anyone through bodily misconduct and the like, gives the gift of fearlessness and binds friends through being dear and agreeable.
"Dhaṃsate" means he departs. "One who practices evil" means one who performs unwholesome deeds such as the taking of life.
Indeed, beings who desire their welfare do not associate with a person of immoral character; rather, they avoid them altogether.

*Avaṇṇaṃ* means a lack of virtue, or blame in one's presence. *Akitti* means infamy and ill-repute. *Vaṇṇaṃ* means virtue. *Kitti* means renown and widespread fame. *Pasaṃsaṃ* means praise in one's presence. *Ādi* means the root.
For morality (*sīla*) is the root of wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*). As it is said: "Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify the beginning among wholesome states.
And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is perfectly pure morality."

"Foundation" (*patiṭṭhā*) means resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). For virtue is the foundation for all superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). Therefore he said: "Being established in virtue," and so forth.
And it is the "mother of the beautiful" (*kalyāṇamātuka*); that is to say, it is the mother, the progenitor, of beautiful qualities such as serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the like.
It is the "foremost of all states" (*pamukhaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ*), meaning it is the foremost among all blameless states such as gladness (*pāmojja*) and the rest.
"Foremost" (*pamukha*) means being the primary [factor], that is, the door of occurrence (*pavattidvāra*). "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because of its status as the beginning and so forth.

"One should purify" (*visodhaye*) means one should bring it to completion by way of being unbroken and so forth. "Limit" (*velā*) means a boundary (*sīmā*) in the sense of being not transgressed by misconduct;

or, it is called a limit because it restrains (*velāyati*), i.e., shakes off or destroys immorality (*dussīlya*). "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) refers to virtue (*sīla*), because it closes the door for the arising of bodily misconduct and the rest.
"Abhihāsa" means gladdening, because it causes the mind to rejoice by being a cause for freedom from remorse.

"And a ford for all Buddhas" means that it serves as a ford for all Buddhas— namely, the disciple-Buddhas (sāvakabuddhas), the solitary-Buddhas (paccekabuddhas), and the perfectly enlightened Buddhas (sammāsambuddhas)—
in washing away the stains of the defilements and plunging into the great ocean of Nibbāna.
Virtue is strength; it is incomparable strength and military might for crushing Māra’s army.
It is the supreme weapon for cutting through the phenomena of defilement. It is an ornament in the sense that it adorns the body of qualities.
It is the most excellent substance, being preeminent at all times. It is a marvelous armor because it protects living beings. "It pierced" (abbhida).
And they recite [this]; "abhejjanti" means "they do not break.
It is a bridge in the sense of not sinking due to the defilements when crossing the great flood of the states of woe and the great flood of saṃsāra.
"Of great influence" means of great power. The fragrance is unsurpassed because it wafts against the wind and pervades all directions.
“Fragrance” is so called because it is pleasing to the minds of all people. Therefore he said, “By which one wafts from region to region”:
by means of that fragrance of virtue, the possessor of it wafts toward every direction, all quarters. There is also a reading, “disodisā,” meaning the ten directions.
“Provisions indeed as a peak”: “provisions” (sambala) refers to food packed in a bundle. Just as one who goes on a journey taking packed food...

Just as a person on a journey does not suffer from the pain of hunger, so too one endowed with virtue, having taken the pure provisions of virtue, does not suffer wherever he travels while traversing the wilderness of *saṃsāra*;

thus, virtue is called the supreme provision. Likewise, virtue is the supreme travel-rations because it is not shared by thieves and the like, and because it produces the desired success in every place.
*Ativāha*: It carries one across, leading or bringing one to whatever place is desired; thus it is a vehicle (*yāna*).
Because it is the cause for reaching a desired destination without being afflicted by anything, virtue (*sīla*) is the supreme vehicle.
"By which": by means of that vehicle, one goes from region to region; thus, one travels with ease to every direction, whether a path of no-going or a path of going.
"He incurs blame right here" means that even in this world, being dejected and his mind defiled by lust and other passions, he incurs blame and censure as one who is "immoral and of evil nature.
Furthermore, after passing away, even in the next world, in the states of misery, he incurs blame from the messengers of Yama and others, such as being called "a wretched man, born of a low birth.
Not only does he incur blame, but moreover, the fool is dejected everywhere.
Because his mind is defiled by the practice of misconduct in this world, suffering arises for him in the next world through such means as being subjected to torture;

thus, in all respects, the fool is unhappy. How so? One who is not concentrated in the precepts—whose mind is not properly established in the precepts, whose mind lacks a firm foundation—even in this world gains a reputation, thinking:
"He is a true person, virtuous, and of noble character. Thus, he is glad even here.
He gains [renown]. Having passed away, even in the next world, in the heavenly realm, he gains fame such as: "This true person was virtuous and possessed of wholesome qualities;
for this reason, he has been reborn in the company of the devas," and so forth. He does not gain fame alone;
rather, being wise (dhīra), endowed with fortitude (dhiti-sampanna), well-composed in his virtues, with a mind well-concentrated, well-absorbed, and well-established in all respects—
In this world, one becomes well-disposed and attains gladness through the practice of good conduct; in the next world, one does so through the attainment of prosperity.
Regarding "virtue alone is supreme here," there are two kinds of virtue: mundane and supramundane.

Among these, mundane virtue brings about a distinction in rebirth within the sense-sphere world among wealthy kṣatriyas and others, as well as in the divine and Brahma worlds, such as the state of being a recipient of gains and so forth.

Furthermore, it serves as a cause [for higher rebirth]. However, because the supramundane virtue transcends the entire suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*), virtue is indeed the foremost. For it has been said:
“By an inferior holy life one is reborn among the Khattiyas;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; and by the supreme, one is purified.”
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,’ [he should think]:
‘May I indeed be one who fulfills the precepts. For, monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.
But as for supramundane virtue, whose opposites have been entirely abandoned, the suffering of saṃsāra from the seventh existence onward—
For one who turns away [from unwholesome states], there is simply nothing to be said regarding their preeminence.

However, by stating "the wise person is supreme," he speaks of the excellence of wisdom itself through a reference to the person, saying: "The wise person is indeed the highest, the most excellent, the best.
Now, demonstrating the excellence of both virtue and wisdom by way of their function, he says: "Victory comes from virtue and wisdom. "Victory" (jaya) means...

And a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa) is to be understood here, or the word *ahū* (was) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. In this context, it is "knowledge" (*paññāṇa*) in the sense of understanding;

and from the standpoint of virtue (*sīla*) and knowledge (*paññā*), there is the conquest of opposing factors. For wisdom does not arise without virtue, nor does virtue fulfill its function without wisdom;
these two are mutually supportive. For it has been said: "Wisdom is purified by virtue, virtue is purified by wisdom..."
"Virtue among humans and devas": this is a demonstration of their specific locations, for there it is that those [qualities] function with particular distinction.

Herein, concentration belongs to the side of virtue because it serves as the foundation for wisdom, or it belongs to the side of wisdom because it is to be developed and because it has virtue as its foundation.

Thus, while teaching the Dhamma to those bhikkhus by way of virtue (*sīla*), the Elder declared his own final knowledge (*aññā*) by demonstrating the excellence of his own perfectly purified virtues, such as virtue.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sīlava is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sunīta.
"Born into a low family," and so forth, are the verses of the Venerable Thera Sunīta. What is his origin?
This one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various states of existence, wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During a period when there was no Buddha, he was reborn into a family home; and upon reaching maturity, he lived about, engaged in play with foolish people.
Having seen a certain Paccekabuddha wandering for alms in a village, [he said]:
"What is the use of your wandering for alms with your entire body covered up as if it were completely wounded? Should you not rather maintain your livelihood through farming, trade, and so forth?
If you are unable to do those, then after carrying away urine, excrement, and the like from house to house..."

“Live by cleaning latrines! he reviled him. Having been cooked in hell because of that deed, and as a remaining result of that same karma, he was reborn in the human world for many hundreds of births into families that discarded flowers, and lived his life in that manner.
And in this current arising of a Buddha, having been reborn in a family that discards flowers, [he lived] by the work of cleaning latrines.
He maintained his life even without obtaining more than mere food and clothing.
Then, during the last watch of the night, the Blessed One entered the Great Compassion Absorption (mahākaruṇāsamāpatti), which is the practice of the Buddhas;
emerging from that, he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and saw [the light] blazing within Sunīta’s heart like a lamp in a jar.

Seeing the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship, when the night had turned to dawn, he dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms surrounded by the community of monks.
He proceeded along the street where Sunīta performed the work of clearing away refuse. There, Sunīta had gathered here and there heaps of filth, excrement, sweepings, and other such waste.
Having placed [the books] into baskets and carrying them on a shoulder-pole, he saw the Teacher approaching surrounded by the community of monks;
becoming terrified and his heart agitated with confusion, finding neither a path to flee nor a place to hide,
he set the pole against the side of a wall and, as if entering through one side, he pressed himself against the wall with palms joined in reverence.
He stood there. Some say he intended to slip away through a hole in the wall.
When the Teacher reached his side, he thought: "This man, though I have approached him impelled by his own roots of merit, is filled with trepidation;
because of his low birth and lowly deeds, he even feels ashamed to face me directly. Well then, I shall instill in him confidence."

Addressing him with the words “Sunīta,” in a voice as deep and excellent as the resonance of the entire city, sweet as the song of the *karavīka* bird and like the Brahma-voice, he said, “Will she be able to go forth into homelessness with such a miserable livelihood?
At these nectar-like words of the Teacher, Sunīta was as if sprinkled; experiencing a sublime sense of joy and gladness, he thought, “Blessed One, if even one such as I...”
“Here they receive the going-forth; why should I not go forth? Let the Blessed One grant me the going-forth,” he said.

The Teacher said, “Come, monk. At that very moment, having received the going-forth and full ordination through the “Come, monk” formula, wearing robes and bowl produced by supernormal power, he appeared like an elder of sixty years standing in the presence of the Teacher.
He stood there. The Blessed One led him to that monastery and explained a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to him.

Having first attained the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), and having further developed insight (*vipassanā*), he became one possessed of the six higher knowledges.
Devas such as Sakka and the Brahmās approached him and paid him homage. Thus it was said:
“Those seven hundred sublime deities, together with Brahmā and Indra, having approached the well-trained one who has overcome birth and old age, pay homage with hearts full of faith,” and so forth.
Seeing him thus honored by that host of gods, the Blessed One smiled and, in praise, said: “By austerity and the holy life...”
He taught the Dhamma in verse. Then, a number of bhikkhus, wishing to make him roar the lion’s roar, asked him:
“Friend Sunīta, from what family did you go forth? How did you go forth? And how did you penetrate the Truths?
He explained all of that:
“I was born into a low family, poor and lacking food;
my work was base—I was a flower-scavenger.
Despised by people, I was treated with contempt and reviled.”
“Having humbled my mind, I would have paid homage to the many people.
Then I saw the Perfectly Awakened One, honored by the community of monks,
the Great Hero entering the preeminent city of Magadha.
“Having set aside my staff, I approached to pay homage;
out of compassion for me alone, the Supreme Person stood there.
Having paid homage at the Teacher’s feet, I then stood to one side.”
I requested the going-forth, supreme among all beings.
Then the compassionate Teacher, who has pity for the entire world, said to me, "Come, bhikkhu"; that was my full ordination.
626. “Thus I, dwelling alone in the forest, unwearied, have carried out the Teacher’s word, just as the Jina instructed me:
‘During the first watch of the night, I recollected my former births.’”
During the middle watch of the night, I purified my divine eye;
during the final watch of the night, I shattered the mass of darkness.
Then, at the end of the night, toward the rising of the sun—
Then Brahmā arrived and, with palms joined in reverence, paid homage to me:
"Homage to you, O noble among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
You whose taints are exhausted—you are worthy of offerings, O Blessed One."
Then, having seen me honored by the assembly of gods,
the Teacher smiled and spoke these words regarding this matter:
“By austerity, by the holy life, by self-restraint, and by self-mastery;”
“By this one becomes a brahmin; this is the supreme brahminhood.
With these verses he let out a lion’s roar.
Therein, “low” means base and utterly inferior. For the state of being high or low among beings is indeed relative to each other. This...
However, showing that he was born into the most wretched of families, he said, "born into a low family. Therefore it was said:

"Low means base and most wretched. "Poor" means destitute; even some who are poor occasionally obtain food and clothing and have an easy livelihood, but as for me, because of my constant state of hardship—
Showing that he was so lowly that he did not see even the slightest thing worthy of being looked at, despite having set up a fire-pot and a mortar, he said, "I had little food.

Showing that while some from low-born and poor families still live by occupations that are not low, his own was not like theirs, he said, "My work was lowly. If one asks what kind it was: he was a flower-sweeper.
This designation, namely "flower-scatterer," came about for him through the metaphorical usage (upacāra), like calling one who lacks hands a "hand-possessor.
Or, he was so called because the dung-hill had the appearance of a bed strewn with withered flowers.
"Despised" means reviled both by birth and by his actions. "Of men" means by men. "Contemned" means treated with contempt.
"Vambhito" means censured. "Having made my mind lowly" means having held other people up like Mount Sineru and making myself inferior even to the dust at their feet;
thus, having made my mind humble and lowly in its conduct.
"I shall worship many people" means that whenever I saw the great multitude, I worshipped them and bowed with palms joined at my head.
Now, *atha* is a particle used to introduce a new section. *Addasāsiṃ* means "I saw. *Magadhānaṃ* refers to the royal princes known as the Magadhans;
even though they were inhabitants of a single province, that province is conventionally called "of the Magadhans" (*magadhānaṃ*), meaning "of the Magadha country.
*Puruttamaṃ* means "the supreme city."
"Byābhaṅgi" means "time. "I requested the going-forth": when the Teacher granted permission, saying, "Sunīta, will you be able to go forth?
I then requested the going-forth. "Ordination was attained instantly": ordination was attained by the mere words of the Teacher, "Come, monk.
"Just as he instructed me": "In this way, develop insight preceded by serenity."
Just as he instructed me, so did I act upon and practice the Teacher’s word. The passage beginning with "During the night," etc., shows the flavor (*rasa*) of that practice.

In this context, because the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*) have many functions, the accusative case is used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*), as in "the first watch" and "the middle watch.
It is not so with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*).
Because it proceeds by way of a single realization, the phrase "in the last watch" should be understood as stated in the locative sense.

"Inda" refers to Sakka, the king of the gods; "Brahmā" refers to Mahābrahmā. By the mention of Indra and Brahmā, it should be understood that the arrival of other sense-sphere deities (*kāmadeva*) and Brahmas is already implied.
For this is a description of the highest possible case, just as one might say, "The king has arrived."
"Namassimsu" means they paid homage both with body and speech.
In this context, having stated "with palms joined" (*pañjalī*) to show the homage performed with the body, the words "namo te" and so forth were spoken to show that performed with speech.
By the mention of "the host of devas" (*devasaṅgha*), even the Brahmās are included by virtue of their status as devas through rebirth.

“Having manifested a smile”: Relying upon the great fruitfulness of his own exhortation and the excellence of the virtues of the devas and brahmās, the Teacher manifested a smile. And in manifesting it, he did not show his teeth like others do;
rather, he opened his mouth slightly. By that much alone, [his smile] surpassed the rays of divine crystal and pearls, and eclipsed the stars and the shimmering rays of the moon.
Dense rays of light, produced from his very white teeth, issued forth and circumambulated the Teacher’s face three times;
seeing this, even those walking behind perceived that the Teacher had manifested a smile.

"By austerity" means by restraint of the sense faculties; some say it means "by undertaking the ascetic practices" (*dhutadhamma*). "By self-restraint" means by virtue (*sīla*). "By self-control" means...
"By wisdom. "By the holy life" means by the remaining supreme conduct. "By this" refers to the aforementioned austerity and so forth.
"He becomes a brahmin" because of the state of having banished evil. "This" refers to the aforementioned austerity and so forth.

"The supreme brahmin" means the highest brahmin, or the most excellent among brahmins; "was" is the ellipsis for the verb. Or alternatively, "brahmin" refers to the state of being a brahmin (*brahmañña*).
Thus, the intention is that the state of a brahmin is supreme, not by birth and so forth. For birth, lineage, locality, clan, excellence, and the like are not the causes for the state of an Ariya;
rather, the training in higher virtue and so forth alone are the causes. Therefore he said:
"Just as in a heap of refuse discarded on the great highway..."
“A lotus might grow there, pure-scented and delightful.
In the same way, among those who have become like refuse, among the blind worldlings,
the disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One outshines them all with wisdom.”
Thus the Elder, answering the matter asked by those monks with these verses, let out a lion’s roar.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sunīta is finished.
The commentary on the Twelfth Chapter is finished.
13. The Thirteenth Chapter. 1.

Commentary on the Verses of the Venerable Soṇa Koḷivisa. In the Thirteenth Chapter, the verses beginning with "In which kingdom... are the verses of the Venerable Soṇa Koḷivisa. What is his origin? He, too—
Having performed services under previous Buddhas, he accumulated merits in various states of existence.
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Anomadassi, having been a very wealthy merchant, he went to the monastery together with lay followers.
Having heard the Dhamma from the presence of the Teacher, with a mind full of faith, he had the Teacher’s walking path (caṅkama) plastered with lime and decorated with various colors.
Having strewn it with flowers, he had a canopy made of various colored cloths tied above; likewise, having constructed a long hall for the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he dedicated it to them.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara into a merchant family, and his name was Sirivaḍḍha.

Having reached adulthood, he went to the monastery and, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those of aroused energy.
Aspiring to that same status himself, he offered a great almsgiving for seven days and made a formal resolution (paṇidhāna).
The Teacher, moreover, [knew] that his aspiration would be fulfilled.
Having seen him and given his explanation, he departed.

He too, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering among gods and humans, was reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī after the Parinibbāna of the Great Sage Kassapa and before the appearance of our own Blessed One. Upon reaching maturity, he lived on the bank of the Ganges.
Having built a leaf-hut, he diligently served a certain paccekabuddha for three months with the four requisites.
When the paccekabuddha had completed the rainy-season retreat and his requisites were fulfilled, he departed for Mount Gandhamādana.
That clansman also performed meritorious deeds there for as long as he lived; passing away from that state, he wandered among gods and humans until [he was reborn] under our Blessed One.
In due time, he took rebirth in the city of Campā in the house of the merchant Usabha.
From the moment of his conception, the merchant’s great mass of wealth increased. On the day of his birth, he was honored with great ceremony throughout the entire city;
because of his previous gift of a crimson woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand pieces to a Paccekabuddha, he possessed a golden complexion.
His physical form was exceedingly delicate, and therefore they gave him the name Soṇa. He grew up with a great retinue;
the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet were the color of the bandhujīvaka flower, and their touch was like that of cotton wool split a hundred times.
On the soles of his feet, hairs grew with the color of jeweled earrings. When he reached maturity...
Having had three palaces built, each suited to one of the three seasons, they provided him with theatrical performances.
He dwelt there enjoying great prosperity like a young god.
Then, when our Teacher had attained omniscience and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, he was residing near Rājagaha.
While he was dwelling there, he was summoned by King Bimbisāra; together with eighty thousand village headmen, he came to Rājagaha.
Having approached the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith.

After obtaining permission from his mother and father, he went forth in the Dispensation and, having received full ordination, took a meditation subject from the Teacher. For the sake of avoiding contact with people—
While dwelling in the Cool Grove, [the Bodhisatta] resolved: "My body is delicate; it is not possible to attain happiness by means of mere ease.
It is right to perform the duty of a recluse after having wearied the body.

Thus, applying himself to striving while intent only on standing and walking, he disregarded the pain that arose even when his soles were cracked and exerted firm energy; however, due to this over-exertion of energy—
Being unable to produce any distinction, he thought: "Even though I strive in this way, I am unable to produce either the Path or the Fruit.
What is the use of my renunciation? I shall return to the low life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
The Teacher, knowing the movement of his mind, went there, exhorted him with the "Lute Simile" instruction, and taught the method for applying balanced effort.
Having bestowed the meditation subject and purified it, he went to Vulture Peak.

The Elder Soṇa, too, having received instruction in the presence of the Teacher, applied himself with balanced energy, accelerated his insight, and established himself in Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Of Anomadassi, the Sage, the Eldest in the World, the Neutral One;”
Having applied a coating of lime, I had a walking path constructed.
I spread that walking path with flowers of various colors;
having fashioned a canopy in the sky, I fed the Supreme Buddha.
“Having raised my hands in reverential salutation and having paid homage to the one of noble vows,
I then offered the Dīghasāla grove to the Blessed One.
Knowing my intention, the Teacher, the unsurpassed one in the world,”
The Blessed One, the one with vision, accepted it out of compassion.
Having accepted it, the Fully Awakened One, who is worthy of offerings in the world including the devas,
sat down amidst the community of monks and spoke these verses:
“I shall praise him who, with a joyful heart, gave me the Dīghasāla house; listen as I speak.
At the time of his death, he was endowed with meritorious deeds.”
A chariot yoked with a thousand [horses] shall stand ready for him.
By means of that vehicle, this person will go to the world of the gods;
the gods will rejoice when he arrives, born into a noble lineage.
“He shall dwell in a most excellent, vast celestial mansion,
plastered with jewels and clay, and adorned with the finest gabled chambers.
For thirty thousand eons, he will delight in the world of the devas.”
For twenty-five eons, he will be a king of the gods.
And seventy-seven times he will be a wheel-turning monarch;
all of them will bear the same name, Yasodhara.
“Having experienced two attainments and increased his store of merit,
in the twenty-eighth aeon he will become a wheel-turning monarch.
There too, he will possess an exquisite celestial palace constructed by Vissakamma.”
He will dwell in the midst of that city, which is uninhabited by the ten types of beings.
"In an immeasurable eon from now, there will be a powerful protector of the earth;
a king named Okkāka will arise in the kingdom."
“Among the sixteen thousand women, she is the most excellent;
this noble-born Kṣatriya lady shall give birth to nine sons.
Having given birth to nine sons, the Kṣatriya lady shall die.”
And a young, beloved maiden shall exercise the sovereignty of a Great Queen.
Having pleased Okkāka, the maiden will receive a boon;
having received the boon, that maiden will cause her sons to go forth into homelessness.
“All of them, having gone forth, shall go to that best of cities;
out of fear of the distinction of birth, they shall all dwell there with their sisters.
And one maiden shall be completely afflicted by diseases.”
"Lest our lineage be split," so the Kṣatriyas will bury [the child].
"Having dug him out, the Kṣatriya shall dwell with her;
then there will be a schism arising from the Okkāka clan."
“From them there will arise a people by birth known as the Koḷiyas;
there they will enjoy no small human wealth.
Having passed away from that body, they will go to the world of the gods.”
There too, he will obtain a most excellent and delightful celestial mansion.
Having passed away from the world of the gods, impelled by the root of his wholesome merit,
he will come back to the human state and become one named Soṇa.
“Ardent in energy, resolute, striving in the Teacher’s dispensation,
having fully understood all taints, I shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
The Blessed One Gotama, the Sakyan bull, possesses infinite vision.”
The Great Hero, who discerns distinctions, will place you in the highest position:
"When the rain has fallen four finger-breadths deep, and the grass on the wind-swept courtyard has been cleared away,
for one who stands engaged in the practice of yoga, there exists no further shore beyond that."
“Tamed in the highest taming, my mind is well-directed;
the entire burden has been laid down by me, I am extinguished and free from taints.
Aṅgīrasa is a great nāga, like a noble-born lion.”
Having sat in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he placed me in the foremost position:
“The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
But having attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he uttered this as an inspired utterance (udāna) and as a declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa):
“He who was preeminent in the kingdom, the foremost attendant of the King of Aṅga—
he, Soṇa, now preeminent in the Dhammas, has gone beyond suffering.
“One should cut off five, abandon five, and cultivate five further.”
The bhikkhu who has overcome the five attachments is called one who has crossed the flood.
For a bhikkhu who is arrogant, negligent, and outward-looking,
virtue, concentration, and wisdom do not reach fulfillment.
“For those by whom what ought to be done is neglected, and what ought not to be done is performed—
those who are arrogant and heedless— their taints increase.
But for those by whom mindfulness directed to the body is constantly and well-undertaken...”
They do not pursue what should not be done, but are constant in doing what should be done;
for those who are mindful and clearly comprehending, the taints come to an end.
"Go upon the straight path that has been declared; do not turn back."
“Exhort yourself by yourself, and direct yourself toward Nibbāna.
“When my energy was excessive, the Teacher, the unsurpassed in the world,
the Visionary, taught me the Dhamma using the simile of the lute.”
Having heard her words, I dwelt delighted in the Teaching.
I practiced tranquility for the sake of attaining the supreme goal;
the three knowledges were realized, and the Buddha’s instruction was fulfilled.
“For one intent on renunciation and for the mind’s seclusion;
for one intent on non-affliction and the destruction of clinging;
for one intent on the destruction of craving and for the mind’s non-delusion.”
Having seen the arising of the sense bases, the mind is rightly liberated.
For that bhikkhu whose mind is peaceful and rightly liberated,
there is no accumulation of what has been done, nor is there anything further to be done.
“Just as a solid stone block does not tremble in the wind,
so too, all forms, tastes, sounds, smells, and tactile sensations—
whether desirable or undesirable— do not shake one who is such (the Tādin).”
“The mind, established and detached, contemplates its passing away”— these verses he spoke. Therein,

“who was pre-eminent in the kingdom” means he who existed— was— pre-eminent, most excellent, and highly distinguished among the eighty thousand village headmen in the kingdom of Aṅga by virtue of his wealth and sovereignty, [being] of King Aṅga.
"Paddhagu" means a distinguished householder who was a retainer of King Bimbisāra—the sovereign lord of Aṅga—in the sense of pleasing the assembly through the four bases of sympathy;
it should be understood that he was a landowner in his kingdom.
"Now he has become pre-eminent in the Dhammas" means that this Soṇa has now become pre-eminent in supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma); even during his time as a householder, by some...
Having been eminent even before, he now remains eminent even at the time of his going forth; thus he represents himself as if he were another.
"One who has gone to the further shore of suffering" means one who has reached the further shore—the limit—of the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
By this, he specifies the state of eminence mentioned without distinction as "eminent among all phenomena," by way of illustrating the attainment of Arahatship.

Now, in order to show by way of a synonym for "higher knowledge" (aññā) the practice through which one has become a goer to the further shore of suffering, he spoke the verse beginning with “pañca chinde.

Its meaning is as follows: A person should cut, by means of the three lower paths, the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana)—which lead to an unhappy destination and bring about a happy rebirth—just as one would cut a rope tied to one’s foot with a knife; [likewise, one should cut] those that lead to existence in the realms of form and formlessness...
A person should abandon the five higher fetters with the highest path, as one would cut a rope tied around one's neck;
furthermore, for the sake of abandoning those higher fetters, he should further cultivate the five faculties beginning with faith.
A bhikkhu who has become thus is free from attachment to lust, and free from attachment to hatred, delusion, conceit, and views.

Having transcended the five attachments, he has become one who has gone beyond the five attachments; because he has crossed over the four floods—the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*), the flood of existence (*bhavogha*), the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*)—he is called "one who has crossed the flood.

And this crossing of the flood occurs only through the fulfillment of the practice beginning with virtue (*sīla*), while virtue and the other factors occur through the abandoning of conceit and the rest.

Showing that [these qualities] reach fulfillment and not otherwise, he spoke the verse beginning with "of the arrogant" (*unnaḷassa*). Therein, "of the arrogant" (*unnaḷassa*) means one whose empty pride has risen up.
For pride is called "reed" (*naḷa*) because, by its mode of functioning as an upward-thrusting state, it is like a reed in its emptiness.

"Of the negligent" (*pamattassa*) means one who has fallen into negligence through the abandonment of mindfulness. "Of the outward-drawn" (*bāhirāsassa*) refers to those [drawn] toward external sense-bases (*āyatana*).
"From this [state]," means for one who is not yet free from passion for sensual pleasures. "Virtue, concentration, and wisdom do not reach fulfillment":
for one who cultivates the opposites of virtue and the other factors, even mundane qualities such as virtue do not reach fulfillment, let alone supramundane ones.
He states the reason for this with the words, "For whatever duty," and so forth. For from the time of his going forth, a bhikkhu must guard the immeasurable aggregate of virtue.
Dwelling in the forest, maintaining the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), delighting in meditation, and so forth—these are called one's duties.
However, those by whom this aforementioned duty of their own has been cast aside—that is, abandoned through non-performance—are negligent.

"Non-duty" refers to the adornment of requisites, such as the decoration of the alms bowl, the robes, the waist-band, the shoulder-strap, the sunshade, the sandals, the fan, the water-strainer, and so forth.
“Excessive indulgence in conditions,” and so forth—this is what is called a monk’s improper task;

it is performed by those who are arrogant in conduct because they have cast aside respect for their teachers, and who are negligent through the abandonment of mindfulness. For them, all four taints (*āsava*) increase.
However, in order to show those in whom qualities such as wisdom increase, the words beginning with “of those who” are spoken. In that context, “well-commenced” means:

"Well exerted. "Mindfulness directed to the body" refers to the cultivation of the contemplation of the body. "This is not your business" means that this—such as adorning oneself—is not your business.

"They do not indulge in it" means they do not perform it. "In what is to be done" refers to the immeasurable protection of the aggregates of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth, which must be performed from the time one goes forth. "Those who act with persistence" means those who act constantly;
through the non-departure of mindfulness, for those who are mindful, there is purposeful clear comprehension (sātthakasampajañña).

"Being clearly comprehending through the four kinds of clear comprehension"—namely, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of the range, and clear comprehension of non-delusion—the meaning is that for those who are thus clearly comprehending, even the four taints (*āsava*) go to their end, reach exhaustion, and come to non-existence.
Now, giving exhortation to the bhikkhus standing near him, he spoke this verse beginning with "On the straight path. Therein:

"Proclaimed on the straight path" means that the Teacher has declared the Noble Path, which consists of the Middle Way and is straight by virtue of avoiding the two extremes and abandoning bodily crookedness and so forth.
"Go" means practice it. "Do not turn back" means do not fall into despondency midway.
"Exhort yourselves by yourselves" means that here, a clansman who desires his own welfare [should exhort himself] by reflecting on the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*) and so forth.
"Chiding himself by himself": "He should bring himself toward Nibbāna" means he should carry himself toward Nibbāna, lead himself to it;
the meaning is that he should practice in such a way that he realizes it.
Now, thinking "I too have practiced in this very same way," in order to show his own practice, [he says] "Accāraddhamhi," and so forth.

It has been said: "When energy is over-exerted" means that while I was developing insight, I failed to bring energy into a state of equilibrium with concentration and instead exerted excessive energy.
The nature of this over-exertion of energy has already been explained above.
Having made the simile of the lute, [the Blessed One said] to the Venerable Soṇa: "Those disciples of the Blessed One who dwell with energy aroused..."
“I am one of them, yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging; therefore, I shall disrobe.
When this thought arose, the Teacher manifested himself before him by means of his psychic power and said:
“Why, Soṇa, did you give rise to the thought, ‘I shall disrobe’? Formerly, when you were a householder, you were skilled at the lute.”
Having asked, "Is the string taut? and being told by him, "Yes, venerable sir," [the Blessed One said]: "What do you think, Soṇa?
When the strings of your lute are too tight, would your lute at that time produce sound or be functional?
Certainly not, venerable sir. What do you think, Soṇa, when the strings of your lute are too loose..."
“Would that lute of yours, at that time, produce sound or be fit for use? “Certainly not, Bhante.

“What do you think, Soṇa? But when the strings of your lute are neither too tight nor too loose, but are settled on even tension, would that lute of yours, at that time, produce sound or be fit for use?”
"So it is, Bhante. In the same way, Soṇa, over-exerted energy leads to restlessness, and overly slackened energy leads to laziness.
Therefore, Soṇa, you should resolve upon evenness of energy and penetrate the evenness of the faculties.
Having spoken thus, he taught me the Dhamma by means of the "Discourse on the Simile of the Lute," which was delivered using the lute as a metaphor.

He taught me. Having heard his words—that is, having heard the Blessed One’s instruction likened to the lute—I abandoned the desire to disrobe that had arisen within me and dwelt delighted and rejoicing in the Teacher’s dispensation.
And while dwelling there, I practiced calm (samatha), applying evenness of energy as I would balance concentration and wisdom.

Bringing about the state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*), I accomplished concentration through insight (*vipassanāsamādhi*) based on the foundation of meditative absorption (*jhānādhiṭṭhāna*) and brought insight to its culmination.
Regarding that, he states the purpose: "for the attainment of the supreme goal" (*uttamatthassa pattiyā*). "For the attainment of the supreme goal" means for the realization of Arahantship.
Now, demonstrating how serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) were perfected by one who practiced accordingly, he speaks by way of another designation:
He spoke the words beginning with “in renunciation” (*nekkhamme*). Therein, “renunciation” refers to the departure from sensual desires through going forth (*pabbajjā*) and so on.
“Of one intent upon it” means of one who is engaged and devoted to it by way of being inclined, leaning toward, and tending toward it;

that is to say, first becoming oriented toward going forth, abandoning sensual pleasures, and having gone forth, [practicing] the purification of virtue, dwelling in the forest, maintaining the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and application to meditation (*bhāvanā*).
"In such blameless qualities as these, he is one who is engaged and devoted"—this is the meaning.

"And with a mind inclined toward seclusion" means that for one whose mind is thus inclined toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*), being devoted to seclusion through the production of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, he is engaged and devoted to seclusion.
"Inclined toward non-affliction" means inclined toward non-affliction, which is the state of being free from suffering.
"For one intent upon the bliss of serenity" means for one who has produced the meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*) and is devotedly engaged in the bliss of calm (*samatha*).
"And for the destruction of clinging" means for one who is inclined toward Arahantship, which is the exhaustion of all four types of clinging;

for this genitive case is used in the sense of a locative. The meaning is: for one who, having made that attained jhāna the foundation, applies himself to insight (*vipassanā*) for the attainment of Arahantship.
"Of one intent upon the destruction of craving": craving is destroyed here, thus it is the "destruction of craving," which is Nibbāna;

of one who is intent upon that, through the vision of the formed (*sa-upādi*) as fearful and the unformed (*an-upādi*) as secure, [one is] inclined toward, sloping toward, and leaning toward cessation.
"And non-delusion of the mind": by way of the clear comprehension of non-delusion, it refers to the non-deluded functioning of the mind through the cutting off of delusion.
Or [it occurs] for one who is intent upon the Noble Path, which is the state of non-delusion of the mind.

Having seen the arising of the sense-bases (*āyatana*)—that is, the moment-to-moment arising of the sense-bases such as the eye by their respective conditions, and their cessation from the opposite standpoint—by means of the wisdom of the Path accompanied by the wisdom of insight, the mind is rightly liberated through that seeing; thus, by the right cause and method, according to the sequence of the Path.
The mind is liberated from all taints.
Regarding the passage beginning with “Of him who is rightly liberated,” this is the summary of the meaning:

for that bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, whose mind is peaceful through absolute tranquility, and who is thus rightly liberated from all defilements in the manner described, whatever wholesome [deed] has been performed...
There is no further accumulation of unwholesome states because they have been completely eradicated by the Path itself;
nor is there any task remaining to be done, such as full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth, because what was to be accomplished has already been achieved.

For one who has become thus—just as a solid, single-mass mountain of rock is not moved or shaken by the natural wind—so too are desirable and undesirable objects such as forms and the rest [unshakable] for the "such-like" one (*tādī*) who has attained the state of such-likeness.
They do not cause the mind—which is established, unshakable, liberated through the abandoning of all sorrow, and dissociated from defilements—to tremble or waver.

And as for that object-condition, by occasionally entering the attainment of fruition and practicing insight, he contemplates its passing away and its nature of breaking up moment by moment; thus he gave the answer.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Soṇakoḷivisa is finished.
The commentary on the Thirteen-Verse Section is finished.
14. The Fourteen-Verse Section.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Revata of the Khadiravana Grove The verses beginning with "When I... belong to the Venerable Elder Revata of the Khadiravana Grove.
What is their origin? Although these verses of this elder have already appeared below in the Ekaka-nipāta, there [in that context] his own...
Only the mere act of reminding his nephews was shown, and thus their inclusion was made in the Ekaka-nipāta (Single Chapter).
However, these verses, which illustrate the Elder’s practice from the time of his going forth until his Parinibbāna, have been included in this Cuddasaka-nipāta (Fourteen Chapter).
Regarding that, the origin story has already been told below. This, however—

The distinction is as follows: it is said that after attaining arahantship, the Elder would from time to time go to attend upon the Teacher and the great elders, such as the General of the Dhamma, staying there for only a few days before returning to the Khadiravana forest.
There he would spend his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) and the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*). As time passed in this manner, he became old and aged.
He had reached old age. One day, while going to pay his respects to the Buddha, he stayed overnight in a forest not far from Sāvatthī along the way.
At that time, some thieves who had committed crimes in the city and were being pursued by the guards fled past the Elder;
they abandoned their stolen goods near him and escaped. The men, pursuing them, [arrived].
Having seen the goods near the elder, they bound the elder and, perceiving him to be a thief, took him and presented him to the king, saying, "Sire, this man is a thief.
The king had the elder released and asked, "Venerable sir, was this act of theft committed by you, or not?
Although the elder had never committed such a deed since birth, he replied:

But from the time of his going forth, since he had not committed such an act and all defilements were utterly eradicated, he—being incapable of doing the like—while teaching the Dhamma to the monks standing nearby and to the king, said:
“When I went forth from home into the homeless life, ... [the rest of the verse follows] ...”
I do not recall any ignoble intention associated with hatred— the thought:
"May these living beings be slain, may they be destroyed, may they meet with suffering"—
nor do I recall such an intention throughout this long interval.
“I know loving-kindness, immeasurable and well-developed;
practiced in successive stages, just as taught by the Buddha.
I am a friend to all, a companion to all, compassionate toward all beings.”
I cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, always delighting in freedom from ill will.
I gladden my mind— unshakable and unassailable—
and I cultivate the divine abodes, which are not practiced by base men.
“Having attained the state free from directed thought,
the disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One is then endowed with noble silence.
Just as a rocky mountain is immovable and well-established,”
Thus, through the destruction of delusion, a bhikkhu does not tremble, like a mountain.
For a person free from blemish, who always seeks purity,
even a hair’s breadth of evil appears as large as a cloud.
“Just as a frontier city is guarded both within and without, so should you guard yourselves;
let not the opportune moment pass you by.
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life.”
I await my time like a wage-earner awaiting his wages.
“I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;
I await my time with clear comprehension and mindfulness.”
“I have served the Teacher; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That for whose sake I went forth from the home life into homelessness—”
“Thus my purpose has been attained: the destruction of all fetters.
Accomplish [your own goal] without negligence; this is my instruction.
Come now, I shall attain final Nibbāna; I am liberated from everything.”—with these verses he spoke.
Herein, this is the commentary on the previously unexplained words:
"In this long interval" means from the time I went forth until this present final period of my life;

during this long interval, I have not entertained any ignoble intention associated with hatred, either through the influence of covetousness such as "May this be mine," or through the influence of ill-will such as "May these beings be slain," and so forth.
The construction is: "I do not recognize [it].

Regarding "and I recognize loving-kindness (*mettā*)," it is called *mettā* because by means of it one is moistened and softened; it is non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*). That which possesses this loving-kindness is *mettā*;

the cultivation of loving-kindness, the divine abode of loving-kindness—that is *mettā*. By the word "and" (*ca*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) are included.
It includes [it] within the other divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). "I directly know" (*abhijānāmi*) means I know from the perspective of direct presence (*abhimukhato*).

For when one reviews the jhāna that has been attained, it becomes present to the reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). To the question "Of what kind?", he says "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*), and so forth.
For, just as it was taught by the Blessed Buddha, it is immeasurable in its objective field (*ārammaṇa*) because it pervades limitless beings by way of non-restriction (*anodissaka-pharaṇa*).
It is immeasurable (*appamāṇa*). It is well-developed (*subhāvita*) because it has been thoroughly cultivated by bringing about a state of proficiency, strength, and mastery.

"I directly know" (*abhijānāmi*) refers to that which was practiced, attended to, and repeatedly cultivated in successive order and sequence—first loving-kindness (*mettā*), then compassion (*karuṇā*), then gladness (*muditā*), and finally equanimity (*upekkhā*).
This is the construction of the sentence.
A friend to all beings, or "all are my friends," is one who is a friend to all (*sabbamitto*). For by cultivating loving-kindness (*mettā*), one becomes dear to sentient beings.
The same method applies here to the term "kinsman to all" (*sabbasakho*). "Compassionate toward all beings" (*sabbabhūtānukampako*) means one who seeks to favor all sentient beings.
"And I develop a mind of loving-kindness" (*mettacittañ ca bhāvemīti*) refers specifically to a mind that is accompanied by and associated with loving-kindness.
“I develop, increase, or make manifest”—even if one does not speak [these words], it is because of the state of having reached the highest excellence (*ukkaṃsagata*) through development.
Alternatively, the reading is “I develop a mind of loving-kindness” (*mettaṃ cittaṃ ca bhāvemī*); its meaning is exactly as explained in the method stated above.

“Delighting in non-affliction” (*abyāpajjarato*) means delighting in the bringing about of welfare for beings, which is non-affliction. “Always” (*sadā*) means at all times; by this, he shows the practice of constancy (*sātaccakiriya*) therein.
"Unassailable" means it cannot be overwhelmed; "unshakeable" means it cannot be dragged away by lust, which is its proximate enemy.
"Imperturbable" means it cannot be disturbed by ill will, which is its distant enemy.

Having made my mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) such as this, I gladden it, I cause it to rejoice, and I cultivate the divine abode (*brahmavihāra*). "Not practiced by base men" means [not practiced] by base men, those of low character.

The meaning is: "I cultivate and increase the sublime, supreme, and faultless abiding in loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth, which has not been practiced by base men, but has been practiced by the Noble Ones, the Buddhas, and others.
Having thus shown his own practice through five verses by way of referring to himself, he now [proceeds] by way of addressing another.

Demonstrating this, he spoke four verses beginning with “without applied thought. Therein, “he has attained the state without applied thought” means he has attained the second jhāna and so forth, which is devoid of applied thought (*vitakka*).
By this, the Elder speaks of his own attainment of the second jhāna and beyond under the guise of the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Since this Elder, having made that very jhāna the basis and having increased his insight (*vipassanā*), [attained liberation] in a single sitting—

He attained arahantship; therefore, in order to show that matter by means of a designation for higher knowledge (*aññā*), he said, "Having entered upon the attainment without applied thought," and added, "The disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One is then endowed with noble silence.
In this context, they call the attainment without applied thought and sustained thought—due to the absence of verbal formations—"noble silence. [Regarding the phrase] "of those who have assembled..."
"But, bhikkhus, two things are to be practiced: either talk on the Dhamma or noble silence.

According to this statement, any meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is called "noble silence. Here, however, the attainment of the fruit of the highest path (*aggaphala-samāpatti*) belonging to the fourth jhāna is intended.
Now, demonstrating by way of a simile that one cannot be shaken by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) due to the realization of that attainment, [the text says]: "Just as a mountain..."

He spoke this verse. Regarding that, "Just as a mountain of rock": the meaning is that it is like a mountain made of stone, a single solid mass of rock, not a mountain of earth nor a mountain of mixed materials. "Immovable and well-established":
its base is firmly established so that it is immovable and unshakable by natural winds; therefore, through the destruction of delusion, a bhikkhu [is like] arahantship and Nibbāna.

"Like a mountain, he does not tremble": because of the complete abandonment of delusion (*moha*), and because all unwholesome states are rooted in delusion, the bhikkhu who has abandoned all unwholesome states does not tremble or shake from worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), just as that mountain is not shaken by natural winds.
Alternatively, "the destruction of delusion" (*mohakkhaya*) refers to both Arahantship and Nibbāna; therefore, it is called "the destruction of delusion."
Because he has attained the destruction of delusion, Nibbāna, and Arahantship, he is firmly established in the Four Noble Truths;
even while not in meditative absorption, he does not waver like a mountain, let alone when he is in absorption—this is the intended meaning.
Now, this so-called "evil" is practiced only by one of impure character, not by one of pure character; for one of pure character, however, that...
Showing that even something as minute as an atom becomes heavy [as a burden], he spoke the verse beginning with “Of one who is without blemish” (*anaṅgaṇassa*). Its meaning is as follows:

For a true person (*sappurisa*) who is without blemish because of the absence of stains such as lust, and who at all times seeks only pure and blameless qualities—even a mere hair’s tip, a mere strand of hair, or even a slight trace of evil, throughout the entire world-system—becomes heavy.
It stands pervading [the body], appearing like a mass of clouds; therefore, the intention is that persons such as I should not be suspected of such deeds.

Since even those free from defilements give rise to such calumnies when they are foolish and blind, he spoke the verse beginning with "Just as a city" while giving this instruction: "Therefore, those who desire their own welfare must carefully protect themselves. Its meaning is as follows: "Just as..."
However, just as people living in a frontier city secure it both internally and externally—
making the gates, walls, and so forth firm on the inside, and making the moats, ditches, and so forth firm on the outside— so too,
by establishing mindfulness and closing the six internal doors, you must guard the city with its doors well-protected.
Without relinquishing mindfulness, guard yourselves by not grasping at the six external sense bases in such a way that they lead to the affliction of the internal ones;
rather, by not grasping them, make them firm, and do not abandon the door-guarding mindfulness that prevents their entry.
Why? Because "let not the opportune moment pass you by. For one who acts thus...

"He does not guard himself; for such a person, this entire opportunity—the moment of a Buddha’s appearance, the moment of human existence, the moment of birth in the Middle Country, the moment of obtaining right view, and the moment of the completeness of the six sense bases—passes away.
May this opportunity not pass you by!"
Thus, having exhorted the assembly including the king as well as the bhikkhus with this verse,
the Elder spoke the words beginning with "I do not rejoice in death," further demonstrating his own equanimity toward both death and life and the fact that he had fulfilled his duty.
The meaning of this has already been explained above.
Having spoken thus, and seeing that the time for his own final Nibbāna had arrived, he gave them a brief exhortation and uttered this concluding verse to announce his Parinibbāna.

In that verse, "fulfill with diligence" means: fulfill with diligence those duties to be fulfilled—such as giving, virtue, and so forth—which are distinguished by their results in the present life and the future life, within the conduct of a householder.
"Be diligent in the guarding of virtue, in the practice of serenity, and in the cultivation of insight.
This is my instruction"—that is, "Do not be negligent regarding generosity, virtue, and so forth"; this is my advice and exhortation.
Having thus illuminated the practice for the benefit of others which has reached its culmination, he now grasps the pinnacle of the practice for one's own benefit as well:
“Come now, I shall attain final Nibbāna; I am utterly liberated from everything,” he said. Therein, “I am utterly liberated from everything” means:
I am completely liberated from all defilements and from all states of existence; therefore, I shall unconditionally attain final Nibbāna.
Having spoken thus, sitting cross-legged in the air, he entered the fire-element, blazed forth, and attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Revata of the Khadiravana Grove is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Godatta:
The verses beginning with "Just as a noble one... belong to the Venerable Elder Godatta. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated wholesome merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he wandered among gods and humans until,
during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a caravan-leader’s family.
Known by the name Godatta, when he reached maturity and his father passed away, he took charge of the household and set out with five hundred carts laden with merchandise.
Traveling from place to place, he made his living through trade and performed meritorious deeds according to his means.
One day, on the road, when the oxen yoked to the cart were unable to pull and collapsed, and the men were unable to raise them up, he went there himself and struck the animal firmly on the tail.
The ox thought, "This is an ignoble person; toward me..."
“Not knowing my strength and weakness, you strike me deeply,” he said, provoked by the words of the man.
“O Godatta, for so long I have carried your burden without concealing my own strength; but today, because of my inability, you press down upon me who has fallen, afflicting me excessively.
Very well; having passed away from here, wherever I am reborn, may I be able to afflict you there.”
Thinking, "May he become my adversary," Godatta reviled him in accordance with that aspiration.

Hearing this, Godatta was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "What is the use of this livelihood which involves harming living beings? Abandoning all his wealth, he went forth into homelessness under a certain great elder.
Practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he soon attained *arahantship* and [dwelt] in the bliss of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
While spending one day teaching the Dhamma concerning worldly conditions to the assemblies of noble laypeople and renunciants who had approached him, he said:
"Just as a noble thoroughbred horse, when yoked to the burden, is capable of bearing that burden;”
Just as a ship, overwhelmed by its heavy load, cannot cross over the battle,
so too those who are satiated with wisdom, like the ocean with its waters,
do not despise others; for the Dhamma of the Noble Ones is indeed the refuge for living beings.
“Falling under the power of time at the appointed hour, subject to the cycle of repeated existence, men undergo suffering;
for this reason, young men, they grieve.
Exalted by the nature of happiness, and depressed by the nature of suffering,”
Fools, not seeing things as they truly are, are struck down by duality.
But those who have transcended the seam between suffering and pleasure—
standing firm like a city gatepost, they are neither elated nor dejected.
“Neither in gain nor in loss, neither in fame nor in reputation;
neither in blame nor in praise, neither in suffering nor in happiness—
these do not smear you at all, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.”
The wise are happy everywhere; they are undefeated everywhere.
Between a gain through righteousness and a gain that is unrighteous, a righteous loss is better than an unrighteous gain.
“The fame of those with little wisdom and the disrepute of the wise—
of the wise, disrepute is better than the fame of those with little wisdom.
And both the praise from the dull-witted and the blame from the wise— ”
It is better for the wise to be censured than to be praised by fools.
Between the pleasure consisting of sensual desires and the suffering of solitude,
the suffering of solitude is better than the pleasure consisting of sensual desires.
“Life lived unrighteously and death lived righteously—
death lived righteously is better than life lived unrighteously.
Those who have abandoned sensual desire and anger, whose minds are peaceful regarding existence and non-existence...”
“They wander in the world unattached; for them there is nothing dear or undear.
Having cultivated the factors of awakening, the faculties, and the powers, and having attained supreme peace, they attain final nibbāna, free from taints.”—he spoke these verses.
In this context, *ājañña* means a noble bull (*usabhājānīya*). *Dhure yutto* means yoked to the burden of a cart.
*Dhurassahe* means one who bears the burden; here, the spelling with two *s*s is used for the sake of metrical ease, meaning "capable of carrying the load of a cart.
*Mathito atibhārena* means oppressed by an excessive burden, that is, by a heavy load. There is also a textual reading of *maddito*, which has the same meaning.
"Yokes" (*saṃyuga*) means that he does not let the yoke placed upon his own shoulders slip off or pass beyond them;
he does not stand aside having properly lifted it and cast off the burden.

"In this way" means just as that draft-ox, by virtue of his noble lineage and his steadfast heroism, does not let his burden slip off or abandon it, even so [are those who are like] the great ocean to water.
Those who are satisfied, sustained, and fulfilled by mundane and supramundane wisdom do not despise or look down upon others of inferior wisdom.
Regarding this, the reason is stated: "The noble Dhamma alone [belongs] to living beings.
Among living beings, this is the Dhamma of the Noble Ones (Ariyas), namely, that because their wisdom has reached fulfillment, they do not exalt themselves on account of gain and so forth.
...not disparaging others because of lack of gain and so forth.

Having thus shown the noble ones’ dwelling in happiness through the fulfillment of wisdom, the words beginning with “at the proper time” (kāle) are spoken to show the ignoble ones’ dwelling in suffering due to the absence of that [fulfillment].
Therein, “at the proper time” means at the time when one is possessed of gain, loss, and so forth. By the power of time...
"Pattā" means having come under the sway of gain and so forth; the meaning is that they are gladdened by gain and the like, and dejected by loss and the like.
"Gatā bhavābhavavasam" means having come under the sway of existence and non-existence; they follow along with increase and decrease.
"Narā dukkhaṃ nigacchanti, tedha socanti māṇavā" means those people, who have received the name "māṇava," undergo suffering and grieve here.
Beings, having fallen into attachment and aversion through gain and loss, or through increase and decrease, grieve in this world;
and in the next world, they go to and encounter the suffering of hell and so forth—this is the meaning.
By the words "puffed up" (*unnatā*) and so forth, he likewise demonstrates how beings meet with misfortune due to the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). In that context, "puffed up" means...

"By means of a pleasant condition" (*sukhadhammena*) means by a cause of pleasure, a condition for pleasure—such as the attainment of wealth—and so forth; the meaning is that they have become uplifted, intoxicated by the pride of wealth, and so on.
"And depressed by an unpleasant condition" (*dukkhadhammena conatā*) means having fallen into inferiority by a cause of suffering, a condition for suffering—such as the loss of wealth—and so forth;
it means having reached a state of wretchedness through poverty and so on. "By both" (*dvayena*) refers to the aforementioned pair of being uplifted and being depressed.
Or, foolish worldlings are struck by the duality of gain and loss, and they are oppressed and afflicted by way of attachment and aversion.

Why? Because they do not see things as they truly are; that is to say, because they have not known the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva) as it really is, and thus they have neither fully understood the aggregates nor abandoned the defilements. It may also be read as "because of not seeing things as they truly are."
They recite [this], meaning "due to non-seeing.

And those who have transcended the seam in suffering, in pleasure, and in between—those noble ones who, by means of attaining the supreme path, have transcended and passed beyond the seam of craving consisting of desire and lust bound to painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neutral feeling; they are like a city gatepost.
They stand unshaken by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma), like [trees] amidst the winds;
they are neither elated nor dejected, for they are never at any time elated or dejected due to the total absence of attraction (anunaya) and aversion (paṭigha).
Having thus shown the Arhat’s stainlessness with respect to feeling, he now analyzes the worldly conditions and demonstrates his stainlessness in every respect.
Demonstrating his state of being unstained, he said, “For indeed not... and so forth. Therein, “gain” (*lābha*) refers to the acquisition of requisites such as robes and the like;
“loss” (*alābha*) refers to the non-acquisition or disappearance of those very same things. “He does not grieve” means in the face of the loss of followers and ill repute.
“Praise” (*kittī*) refers to being extolled in one’s absence with a spreading fame. “Censure” (*nindā*) refers to being reviled in one’s presence. “Honour” (*pasaṃsā*) refers to...
Regarding "praising virtues through direct experience": "in suffering" means when suffering has arisen; "in happiness"—here too the method is the same.
"In all cases" means in all eight kinds of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) as previously described, or in all objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are not smeared by them because their defilements have been entirely abandoned. How is this so? Like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
Just as a drop of water, though it remains clinging to a lotus leaf, does not smear it, nor does the drop of water smear the lotus leaf, but rather they are entirely detached from one another;
even so, these wise and learned ones remain detached from gains and the like when they arise, and from visible objects and other sense-objects that come within their range.
For this very reason, in all matters such as gain and the rest, through the gateway of wisdom, they [do not grasp] at the signs of the pleasant.
Due to the absence of sorrow and the like, they are happy; and because they cannot be overcome by gain and the rest, they remain entirely undefeated.
Now, having distinguished the superior among gain, loss, and so forth, he says, "By means of the Dhamma," and so on.
In that context, "loss through the Dhamma" refers to the loss of gain—the absence of gain—that occurs for one who guards the Dhamma, caused by that very reason. It is the decline of gain.
And as for gain that is unrighteous, obtained by an unrighteous and improper method, condemned by the Buddha—between those two, non-gain that is righteous and conducive to the Dhamma is better;
such non-gain, which causes unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase for one who avoids such gain, is more praiseworthy and brings about welfare. And whatever...
"Gain that is unrighteous" means that gain which has arisen through unrighteous means is not good;

this is the intended meaning. "Fame among those of little wisdom and infamy among the wise" means that whatever fame a person obtains by way of those of little wisdom and poor understanding, and whatever infamy or loss of fame occurs by way of the wise and learned—among these...
Of these two, for the wise, fame is indeed better. For they would desire the loss of fame only in such a way that unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase;
and being of a capable nature, he would abandon that lack of virtue and become established in virtue.
Fame is not for those of little intelligence—by way of the dull-witted, fame is considered better, for they...
For they might even produce it by means of proclaiming qualities that are unreal;
and this would bring him harm, both here through the censure of the wise and others, and in the future life through suffering and affliction in the miserable states. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Gain, fame, honor, and the reputation wrongly acquired," and "Honor kills the base man."
"By fools" means by those lacking in wisdom (*nippaññehi*). "And whatever praise of fools" refers to that which is called praise by the ignorant and unlearned.
"Consisting of sensual desire" means consisting of sense-objects (*vatthukāma*); it arises dependent upon the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
"And the suffering of seclusion" is the bodily suffering produced from seclusion, occurring through physical exhaustion and caused by such things as the affliction of an uneven posture.

That suffering, moreover, is praised by the wise because it serves as a support for the spiritual turning away from worldly life (*nirāmisavivaṭṭūpanissaya*). Therefore it is said: "The suffering of solitude is better.
And regarding "living by unrighteousness": this refers to making a livelihood through unrighteous means, that is, practicing unrighteousness for the sake of one's life.
As for "death by righteousness," even if someone says, "I will kill him who does not commit such-and-such an evil deed," and one kills him [for that purpose].
For one who has committed no evil and does not violate the Dhamma, death for the sake of the Dhamma is a righteous and superior kind of death.
Because such a death does not depart from the Dhamma, it leads to heaven and serves as a necessary condition for Nibbāna; therefore, it is more praiseworthy in the eyes of the wise. Thus it is said:
"One should give up wealth for the sake of a noble limb; one should give up a limb while protecting one's life."
“A man, recollecting the Dhamma, should renounce even his limb, his wealth, and his very life.

The meaning of “if one should live unrighteously” is that a person should not pursue a livelihood that deviates from the Dhamma, because it is censured by the wise and leads to states of misery; this is the intended sense.
