Now, demonstrating the reason for the stainlessness of those whose taints are destroyed as previously described, he spoke the verse beginning with “having abandoned desire and anger.”
Therein, "those who have abandoned desire and anger" means that through the Noble Path, all forms of attachment and aversion have been entirely abandoned.

"With peaceful minds regarding existence and non-existence" means their minds are tranquil because the fever of the defilements has been completely eliminated with respect to both minor and major states of being.
"In the world" refers to the world of the aggregates and so forth. "Unattached" means they are independent of the basis of craving and views. "For them there is nothing dear or undear."
For those whose taints are exhausted, there is nothing pleasant or unpleasant regarding any gain and so forth, nor regarding objects such as forms,
because the defilements that have those as their objective support have been entirely eradicated.
Now, having shown by means of which development they have become such as this, [the Buddha proceeds] with a teaching on the element of Nibbāna without residue.
While reciting the *kūṭa*, he uttered the concluding verse: “Having cultivated... Therein, “pappuyya” means having reached.
The rest is exactly according to the method explained below. And these very verses also served as the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Godatta is finished.
The commentary on the Cuddasakanipāta is finished.
15. The Soḷasakanipāta. 1.
Commentary on the verses of the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña.
In the *Soḷasakanipāta*, the verses beginning with "This one is superior" (*esa bhiyyo*) are those of the Venerable Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña. What is their origin?
He too, having been born during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great householders, attained maturity;
one day, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher [predict] a certain bhikkhu...
Seeing the Teacher appointing him to the foremost position among those who first realized the Dharma within his own dispensation, he himself aspired to that same status.
Having offered a great almsgiving for seven days to the Teacher, who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand monks, he made a formal resolve.
The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, prophesied his future success.
Thus, having performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna and a stupa was being erected,
he had a jeweled chamber constructed within the stupa and had a thousand precious ornaments made to surround the stupa.
Having thus performed these meritorious deeds, after passing away from there, he wandered among gods and humans until the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
At that time, having become a householder named Mahākāla, he plowed a field measuring eight karīsas to expose the sheaves of rice.

Having prepared milk-rice (*pāyāsa*) from the rice grains he had gathered—unmixed with any other milk—and having added honey, clarified butter, sugar, and so forth, he gave it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. At each place where he had plowed to gather the rice sheaves...

It filled up again, and at the time of the threshing, he gave the "top-portion of the threshed grain" (*puthukagga*). At the time of winnowing, he gave the "top-portion of the winnowed grain" (*lāyanagga*);

at the time of making bundles, the "top-portion of the bundles" (*veṇagga*); at the time of making sheaves, the "top-portion of the sheaves" (*kalāpagga*); [and likewise] the "top-portion of the threshing floor," the "top-portion of the granary," the "top-portion of the measuring," and the "top-portion of the storehouse.
In this way, for a single crop, he gave what is called the "top-portion gift" nine times. Yet that crop became even more abundant and successful.
Having thus performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, he passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the devas.

Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born even before the appearance of our Blessed One, in a prominent brahmin family in the brahmin village named Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu. He was known by the clan name Koṇḍañña.
The name Āgata was given to him. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas and attained mastery in the science of marks and mantras.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having descended from the Tusita heaven, was born in the city of Kapilavatthu in the house of King Suddhodana.
On the day of his naming ceremony, when one hundred and eight Brahmins were brought forward, those eight—
The brahmins were brought to the great terrace for the purpose of examining his marks. Being the youngest among them all, he observed the perfection of the Great Man’s marks;
having reached the conclusion that "this one will certainly become a Buddha," he wandered about, awaiting the Great Being’s Great Renunciation.
The Bodhisatta, too, growing up with a great retinue, gradually reached maturity and attained the ripening of his wisdom.
In his twenty-ninth year, when he was departing on the Great Renunciation, he went forth on the banks of the river Anomā.
Proceeding by stages, he went to Uruvelā and undertook the practice of striving. At that time, the young brahmin Koṇḍañña learned of the Great Being’s state of having gone forth.
Having heard this, he went forth with four others, including the young brahmin Vappa—the sons of the brahmins who had examined his marks—making himself the fifth.

Proceeding by stages, he approached the Bodhisatta; after attending upon him for six years, becoming weary of the consumption of substantial food, he departed and went to Isipatana. Then the Bodhisatta...
Having gained physical strength through the consumption of coarse food, he sat upon the invincible throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the full moon day of Vesākha;
having crushed the heads of the three Māras and attained supreme enlightenment, he spent seven weeks right there at the seat of awakening.
Then, knowing that the wisdom of the group of five monks had reached maturity, he went to Isipatana on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī.

He taught them the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*. At the conclusion of that teaching, the Elder Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). Then, on the fifth day of the fortnight, through the teaching of the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*, he realized Arhatship.
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“First, I beheld the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara, the eldest in the world, the Leader who had attained the plane of a Buddha.
As far as the foot of the Bodhi tree, all the yakkhas had assembled there.”
Surrounding the Perfectly Enlightened One, they pay homage with palms joined together:
“All the gods, their minds filled with joy, move through the sky;
this Buddha has arrived, the dispeller of the darkness of gloom.”
As they were overcome with laughter, a great cry arose:
“We shall burn away the defilements in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One!
Having understood the speech of the devas, I uttered this lion’s roar:
Joyful with a joyful heart, I gave the first alms.
Knowing my intention, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world,
sat amidst the assembly of devas and spoke these verses:
“Having gone forth for seven days, I attained enlightenment;
this was my first meal, sufficient for the life of one practicing the holy life.
For it was he who, coming here from the Tusita heaven, brought me almsfood.”
I shall proclaim this; listen as I speak.
"For thirty thousand eons he will exercise sovereignty over the gods;
having surpassed all the gods, he will dwell in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three."
“Having passed away from the world of the gods, he will go to the human state;
there, as a wheel-turning monarch with a thousandfold power, he will exercise sovereignty.
In a hundred thousand aeons, born into the lineage of Okkāka—”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
Having passed away from the realm of the Thirty-Three, he will come to human existence;
having gone forth from the home, he will dwell for six years.”
“Then, in the seventh year, the Buddha will proclaim the Truth;
one named Koṇḍañña by name shall be the first to realize it.
Having gone forth when he himself had gone forth, I have accomplished my striving well.”
For the sake of burning away the defilements, I went forth into the homeless life.
Having approached the All-Knowing Buddha in the world together with its devas at the Migāra’s Grove in Isipatana,
he beat the drum of the Deathless.
“Thus now I have attained the Deathless, the unsurpassed state of peace;
having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
The four analytical knowledges... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Then, at a later time, while seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher—proclaiming the state of having first penetrated the Dhamma—placed him in the foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are long-standing in the faith: namely, Aññā Koṇḍañña. Together with the two chief disciples, he...
Desiring to avoid the supreme display of hospitality being performed for him and the crowded living conditions in a village monastery,
and wishing to dwell in the delight of seclusion, he regarded even the reception of laypeople and renunciants who approached him as a source of proliferation (*papañca*);
thus, having taken leave of the Teacher, he entered the Himālayas, where he was attended by the Chaddanta elephants.
He dwelt for twelve years on the banks of the Chaddanta Lake.

While the Elder was living there, one day Sakka, the king of the gods, approached him, paid homage, and stood to one side, saying: "It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble one would teach me the Dhamma.
The Elder [taught] him the Dhamma, which contains the four truths, is struck by the three characteristics, is associated with emptiness, and is variegated by various methods.
He taught the Dhamma, which plunges into the Deathless, with the playful grace of a Buddha. Having heard it, Sakka, expressing his own faith, recited the first verse:
“Having heard this Dhamma of great flavor, I am even more filled with confidence;
the Dhamma taught is dispassion, leading entirely to non-clinging.”
In this matter, I have even greater confidence, having heard the Dhamma which is of great savor.

Although I was already deeply convinced after hearing the Dhamma many times in the presence of the Teacher, now, having heard from you the Dhamma of great savor—diverse in its various methods and utterly refreshing—I have even greater confidence than before. Dispassion has been taught.
The Dhamma is "the complete non-clinging" because it is the fading away from all defilements and all formations,

and because it generates dispassion (*virāga*). For that very reason, it is taught as being entirely without clinging, since it proceeds by way of accomplishing liberation without clinging to or grasping at any phenomenon whatsoever, such as form and the rest.
Thus, having praised the Elder’s teaching and paid homage to him, Sakka, the king of the gods,
returned to his own place. Then, one day, the Elder, observing the mental conduct of certain worldlings who were being overwhelmed by wrong thoughts,
recalled the sequence of practices that serve as their antidotes, as well as his own state of having completely turned his mind away from them.
Having reflected on this and illuminated its meaning, he said:
“Many wonders are there in the world upon this circle of earth;
They seem to churn away my intention, that beautiful thought associated with lust.”
“Just as dust is settled by the wind when the clouds have dispersed, so too are intentions stilled when one sees with wisdom. He spoke these two verses.
Therein, “many diversities in the world” refers to [the diversity] by way of form and so forth, and therein also by way of blue, yellow, and so forth, and by way of woman, man, and so forth.
And there are many various kinds of objects in the world.
By the phrase "on this circle of earth," he speaks with reference to the human world as it is directly perceived.
They churn, as it were—they intend, they conceive—those wrong intentions fashioned by improper attention, accompanied by human effort, like fire produced from friction.
I think they stand as if churning. Of what kind? "Beautiful," meaning a thought of sensual desire accompanied by lust;
for that is conventionally designated as "beautiful" by way of grasping the aspect of beauty.
"And like dust raised by the wind"—the word *ca* is merely a particle. Just as in the last month of summer, [dust] is raised by the wind...
Just as a great cloud raining down would settle and pacify dust that has arisen, so too are intentions pacified when one sees with wisdom.
When the noble disciple sees those worldly diversions with wisdom, as they truly are— in terms of their origin, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them— then,
just as that dust is settled by the cloud, [so too are his intentions stilled].
In this way, all wrong intentions are stilled by wisdom. For when right view has arisen, wrong intentions find no foothold.
To show how one sees with wisdom, it is said:
"When one sees with wisdom that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent';"
Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.

"All conditioned phenomena are suffering" … [as before] … this is the path to purification. When one sees with wisdom that "all phenomena are non-self," [then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification].
“Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.”—Thus he spoke these three verses.
Therein, “all conditioned phenomena” (*saṅkhārā*) refers to all the five aggregates of the three planes, comprised within the six objects of experience. “Impermanent” (*anicca*)...

“When one sees with the wisdom of insight that [the aggregates] are impermanent because they possess a beginning, middle, and end; because they are subject to termination; because they are merely temporary;
and because they break up here and there—then one becomes disenchanted with suffering. Thus, one becomes disenchanted with this suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
Becoming disenchanted, one penetrates the Truths by means of the method beginning with the full understanding of suffering. This is the path.

"By means of purification": this aforementioned method of insight (vipassanā) is the path and the means for attaining the purification of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) and ultimate purification.

"As suffering": it is suffering because it is fearful, because it is oppressed by arising and passing away, because it is inherently painful, and because it is the opposite of pleasure. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
"All phenomena are non-self" means that all phenomena belonging to the four planes are non-self. Here, however, only the phenomena of the three planes are to be taken.
For these should be seen through insight as non-self because they are without essence, because they do not admit of mastery, because they are empty, and because they are the negation of a self.
The rest is exactly as before.
Having thus shown the method of insight (vipassanā), he shows himself as having performed the task by that method, making himself appear as if someone else:
“The elder Koṇḍañña, who awakened after the Buddha, was one of swift exertion;
he has abandoned birth and death, perfected in the holy life.”
“The flood, the snare, the firm stake, the mountain difficult to shatter—
having cut through the stake and the snare, having split the rock that is hard to break,
the meditator has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and is released from the bonds of Māra.”
He spoke two verses.

Therein, "awakened after the Buddhas" (*buddhānubuddho*) means awakened after the Buddhas; the meaning is that he awakens to the truths realized by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*) in accordance with their teaching.
He is endowed with the stable qualities of those beyond training (*asekha*), such as the essence of virtue (*sīlasāra*).
"Thera": an elder. "Koṇḍañña": a designation of his clan. "Tibbanikkama": one of firm energy, of steadfast exertion. "Pahīnajātimaraṇo":
because he has abandoned birth and death, he is one who has abandoned birth and death. "Brahmacariyassa kevalī": one who possesses the entirety of the holy life;
that is, one who has fulfilled the holy life of the Path without remainder, or alternatively, one who is called "kevalī" (complete) due to being unmixed with defilements.
Path-knowledge and fruition-knowledge; because these exist in him, he is called *kevalī*.
Furthermore, since both of these arise by means of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) and not otherwise, it is said: "the possessor of the whole of the holy life.
The "floods and bonds" refers to the four floods mentioned as follows: the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
The "snare that moves through the air, which roams the mind"—this refers to the snare of lust (*rāga-pāsa*). The "firm stake" refers to the fivefold firm and stable [stake] described as follows:
"He doubts the Teacher, he doubts the Dhamma, he doubts the Saṅgha, he doubts the training;
he is angry with his fellow celibates, displeased, with a resentful heart, and stubborn."
And the mental barrenness (*cetokhila*). Because it cannot be split by ordinary people, it is difficult to split (*duppadālaya*);

for that very reason, because it resembles a mountain, it has come to be designated as a "mountain" (*pabbata*). Alternatively, it refers to the various types of ignorance (*aññāṇa*) described by the method beginning with "ignorance regarding suffering.
Thus, having cut off all this—both the barrenness and the snare—among these fourfold defiled phenomena...

Having severed both the thicket and the snare with the sword of knowledge of the Noble Path; having shattered the rock—that rock of ignorance which is difficult to break and impossible to cut by any other means—with knowledge resembling a thunderbolt;

having crossed over all four floods; and because he stands upon the further shore of Nibbāna, he is "crossed over" and has "gone to the further shore. By means of the characteristic of meditative reflection upon the object...
"He meditates by means of both kinds of characteristics: the characteristic of the marks [of a Great Man] and the characteristic of close contemplation.
"He is freed from Māra’s bonds" means that such a one, whose taints are exhausted, is freed, utterly liberated, and dissociated from every bond of the defilements of Māra.
The Elder speaks this with reference to himself.
Then one day, the Elder, seeing his own co-resident bhikkhu living with unwholesome friends—lazy, lacking in energy, restless, and arrogant—went there by means of psychic power and said to him:
"Friend, do not act thus; abandoning unwholesome friends and associating with wholesome friends, practice the duty of a recluse."
He exhorted him. But he did not heed the Elder’s words. Because he would not listen, the Elder was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma;
and in a discourse addressed to the individual, he censured wrong practice while praising right practice and dwelling in seclusion:
“A bhikkhu who is agitated and fickle, having come to evil friends...”
One sinks in the great flood, overwhelmed by the waves.
“Unagitated, not fickle, prudent, with senses restrained,
possessing good friends and being wise— one shall be an ender of suffering.”
“Resembling a black antelope’s leg, emaciated and with veins showing,
a man who knows moderation in food and drink, his mind undepressed;
though touched by gadflies and mosquitoes in the forest, the great woodland— ”
Like an elephant at the head of battle, mindful, one should endure it there:
“I do not rejoice in death… [as before] …fully aware and mindful.
‘The Teacher has been served by me… [as before] …the conduit to existence has been uprooted.’”
“For whose sake I went forth from the home life into homelessness—
that purpose of mine has been attained; what need have I for a co-resident?”—
he spoke these verses.
In this context, "agitated" means one who is possessed by restlessness, lacking concentration, and whose mind is distracted.

"Fickle" means one who is endowed with fickleness through the adornment of bowl and robes, being of a restless nature. "Doing evil by resorting to friends" means not practicing the duty of a recluse by relying on unwholesome friends.
"Sinks in the great flood, overwhelmed by the wave" means just as a person who has fallen into the great ocean [is swept away].
Just as one who is overwhelmed by the waves of the ocean and unable to raise his head sinks right there, so too one wandering in the great flood of saṃsāra,
struck and overwhelmed by the waves of anger and distress, being unable to raise the head of wisdom through the means of insight (vipassanā),
sinks right there.

“Circumspect” means skillful; “diligent” means clever. “Skilled in his own welfare and that of others” is explained thus. “With faculties restrained” means one whose faculties are closed by the restraint of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
“Possessing good friends” means endowed with virtuous friends. “Wise” means possessed of the wisdom born of the essence of the Dhamma (*dhamma-joja*).
“May he be one who makes an end of suffering”: such a person as this may become the bringer of an end to the entire suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*).

The passage beginning with "Resembling a black bamboo joint" and so forth is a praise of delighting in seclusion. The passage beginning with "I do not rejoice" and so forth, however, demonstrates that one's duty has been fulfilled.
All of this has already had its meaning explained above. At the conclusion, however, the words "What have I to do with my co-resident?
were spoken with reference to his own co-resident. Therefore, what purpose do I have for such a co-resident who is difficult to speak to and disrespectful?
"The meaning is: 'Dwelling alone is what pleases me.

Having spoken thus, he went to the Chaddanta Lake itself. Having lived there for twelve years, when his final passing was near, he approached the Teacher, requested permission for his final passing, and having gone back to that very place, he attained final nibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña is finished."
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Udāyi.
The verses beginning with "When he became a human being," etc., belong to the venerable Elder Udāyi. What is his origin?

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in Kapilavatthu.
Having received the name Udāyī, when he reached maturity, he witnessed the majesty of the Buddha during a gathering of the Teacher’s kinsmen.
Having gained faith and gone forth into homelessness, he applied himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā) and before long attained arahantship. Indeed, there were three Elders named Udāyī.
Formerly, there was Kāḷudāyī, the son of a minister; Lāludāyī, the son of a cowherd; and this Mahāudāyī, the son of a brahmin.

One day, when the Teacher, taking the white elephant adorned with all ornaments and being praised by the great multitude as the occasion for his discourse, taught the Nāgopama Sutta, at the conclusion of that teaching, [Mahāudāyī], in accordance with the power of his own knowledge—
Recalling the virtues of the Teacher, his mind uplifted by joy directed toward the Buddha, he thought:
"This great multitude praises this elephant among animals, not the Great Elephant among Buddhas. Come now, I shall make manifest the virtues of the Great Fragrant Elephant that is the Buddha.
Thus, extolling the Teacher—
“The Fully Awakened One, become human, self-tamed and composed;
walking upon the path of the Brahmās, delighting in the tranquility of the mind—
him whom people revere as one who has gone beyond all phenomena.”
"The gods pay homage to him," so I have heard from the Arahant:
"He has transcended all fetters and come from the forest to the state beyond the forest;
delighting in renunciation of sensual pleasures, he is freed like gold from the rock."
“He indeed is the most excellent Nāga, like Himavat among other mountain ranges;
among all who bear the name ‘Nāga,’ he is the peerless one whose name is true.
I shall proclaim the virtues of this Nāga, for he commits no offense.”
Loving-kindness and non-violence are the elephant’s two forefeet.
Mindfulness and clear comprehension are the other two feet of the elephant.
The Great Elephant has faith as his trunk and equanimity as his white tusks.
“Mindfulness is his neck, wisdom his head; investigation is his reflection on the Dhamma;
dwelling in the belly of the Dhamma, seclusion is his tail.
He is a meditator, delighting in inhalation and exhalation, well-composed within.”
The Nāga is concentrated while walking; the Nāga is concentrated while standing.
“The Nāga is concentrated while sitting; the Nāga is concentrated even while reclining.
The Nāga is restrained in every way—this is the perfection of the Nāga.”
“He eats what is blameless and does not eat what is blameworthy;
having obtained food and clothing, he avoids hoarding.
Having cut off every fetter, both subtle and gross, and all bonds;”
Wherever he goes, he goes without attachment.
Just as a white lotus born in the water grows there,
yet is not defiled by the water— pure-scented and delightful.
“Just so, though born in the world, the Buddha dwells in the world;
he is not defiled by the world, just as a lotus is not wetted by water.
Even a great blazing fire is extinguished without fuel.”
And while there are still burning coals, one is said to be "extinguished.
This simile, taught by the wise, is for the purpose of making the meaning known.
The Great Nāgas will understand this Nāga-teaching taught by a Nāga.
“Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, and taintless;
casting off the body, the Naga, taintless, will attain final Nibbāna”—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, “become among humans” means born among humans, arisen; or, having attained the human state of existence. The Teacher...

Indeed, although he is liberated from all states of existence through the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), he is nevertheless designated simply as a "human" by virtue of having taken rebirth in his final body.
Yet, by way of his qualities, he is the "super-god" among gods and the "super-Brahmā" among Brahmās.

He is called the "Fully Awakened One" (*Sambuddha*) because he possesses the awakening that must be awakened by himself alone. He is the "Self-Tamed" (*Attadanta*) because he has been tamed by himself alone. Thus [is] the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*).
For he is tamed by the supreme taming through both the eye and so forth up to the mind, by means of the Noble Path generated by himself alone.
"Concentrated" means concentrated by means of the eightfold concentration and the concentration of the Paths and Fruits.
"Wandering on the path to the Brahma-world" refers to the fourfold path of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), or to the supreme path of the attainment of the Fruit.

It is that which proceeds by way of attaining meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Although the Blessed One does not at all times conduct himself according to the aforementioned divine path (*brahmapatha*), he is nevertheless described as "conducting himself" (*iriyamāna*) with reference to his capacity for such conduct and his inclination toward it.
"Delighting in the tranquility of the mind" means being devoted to Nibbāna—the stilling of all conditioned phenomena—which is the cause of the mind’s tranquility.

"Whom humans revere as one who has gone beyond all phenomena": this refers to the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), who has reached the further shore in six ways regarding all phenomena such as the aggregates (khandhas) and the bases (āyatanas)—namely, the further shore of direct knowledge (abhiññā), the further shore of full understanding (pariññā), the further shore of abandonment (pahāna), the further shore of cultivation (bhāvanā), the further shore of realization (sacchikiriyā), and the further shore of attainment (samāpatti).
Humans, including noble warriors (khattiyas) and wise men (paṇḍitas), revere him whose excellence has reached the highest pinnacle.
Worshipping through practice in accordance with the Dhamma by means of body, speech, and mind, they become inclined toward it, leaning toward it, and bent toward it.
"Even the gods pay homage to him" means that not only humans, but indeed the gods throughout immeasurable world-systems also pay homage to him.
"Thus have I heard from the Arahant" means that thus have I heard from the Arahant on account of reasons such as his being far removed (*ārakatta*).

This shows that [the teaching] was heard in the presence of the Blessed One and the Dhamma-Generals (Sāriputta and others) as they were saying, "The Teacher of gods and men," and so forth. "One who has transcended all fetters" means one who,
by means of the four paths as appropriate, has [transcended] all ten fetters along with their underlying tendencies (*vāsanā*).

"Transcended": it has arrived at the "vanless" (nibbāna) from the forest of defilements (*kilesa-vana*), having reached that which is devoid of them. "Delighting in renunciation through sensual pleasures":

having completely emerged from all sensual pleasures, it delights in renunciation (*nekkhamma*) in its various forms such as the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), meditative absorption (*jhāna*), and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Like gold released from rock": because its essential nature has escaped from what is insubstantial, it is like gold released from rock.
The construction is: "Even the gods pay homage to him.
"He indeed is the Nāga of supreme radiance" means that he does not, in any way whatsoever, commit an offense (*āgu*); he does not go to renewed existence; he is powerful like a *nāga*.
The one named "Nāga," the Perfectly Enlightened One, is "of supreme radiance" (*accaruci*) by virtue of the radiance of his own body and the radiance of his knowledge.
And having transcended the world together with its devas, his radiance shone. How so? Like the Himalayas among other mountain ranges;

for just as the Himalayas, the king of mountains, outshines all other mountains by virtue of qualities such as his own stability, weightiness, and great essence, even so he outshone them—this is the meaning.
"Of all those named 'Nāgas'" refers to the snake-nāgas, elephant-nāgas, human-nāgas, and the nāgas who are trainees (sekha), non-trainees (asekha), and paccekabuddhas.
Or: *Saccanāma* means one whose name is true by virtue of truth itself. That quality of having a true name he will explain himself with the words, "For he does not commit sin," and so forth.
Now, demonstrating the Buddha-nāga both analytically and as a whole, he first shows him by name, saying, "For he does not commit sin.
Because he does not commit sin—that is, evil—in every way whatsoever, therefore he is called a *nāga*; this is the meaning. *Soraccaṃ*... [etc.]
Virtue (*sīla*) and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*), which is compassion (*karuṇā*):
since these two are the forerunners of the entire mass of qualities, it is fitting that they constitute the two front feet of the Buddha-elephant; thus he said, "Those two are the elephant's feet.
Speaking of the other [rear] feet, he said, "Mindfulness and clear comprehension—those others are the elephant's feet. "Those others" means...

Or there is another reading. The analysis of the words for those [terms] is as follows: he whose hand is faith (*saddhā*) in the undertaking of blameless qualities is "one who has faith as his hand" (*saddhāhattha*).

He who possesses well-purified feeling (*vedanā*), the various kinds of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) as his white teeth is "one who has equanimity as his white teeth" (*upekkhāsetadantavā*).
Wisdom (*paññā*) is the head; mindfulness (*sati*) is its support. Thus it is said: "Mindfulness is the neck, wisdom is the head. Inquiry (*vīmaṃsā*)...

“Contemplation of the Dhamma” (dhammacintanā) means that just as the touching and smelling with the trunk of a noble elephant of what is edible and what is inedible is called its “investigation,” so too the contemplation of wholesome and other states by the Buddha-elephant is an “investigation.
It is a “common abode” (samāvāsa) because they dwell together therein; the vessel, namely the belly, is the common abode, because it serves as the receptacle for the higher knowledges and serenity.
One whose dwelling in the Dhamma is in the belly—that is, one for whom the Dhamma consisting of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) is the internal abode—is a "Dhamma-belly-dweller.
"Seclusion" (*viveka*) refers here to seclusion from the substrata of existence (*upadhiviveka*). "Of him" refers to the Buddha-elephant. "Tail" is used because it is the final limb.
"A meditator" (*jhāyī*) means one whose nature is to meditate through the close contemplation of an object. "From the stream of consolation" means from Nibbāna, which is the supreme consolation.
“Delighted. Regarding “well-composed within,” this refers to being perfectly composed in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) while dwelling upon internal objects.
To show that this state of composure is excellent and persists at all times, it is said: “The Naga goes composed,” and so forth.
For the Blessed One, because he has abandoned restlessness along with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), there is no distraction; thus, he is always indeed composed. Therefore, whatever...
Whatever posture he adopts, he adopts it while remaining concentrated.
"In all instances" means in every object of experience (*gocara*) and at every door (*dvāra*), with his conduct entirely closed off [to unwholesome states]. Therefore he said:
"All bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge," and so forth. "This is the perfection of the Nāga" refers to this: "Not..."

By such passages as "for he performs [the arrival]" and so forth, or by "the Fully Awakened One" and so forth, the perfection of the qualities of the Buddha-elephant— both those already mentioned and those yet to be described—
is shown. "He partakes of blameless things" means that, through having reached the highest excellence of right livelihood, he partakes of things that are beyond reproach.
The construction is as follows: because wrong livelihood has been abandoned in its entirety along with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), he does not consume what is blameworthy or censurable;
and while consuming what is blameless, he consumes it while avoiding hoarding (*sannidhi*).
"Fetter" (*saṃyojana*) is so called because it fetters the continuum together with the suffering of the round of existence, and is thus capable of causing one to sink into the round.
The tenfold fetter (*saṃyojana*) consists of both the subtle and the gross—that is, the small and the great.

"Having cut all bonds" means having severed the bond of the defilements without remainder by means of the knowledge of the Path (*magga-ñāṇa*). "In whatever direction" means in whichever particular quarter or region.
For just as the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) born in water grows in water yet is not defiled by the water, because its very nature is to be unstained; [so too is the Tathāgata].

Likewise, the Buddha, born in the world, dwells in the world; he is not defiled by the world because of the absence of the stains of craving, views, and conceit—this is the construction [of the meaning].
*Gini* means fire. *Anāhāra* means without fuel.
*Atthassāyaṃ viññāpanī* means it is an illuminator of the meaning to be illustrated, namely, the Teacher’s qualities which constitute the subject of the simile; it is an elucidator.

This is the "simile of the elephant. "By the wise" refers to those who, with reference to themselves, fully understand the Dhamma of the Four Truths realized by the Teacher. "They will understand," and so forth, is a statement of the reason:

because the great elephants—the Arahants whose taints are destroyed—standing within their own domain, will discern the elephant, that is, the Tathāgata, the scent-elephant, taught by me, who am an elephant. Therefore...
The intention is that this simile was spoken by us for the purpose of making it known to other ordinary people (*puthujjana*).

"The Nāga, casting off his body, will attain final Nibbāna without taints" means that the Nāga who is the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, free from taints, having attained final Nibbāna with residue remaining at the foot of the Bodhi tree,
will now, casting off his body— his personal existence— attain final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*).

Having thus adorned [the teaching] with fourteen similes, sixteen verses, and sixty-four lines, he brought the instruction to its conclusion by extolling the virtues of the Teacher through the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Udāyī is finished.
The commentary on the Sixteen-Fold Chapter (*Soḷasakanipāta*) is finished.
16. Vīsatinipāta 1.
Adhimutta Thera-gāthā-vaṇṇanā:
In the Vīsatinipāta, the verses beginning with "yaññatthaṃ vā" are the stanzas of the venerable second Adhimutta Thera. What [is their meaning]?

As for his birth: this person, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.
Upon reaching maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and distributed great almsgivings. By that meritorious deed...
While wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in the womb of the sister of the Venerable Saṅkicca Thera during this current dispensation of a Buddha;

his name was Adhimutta. Upon reaching maturity, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of his maternal uncle, the Elder, and while practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship while still remaining on the level of a novice (sāmaṇera).
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the Protector of the World, Atthadassī, the supreme among men, had attained Nibbāna,
I attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with a serene mind.”
“Having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus— upright and concentrated—
I constructed a pavilion of sugarcane and fed that supreme Saṅgha.
Whichever womb I was reborn into, whether among the gods or among humans,”
“I overcome all beings—this is the fruit of meritorious karma.
Because I gave that gift of sugarcane eighteen hundred eons ago, I have never known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of the gift of sugarcane.”
“The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship and wishing to enter upon it while spending his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, he thought, “I shall ask my mother for permission,” and as he was going to his mother’s presence, he encountered a man searching for meat in order to perform an offering to a deity along the way.
He encountered five hundred bandits who were traveling along. The bandits seized him, thinking, "He shall be an offering for our deity.

Although he was captured by the bandits, he stood there fearless, undaunted, and with a serene face. Seeing this, the village headman of the bandits was struck with wonder and amazement, and praising him, he said:
"Those whom we formerly slew for the sake of sacrifice or for the sake of wealth..."
The rest were filled with fear, trembling and lamenting: “Yet you have no fear;
on the contrary, your complexion brightens.
Why do you not lament in such a time of great terror?”—thus he spoke these two verses.
In that context, "for the sake of sacrifice" (*yaññatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of sacrificing or for the purpose of making offerings to the deities; the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative.
"For the sake of wealth" (*dhanatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of seizing property. "Those whom we formerly slew" (*ye hanāma mayaṃ pure*): this is a present-tense verb used in the sense of the past.
"Having subjected them" (*avasetvā*) means having made them dependent or slaves. "Their" (*taṃ*) refers to those [beings]. There is also the reading "the remainder" (*avasesaṃ*).
They recite [this]. Of those taken by us, with the exception of that one, for the rest;
or rather, this is the very reading. "Fear arises" means the fear of death arises. By which they are pierced and lament: they are pierced by mental terror;
lamenting, they say such things as, "Master, we will give you this and that; we will become your slaves."
“Of you” means: of you who were threatened by us—who, desiring to deprive you of life for the sake of making an offering to the deity—while we had our swords raised.
“State of being afraid” (*bhītatta*) means the condition of being afraid; the sense is “fear.

“The complexion becomes even more serene” means that your facial complexion becomes clear and bright, surpassing even your natural color. It is said that at that time the Elder thought: “If these men kill me...”
"Right now I shall attain final Nibbāna without clinging; the burden of suffering will vanish"—with these words, a sublime joy and gladness arose in him.
"In such great fear" means when such a great terror of death has presented itself. Alternatively, this locative case is used in the sense of cause.
Now, the Elder, while giving a reply to the village headman of the thieves, taught the Dhamma as follows:
“There is no mental suffering for one who is free from longing, O village headman;
indeed, all fears have been transcended by one whose fetters are destroyed.
With the conduit to existence destroyed, he sees the Dhamma as it truly is in this very life.”
There is no fear of death for me, as if it were merely laying down a burden.
"The holy life has been well-practiced by me, and the path has been well-cultivated;
there is no fear of death for me, just as when diseases are brought to an end."
“The holy life has been well-practiced by me, and the path has been thoroughly cultivated;
states of existence have been seen as devoid of essence, like discarded poison once it has been drunk.
Having reached the further shore, free from clinging, my task is done and I am without taints.”
He is content with the exhaustion of his life, like one released from the place of execution.
Having attained the supreme state of Dharma and having no concern for anything in the whole world,
he does not grieve at death, like one released from a burning house.
“Whatever association there is, or whatever state of existence is found— All this is without escape;
so it was said by the Great Seer.
Whoever understands that in accordance with how it was taught by the Buddha,”
He grasps at nothing whatsoever, like a red-hot iron ball.
"It was," I do not think; "it will be," I do not think of mine.
Formations will pass away; what lamentation can there be in that?
“For one who sees, as it truly is, the pure arising of phenomena and the pure continuity of conditioned formations, there is no fear, O headman.
When one perceives with wisdom the world as being like grass and sticks,”
Not finding anything to call his own, he does not grieve, thinking, "It is not mine.
"I am weary of this body; I have no desire for further existence.
This body will break apart, and another shall not come to be."
“Whatever you wish to do with this body,
do that as you desire; because of that, neither blame nor affection shall arise in me.”—
Thus he spoke these verses.
“Having heard those words of his, so wonderful and hair-raising,
the young men laid down their weapons and spoke thus”—
this is the verse uttered by the compilers of the Council. Following this are three verses consisting of the speech and counter-speech of the robbers and the Elder:
“Having done what, O Venerable One, or who is your teacher?
Having relied upon whose instruction is this state of sorrowlessness obtained?
“The All-Knowing, the All-Seeing Victor is my teacher.”
The Teacher is the Greatly Compassionate One, the healer of the entire world.
Therefore, this Dhamma has been taught by him—supreme and leading to the destruction [of suffering].
By resorting to his teaching, that state of sorrowlessness is attained.
“Having heard the well-spoken words of the Seer, the bandits laid aside their swords and weapons;
some desisted from that work, while others took delight in going forth. Having gone forth in the teaching of the Sugata, those wise ones developed the powers of the factors of enlightenment.”
"With uplifted minds, joyful and with faculties composed, they have touched the unconditioned state of Nibbāna.
These are also verses uttered by the compilers of the Council.
In this context, "there is no mental suffering for one who is without longing" (*anapekkhassa*, O village headman); "longing" (*apekkhā*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*).
For one such as I, who is indifferent due to the absence of [craving], there is no mental suffering or dejection, just as pus lacks the nature of blood.
By way of stating the absence of dejection, he speaks of the absence of fear. Therefore he said: "All fears have been transcended.
"All fears have been transcended" refers to the twenty-five great fears and other [fears] of the Arahant whose fetters are destroyed.
The meaning is that all fears have been entirely transcended, passed beyond, and removed.

"In this very life, as it truly is" means having seen according to reality by means of the wisdom of the path, through the modes of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing regarding the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "In death" means for the sake of death. "As in the laying down of the burden" means just as...

The meaning is: just as a certain man, sinking under a great heavy burden placed upon his head, does not fear its being set down or removed, so it is in this case. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"The five aggregates are indeed the burden, and the person is the bearer of the burden."
“Taking up a burden is suffering in the world; laying down the burden is happiness.
“Well-practiced” means well-conducted. “The holy life” (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the three trainings.
For that very reason, the Noble Eightfold Path—the path itself—is also rightly cultivated, just as one would [treat] diseases.

Regarding "at the destruction" (*saṅkhaye*): just as a patient overwhelmed by many diseases experiences only joy and gladness at the destruction of those diseases, so too for one like me there is no fear in death, which is the destruction of the disease of the aggregates.
Existences have been seen as devoid of gratification; they are overwhelmed by the three types of suffering and set ablaze by the eleven fires. The three...
"I have seen that existences are devoid of relish and lacking in satisfaction.
'Like one who has drunk poison and discarded it' means that through negligence, as if having drunk poison and discarded it by such a means, there is no fear of death for me.
"As if released from the place of execution" means just as one who has been led to the place of execution by thieves for the purpose of being killed [is released] by some means from there...

Being liberated, he is joyful and elated. Thus, because he has gone to the further shore of saṃsāra—nibbāna—he is one who has reached the further shore (pāragū). Because he does not cling through any of the four types of clinging, he is without clinging (anupādāna).

Because he has performed the sixteen tasks beginning with full understanding (pariññā), he has done what was to be done (katakicca). Because he is free from the taints of sensual desire and the rest, he is without taints (anāsava).
With the exhaustion of his lifespan, he is joyful and glad on account of that exhaustion of his lifespan.

"Uttama" means supreme. "Dhammatanti" means the nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*). When arahantship is accomplished, the cause for its accomplishment is the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) toward desirable objects and so forth.
"In the whole world" (*sabbaloke*) means even in the entire world; that is, even in a world connected with long life, abundance of happiness, and so on.
"One who has no need" (*anatthiko*) means one who is without longing. "Like one escaped from a burning house" means just as some person [escaped] from all sides...
Just as one who has escaped from a house that is burning and ablaze does not grieve for the sake of escaping from it, so too the one whose taints are destroyed does not grieve for the sake of death.
"Whatever is clung-to" means whatever exists, is found, or is obtainable in this world that is clung-to.
It is the meeting or the convergence with beings or with formations (*saṅkhāra*). There is also the reading *saṅkhata* (the conditioned); its meaning is:
whatever is made by coming together and uniting through conditions, that is, dependently arisen. Or, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to where it is found;
that is, whichever existence-at-birth is found within a particular class of beings. All this is without escape. All this...
It is devoid of a lord; herein no one is able to exercise sovereignty by saying, "Let it be thus.
Thus it was said by the Great Seer—by the Perfectly Enlightened One who spoke thus: "All phenomena are non-self. Therefore, the construction is:
understanding that "this is without a master," one does not grieve at death.

“He grasps at nothing whatsoever”: the noble disciple understands those three states of existence exactly as they were taught by the Blessed Buddha—beginning with “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent”—by means of path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom.
Just as a man desiring comfort would not grasp with his hand an iron ball heated all day long, so too...
It does not grasp at any state of existence, whether small or great; the meaning is that it does not create craving for it.

Through the view of self, there is no occurrence of thought in me such as "I existed" or "In the past I was like this," because views have been completely uprooted and the true nature of phenomena has been clearly seen.
The thought "I shall be" does not occur to me; for that very reason, the thought "In the future, how indeed might I become such-and-such?
does not occur to me either. However, the thought "Formations will pass away" does occur to me: "It is merely formations proceeding according to their conditions;
herein there is no self or anything belonging to a self, and these formations will simply pass away."

“They will perish; they will break up moment by moment. In this regard, what lamentation is there? For one such as I who sees things thus, what lamentation indeed can there be concerning the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*)?
“Pure” means absolute, unmixed with the conceit of a self. “The arising of phenomena” means the arising of phenomena through conditions and their being produced from conditions.

The mere occurrence of phenomena such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) through conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*). The "continuity of volitional formations" (*saṅkhārasantati*) refers to the succession of volitional formations divided into the categories of defilements (*kilesa*), karma, and result (*vipāka*).
"Seeing it as it truly is" means knowing it according to reality by means of the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*) together with insight (*vipassanā*).
"The world is like grass and sticks" means that just as when grass and sticks in a forest that is not claimed as property are being taken by one person, they do not belong to another.

When he perceives with wisdom that the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*)— being ownerless— is like grass and sticks, such that the thought "this person is taking what belongs to me" does not arise,
he finds no sense of "mine" therein; finding it not, obtaining it not, and making none for himself,
he does not grieve, thinking, "It was mine," or "Alas, I am no more," or "That which was mine is now gone."
“I am weary of this body” means: I am weary of this body which is essence-less, hollow, painful, ungrateful, and by nature impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive;
it is with such disenchantment toward this body that I stand thus. “I have no need for existence” means:
I have no need for any kind of existence whatsoever; I do not long for any state of being. “This body will break up.”
"This body of mine will now break up either by your efforts or otherwise;
and there shall be no other" means that another body will not exist for me in the future, due to the absence of renewed existence (*punabbhava*).
"Whatever task [you have] with this body" means: do whatever you desire, whatever purpose you have for this body.
“If you so desire”: “It is not for that reason [of yours]”—that sign is the cause for you to perform whatever service you wish for this body.

“Therein,” meaning while they are performing it or not performing it, “hatred and affection will arise”—meaning, respectively, aversion and attachment will not occur, because of having completely abandoned concern for one’s own existence; this is the intended meaning.
The expression "therein" (*tattha*) is stated according to how it was attained, even though there are no other conditions and no aversion or attachment present;
it refers to those conditions. "His" (*tassa*) refers to the Elder Adhimutta.
"That statement" (*taṃ vacanaṃ*) refers to the statement regarding death, beginning with "There is no mental suffering," and so forth.
Having heard those words—which illuminate the absence of fear and are therefore marvelous and hair-raising—the young men (māṇavā) [asked]:
"What, venerable sir, have you done?"—that is, what kind of ascetic practice (tapokamma) have you performed? Or who is your teacher, and whose [disciple] are you?
Relying upon the Teaching (sāsana) and the instruction (ovāda), they spoke this meaning—that this state of being without sorrow (asokatā), the absence of grief at the time of death—is obtained;
they explained it by way of questions, they declared it.

Having heard that, the Elder, giving them a reply, said, "The All-Knowing One" (sabbaññū), and so forth. Therein, "the All-Knowing One" (sabbaññū) refers to [knowledge] not through the instruction of another.

He is "all-knowing" (*sabbaññū*) because, through the attainment of unobstructed knowledge—which is capable of awakening to all phenomena in every way and functions according to his own wish—he knows everything divided into the past and so forth.

He is "all-seeing" (*sabbadassāvī*) because he sees everything with that very same "universal eye" (*samantacakkhu*). That which is unobstructed knowledge is itself the knowledge of omniscience; there is no separate textual tradition for a distinct "unshared knowledge."
The contradiction [in the texts] is for the purpose of showing that this single knowledge is unique compared to others by way of its arising in different objects, because it is stated in two ways.
Furthermore, whatever needs to be said here has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the *Itivuttaka*;

therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated therein. He is the "Victor" (*jina*) because of his victory over the five Māras. [He is the one] distinguished by the divisions of inferior and so forth...
He is the Great Compassionate One because he is endowed with great compassion due to his disposition and conduct toward the entire multitude of beings;
he is the Teacher because he instructs those to be trained according to their needs through the ultimate truths pertaining to the present life and the future life;
for that very reason, he is the Healer of the Entire World because he cures the disease of the defilements of the whole world; he is the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Master.
The construction is "mine" (*mamāti*). "Leading to destruction" (*khayagāmī*) means leading to Nibbāna.

When the Elder had thus proclaimed the virtues of the Teacher and his Dispensation, some of the thieves, having gained faith, went forth into homelessness, while others declared themselves lay followers (*upāsaka*).
Illuminating this matter, the compilers of the Dhamma [said]: "Having heard... and so forth.
They spoke two verses. In that context, "sages" (*isino*) refers to those who seek (*esanatthena*) the training in higher virtue and so forth; [this refers to] the Elder Adhimutta.

"Having laid aside" (*nikkhippa*) means having abandoned. "Weapons and missiles" (*satthāni ca āvudhāni ca*) refers both to weapons such as swords and the like, and to missiles such as bows, quivers, and so forth.
"And from that work" (*tamhā ca kammā*) means from that work of banditry.

"Having gone forth in the teaching of the Sugata"—those thieves, having entered the going-forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One, the Sugata, by virtue of his beautiful gait and other such qualities;
"with uplifted minds," through being endowed with the joy characterized by rapture attained through a specific stage of meditation (*bhāvanā*);

"joyful," having reached a state of mental gladness (*somanassa*); "with developed faculties," meaning their faculties were cultivated; "they touched," by means of attaining the supreme path (*aggamagga*).

They attained the unconditioned Nibbāna. It is said that Adhimutta, having made the thieves cease their criminal activities and having stationed them right there, went to his mother, took leave of her, and returned. He then went with them into the presence of the preceptor;
having been ordained, he received full admission (upasampadā). Then, he explained a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to them. They...
Before long, they were established in Arahatship. Therefore it was said: “Having gone forth... [pe] ...the Unconditioned.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Adhimutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Pārāpariya.
The verses beginning with "A thought arose for the ascetic" belong to the Venerable Pārāpariya Thera. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence throughout various births, wandered only among happy destinies.
Then, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was born into a certain prominent brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
Having been born as a son, he was given the name Pārāpariya according to his clan.
When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas and attained perfection in the brahminical arts.

One day, at the time of the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he went to the Jetavana monastery and sat at the edge of the assembly. The Teacher, observing his disposition, [preached] the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta.
He taught it. Having heard this, he gained faith and went forth. Having mastered that discourse, he reflected upon its meaning.
The manner in which he reflected will be made clear through the verses themselves.
While reflecting in that way, he established insight by way of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) and before long attained *arahantship*. Later on, by himself...
Explaining the nature of his thought:
“A thought arose in the recluse, the bhikkhu Pārāpariya,
as he sat alone, secluded and meditating.”
“What is it that a person should practice in succession? What is the vow?
What is the conduct? How should one perform their own duty so as not to harm anyone?
The faculties of human beings lead both to welfare and to harm.”
Unprotected, they lead to harm; protected, they lead to welfare.
"One who guards the very faculties, protecting and guarding the faculties, performs his own duty and does not harm anyone."
“If one does not restrain the eye-faculty as it moves toward forms,
failing to see the danger therein, one is surely not released from suffering.
If one does not restrain the ear-faculty as it moves toward sounds...”
One who does not see the danger is not released from suffering.
If one who does not see the escape indulges in odors, being infatuated with odors, he is not released from suffering.
“Recalling the sour, the sweet-tasting, and the bitter-tasting,
one who is gripped by craving for flavors does not understand the heart.
Recalling beautiful and non-repulsive tactile sensations...”
One who is lustful finds manifold suffering on account of that lust.
"If one is unable to guard the mind against these phenomena,
then suffering follows him from all five of them."
“Full of pus and blood, and with much carrion;
made by a hero among men, beautiful like an inlaid casket.
Bitter, yet sweet-tasting; a bond of love that is suffering.”
Like one licking a razor blade smeared with honey, he does not perceive the danger.
One who is passionately attached to the form of a woman, to the voice of a woman, to the touch of a woman,
and to the fragrance of a woman, experiences manifold suffering.
“All these streams flow fivefold into five;
he who possesses energy is able to build a dam across them.
He is one who acts for the welfare of others, he is established in the Dhamma, he is skillful, and he is discerning.”
Even while enjoying himself, one should perform duties connected with the Dhamma and the goal.
Furthermore, one should avoid useless tasks that lead to exhaustion;
considering such things not to be true duties, the wise person remains heedful.
“Whatever is connected with the goal, and whatever delight is centered on the Dhamma—
taking that up, you should practice it, for that indeed is the supreme delight.
With various high and low means, one seeks to overcome others.”
Having struck, having slain, and then having caused grief, he who by violence plunders others—
just as a strong man, striking wedge with wedge, drives it home,
so too does the skillful one strike down the sense-faculties by means of the sense-faculties themselves.
“Cultivating faith, energy, concentration, mindfulness, and wisdom—
having struck down the five [hindrances] with the five [faculties], the brahmin goes free from distress.
He is one who possesses the goal, he is established in the Dhamma, having followed the instruction of the words.”
He prospers in happiness in every way toward the Buddha.”—he spoke these verses.
Therein, “of the ascetic” (*samaṇassa*) means of one who has gone forth. “Was” (*ahū*) means it came to be. “Thought” (*cintā*) means reflection on the Dhamma, investigation of the Dhamma.
“Of Pārāpariya” means of one of the Pārāpara clan. They also read it as “of Pārācariya. “Bhikkhu” means in the cycle of existence...
Fear belongs to one who is prone to craving. "Of one alone" means of one without a companion; by this he shows physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).

"Of one secluded" means of one who has begun seclusion through the suppression of the defilements by means of seclusion; by this he shows mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). Therefore he said, "of one who meditates" (*jhāyino*).
"One who meditates" means one whose nature is to meditate; the meaning is: one who is engaged in proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
The Elder speaks of all this as if he were another person.
With the words beginning “What is the sequence? (*kimānupubbaṃ*), he shows that reflection. Therein, in the first verse, “what is the sequence?
(*kimānupubbaṃ*) means: what is the succession (*anupubbaṃ*); what is the order (*anukkamo*) among the vows and practices that are about to be described; by what sequence?

The meaning is: "These are to be practiced. Regarding the phrase "What vow? What conduct?": a person desiring their own welfare should practice such virtue (*sīla*) as is called a "vow" (*vata*) in the sense of something to be undertaken, and such conduct (*samācāra*). By practicing it, one would be a doer of one's own duty, a doer of what ought to be done;
one would not harm or oppress any living being—this is the meaning. One's own duty is indeed the *samaṇadhamma* (the duty of a recluse).
In brief, these are virtue, concentration, and wisdom. For one who fulfills them, there is not even a trace of harming others;
for if such harm exists, the state of being a recluse itself would be non-existent.
As the Blessed One said: "One who harms others is not a renunciant; one who oppresses another is not a recluse."
And here, by the mention of "restraint" (*vāra*), the morality of abstention (*vāritta-sīla*) is included;

by the mention of "conduct" (*samācāra*), together with the morality of performance (*cāritta-sīla*), there are also the meditations, insight, and so forth, because these are to be practiced. Therefore, the morality of abstention is primary.

Furthermore, since when the restraint of the sense faculties is accomplished, all morality becomes well-guarded and well-protected, one should first [consider] the morality of restraint of the sense faculties.
Desiring to show this, and elucidating the dangers and benefits respectively in the non-protection and protection of the faculties, he said: "The faculties of men," and so forth.
Therein, "the faculties" is an indication of the phenomena that ought to be protected; therefore, it is meant that the six faculties beginning with the eye are intended.
"Of men" is an indication of the persons who are capable of protecting them. "For their welfare" means...
"For welfare" (*atthāya*). "For harm" (*ahitāya*) means for non-welfare (*anatthāya*). The word "become" (*honti*) is a remainder of the sentence.
But how can those very same [faculties] become both for welfare and for harm? To this he says: "When guarded," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:

For one whose faculties, such as the eye, are not covered by the door-panel of mindfulness, they lead to harm because they serve as the gateway for the arising of evil states such as covetousness toward forms and the like; whereas when they are covered, they lead to welfare.
They lead to welfare because of that absence.
For it is the very faculties that one guards; since the restraint of the faculties, when fulfilled, fulfills the perfection of virtue (*sīla-sampadā*);

the perfection of virtue, when fulfilled, fulfills the perfection of concentration (*samādhi-sampadā*); and the perfection of concentration, when fulfilled, fulfills the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-sampadā*).
Therefore, showing that the guarding of the sense faculties is indeed the root of the practice for one's own welfare, he said:

"One should guard the very sense faculties. By means of protection preceded by mindfulness, guarding the sense faculties themselves properly through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), [one ensures] that unwholesome thieves do not enter through those various doors and [steal] the wholesome goods within the continuum of consciousness.
They do not plunder; thus, the meaning is that they close those [doors]. And it is said with the inherent form of the prefix *saṃ* as in "passion" (*sārāga*) and so forth.
There is also the reading *saṃrakkhanti*. And "they guard the faculties" is a synonym for that very same thing;
the purpose of using a synonym is as stated in the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*.
It should be understood as follows: by the phrase "one who performs one's own duty," he shows the practice for one's own welfare;

by the phrase "and does not harm anyone," he shows the practice for the welfare of others. Alternatively, by both together, he shows only the practice for one's own welfare, since non-harming of others is itself a form of practice for one's own welfare. Or else, by both phrases, he shows the practice for one's own welfare.
He shows that for both the worldling and the trainee, the practice for the benefit of others is also a practice for one's own benefit.
Having thus shown the side of purification in brief— that guarded faculties lead to welfare—
he then spoke the passage beginning with "If the eye-faculty," showing analytically the side of defilement— that unguarded faculties lead to harm.
In this context, regarding the phrase "if one does not restrain the eye-faculty as it moves toward forms": if one who fails to see the danger does not restrain the eye-faculty—
which is moving toward and proceeding according to its own inclination toward desirable and undesirable sense-spheres of form, such as the various types of blue, yellow, and so forth—
and while failing to restrain or ward it off, does not perceive the danger in such engagement, then [there is] danger pertaining to the present life.
And if he does not see the danger and fault pertaining to the future life. There is also the reading: “One who sees no escape should restrain one who is going.

In that context, one who—abiding in the mere seen according to the method stated as “there will be only the mere seen”—proceeds within the sense-sphere of visible form by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension, is called “one who sees the escape from it.”
By the reverse of what was stated, one who sees no escape should be understood.
"He is not released from suffering" means that such a person is indeed not released from the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).

And here, the non-restraint of the eye-faculty refers to its functioning in such a way that evil states such as covetousness might flow in through that door; and this, in terms of its actual meaning, is...
The non-fulfillment of mindfulness and clear comprehension is to be understood [as the cause]. The same method applies to the remaining faculties as well.
"Adhimucchito" means one who has fallen into a swoon through the infatuation of craving (*adhimutta-taṇhā*).

"Ambilaṃ" means sour taste. "Madhuraggaṃ" means a portion of sweet taste. Likewise for "tittakaggaṃ. "Anussaranto" means reflecting upon each respective taste by way of its gratification. "Ganthito" means...
One is bound and fettered by craving for tastes in this or that particular taste. Some read "gadhito," which means "one who has fallen into greed.
"The heart does not understand" means that one does not know or discern the mind that arose at the time of going forth with the thought, "I shall bring an end to suffering";
it does not grasp the heart of the Teaching, that is, the internal, blameless states.
The meaning is that one who is gripped by craving for the taste of touch does not understand, does not know, and does not practice accordingly.
"Beautiful" means lovely. "Not repulsive" means delightful and desirable. "Tangible objects" refers to contacts (phassa) divided into those that are appropriated and those that are not.
"Lusting" means colored by passion through its inherent nature of lustful attachment. "On account of lust" means with lust as the cause. "Various..."

"He experiences suffering" means that he obtains various kinds of suffering, both pertaining to the present life by way of the fever of passion (*rāga-pariḷāha*) and so forth, and pertaining to future lives by way of the torments of hell and so forth.

"And mind [is affected] by these" means that the mind is [affected] by these objects of form and so forth, which are distinguished as objects of mental phenomena (*dhamma*). "Him" refers to the person.

"By all" means by all five. This is what is meant: whichever person is unable to guard and protect the mind—the mind-faculty—from these aforementioned five things, beginning with visible forms, according to their classification as objects of consciousness;
because he cannot guard it by preventing the unwholesome kamma that arises therein, due to that lack of protection, suffering arises for that person on account of that [unrestrained mind].

It follows; it goes along with. And while going along, it goes together with all these objects—beginning with the five objects such as visible forms—and together with the sixth object, by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Herein, because the eye-faculty and the ear-faculty apprehend what is not reached, it is said:
"do not obstruct that which is going"; whereas the others are apprehenders of what is reached, [as in the case of] "scents..."

This is stated in the passage beginning with, "he partakes of this," and so forth. Furthermore, among those [cravings], craving for flavors (*rasataṇhā*) and craving for tangibles (*phoṭṭhabbataṇhā*) are especially powerful in sentient beings;
thus, it should be understood that it is said, "addicted by craving for flavors, recollecting tangibles.
In this way, for a person who does not guard the doors of the senses, there is non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) regarding all six objects through the six doors.

Having shown the suffering that arises, [the Blessed One] spoke these two verses beginning with "filled with pus and blood" while investigating the true nature of the body, because this lack of restraint occurs through a failure to understand the body's actual nature. The meaning of this is as follows:
this so-called "body" is filled and packed with pus and blood, and with other things such as bile, phlegm, and so forth.
With much effort, this [body] has been made beautiful and polished by that hero among men, a skilled master of arts, through the application of lacquer and other treatments;
yet it is filled within with impurities such as excrement, like a casket charming only in its outer skin, deluding the foolish,
and bitter because its nature is suffering and because it brings about the torments of hell and other realms of misery, arising from mere conceptual construction.
Because it is baseless, it is merely a gratification; because of its sweetness, it is a sweet taste; for that very reason, due to the bond of endearment, it is a bond of affection;

and because of its unendurability and lack of satisfaction, it is suffering. Thus, the world—failing to realize that within such a body great suffering is being experienced through greed for gratification—should be regarded as one who is greedy for sweetness, like a man licking the edge of a razor blade.
Now, these forms and so forth, which have been described as the objects of the eye and the other senses, are specifically desirable for a man because they are connected with women;
thus, showing that restraint must be exercised therein, he says, "In the form of a woman," and so on.

Therein, "in the form of a woman" means in the color (vaṇṇa) comprised within the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) produced by the four causes, belonging to a woman. Furthermore, whatever [form] of a woman’s clothing...
The color of an ornament, or of perfumes, pigments, and so forth, or of garlands worn on the body, when attached to the person, serves as an object for a man’s visual consciousness;
all this should be understood as "female form" (*itthirūpa*).
"Female sounds" (*itthisara*) refers to the sounds of a woman's singing, lamenting, laughing, and weeping. Furthermore, it includes even the sound of a woman’s clothing.

It should be understood that here, by the term "the voice of a woman," the sounds of flutes, lutes, conchs, drums, and so forth—though they are produced through the employment of women and even though they are themselves embellished with ornaments—are included. All of this draws the mind of a man.

However, the phrase "in the essence of a woman" (*itthirase*) is stated in the Pāḷi in terms of the sense-sphere of taste (*rasāyatana*) arising from the fourfold origination; it refers to the state of being obedient to a woman's command and so forth.

Some say that the "essence of woman" consists of the taste of her saliva and the taste of her enjoyment. However, whatever is the taste of the saliva and so forth smeared on a woman's lips, and whatever is the taste of the rice-gruel, food, and so forth given by her to a man—all this indeed should be understood as the "essence of woman.
As for tangibles, there is the contact of a woman’s body, as well as the clothes, ornaments, garlands, and so forth worn upon her body.

Contact should be understood as "the touch of a woman. And here, for those in whose text the reading is *itthirūpe itthisare*, the inclusion of *itthirasā* (the taste of a woman) should be understood by means of the word *api*.
Regarding "in the scents of a woman": this refers to the odor-spheres (*gandhāyatana*) of a woman arising from the four causes.
The so-called body-odor of a woman is indeed a foul smell; for some women have the odor of a horse, while others have the odor of a ram.
Some have the smell of sweat, some the smell of blood; nevertheless, the blind fool still becomes attached to them.
However, from the body of the Woman-Treasure (itthiratana) of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti), the fragrance of sandalwood wafts forth, and from her mouth, the fragrance of a blue lotus;
this does not belong to all women. Therefore, the "smell of a woman" (itthigandha) should be understood as the adventitious scent of ointments and the like applied to a woman's body.
"Sāratto" means well-attached, deeply clinging, infatuated; this term, moreover, should also be applied to "the form of a woman" and so forth.

"Vividhaṃ vindate dukkhaṃ" means that one encounters various kinds of suffering—pertaining to the present life through killing, imprisonment, and so on, regarding the signs of lust such as the form of a woman, and pertaining to future lives through the fivefold bonds and so forth.
"All these streams of women" means that all five streams of craving—without exception—flow toward the objects of a woman’s form and so forth.
"In the five" refers to the five doors of a man. "Of those" refers to those five streams.
"Blocking" means restraining; it is the establishing of mindfulness and clear comprehension as a restraint so that non-restraint does not arise.
He who is able to set this in motion is "possessed of energy" (*vīriyavā*), meaning he has "aroused energy" for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states.
Having thus shown the practice for one who has gone forth within the sphere of form and so forth, [the text] now shows that for the householder: "He..."
The passage beginning with “He is one who possesses welfare” has been stated.

In this context, “he is one who possesses welfare, he is one who stands on the Dhamma, he is skillful, he is discerning” means that such a person in this world is one who possesses welfare, is intelligent, is established in the Dhamma, is skillful in the Dhamma, is proficient in the Dhamma, or is diligent and discerning—meaning he is skilled in what ought to be done. He would perform even while enjoying himself that task which is connected to the welfare and the Dhamma.
