Even while enjoying himself with delight in the pleasures of the household life, he should perform each of those duties that are connected with the Dhamma and consistent with the Dhamma—that is, not departing from the Dhamma in terms of both principle and purpose.
He should bring about the acquisition of wealth not yet acquired, protect what has been acquired, and enjoy it;
and he should apply himself to the welfare of the three groups (the wife, children, and servants) without mutual conflict and without mutual obstruction.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). And this method should be understood as being stated with reference to those—such as the great king Bimbisāra and others—for whom it applies by way of the three aggregates of welfare (*tivagga-attha*) without contradicting right practice; it is not meant for just anyone.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it sinks when conjoined": if one grasps a purpose pertaining to this world (*idhaloka*), that is, a benefit belonging to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), [then it sinks].

"Steadfast. Regarding "what should be avoided": even if one were to relinquish or abandon an action that is purposeless—meaning an action devoid of benefit for future lives and associated with harm—one should not consider it a duty.
Being "heedful and discerning" means being heedful through the non-abandonment of mindfulness and discerning through the arising of investigative wisdom regarding what is associated with harm.
Thinking, "That task should not be done by me," one should avoid it.
But having avoided it, one should practice by undertaking that which is connected with purpose and that delight which pertains to the Dhamma.
Whatever is connected with purpose—that is, with benefit—distinguished as pertaining to the present life or the future life, and which brings about both kinds of welfare; [that one should undertake].
And whatever delight is directed toward superior wholesome states and accompanied by serenity and insight— one should practice after correctly undertaking and embracing both of these.
For, according to the statement, "Delight in the Dhamma conquers all delight," that is indeed called the supreme delight because it leads unilaterally to the highest goal.

However, regarding that which was stated—that an activity connected with sensual delight is useless—it was said, "By various means," and so forth, in order to demonstrate its lack of connection with the beneficial.
Therein, "various" (*uccāvacehi*) means both great and small.
"Means" (*upāyehi*) means methods. "He seeks to conquer others" means he desires to take away what belongs to others; [he seeks] others...
Or he entirely ruins it; having struck down another, having killed them, and then having caused them to grieve, he who violently plunders the property of others.

This is what is meant: that person, for the sake of sensual pleasure, while striking others, causing them to be slain, or causing them to grieve, strives to seize the belongings of others through various improper means such as breaking into houses, climbing over walls, or using forceful seizure.
He acts with recklessness, he violates [the law], he seeks to seize, and by means of his wealth, he causes others to suffer loss;
that deed of his is based on sensual pleasure, leads to harm, and is entirely base.
By this, he demonstrates through contrast that delight directed toward the Dhamma is, in every respect, supreme.
Now, regarding that which was stated as "he who is able to create an obstruction for them," the obstruction of the faculties is explained along with the means:
"Just as a strong man, striking pin with pin, drives it out.
This means that just as a carpenter endowed with physical strength and the power of knowledge, desiring to extract a pin fixed within a tree trunk, [proceeds to do so].

Then, by turning a strong wedge, he draws it out; in the same way, a skilled bhikkhu who wishes to destroy the faculties such as the eye by the power of insight (vipassanā) destroys them by means of the very faculties themselves.

To the question "By which ones?", he says: "Faith," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: faith has the characteristic of resolution (adhimokkha); energy has the characteristic of exertion (paggaha).

By developing and increasing these five faculties that bring liberation to maturity— namely, energy, concentration characterized by non-distraction, mindfulness characterized by establishment, and wisdom characterized by seeing—
one destroys the state of being a gateway for the arising of defilements such as attachment and aversion in the case of the five faculties beginning with the eye, by means of these five faculties.

Having slain—that is, having utterly eradicated the defilements that serve as the necessary conditions for those [sufferings] by means of the Noble Path—the brahmin, being thus free from distress (*anīgha*) and devoid of suffering, goes to, or attains, *parinibbāna* without remainder (*anupādisesa*).

He is "one who possesses the goal" (*atthavā*): because he is endowed with the highest sense of purpose, that aforementioned brahmin is one who possesses the goal; [he is so called] because he has attained that [goal].
Because he is established in the Dhamma, he is "one who stands in the Dhamma. Having performed, in its entirety and by every method without exception,
the instruction consisting of the word of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and having stood practicing according to that instruction,
for that very reason, that man— the supreme person— thrives, cultivates, and increases the bliss of Nibbāna.

Thus, because the Elder has elucidated his practice by way of explaining the manner of his own reflection, this very [verse] should be regarded as his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Pārāpariya is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Telakāni.
The verses beginning with "For a long time indeed, being ardent" are those of the Venerable Elder Telakāni. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to dispassion in various states of existence, was reborn in this present age of a Buddha in the city of Sāvatthī within a certain brahmin family, even before the Teacher’s birth.

One who had received the name Telakāni, having reached maturity, felt revulsion for sensual pleasures due to his possession of the necessary causes. Abandoning the household life, he went forth into the wandering life of a paribbājaka.

With a mind inclined toward liberation (*vivaṭṭajjhāsayo*), while seeking deliverance by means of such inquiries as "Who in this world has gone to the further shore?", he approached various recluses and brahmins and asked them questions; however, they were unable to satisfy him. He...

With his mind thus unappeased, he wandered about. Then, one day, when our Blessed One had arisen in the world and was turning the sublime Wheel of Dhamma for the benefit of the world, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, went forth.
While practicing insight meditation, he soon established himself in Arahantship. One day, he—
Sitting together with the bhikkhus, he reflected upon the distinction he had attained,
and following that, recollecting his own practice, he declared it all to the bhikkhus:
"For a long time indeed, being ardent, I have reflected upon the Dhamma;..."
I found no equanimity of mind when questioning the ascetics and brahmins:
“Who in this world has gone to the further shore? Who has reached the state immersed in the Deathless?
Whose Dharma shall I accept—that which brings knowledge of the ultimate truth?”
“I have entered into a crooked place like a fish seeking bait;
bound by Mahinda’s snare, I am like the Asura Vepacitti.
I will pull him out, I will not release him from this lamentation and wailing.”
“Who in this world will release me from bondage and make known full enlightenment?
Which ascetic or brahmin, proclaiming the perishable,
shall I accept as my teacher— the one who carries away old age and death?”
“Bound by the fetters of doubt and uncertainty, constrained by the force of aggression,
with a mind hardened by anger and reached by wrath— this is the tearing asunder of longing.
Arising from the bow of craving, it is joined with two [factors] and fifteen [qualities].”
Behold, it remains piercing me deeply in the chest.
Because I have not abandoned my dogmatic views, and am incited by the power of my intentions,
I tremble, pierced by that, like a leaf stirred by the wind.
“Arising within myself, it quickly ripens upon me:
this body with its six bases of contact, wherein [the mind] always dwells.
I do not see any physician who can extract this arrow from me.”
Not by a sword with various blades, nor by any other means, can this doubt be removed.
"Who is my surgeon without a blade, who has no wound,
yet will extract the arrow resting within me— the arrow that pierces all my limbs?"
“Indeed, he is the best of Dhamma-physicians, the one who flushes out the poison of defilements;
to me who had fallen into the deep, he has shown the dry land and extended a hand.
I have plunged into this lake filled with dust and mud that is unfit to be taken.”
Deceit, envy, and aggression, enveloped by sloth and torpor;
the thundering clouds of restlessness and the storm-clouds of the fetters—
these currents carry away one of evil view, whose intentions are rooted in passion.
“Streams flow everywhere; a creeper grows up and stands firm.
Who could block those streams? For who indeed could cut that creeper?
O venerable ones, make a dam to hold back the flowing streams.”
“Let not your mind-made stream be suddenly lopped off like a tree. For me,
who am thus born of fear and seeking the further shore from this shore,
the Teacher— armed with wisdom and served by the host of seers— is my refuge.”
“You have given me a ladder that is well-constructed, pure, firm, and made of the essence of the Dhamma,
for me who was being swept away,” and he said to me, “Do not fear.
Having ascended the palace of the foundations of mindfulness, I reflected.
That which I previously did not understand was this generation, delighting in personal existence (sakkāya).
But when I saw the path for embarking upon the ship,
and without clinging to a self, I beheld the supreme ford.
“The arrow arising from oneself, produced by the conduit of existence—
for the non-occurrence of these, he taught the supreme path.
Lying latent for a long time, firmly established for a long time.”
"Buddha, may you dispel my bondage, you who carry away the poison of defilements"—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, "for a long night indeed" means for a long time. "Ardent" means possessing energy, having exerted effort in the search for the Dhamma of liberation.
"Reflecting upon the Dhamma" means [reflecting]: "Of what nature is the Dhamma of liberation, and how is it to be attained?"
While investigating and searching for the Dhamma of liberation, he did not find equanimity of mind.

"He asked various recluses and brahmins"—that is, while asking various sectarian recluses and brahmins about the Dhamma of liberation, he did not find, nor did he attain, the noble Dhamma which is by nature a state of peace, a complete tranquility of a mind that was previously unpeaceful by nature, and which is an escape from the suffering of saṃsāra; such is the meaning.
"Who is he who has gone to the further shore? and so forth is a demonstration of the manner in which the question was asked.
Therein, "In this world, among those ascetics and brahmins who claim to be founders of sects, who indeed is he who has reached the further shore of saṃsāra, which is Nibbāna?
Who has attained the state immersed in the Deathless? means: who has attained and realized the path of liberation that is established in Nibbāna?
The meaning [is as follows]: "Whose Dhamma shall I accept? means: from which ascetic or brahmin shall I receive and practice the Dhamma of instruction?

"Knowledge of the ultimate truth" (paramatthavijānana) means the knowing of the ultimate truth; the meaning is that they proclaim the occurrence and cessation of things in their non-erroneous state. "He was one who had entered into a crookedness within":
here, "crookedness" (vaṅka) refers to a state of wrong view because it is a crookedness of the mind, or else it refers to all defilements (kilesa).
"Within" (*anto*) means inside the crookedness of the heart, or rather, that the crookedness of the defilements has entered within the heart; this is the meaning.
"Like a fish devouring bait" (*macchova ghasamāmisam*): the intention is that he was like a fish devouring—eating—the bait, or like a fish caught on a hook.
"Bound by Mahinda’s snare, like the asura Vepacitti": by the snare of Mahinda, who is Sakka.

Just as Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, was bound, dwelling in misery and fallen into great suffering, so too was I formerly bound by the snare of the defilements, dwelling in misery and fallen into great suffering—this is the intended meaning. "I pull" means I drag.
"Him" refers to the snare of the defilements. "I do not release" means I do not let go. "From this lamentation and wailing."

"From this cycle of sorrow and lamentation. This is what is meant: just as a deer or a pig bound by a snare, not knowing the means of release, thrashes about and pulls against it, thereby making the bond tighter;
even so, I was previously ensnared by the snare of the defilements, and not knowing the means of release, I thrashed about by way of bodily volition and the rest.
I did not release him; rather, by making it even firmer, I led him to further defilement such as sorrow and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Who in this world will release my bond and make known full enlightenment (*sambodhi*)?", who in this world, releasing me from this bond of defilements, will realize—that is, awaken by means of it—the path to liberation which has received the name "full enlightenment" (*sambodhi*)?
“Vedayissati” means he will declare or explain. Some also read it as “bandhamuñcam”; the construction is:
“the awakening that releases from bondage, or the release from bondage.
“Ādisantam” means teaching. “Pabhaṅgum” means that which shatters, the destruction of the defilements; [it is] pabhaṅguṇaṃ.
Or, regarding one who reveals and proclaims the manifestation of the Dhamma—the driving away of old age and death—to whom shall I receive the Dhamma?

Alternatively, the reading is “paṭipajjāmi,” which has the same meaning. Regarding the knot of doubt and perplexity: this refers to the state of moving about by way of gliding and crawling, consisting of doubt that proceeds in the manner of “Was I indeed in the past? and so forth.
"And bound by doubt. "Endowed with the force of aggression" means joined with an aggression that has attained strength, characterized by the act of seeking superiority.
"With a mind hardened by anger" means having reached a state of rigidity through a mind possessed of anger in all respects.
"Tearing apart through longing": for craving, by way of not obtaining what is desired and so forth, tears apart the minds of beings.
It proceeds as if [an arrow]. Because it stands near as a means for piercing even one standing at a distance, craving itself is established as the bow;

that from which this arises is "originating from the bow of craving," namely, the dart of views. Since that, moreover, consists of thirty varieties—namely, the twenty-based view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the ten-based wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*)—therefore it is said: "and two [times] fifteen."
The meaning is: "twice fifteen-fold. Regarding the phrase "behold the heart-born, having pierced through the firm":

he addresses himself, saying, "behold that which, being 'heart-born' (urasika) because it is connected to the heart, is 'firm' (bāḷha)—that is, exceedingly strong—and having pierced through, having penetrated the heart, remains right there in that very heart."
"Non-abandonment of secondary views" means the cause for not abandoning the remaining views that have become secondary views.
For as long as the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) does not depart from the continuum, so long there is indeed no abandonment of views such as eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

"Stimulated by the fire of intention" means stimulated—that is, incited—by intention, which is wrong thought, toward others, meaning toward other people who have fallen away from the characteristic of reliance.
"Struck by that, I tremble": struck by that dart of wrong view (*diṭṭhi-salla*) in such a way that it remains piercing the heart, I tremble;
I am agitated and tossed here and there by way of eternalism, annihilationism, and so forth.
"Like a leaf stirred by the wind": like a tree leaf released from its stalk and shaken by the *māluta*—the wind.
"Arising within myself": this is not like a dart in the world that, having arisen from the outside, pierces and afflicts from within.

Rather, this [fever] arises within me, in my own personal existence (*attabhāva*), and it quickly and swiftly cooks and burns that body consisting of the six bases of contact which is designated as "personal existence.
How is it like? It is like a fire that burns along with its own support.
While burning that very personal existence (*attabhāva*) which belongs to me and is mine, it remembers and functions right where it has arisen.
"I do not see such a physician" means: because he is appointed to such a medical treatment, I do not see a physician, a surgeon, a healer (*bhisakka*), who is a *tekiccha*.
"Who might extract this dart for me" refers to a physician who [might extract] this dart of wrong view (*diṭṭhisalla*).

One should extract the dart of the defilements; and while extracting it, one should insert a probe known as a "cord" (rajjusadisa) made of various cords, and having cut with a blade, one must bring it forth and apply it, for it is not possible to treat a dart that has taken root through doubt by any other application of mantras or medicinal herbs.
Furthermore, "doubt" is mentioned here merely as an illustration; this applies to all [defilements] as well.
The meaning should be understood by way of the arrow of the defilements (*kilesasalla*).
"Without a weapon" (*asattha*) means devoid of a weapon. "Without a wound" (*avaṇa*) means without an opening.

"Resting within" (*abbhantarapassaya*) means situated in dependence upon the heart, which is reckoned as "within. "Not harming" (*ahiṃsa*) means not pressing or afflicting. There is also the reading "ahiṃsā," [meaning] by non-harming, that is, by not afflicting.

The meaning. This is the summarized meaning here: "Who indeed, without taking up any weapon and without making a wound—and thus without causing pain to any of my limbs—will extract, in the ultimate sense, the shaft of the defilements which has become a shaft because it produces affliction within my heart, because it pierces within, and because it obstructs within?"

Having thus shown the manner in which he previously reflected by means of these ten verses, he spoke the passage beginning with “For he is the best among those who have the Dhamma as their refuge” in order to show that same matter again by way of another method.
In this context, *dhammappati* means having the Dhamma as its sign or cause. *Hi* is merely a particle.
*So seṭṭho* means that person is supreme. *Visadosappavāhako* refers to one who carries away the poison of my own defilements, such as lust and the rest.
The one who carries away, the one who cuts off. Who indeed would show me the dry land and the hand when I have fallen into the deep—
showing the dry land of Nibbāna and the hand of the Noble Path that leads to it, while consoling me, who have fallen into the exceedingly deep great flood of saṃsāra, saying, "Do not fear"?
“I have plunged into the lake of existence”: I have descended and entered the great lake of *saṃsāra* by way of submerging myself up to my head.

“The lake whose mud and dust are irremovable”: it is called a lake whose mud and dust—the mud consisting of passion (*rāga*) and so forth—are irremovable (*ahāriya*), meaning impossible to take away; [I am] in that lake. Or alternatively: “in the mud and dust that is irremovable.”
The meaning of "pāṭho" is that it is a pool where the dust of passion and the like, which is difficult to remove, remains close at hand.

Deceit (māyā) has the characteristic of concealing one's own faults; envy (usūyā) has the characteristic of being unable to bear the success of others; contentiousness (sārambho) has the characteristic of acting with overbearing pride;
sloth (thina) has the characteristic of mental sluggishness; and torpor (middha) has the characteristic of physical sluggishness. In that pool where these evil states (pāpadhammā) are spread out—
"Spread with deceit, envy, exertion, and sloth"—here the letter *m* is used as a sandhi-conjunction (*padasandhikara*).
The meaning is: "spread with these aforementioned evil qualities.

"Thundering with the clouds of restlessness"—this is stated by means of a reversal of word-order (*vacanavipallāsa*), [meaning] having the nature of turbulence, [described as] "the cloud of the fetters."
Restlessness is the thundering and roaring of clouds; those who possess it are "those with restlessness as their cloud-thunder. The ten kinds of fetters themselves are the clouds;
those who possess them are "those with fetters as their clouds. The currents are like great torrents of water;

the meaning is that wrong intentions based on passion, which abide in [the contemplation of] the foul and so forth, carry me away toward a false view, dragging me along specifically toward the ocean of the states of woe.

"Flowing everywhere" (*sabbadhi savantī*): these are the five streams—the stream of craving (*taṇhāsota*), the stream of views (*diṭṭhisota*), the stream of conceit (*mānasota*), the stream of ignorance (*avijjāsota*), and the stream of defilements (*kilesāsota*).
They "flow everywhere" because they flow toward all objects, such as forms and so forth, by means of the eye-door and the other doors;

or alternatively, because they flow in every respect through the various modes [of craving], such as "craving for forms" (*rūpataṇhā*) up to "craving for mental phenomena" (*dhammataṇhā*). "Entanglements" (*latā*) is in the sense of entwining.
It is called a "creeper" (*latā*) because it binds together like a creeper; this refers to craving (*taṇhā*).

"It stands having burst forth" means that having burst forth through the six sense-doors, it persists among objects such as visible forms. Regarding "those streams": who, being a distinguished person, could block those streams of craving and so forth flowing within my continuum by means of the dam of the Path?
That "creeper" is the creeper of craving; who will cut it? Who will sever it with the sword of the Path?
"Make a bank" means: make a bank, a dam, a barrier for those streams. "Venerable sir" (*bhaddante*) is a demonstration of the manner of address.
"Let there not be a mind-made stream for you"—the water-stream is coarse; even by foolish common people it is possible to make a dam and prevent it.
But this mind-made stream is subtle and difficult to prevent. Just as a water-stream, when it increases...

Just as one destroys a tree standing on the bank by felling it right there, so too, do not let him—having suddenly felled you who stand on the shore of the states of woe and casting you into the ocean of the states of woe—break you, ruin you, or bring about your misfortune and calamity; this is the meaning.

Thus, because this Elder had thoroughly mastered conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) in previous existences and because his knowledge had reached full maturity, [he understood] the suffering of phenomenal existence (*pavattidukkha*).
Having shown the manner in which he examined the defiled states such as doubt, and having now demonstrated how, having become stirred by spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*),

he went into the presence of the Teacher seeking what is wholesome, [the Buddha] spoke the words beginning with "Thus, to me who was born of fear," in order to show the specific distinction to which he became intent.
Therein, "Thus, to me who was born of fear" means in the manner just described.

For one who has conceived fear for *saṃsāra*—fearing the shore of this world on this side, which is full of peril—and who seeks and searches for the further shore, *nibbāna*, [asking] "How indeed might I be liberated?", wisdom (*paññā*) is his weapon;
it is a refuge for the world including the devas, and it is the instrument that utterly cuts off the defilements (*kilesa*).
He is thus called "one whose weapon is wisdom" (*paññāvudho*). This is because he instructs beings as is appropriate for them, according to the meaning of the present life and so forth.

It was "frequented by the host of seers" (*isisaṅghanisevita*), meaning it was resorted to and attended upon by the Teacher together with the assembly of seers—the multitude of noble persons beginning with the chief disciples.
It was "well-made" (*sukata*) because it was well-executed and constructed through the knowledge of teaching;

it was "pure" (*suddha*) because it is free from defilements; it was "made of the essence of Dhamma" (*dhammasāramaya*) because its core consists of such essentials as faith and wisdom; and it was "firm" (*daḷha*) because it cannot be shaken by opposing factors.
To me, who was being swept away by the great flood, the Teacher gave the staircase known as *vipassanā*;
and while giving it, he comforted me, saying, "By this you shall find safety," and spoke thus: "Do not fear.

He spoke of the "palace of the foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna-pāsāda*), which is to be attained through that staircase of *vipassanā*—namely, through the fourfold distinctions of the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) beginning with the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).

Having ascended the palace of the foundations of mindfulness, which is endowed with the four stages, I reflected upon the Dhamma of the Four Truths; I reviewed and penetrated it with the knowledge of the Path.

Regarding that multitude whom I previously did not understand—the people who delight in self-identity (sakkāya), namely those followers of other sects who delight in self-identity thinking "I" and "mine"—and their imagined self, I [penetrated them].

"Previously I thought it was substantial. And when I saw the path, as in the phrase "embarking upon the ship," when I saw the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*)—which serves as the means for embarking upon the ship of the Noble Path—as it truly is;
from that point on, not fixing, not establishing, and not grasping that class of sectarians and myself within the mind, [I reached] the ford known as *nibbāna*.
"I saw the vision of the Noble Path, which serves as a ford to the great shore of the Deathless; it is the most excellent of all paths and all wholesome states.
This means that I did not see [anything else] according to reality.
Having thus proclaimed his own unsurpassed attainment of the Path, he now [praises] the Teacher of that Path, the Fully Enlightened One.
He says, "The arrow arising from oneself," and so forth. Therein, "arrow" refers to the arrows of defilements such as views and conceit.
"Arising from oneself" means produced within the personal existence (*attabhāva*) which has received the name "self" because it is the locus of the conceit "I am.

"Developed by the craving for existence" means originated from the craving for existence and dependent upon the craving for existence; for that [craving] is the basis for views, conceit, and the rest.
"Origination": for the non-occurrence and non-arising of these aforementioned evil states.
"He taught the supreme path": he explained the supreme, most excellent, noble Eightfold Path, as well as the path of insight (*vipassanā*) which is the means to that end.

"Lying dormant for a long time": having lain down continuously within the mental continuum throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) for a vast period, [it arises] upon obtaining the necessary conditions.
It has become firm by way of its fitness to arise, and having ascended and remained upon a continuum that has been resolved for a long time.

As for "bonds" (*gantha*), the Buddha, the Blessed One, who removes the poison of the defilements that have become bonds within my continuum—namely, the bodily bond of covetousness and so forth—has dispelled them and caused them to be abandoned through the power of his own teaching. For among the bonds...
When [defilements] have been abandoned without remainder, there is no defilement left unabandoned.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Telakāni is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla.
The verses beginning with "Behold the mind-made" are those of the Venerable Elder Raṭṭhapāla. What is their origin?
It is said that long before the appearance of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great householders.
Upon reaching maturity, he established himself in the life of a householder following his father’s passing, serving as the superintendent of the jewel storehouse.

Seeing the immeasurable wealth inherited through his family lineage thus displayed, he thought, "My father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth, were unable to take even this much heap of wealth away with them;
yet it is fitting that I should take it and go.
Having reflected thus, he gave a great alms-giving to the poor, the destitute, and others. He [was] one who had attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).

While attending upon the ascetic, he was appointed by him to the sovereignty of the deva-world; having performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, he passed away from there and was reborn in the deva-world, where he enjoyed celestial splendor.
Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn in the human world as the only son of a family capable of restoring a divided kingdom.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, having appeared in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma,
was leading those beings capable of being trained to the land of safety known as the great city of Nibbāna. Then, that son of good family,
having gradually attained maturity, went one day to the monastery with lay devotees and saw the Teacher teaching the Dhamma.

Having seen this, with a mind full of serene confidence, he sat at the edge of the assembly. Now at that time, the Teacher placed a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who had gone forth out of faith.

Seeing him, he set his heart on that goal with a devout mind and, for seven days, offered a great almsgiving with great honor to the Blessed One, who was surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
Having made his aspiration, he performed it. The Teacher, seeing that it would succeed without obstacle, prophesied:
"In the future, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, he will be the foremost among those who have gone forth out of faith.
Having paid homage to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, he rose from his seat and departed. There, he remained for as long as his lifespan lasted.
Having performed meritorious deeds and passed away from there, he wandered among gods and humans; ninety-two aeons ago,
during the time of the Blessed One Phussa, while three princes who were the Teacher’s paternal cousins were attending upon the Teacher,
he performed service for them in their performance of meritorious acts.
Thus, having accumulated much merit in various states of existence and wandering only among happy destinies,
he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in the merchant Raṭṭhapāla’s house in the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika in the kingdom of Kuru.
Because he was born into a family capable of restoring a broken kingdom, he received the name Raṭṭhapāla, which was indeed consistent with his lineage.
Such was his name. As he grew up with a great retinue, he gradually reached youth and was united by his parents with a suitable wife;
established in great glory, he experienced a prosperity resembling that of the divine realms.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the countryside through the kingdom of Kuru, arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. Having heard of this, [the people...]
The clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Teacher; having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and desired to go forth.
After fasting for seven days, and with great difficulty and hardship having obtained his parents' permission, he approached the Teacher and requested the going-forth.
By the Teacher's command, he went into the presence of a certain elder.
Having gone forth, by applying himself with wise attention and increasing his insight, he attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the World’s Elder, the Neutral One;”
“I gave away the elephant Varana, who had tusks like plow-poles and was of great stature.
Adorned with a white parasol, equipped with a crest and a hand-ornament,
I had all that valued and caused a monastery for the Saṅgha to be built.”
“I had eighty-four thousand palaces built;
having made this great flood of alms, I offered them to the Great Sage.
The Great Hero, the Self-Existent One, the Supreme Person, gave his approval.”
Making all people laugh with joy, he taught the deathless state.
"The Buddha named Jalajuttara,
sitting amidst the community of monks, explained that to me and spoke these verses."
“This person had eighty-four thousand palaces built;
I shall describe their result—listen to me as I speak.
There will be eighteen thousand gabled chambers.”
They were reborn in the highest heaven of Brahmā, and they were made entirely of gold.
Fifty times the lord of gods will exercise sovereignty over the devas;
and fifty-eight times he will become a wheel-turning monarch.
“In a hundred thousand eons, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a teacher in the world.
Having passed away from the deva realm, impelled by the root of merit [of his past deeds],”
"For now, he will be reborn into a wealthy family of great fortune.
Later, having gone forth and urged on by the root of his white virtue,
he will become a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Raṭṭhapāla."
“Dedicated to the exertion, peaceful and free from acquisitions,
having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, being without taints.
Having risen and gone forth, having abandoned the abundance of wealth...”
“Toward worldly enjoyments, I have no affection, like [a dog’s] for a lump of spittle.
My energy is the yoke-bearer that carries the burden, bringing about security from bondage;
I maintain this final body within the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“The four analytical knowledges, these eight liberations, and the six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship and received the Teacher’s permission, he went to Thullakoṭṭhika to see his mother and father.
There, while wandering for alms in regular succession, he received stale sour gruel at his father’s residence;
partaking of it as if it were nectar, he accepted his father’s invitation for the following day.
On the second day, having eaten his alms-food at his father’s house, he approached the women of the harem who were dressed in their finery and asked, "Of what kind..."

Having said such things as, "O noble son, these are those very nymphs for whose sake you lead the holy life," when they began to employ their seductive arts, he turned their intention aside and, preaching the Dhamma connected with impermanence and other such themes, spoke thus:
"Behold this painted image, a heap of sores piled together; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“Behold this form fashioned by the mind, afflicted and full of many thoughts, which possesses no lasting stability— adorned with jewels and earrings,
yet it is but bone wrapped in skin, appearing beautiful only with its garments.”
“Feet adorned with anklets, face smeared with powder—
these are enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
Hair arranged in eight-strand braids, eyes anointed with collyrium— ”
It is enough to delude the fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
Like a freshly painted eye-ointment box, this putrid body is adorned;
it is enough to delude the fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
“The hunter set the snare, yet the deer did not fall into the trap;
having eaten the bait, we depart while the deer-trappers wail.
The snare of the hunter is broken; the deer did not fall into the trap.”
"Having partaken of the bait, we shall go, while the deer-trappers grieve"—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, *cittakataṃ* means "made variegated"; the sense is that it was made diverse by means of garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth.
*Bimbaṃ* refers to the physical form (*attabhāva*) adorned with long and other limbs in those places where length and such are appropriate.
*Arūkāyaṃ*: This refers to a body from which impurities flow out by way of the nine openings and the pores of the skin, and which is entirely ulcerated and wound-like, or a body consisting of wounds.
*Samussitaṃ*: It is "constructed" by means of three hundred bones. *Āturaṃ*:
It is "afflicted," meaning it is constantly ill because it must be maintained through various postures and so forth at all times. *Bahusaṅkappaṃ*: [It is] full of many thoughts.
It should be conceptualized in many ways by foolish people through superimposing what is unreal.

"Of which there is no lasting stability" means that for this body there is no state of permanence or a nature of endurance; it is, in every respect, subject solely to the nature of breaking up, scattering, and destruction.
"Behold that" refers to a person standing nearby, or he speaks with reference to himself.

"Form" (*rūpa*) means the body. For even the body is called "form" in such passages as: "That which is surrounded by space, depending on bones, depending on sinews, depending on flesh, and depending on skin, comes to be designated simply as 'form'.
By "jewel and earring," it is meant that which is fashioned with jewels and earrings belonging to head-ornaments and the like. Bone...
"Covered with skin" means it is enveloped in raw hide; "one sees the bone"—this is the construction.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in "and with earrings," one includes the remaining ornaments and decorations.
"It shines together with clothes" means that this form, even when inlaid with jewels, shines only when covered by clothes, not when uncovered.
The meaning [is as follows]. However, for those who read "aṭṭhitacena," the meaning is: "It shines when covered by a skin of bone;

it is called 'aṭṭhitacena' because it is covered. "Alattakakatā" means dyed with lac, colored with red resin (lākha). "Pādā" means feet. "Mukhaṃ cuṇṇakamakkhitaṃ" means the face is smeared with powder.

The face is smeared with powder; this refers to those devoted to adornment who, having removed facial pimples and the like with mustard-paste and having removed impure blood with salt-clay, apply facial powders and ointments.
"Alaṃ" means it is enough for the foolish, blind worldling who does not seek the further shore, for the sake of deluding and utterly confusing him as he delights in the cycle of existence.

It is sufficient and adequate to delude the mind of one who seeks the further shore but delights in the cycle of existence; however, it is not enough and not adequate for one who seeks the further shore and delights in turning away from it.

"Made in the pattern of eight squares" (*aṭṭhāpadakatā*): this refers to the arrangement of hair on the forehead made in the shape of eight squares, gathered together and fashioned after trimming the hair at the front, intended to cover the forehead;
this arrangement of hair is called "eight squares," which is also termed *alaka*. "The eyes" (*nettā*).
"Anointed with collyrium": both eyes are so anointed that the reflection of the collyrium is visible inside and at both edges, just as it appears when they have been smeared with it.
"Like a new painted ointment-box, this putrid body is adorned":

just as an ointment-box—an ointment tube—that is new, freshly made, painted with floral designs, crocodile teeth patterns, and so forth, is smooth, bright, and beautiful to behold on the outside, yet not beautiful to behold on the inside.

In the same way, the meaning is that their body, though adorned externally with baths, unguents, clothing, and ornaments, remains bright on the outside while inside it is putrid and filled with various kinds of impurities.
*Odahī* means he set [the trap]. *Migavo* means a deer-hunter. *Pāsaṃ* means a snare or a staff-trap. *Nāsadā* means he did not strike.
“Snare” (*vāgurā*) means a trap. “Bait” (*nivāpa*) refers to grass and other fodder thrown down for the sake of feeding deer.
This simile was employed by the Elder in order to make the meaning understood. Herein, the meaning is this:
just as when a hunter has set a snare with a pole for the purpose of killing deer, scattered bait thereon, and remained hidden nearby, one deer among them—endowed with speed and prowess—[escapes].
A clever deer, without even touching the snare, eats the bait as he pleases and departs while the deer-trapper is still crying out, "Oh, the deer has cheated me!
Another deer, strong, clever, and endowed with great speed, goes there, eats the bait, and breaks the snares here and there, thinking, "The deer has indeed cheated me; the snare is broken!"

"The deer hunter departs even while grieving; so too we, having previously in our time as worldlings enjoyed wealth provided by our parents for the sake of sensual indulgence, went forth without being attached to this or that.
But now, having completely severed the defilements and standing as those who are no longer dependent, we eat the food given by them and depart even while they are grieving."
Thus the Elder showed himself as one who, like a deer-hunter, had abandoned his parents; who, like a snare of nets, had abandoned gold, silver, and the female court;
who, like grass for a meal, had abandoned the wealth he had enjoyed in the past and the food he was now eating;
and who, like a great deer, had shown himself as having cast off all these things. Having spoken these verses, he rose up into the air before King Koravya.
He sat down on the auspicious stone slab in the Migājina Park. It is said that the Elder’s father had bolts placed at the seven gate-towers and commanded the Mallas:
"Do not allow anyone to exit; remove their saffron robes and have them dress in white.
Therefore, the Elder traveled through the air. Then King Koravya, having heard that the Elder was seated there, [approached].
Having approached him and exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he asked:
"Master Raṭṭhapāla, one who goes forth here does so having encountered the loss of health through illness, or the loss of wealth, or the loss of relatives.
But you have not experienced any such loss; for what reason have you gone forth? Then the Elder said to him: "It is being carried away..."

Having explained the state of solitude for himself through these four summaries of the Dhamma—"The world is unstable; the world is without refuge and without a lord; the world is ownerless, everything must be abandoned and departed from;
the world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving"—he spoke this verse in response to that teaching:
“I see people in the world with wealth who, having acquired riches, do not give them away out of delusion;
greedy, they hoard their wealth and desire even more sensual pleasures.
A king, having conquered the earth by force and dwelling upon the great earth bounded by the oceans...”
Unsatisfied with this side of the ocean, one might long for the far shore as well.
Both kings and many other people, not having overcome craving, meet their death;
they cast off the body while still incomplete, for there is no satiety with sensual pleasures in this world.
“His kinsmen weep, tearing at their hair, crying out, ‘Alas! Oh, that he were not dead!
Having wrapped him in a cloth, they carry him out, pile up a funeral pyre, and then burn him.
He is burned while being pierced by stakes, having abandoned his wealth for a single cloth.”
For one who is dying, there are no refuges—neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor companions.
His heirs take away his wealth, while the being goes wherever its karma leads.
Nothing at all follows the one who dies—not sons, nor wives, nor wealth, nor kingdom.
“One does not obtain long life through wealth, nor does one ward off old age with riches.
The wise say that this life here is short, impermanent, and subject to change.
Both the wealthy and the poor experience contact; likewise, both the fool and the wise man are touched by it.”
For the fool lies as if slain by his own folly, while the wise man does not tremble when touched by sensory contact.
Therefore, wisdom is indeed better than wealth, for it is through wisdom that one attains final peace here.
For it is through lack of peace regarding various states of existence that one commits evil deeds out of delusion.
“He enters the womb and the other world, undergoing the cycle of existence in succession;
the one of little wisdom, placing full faith in him, likewise enters the womb and the other world.
Just as a thief caught at the mouth of a tunnel is executed for his own deed, so too is the evil-natured person slain by his own karma.”
Thus, when people pass away to the world beyond, one of evil nature is destroyed by their own karma.
"For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful; they agitate the mind in their various forms.
Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, therefore, O King, I have gone forth."
“Like ripe fruits falling from trees, young and old alike fall when the body breaks up.
Seeing this too, O King, I have gone forth; the life of a recluse alone is surely better, for it is unerring.
Out of faith I have gone forth, devoted to the teaching of the Conqueror.”
My renunciation has not been in vain; free from debt, I enjoy my food.
Having seen sensual pleasures as a blazing fire, gold as a blade, conception in a womb as suffering, and the great terror in the hells.
“Having understood this danger, I then attained a sense of spiritual urgency;
being pierced by that [realization], I have now reached the destruction of the taints.
The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.”
“Heavy is the burden that has been laid down; the fetter to existence has been utterly destroyed.
That purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me. He spoke these verses.
"In this regard, O Great King, I see that in this world there are wealthy people, endowed with riches and possessing great fortune;
yet, having acquired wealth and being established in the abundance of enjoyments, they give nothing at all to any ascetics, brahmins, or others. Why?
Because of delusion and the absence of the wisdom that understands one's own karma as one's own property. They are greedy, overcome by avarice."
They make a complete accumulation and hoarding of whatever wealth they have acquired. Furthermore,
beyond their already attained desires, they long for and yearn for further sensual pleasures and objects of desire, thinking,
"May I obtain such enjoyments as these," and they exert themselves toward that end.
Showing further examples of the pursuit of sensual pleasures (*kāmapatthanā*), he said, beginning with “The king.
Therein, “having conquered the earth by force” means having forcibly subdued the earth inherited through his own lineage. “Dwelling” means ruling over it.
“On this side of the ocean” means that even though he had obtained the entire region on this side of the ocean, being unsatisfied with that, [he sought] the further shore.
One might even desire another island in the ocean. "Not free from craving" means craving has not departed.

"As if incomplete" means as if their desires were unfulfilled. "There is no satiety with sensual pleasures in this world": for those possessed by craving, there is no such thing as satiety with the objects of sense-desire in this world.
"They wail" means they cry out, lamenting while praising the virtues of a deceased man. "Oh, alas!"... [etc.]
They say "no amarā," meaning "O, alas! may our kinsmen become immortal," and they speak thus; here, the word *vatā* is pronounced with a long vowel for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukhattha*).

"He is burned while being pierced by stakes" means that the deceased being is being properly cremated by the corpse-burners while being pierced by stakes. "Refuges" (*tāṇā*) are those which provide protection.
“Yenakammaṃ” means according to one’s kamma. “Dhanaṃ” refers to any object that is to be valued as wealth. Again, he says “dhanaṃ” with reference specifically to gold and bullion.
Having stated by the words “na dīghamāyuṃ,” etc., that there is no remedy for sensual pleasure and for aging, he then said “appaṃ hi,” etc., to demonstrate their absolute certainty.
“Phusanti” means they touch or encounter undesirable contact; therein—

This shows that being rich or poor is not the cause [of suffering]. "The fool and the wise man are touched by contact in the same way" means that just as the fool is touched by desirable or undesirable contact, so too the wise man is touched by desirable or undesirable contact;
there is no difference here between the fool and the wise man. But this is the difference: the fool indeed lies prostrate, struck down by his own foolishness.
When a foolish person is touched by any painful state, he lies down and sleeps as one who is smitten and oppressed by his own foolishness—sorrowing, wearying, and wailing with his chest beating.
Turning this way and that, twisting and contorting, he trembles when touched by contact.
But the wise man, the sage, when touched by the impact of suffering, does not tremble; not even the slightest shaking occurs in him.
Therefore, since such is the conduct of fools and the wise regarding worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), wisdom alone is better than wealth—that by which one attains finality here.
Wisdom is more praiseworthy than wealth, for by means of that wisdom one attains *nibbāna*, the end of existence, which constitutes the finality of becoming.
"Because of non-finality" means because the ultimate goal has not been attained. "In various states of existence" means...
Among great and mighty beings,
he enters the womb and the next world; having entered the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) through successive succession— having committed evil deeds and undergone wandering from one state to another—
he enters the womb and the next world, that is, by lying in the womb and arising in the next world.
And one who does not believe in the action of that person who has committed evil deeds, yet thinks, "I myself shall exist," and assents to this—
such another foolish person of little wisdom, by practicing accordingly, enters the womb and the next world, and is not liberated from it.
Just as a thief— a person of evil nature— while breaking into a house,
is caught at the opening of the breach by the guards, and because of that very act of his— the act of breaking the breach— is beaten with whips and the like,
and is tormented and bound by the king’s men; even so, O monks, does this world of beings here [suffer].

Having committed evil deeds, after passing away and reaching the next world by means of that karma, one is slain in the hells and other realms, and is afflicted through the fivefold tortures of imprisonment and penal servitude. Thus,
having explained the four summaries of the Dhamma as appropriate with these eleven verses,

[the author] now, seeing the danger in sense pleasures and in saṃsāra, [declares] his own state of having gone forth out of faith, and the attainment of the pinnacle of the duties of one who has gone forth.

While analyzing them, he says, "Sensual pleasures (kāmā)," and so forth. Therein, "sensual pleasures" refers to both object-sensual-pleasures (*vatthukāmā*), which are agreeable phenomena such as visible forms and so on, and defilement-sensual-pleasures (*kilesakāmā*), which comprise all varieties of lust.
However, in this context, object-sensual-pleasures are to be understood.

For these are variegated (*citrā*) due to their manifold nature consisting of visible forms and so on; they are sweet (*madhurā*) due to their desirable aspect, by virtue of being the gratification of the world; [and they are] for foolish worldlings...
They delight the mind, thus they are "mind-delighting" (*manoramā*). "In various forms" (*virūparūpena*) means by way of diverse forms; the sense is that they possess many kinds of characteristics.
For those [objects] are variegated by way of visible form and so forth, and manifold in appearance by way of blue and so forth.

Thus, having displayed gratification in such and such ways through those various forms, they agitate the mind and do not allow it to find delight in the life of renunciation—this is by way of their having little gratification and much suffering, and so on.
Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), I went forth for that very reason.
Just as the fruits of a tree fall—whether ripe or unripe—from external impact or by their own inherent nature, so too do beings, both young and old, fall upon the dissolution of the body.
"Having seen this" means having seen such impermanence with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*).
Having seen this, the intention is that it is not only the disadvantage [of sensual pleasures] due to their lack of satisfaction and so forth. "Infallible" (*apaṇṇaka*) means unerring;
the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*), which is the very nature of a monk (*samaṇabhāva*), is better and superior.
"By faith" (*saddhāya*) means [faith] in karma and its fruit, in the Buddha’s perfect Buddhahood, in the Dhamma’s perfect Dhamma-nature, and in the Saṅgha’s correct practice.
"Having placed my faith": "Endowed with the Victor’s teaching" means having entered into the correct practice within the Teacher’s dispensation.

"My renunciation has not been in vain" because of the attainment of Arahatship. For that very reason, "I eat my food free from debt," because I enjoy it as a master through the absence of defilements, enjoying it as one who possesses mastery.

"Seeing sensual pleasures as aflame" means seeing both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*) as being in a state of combustion due to eleven fires.
"Gold from the sharp-edged sword" refers to all varieties of gold, whether wrought or unwrought, as being like a sharpened blade because they bring about harm.
"Suffering from the descent into the womb" refers to the suffering of the entire process of saṃsāra beginning from the moment of conception.
The construction is as follows: "Having seen the great terror found everywhere in the eight great hells, which are full of suffering, [one thinks] 'In the hells there is great terror.
"Knowing this danger" means knowing this danger and fault of saṃsāra, such as the burning nature of sensual pleasures.
"I attained spiritual urgency at that time" means that at the time of hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, I attained spiritual urgency regarding existence and so forth.

"Pierced then" means that while he was still a householder, being pierced by the thorns of passion and the like, he has now, having come to the Teacher’s dispensation, attained the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*); or else, "pierced" means he has penetrated the Four Noble Truths.
The remainder is easy to understand, as it has already been explained in various other places.

Thus, having taught the Dhamma to King Koravya, the Elder went back into the very presence of the Teacher. And at a later time, while seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who had gone forth out of faith.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Māluṅkyaputta.
“Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost,” and so forth—these are the verses of the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta. The account of this Venerable One has already been told below in the *Chakkanipāta*.
Those verses were spoken by the Elder, once established in Arahantship, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to his kinsmen.
Here, however, it refers to the time when he was still a worldling (*puthujjana*), [when he said]: “It would be well for me, Bhante, if the Blessed One would [explain] in brief...”
When the Teacher was thus entreated, "Please teach the Dhamma," he said: "What do you think, Māluṅkyaputta?

Regarding those forms cognizable by the eye that have not been seen, have never been seen before, which you do not see now, and for which you do not have the thought 'may I see them'—is there in you any desire, lust, or affection for them?
"Certainly not, Bhante. "Regarding those sounds cognizable by the ear... [and so on]."

“Are odors cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tangibles cognizable by the body... mental phenomena cognizable by the mind such that they have not been cognized, have not been cognized before, you do not cognize them now, and you do not think ‘I might cognize them,’ yet there is in you toward them desire, lust, or affection? “No, venerable sir.
“In this case, Māluṅkyaputta, regarding those things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, as for what is seen, it is merely what has been seen.”
There will be, Māluṅkyaputta, in what is heard, merely what is heard; in what is sensed, merely what is sensed; in what is cognized, merely what is cognized.

But when, Māluṅkyaputta, regarding phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, there is in what is seen merely what is seen, in what is heard merely what is heard, in what is sensed merely what is sensed, and in what is cognized merely what is cognized—then, Māluṅkyaputta, you...
"Not by that. Since you, Māluṅkyaputta, are not by that, therefore you, Māluṅkyaputta, are not there.
Since you, Māluṅkyaputta, are not there, therefore you, Māluṅkyaputta, are neither here, nor in the world beyond, nor in between the two;
this itself is the end of suffering. Thus he spoke, demonstrating that the Dhamma had been thoroughly mastered when the teaching was given in brief.
“Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of lust, he feels it and remains absorbed in it.
For him, manifold feelings born of forms increase.”
Covetousness and ill will—by these the mind is struck down;
for one who thus accumulates suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost by one who attends to a pleasing sign.
With a mind full of passion he experiences it, and he remains clinging to it.
For him, many sensations arise from sounds;
through covetousness and ill-will, his mind is struck down.
For one who accumulates suffering in this way, it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having smelled a scent, mindfulness is lost by one who attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of passion, he experiences it and remains clinging to it.
“For him, feelings arise in manifold ways born of scents;
covetousness and cruelty afflict his mind.
For one who thus accumulates suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is far away.”
“Having tasted [the flavor], mindfulness is lost as one attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of lust, one experiences it and remains absorbed in it.
For such a person, manifold sensations born of that flavor increase.”
Covetousness and ill will—by these the mind is struck down;
for one who thus accumulates suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
“When contact has been made and mindfulness is lost, as one attends to a pleasing sign;”
With a mind full of passion he experiences it, and he persists by cleaving to it.
His feelings increase, arising from manifold contacts;
covetousness and ill-will assail his mind.
For one who accumulates suffering in this way, it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having understood the Dhamma, if mindfulness is lost while attending to an attractive object,
one experiences it with a mind full of passion and remains clinging to it.
“For him, feelings increase, arising from many phenomena;
covetousness and ill will afflict his mind.
For one who thus accumulates suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is far away.”
“He is not infatuated with forms, being mindful when he sees a form;
with a mind detached, he experiences it, and he does not remain clinging to it.
Just as he perceives the form, and as he experiences the feeling while indulging in it...”
He diminishes and does not accumulate; thus he fares mindfully.
For one who thus diminishes suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is near.
"He is not stained by sounds; having heard a sound, he remains mindful."
With a mind detached, he experiences [feeling], yet he does not remain clinging to it.
"Just as his hearing of sounds and his indulging in feeling cause him to diminish rather than to accumulate, so does he live with mindfulness."
For one who thus diminishes suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.
"He does not take delight in odors; having smelled an odor, he remains mindful.
With a mind detached, he experiences it, and he does not remain clinging to it."
“When, while smelling an odor and experiencing the feeling that arises from it,
one’s defilements diminish and do not increase— one who acts thus is mindful.
For one who thus wears away suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is near.”
“He is not attached to flavors, being mindful while tasting a flavor;
with a detached mind he experiences it, and he does not remain clinging to it.
Just as he tastes the flavor, and as he experiences the sensation from indulging in it...”
It diminishes and does not accumulate; thus he dwells mindful.
For one who thus reduces suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is near.
He is not stained by contacts; having experienced a contact, he remains clearly comprehending.
With a detached mind he experiences [feeling], and he does not remain clinging to it.
Just as his contact, when touched, and his feeling, when indulged in,
diminish rather than accumulate— so does he live with mindfulness.
For one who thus diminishes suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.
"He does not take delight in phenomena, being mindful and having understood phenomena;
with a detached mind he experiences them, and he does not remain clinging to them."
“As one who understands phenomena as they are, and experiences feelings as they arise,
wastes away and does not accumulate— thus he dwells mindful.
For one who thus diminishes suffering, it is said that Nibbāna is near.”
He spoke these verses.
Therein, "having seen a form" means having perceived with the eye-door a form cognizable by the eye.
"Mindfulness is lost, he attends to a pleasing sign" means that, instead of remaining right after merely seeing that form, he attends to a beautiful sign (*subhanimitta*).
For one who attends to it improperly by way of grasping at the aspect of beauty, mindfulness becomes lost.
And with such mindfulness, his mind being inflamed, he experiences that objective field of form; having become impassioned, greedy, and infatuated, he feels it, relishes it, and delights in it.
Being thus disposed, he cleaves to it and persists in that objective field of form.
Clinging, adhering, and being convinced that "pleasure is pleasure," he swallows it and makes it his final conclusion.

For such a person, various feelings arising from form—having form as their object and distinguished by pleasure and so forth—increase; these are the causes for the arising of defilements. Covetousness...

"And vexation": the mind of this person is struck and oppressed by covetousness (*abhijjhā*), which arises through attachment to what is pleasant, and by vexation (*vihesā*)—characterized by sorrow and so forth—which arises through resentment toward what is unpleasant, and which occurs due to the transformation and alteration of that very same pleasant object.
"Suffering for one who accumulates" refers to the manner already described.
As one accumulates the formative volitions for existence (*bhavābhisaṅkhāra*) by means of relishing various feelings, the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) proceeds.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “With feeling as condition, craving arises... [and so on] ...this is the origin of this mass of suffering.

For one who has become thus, Nibbāna is said to be far away, remote, distant; the meaning is that it is difficult for him to attain. This is also the case in the verses beginning with “Having heard a sound,” and so forth.
The meaning should be understood in the manner already stated. Therein, "having smelled" means having olfactorily perceived; "having tasted" means having gustatorily perceived;
"having touched" means having tactually perceived; "having known the phenomenon" means having cognized the mental object as a phenomenon.

Having thus shown the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) for one who is attached to the range of the six doors, he now shows the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*) for one who becomes dispassionate toward that same range.
Demonstrating this, he said: “He does not lust after forms,” and so forth. In that context, regarding the phrase “he does not lust after forms, being mindful when seeing a form”:

that person who, having seen a form—that is, having apprehended a form-object that has come into the range of vision by means of the stream of consciousness through the eye-door—becomes mindful through the practice of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) by way of the fourfold clear comprehension, does not [lust] after form-objects.
One does not lust, nor does one generate passion; rather, one experiences with a mind entirely dispassionate.

Understanding the object of form (rūpārammaṇa) as it truly is—from its arising onwards—one becomes disenchanted. Becoming disenchanted, one experiences the feeling arisen therein with a dispassionate mind;
being thus disposed, one remains without adhering to it. Thus, that object of form is [abandoned] precisely through the state of having a dispassionate mind.
He does not stand attached, thinking, "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"; he does not adhere by way of craving, conceit, or views.
Just as for one who sees "form" these states such as covetousness do not arise, so it is for the yogi who sees form as impermanent and so forth.
And "of one who pursues feeling": [this refers to] the feeling arisen with reference to that [object].
And for one who cultivates those states associated with it by frequenting their objective domain, [it is said:

"It is exhausted" means that the entire cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) goes to its complete destruction and exhaustion. "It is not accumulated" means it is not built up, it does not reach an accumulation.
"Thus he walks mindful" means that, having become mindful and clearly comprehending through this practice of removing the defilements, he walks and dwells.

"For one who thus diminishes suffering" means for one who, by means of the wisdom of the path leading to diminution according to the method already stated, diminishes the entire suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).

"Nirvana is said to be near" means it is said to be in the very vicinity of the element of Nirvana with remainder (*saupādisesa*) and without remainder (*anupādisesa*), because of the realization of the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). In the passages beginning with "he does not take delight in sounds," it is also by this same [principle].
The meaning is to be understood according to this method.

Thus, having declared through these verses that he had grasped the Teacher’s instruction for himself, the Elder rose from his seat, paid homage to the Teacher, and departed. Before long, having further developed insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship*.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Māluṅkyaputta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sela.
The verses beginning with “Paripuṇṇakāyo” belong to the venerable Elder Sela. What is his origin?

It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a noble family; having reached maturity, he became a leader of a group and, after persuading three hundred men [to follow him],...

Having had a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) built for the Teacher together with them, and having offered a great almsgiving to the Blessed One and the community of monks once the fragrant chamber was completed, he clothed the Teacher and the monks in the three robes (ticīvara).
By that meritorious deed, he dwelt in the world of the gods for the duration of one interval between Buddhas; having passed away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During this dispensation of the Buddha, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the brahmin village named Āpaṇa among the Aṅguttarāpas, and received the name Sela.
Upon reaching maturity, having attained proficiency in the three Vedas and the brahminical arts, he resided in Āpaṇa teaching the mantras to three hundred young brahmins. At that time, the Teacher—
Having departed from Sāvatthī, while wandering on tour among the Aṅguttarāpans together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus,
the Blessed One, seeing that the knowledge of Sela and his pupils had reached maturity,
stayed in a certain grove. Then a matted-hair ascetic named Keṇiya, having heard of the Teacher’s arrival, went there together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having invited the Teacher for the following day, he prepared an abundance of hard and soft food in his own hermitage.
At that time, the brahmin Sela, while wandering on foot with three hundred young brahmin students,
entered Keṇiya’s hermitage and [observed] the matted-hair ascetics engaged in the preparations for the gift, such as splitting wood and preparing the hearth.
Seeing him making preparations, [the Teacher] asked, "What is it, Keṇiya, that such a great sacrifice has been set forth?
When he replied, "The Buddha, the Blessed One, has been invited by me for tomorrow," the moment he heard the word "Buddha," he became joyful, elated, and filled with rapture and gladness;
he immediately approached the Teacher together with his young brahmin students.
Having exchanged greetings and sat down to one side, he saw the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One’s body and thought:
“One endowed with these marks is either a wheel-turning monarch or a Buddha in this world who has rolled back the veil [of ignorance].
But this man is a renunciant; I do not yet know whether he is a Buddha or not. However, I have heard this:”
When the elder brahmins, the seniors, and the teachers of teachers were speaking, [the Buddha thought]:
"Those who are Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, reveal themselves when their own praise is being spoken.

For, standing face-to-face while being extolled for the qualities of a Buddha, one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One becomes embarrassed and falls into a state of diffidence because he has not attained fearlessness.
"Because he is unable to endure my questioning, what if I were now to praise the ascetic Gotama to his face with appropriate verses?
Having thought thus, he said:
"Full-bodied, radiant, well-born, and beautiful to behold;"
"O Blessed One, you are golden-hued, with most white teeth and endowed with vigor.
For all those marks that belong to a well-born man,
they are all present upon your body as the characteristics of a Great Man."
“With clear eyes and a pleasant face, tall, upright, and majestic,
you shine like the sun in the midst of the community of monks.
O monk of auspicious appearance, your skin is like refined gold.”
"What use have you for the state of a recluse, when you possess such a supreme complexion?
You ought to be a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a lord of chariots,
a conqueror of the four quarters, and a sovereign of the Jambusaṇḍa."
“Khattiyas, lords of wealth, they become your followers;
O King of kings, lord of men, rule your kingdom, O Gotama!”—
with these six verses they praised the Blessed One.

In this context, "one with a complete body" means one whose physical form is complete due to the perfection of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*) and because of having no deficiency in limbs or members.

"Radiant" (*suruci*) means one whose bodily luster is beautiful. "Well-born" (*sujāta*) means one who is well-developed through the excellence of height and girth, as well as the excellence of physical proportions.
"Pleasant to behold" (*cārudassana*) means one who produces no sense of satiety even for those looking at him for a very long time.

“Of lovely appearance” (*cārudassano*) means that his appearance is not repulsive, but rather delightful and beautiful to behold. Some, however, say: “‘Of lovely appearance’ means having beautiful eyes.
“Golden-colored” (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇo*) means having a complexion like gold. “You are eighty”—this word is to be connected with all the subsequent phrases, such as “you have a full body” and so forth.
“With very white teeth” (*susukkadāṭho*) means having teeth that are perfectly white. For the Blessed One’s...
From his fangs, white rays of light stream forth like the rays of the moon.

He is "endowed with vigor" because he is preeminently possessed of the perfection of vigor, of the resolve for vigor endowed with its four factors, and of the attainment of the fourfold right exertion.
Indeed, he is "well-born among men" because he has fulfilled the thirty perfections, or because he has completed the conduct of a noble wheel-turning monarch.
"Of one truly and perfectly born"—the meaning is "of a Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*).

"All those" refers to the physical qualities consisting of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—such as having well-placed feet—which are designated by the conventional term "marks" (*byañjana*) because they manifest the state of a Great Man and the state of being the foremost person in the world;
and also the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), such as copper-colored nails and prominent nails. All these, without exception, belong to you.
The phrase "they exist in the body" is an elliptical expression (*vacanaśeṣa*).
Having concluded by restating through a different formulation the very same characteristics of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakkhaṇa*) that were previously mentioned,
he now speaks the words beginning with "serene-eyed" (*pasannanetto*) as a way of honoring the Blessed One with those characteristics among them that he personally prefers.
For the Blessed One has eyes clear with the perfection of the five-colored *pasāda* [tissue].

He is fair-faced due to having a face resembling the full orb of the moon. He is tall due to the perfection of height and girth. He is straight due to his Brahma-like symmetry. He is majestic due to his radiance.
Now, illustrating that very majesty through a simile of the sun, he said: "In the midst of the community of recluses," and so forth.

In this context, "you shine like the sun": just as the sun, rising up, dispels all darkness and shines forth by creating light, so too do you shine, having shattered all the darkness of ignorance both within and without, and creating the light of knowledge.

You are "of beautiful appearance" because you bring about the perfection of sight for those who have come to possess it, and because you are endowed with the five kinds of auspicious vision. "Possessing supreme beauty" means being endowed with the highest form.
*Cakkavattī* means he sets the wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*) in motion; he sets the four wheels of prosperity in motion, and by means of them, he causes others to move.
He is a *cakkavattī* because in him there is the turning (*vatta*) of the wheels of postures for the sake of the welfare of others.

Alternatively, it is because in him there is the turning of the wheel of authority (*āṇācakkassa vatto*), which cannot be overcome by others due to his possession of the four wonderful qualities and the bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
"There is a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī). "A bull among chariot-warriors" means a man who is a thoroughbred bull among those who drive chariots;

the sense is "a great chariot-warrior. "Lord of the four quarters" means the master of the earth bounded by the four oceans. "Victorious" means one who has won victory. "Of Jambusaṇḍa" refers to Jambudīpa;
for he speaks thus while demonstrating his sovereignty over what is well-known. But the wheel-turning monarch [rules] over the surrounding islands as well.
He is the sovereign of all four great continents.
"Khattiyas" refers to those of noble birth; "bhogīs" refers to wealthy landowners; "rājāno" refers to whoever exercises rule; "anuyantā" refers to followers and servants;
and "rājābhirāja" means being a king worthy of honor by other kings—the intended meaning is that he is a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattī*).
“Manujinda” means lord of men; the meaning is the supreme ruler of human beings.
When Sela had spoken thus, the Blessed One—fulfilling Sela’s wish by saying, “Those who are Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, reveal themselves when their own praise is being recited”—said:
“I am a king, O Sela,” (the Blessed One said), “an unsurpassed Dhamma-king.”
“I turn the wheel by means of the Dhamma, a wheel that cannot be turned back”—thus he spoke this verse.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: “O Sela, as for what you ask of me, ‘You ought to be a king, a wheel-turning monarch,’ let go of that concern;
I am a king. And while being a king, just as no other king, though equal to me, [can turn] a hundred leagues...”
Or he instructs [a realm] of two, three, four, or five hundred yojanas, or even a thousand yojanas;
or, having become a wheel-turning monarch, [he rules] only as far as the four continents. But my domain is not limited in this way. For I am the unsurpassed King of Dhamma;
from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, and across immeasurable world-systems in the horizontal directions, I exercise my instruction.
For as far as there are beings distinguished by their lack of feet and so forth, I am the foremost among them. Indeed, there is no one equal to me in virtue...

[and so on] ...or in the knowledge and vision of liberation, much less anyone superior. Thus, being such an unsurpassed King of Dhamma, I turn the Wheel with the unsurpassed Dhamma known as the factors of enlightenment—divided into the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth—and the Wheel of Command, saying: "Abandon this; enter upon and abide in that," and so on.
“Furthermore, monks, this is the noble truth of suffering,” and so forth; thus, by means of the Dhamma of the scriptures, it is indeed the Wheel of Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase “the wheel that cannot be turned back”: that wheel which cannot be turned back by an ascetic, or by anyone else in the world.
