Having seen the Blessed One thus revealing himself, Sela, filled with rapture and joy, spoke again for the sake of strengthening his conviction:
“You claim to be a Perfectly Awakened One,” said the brahmin Sela, “a supreme King of Dhamma;
‘I turn the wheel by means of the Dhamma,’ thus you speak, Gotama.
Who then is your general, your disciple who follows the Teacher?”
"Who now follows after you, turning the Wheel of Dhamma that has been set in motion?"—thus he spoke these two verses.

Therein, "Who indeed is the general? he asked, questioning who might be the general who turns in accordance with the Wheel of the Dharma King, the Blessed One, who has been proceeding by means of the Dhamma.
At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was seated on the Blessed One’s right side, shining with glory like a heap of gold. Pointing him out, the Blessed One said:
“The wheel set in motion by me—the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma—Sāriputta turns in accordance with it, for he is born after the Tathāgata,” the Blessed One said, reciting this verse.
In that context, “born after the Tathāgata” means he is born after the Tathāgata; the meaning is that he is born through noble birth, having the Tathāgata as his cause.

Having thus answered the question posed by Sela, “Who indeed is your general?”, and wishing to make him free from doubt regarding what Sela had said—“You claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One”—he spoke in order to make it known: “I do not claim to be so merely on account of my word;
rather, for this reason I am a Buddha.”
“What is to be directly known has been directly known; what is to be developed has been developed;
what is to be abandoned has been abandoned by me—therefore, O brahmins, I am a Buddha. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “what is to be directly known” refers to the four truths, the four noble truths. For regarding the four truths and the four noble truths...

This term "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) is used in a general sense. In that context, among the Noble Truths, both the Truth of the Path (*maggasacca*), which is to be developed, and the Truth of Origination (*samudayasacca*), which is to be abandoned, are included.

By including these two, their results—the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasacca*) and the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*)—are also necessarily included, because the result is established simply by grasping the cause.
Therefore, in that regard, [the phrase] "that which is to be realized has been realized" (*sacchikātabbaṃ sacchikataṃ*) [is understood].
"‘That which is to be fully understood has been fully understood’—this too has already been stated.

Or, having shown by way of summary that all that is to be known has been directly known and perfectly awakened to through the phrase "‘That which is to be directly known has been directly known’," he speaks of "‘That which is to be developed has been developed,’ etc.," showing it by way of exposition as a portion of that [whole].
Alternatively, "‘That which is to be developed has been developed’..."
By the statement, "What is to be abandoned has been abandoned," all the qualities of a Buddha are praised by way of proclaiming the perfection of his own knowledge and abandonment;
since all those qualities are rooted in that [realization], he says, "Therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha.

For, by the inclusion of both what is to be directly known and what has been directly known, the state of the Four Truths together with their fruit and the excellence of its cause is entirely encompassed.
By showing that he has awakened to everything that ought to be awakened to, he clarifies his own state of Buddhahood through this method and reasoning, thinking, "I have become a Buddha.
Having thus manifested himself in a non-figurative sense, he encourages the brahmin to overcome his doubts regarding him:
"Dispel your doubt concerning me; be resolved, O Brahmin."
“Rare is the sight of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, occurring but seldom. O Brahmin,
for those whose manifestation in the world is indeed rare,
I am that Buddha, the unsurpassed surgeon who extracts the arrow.”
“Having become Brahmā, peerless, the crusher of Māra’s army;
having brought all enemies under my control, I rejoice, free from fear from any quarter.”—thus he spoke these three verses.
Therein, *vinayassu* means “remove,” that is, cut away. *Kaṅkhaṃ* means doubt. *Adhimuccassu* means resolve.
Believe that he is the "Perfectly Enlightened One. For the sight of Buddhas is rare, since even for incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) the world remains empty of Buddhas.
"The Surgeon" means one who extracts the thorns of passion and the like. "Become Brahma" means become supreme.
"Incomparable" means having passed beyond all measure; the meaning is "without peer. "Crusher of Māra’s army": [Māra is] "desire..."

"Those are the first army"—thus he is the crusher of Māra’s host that has thus arrived. "All enemies" refers to all adversaries, namely the aggregates (khandhas), the defilements (kilesas), the formations (abhisaṅkhāras), Death (Māra), and the Son of the Devas (Devaputtamāra).
"Having brought under my control" means having brought them under one's own power. "I rejoice, free from fear from any quarter":
being fearless from any source, I rejoice in the bliss of concentration and in the bliss of the fruit of Nibbāna.
When this was said, the brahmin Sela immediately conceived faith in the Blessed One. Desiring the going-forth, he said:
“Listen, sirs, to what the Visionary One declares;
The Great Hero, the Surgeon, roars like a lion in the forest.”
“Who, even one born of the dark race, would not feel confidence upon seeing him who has become Brahmā, the incomparable crusher of Māra’s army?
Let whoever wishes to follow me do so; or let whoever does not wish to go depart.”
“Here I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the one of excellent wisdom”—
thus he spoke these three verses, being urged on by the perfection of his supporting conditions that had reached full maturity.
In this context, “one of dark birth” means one of low birth, situated in a state leading from darkness to further darkness.
Then those young brahmins, because they were endowed with the necessary causes, became desirous of going forth right there, saying:
"If this teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One is pleasing to you, sir,
we too shall go forth in the presence of him of supreme wisdom."
They spoke these verses, as was the custom for noble sons who had performed meritorious deeds in his presence.
Then Sela, with a joyful heart, showing himself among those young brahmins and requesting ordination, said:
"These three hundred brahmins, with palms joined in reverence, make their request."
“Blessed One, we shall lead the holy life in your presence. Thus he spoke this verse.

Then the Blessed One [considered] that since Sela had, in the manner previously described during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, been the leader of the group among those same three hundred men and had planted roots of merit, now, even in his final existence, he was among those very same [men].
Having been reborn as a teacher, his own knowledge and theirs had reached maturity, and there was the necessary condition for the state of "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu).
Therefore, ordaining them all through the "Come, monk" formula, the Blessed One said:
"Well-proclaimed is the holy life (brahmacariya), O Sela, which is visible here and now and timeless."
He spoke this verse: “Where renunciation is not in vain for one who trains with diligence.
In that context, *sandiṭṭhika* means directly visible. *Akālika* means that because the fruit arises immediately after the path, it is not a fruit to be attained at some other time.
*Yattha* means “on account of which”; for renunciation is not in vain on account of the holy life of the path.
"Nor are they fruitless"—that is to say, in whatever teaching one trains in the three trainings, being diligent and free from lapses in mindfulness.
Having said this, the Blessed One spoke: "Come, monks. At that very moment, they all became bearers of miraculous robes and bowls;
appearing like elders of sixty years' standing, they paid homage to the Blessed One and surrounded him. Thus he went forth.
While practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), on the seventh day he and his retinue attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a street-leader;
having gathered my kinsmen together, I spoke these words.”
“A Buddha has arisen in the world, an unsurpassed field of merit;
he was the recipient of offerings for the entire world.
The kshatriyas, the townspeople, the great householders, and the brahmins—”
With serene minds and joyful hearts, they performed acts of merit for the community.
The elephant riders, the cavalrymen, the charioteers, and the foot soldiers—
with serene minds and joyful hearts, they performed acts of merit for the community.
“Uggas, princes, vessikas, and brahmins—
With hearts full of faith and joyful minds, they performed the duty of the assembly.
Cooks, barbers, bath-attendants, and garland-makers...”
With serene minds and joyful hearts, they performed the duty of honoring the Saṅgha.
“The dyers, the weavers, the leather-workers, and the barbers—
with serene minds and joyful hearts, they performed the duty of honoring the Saṅgha.”
“Fletchers, weavers, leather-workers, and carpenters,
with serene minds and joyful hearts, performed the duty of honoring the Saṅgha.
Blacksmiths, goldsmiths, and likewise those who work with the three metals,”
With clear minds and joyful hearts, they performed acts of merit for the community.
"The many hired servants, slaves,
and laborers likewise performed acts of merit for the community, each according to their own strength."
“Water-carriers, wood-gatherers, farmers, and grass-cutters—
each according to their own strength, they performed the duty of the Saṅgha.
Flower-sellers, garland-makers, vegetable-vendors, and fruit-gatherers likewise did so.”
According to their respective means, they performed the duty of honoring the Saṅgha.
“The courtesan, Kumbhadāsī, Pūvikā, and Macchikā as well—
according to their respective means, they performed the duty of honoring the Saṅgha.”
“Come, let us all gather together and form a group as one;
we shall perform meritorious service in this unsurpassed field of merit.
Having heard my words, they immediately formed a group.
They had a well-constructed assembly hall built for the community of monks.
Having completed that hall, joyful and with a delighted mind,
surrounded by all of them, I approached the Fully Awakened One.
“Having approached the Fully Awakened One, the Lord of the World, the Bull among Men,
and having paid homage at the Teacher’s feet, I spoke these words: ‘O Hero,
here are three hundred men, a single group together.’”
“You have dedicated this well-constructed assembly hall, O Sage.
Having accepted it in the presence of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
the Visionary One spoke these verses before three hundred [monks].
“The three hundred and the eldest shall follow together;
having first attained prosperity, you shall all experience it.
When the final existence is reached, the unsurpassed state of coolness [nirvana] will be attained.”
“You shall touch Nibbāna—the unaging, deathless, and peaceful.
Thus the Buddha, the omniscient and unsurpassed, gave this explanation.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, I experienced great joy.
“For thirty thousand eons, I delighted in the world of the gods;
for five hundred [eons], I exercised divine sovereignty as a lord of the gods.
A thousand times, moreover, I was a wheel-turning monarch.”
While he was exercising sovereignty over the gods, the great deities paid him homage.
"In this human kingdom, there were assemblies and kinsmen;
when his final existence arrived, he was a brahmin named Vāseṭṭha."
“I was the son of one who possessed a hoard of eight hundred million;
my name was Sela, and I had reached perfection in the six factors.
While wandering on foot for exercise, preceded by my disciples,”
To the ascetic named Keṇiya, who was burdened by his heavy mass of matted hair,
I spoke these words upon seeing the prepared sacrificial offering:
"Is it a marriage, or a wedding, or has the king invited you?"
“I desire to offer an oblation to the brahmins who are honored by the gods;
I do not invite the king, for no such oblation exists for me.
There has been no marriage for me, nor does any wedding exist for me.”
The one who brings joy to the Sakyans, the best in the world including the devas—
“For the benefit and welfare of the entire world, bringing happiness to all beings,
he has been invited by me today; this is the preparation for him.”
“Resplendent with the color of a timbarūsaka flower, immeasurable and peerless;
the Buddha, matchless in form, has been invited for tomorrow.
Like [a gem] struck by the mouth of a furnace, resembling glowing acacia coals;
The Great Hero is like a flash of lightning; that Buddha has been invited by me.
Like a flame on a mountain peak, like the full moon, resembling the color of a reed-flame—that Buddha has been invited by me.
“Unfrightened, having transcended fear, the Sage who brings about the end of existence;
like a lion, a great hero—he, the Buddha, has been invited by me.
Skilled in the qualities of a Buddha, he is invincible to others.”
The Great Hero is like a nāga; that Buddha has been invited by me.
Skilled in practicing the True Dharma, the peerless Buddha-nāga;
the Great Hero is like a bull; that Buddha has been invited by me.
“Of infinite beauty and immeasurable fame, possessing every diverse mark, the Great Hero is like Sakka; that Buddha has been invited by me.
Masterful, a leader of a group, majestic, radiant, and difficult to approach.”
The Great Hero, like Brahmā, that Buddha has been invited by me.
The One Who Has Attained the Dhamma, the Ten-Powered One, who has gone beyond strength and superior strength;
the Great Hero, like the earth, that Buddha has been invited by me.
“Studded with the waves of virtue, stirred by the consciousness of the Dhamma, like the ocean—such is the Great Hero; that Buddha has been invited by me.
Difficult to approach, difficult to overcome, immovable, lofty, and sublime.”
The peerless Great Hero, that Buddha has been invited by me.
“Of infinite wisdom, unequaled and incomparable, immeasurable, having reached the pinnacle;
like the sky, the Great Hero—that Buddha has been invited by me.”
“The refuge for those terrified by fear, the shelter for those who go for protection,
the consoler— the Great Hero, that Buddha has been invited by me.
He is the abode of the wise, the field of merit for those seeking happiness.”
The great hero Ratanākara, that Buddha has been invited by me.
The one who provides consolation, the maker of knowledge, the giver of the fruits of recluseship;
the great hero like a rain cloud—that Buddha has been invited by me.
“The Eye of the World, of great majesty, the dispeller of all darkness;
like the sun is the Great Hero—He, the Buddha, has been invited by me.
The Sage who perceives the true nature of things, liberated from all objective referents.”
The Great Hero, resembling the moon, that Buddha has been invited by me.
The Buddha, exalted in the world, adorned with the marks [of a great man],
immeasurable, the Great Hero— that Buddha has been invited by me.
“He whose knowledge is immeasurable, whose virtue is incomparable,
and whose liberation is peerless— he, the Buddha, has been invited by me.
He whose steadfastness is matchless and whose power is inconceivable...”
“He for whom effort is supreme—he, the Buddha, has been invited by me.
Passion, hatred, and delusion—all poisons have been uprooted;
like an antidote is the Great Hero—he, the Buddha, has been invited by me.”
“The Great Hero, like a physician, who dispels all suffering and the many ailments of the defilements—
he, the Buddha, has been invited by me. O sir,
as for this word ‘Buddha’ which you speak, even the sound of it is very difficult to obtain.”
Having heard "Buddha, Buddha," joy arose within me.
Though not grasping it internally, that joy overflowed from me outwardly.
Being thus joyful in mind, I spoke these words:
“Where indeed is that Blessed One, the eldest in the world, the bull among men?
Having gone there, I shall pay homage to him, the giver of the fruits of recluseship.
Raising my right arm, filled with rapture and with palms joined, I shall go.”
The King of Dhamma has explained to me the dispeller of the dart of sorrow:
"Behold this great forest, rising up like a massive cloud, dark as collyrium, appearing like the ocean."
“Here dwells that Buddha, the Sage who tames the untamed;
training those to be trained and awakening them to the factors of enlightenment.
Like one parched with thirst seeking water, or like one famished seeking food,”
Just as a cow is greedy for her calf, so am I longing for the Conqueror.
“Knowing the proper conduct and etiquette, and the restraint appropriate to the Dhamma,
I train my own disciples as they go into the presence of the Conqueror.”
“The Blessed Ones are difficult to approach; they move alone like lions.
O young men, you should come placing one foot after the other.
Like a terrible venomous snake, like the maned king of beasts, the lion.”
Just as a tusker elephant has musth, so too are the Buddhas difficult to approach.
“O young men, disregard what is coughed or spat out;
placing one foot after another, come into the presence of the Buddha.”
“Venerating seclusion, quiet, and difficult to approach;
difficult to visit, the Buddhas are revered in the world with its devas.
When I ask a question or exchange greetings with them...”
“Be quiet then; remain as if you have become sages.
Listen intently to that very teaching which the Fully Awakened One proclaims for the attainment of the secure state of Nibbāna;
hearing the True Dhamma is bliss.”
“Having approached the Perfectly Awakened One, I exchanged greetings with the Sage;
having concluded that conversation, I examined his marks.
Regarding two marks I was in doubt, yet I saw thirty-two marks.”
The Sage, through his supernormal power, revealed that which was hidden by his lower garment.
Extending his tongue, the Conqueror reached his ears, nostrils,
and even the hairline on his forehead, covering it entirely.
“Having observed his marks, complete and with all their characteristics,
and having reached the conclusion that he was a Buddha, I went forth together with my disciples.
Accompanied by three hundred followers, I went forth into the homeless life.”
Before half a month had passed, we all attained Nibbāna.
Having performed deeds together in this unsurpassed field of merit,
and having wandered through saṃsāra together, they have now turned back from it together.
“Having provided rafters, I lived according to the Dhamma of the community.
By that well-performed deed, I obtain eight benefits:
I am honored in all directions, and my wealth is immeasurable.”
I am a refuge for all; no fear exists within me.
No diseases exist for me, and I preserve my long life;
I possess delicate skin and dwell in whatever dwelling I desire.
“Having offered eight rafters, I lived according to the Dhamma of the Saṅgha;
the analytical knowledges and arahantship—this was my eighth attainment.
With all that was to be accomplished fully accomplished, having done what was to be done, free from taints;”
“The eight rafters, my son, are the Great Sage.
Having given five pillars, I dwelt in the Dhamma of the Saṅgha;
by that well-performed deed, I obtain five causes.”
“Through loving-kindness I am unshakable, and I remain with all my faculties intact;
I become one whose words are worthy of being accepted, and I do not disparage others as I am myself.
My mind is not wavering, and I am free from harshness toward anyone.”
By that well-performed deed, I have become stainless within the Teaching.
"Reverent and respectful, having fulfilled my task and being free from taints, I am your disciple, O Great Hero; as a monk, I pay homage to you, O Sage."
“Having prepared a well-made couch, I had it displayed in the hall;
by that well-performed deed, I obtain five fruits.
Having been born into a noble family, I become one of great wealth.”
I possess every prosperity; stinginess does not exist within me.
When I desire to go, a palanquin stands ready for me;
together with that most excellent palanquin, I travel wherever I wish.
“By that gift of a palanquin, I dispelled all darkness;
having attained the power of all direct knowledges, this elder, a sage, pays homage to you.
Having fulfilled my duties and completed all tasks, I have accomplished every obligation.”
By that well-performed deed, I entered the city free from fear.
When the hall was completed, I gave it for communal use;
by that well-performed deed, I attained the status of a guild-leader.
“Whatever tamers there are in the world who tame elephants and horses,
they do so by inflicting various punishments and subduing them with cruelty.
But you, O Great Hero, do not tame men and women in such a way.”
Without staff or sword, he tamed them with the highest taming.
Praising the virtue of giving,
the Sage skilled in teaching awakened three hundred people while answering but a single question.
“Tamed by the Charioteer, we are well-liberated and free from taints;
having attained all the powers of direct knowledge, we are extinguished through the destruction of acquisitions.
That gift which I gave back in a hundred thousand aeons—”
“All fears have been transcended; this is the fruit of the gift of the sāla tree.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahatship, he approached the Teacher and declared his realization.”
“We have come for refuge to you, O Visionary One, eight days ago from now;
in seven nights, Blessed One, we have been tamed by your teaching. Thus he spoke this verse.
Its meaning is as follows: O Visionary One, Blessed One, who possesses the five eyes, since we [have come to you] eight days ago from now...
On that very day we went to you for refuge. Therefore, within seven nights, we have been tamed by your teaching as a tamer.
Oh, how great is the power of going for refuge to you! Thereafter:
“You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher; you are the Sage who has overcome Māra.”
“Having cut off the underlying tendencies, you have crossed over and are carrying this generation across.
‘The acquisitions have been transcended by you; the taints have been shattered by you.
Like a lion, free from clinging, you have abandoned fear and terror.’”
Having praised him with these two verses, he requested the Teacher’s blessing with the concluding verse:
“These three hundred bhikkhus stand here with palms joined;
O Hero, stretch out your feet, so that the Nāgas may pay homage to the Teacher.”
In this context: "You are the Buddha" means that you alone are the omniscient Buddha in this world.

Because you instruct sentient beings in matters pertaining to the present life and so forth, you alone are the Teacher (*satthā*). Because you have overcome all Māras, you are the Conqueror of Māra (*mārābhibhū*).

Because of your state as a sage (*muni*), you are the Sage. "Having cut off the underlying tendencies" means having severed the underlying tendencies such as sensual lust with the sword of the Noble Path. "Crossed over" means...
Having himself crossed the great flood of *saṃsāra*, he has, by means of the hand of his teaching, delivered this generation, this collection of beings.

"Bases" (*upadhi*) refers to all bases, such as the basis of the aggregates (*khandhūpadhi*). "Without clinging" (*anupādāna*) means one who has completely abandoned the clinging to sense-desires (*kāmupādāna*) and the rest.
Having spoken thus, the Elder, together with his retinue, paid homage to the Teacher.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sela is finished.
7. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷigodhā:
“*Yātaṃ me hatthigīvāya*,” etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Bhaddiya. What is his origin? He too—
Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, he was reborn into a family of great wealth during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

Upon reaching maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those from noble families.
He himself then aspired to that same status and, for seven days, [honored] the Sangha headed by the Buddha...

Having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he made a formal aspiration (paṇidhāna). The Teacher, seeing that it would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him a prediction (byākāsi).

Having heard that prediction, he asked about the karma conducive to birth in a high-born family, and [the Teacher explained] the making of an offering for the hearing of the Dhamma, the giving of a seat in the Dhamma-maṇḍapa, the giving of a fan, and [the support of] those who preach the Dhamma.

Having performed much merit throughout his life—such as making offerings and showing honor, and providing lodging in the Uposatha hall—and having passed away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.

Subsequently, after the time of the Blessed One Kassapa and before the arising of our own Blessed One, he was reborn in a householder’s home in Bārāṇasī. There, [he saw] many Paccekabuddhas entering for alms...
Having practiced his service, he saw them gathering at one and the same place to break their fast;
thereupon, having spread out stone slabs and providing water for washing the feet and other necessities, he attended upon them for as long as he lived.
After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, he was born in this present age of a Buddha in the city of Kapilavatthu.
He was reborn in the Sākiya royal family, and his name was Bhaddiya.

When he reached maturity, together with five other khattiyas including Anuruddha, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher while the Teacher was dwelling in the Ambavana at Anupiya; having done so, he attained arahantship.
Later, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones in Jeta’s Grove, [he spoke] regarding the bhikkhus from high-born families.

He placed him in the foremost position. Passing his time in the bliss of the fruits [of the path] and the bliss of Nibbāna, whether gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, he frequently uttered this inspired exclamation: “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
Hearing this, the bhikkhus reported it to the Teacher: “Venerable Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷigodhā, frequently says, ‘Oh, what happiness!’”
“‘Oh, what happiness! he says; I think he practices the holy life without being truly delighted.
The Teacher summoned him and asked, “Is it true, Bhaddiya, that you constantly say, ‘Oh, what happiness!
Oh, what happiness!’? He replied, “It is true, Blessed One. [The Teacher continued: “Formerly, when I was ruling as king, my protection was well-arranged...”
“Even though I was thus, I lived afraid, agitated, and apprehensive. But now, having gone forth, I dwell without fear, without agitation, and without apprehension.
Having said this, he added:
“The fine garments that were worn upon my elephant’s neck—”
He used to eat fine rice served with pure meat broth;
now he is blessed and constant, delighting in what comes into his alms-bowl from gleanings.
Without clinging, Bhaddiya, the son of Godhā, meditates.
“Wearing rag-robes, constant in effort, delighting in what comes into his alms-bowl,
he meditates without clinging— the son of Godhā, Bhaddiya.
“A mendicant for alms, constant in effort…” [and so forth].
“One who wears but a single set of robes and is constant...
[as before] ... One who goes for alms in regular order and is constant... [as before] ... One who eats at a single sitting and is constant... [as before] ...”
“One who eats only what is received in the alms-bowl and is constant...
[as before] ...One who eats only after the meal has been prepared and is constant... [as before] ...One who dwells in the forest and is constant... [as before] ..."
“One who dwells at the foot of a tree and is constant...
[as before] ... One who dwells in the open air and is constant... [as before] ...
One who dwells in a charnel ground and is constant... [as before] ...”
“One who is content with whatever seat is provided, constant... [as above]...
One who is a sitter, constant... [as above]...
One who has few desires, constant... [as above].”
“Contented and constant...
[as above] ...Secluded and constant...
[as above] ...Unsocialized and constant... [as above] ...”
“Exerting energy, constant... [as above] ...
Having abandoned the bronze bowl weighing a hundred palas, adorned with a hundred royal lines, he took up a clay alms-bowl; this was his second consecration.”
“In the past, I dwelt in a supreme city, protected by high circular walls, strong watchtowers and gatehouses, and guarded by men with swords in hand.
But now I am blessed and fearless, having abandoned all fear and terror.”
“Having entered the forest, Bhaddiya, the son of Godhā, meditates:
‘Established in the aggregate of virtue, developing mindfulness and wisdom,
I have gradually attained the destruction of all fetters.’”
With these verses, he let out a lion’s roar before the Teacher.
Regarding the phrase "I have traveled on the neck of an elephant": "Venerable Sir, in the past, even when traveling, I would travel seated upon the shoulder of an elephant;
and even while wearing garments, I wore exquisite Kāsī cloth of fine texture and pleasant touch."

It was maintained. Even while eating rice—rice of three-year-old *purāṇa-gandha-sāli* paddy, sprinkled with the pure meat of partridges, francolin partridges, and the like—he ate it as "pure-meat-sprinkled";
nevertheless, that pleasure did not bring satisfaction to his mind in the way that the pleasure of seclusion does now. Demonstrating this, he said, "Sojja bhaddo," and so forth.
And here it should be understood that by the mention of "elephants," horses, chariots, and vehicles are included; by the mention of "clothing," all royal ornaments are included;
and by the mention of "boiled rice," all varieties of food are included. "Soñño" means he who now stands today in the state of renunciation.

"Bhadde" means auspicious because of being endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). "Sātato" means [devoted] to the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) and to dwelling in happiness in this very life.
“Constantly devoted” means: “Delighting in what comes into the alms-bowl from the gleanings” means he delights in what has been gathered into his bowl through the practice of gleaning;
the intention is that he is satisfied with just that. “He meditates” means he meditates by means of the meditation of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
“The son of Godhā” means the son of the Kṣatriyan woman named Kāḷigodhā. “Bhaddiya”—thus the Elder speaks of himself, referring to himself as if he were someone else.
Having rejected robes offered by householders, he is a wearer of rag-robes through his undertaking of the practice of wearing rag-robes.
Having rejected meals provided by the Sangha, he is an alms-food eater through his undertaking of the practice of eating almsfood.

Having rejected extra robes, he is a wearer of the three robes through his undertaking of the practice of wearing the three robes. Having rejected greedy behavior, he is one who goes for alms in regular order through his undertaking of the practice of going for alms in regular order.
He is one who goes on alms-round from house to house. Having rejected eating at various seats, he is a "one-seater" by undertaking the practice of the single-seat discipline.
Having rejected a second vessel, he is a "bowl-almsman" by undertaking the practice of the bowl-alms discipline.
Having rejected leftover food, he is a "refuser of later-food" by undertaking the practice of the discipline of not eating after the proper time. Having rejected lodgings within a village...
By undertaking the practice of dwelling in the forest, he is a forest-dweller (*āraññika*).

Having rejected living in a sheltered place, by undertaking the practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree, he is a tree-root dweller (*rukkhamūlika*). Having rejected both sheltered places and the roots of trees, by undertaking the practice of dwelling in the open air, he is an open-air dweller (*abbhokāsika*).
Having rejected cemeteries, by undertaking the practice of dwelling in a cemetery, he is a cemetery dweller (*sosānika*). Having rejected greed for lodgings...

By undertaking the practice of the "as-it-is-spread" factor, one is an "as-it-is-spread" practitioner (*yathāsanthatika*). By undertaking the practice of the "always-sitting" factor after rejecting lying down, one is an "always-sitting" practitioner (*nesajjika*).
This is the summary here. For a detailed account of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), however, it should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"High" (*ucca*) means in a high location, or because it is situated on an upper story of a palace. "Enclosed by a circular wall" (*maṇḍalipākāra*) means surrounded by a wall in the shape of a circle.
“With strong watchtowers and gatehouses” means possessed of firm watchtowers and gate-chambers; this refers to the city.

Regarding the phrase “mindfulness and wisdom,” here he speaks of concentration by way of the term “mindfulness. Having in mind the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), he said, “cultivate mindfulness and wisdom. The rest is clear, as it follows the method explained in various other places.
Thus the Elder let out a lion’s roar in the presence of the Teacher. Hearing it, the monks became deeply inspired with faith.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷigodhā, is finished.

8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Aṅgulimāla The verses beginning with "Gacchaṃ vadesi" (As you go, you speak) belong to the Venerable Elder Aṅgulimāla. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties in various existences and accumulated wholesome merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*),
he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a brahmin named Bhaggava, who was the chaplain to the King of Kosala.
On the day of his birth, weapons throughout the entire city burst into flames, and the king’s auspicious weapon ignited upon his bed.
Once set down, it blazed up. Seeing this, the king became terrified and agitated, and he could not find sleep.
At that time, the court chaplain, observing the conjunction of the constellations, reached the conclusion: "He was born under the constellation of thieves.
When the night had turned to dawn, he went into the presence of the king and asked after his comfortable rest. The king replied, "How could there be a comfortable rest, Teacher?"
“Last night my auspicious weapon flared up; what will be the result of that? “Do not fear, Great King.
A son has been born in my house. By his power, the weapons have flared up throughout the entire city.
“What will happen, Teacher? “The boy will become a thief. “Will he be one who goes alone?”
“Is he a thief, or rather the leader of a band? “He is a solitary wanderer, Your Majesty. “Then why should we kill him?

“If he is a solitary wanderer, let us look after him for now,” he said. When they were giving him a name, because he was born troubling the king’s mind as he was being born, they called him Hiṃsaka (the Troubler);
yet afterwards, as if what was seen were unseen, they began to call him Ahiṃsaka (the Non-Troubler).
Thus, having reached maturity, by the power of his former karma he possessed the strength of seven elephants. This was his former deed:
when the world was empty of Buddhas, he had been reborn as a farmer.
Seeing a certain Paccekabuddha who had come to his field, drenched with rainwater, his robes wet, and oppressed by the cold, he thought, "A field of merit has appeared before me."
Filled with joy, he kindled a fire and gave it as an offering. By the power of that deed, in every place where he was reborn, he became endowed with steadfastness, speed, and strength;
and in this his final existence, he possesses the strength of seven elephants.
Having gone to Takkasilā, he became a Dhamma-pupil under a world-renowned teacher.
While learning a craft, he carefully attended upon his brahmin teacher and his wife.

Consequently, that brahmin woman provided him with hospitality consisting of food and other necessities available in the house. Unable to tolerate this, other young men created a rift between him and the teacher.
The brahmin, however, did not believe their words for two or three times.
Having made the offering and subsequently gained faith, he thought, "The young brahmin Mahābala cannot be killed by anyone;
I shall kill him by some stratagem. Then, addressing the young brahmin who was asking for leave to go to his own city after completing his training, he said:
"Dear Ahiṃsaka, a pupil who has completed his training must present a teacher’s fee to his preceptor."
“Give that to me. “Very well, teacher; what shall I give? “Bring the right-hand index fingers of a thousand men!
It is said that this was the brahmin’s intention: that when many were being killed, one would surely kill him.
Having heard this, Ahiṃsaka, placing his long-practiced cruelty before him, equipped himself with the five weapons.
Having entered the Jālinī forest within the realm of the King of Kosala, he lived among the mountains near a great highway.
Standing upon a mountain peak, he watched people passing along the road; then, rushing down with speed, he seized their fingers and hung them from the tops of trees.
There, both vultures and crows devoured them, and once cast upon the ground, they became putrid. Thus...
As his counting remained incomplete, he would take each finger he captured, tie it with a thread to make a garland, and hang it over his shoulder as if it were a sacrificial offering.
From that time on, he was known by the name Aṅgulimāla.
Thus, while he was killing people along the road, the path became impassable. Finding no more people on the road, he went to the vicinity of a village.
Having gone and hidden himself, he would kill people as they came and went, taking their fingers with him as he departed.
When the people realized this, they fled from the village; the village became empty, and likewise the market towns and the countryside. Thus that region was terrorized by him.
And for Aṅgulimāla, there were nine hundred and ninety-nine fingers collected. Then the people...
They reported that great calamity to the King of Kosala. At dawn, the king had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming:
"Let us quickly capture the bandit Aṅgulimāla; let the army assemble! When she heard this, the brahmin woman named Mantāṇī, Aṅgulimāla’s mother, said to his father:
"It is said that your son has become a bandit and is doing such and such things; him—"
“Convince him, saying, ‘Do not do such a thing,’ and bring him back; otherwise, the king will have him executed.
The brahmin replied, “I have no need for sons such as these; let the king do whatever he wishes.
Then the brahmin woman, out of affection for her son, took provisions for the journey and set out on the road, thinking, “I shall convince my son and bring him back.”
The Blessed One, knowing—"This man is going with the thought, 'I will bring Aṅgulimāla.
If she goes, Aṅgulimāla, thinking, 'I will complete my thousand fingers,' will kill even his mother. Furthermore, he is in his final existence;
if I do not go, there will be a great loss"—took his own bowl and robe after returning from his almsround following the meal and set out himself.

Setting out on foot along a road thirty *yojanas* in length for the sake of Aṅgulimāla, he approached the Jālinī forest even though he was being restrained by cowherds and others along the way. At that moment, his mother was seen by him;
seeing her from afar, he thought, "Today I shall complete my collection of fingers even by killing my own mother," and raising his sword, he ran toward her.
Between those two, the Blessed One revealed himself. Upon seeing the Blessed One, Aṅgulimāla thought, "What is the use of my killing my mother and taking her finger?
Let my mother live; what if I were to deprive this ascetic of life and take his finger?
Raising his sword, he pursued the Blessed One from behind, right on his heels.
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that even though he moved with his natural gait,
Aṅgulimāla could not catch up to him despite running with all his might. His speed exhausted,
gasping for breath with loud wheezing, sweat pouring from his armpits, he was unable even to lift his foot.
Standing like a pillar, he said to the Blessed One, “Stop, stop, ascetic! The Blessed One, while still walking, said, “I have stopped, Aṅgulimāla;
you, too, stop. He thought, “These ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, are speakers of truth;
for even as this ascetic was walking, he said, ‘I have stopped, Aṅgulimāla; you, too, stop,’ and I am...”
“Who indeed could this be? What is his intention? Having asked him, I shall know. Thinking thus, he addressed the Blessed One with a verse:
“You say you are walking, O ascetic, yet you stand; and of me, who am standing, you say that I am not standing.
I ask you, ascetic, about this matter: how is it that you are standing while I am not standing?”
In this context, "ascetic" (*samaṇa*) is an address to the Blessed One. "Me" (*mamam*) means "to me.
"How" (*katham*) means "in what manner. This is the meaning here: "O ascetic, while you yourself are walking, you say, 'I am standing.
And while I am indeed standing, you call me 'not standing,' you say so. There must be a reason for this; therefore, O ascetic, I ask you about this matter."
“In what way, in what manner were you standing while I was not standing? When this was said, the Blessed One replied:
“I have always stood, Aṅgulimāla, having laid aside the rod toward all living beings;
but you are unrestrained toward breathing creatures. Therefore, I am standing and you are not standing.”
He addressed him with this verse:
"Standing there, Aṅgulimāla, I am at all times laying aside the rod toward all beings.
Aṅgulimāla, I—at all times, at all seasons, from beginning to middle to end—toward all beings, whether moving or stationary, have laid aside the rod.
"Having laid aside the rod, having laid aside the weapon, modest and compassionate"—because he does not act otherwise than this, he stands in such a state.
"But you are unrestrained toward living beings": you, however, are devoid of self-restraint toward sentient beings; you are cruel, blood-stained, intent on killing and striking, and merciless;
therefore, you are unrestrained and do not stand by way of abstinence from those [actions]. For that very reason, toward them...
"Even though you have wandered through those various realms of existence, even now, though you stand in the [four] postures, you are not truly established;

I, however, am established in the manner already described. Then Aṅgulimāla, because he had previously heard of the fame of the Blessed One—which stood pervading the entire world like oil spread upon the surface of water—due to the excellence of its causes, and because it was manifested by his qualities as they truly are, [was moved].
Because his knowledge had reached full maturity, he was filled with joy and gladness, thinking: "This is that Blessed One. "This is a great lion’s roar, a mighty thundering;
this cannot belong to anyone else; it must be the thundering of the ascetic Gotama.
I have surely been seen by the Great Seer, the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Blessed One has come here for the sake of gathering me to himself. Having reflected thus—
“After a long time, indeed, the Great Seer who is honored by me has entered the great forest as a recluse;
having heard this verse of yours connected with the Dhamma, I shall renounce my thousandfold evil.
Thus he spoke this verse.
In that regard, "for so long indeed" means for a long time. "Me" refers to me, for the sake of favoring me.
"Honored" means honored with great worship by the world together with its devas. "Mahesi" means one who seeks or searches for the great qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).
"The ascetic has entered the Great Forest" means that the Blessed One, having stilled all evil, has set out into this great wilderness. Such as I am, I shall renounce.
"Having heard your verse, which is connected with the Dhamma, I have heard your verse that is joined to the Dhamma and associated with the Dhamma.

Having heard it, I thought: 'Even though it has been accumulated and familiarized over a long time—even for a very long duration—I shall abandon this thousandfold evil. The meaning is: 'Now I shall relinquish it entirely.'"
Having spoken thus, in order to show how he acted and how he was favored by the Blessed One, [the text says]:
"Thus the robber cast his sword and weapon into a pit, a precipice, and a hell;
the robber bowed at the feet of the Sugata and right there requested ordination from the Buddha."
“The Buddha is indeed the compassionate Great Seer, the Teacher of the world together with its devas;
‘Come, monk,’ he then said to him—this was his becoming a monk.
The compilers of the collection placed these two verses [there].
In this context, *icceva* means "having spoken thus" (*iti evaṃ vatvā*), immediately thereafter. *Coro* refers to Aṅgulimāla. *Asi* refers to the sword. *Āvudhaṃ* refers to other weapons.
*Sobbhe* refers to places where the banks are cut away on all sides. *Papāte* refers to places where the banks are cut away on one side. *Narake* refers to fissures split open in the earth.
Furthermore, here by all three terms, it is meant that place where once fallen, one cannot be recovered by another.
He spoke of nothing other than such a mountain-like [obstacle]. "Anvakāsi" means he followed after;
he threw away—that is, discarded—his fivefold weaponry. Having discarded those, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said, "Venerable Sir, grant me the going-forth.
Therefore it was said: "The robber paid homage at the Sugata’s feet and there and then requested the going-forth."

“Buddha! Thus, when he had requested the going-forth, the Teacher, looking back at his past karma and seeing the perfection of the necessary causes for the state of an "Ehi-bhikkhu" (Come, monk), extended his right hand and said: “Come, bhikkhu! The Dhamma is well-expounded;
lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering. That itself was his going-forth and his full ordination.
And so it happened. Therefore he said: “Come, monk,” he then said to him; that very thing became his state of being a monk.

Thus the Elder, having received the going-forth and the full ordination through the “Come, monk” formula in the presence of the Teacher, performed the work of insight, attained Arahantship, and experiencing the bliss of liberation, filled with joy and gladness, uttered this inspired utterance:
“He who, having been negligent in the past, Is not negligent later on;”
He illuminates the world like the moon released from clouds.
“He whose evil deed is covered over by a wholesome one,
illuminates the world like the moon released from clouds.”
“He who, being a young bhikkhu, applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching, illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds. Thus he spoke these three verses.
Their meaning is as follows: whoever—whether a householder or one gone forth—due to association with a virtuous friend, rather than previous association with evil friends...
Or, having neglected through a lack of personal reflection and fallen into heedlessness regarding right practice,
he later— emerging through wise consideration by association with virtuous friends— does not neglect, practices rightly, and by devoting himself to serenity and insight,
he attains the three true knowledges and the six direct knowledges; thus, he is freed from the clouds and other obscurations.
Just as the moon illuminates the physical world with its own attained knowledge and supernormal powers (vijjā-abhijñā), so too does he illuminate this world of aggregates and so forth.

For that person whose committed and accumulated evil karma is shut off and blocked from producing its result—by means of the closing of the door to the arising of ripening through supramundane wholesome states that cause the exhaustion of karma—the rest is exactly as previously stated.
"Dahara" means young; by this, he shows that his body is capable of yoga. For he [is able to endure] the arisen perils of wind and heat...
Having overcome [obstacles], he is able to apply himself to practice. He applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching, being properly engaged in the three trainings;
the meaning is that he accomplishes them with diligence.
Thus, having become filled with rapture and joy and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, when he enters the city for alms, then—
A clod thrown by one person fell upon the elder’s body; a staff thrown by another likewise fell upon his very body.
With his bowl broken, he entered the monastery and went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher exhorted him: “Endure it, O brahmin! Endure it, O brahmin! For that which you [endure]...”
“Brāhmaṇa, as the result of that karma you would have been cooked in hell for many thousands of years;
however, Brāhmaṇa, you have experienced the result of that very karma in this very life.
Then the Elder, having established a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings without exception—
“May people in all directions hear my discourse on the Dhamma; may people in all directions apply themselves to the Buddha’s teaching;
may people in all directions associate with those virtuous men who cause the Dhamma alone to be practiced.
For in all directions are those who speak of forbearance and praise non-conflict.”
Let them hear the Dhamma at the proper time, and let them act in accordance with it.
"For once he has attained supreme peace, he will never harm me, nor anyone else;
having reached that ultimate tranquility, he shall protect both the timid and the stationary."
“Indeed, channel-makers lead water; fletchers straighten the arrow-shaft;
carpenters shape wood; but the wise subdue themselves.
Some subdue [themselves] with the rod, with hooks, and with whips.”
“Without staff, without sword, I am tamed by suchness.
‘Non-violent’ is my name, though formerly I was violent;
today I am truly named, for I do not harm anyone at all.”
“In former times I was a robber, known as Aṅgulimāla;
being swept away by a great flood, I went for refuge to the Buddha.
In former times I was blood-handed, known as Aṅgulimāla.”
Behold this going for refuge: the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
Having performed such deeds that lead to many miserable destinies, though touched by the ripening of that karma, I now enjoy my food free from debt.
“Fools of little intelligence devote themselves to negligence;
but the wise person guards heedfulness as one would guard the most excellent treasure.
Do not devote yourself to negligence, nor to intimacy with the pleasures of sensual desire.”
For one who meditates with diligence attains supreme happiness.
"Welcome, not departed—this was not ill-considered by me;
among all analyzed phenomena, I have attained that which is best."
“Welcome! It has not departed; this was not poorly resolved by me.
The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Whether in the forest, at the foot of a tree, on mountains, or in caves...”
I stood right there, my mind then filled with agitation:
"I lie down in comfort, I stand in comfort, I lead my life in comfort;
I am beyond the reach of Māra—oh, how I am compassionated by the Teacher!"
“Formerly I was of brahmin birth, an up-country man on both sides.
Now I am the son of the Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dhamma.
Free from craving, without grasping, with guarded sense-doors and well-restrained.”
“Having destroyed the root of evil, I have attained the destruction of the taints.
The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.”—he spoke these verses.
In this context, "even my enemies" refers to those who are my adversaries and foes who revile me thus:
"Just as we have been overcome by the suffering of separation from our kinsmen through Angulimāla and have encountered such misery, may Angulimāla likewise encounter misery!
"May they hear my discourse on the Dhamma" means that which was heard by me in the presence of the Teacher, connected with the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
"How shall they hear? Having heard [the words] 'Let them apply themselves,' let them practice for that purpose.

Let them associate with those men' means let them associate with, serve, and rely upon such superior persons who are virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta). 'Those who cause one to attain only the Dhamma, being peaceful' refers to those superior persons who cause one to attain only wholesome states (kusala-dhamma), only superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma), and only the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) that have been realized."
They cause [others] to undertake, incite, and take up [the practice].
"Of those who speak of forbearance" means of those who speak only of the forbearance of endurance;

"of those who praise non-opposition" means of those whose nature it is to praise only loving-kindness (*mettā*), which is non-oppositional toward anyone. "Let them hear the Dhamma at the proper time" means at the appropriate and suitable time.

"May they hear the Dhamma in their presence; may they follow it"—the meaning is: having properly mastered that Dhamma exactly as it was heard, may they emulate it and practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma).
"For he shall never harm me"—that adversary of mine, facing me, shall by no means at all harm me.
He should not harm; nor should he injure anyone else—meaning he should not harm not only me, but any other being whatsoever.

Having attained supreme peace—he should attain the supreme, most excellent peace that is Nibbāna—and having attained it, he should protect all beings, both those who are vulnerable and those who are stable, protecting them with the highest protection.
The meaning is that he should protect [others] like a son protects his own child.

Thus, by means of these verses, the Elder, liberating others from evil and performing what is called a protective rite (*paritta*), proclaimed his own practice by uttering the verse beginning with "Water. Therein, having dug up a dry spot on the earth...

They are called *nettikā* (channel-makers) because, having filled a depression or having constructed a channel-basin (*mātikā*) or set up a wooden trough (*rukkhadoṇi*), they lead water to whatever place they desire;
thus they are water-carriers. *Tejanaṃ* means an arrow-shaft. This is what is meant:
the channel-makers lead water according to their own preference, and fletchers also remove the crookedness from an arrow-shaft (*tejanaṃ*) by heating it.

"Damayanti" means they make straight. Just as carpenters, when fashioning wood for the sake of rims and so forth, tame the wood and make it either straight or curved according to their own preference;
even so, the wise and discerning ones, making this much an object of focus, tame themselves while giving rise to the Noble Path.
But those who have attained Arahantship are called "absolutely tamed."
Now, the Teacher, the charioteer of those who are to be tamed by men, desiring to reveal his own manner of taming and his gratitude, spoke these five verses beginning with “Some tame with the rod.

Therein, “some tame with the rod” means that kings, royal ministers, and others tame their enemies and so forth with punishment, as well as with an army consisting of elephants, horses, and the like; and cowherds and others tame cattle and the like with a stick or staff.
"Trainers tame elephants with goads, and horse-trainers tame horses with whips. But I, O Such-a-One (Tādin), have been tamed without punishment and without weapons;

indeed, I have gone forth, tamed and free from worldly attachments, by means of the Perfectly Enlightened One who has attained the state of equanimity (tādi-bhāva) toward the desirable and the undesirable.
Thus, apart from punishment and weapons—that is, by virtue of having laid aside both punishment and weapons—I have been tamed, subdued, and have gone forth.
"Ahiṃsaka" was my name; previously, while I was a harmful person before meeting the Teacher, I had the mere name "Ahiṃsaka.
But now, indeed, I am truly named "Ahiṃsaka"—my name is real and not false.
Therefore, I do not harm any being whatsoever; I do not injure or oppress them. "Na" is a mere particle used for emphasis.

*Vissuto*: "Renowned" means well-known through such descriptions as "a killer of living beings, cruel, with blood-stained hands. *Mahoghenā*: "By the great flood" refers to the great flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*) and so forth;
I went to, that is, approached, the Buddha—known as the Buddha—as a refuge, which cuts off that flood. *Lohitapāṇī*:

"Blood-stained hands" means hands smeared with the blood and gore of others by the act of taking life. *Saraṇagamanaṃ passa*: "Behold my going for refuge"—this is an address to himself, meaning "behold my going for refuge, which is of great fruit."
"Such a deed" refers to a terrible and similar evil deed, such as the slaughter of many hundreds of men.
"Touched by the ripening of karma" means touched by the ripening of evil karma committed in the past; one who has entirely abandoned karma and is experiencing only its ripening.
Alternatively, "touched by the ripening of karma" means [touched] by the supramundane path, which is the fruit of wholesome karma that served as the decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Or rather, he is touched by the bliss of liberation, which is the fruit of supramundane action (*lokuttara-kamma*) itself.
Because all defilements (*kilesa*) have been exhausted, he is "debt-free" as he partakes of food; by way of this term "food," he refers to all four requisites (*paccaya*).
Now, while censuring his former state of negligence through the gateway of reproach, he praises his subsequent practice of diligence (*appamāda*).
And there, inspiring others, he spoke the verse beginning with "Those who indulge in negligence.
In this context, "fools" (*bālā*) refers to those possessed of folly who do not understand the welfare of this world or the world beyond. "The dull-witted" (*dummedhino*) means those lacking wisdom;
seeing no danger in negligence, they indulge in it, engage in it, and pass their time solely through negligence.
But the wise man, endowed with the wisdom of the essence of the Dhamma,
protects heedfulness as a learned man guards the supreme and most excellent wealth of the seven treasures inherited through his family lineage.

For just as those who perceive the benefits in wealth think, "By means of this supreme wealth we shall attain prosperity, support our children and wife, and clear the path to a happy destination," so too does he guard heedfulness.

They guard their wealth; likewise, the wise person—seeing the benefit in heedfulness, thinking, "By relying on heedfulness I shall attain the first jhāna and so forth, I shall reach the paths and fruits, and I shall accomplish the three knowledges and the six direct knowledges"—guards heedfulness as if it were his most excellent wealth. This is the meaning.
"Do not be negligent" means: do not devote yourself to negligence; do not let your time pass away in negligence.

"Do not indulge in intimacy with the delight of sensual pleasures" means: do not devote yourself to, do not experience, and do not obtain even that intimacy of craving known as delight in both material objects (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*).
"For one who is diligent" means: a person who is diligent by virtue of established mindfulness, meditating and devoted to meditation.
One attains the supreme, most excellent bliss of Nibbāna.

Regarding the phrase "the welcome has not departed": that arrival which occurred then in the presence of my Teacher, or the arrival of the Teacher in that great forest—that welcome, that coming, has not departed; in its true sense, it has not gone away or vanished.
"This was not ill-considered by me": that which was considered by me at that time—"I shall go forth in the presence of the Teacher"—this too was not ill-considered by me;
it was indeed well-considered. Why? "Regarding phenomena analyzed in detail":

regarding phenomena analyzed in their various aspects by way of what is blameworthy and what is blameless, etc., that which is the best, the highest, the most excellent—Nirvana. "He approached that": the meaning is that he went to that very [Nirvana].
“Then, during the time of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), because my application and disposition were impaired, I dwelt in suffering in the forest and other such places;

now, because my application and disposition are perfected, I dwell there in happiness. Thus he spoke the words beginning with “in the forest,” demonstrating both his state of dwelling in happiness and his status as a brahmin in the ultimate sense (*paramattha-brāhmaṇa*), saying: “Formerly I was a brahmin by birth alone; now I am a brahmin by being the Teacher’s own son.”
Therein, "I lie down happily": even while lying down, I lie down happily, with ease and without suffering, being free from mental pain due to the absence of mental terror and the like.
"I stand": I stand. "Beyond the reach of Māra's hand": outside the domain of the defilement-māra and the others. "Oh, how the Teacher has shown compassion! means:
oh, how he has been favored by the Teacher!

"Brahmajacco" means one born of the brahmin caste. "Udicco ubhato" means noble on both sides, both from the mother’s side and the father’s side, being of pure descent. The rest is exactly as explained in their respective places.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Aṅgulimāla is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Anuruddha.
"Having abandoned mother and father," and so forth, are the verses of the Venerable Elder Anuruddha. What is their origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara as a wealthy householder.
One day, having gone to the monastery and listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher [pointing out] a certain bhikkhu...
Seeing him being placed in the foremost position among those with the divine eye, he himself aspired to that same status.
He then offered a great almsgiving for seven days to the Blessed One, who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.

On the seventh day, having given the most excellent robes to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he made a formal aspiration. The Teacher [prophesied] that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle.
Having seen him, he prophesied: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, he will become the foremost among those possessing the divine eye.

He too, while performing meritorious deeds there, after the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, at the completion of the seven-yojana golden cetiya, lit it with many thousands of lamp-trees and small oil-lamps, [vowing]: "For the sake of the knowledge of the divine eye..."
Thinking, “May this be a strong supporting condition,” he performed a magnificent offering of lamps.

Having thus performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa in a householder’s home in Bārāṇasī.
Upon reaching maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna and the golden stupa one league in height had been completed, he...
Having had many bronze bowls made and filled with the cream of ghee, and having placed a single lump of sugar in the center of each,
he had them arranged so that the rim of one touched the rim of another, surrounding the stupa. Then, having himself had one large bronze bowl made and filled with the cream of ghee,
he had a thousand wicks lit and, placing them upon his head, [remained there] throughout the entire night.
He circumambulated the cetiya.
Thus, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his entire life even in that existence, he passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the devas;
remaining there for the full span of his lifespan, he passed away from there and, since no Buddha had yet arisen, was reborn in Bārāṇasī itself into a family of the poor.
His name was Annabhāra. He lived by performing work in the house of a merchant named Sumanaseṭṭhi.

One day, he saw the Paccekabuddha named Upaṭṭha emerging from the attainment of cessation, coming through the air from Mount Gandhamādana, descending at the gate of the city of Bārāṇasī, putting on his robe, and entering the city for alms.

Seeing this, with a heart full of faith, he took his alms-bowl, placed into it a portion of rice set aside for himself, and began with the desire to give it to the Paccekabuddha. His wife also placed her own portion of rice right there into it.
He then led him away and placed it into the hand of the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha, having taken it—
Having offered his appreciation, he departed. Seeing him, the deity dwelling in the parasol of the merchant Sumanas during the night exclaimed with a great roar:

"O, what a gift! A supreme gift! Well-established, O Upaṭṭha! Hearing this, the merchant Sumanas thought, "Since this very gift has been thus commended by the deity, it is indeed the most excellent gift," and he dedicated the merit therein.

He made a request. Annabhāra, however, gave him his share. With a mind full of faith, the merchant Sumanas gave him a thousand [pieces of gold] and said, "From now on, you have no need to perform manual labor with your own hands;
build yourself a suitable house and live there permanently."

Because almsfood given to a Paccekabuddha who has emerged from cessation yields an even more exalted result on that very day, the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi took it with him when he went to the presence of the king that same day.
The king, however, looked at it with great respect. The merchant said, "Great King, this is indeed worthy of being looked upon."
Having said this, he then told him about the merit he had performed and how he himself had given him a thousand [pieces of gold]. Hearing that, the king was pleased;
he gave him the thousand pieces and commanded him, saying, "Build a house in such-and-such a place and dwell there," and thus he assigned him the site for the house.
As he was having that site cleared, large jars of treasure rose up. Seeing them, [he...]
He reported this to the king. The king, having had all the wealth brought out and seeing it piled up, asked, “In whose house in this city is there such an amount of wealth?
“No one’s, Your Majesty,” they replied.
“In that case, let this Annabhāra be known as the Great Wealthy Merchant of this city. On that very day, he raised the merchant’s parasol over him.

From that time forth, having performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life, he passed away and, after wandering through the realms of gods and humans, took rebirth in this present age of a Buddha in the city of Kapilavatthu in the house of the Sakyan Sukkodana;
his name was Anuruddha. He was the younger brother of Mahānāma the Sakyan and the son of the Teacher’s junior father.
His son, who was exceedingly delicate and possessed of great merit, was experiencing celestial-like prosperity while residing in three palaces suited to the three seasons,
surrounded by adorned dancing girls; meanwhile, at the request of King Suddhodana, the Sakyan princes such as Bhaddiya Kumāra and others—
sent to serve as an entourage for the Teacher— approached the Teacher as he was dwelling in the Anupiya Mango Grove.
Having approached and gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, he developed the divine eye within the very same rainy season retreat.
Then, having received a meditation subject from the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and gone to the Pācīnavaṃsa Grove in the Cetiya country,
while practicing the duties of a recluse and reflecting upon the seven thoughts of a Great Man, he was unable to comprehend the eighth.

Having learned of his conduct, the Teacher spoke the eighth thought of a Great Man and taught the practice of the Great Noble Lineage, adorned by contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation.
Following that teaching, he increased his insight and realized Arahantship, accompanied by the higher knowledges and analytical insights.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“I saw the Blessed One Sumedha, the eldest in the world, the bull among men;
I saw the Leader of the World dwelling in seclusion.
Having approached the Perfectly Enlightened One, Sumedha, the Leader of the World...”
Raising my hands in reverential salutation, I made this request to the Supreme Buddha:
“Have compassion on me, O Great Hero, Foremost in the World, Bull among Men!
I shall provide a lamp for you as you meditate at the foot of the tree.”
The wise one, the Self-Existent, the best among speakers, consented;
at that time, having pierced through the trees, I harnessed the chariot.
I gave a thousand-spoked wheel to the Buddha, the Kinsman of the World.
Having blazed for seven days, my lamps were extinguished.
Through that clarity of mind and through my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I was reborn in a celestial mansion.
“Having been reborn in the divine realm, my celestial mansion was exquisitely fashioned;
it blazed forth on all sides—this is the fruit of giving a lamp.
At that time, I shone for a hundred yojanas in every direction.”
“I surpass all the gods; this is the fruit of giving a lamp.
For thirty eons I exercised sovereignty as the Lord of Gods;
no one ever despised me—this is the fruit of giving a lamp.”
“Twenty-eight times I was a wheel-turning monarch;
at that time, I could see for a league all around, both by day and by night.
Through my knowledge, I saw a thousandfold world-system within the Teacher’s dispensation.”
Having attained the divine eye—this is the fruit of the gift of a lamp.
"Thirty thousand aeons ago, there was a Perfectly Enlightened One named Sumedha;
to him a lamp was given by me with a serene mind."
“The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Later, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those possessing the divine eye, saying:
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who possess the divine eye.”
"Namely, Anuruddha.

While dwelling experiencing the bliss of liberation, one day, having reflected upon his own practice, he became filled with rapture and joy and uttered, by way of a spontaneous exclamation (*udāna*), the verses beginning with "Having left behind mother and father. However, some [say]...
“They say: ‘The first four verses were spoken by the compilers of the Council (saṅgītikāra) in order to proclaim the Elder’s going forth and his attainment of Arahantship.
Those following that were spoken by the Blessed One, whose mind was won over by the Elder’s practice of the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa).
All the others were spoken by the Elder himself for various reasons. Thus, in every respect, these—”
It should be understood that even when a verse is spoken by an elder, or spoken with reference to an elder, it is still "the elder’s verse. For example:
"Having abandoned mother and father, sisters, kinsmen, and brothers, and having left behind the five strands of sensual pleasure, Anuruddha alone meditates."
“Accompanied by dancing and singing, awakened by the sound of drums and cymbals—
he did not attain purity through that, being delighted in the realm of Māra.
But having transcended even this, he took delight in the Buddha’s teaching.”
Having completely transcended all floods, Anuruddha meditates alone.
"Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and delightful tangibles—
having transcended these as well, Anuruddha meditates alone."
“Having passed beyond the search for alms-food, the sage, alone and without a companion,
Anuruddha, free from taints, seeks out rag-robes. The sage sorted them,
took them, washed them, dyed them, and wore them.”
The wise Anuruddha, free from taints, wears robes made of discarded rags.
For one who is full of great desire, discontented, socializing, and agitated,
these evil and defiling qualities arise.
“He is mindful and of few desires, contented and free from distress;
delighting in seclusion, satisfied, and always energetic.
For him these wholesome qualities conducive to enlightenment arise.”
"And he becomes one free from taints," so it was said by the Great Seer:
"Having understood my intention, the Teacher, the unsurpassed in the world,
approached me by means of psychic power with a mind-made body."
“When my intention arose, he taught even further:
the Buddha, who delights in the unproliferated, taught the unproliferated.
Having understood his Dhamma, I dwelt delighting in his teaching.”
The threefold knowledge has been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
“For fifty-five years I have remained sitting, and for twenty-five years sleep has been utterly destroyed.”
“There are no in-breaths or out-breaths for the Stable One whose mind is established;
unmoving, having undertaken peace, the Visionary has attained final Nibbāna.
With a mind that does not shrink back, he endured all sensations.”
Like the extinguishing of a lamp, there was the liberation of his mind.
"These, now, are the last sensations for the Sage, with contact as the fifth;
no other phenomena shall arise once the Perfectly Awakened One has attained final Nirvana."
“There is now no further dwelling, O Jālinī, within the host of gods;
the wandering through births is exhausted, and there is now no more renewed existence.
By him in a single moment the world was fully known in its thousandfold aspects, including the Brahmā realm.”
Mastered in the qualities of psychic power and in the passing away and rebirth of beings, that bhikkhu beholds the deities at the proper time.
"In the past, I was Annabhāra, a poor man who carried fodder.
I offered it to the illustrious ascetic Upāriṭṭha."
“I was born in the Sakyan clan; I am known as Anuruddha.
I was devoted to dance and song, and was awakened by the sound of drums and cymbals.
Then I saw the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Teacher who is fearless from any quarter.”
Having gained confidence in that mind, I went forth into the homeless life.
"I know my former abodes, where I dwelt in the past:
among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, I stood in the lineage of Sakka."
“Seven times I was a lord of men; I exercised sovereignty, having conquered on all four sides and being the master of the Jambusaṇḍa continent.
Without punishment and without weapons, I ruled according to the Dhamma.”
“Seven times from here, and seven times from there— fourteen existences in all—
I shall recognize as my dwelling, remaining then in the world of the gods.
In the five-factored concentration, peaceful and developed in solitude.”
When [the mind] had attained tranquility, my divine eye was purified. Standing firm in the five-factored jhāna,
I know the passing away and rebirth of beings— their coming and going,
their state as it is and their change into another state.
“I have served the Teacher... [as before] ...the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
In the village of Veḷuva among the Vajjis, at the end of my life, beneath a bamboo thicket, I shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints.”
In this context, “having abandoned” means having relinquished. “Mother and father” means both mother and father. This is the intended meaning here:

“We do not go forth like others who, overcome by the loss of relatives or the loss of wealth, go forth and then dwell intent upon other worldly duties; rather, we [go forth] leaving behind a vast circle of kinsmen.”
"Having abandoned a great mass of wealth, they went forth, indifferent to sensual pleasures.
"He meditates" means he dwells devoted to both kinds of meditation: meditation upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and meditation upon characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).
"Accompanied by dancing and singing" means being endowed with dancing and singing; that is, seeing dances and hearing songs.

The meaning is as follows: some read "sammato," which means "honored" by means of dance and song. "Sammatāḷappabodhano" means one who is to be awakened at the time of dawn by the sounds of drums and cymbals.
"Na tena suddhim ajjhagam" means that through that enjoyment of sensual pleasures, one does not attain purification from saṃsāra.
"Rato mārasa visaye" means [delighting] in the strands of sensual pleasure, which constitute the domain of the defilement-māra (kilesamāra).

“Delighting”: the meaning is that he did not hold such a view as, “Purification from saṃsāra occurs through the enjoyment of the strands of sensual pleasure, which are the domain of the Māra of defilements.
Therefore he said, “And having transcended this,” and so forth. Therein, “this” refers to these fivefold strands of sensual pleasure.
“Having transcended” means having transcended them; the meaning is, having discarded them without regard for them. “All floods” (sabboghaṃ).
All floods, beginning with the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*), are included.
To show the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) in their own form, it is said: "Forms, sounds," and so forth.
In that context, "delightful" (*manoramā*) means they delight the mind in the sense of being alluring; thus, it is said they are "pleasing. As it has been said: "Which five are pleasing?"
"Forms, pleasant sounds," and so forth.
"One who has transcended the taking of alms-food" means one who has gone beyond the grasping for alms-food; the meaning is that he turns away from the grasping for alms-food.
"Alone" means solitary, without a companion-monk. "Without a second" means free from craving; for craving is indeed called the "second" of a person.
As it is said: "A person has craving as his companion. *Esati* means he seeks. *Vicināti*:
while seeking, he searches here and there at places where refuse rags are found, such as heaps of rubbish and the like. *Aggaṇhī*:
having searched, he took them without feeling disgust even though they were smeared with filth. *Dhovī*: he washed them. *Rajayī*: having washed them...
Having taken it and sewn it, he dyed it with permissible dye. "He wore it" means that after dyeing it and applying the allowable spots (*kappabindu*), he wore it;
he both used it as an undergarment and as an upper robe.
Now, demonstrating the instruction given by the Teacher in the Eastern Vamsa Grove and how he himself had reached the pinnacle of its realization:
