He spoke the verse beginning with, “One who has great desire and is discontented,” and so forth. Therein, “one who has great desire” (*mahiccha*) means one endowed with a great longing for requisites;
the meaning is that he desires requisites that are magnificent, excellent, and numerous. “Discontented” (*asantuṭṭha*) means lacking contentment;
it means being devoid of contentment such as being satisfied with whatever is obtained. “Intimate” (*saṃsaṭṭha*) means [intimate] both with householders and with those gone forth.
“Associated with what is unwholesome” means being associated through improper contact. “Agitated” means tossed about.
“Of him” refers to the person described by the terms “one of great desire,” and so forth. “States” refers to such things as great desire, lack of contentment, association, and distraction.
They are “evil” in the sense of being base. They are “corrupting states” because they cause the defilement of that mind.

"He is mindful and of few desires" means that when this person, while attending upon, associating with, and honoring spiritual friends, listening to the true Dhamma, and applying wise attention, becomes mindful and, having abandoned great desire, possesses few desires;
having abandoned lack of contentment, he is contented; and having abandoned mental agitation which causes distress to the mind, he is free from distress.
Undistracted and concentrated, having abandoned the company of crowds, he delights in solitude;
filled with the joy of the Dhamma through his delight in seclusion and his sense of disenchantment, he is happy and glad-hearted; and by completely abandoning laziness, he has aroused energy.
For one thus endowed with such qualities as fewness of wishes, these thirty-seven factors beginning with the foundations of mindfulness [arise].

In the sense of being produced through skill, they are wholesome (*kusala*) as they comprise the threefold insight; these are the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhika-dhamma*) included within the Path.
One endowed with them becomes free from taints (*anāsava*) from the moment of the supreme path onwards, by the complete exhaustion of all taints (*āsava*).
Thus was it spoken by the Great Seer, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the Mahāpurisa-vitakka at Pācīnavaṃsadāya.
The intention is: "by way of bringing it to its culmination.
"Having understood my intention" refers to that which was undertaken by way of the thoughts of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*), such as: "Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one with few desires;
this Dhamma is not for one with great desires," and so forth—and which remained [unfulfilled] because those thoughts were incapable of reaching their culmination.
"Having known my intention. "By means of the mind-made" (*manomayena*) means as if made by mind, having been transformed into something resembling what is fashioned by the mind;
this is the meaning. "By means of psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) refers to the psychic power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) that proceeds thus: "Let this body become like this mind.
"When there was an intention in me" (*yadā me ahu saṅkappo*) refers to the time when [the thought arose]: "What indeed is the eighth thought of a Great Man?"
There was a reflection. Then, having understood my intention, he approached by means of psychic power—this is the construction of the sentence.

"He taught further" means that, fulfilling this eighth thought of a Great Man—"Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in the unproliferated (*nippapañca*), for one who finds pleasure in the unproliferated; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in proliferation (*papañca*), for one who finds pleasure in proliferation"—he taught what follows. That which was thus taught...
While teaching the Dhamma, he said: "The Buddha delights in the state free from conceptual proliferation (nippapañca) and taught the state free from conceptual proliferation.

Conceptual proliferations (papañcā) are the defilements such as lust and the rest; because they have been stilled and because they are absent, the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are called "free from conceptual proliferation.
The Fully Enlightened One, delighting in—that is, taking great pleasure in—that state free from conceptual proliferation, taught such a Dhamma so that others might likewise attain it.
"Taught" (*adesayi*) means he proclaimed the Dhamma teaching that elevates one to the highest point, namely the teaching on the Four Noble Truths.

"Having understood his Dhamma" (*tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ aññāya*) means having known the Dhamma of that Teacher's teaching, I dwelt practicing according to the instructions, being delighted and rejoicing in the Dispensation comprised of the Three Trainings.
Having thus shown the meeting with the Teacher and the purpose accomplished by him, [the author now speaks] from the time of his own going forth...

From the time he began to exert energy, showing his disregard for the body through the renunciation of the pleasures of lying down and reclining, and his exertion from the time he ceased sleeping, he spoke this verse: "For fifty-five years.
Therein, "since I became one who never lies down" means from the time when there was conformity to yoga and the conduct of a true person devoted to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having seen such qualities as "living with austerity" (*sallekhavutti*), I remained one who never lay down for those fifty-five years.
"Since drowsiness was eradicated": from the time I abandoned sleep onwards, it has been twenty-five years.
[This refers to] while the Elder had been one who never lay down for fifty-five years, during the first twenty-five years he slept.
"There was no [sleep], and after that, in the final watch of the night, there was sleep due to bodily fatigue," so they say.

The three verses beginning with "There were no inhalations and exhalations" were spoken by the Teacher at the time of his Parinibbāna, when he was asked by the bhikkhus, "Has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna?
and he announced the fact of his Parinibbāna. Therein, "There were no inhalations and exhalations":

"Of the one whose mind is steady, who is such-like": having entered and emerged from all the attainments in many modes and permutations both forward and backward, and finally remaining in the fourth jhāna, for the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is such-like and whose mind is steady, there were no—indeed, there could be no—inhalations and exhalations.
This is the meaning. By this it is shown that for one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the bodily formations cease.
"Body-formations" (kāyasaṅkhāra) refers to inhalation and exhalation; therefore, he shows that from the moment of the fourth jhāna onwards, inhalation and exhalation no longer exist.
It is "unshaken" (aneja) because of the absence of the "urge" (ejā) known as craving, or because it is unshaken due to being established in concentration.
"Aiming for peace" means aiming for, depending upon, or with reference to Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa). "One who possesses vision" (cakkhumā)—
He was possessed of vision through the five eyes. "Parinibbuto" means he attained final Nibbāna. This is the meaning here:

having entered the attainment of the fruit of the fourth jhāna with Nibbāna as its object, he immediately thereafter attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
"With unflagging mind" means with a mind that is not sluggish, not contracted, but rather fully blossomed. "He endured the feeling" means mindfully.
Being fully aware, he endured the sensations of his final passing; he did not follow after those sensations nor roll about here and there.

"As for a lamp, its extinction occurred; there was liberation of the mind"—just as a lamp, burning in dependence upon oil and a wick, goes out when those are exhausted, so too did he become extinguished. And being extinguished...
Having gone somewhere, it does not remain; rather, it simply vanishes and goes out of sight.

In the same way, the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna), which proceeds dependent upon the defilements (kilesas) and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāras), is extinguished when those are exhausted.
And having been extinguished, it does not go anywhere to remain; rather, it simply vanishes and goes out of sight.
This is shown. Therefore it was said: "The wise are extinguished just as this lamp," and "As a flame cast by the force of the wind," and so forth.
"These" refers to what was spoken because of the direct personal experience (*paccakkha*) of the phenomena (*dhamma*) occurring within the Teacher’s continuum at the moment of final *parinibbāna*.
"Last" means that there is no further arising of consciousness beyond that point. "Now" means at this very time. "With contact as the fifth" means...

This is stated because the phenomena consisting of contact as the fifth member are manifest. For even in the discourse on the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), only those beginning with contact as the fifth are mentioned from the outset.

"Other phenomena" refers to other mental states and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*) together with their support (*nissaya*), but not the mental states and mental factors of final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*). [Objection:
Will not those too cease to exist? [Reply: True, they will not exist.
However, with reference to them, because there is no possibility of attachment, it is simply not to be said that "they will not exist.

But as for the others—the trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*)—there might be the suspicion, "Will they perhaps exist? It is in order to dispel that suspicion that it is said, "No other phenomena will exist.
Regarding the verse, "There is now no returning again to the realm of gods, O Jālinī," here *Jālinī* is the deity being addressed; "O deity..."
"In the body of a god," that is, among the host of gods, "dwelling" (*āvāsa*) means a place of residence; the meaning is: "Now I have no such dwelling.
He states the reason for this with the words beginning, "It is exhausted" (*vikkhīṇo*). It is said that in a previous existence, that deity was the Elder’s attendant;
therefore, seeing the Elder now old and aged, she came out of her former affection and [said], "There..."
“Make a resolve for that place where you formerly dwelt,” she said, requesting rebirth as a deity.
Then, with the words “Now there is none,” and so forth, the Elder gave her his reply. Having heard this, the deity, her hopes shattered, vanished right then and there.
Then the Elder, ascending into the air, manifested his own spiritual power to his fellow celibates, saying: “For whom—”
He spoke this verse: “In a mere moment. Its meaning is as follows:

for that bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, in a mere moment, the world—in its thousandfold variety, its classification into three thousand great thousands, including the Brahmā-world and together with the Brahmās—is thoroughly known, perfectly understood, realized, and made manifest.
Thus, through the quality of psychic power (*iddhi*), by means of the perfection of psychic power, [he knows] both passing away and rebirth.
Having attained mastery, that bhikkhu sees the deity at the time of approach; there is no decline for him in his vision of the deities.

It is said that when the Elder spoke the verse beginning with “There is none now” as a reply to the deity Jālinī, the bhikkhus, not seeing Jālinī, wondered: “What indeed is the Elder saying to her by way of conversing on the Dhamma?”
They reflected. Knowing their state of mind, the Elder spoke this verse: "Yassa muhuttena... [and so forth].
"Annabhāro pure" means one who, in a previous existence, was known by that name. "Ghāsahārako" means one who lived by performing service for the sake of mere food.
"Samaṇaṃ" means one who has stilled evil. "Paṭipādesin" means I presented [the food] facing him, out of faith.
The intention is that he gave a gift of food while facing [the recipient]. "Upariṭṭha" refers to the Paccekabuddha of that name.
"Yasassin" means one who possesses fame, one whose renown is widespread. With this verse, he shows his own past karma, which served as the cause for his exalted success up until his final existence.
Therefore, he said: "I am born in the Sakyan clan," and so forth.
"Seven from here" means having passed away from this human world, they will be reborn seven times in the deva realm with divine sovereignty.
"Seven from there" means having passed away from that deva realm, they will be reborn seven times in the human world as universal monarchs (*cakkavatti*).

"Fourteen rounds of saṃsāra" refers to fourteen transmigrations through different states of existence. "They will know their dwelling" means he has directly known his own previous dwellings. [In the deva realm...]

"Standing then" means that this was not only in this very present existence, but rather when he was standing in the world of the gods in the immediately preceding past existence; the meaning is that at that time he knew [the future].

Now, demonstrating the manner in which he had attained the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*), he says "five-factored," and so forth.
He spoke two verses. Therein, "in the five-factored concentration" (*pañcaṅgike samādhimhi*) refers to the fourth-jhāna concentration that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

For that is called "five-factored concentration" because it is endowed with these five factors: the pervasion of rapture (*pīti*), the pervasion of pleasure (*sukha*), the pervasion of the mind (*ceto*), the pervasion of light (*āloka*), and the sign of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇanimitta*). "Peaceful" (*sante*) means by the subsiding of opposing states.
"And while it was continuous in its factors. "Developed to unification" means having reached the state of unification; the meaning is that mastery has been attained over what has been well-practiced.
"Obtained through subsiding" means obtained through the subsiding of the defilements.
"My divine eye was purified"—when such concentration had been accomplished, my knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) was purified of the eleven imperfections.
It became purified by liberation.
"I know passing away and rebirth" means that I know the passing away and rebirth of beings; and knowing it, [I know]:
"These beings, having come from that world, have been reborn here; and having gone from this world, they will be reborn in that world."

I know the coming and going of beings; and knowing it, I know their state as such—that is, their human state—and their state as otherwise, namely, their existence as other than human, prior even to their rebirth.
Showing that all this is accomplished only when the five-factored concentration is perfected, he said: "Standing in the five-factored jhāna. Therein:
The meaning is: having stood and being firmly established in the five-factored jhāna, he knows thus.

Having thus shown the threefold clear knowledge (vijjāttaya), and as a related topic, showing the third clear knowledge—which was previously mentioned—along with the accomplishment of its task, he spoke the two verses beginning with, “The Teacher has been served by me.
Therein, “in the Vajjīs’ village of Veḷuva”:
In the Vajji country, at Veḷuva Village— where he entered the final rains retreat in the Vajji country—
at the foot of a bamboo thicket: "they will be extinguished" means "I shall be extinguished," that is,
I shall attain final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Anuruddha is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Pārāpariya:
"A thought arose in the recluse," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Pārāpariya. The story concerning him is found below.

It has indeed come to pass. Those verses were spoken by the Teacher while he was still living, as a means of explaining his own reflection on the restraint of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, during his time as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

These [verses], however, were spoken later, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna and when his own final Nibbāna was imminent, as a means of explaining to the monks the future practice of the higher Dhamma. In this regard—
“The contemplative had a thought while the great forest was in bloom, as he sat alone, secluded, and meditating”—this verse was placed by the compilers of the collection.
Its meaning is exactly as explained above. This, however, is the connection [of the narrative]:
When the Teacher, the foremost disciples, and many great elders had attained final nibbāna, and while the Dispensation was without its Master,
there were monks who were easy to admonish and desirous of training, yet such monks became rare; when monks who were difficult to admonish and full of wrong practice had arisen,
[he spoke] to one who was secluded, one-pointed, and habituated to meditation, sitting in a vast, blossoming *sāla* grove.
Based on the conduct of the ascetic Samaṇa Pārāpariya, who had stilled all evil, another [thought] arose as an inquiry:
"In one way was the behavior of the monks while the Protector of the World, the Supreme Person, was still present; now it is seen to be otherwise."
“[They used] protection against cold winds, a covering for modesty and shame;
they ate only what was sufficient, content with whatever was available.
Whether it was fine or coarse, whether little or much—”
They ate for the sake of sustenance, free from greed and without infatuation.
They were not intensely eager for the requisites of life,
nor for medicines and other necessities, as they were for the destruction of the taints.
“In forest groves, at the roots of trees, in ravines and caves,
they dwelt devotedly, cultivating seclusion.
Lowly in their station, easy to support, gentle and without arrogance of mind.”
Unstained, not loquacious, following after the pursuit of what is beneficial.
Then, whatever was seen, heard, eaten, or practiced became pleasing;
their deportment was as smooth as a stream of oil.
“With all taints utterly destroyed, great meditators, great benefactors—those elders are now extinguished; such as they are now rare indeed.
Through the exhaustion of wholesome qualities and through the exhaustion of wisdom,”
Endowed with the excellence of all modes, the teaching of the Conqueror is decaying.
[There are] those who are the breeding ground for evil states and defilements,
those who are established in seclusion, and those who are the remnants of the true Dhamma.
“Those defilements, as they increase, invade many people;
they seem to play with fools, like demons with the insane.
Overcome by those defilements, they run hither and thither.”
Men, amidst the bases of defilement, are proclaimed to be like those in a battle.
Having abandoned the true Dhamma, they quarrel with one another;
pursuing various speculative views, they imagine, "This is better."
“Having abandoned wealth, children, and wife, they have gone forth;
even for the sake of a spoonful of alms-food, they endure hardships.
Having eaten until their bellies are full, they lie down on their backs.”
The awakened ones increase their discourse with that talk which does not disparage the Teacher:
“Having made a commitment, one should train in all the crafts and skills;
yet for one who is not inwardly tranquil, the goal of asceticism remains unattained.”
“Clay, oil, powder, water, seats, and food—
these they offer to householders, desiring much more in return.
Tooth-sticks, wood-apples, flowers, and various edibles;”
When alms-food is obtained, and likewise when *āmalaka* fruits are given by one’s mother;
as physicians are toward medicines, as householders are toward what should and should not be done;
as courtesans are toward adornment, and as Kṣatriyas are toward their lords.
“Deceitful and fraudulent, false witnesses and untruthful,
they consume material gain through many various contrivances.
Pursuing their schemes with artful methods and stratagems, they run hither and thither in pursuit of their plans.”
Seeking a livelihood, they amass great wealth by means of crafty schemes.
They gather a following through their work and not through the Dhamma;
they teach the Dhamma to others for the sake of gain and not for the sake of the true goal.
“They quarrel over gains belonging to the Saṅgha, having been excluded from the Saṅgha;
subsisting on the gains of others, they are shameless and feel no remorse.
Likewise, some who are not truly devoted, though shaven-headed and clad in the outer robe of the Saṅgha,”
Those intoxicated by gain and honor desire only esteem.
"Now that things have become so diverse, it is no longer easy to attain what has not been attained, nor to preserve what has been attained."
“Just as one might walk barefoot in a place full of thorns,
so should the sage walk through the village, having established mindfulness.
Remembering the yogis of old and following their conduct,”
"Even though it be the final hour, one may touch the deathless state.
Having said this in the Sāla grove, the ascetic with developed faculties, the brahmin,
the sage whose renewed existence is exhausted, attained final Nibbāna.
These verses were spoken by the Elder himself.

Regarding the phrase "the conduct of the bhikkhus was such": while the Supreme Person, the Lord of the World, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was still present and remaining—because of the current state of practice at that time—the conduct and behavior of the bhikkhus was otherwise; that is, it was in a different manner.

"It was as instructed" because of the cultivation of practice according to the instructions. "Now it is seen otherwise" means that now, however, the conduct (*iriyā*) of the monks is seen to be different from that, due to their practice not being in accordance with reality; this is the intended meaning.
Now, in order to first show the manner in which the practice of the monks was while the Teacher was still living:
“‘Protection against cold winds,’ and so forth, was said. Therein, ‘just enough’ (*mattaṭṭhiya*) means that measure is the purpose.
They made use of the robe-cloth only to the extent of protection against cold winds and only to the extent of covering the private parts out of a sense of shame.
How so? Being content with whatever they received—whether inferior or superior—they attained satisfaction in those very requisites.”
"Exquisite" (*paṇīta*) means superior, mixed with ghee and so forth; by the absence of such things, it is coarse (*lūkha*).

"Little" (*appa*) means even as much as four or five mouthfuls. "They ate much for the sake of sustenance" (*yāpanatthaṃ abhuñjiṃsu*) means that even while eating much exquisite food, they ate only a quantity of food sufficient for maintenance.
For that very reason, they were not greedy (*agiddhā*), having not fallen into grasping (*gedha*); they were not infatuated (*nādhimucchitā*) nor attached (*na ajjhositā*), just like axle-oil.
The carters ate like merchants who have applied ointment to their wounds.
Regarding the requisites for life: medicinal requisites, that is, those conditions reckoned as medicine which serve as the equipment for the maintenance of life;
"just as they" means just as those former bhikkhus [attained] the destruction of the taints.
"Zealous and diligent" means that even though they were overcome by illness, they did not become excessively or intensely zealous for the requisites of the sick.

"Having that as their supreme resort" means having seclusion as their supreme resort and being inclined toward seclusion. Thus, by means of these four verses, the practice of the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa) was shown by demonstrating contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation.
"Humble" means that, without engaging in self-exaltation or disparagement of others—thinking, "We are rag-robe wearers, we are alms-food eaters"—they lived in a humble manner.
The meaning is "those of humble conduct. "Established" means established in faith within the Teaching (*sāsana*). "Easy to support" means easy to nourish by virtue of having few desires and so forth.
"Gentle" means gentle in the performance of duties and in the entire holy life (*brahmacariya*);
they are capable of being employed like well-refined gold. Alternatively, "gentle" means without frowning, with open faces, and conducting themselves with a welcoming expression.

It means that it brings happiness like a good landing-place. "With minds not stubborn" (*athaddhamānasā*) refers to a mind that is not rigid; by this, he expresses the state of being easy to speak to.

"Unstained" (*abyāsekā*) means free from the staining of defilements due to the absence of any lapse in mindfulness; the meaning is that they are not intermittently beset by craving, views, pride, and so forth.
"Not loquacious" (*amukharā*) means not talkative; they are not harsh with their mouths, being devoid of verbal impudence.

Or it means "the purpose. "Following the conclusion of the reflection on welfare" means following the conclusion of the reflection on benefit, being dependent upon the reflection on benefit; that is, those who revolve solely around the reflection on the welfare of themselves and others.
"Therefore" means for that reason, due to such causes as living humbly. "Inspiring confidence" means [a state] which produces serene confidence in those who see or hear the practice.
"Bringing confidence": "Gone" refers to the movement of going forward, returning, turning around, and so forth;
or alternatively, it refers to the activity of body and speech. "Eaten" refers to the utilization of the four requisites.

"Enjoyed" refers to the frequenting of one's range of resort. "Smooth like a stream of oil": just as a continuous stream of oil poured by skilled people flows without turning back, uninterrupted, smooth, and glossy.
It was beautiful and pleasing to behold; likewise, the posture of those who were perfected in their deportment was flawless, gentle, smooth, beautiful, and pleasing to behold.
"Great meditators" (mahājhāyī) means those whose nature it is to meditate with great jhānas, or those who meditate upon the great Nibbāna; thus they are called "great meditators."
Therefore, they are "of great benefit" (mahāhitā), meaning they are endowed with great benefits.
"Those elders" (te therā) means those elders of the aforementioned type, who were devoted to such practice, have now attained final Nibbāna.
"Now they are few like that" (parittā dāni tādisā) means that in this present final period, elders of such a kind and character are few, limited, and only a small number—this is what is being said.

"Of wholesome states" means of those blameless states that are the requisites for liberation (*vimokkha-sambhāra*) and serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
"And by wisdom" means by such wisdom as that. "By its complete destruction" means by its non-existence and non-arising.
Granted that wisdom here too may be considered a blameless state, it is nevertheless mentioned separately in order to show its great efficacy.

"Accumulations of merit and knowledge. "Endowed with the excellence of all modes" means it is possessed of and equipped with all the most excellent modes, that is, the specific distinctions such as being auspicious in the beginning and so forth;
the teaching of the Conqueror, the Blessed One, "is crumbling and perishing"—this is the meaning.
And "of evil states and defilements": of the evil states such as bodily misconduct and so forth, and of the defilements such as greed and so forth, that which is the "season" (utū) [is meant].
The remainder of the sentence is: "That which is the season and the time for the defilements—that is what is occurring.

Furthermore, those who are established in seclusion and who possess the remnants of the true Dhamma—meaning those who, at such a time, have exerted their energy for the sake of physical, mental, and material seclusion—they become those who possess the remaining practice of the true Dhamma.
This is the intended meaning here: even those whose virtue and conduct are perfectly purified...
Now, some bhikkhus, having first performed preliminary duties such as establishing the postures,
the method for developing serenity and insight, the severing of major impediments, and the severing of minor impediments, apply themselves to meditation. Yet,
being deficient in the true Dhamma of the remaining practices, they are unable to bring those practices to their ultimate perfection.
"Those defilements are increasing" means that those very defilements which were brought to exhaustion and total destruction by the Blessed One’s own sons (the noble disciples) at that time,
are now finding their opportunity and are attaining growth, increase, and abundance among the monks.
"They infest many people" means they infest the blind, foolish folk who lack virtuous friends and are full of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
Having overcome them and brought them under their control, they enter the mental continuum and penetrate it.
Being thus, I think those defilements sport with fools like *rākṣasas* with the insane;

just as *rākṣasas* who are fond of play, having entered those insane persons who lack a physician, sport with them while leading them to ruin and disaster, so too do those defilements sport with those who lack the Greatly Enlightened One as their physician.
Having possessed the ignorant bhikkhus and causing them harm categorized as pertaining to the present life and so forth, they seem to play with them;
the meaning is that they act as if they were playing.
"By this and that" means by this and that portion of an object (*ārammaṇabhāga*). "They run about" means they run about in a distorted way, by way of what is unsuitable (*asāruppa*).

While practicing. Regarding the phrase "in the bases of defilement" (*kilesavatthūsu*): because those defilements that arise later have the previously arisen defilements as their cause, the defilements themselves are called the "bases of defilement.
When those bases of defilement have been removed, [the village] was proclaimed as "free from strife" (*sasaṅgāma*).
Having scattered wealth such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls, [it was declared]: "Whatever gold, silver, and so forth has come into the hands of anyone, let that belong to him."
"Let it be for that very person"—this is what is called the proclamation of desire, which is like the proclamation of a battle with attachments. Herein, this is the meaning:

among the bases of defilement, "Whichever defilement seizes and overcomes whichever being, let that [defilement] belong to that very person"—just as if Māra, the commander-in-chief of the army of defilements, were to proclaim a battle with attachments.
Those foolish worldlings, overcome by those various defilements, by him...
"Driven by that objective, they have run about and become exhausted.
To the question, "What do they do once they have thus run about? he says: "Having abandoned the true Dhamma, they quarrel with one another.
The meaning of this is: having discarded the true Dhamma of practice, for the sake of mere material gain, they quarrel with one another.

"Engaging in quarrels" means: following and pursuing these "wrong views"—such as the views that "only consciousness exists, material phenomena do not exist at all," or "just as a person does not exist in the ultimate sense, so too intrinsic phenomena do not exist in the ultimate sense and are merely conventional designations"—while clinging to such false graspings. This...
They think, "This alone is better; this is supreme; anything else is wrong.
"Those who have gone forth" means those who have departed from the home life. "Even for the sake of a spoonful of alms" means even for the purpose of receiving a mere spoonful of food.
For a householder giving such [alms], there is improper association; by virtue of that, there are duties not to be performed by one who has gone forth.
They perform and carry out their tasks.
Having eaten until the belly is full means: having eaten to satiety without considering the statement, "one should eat moderately, with an empty stomach.
Lying down on one's back means: "he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other."
"Without recollecting the manner prescribed as 'mindful and clearly comprehending,' they lie down like those who have just been born.
When it is said, "discourse censured by the Teacher," this refers to talk about kings and so forth, up to talk about spirits (tiracchānakatha).
"All the crafts and skills" refers to all the tasks to be performed by craftsmen such as Vaiśyas, including the making of bowls, fans, and salt-spoons.
*Hatthasippāni*: manual arts. *Cittiṃ katvāna*: having made it a matter of the heart; that is, having done so with care and respect. *Avūpasantā ajjhattaṃ*:

"unpeaceful within" means that because of the absence of the subsiding of defilements (*kilesa*) and because there is not even for a moment the steadiness [of mind] required for milking a cow, they are unpeaceful within; the meaning is that their minds are unpeaceful. *Sāmaññattha*:
the state of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). *Atiacchati*: it does not reach them, because they are intent upon the business of their livelihood and thus do not touch upon even a single part of it.
"He sits apart" means he does not cling [to worldly things].
"Clay" refers to ordinary clay or five-colored clay suitable for the use of householders.
"Oil and powder" refers to both oil and powder, whether natural or prepared. "Water, seat, and food" refers to water and a seat.
"And food": "Desiring more" means desiring much alms-food and so forth, one after another;

the meaning is that they present [the requisites] to householders with the intention: "When we have given clay and such things, people will become firm in their devotion and give us many successive kinds of the four requisites."
“Dantapoṇaṃ” means that by which teeth are cleaned and purified; it is a tooth-stick (*dantakaṭṭha*). “Kapitthaṃ” means the kapittha fruit.
“Pupphaṃ” means flowers such as jasmine (*sumana*) and champak. “Khādanīyāni” refers to the eighteen kinds of special edible snacks.

“And when alms-food is available” refers to specific types of cooked rice endowed with excellence of color and other qualities. By the word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “mangoes and *āmalaka* fruits,”...
It includes fruits such as the citron, the palmyra, and the coconut, even though they were not explicitly mentioned.
In all cases, the construction is to be understood as:

"They offer these to householders who desire them in great abundance. Regarding medicines, the phrase "just as physicians" means that monks proceed in the application of medicines for householders in the same manner as physicians do.
The intention [is as follows]: "Like householders in matters of duty and non-duty" means that, regarding both small and great duties to be performed, they act like householders.
"Like courtesans in their adornment" means that, in the matter of adorning their own bodies, they are like those who live by their beauty.
"Like kṣatriyas among lords" means that, just as kṣatriyas act in the exercise of lordship, so too do they conduct themselves as heads of families (*kulapati*). This is the meaning.
“Deceivers” (*nekatika*) means those engaged in deception; having made what is not a gem into a gem and what is not gold into gold, they delight in counterfeit and fraudulent combinations.
“Fraudulent” (*vañcanika*) means those who deceive by means of false measures and the like. “False witnesses” (*kūṭasakkhī*) means those whose testimony does not correspond to reality.

“Cunning” (*apāṭuka*) means crafty; the meaning is that their conduct is unrestrained. “By many devices” (*parikappehi*) means by the various modes of wrong livelihood already mentioned and others besides.

*Lesakappeti*: to designate as allowable, as something resembling the allowable, or as a semblance of the allowable. *Pariyāyeti*: in the application of an alternative regarding the requisites (*paccaya*).
*Parikappeti*: in the imagining of possibilities such as increase and so forth; in all these instances, the locative case is used for the object. *Anudhāvitā*:
pursued or overcome by evil qualities such as great desire and the like. *Jīvikatthā*: having livelihood as their purpose, caused by livelihood. *Upāyena*: by means of a stratagem.
By means of such methods as indirect discourse (*parikathā*), that is, by way of generating the requisite conditions (*paccaya*). "They gather together" (*saṅkaḍḍhanti*) means they collect.
"They attend upon" (*upaṭṭhāpenti*): they cause themselves to be attended upon by the assembly; the meaning is that they win over the assembly just as the assembly attends upon them.
"By way of work" (*kammatoti*) means for the sake of work. For they [do so] on account of the services (*veyyāvacca*) that ought to be performed by themselves.
They attend to [the assembly], yet they do not attend to it according to the Dhamma; that is, they do not attend to the sign of the Dhamma.

The meaning is that they do not support the assembly with that kind of gathering which was authorized by the Teacher for an assembly established in a nature of mutual upliftment. "On account of gain" means for the sake of gain:
thinking, "The noble one is learned, an eloquent speaker, a preacher of the Dhamma," the great multitude honors me with gain and respect.
"Will bring [them] near"—thus, standing in a way of life driven by desire, they teach the Dhamma to others for the sake of gain.

"But not for the sake of the goal" means that they do not teach the Dhamma for the sake of benefit—such as that pertaining to the present life and so forth—which is to be attained by one who stands at the head of the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana) and proclaims the true Dhamma; this is the meaning.
"Quarreling over gains from the Saṅgha" means they quarrel for the sake of gains from the Saṅgha, engaging in strife by saying things such as, "It falls to me, not to you.
"Excluded from the Saṅgha" means they are outside of the Noble Saṅgha because that [quality] is absent in them within the Noble Saṅgha.

"Living off the gains of others" refers to those who, while there is gain in the Teaching, live off the gains of others—namely, those ordinary worldlings who are blind and foolish—as opposed to those endowed with virtues such as moral discipline.

Because it has arisen for the sake of those in training (sekha), those quarrelsome monks who subsist upon that gain from others—that is, gain obtainable from other donors—being devoid of shame due to the absence of loathing for evil, do not feel ashamed or feel a sense of moral dread (*hirī*) even as they think:
"We are consuming the gains of others; our livelihood is dependent on others."
"Not devoted" means not devoted to those qualities that make one a true ascetic. "In that way" means just as previously mentioned, such as the makers of bonds and so forth.

"Some" means a certain number. "Shaven-headed and clad in the *saṅghāṭī*" means they are shaven-headed merely because their hair has been shaved off, and their bodies are covered with a robe named "*saṅghāṭī*" in the sense of being composed of patches of ragged cloth. They desire only honor.
“Intoxicated by gain and honor” means being infatuated with and clinging to the hope for gain and honor;
or, being devoted to sweet speech, thinking “he is amiable, a proponent of the ascetic practices (dhuta),
and learned,” they desire and seek only esteem and high regard as an “Ariyan,” but not the actual qualities that constitute such a state— that is the meaning.
Thus, according to the method stated as "through the complete exhaustion of wholesome states and through wisdom" (*kusalānañca dhammānaṃ paññāya ca parikkhayā*).

"In the midst of manifold wandering" (*nānappakāramhī*) means when one has set out or engaged in various kinds of things subject to disintegration, or when one has begun to proceed toward or engage in various kinds of defiled states.
"Now it is not easy to do so" (*na dāni sukaraṃ tathā*) refers to this present time, when a virtuous friend is difficult to find and hearing the true Dhamma that is beneficial is difficult to obtain.
And when the Teacher is still living, it is not easy—at that time—to touch or attain the as-yet-unattained meditative absorption (jhāna) and insight (vipassanā);

nor is it easy to guard and preserve what has already been touched, so that instead of being subject to decline or remaining static, it becomes something characterized by distinction; such is the meaning of "it is not easy to accomplish."

Now, because the time for his own final Nibbāna was near, he spoke the words beginning with "Just as a man in a place full of thorns... while giving brief instruction to his fellow celibates. The meaning of this is as follows:
Just as a man walking barefoot in a place covered with thorns for some purpose would establish mindfulness, thinking, "May a thorn not pierce me," [so should one dwell].
It is said that just as one moves about, so too the Sage, moving for a purpose through the village of his range—

which is strewn with the thorns of defilements— should move about only with diligence, having established mindfulness and being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, never abandoning his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Remembering the yogis of old" means that they remember the conduct of those former ones because they were devoted to the development of yoga in their previous practice.
Remembering those who have initiated insight and recollecting the method for the cultivation of right practice according to their conduct and the tradition,
one should proceed accordingly without laying down the burden. Even though this is the final period and the Teacher has passed away,
by practicing exactly in accordance with the Dhamma and exerting oneself in insight, one may still attain realization.
"May he attain the deathless state, Nibbāna.

Having said this—meaning, having explained this method of practice regarding defilement and purification as it has been shown—it should be understood that this final verse was spoken by the elders who compiled the collection in order to announce the Thera’s Parinibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Pārāpariya is finished.
The commentary on the Vīsatinipāta is concluded.
17. Tiṃsanipāta 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Phussa.
The verses beginning with "Having seen many beautiful [forms] in the Tiṃsanipāta" belong to the Venerable Elder Phussa. What is their origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, wandered among gods and humans until, during the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a certain provincial king.
His name was Phussa. When he reached the age of discretion, he attained mastery in all the arts and crafts to be learned by khattiya princes.
Because he was endowed with the necessary conditions, his mind was unattached to sensual pleasures;
having heard the Dhamma from a certain great elder, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and, taking up a meditation subject suited to his temperament, devoted himself to its cultivation.
Having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and established insight (*vipassanā*) based upon them, he soon became possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Then one day, an ascetic named Paṇḍaragotta, having heard the Dhamma in his presence, sat down;
seeing many monks endowed with virtue and conduct, well-restrained in their faculties, with bodies developed and minds developed, he felt a heart full of serene confidence.

Thinking, "May this practice indeed endure for a long time in the world," he asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, how will the practice of the bhikkhus be in the future? To show this matter, the compilers of the collection [said]:
"Having seen many who were inspiring, with developed minds and well-restrained..."
“Isi paṇḍarasagotto, apucchi phussasavhayan”ti—this verse they placed at the beginning.

Therein, “gracious” (pāsādika) means worthy of inspiring confidence through one’s own practice. “Many” (bahū) means numerous. “Of developed self” (bhāvitatta) means those whose minds have been developed through the cultivation of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
“Well-restrained” (susaṃvuta) means those whose sense faculties are well-restrained. “Seer” (isi) means an ascetic. “Paṇḍarasagotta” means of the Paṇḍara clan.
Because he was born in the lineage of the seer Nāma, he is of the same clan as him. "Phussasavhaya" means that which is to be called by the word "Phussa";
the meaning is "named Phussa.
"What will their desires be, what their intentions, and what their conduct?"
“In the future time, answer this question for me when asked.
This is the verse of inquiry from that seer.
Therein, “What will their inclinations be? means: in this dispensation, in the future, what will be the inclinations and what will be the resolute intentions of the bhikkhus?
"Of low disposition" means: are they of inferior inclination or of sublime inclination? "With what intention" means:
what kind of intention, what kind of underlying tendency (*ajjhāsaya*) do they have; is their underlying tendency defiled or is it pure? Alternatively, "zeal" (*chanda*) is the desire to act;
therefore, the meaning is: what kind of desire to act do they have? "Intention" (*adhippāya*) is the same as the underlying tendency (*ajjhāsaya*).

“What kind of conduct? means what sort of conduct. “Conduct” (ākappa) means one who possesses the deportment, dress, and so forth, as well as the proper behavior and practice. “Will be” means they will exist. “Tell that to me” means:
having been asked about that future classification of the monks’ intentions and conduct, tell and explain it to me;
thus he requests the Elder. As the Elder explains this matter to him, [he first] urges him to listen attentively:—
“Listen to my words, O seer named Paṇḍara;
attend carefully, for I shall declare what is yet to come. Thus he spoke this verse.
Its meaning is: “O seer named Paṇḍara, that which you ask me, I shall declare to you as it pertains to the future.”
"But listen to my words as I speak them; since they reveal what is to come and bring about a sense of spiritual urgency, attend to them with care.
Then the Elder, having seen the future course of events for the monks and nuns exactly as it would be through his knowledge of the future, spoke to him:
"Many will be wrathful and resentful, Spiteful, stubborn, and deceitful;..."
In the future, there will be those who are envious and proponents of various doctrines.
Thinking they have realized the Dhamma when it is profound, they will range only along the shore;
being light-minded and disrespectful toward the Dhamma, they will show no reverence for one another.
“Many dangers will arise in the world in the future;
those of weak intellect will corrupt this well-taught Dhamma.
Even those devoid of virtue, speaking confidently within the Saṅgha,”
They will be powerful, talkative, and unlearned.
Even those who possess virtues and speak within the Saṅgha according to the truth will become weak, modest, and indifferent to their welfare.
“Silver and gold, fields and land, goats and sheep,
And female and male slaves— the dull-witted will accept these in the future.
Fools, perceiving them as blameless, will remain unconcentrated in their virtue.”
“Roaming about with their necks upraised, these birds will delight in quarreling.
They will become arrogant, clothed in blue robes;
deceitful, stubborn, talkative, and haughty, they will wander about like noble ones.”
“With hair matted in thirteen ways, fickle and with eyes like collyrium, they will go along the streets, draped in garments the color of ivory.
[But others] will wear the most loathsome [robes], having renounced [worldly things], the beautifully dyed banner of the Arahants.”
Attached to white robes, they will loathe the saffron-colored one.
Desiring gain, lazy, and lacking in energy,
they will find forest retreats difficult and dwell instead among villages.
“Those who always delight in wrong livelihood will gain whatever gains they obtain;
by training after their example, the unrestrained will associate with them.
Those who do not gain what they have not gained will not be honored.”
Even though you are steadfast, they will not serve you then. "Censuring their own red banner,
the people of the borderlands will wear the white banners of the heretics."
“Then there will be a lack of respect for the saffron robes among them;
and there will be no reflective discernment regarding the saffron robes for the bhikkhus.
For one who is overcome by suffering, pierced by arrows, and tormented—”
Reflecting upon that most terrible [event], the elephant’s thought was inconceivable:
“Having then seen the well-colored banner of the Arahant,
the six-tusked elephant immediately spoke this verse, which was full of meaning.”
“He who, being impure, shall wear the saffron robe,
devoid of self-restraint and truthfulness— he does not deserve the saffron robe.
But he who has vomited out impurity and is well-composed in his virtues— ”
One endowed with self-control and truthfulness truly deserves the saffron robe.
But one of failed virtue, dull-witted, openly acting according to his own desires,
distracted in mind, and devoid of energy— he does not deserve the saffron robe.
“He who is perfected in virtue, free from passion, composed,
and pure in mental intention— he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.
But the fool who is agitated and arrogant, in whom virtue does not exist— ”
He deserves the white robe; what will the saffron robe do?
In the future, monks and nuns with wicked minds and lacking respect will rebuke those who are such-like and possess hearts of loving-kindness.
“Even when being instructed by the elders regarding the wearing of robes, those fools,
being dull-witted and acting according to their own whims, will not listen.
Having been thus instructed, those fools will show no respect for one another.”
They will not heed their preceptors, like a wild colt disregarding its trainer.
"Such will be the practice for monks and nuns in the future, when the final time has arrived."
“Before this great danger arrives in the future,
be gentle-spoken and kindly, showing mutual respect for one another.
Be of loving mind and compassionate, and be restrained in your virtuous conduct.”
“Exerting energy, resolute, always firm in their perseverance,
seeing heedfulness as fear and heedlessness as security,
they should develop the Eightfold Path, touching the deathless state”— these verses he spoke.
In this context, "prone to anger" means having a habit of being angry; this is to be connected with the words "will exist in the future.
One might ask: "Did they not exist so [prone to anger] in the time of the Elder? They were not non-existent.

However, at that time, because there was an abundance of virtuous friends—many fellow practitioners acting as instructors and exhorters—and because of an abundance of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) even when the defilements were powerful, [they did not become so].
For the most part, the monks were free from anger, whereas in the future they will become excessively angry as the opposite of that;

therefore, it is said, "in the future. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. One who is *upanāhī* is so called because of the habit of harboring resentment (*upanayhana*) toward the bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), or because of the arising of resentment.
In this context, anger (*kodha*) is the ill-will (*byāpāda*) belonging to the earlier period, while [malice] belongs to the subsequent period.
Enmity (*upanāha*). Hatred that arises once is anger (*kodha*); that which arises many times is enmity.

They smear and heap up the existing virtues of others; or, like a water-scraper (*udakapuñjanī*) for water, they possess this "smearing" (*makkha*)—the act of smearing and heaping—thus they are "smeared ones" (*makkhī*).

Those who possess "stiffness" (*thambha*), characterized by arrogance, are "stiff ones" (*thambhī*). "Crooked ones" (*saṭhā*) refers to those characterized by the manifestation of non-existent virtues.
They are possessed of deceit. "Envious" means they are possessed of envy, which has the characteristic of disparaging the prosperity of others.
"Holding various doctrines" means they hold mutually contradictory views and opinions; the meaning is that they are makers of strife.
Regarding the Dhamma, "which is deep, difficult to see, and whose shore is their domain": while the True Dhamma is indeed deep and hard to perceive, they [claim] it is not known.
“Known” means “seen”—thus they are conceited; for that very reason, because their activity is directed toward the lower part [of the path], they have the near shore as their domain.
“Light” means having a light nature, being fickle. “Without respect for the Dhamma” means devoid of reverence for the true Dhamma.
“Mutually disrespectful” means lacking deference toward one another, and devoid of heavy respect for the Saṅgha and their fellow celibates. “Many dangers” means...
There are many various obstacles and manifold faults of the kind already mentioned and those yet to be described. "In the world" means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*).

"Will arise in the future" means they will manifest in the future. "This well-taught Dhamma" refers to this true Dhamma of the scriptures (*āgamasaddhamma*) taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) perfectly and without error, in its aspects such as being excellent in the beginning and so forth. "They will defile" means they will become stained and corrupted by defilements (*kilesa*).
They will act with the corruption of misconduct and the non-Dhamma, saying, “An offense is ‘no offense,’” or “A grave offense is ‘a light offense,’” and so forth;
they will reject the subtle and refined phenomena of form and formlessness.
Through the corruption of views and the corruption of craving in both respects, they will become defiled and stained. “Dull-witted” means lacking wisdom. For this has been said:
The Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, in the future there will be bhikkhus...
who, while discussing Abhidhamma and Vedalla discourses, will fall into dark states and fail to understand.

"Devoid of qualities" means devoid of qualities such as virtue; they are immoral and shameless. Alternatively, "devoid of qualities" refers to being lacking in qualities such as restraint according to the Vinaya.
"Inferior in the Dhamma and Vinaya" means those who have little knowledge. "In the Saṅgha" means in the midst of the Saṅgha. "Speaking" means talking;
that is, saying whatever they please while a formal discussion is taking place in the Saṅgha. "Confident" means fearless and impudent.
"Powerful" means powerful by virtue of the strength of their faction. "Garrulous" means harsh-mouthed or speakers of harsh words. "Unlearned" means...
The learned will not become powerful by merely relying on gain, honor, and fame to act as possessors of virtue,

establishing whatever matter they desire within the midst of the Saṅgha, such as declaring what is Dhamma to be "non-Dhamma," non-Dhamma to be "Dhamma," Vinaya to be "non-Vinaya," and non-Vinaya to be "Vinaya."
"Virtuous" means endowed with qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*). "Speaking according to the facts" means explaining in accordance with the truth and without distortion:
teaching what is Dhamma as "Dhamma," what is not Dhamma as "not Dhamma," the Vinaya as "Vinaya," and what is not Vinaya as "not Vinaya.
"They will be weak" means they will be devoid of strength because of the prevalence of shamelessness within the assembly.
There will be those whose words will not stand firm. "Modest and not desiring" means that those who possess a sense of shame (*hiriman*) have no desire for anything [unwholesome].
For even though they are capable of speaking according to the Dhamma, because of their revulsion toward evil and their lack of worldly involvement, they do not engage in conflict with anyone;
nor do they strive to establish their own position, nor do they make a public declaration of their views or a formal resolution.
Or, having not done so, they remain silent.
"Silver" (*rajata*) means coined money; by this, the inclusion of *kahāpaṇas*, copper coins, *māsakas*, and so forth, should be understood.
"Gold" (*jātarūpa*) means bullion; by this, the inclusion of gems, pearls, and so forth, should be understood. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction: "apadā... [and so on].
As in the phrase "or" (*vā*) and so forth. Alternatively, the reading is "silver and gold" (*rajatajātarūpañca*).

"Field" (*khettam*) refers to that place where the primary and secondary crops grow; the plot of ground not yet prepared for that purpose is "site" (*vatthu*). Regarding "goats and sheep": "sheep" (*eḷakā*) are indeed goats;
with the exception of those, the remaining species of livestock are called "goats" (*ajā*). By the inclusion of "goats and sheep" here, cattle, buffalo, and so forth are also included.
"Saṅgaho kato" means a gathering was made. "Dāsidāsañca" means female slaves and male slaves. "Dummedhā" means the ignorant;
those who do not know what is allowable and what is unallowable, what is proper and what is improper, will consent to and accept [these things] for their own sake.
"Ujjhānasaññino" means those whose minds look down upon others with contempt, or those whose nature is to find fault even in matters that should not be found fault with.
They are "fools" because they are endowed with the characteristics of a fool, such as thinking ill-thought thoughts;

for that very reason, they are "unconcentrated in virtue," meaning their minds are not settled in the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). They are "haughty," meaning they have raised up a hollow pride.

They will "wander about," meaning they will wander about having hoisted the banner of pride. They are "delighting in quarrels," meaning they are intent on superiority due to their abundance of contentiousness.
"Delighting in quarrels" means they are like deer seeking their own welfare, intent on searching for food; the sense is that they are intent on harming the weak.
"Agitated" means possessed of restlessness (uddhacca) and devoid of one-pointedness of mind (citt’ekaggatā).
"Clad in blue robes" means clothed in blue-colored robes dyed with an improper dye; it refers to those who wander about having put on and wrapped themselves in such robes.

They are "deceivers" (kuhā) because they deceive others by practicing fraud through such means as hinting to neighbors; having created deceit out of a desire for the esteem of qualities they do not possess, they cause wonderment in others.
They are "obstinate" (thaddhā) because their minds are hardened by anger and pride, and their hearts are cruel.
They are "flatterers" (lapā) because they live by the livelihood of flattery, [saying] to people whose minds are full of faith: "Venerable sir, what does your honor require?"
The meaning is: those who speak to obtain requisites from the givers of requisites, by means of indirect speech and by means of insinuation (*nippesikatā*).
Regarding "flattery" (*siṅgi*): it refers to the manifest defilements similar to a horn, as described in the passage:
"In this context, what is a 'horn'? That which is a horn, flirtation, wantonness, cleverness, artfulness, and guile."
“Endowed with” means they possess a graceful manner of conduct. The phrase “like noble ones” is an explanation of the meaning of the word “deceitful” (*kuhā*).
For, showing that these deceivers maintain an appearance similar to that of noble ones, he said they “wander about like noble ones.
“With oil-smears” means smeared with either rice-paste oil or water-oil. “Fickle” refers to [their preoccupation] with the adornment of the body and the adornment of requisites, and so forth.
"Endowed with frivolity. "With eyes anointed with collyrium" means having their eyes smeared with decorative ointment.
"They will go along the carriage road" means they will wander here and there on the main highway under the pretext of going for alms or visiting families.
"Clad in ivory-colored robes" means having their bodies covered with saffron-colored robes dyed with the color of ivory.
They feel disgust for that which should not be felt with disgust. "By those who are liberated" means by the Noble Ones (ariyas). "Well-dyed" means well-colored with permissible dye;
they will feel disgust for the saffron robe, the banner of the Arahants, because it was worn by the Arahants such as the Buddha and others.
Why? Because they are attached to white garments and have fallen into greed for them. For this is the statement of the reason why they do not wear robes of the color of ivory. They...

Thinking that if they were to wear white robes, "if the white robes were taken away entirely, there would be nothing but the abandonment of their monastic marks," they put on robes the color of ivory.
"Desirous of gain" means greedy for gain. "Lax" because of being addicted to indolence even in the practice of alms-gathering.

"Of inferior energy" due to the absence of enthusiasm in the mind to perform the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). "Distressed" means weary; distressed by the thought of dwelling in forest retreats (*vanapattha*).

The meaning is "with weary minds. "In the vicinity of villages" means in dwellings near a village, in dwellings close to a village, or in dwellings at the gates of a village. "They will live" means they will dwell.
"Learning after them" means learning after those very individuals who have obtained gains through the practice of wrong livelihood.
"They will wander about. "They will wander about" means they will roam about, serving royal families and the like, in order to produce gain through wrong livelihood just as those [others] do.
Or the reading is "they will resort to" (*bhajissantī*); the meaning is "they will serve. "Unrestrained" (*asaṃyatā*) means devoid of the restraint of virtue (*sīla*).
"Whosoever are without gain, [seeking] gain" refers to those monks who, by avoiding wrong livelihood and due to their lack of merit, are without gain.
Those who do not obtain requisites will then, in that future time, no longer be worthy of honor, worthy of worship, or praiseworthy.
Even toward those monks who are steadfast—meaning those endowed with fortitude—and who are exceedingly gentle, they will not associate;
the meaning is that in that future time, those monks will be seekers of gain alone.
"Red with the dye of a barbarian" means dyed with the dye of *kālakacchaka* (a type of plant). This is a compound word;
the nasalization (*sānunāsika*) is used for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. "Censuring their own banner" means loathing the saffron robe, which serves as their banner.

For those who have gone forth in the Dispensation, the saffron robe is indeed called the "banner. "Some [censuring] the banner of the sectarians" refers to some [who censure] the state of being a follower of the Sakyan son.
Claiming [to be true followers], they will wear white garments—those very white clothes that serve as the banner of the sectarian heretics.
And there will be a lack of respect for the saffron robe; at that time in the future, there will be no reverence or esteem for the saffron robe, which is the banner of the Arahants.
Furthermore, there will be no reflection regarding the saffron robe, such as: "I use this robe with wise reflection," and so forth.
According to this method, there will not be even a mere reflection upon the wearing of the saffron robe.

To one who wears the saffron robe with great respect, thinking, "One must desist from misconduct," [the Buddha], illustrating the weightiness of the saffron robe by citing the *Chaddanta Jātaka*, spoke the verse beginning with "By one overcome by suffering. In that context, "of one pierced by the arrow" means:
Of one pierced by a sharp and various arrow, and thus overcome by great suffering;
"is being afflicted" means undergoing a transformation of the body. "Great and terrible" means fearsome and more intense due to indifference toward both body and life;
it was a reflection beyond the reach of others, inconceivable by mere thought, which occurred to the Great Elephant Chaddanta.
It was thus. For at the time of his birth as the Elephant King Chaddanta, the Bodhisatta was standing in a secluded place when he was pierced by a hunter named Soṇuttara with a poison-tipped arrow.
Overcome by great pain, he saw the saffron robe (kāsāva) wrapped around the hunter and thought, "This man is covered by the banner of the Noble Ones;
he must not be harmed by me," and thereupon directed a mind of loving-kindness (mettā) toward him.
Having established himself, he taught the higher Dhamma, as it is said:
"Though pierced by a broad arrow, the elephant,
with a mind free from ill-will, spoke to the hunter."
“For what purpose, for what reason, O friend, have you killed me?
Or whose design is this?”—it was in order to show this meaning that the Elder spoke the verse beginning with “The six-tusked one. In that context, “the well-colored banner of the Arahant” means:

This is said with reference to Soṇa Uttara, who was wearing saffron robes (*kāsāva*). "He spoke" (*abhaṇi*) means he uttered. "Verses" (*gāthā*) means verses. "The elephant" (*gaja*) refers to the royal nāga-king Chaddanta.
"Connected with the goal" (*atthopasaṃhitā*) means dependent upon the goal, beneficial; the meaning is that they are endowed with welfare.

Regarding the verses spoken by the royal nāga-king Chaddanta, "not free from impurity" (*anikkaṣāvo*) means one who is impure through the impurities (*kasāva*) such as lust and the like; "he will wear them" (*paridahissati*) [means he will be clothed in them].
He will use it as an undergarment, an upper robe, and a covering. Alternatively, the reading is "he will wear it.
"Devoid of self-control and truth" means he is devoid of both the restraint of the sense faculties and the truth of speech which belongs to the side of ultimate truth;
the meaning is that he is separated from and has abandoned them. "Not he"—such a person is not worthy to wear the saffron robe.
"Vantakasāva" means one who has vomited out the taints; the sense is that he should be one whose taints have been discarded and abandoned by means of the four paths.
"In the precepts" (sīlesu) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue. "Well-composed" (susamāhita) means thoroughly concentrated.
"Endowed" (upeta) means arrived at and possessed of both the taming of the faculties and the aforementioned truth. "He, indeed" (sa ve)—that person of such a kind, that...
The meaning is that he is entirely worthy of the saffron-colored robe.
"One of failed virtue" means one whose virtue is broken. "Dull-witted" means lacking wisdom, being devoid of the wisdom that purifies virtue.
"Notorious" means notorious or well-known as "this person is immoral," or else it means "one with notorious faculties" due to having distracted sense-faculties.
"Acting according to his own will" means acting as he desires because his restraint has been broken; or, he is one who can be made to do whatever Māra—the god of desire—wishes.

"With distracted mind" means having a mind scattered among sense objects such as forms and so forth. "Lacking zeal" means being unzealous—that is, devoid of the quality of purity (sukka), lacking moral shame and dread of blame, or lacking the eagerness to accomplish wholesome qualities.

"Free from passion" (*vītarāga*) means one whose desire and lust have departed. "With pure mental intention" (*odātamanasaṅkappa*) means one whose thoughts of the mind are thoroughly purified, or whose intentions are untroubled.
"What will the saffron robe accomplish?"—for one who lacks virtue, what purpose indeed will the saffron robe fulfill? The meaning is that his emblem of renunciation is like a mere painting.

"With corrupt minds" (*duṭṭhacitta*) means those whose minds are defiled by the faults of passion and so forth. "Without respect" (*anādara*) means lacking reverence for the Teacher, the Dhamma, and one another.

"Without respect. Regarding "those who possess a mind of loving-kindness": this refers to those who, through the very attainment of Arahatship, have reached a state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) toward the desirable and so forth, while their hearts are associated with the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*).
This genitive case is used here in the sense of the accusative. "They will restrain [us]" means:
"Seeing those endowed with virtue and other qualities, and honoring them, they will not think much of us who have failed in virtue," thus [thinking] regarding themselves.
The meaning is that they will trouble them in such a way that, out of fear of disrespect, they will depart as they are harassed.
"Even while teaching" means even while being taught; for this is a designation of the agent used in the sense of the object.
"By the elders" means by their own teachers and preceptors. "Wearing the robes" is merely an illustration of the practice of a recluse; therefore—
The meaning is: even when being instructed with such words as, "In this way you should advance; in this way you should retreat," and so forth.
"They will not listen" means they will not accept the exhortation.
"Those fools, though thus instructed," refers to those blind fools who, despite being instructed by their teachers and preceptors, [act] out of disrespect.
"Untrained": they do not respect their preceptor or teacher; they do not abide by their instructions.

How is this so? Like a wild colt [does not respect] its trainer—just as a wild colt, a wicked horse, does not respect its horse-tamer and does not abide by his guidance—even so they do not fear their preceptors and teachers.
The meaning is "they do not become attached.
"Thus," and so forth, is the conclusion of the very meaning already stated. Therein, "thus" means in the manner described.
"Of the future time" (*anāgataddhāna*) means the future period; the meaning is "in the future time. Showing that very [time] by its specific form: "when the time has arrived..."
He said, "In the final period. In this regard, what is the final period? Some say, "The final period begins from the Third Council," but some do not accept that.
For there are five pairs in the Dispensation: the pair of liberation, the pair of concentration, the pair of virtue, the pair of learning, and the pair of giving.
Among these, the first is the pair of liberation; when that has disappeared, the pair of concentration [arises].
When that has disappeared, the pair of the precepts (sīla-yuga) prevails; when that too has disappeared, the pair of learning (suta-yuga) continues to prevail.
For one whose virtue is impure may persist, having acquired some portion of extensive mastery of the scriptures out of a desire for gain and the like.
But when the scripture, down to its very matrices (mātikā), disappears entirely, from that point on there remains only the outward mark (liṅga).
When only that much remains, they gather whatever wealth there is and distribute it by way of giving;

this, it is said, was their final practice of right conduct. Regarding this, some say it was the final period starting from the pair of the *Sutta* [Nikāyas], while others say it was starting from the pair of the *Sīla* [Vagga].
Thus, having shown the great danger arising in the final period, the Elder further addressed the monks assembled there:
While giving this advice, he spoke these three verses beginning with "Before it comes.

Therein, "Before it comes" means that before this future great danger—which I have described to you as an obstacle to your practice—arrives, while it is still yet to come, at that very time [you must act].
"Subbaca" means those who are patient in speech, those who make themselves easy to speak to.
The meaning is: "Being endowed with these qualities, you should be receptive to the instructions of your teachers. *Sakhilā* means having gentle hearts.
*Mettacittā* means having minds associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*), which is characterized by the promotion of the welfare of all beings.
*Kāruṇikā* means devoted to compassion (*karuṇā*), being endowed with compassion that functions in the manner of removing the suffering of others. *Āraddhavīriyā* means... [having initiated energy].
They have exerted energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states.
"With minds directed toward Nibbāna" means having set their hearts upon Nibbāna. "Always" means at all times. "Firm in effort" means possessing steady energy. "Negligence" means neglect;
it is the non-performance of wholesome states and the surrendering of the mind to unwholesome states. For it has been said:

“In this context, what is negligence (*pamāda*)? It is the relinquishing of the mind, the continued granting of relinquishment, toward bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct, or toward the five strands of sensual pleasure; it is the lack of earnestness in the cultivation of wholesome states,” and so forth.
"Appamāda" means non-negligence; it should be understood as the opposite of negligence (*pamāda*).
In terms of its essential meaning, "appamāda" is the non-separation from mindfulness; it is a name for precisely established mindfulness. This is the meaning here:
since all misfortunes have negligence as their root, and all benefits have non-negligence as their root, therefore one should regard negligence as fear.
Seeing heedlessness as a calamity and seeing heedfulness as security and freedom from calamity,
you should develop the Noble Eightfold Path— which consists of the eight factors beginning with right view and which comprises the three aggregates beginning with virtue,
being the pinnacle of the practice of heedfulness— while touching and realizing the deathless Nibbāna; thus, generate it within your own mental continuum.
"Do not remain at the mere path of seeing, but grow by means of the arising of the three higher paths;
in this way, your development through diligence will reach its culmination.
Thus the Elder exhorted the assembled company. These very verses were his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Phussa is finished.
2. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāriputta:
"According to his conduct, according to his mindfulness," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta. Of that Venerable One, [in relation] to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna...

And the background story should be understood as follows: In the past, more than a hundred thousand aeons ago, at the end of an incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeyya*), the Venerable Sāriputta was reborn in a prominent brahmin family;
by name he was known as the young brahmin Sarada. Mahāmoggallāna was reborn in a prominent householder family;
by name he was known as Sirivaḍḍha the householder. Both of them were childhood playmates who grew up together.

They were as follows. Among them, when his father had passed away, the young man Sarada took possession of the family wealth and one day, having gone into seclusion, thought: "Death is an absolute certainty for these beings;
therefore, I must go forth into homelessness and seek the path to liberation. He approached his friend and said, "Friend, I wish to go forth."
Having asked, "Will you be able to go forth?", when he replied, "I will not be able," [the king said], "Very well, I myself shall go forth.

He had the treasuries opened, gave a great alms-giving to the poor, the destitute, and others, went to the foot of a mountain, and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*. Following his example, seventy-four thousand people went forth as well.

They became sons of brahmins. Having realized the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), he taught the practice of the kasiṇas to those jaṭilas as well. They too all realized the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments.
At that time, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Anomadassī appeared in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma.

Having delivered beings from the great flood of saṃsāra, one day [the Buddha], thinking, "I shall show favor to the ascetic Sarada and his disciples," took his bowl and robes and went through the air alone, without a companion.
Thinking, "Let him know my state as a Buddha," he descended from the sky while the ascetic Sarada was looking on and stood firm upon the earth. The ascetic Sarada [beheld] the Teacher...

Having examined the marks of a Great Man on the Teacher’s body and reached the conclusion that he was indeed an omniscient Buddha, the ascetic Sarada went out to meet him, prepared a seat, and offered it to him. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The ascetic Sarada sat down to one side in the presence of the Teacher.
At that time, his seventy-four thousand attendant matted-hair ascetics arrived carrying various excellent and succulent fruits.

Upon seeing the Teacher, faith arose within them; observing the manner in which both their own teacher and the Teacher were seated, they said, "Teacher, previously we thought, 'There is no one greater than you.'"
“Let us deliberate; however, this man seems to me to be greater than you,” they said. “What are you saying, dear ones?
Do you wish to make Mount Sineru, which rises sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas high, equal in height to a mustard seed?
Do not compare me with an omniscient Buddha! Then those ascetics, having heard the words of their teacher, [fell silent].
“‘How great indeed is this Supreme Person! saying this, they all prostrated at his feet and paid homage to the Teacher.
Then the teacher said to them: ‘Sons, we have no gift suitable for the Teacher;
yet the Teacher has arrived here at the time for the alms-round. Come now, let us give a gift according to our means. You—’”
"Bring whatever choice fruits have been brought," he said; having had them brought, he washed his hands and personally placed them into the Tathāgata’s bowl.
As soon as the Teacher had accepted the fruits, the deities infused them with divine essence.
The ascetic himself also strained the water and gave it to him. Then, the meal was finished.
When he had finished and the Teacher was seated, he summoned all his resident pupils and sat down conversing with the Teacher on a memorable discourse.
The Teacher thought, "Let the two Chief Disciples come together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Knowing the Teacher's mind, the two Chief Disciples, surrounded by a retinue of a hundred thousand who were free from the taints (khīṇāsavā), arrived at that very moment.
Having approached and paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side.
Then the ascetic Sarada addressed his pupils: "Sirs, an offering of flowers must be made for the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
therefore, bring flowers. At that very moment, by means of their psychic power (iddhi), they brought flowers endowed with excellent color and fragrance.
