Having brought flowers, they prepared a flower-seat for the Buddha measuring one *yojana* in extent; for the two chief disciples, three *gāvutas*;
for the rest of the monks, various sizes starting from half a *yojana*; and for the youngest member of the Saṅgha, they prepared a seat the measure of a bull (*usabha*).
When these seats had thus been prepared, the ascetic Sarada stood before the Tathāgata with his hands joined in reverential salutation.
“Venerable Sir, please ascend this flower-seat out of favor to me,” he said. The Blessed One sat down on the flower-seat.
When the Teacher was seated, the two chief disciples and the remaining monks each sat down on their own respective seats.
The Teacher, thinking, “May this be of great fruit for them,” entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). [He perceived] the Teacher’s state of having entered that attainment...
Having understood this, the two chief disciples as well as the rest of the bhikkhus entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

The ascetic stood for seven days continuously holding a flower parasol over them; the others, however, subsisted on forest roots and fruits, and at other times stood with their palms joined in reverent salutation.
At the end of seven days, the Teacher emerged from cessation and addressed the chief disciple, the Elder Nisabha:
"Offer words of thanksgiving for the flower-seats of the ascetics. Standing upon the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple, the Elder offered words of thanksgiving for their flower-seats.
At the conclusion of his discourse, the Teacher addressed the second chief disciple, the Elder Anoma: "You too..."
"Teach them this Dhamma. He too, having reflected upon the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, preached the Dhamma to them.

Yet, despite the teaching given by both of them, not even a single person attained the realization of the Dhamma. Then the Teacher, standing on the ground of his own Buddhahood, began the preaching of the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of that discourse, with the exception of the ascetic Sarada, all the remaining seventy-four thousand beings—altogether numbering about seventy-four thousand—[attained realization].
The matted-hair ascetics attained Arahatship. The Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, they vanished from their appearance as ascetics and appeared wearing the eight excellent requisites, looking like elders of sixty years' standing.
However, the ascetic Sarada thought, "Oh, would that I too, like this elder Nisabha, might [attain the same] for a future Buddha!"
Thinking, "May I become the foremost disciple," he was distracted by a reflection that had arisen at the time of the Teacher’s discourse;
consequently, he was unable to penetrate the paths and fruits. Then, having paid homage to the Tathāgata, he made that aspiration.
The Teacher, seeing that it would be fulfilled without obstacle, said: "From now on, after more than a hundred thousand aeons..."
"Having passed through one incalculable aeon, you will become the chief disciple named Sāriputta of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama," he declared.
Having thus spoken and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he leaped into the air, surrounded by the community of monks.
The ascetic Sarada also went to his friend Sirivaḍḍha and said, "Friend, by me [the teaching] of Anomadassi..."
"At the feet of the Blessed One, he has aspired to the position of chief disciple of the future Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama;
you too should aspire to the position of his second disciple.
Having heard this instruction, Sirivaḍḍha leveled a space measuring eight *karīsa* at the gate of his residence.
Having had flowers with parched grain as the fifth scattered, having had a pavilion with a canopy of blue lotuses constructed,
having prepared a seat for the Buddha and seats for the monks as well, and having arranged a great show of honor and respect,

he invited the Teacher together with the company of monks headed by the Buddha through the ascetic Sarada; then, having offered a great almsgiving for seven days, [he presented it] to the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at its head.
Having clothed him in costly garments, he made an aspiration for the state of being a second disciple.

The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave a prediction according to the established method, and after delivering a discourse of thanksgiving for the meal, he departed.
Sirivaḍḍha, with a heart overflowing with joy, performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and, at the end of his second cycle of consciousness, was reborn in the world of the sense-sphere devas.
He was reborn. Having cultivated the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), the ascetic Sarada was reborn in the Brahma-world.
From that time forth, no further account of either of them is related.
However, even before the appearance of our Blessed One, the ascetic Sarada [was born] in the village of Upatissa, not far from Rājagaha, to the Brahmin woman Rūpasārī.
He took rebirth in a womb. On that very same day, his friend also took rebirth in the womb of a Brahmin woman named Moggalī in the village of Kolita, not far from Rājagaha.
It is said that these two families had been close, bound together as friends for seven successive generations. On that same day, they provided the necessary care for both pregnancies.
When ten months had passed, they provided sixty-six nurses for those who were born.
On the day their names were given, because the son of the Brahmin woman Rūpasārī was the son of the eldest family in Upatissa Village, they gave him the name Upatissa.
Because the other was the son of the eldest family in Kolita Village, they gave him the name Kolita. Both of them...
Growing up with a large retinue, they reached the further shore of all arts as they matured.

Then one day, while observing a mountain-top festival in Rājagaha and seeing the great multitude gathered there, their wisdom having reached full maturity, they emerged through wise reflection, thinking:
"All these people, too, within a hundred years will fall into the jaws of death."
Having attained a sense of spiritual urgency, they made the resolution: "We must seek the Dhamma of liberation, and in seeking it, it is necessary for us to obtain the going-forth (pabbajjā).
Having made this decision, they went forth together with five hundred young brahmins into the presence of the wanderer Sañcaya.
From the time they went forth, Sañcaya attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame.
It came to pass that within a few days, having scrutinized the entire system of Sañjaya’s teachings and finding no essence therein, they departed from him.
They then went here and there, posing questions to various ascetics and brahmins who were esteemed as wise men;
yet when questioned by them, those teachers could not provide an answer, but instead had their own questions answered by the seekers themselves. Thus...
Seeking liberation, they made an agreement: "Whichever among us first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other.
And at that time, our Teacher, having attained supreme enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma...

Having gradually tamed the thousand matted-hair ascetics, beginning with Uruvelakassapa, while he was dwelling at Rājagaha, one day the wanderer Upatissa, while going to the wanderers’ park, saw the Venerable Elder Assaji walking for alms in Rājagaha and thought:
"I have never before seen a renunciant so perfected in deportment; by his peaceful nature..."
Thinking, "There must be something here," he followed closely behind the Venerable One, watching him with growing confidence as he waited to ask a question.
When the Elder had obtained almsfood, he went to a suitable place to eat.
The wanderer prepared his own wanderer’s seat and offered it to him. At the conclusion of the meal, for him—
He gave water from his own water-pot.
Having thus performed the duties toward his teacher, and having exchanged greetings with the Elder who had finished his meal, he asked:
"Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you find pleasing? The Elder pointed to the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Again, when asked by him, "But what does the Venerable One’s Teacher teach?", [the monk], thinking, "I shall demonstrate the profundity of this teaching," announced his own status as a novice and spoke the teaching of the Dhamma in brief, reciting the verse: "Of those phenomena that arise from a cause...
Having heard only the first two lines, the wanderer [attained] the thousand-fold method...
He was established in the fruit of stream-entry; the other two stages were completed at the time he became a stream-enterer.
However, at the conclusion of the verses, seeing that no further distinction arose despite his becoming a stream-enterer, he reflected, "There must be a reason for this," and said to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, do not increase the teaching of the Dhamma further; let it remain just this much. Where..."
“Does our Teacher reside there? “In Veḷuvana. “Venerable sir, you go on ahead;

I shall release my promise to my friend, take him with me, and return,” he said. Having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, circumambulated the elder three times, and dismissed him, he went to the wanderers’ park.
When the wanderer Koliya saw him approaching from afar, he thought, "His complexion is not as it was on other days;
surely he must have attained the Deathless through his journey. Suspecting thus that he had achieved some distinguished attainment, he asked about his realization of the Deathless.
He [Koliya] acknowledged, "Yes, friend, I have attained the Deathless," and recited that very same verse. At the conclusion of the verse—
Having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry, Kolita asked, "Where is our Teacher? "In the Veḷuvana," he replied.
"In that case, friend, let us go; we shall see the Teacher. Upatissa was always a worshiper of his teacher;
therefore, having gone to Sañjaya and proclaimed the virtues of the Teacher, he desired to lead him as well into the presence of the Teacher.
He was driven by a desire for gain and, unwilling to remain a pupil, refused, saying, "I cannot become a water-sprinkler just to act as a ladle.

When they were unable to persuade him through various means, they went to Veḷuvana together with two hundred and fifty pupils who were abiding by their own instructions. The Teacher saw them approaching from afar.
Having seen them, he said, "This shall be my pair of disciples, a supreme and auspicious pair.
Then, having taught the Dhamma according to the conduct of their assembly and established them in Arahatship, he granted them full ordination by the formula "Come, monk!
Just as it was for them, so too did the supernaturally produced bowl and robes come to the Chief Disciples. The task of the three higher paths [was thus completed].
But it does not reach its conclusion. Why? Because of the greatness of the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections (pāramīñāṇa).

Among them, on the seventh day after his going forth, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was practicing the duties of a recluse at the village of Kallavāla in the kingdom of Magadha, he was overcome by sloth and torpor;
being stirred by the Teacher, he dispelled that sloth and torpor.
While listening to the meditation subject on the elements (dhātukammaṭṭhāna), he attained the three higher paths and reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s knowledge of perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa).

Having passed half a month from the day of his going forth, the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling with the Teacher at the Sūkarakhatā Cave in Rājagaha when [the Teacher spoke] to his own nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha.

While the *Vedanāpariggaha Sutta* was being taught, he directed his knowledge according to the discourse and reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*), like one eating a meal prepared by another.
Thus, the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge was attained by both chief disciples in the very presence of the Teacher. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
"Not far from the Himālaya is a mountain named Lambaka;
there my well-constructed hermitage stands, with its leaf-hut beautifully arranged.
There is a river with shallow banks, easy to ford, and delightful."
"Strewn with very pure sand, not far from my hermitage,
a river flows there— free of gravel, without precipices, sweet, and without foul odor— beautifying my hermitage."
“Here, crocodiles, sea-monsters, and likewise sharks and turtles move about in that river, beautifying my hermitage.
There are also pāṭhīna fish, pāvusa fish, balaja, muñja, and rohita fish.”
The vaggaḷā birds, as they swoop down, beautify my hermitage.
On both banks of the river, trees laden with flowers and fruit hang down on both sides, beautifying my hermitage.
“The ambā, sāla, and tilaka trees, the pāṭalī and sinduvāraka—
blooming in my hermitage, they emit a divine fragrance.
The cammaka, saḷala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka trees [do the same].”
Divine fragrances waft about, as flowers bloom in my hermitage.
The *atimutta* and the *asoka* have blossomed, and the *bhaginīmālā* has flowered;
The *aṅkola* and the *bimbijāla* have blossomed in my hermitage.
“Ketaka trees and kandali plants, godhuka and grass-stalks,
wafting a divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.
Kaṇikāra and kaṇṇika trees, asana and many ajjuna trees [also adorn it].”
Exuding a divine fragrance, they beautify my hermitage.
“Punnāga trees, mountain-punnāgas, and blooming koviḷāra trees,
exuding a divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.”
“Uddālakas and kuṭajas, kadambas and many bakulas,
wafting divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.
Āḷakas and isimuggas, plantains and mātuluṅgis— ”
Nourished by scented water, they bear fruit.
"Some lotuses bloom, others are born with filaments;
some lotuses are already flowering, while others in the pond have blossomed at that time."
“The lotuses conceive seed, the water-lilies run forth;
strewn with *siṅghāṭa* leaves, the ponds then shine.
The *nayita*, the mango-scented, the *uttalī*, and the *bandhujīvaka* [blossom].”
Then, having blossomed in the pond, divine fragrances wafted forth.
“The pāṭhīna, pāvusa, and balaja fish, as well as the muñja and rohita,
saṃgula, and maggura, all dwell in that pond at that time.”
“Then crocodiles, water-monsters, stingrays, and rākṣasas;
owls, pythons, and snakes dwell in that pond.
Pigeons, ravens, swans, ruddy geese, and river-dwelling birds [are there too].”
Cuckoos, parrots, and mynas depend upon that lake.
Loud-cackling ducks, water-fowls, wood-peckers, Dindibhas,
and young swans depend upon that lake.
“Swans, cranes, and peacocks, cuckoos and *tambacūḷaka* birds,
*pampakas* and *jīvaṃjīvas*— they all depend upon that lake.
*Kosikas*, *poṭṭhasīsas*, ospreys, and many *senakas* [also dwell there].”
And mahākāḷa birds depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
“Deer, wild boars, yaks, and many gaṇḍaka antelopes;
ruddy geese and white pigeons also depend upon that lake for their livelihood.”
“Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, and brown bears,
as well as elephants of three-fold breed, depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
Kinnaras, monkeys, and even forest-dwellers likewise do so.”
The servants and the hunters alike subsist upon that lake.
"The *tinduka* trees, the *piyāla* trees, the *madhuka* and *kāsumārī* shrubs—
surely they bear fruit not far from my hermitage."
“The *kosamba*, *saḷala*, and *nimba* trees, endowed with sweet fruit,
surely bear their fruit not far from my hermitage.
There are *harītaka*, *āmalaka*, mango, *jambu*, and *vibhītaka* trees as well.”
The kolā, bhallātaka, and billā fruits grow there.
And āluvā, kaḷamba, biḷālī, and takkaḷa,
as well as jīvaka and sutaka— these are found in abundance in my hermitage.
“Not far away, there were well-constructed ponds,
with clear water, cool and refreshing, with beautiful landing-stairs and enchanting to the mind.
They were covered with lotuses and water-lilies, and filled with white lilies.”
Covered with mandārava flowers, it wafts a divine fragrance.
"In such a forest, endowed with every excellence, in full bloom and laden with fruit,
I then dwelt in that well-constructed and delightful hermitage."
“Virtuous and perfected in vows, always meditative and delighting in jhāna,
having attained the power of the five higher knowledges— such was the ascetic named Suruci.
Twenty-four thousand disciples attended upon me.”
"All these brahmins are of noble birth and renowned.
They are experts in the marks [of a great man], in traditional lore, and in the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha lexicons;
they are versed in the analysis of words and grammar, having reached perfection in their own Dhamma."
“Skilled in portents, omens, and marks,
my disciples are well-trained in the earth, the ground, and the sky.
These men have few desires, are prudent, eat little, and are free from greed.”
Content with gain and loss, they always attend upon me.
Meditators, delighting in jhāna, wise, peaceful in mind and concentrated,
aspiring for the state of nothingness, they always attend upon me.
“Having reached perfection in direct knowledge, delighting in their ancestral domain,
those wise ones who travel through the air always attend upon me.
Restrained at the six sense-doors, unshakable, with their faculties guarded.”
“Those wise ones are unattached; my disciples are difficult to approach.
By sitting cross-legged and by standing or walking, my disciples, who are difficult to approach, pass the night.”
“They do not lust for what is lust-inducing, they do not hate what is hate-inducing,
and they are not deluded by what is delusion-inducing— my disciples are difficult to overcome.
Examining spiritual power, they conduct themselves at all times.”
They cause the earth to tremble, difficult to approach because of their intensity.
And those disciples of mine play, playing the play of meditative absorption.
My disciples, difficult to approach, bring back fruit from the rose-apple tree.
“Some go to Goyāna, others to Pubbavideha;
others still to Uttarakuru—difficult to approach in their quest.
They carry a basket before them, yet they walk behind it.”
The sky was covered by twenty-four thousand [monks].
Some were fire-cookers and some were not;
some used their teeth as mortars, while others ground with stones or subsisted on fallen fruit.
“Some of my disciples, having bathed in water early and late, remain pure for a long time;
they perform ritual sprinklings with water and are difficult to overcome.
With their armpits, nails, and body hair grown long, their teeth stained with mud and their heads covered in dust,”
Fragrant with the scent of virtue, my disciples are difficult to approach.
Having assembled at dawn, those matted-hair ascetics of fierce austerities announce their gains and losses,
and then they depart through the air.
As they depart, a great sound arises;
with the sound of their deerskin robes, the deities are gladdened.
The seers who travel through the sky depart in every direction.
Supported by their own power, they go wherever they wish.
These are shakers of the earth, all of them travelers through the sky;
possessed of fierce energy and difficult to overcome, they are unshakeable like the ocean.
“Some of my disciples are those who stand and walk in meditation, some are seers who remain seated;
some subsist on food as it is provided—my students are difficult to approach.
They dwell in loving-kindness, seeking the welfare of all living beings.”
All those who do not praise themselves do not disparage anyone.
"Like the lion king, they are fearless; like the elephant king, they are steadfast;
like the tiger, they are difficult to approach—they come into my presence."
“Vidyādharas and deities, nāgas, gandhabbas, and rakkhasas;
kumbhaṇḍas, dānavas, and garuḷas—all depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
They, with matted locks piled high and wearing deer-skins as upper garments...”
All those who move through the air depend upon that lake.
"These are always appropriate to one another, full of mutual respect;
among these twenty-four thousand [birds], no sound of flapping wings is heard."
“Placing foot upon foot, making little noise and well-restrained,
they all approached and paid homage to me with their heads.
Surrounded by those disciples, peaceful and ascetic, I— ”
I dwell there in that hermitage, a meditator devoted to meditation.
The hermitage is perfumed by the fragrance of the sages' virtue, by the fragrance of flowers on both sides,
and by the fragrance of the fruits of those who bear fruit.
“I know not night nor day, nor does discontent exist within me;
instructing my own disciples, I find ever-increasing joy.
Amidst flowers blooming and fruits ripening—”
Divine fragrances wafted forth, beautifying my hermitage.
Having emerged from meditative concentration, diligent and wise,
I took up my basket-load and entered deep into the forest.
“Highly trained in portents, dreams, and bodily marks,
I was at that time upholding the recitation of the mantra-words as they were being transmitted.
The Blessed One Anomadassi, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men— ”
Desiring seclusion, the Fully Awakened One went to the Himalayas.
Having plunged into the Himalayas, the foremost, compassionate Sage,
the Supreme Person, sat down after folding his legs crosswise in the lotus posture.
“I beheld the Fully Awakened One, radiant and enchanting;
like a blooming blue lotus, like a blazing sacrificial fire.
He was like a flaming lamp-tree, like lightning flashing in the sky.”
I saw the Leader of the World, like a fully blossomed king of *sāla* trees:
"This Naga, the Great Hero, the Sage who brings an end to suffering—
by coming into his presence, one is liberated from all suffering."
“Having seen the God of Gods, I examined his marks:
‘Is he truly a Buddha, or is he not? Come, let me see the One with Vision.
Upon his supreme feet, wheels with a thousand spokes are visible.”
"Having seen his marks, one should reach a conclusion regarding the Tathāgata.
Having taken up a broom and swept at that time,
and then having gathered flowers, I worshipped the Best of Buddhas."
“Having worshipped the Fully Awakened One, who has crossed the flood and is free from taints,
I placed my deerskin on one shoulder and paid homage to the Leader of the World.
By means of that same knowledge by which the Fully Awakened One dwells free from taints, [I too have attained it].”
I shall praise that knowledge; listen as I speak.
“Self-become one of immeasurable rise, you have lifted this world up;
by coming to see you, they cross over the stream of doubt.”
“You are the Teacher and the banner, the standard and the sacrificial post for living beings;
you are the ultimate refuge, the foundation, and the island—the supreme among bipeds.
It might be possible to measure the water in the ocean with a dry-measure;”
But it is not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge.
It is possible to hold the earth upon the surface of a scale,
but it is not possible to hold your omniscient knowledge.
“Space can be measured with a cord or with a finger,
but your omniscient knowledge, O All-Knowing One, cannot be measured at all.
Even if one were to abandon the water of the great ocean and the entire solid earth,”
When compared with the Buddha’s knowledge, these similes are not appropriate:
“Those whose minds operate throughout the world including the devas—
O Seer, they are caught within the net of your knowledge.”
“By that same knowledge through which you attained the supreme, absolute enlightenment,
by that same knowledge, O Omniscient One, you have crushed the followers of other sects.
Having praised him with these verses, the ascetic named Suruci—
Having spread out his antelope skin, he sat down upon the earth:
"The King of Mountains is said to be eighty-four thousand [yojanas] deep in the great ocean,
and it is likewise as high above [the water].”
“Mount Meru is so exceedingly high, long, and broad;
yet when ground into minute particles by the hundreds of thousands of millions,
even if one were to count for a hundred thousand lakhs, it would not reach exhaustion.”
But it is not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge.
It would be as if someone were to cast a fine-meshed net over the water;
whatever living beings there might be in the water would all be caught within the net.
“Even so, O Great Hero, those who belong to various other sects,
having plunged into the thicket of views, are deluded by their own dogmatic attachments.
Yet, through your pure knowledge, you see all things without obstruction.”
"These are mere inner webs; knowledge does not transcend them.
At that time, the Blessed One, Anomadassī of great fame, the Victor, having emerged from meditative concentration, surveyed the directions.
“The disciple of the Buddha Anomadassi was named Nisabha;
he was surrounded by a hundred thousand who were peaceful in mind and poised in equanimity—
those whose taints were destroyed, who were pure, possessed of the six direct knowledges, and devoted to meditation.”
Knowing the mind of the Buddha, they approached the Leader of the World.
Standing there in the sky, they performed circumambulations;
paying homage with palms joined, they descended into the presence of the Buddha.
“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the World’s Elder, the Bull among Men, the Conqueror,
while seated with the community of monks, manifested a smile.
Varuṇa was the name of the attendant of the Teacher Anomadassī.”
Having arranged his robe over one shoulder, he asked the Leader of the World:
“What, O Blessed One, is the cause for the Teacher’s smile?
For those Buddhas do not manifest a smile without a reason.”
“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,
sat in the midst of the bhikkhus and spoke this verse:
‘He who honored me with a flower and also praised my wisdom— ’”
I shall praise him; listen as I speak.
"Having understood the speech of the Buddha, all the devas assembled;
desiring to hear the true Dhamma, they approached the Perfectly Enlightened One."
“In ten world-systems, divine hosts of great psychic power,
desiring to hear the True Dhamma, approached the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— the fourfold army— [also gathered].”
“They shall always attend upon me; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Sixty thousand musical instruments and well-adorned drums shall always serve me;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”
“Sixteen thousand women, well-adorned,
with variegated garments and ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings;
with arched brows and long lashes, smiling, graceful, slender-waisted, and lithe.”
“They shall always attend upon me; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
For a hundred thousand eons, they will delight in the world of the gods;
a thousand times, they will become a universal monarch (cakkavattī) ruling over a kingdom.”
“One thousand times he will exercise divine sovereignty as Lord of the Devas,
and local kingship on a vast scale beyond counting.
When his final existence is reached, he will attain the human state.”
A brahmin woman named Sārī will carry him in her womb.
By his mother’s name and clan, this man shall be known;
by the name Sāriputta, he will be of sharp wisdom.
“Having abandoned eighty crores, he will go forth as one possessing nothing;
seeking the state of peace, he will wander this earth.
In an immeasurable eon from now, born in the Okkāka clan...”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born from them and fashioned by the Dhamma,
will be the foremost disciple known by the name Sāriputta.”
“This Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, flowing forth from the Himavat mountains,
enters the great ocean, satisfying the vast sea.
In the very same way, this Sāriputta, confident in his own three knowledges,”
Having reached the perfection of wisdom, he will satisfy all living beings.
From the Himalayas up to the great ocean, the vast sea—
whatever sand lies within that interval is beyond counting.
“Even that [number] could be calculated in its entirety by means of counting,
but the wisdom of Sāriputta will not be measured. Even if one were to place marks at every hundred thousand,
the sands of the Ganges would be exhausted.”
But it will not be possible to measure the wisdom of Sāriputta.
"The waves in the great ocean are beyond counting;
even so, it will not be possible to measure the wisdom of Sāriputta."
“Having propitiated the Fully Awakened One, Gotama, the bull among the Sakyas,
and having reached the perfection of wisdom, he will become the foremost disciple.
When the Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the Sakyan son, the Imperturbable One...”
“He will follow correctly, raining down showers of Dhamma.
Having directly known all this, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans,
will sit amidst the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and establish it in the highest state.”
“Aho! Well done is the deed I have performed for the Teacher Anomadassi!
Having rendered service to him, I have reached perfection in every respect.
The deed performed in immeasurable time displays its fruit here to me now.”
“Like an arrow released from a bow, I have consumed my defilements.
Seeking the unconditioned, the unshakable state of Nibbāna,
and scrutinizing all the various sectarians, I wandered through the realms of existence.”
“Just as a sick man would seek out medicine,
searching through the entire forest for release from his illness; so too,
one seeking the unconditioned, the deathless state of Nibbāna.”
Accompanied by five hundred followers, I went forth into the ascetic life of a seer.
Burdened by the weight of my matted locks and clad in an upper garment of antelope skin,
I reached the perfection of direct knowledge and departed for the Brahma world.
“There is no purity among outsiders, except for the teaching of the Victor;
whatever sentient beings possess intelligence, they find purification within the teaching of the Victor.
This is based on personal realization; it is not mere hearsay.”
Seeking the unconditioned, I wandered through false fords.
Just as a man seeking heartwood might cut down a plantain tree and split it open,
yet find no heartwood therein— for it is empty of heartwood.
“In the same way, the many people among the world’s sectarians hold various views;
they are empty of the unconditioned, like a plantain tree devoid of pith.
When my final existence was reached, I became a mere kinsman of Brahmā.”
Having abandoned great wealth, I went forth into the homeless life.
I was a reciter, a bearer of mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas—
a brahmin named Sañcaya— and it was at his feet that I dwelt.
“O Great Hero, that disciple of yours, a brahmin named Assaji,
was then wandering for alms— difficult to approach and of fierce energy.
I saw that wise sage, absorbed in silence.”
“Seeing the Great Elephant with a peaceful mind, like a lotus in full bloom, my thought arose:
‘This one has been well-tamed, his mind is pure;
he is a bull, a preeminent hero—he will become an Arahant.’”
“Gracious he moves, handsome and well-restrained;
tamed in the supreme taming, he will become a seer of the Deathless.
What if I were now to ask about the highest goal him whose mind is satisfied?”
Thus questioned, he will speak to me, and I shall then ask him in return:
"As I was walking for alms, I followed behind you,
waiting for an opportunity to ask about the deathless state."
“Having approached you who had not yet reached the street, I asked:
‘How is your lineage, O Hero? Whose pupil are you, dear sir?
Being thus questioned by me, he answered like an unafraid lion.”
“A Buddha has arisen in the world; I am his disciple, friend.
What kind of teaching and Dharma of the Buddha have you followed, O Great Hero of great renown? Please explain it well to me, sir.”
“Thus questioned by me, he explained everything— the profound and subtle state,
the slayer of the arrow of craving, the dispeller of all suffering.
‘Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has stated their cause;’”
And their cessation—such is the teaching of the Great Recluse.
Having answered this question, I attained the first fruit;
having heard the Conqueror’s instruction, I became stainless and pure.
“Having heard the words of the Sage and having seen the supreme Dhamma, I,
having fully penetrated the true Dhamma, spoke this verse:
‘If only one could realize that very Dhamma right now, the state free from sorrow!’”
“Unseen for many hundreds of thousands of eons,
that goal for which I wandered through difficult places seeking the Dhamma has now been attained by me; it is time for me not to be negligent.”
“Satisfied am I with Assaji, having attained the unshakable state;
seeking my companion, I went to his hermitage.
Having seen me from afar, my well-trained companion—”
Endowed with perfect deportment, he spoke these words:
"Your face and eyes are serene; the state of a sage is indeed visible.
Have you attained the Deathless? Is it the immortal state of Nibbāna?"
“You have come with a serene appearance, as if you have performed the practice of imperturbability;
like one tamed, you are subdued by self-control, O Brahmin—you are at peace.
The Deathless has been attained by me, which removes the sting of sorrow.”
“You too shall attain that; let us go into the presence of the Buddha.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” my well-trained companion took my hand in his, and we approached you.
“Both of us shall go forth into homelessness under you, O Son of the Sakyas;
having come to your teaching, may we dwell free from taints.
Kolita is supreme in psychic power, and I am one who has reached the further shore in wisdom.”
“Having come together as one, let us both adorn the Dispensation.
With my purpose unfulfilled, I wandered at a wrong ford;
but having come into the sight of you, my purpose has been fulfilled.”
“Established upon the earth, trees blossom in due season;
they emit divine fragrances and gladden all living beings.
In the same way, O Great Hero, Son of the Sakyas, of great renown;”
Having established myself in the Teaching, I cause it to blossom.
Seeking the flower of liberation that releases one from the cycle of existence,
by attaining that flower of liberation, I gladden all living beings.
“Within the entire field of the Buddhas, setting aside the Great Sage himself,
there is no one equal to your son in wisdom, O Visionary One.
Your disciples are well-trained, and your assembly is well-disciplined.”
Tamed by the highest taming, they always surround him.
The wise ones, meditative, delighting in jhāna, with peaceful minds and concentrated,
sages endowed with sagehood, always surround him.
“Those who have few desires, who are prudent and wise, who eat little and are free from greed,
and who are content whether they gain or do not gain— these always attend upon him. Those who dwell in the forest,
who delight in the ascetic practices, who are absorbed in meditation, and who wear coarse robes;”
The wise, delighting in discernment, always surround him.
Those practicing the path and those established in its fruits, those in training and those possessing the fruits,
aspiring for the supreme goal, always surround him.
“Stream-enterers, stainless ones, and those who return but once;
non-returners and arahants always surround him.
Skilled in the foundations of mindfulness, they delight in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.”
All your many disciples always attend upon you.
Skilled in the bases of psychic power, delighting in the cultivation of concentration,
and devoted to the right efforts, they always attend upon you.
“Possessing the threefold knowledge and the six direct knowledges, having reached perfection in supernormal powers,
and having attained perfection in wisdom— they always surround you,
O Great Hero. Such are your well-trained disciples.”
Difficult to approach and of fierce splendor, they always surround you.
Surrounded by those disciplined ascetic disciples,
you shine like the fearless king of beasts, or like the lord of the stars.
“Established upon the earth, the plants that grow from the ground reach full maturity and display their fruit. You,
O Son of the Sakyas of great renown, are like the earth.”
Having established themselves in the Teaching, they obtain the fruit of the Deathless.
“The Sindhu and the Sarassatī, the Nandiyā and the Candabhāgā;
the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the Sarabhū and the Mahī.”
“As these rivers flow onward, the ocean receives them all;
they abandon their former names and are known simply as ‘the ocean.
Even so, these four classes of people, having gone forth into homelessness in your presence,”
They cast off their former names and are known as "Sons of the Buddha.
Just as the stainless moon, moving through the expanse of space,
outshines all the hosts of stars in the world with its radiance.
“Even so, O Great Hero, surrounded by gods and humans,
you alone shine forever, having transcended them all.
Just as waves arising from the deep do not overstep the shore,”
Just as all the waves reach the shore, only to be crushed and scattered,
so too do the many people of various views among the world’s sectarians,
though desiring to proclaim their own doctrines, never surpass that Sage.
“But if they do reach you, O Visionary One, repel them;
having come within your reach, they will be utterly crushed.
Just as many water-born lilies and mandārava flowers [are swept away] in the water...”
They are smeared with water and with mud and mire.
In the same way, many beings born in the world grow up in filth;
they are distressed by passion and hatred, like a white lotus in the mud.
“Just as a lotus born of water grows in the midst of water,
yet it is not smeared by the water, for its filaments are pure;
even so, O Great Hero, O Great Sage, you were born in the world.”
One does not stain the world, just as a lotus is not stained by water.
"Just as in the month of Ramman, many water-born flowers bloom;
they do not exceed that month, for it is the season for their blossoming."
“In just that way, O Great Hero, you are in full bloom through your liberation;
they do not overstep your teaching, just as the water-born lotus [is not submerged].
The king of sāl trees is in full bloom and wafts a divine fragrance.”
Surrounded by other *sāla* trees, he shines like the king of *sāla* trees.
"In just that way, O Great Hero, you, blossomed with the wisdom of a Buddha,
surrounded by the community of monks, shine like the king of *sāla* trees."
“Just as the Himavat mountain is the abode of all living beings,
of nāgas, asuras, and deities, and is like a healing herb for them;
even so are you, O Great Hero, like a healing herb for all living beings.”
Possessing the three true knowledges and the six direct insights, they have reached perfection in spiritual powers.
"Instructed by you, O Great Hero,
those compassionate ones delight in the joy of the Dhamma and dwell within your teaching."
“Just as the lion, king of beasts, having emerged from his lair,
surveys the four quarters and roars three times;
all the animals tremble with fear at the roar of the king of beasts.”
For thus it is: "This one who possesses birth always terrifies animals.
When you roar, O Great Hero, the earth trembles;
those capable of being awakened understand, and the hosts of Māra are terrified."
“All the sectarians tremble at the roaring of that Great Sage,
like a scattered flock of crows before a lion-king of beasts.
Whatever teachers are called ‘leaders of a group’ in the world— ”
“They teach the Dhamma handed down through tradition to the assembly.
But you, O Great Hero, do not teach the Dhamma to living beings in that way;
having yourself awakened to the Truths, you teach the entirety of the factors conducive to enlightenment.”
“Having known their underlying tendencies and latent dispositions, having understood the strength and weakness of their faculties,
and having discerned who is capable and who is incapable, you thunder like a great cloud.
Even if an assembly were seated as far as the limits of the world-system...”
To you who investigate various views in order to cut through doubt:
"Having understood the minds of all, the Sage, skilled in similes,
cuts away the doubts of living beings even while speaking a single question."
“Even if the earth were filled with beings exactly like Upatissa, and they all,
with palms joined in reverence, were to praise the Leader of the World—
praising him for an entire eon, they would praise him with various epithets.”
They would not be able to measure him; the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Just as the Victor has been praised by me according to my own power, even if they were to praise him for ten million eons, they would praise him in exactly this same way.
“Indeed, if any god or human, however well-trained,
were to attempt to deceive you, he would only meet with frustration.
Having established yourself in your teaching, O Sakyaputta of great renown!”
Having reached the perfection of wisdom, I dwell free from taints.
I crush the followers of other sects and maintain the teaching of the Conqueror;
today, as the General of the Dhamma, I stand within the dispensation of the Son of the Sakyans.
“Karma performed in immeasurable time has shown its fruit here to me;
like an arrow shot by Sukhitta, it has incinerated my defilements.
Whatever person might always carry a burden upon their head;”
“I was pained by a burden, likewise weighed down by many burdens.
Wandering through states of existence while burning with the three fires,
I was laden with the burden of becoming, like a mountain that has been uprooted.”
“The burden has been laid down by me; existence has been shattered by me;
everything that was to be done has been accomplished in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans.
As far as the field of the Buddhas extends, setting aside the Bull of the Sakyans...”
“I am supreme in wisdom; my equal is not to be found.
I am highly skilled in concentration and have reached the perfection of psychic power (iddhi).
If I wished, I could manifest a thousand [forms] this very day.”
“The Great Sage, having attained mastery over the successive dwellings, taught my instruction to me: ‘Cessation is my bed.
My divine eye is purified, and I am skilled in concentration.”
Devoted to the right efforts, delighting in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment:
"Whatever is to be attained by a disciple has all been accomplished by me;
with the exception of the Lord of the World, there is no one equal to me."

“Skilled in the meditative attainments, swiftly obtaining the jhānas and liberations, delighting in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, I have reached the perfection of the qualities of a disciple.
Even by the quality of a disciple, I am like Phussa; with wisdom, I am one who has cast off all burdens.”
That mind which is embraced by faith toward my fellow practitioners at all times—
like a snake whose venom has been extracted, like a bull whose horns have been broken,
and with pride and arrogance cast aside— I approach the community with profound reverence.
“If wisdom were to have a physical form, it would not equal even the earth in measure.
This is the fruit of the veneration of knowledge for the Blessed One Anomadassi.
The Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion by the Sakyan Son, the Imperturbable One.”
I have followed rightly; this is the fruit of praise for my knowledge.
"May I never, at any time, be one of evil desires, lazy, lacking in energy, of little learning, or of bad conduct, even when gathered with others."
“Learned and wise, well-composed in moral virtues,
devoted to mental tranquility— let him stand even upon the summit.
I say this to you, O venerable ones, all of you gathered here.”
“Be of few desires and contented, always meditative and delighting in jhāna.
He whom I first saw, by whom I became stainless and pure—
he was my wise teacher, the disciple named Assaji.”
“By virtue of that merit, today I have become the General of the Dhamma;
having reached perfection in every respect, I dwell free from taints.
He who was my teacher, the disciple named Assaji—”
"In whatever direction he dwells, I place him upon my head.
Remembering my deed, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas,
sat in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and established me in the foremost position."
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s instruction has been accomplished.

Later, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher, establishing his disciples as foremost among them for their various specific qualities, said: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples...”
“Of those with great wisdom, this is Sāriputta”—thus the Blessed One placed the Elder in the foremost position among those of great wisdom.
Having thus reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple and established himself in the office of General of the Dhamma, he worked for the welfare of beings.
One day, while explaining his own past conduct to his fellow celibates as a means of declaring his final knowledge (aññā), he said:
“Acting as he does, dwelling as he does, mindful, with intentions restrained, meditative, and heedful;
delighting in the internal, his self composed, alone and contented—he is called a bhikkhu.
Whether eating fresh food or dried, he should not be excessively full.”
With a small stomach and moderate food, let the mindful bhikkhu wander.
Having eaten only four or five morsels, he should drink water;
this is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute in himself.
“If that which is allowable covers him, this robe serves its purpose;
it is sufficient for a bhikkhu of resolute self to dwell in comfort.
When he sits cross-legged, the rain does not fall upon his knees.”
It is sufficient for the comfort and ease of a bhikkhu who is resolute:
“He who has seen pleasure as suffering, and has seen suffering as a dart,
and does not exist between these two— by what means could anything exist for him in the world?”
“May I never be one who has evil desires, lazy, and lacking in energy;
may I not be of little learning or disrespectful—by what [means] might I be anything at all in this world?
Being of great learning and wise, well-composed in moral virtues...”
“Let one devoted to mental tranquility stand even upon the crown of the head.
But the fool who is intent on conceptual proliferation, delighting in proliferation—
he has missed Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.”
“Whoever, having abandoned conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), delights in the path free from proliferation (*nippapañca*),
has attained Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Whether in a village or in the forest, whether in a low-lying place or on high ground;”
Wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful.
“Delightful are the forest retreats where people find no pleasure;
those free from passion will delight there, for they do not seek sensual desires.”
“One should associate with such a wise person, one who points out faults, who speaks with restraint, and who is discerning— just as one seeks the discoverer of hidden treasures.
For one who associates with such a person, it becomes better, not worse.”
“One should advise and instruct, and restrain one from what is unwholesome;
for such a person is dear to the virtuous, but is disliked by the wicked.
The Blessed One, the Buddha, the Visionary, taught the Dhamma to another.”
While the Dhamma was being taught, I applied my ear with intent;
thus my hearing has not been in vain, for I am liberated and free from taints.
Neither for the sake of recollecting past lives, nor for the divine eye—
In the supernormal power of reading others' minds, in the knowledge of death and rebirth,
and in the purification of the divine ear-element, I have no further aspiration.
"Like one who has taken refuge at the foot of a tree, shaven-headed and clad in the outer robe..."
The Elder Upatissa, supreme in wisdom, meditates thus:
“Having attained the state free from directed thought,
the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One is then endowed with noble silence.”
“Just as a rocky mountain, immovable and well-established, so too,
through the destruction of delusion, the bhikkhu does not tremble like a mountain.
For a person free from blemish, who always seeks purity— ”
Even a hair’s tip of evil appears as large as a cloud.
“I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;
I shall cast off this body, mindful and clearly comprehending.”
“I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;
I await my time like a servant awaiting his wages.
For both [paths], this is indeed death—whether later or sooner.”
Practice [the path]; do not perish; let not the opportune moment pass you by.
Just as a frontier city is guarded both within and without, so should you guard yourselves;
let not the opportune moment pass you by.
For those who have let the opportune moment pass grieve when they are cast into hell.
One who is peaceful, restrained, measured in speech,
and unagitated shakes off evil states like the wind shakes leaves from a tree.
“Peaceful, restrained, measured in speech, and unagitated;
he has cast off evil states like the wind sheds a leaf from a tree.
Peaceful, free from distress, serene and undisturbed.”
One of virtuous character and wise shall be a maker of an end to suffering.
"One should not place trust in certain individuals, whether they be householders or those who have gone forth;
for having been good, they become bad, and having been bad, they become good again."
“Sensual desire and ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and doubt— these five are stains upon the mind of a bhikkhu.
For one who is being honored, or for one who is not honored— both cases alike— ”
The concentration of one who dwells in heedfulness does not waver.
Of that meditator who is constant, who perceives with subtle vision,
and who delights in the destruction of clinging, they say, "He is a true person."
“The great ocean, the earth, the mountain, and even the wind—
these do not serve as adequate similes for the Teacher’s excellent liberation.
The Elder who follows the Wheel, possessed of great wisdom and concentrated in mind,”
Treating the earth like fire, he is neither attached nor repelled.
Having reached the perfection of wisdom, possessing great intelligence and great discernment, though not dull-witted, he appears as if dull-witted;
ever extinguished, he moves about.
“I have served the Teacher... [as before] ...the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
‘Accomplish [your goal] through diligence; this is my instruction.
Now I shall attain final Nibbāna; I am utterly liberated from everything.’”

He spoke these verses. For some of these verses were spoken by the Elder, while others were spoken by the Blessed One concerning the Elder; yet because they were all subsequently spoken by the Elder himself as a proclamation of his own conduct, they became the Elder’s own verses.
In this context, *yathācārī* means one who, having become restrained and self-controlled, conducts himself or dwells according to [his practice];

or, *yathācārī* means one whose character is such that he conducts himself accordingly—the meaning is "one perfected in virtue" (*sīlasampanna*). *Yathāsato* means "as he truly is. The nasal vowel has been elided for the sake of the meter of the verse.

Having done so, the exposition is made; the meaning is that he is indistinguishable from the Noble Ones (*ariya*), as if he were one who is truly peaceful. "Possessed of mindfulness" means endowed with supreme mindfulness.

"One who meditates with restrained intention" means having abandoned all wrong intentions (*micchā-saṅkappa*) and, being one whose intentions are restrained through renunciation-intention (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) and so forth, he is by nature one who meditates through both meditation upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and meditation upon characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). "Diligent" means...
In that very state of conduct, being one whose intention is resolute, through meditation he is free from negligence and possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension well-established in all respects.
"Delighting in the internal" means he delights in the cultivation of the meditation subject within the internal field of activity.

"With mind concentrated" means his mind is one-pointed by means of that very cultivation. "Alone" means without a companion, avoiding both association with crowds and association with the defilements.

Having abandoned seclusion of body and cultivating seclusion of mind, he is "contented" (*santusita*), being rightly satisfied and pleased through contentment with requisites and contentment with delighting in meditation.
For from meditation that brings about ever-increasing distinction, a sublime rapture and joy arise;
but when it has reached its peak, there is nothing further to be said. Of this they say:

Regarding the term *bhikkhunī*: they call such a person a *bhikkhu* because of their looking with fear at the non-fulfillment of the three trainings, and because of their having shattered the defilements (*bhinnakilesatā*).
Now, showing first the contentment regarding requisites (*paccayasantosa*) among the two kinds of contentment already mentioned, he says: "Whether wet or dry," and so forth.
In this context, *alla* means moist and oily due to being mixed with ghee and other liquids; *sukkha* means coarse because of the absence of such [moisture].
The word *vā* has the sense of non-restriction, meaning "either moist or dry. *Bāḷha* means excessively. *Suhito na siyā* means one should not be well-fed or satiated.
To the question, "How then should one be? he says: "With a small stomach and moderate food," whether the meal be choice or coarse.
While eating, a bhikkhu, having eaten as much as he needs, should dwell wandering about mindful, being moderate in his belly and light in his stomach,
and thus moderate in food and limited in his meals, consuming food endowed with the eight factors through moderation therein and with mindfulness of reflection.
To show how one becomes "thin-waisted" and "moderate in food," the passage beginning with "four" was spoken.
Therein, "without having eaten" means that without consuming four or five mouthfuls (ālopa-kabaḷa), one should drink water after leaving room for that much food;
for this is living very lightly on food. Indeed, for one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna...
The meaning is: "It is sufficient for the comfort of a bhikkhu, for the attainment of jhāna and so forth, and for dwelling in happiness.
By this, while speaking of almsfood that merely sustains the belly, he demonstrates contentment with whatever is obtained in the matter of almsfood.
Alternatively, there is the reading "bhutvāna" (having eaten); this refers to one who is capable of sustaining the body even with food consisting of only four or five mouthfuls.
This may have been stated with reference to a person of an exceedingly stable character;
it is indeed consistent with the subsequent verses as well, because of the fact that only a small amount of robe-cloth and bedding will be mentioned.
"Suitable" (kappiya) means any one among the items such as linen (*khoma*) and so forth, which are suitable or conformable to what is suitable. "If that covers [the body]"—
If it covers the place that ought to be covered while being a permissible robe (*kappiya-cīvara*), the meaning is:
provided it is of a type permitted by the Teacher and possesses, at the very least, the dimensions permitted [by him]. "This is for the purpose" means:

for the sake of a specific purpose stated by the Teacher as its purpose—that is, solely for the purpose of warding off cold and so forth, and for the purpose of concealing the private parts out of a sense of shame (*hirī*).
This refers to the robe that serves as a protection for the body and to contentment with whatever is available.
"Of one sitting cross-legged" (*pallaṅkena nisinnassa*): "cross-legged" (*pallaṅka*) means a seat bound around the thighs on all sides;

"of one sitting" by that means "of one sitting having folded the legs into a three-jointed cross-legged posture"—this is the meaning. "The rain does not fall upon the knees" (*jaṇṇuke nābhivassati*) refers to whichever hut...
While sitting there in such a way, even when it rains, his two knees are not soaked by the rainwater; this much alone constitutes a complete and excellent lodging.
Indeed, a clansman who desires his own welfare can accomplish his goal while sitting there. Therefore, he said:
"It is sufficient for a bhikkhu of resolute mind to dwell in comfort."

Thus, having proclaimed through these four verses the instruction on effacement (*sallekha*) in its highest excellence for those monks who were of great desire and discontented, the Elder now spoke the verse beginning with "He who [knows] pleasure," etc., showing contentment in the delight of meditation by way of feeling (*vedanā*).

Therein, "pleasure" means pleasant feeling. "From suffering" means from the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-dukkha*). "Adda" means he saw, by means of wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
The meaning is: "he who saw [it] as it really is through the wisdom of the path.

For even though a pleasant feeling is enjoyed at the time of its experience, like food mixed with poison, it becomes nothing but suffering at the time of its transformation. Therefore, this demonstrates the contemplation of suffering therein.
"He saw suffering as a dart" means that he saw the painful feeling as a dart. Painful feeling...

For just as a dart, whether it is entering the body, having already entered and remaining there, or being extracted, produces only affliction, so too [feeling] afflicts even while arising, while established, and while dissolving.
By this, he speaks here extolling the contemplation of suffering itself; and by that, because of the statement, "That which is suffering is not-self."
He dispels the grasping for a self or what belongs to a self regarding the two types of feeling. "Between the two" means between those two;

the meaning is that which exists in the middle of pleasant and painful feelings, namely, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. "It was not" refers to the absence of the insistence on a self or what belongs to a self through the realization of things as they truly are.
Having thus fully understood even the five aggregates of clinging by way of feeling, [one realizes]: "By what means could there be anything in the world?"
Having completely severed the entire web of defilements bound to that [body], by what defilement indeed would he be bound in the world?
What future state could there be for him among gods and others? The intention is that he is simply one whose bonds are cut and who is beyond description.
Now, censuring the person who practices wrongly and praising the one who practices rightly, [the Blessed One] says, beginning with "Mā me... (May not...).
He spoke four verses. Therein, "May I never be one of evil desires" refers to one who is of evil desires because of the longing to be esteemed for qualities he does not possess;
who is indolent due to a lack of enthusiasm for the ascetic’s duty (samaṇadhamma); and for that very reason, of inferior energy;

who is of little learning due to the absence of hearing the teachings connected with truth, dependent origination, and so forth; and who is disrespectful due to a lack of reverence toward exhortations and instructions—such a person is an exceedingly base individual.
"May such a person never be in my presence. Why? Because by what instruction, or by doing what, could anything be achieved for that kind of individual within this world, among the classes of beings?
The meaning is that it would be entirely useless."
And "one who is learned" (*bahussuta*) is a person who, by virtue of possessing much learning consisting of the Suttas,

Geyyas, and so forth, connected with virtue (*sīla*) and the rest, is wise (*medhāvī*) through the wisdom of the essence of the Dhamma (*dhamma-oja*), the functional wisdom (*pārihārika-paññā*), and the wisdom of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññā*);
and because he is well-established in the precepts (*sīla*), he is well-concentrated (*susamāhita*), [possessing] mental tranquility (*cetosamatha*) distinguished as mundane and supramundane.
One who is devoted to the concentration of the mind—such a person may stand even upon my head, let alone live in my company.

But as for the person "devoted to conceptual proliferation" (*papañca*): this refers to a person who, through delighting in kamma and so forth, and through attachment to forms and so forth, is devoted to *papañca*—which consists of craving and its divisions—in the sense of the proliferating activity of the process; and who, moreover, fails to see the danger therein.
One who delights in the path is like a traveler on a road; he has missed out on Nibbāna and stands very far, indeed, from Nibbāna.

But as for the person who, having abandoned *papañca*—that is, having abandoned the *papañca* of craving—delights in the Noble Path, which is the means for attaining the state free from *papañca* (the *nippapañca* of Nibbāna), and who delights in its cultivation and realization, he [attains] Nibbāna.
"Ārādhayi" means he accomplished and attained.

Then one day, the Elder, seeing that his own younger brother, the Elder Revata, was living in a waterless wilderness thick with thorny khadira trees, spoke the two verses beginning with "In a village... while praising him. Therein:
"In the village": although Arahants do not obtain physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) in a village, they certainly obtain mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*).
For even objects resembling those of the divine realms cannot disturb their minds;
therefore, whether it be in a village or in any other place such as the forest, wherever Arahants dwell, that region of ground is "delightful"—that is, that specific locality.
The meaning is "truly delightful.
The connection is that the forests—adorned with groves of trees in full bloom and endowed with pure reservoirs of water—are delightful.
"In which" means in those forests which, as if blossoming, provide delight; therein, one who belongs to the side of sensual pleasure and seeks sensual pleasures [dwells].
"Ordinary people do not find delight there. But those who are free from passion—those whose taints are destroyed—will find delight in such forest retreats, just as bees do in lotus groves.
"They do not seek sensual pleasures": the meaning is that because they are free from passion, they are not seekers of sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, out of compassion for a poor brahmin named Rādha, the Elder ordained him and granted him full admission (upasampadā). To him...

While wandering about with him acting as his attendant monk, the Teacher, being pleased one day by the latter’s tractable nature, spoke the verse beginning with "As of treasures" while giving him exhortation.
In that context, "of treasures" refers to jars of treasure filled with gold, silver, and so forth, which have been deposited and stored here and there.
"A distributor" refers to a person in a state of misery who finds it difficult to make a living.

It is like one who, out of compassion, says, "Come, I will show you a means by which you may live in comfort," and having led him to the location of a hidden treasure, extends his hand and points it out, saying, "Take this and live happily. Regarding "one who sees faults":
there are two kinds of those who see faults—the one who seeks a flaw, thinking, "I will restrain him in the midst of the Saṅgha for this unseemly conduct or this lapse"; and [the other].

Furthermore, one who desires to make known what is not yet known, who relishes what is already known, and who, out of a desire for the growth of virtue and so forth, examines various faults while being established in a nature of uplifting—
this is the one intended here. For just as a man in distress,
even when being pressured with the words "Take this treasure," does not become angry at the pointing out of the treasure but remains joyful, so too...
When seeing something unbecoming or a lapse in such persons, one should not become angry;
rather, one should remain with a joyful mind and even invite them, saying, "Venerable sir, please tell me again when I am like this.
One who speaks reprovingly is one who, upon seeing a fault, does not consider, "This is my co-resident, my pupil, or my benefactor," but instead speaks in accordance with that fault.
One who restrains, sends away, and administers disciplinary measures while training is called a "reprover," just like the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For this has been said: "Restraining again and again, Ānanda, I shall speak; driving out again and again, Ānanda, I shall speak.
That which is the essence will remain. "Wise" means endowed with the wisdom of the Dhamma-fuel. "Such a one" [refers to one]...
"One such as this is a wise person. "One should associate with" means one should attend upon him. For a resident pupil who associates with such a teacher, it is better and not worse;
there is only progress, not decline—this is the meaning.
Then, on one occasion, when the dwellings at Kīṭāgiri had been defiled by Assaji and Punabbasuka, the Teacher commanded his own retinue:
Having gone there together with Mahāmoggallāna, the General of the Dhamma spoke this verse when Assaji and Punabbasuka would not accept his exhortation.
Therein, "ovadeyya" means he should give exhortation or instruction; "anusāseyya" is a synonym for that same thing.
Alternatively, one is said to "exhort" (ovadati) when speaking regarding a matter that has already arisen, whereas... [regarding a matter not yet arisen]...
When one speaks regarding the future, saying, “It may even be iron for you,” and so forth, one is said to *instruct* (*anusāsati*).
Speaking in the presence [of the person] is called *exhorting* (*ovadati*), while speaking by sending a messenger or a message when they are absent is called *instructing*.
Speaking once is called *exhorting*, while speaking repeatedly is called *instructing*. And the phrase “unrefined” (*asabbhā*) means unwholesome (*akusala*).
The meaning is: "one should restrain unwholesome states and establish one in wholesome states.

For such a person is dear to the virtuous; however, for those who are non-existent, who are not true men, who have disregarded the world beyond, whose eyes are fixed on material gain, and who have gone forth merely for the sake of a livelihood—he is their instructor and admonisher, [saying]: "You are not our preceptor, nor..."
"Teacher, why do you speak to us?"—thus one becomes disliked by those who pierce with the arrows of their words.

When a discussion arose among the monks, "Only he for whom the Teacher teaches the Dhamma is one endowed with the necessary support (upanissaya)," [the Buddha], showing that this was not so, spoke the verse beginning with "Of another. In that context, "of another" refers to himself.
This was said with reference to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha.

For while the Teacher was teaching the *Vedanāpariggaha-sutta*, this Great Elder attained the path of meditation and reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).
"He opened his ear to the summit": standing fanning the Teacher, he became intent and, desiring to hear, he opened his ear.
“Hearing that was not in vain for me”: thus, that hearing which I heard in such a manner became fruitful and not barren for me;
it became the support for the attainments to be reached by a chief disciple. Therefore he said, “I am liberated,” and so forth.
In that context, “neither for the sake of recollecting past lives” means there was no aspiration for the knowledge that knows one’s own and others’ past lives.

The construction is: "it does not exist for me. By way of performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*), even a mere mental aspiration for that purpose neither exists nor has it existed—this is the meaning.

"Of the penetration of minds" (*cetopariyāya*) means of the knowledge of the penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*). "Of psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) means of the knowledge of the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*).

"Of passing away and rebirth" (*cutiyā upapattiyā*) means for the sake of the knowledge of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapātañāṇa*), which is the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

"By the purification of the ear-element" means by means of the knowledge of the divine ear. "I have no aspiration" means that I have no aspiration or mental application of the mind toward these specific higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) as a preliminary exercise; the meaning is that such an aspiration did not exist for me.
For just as the qualities of omniscience belong to the Buddhas, all the qualities of disciples come into the hands of disciples only through the attainment of the supreme path.
These [qualities] exist; there is no need for them to perform a separate preparatory exercise (*parikamma*) for their attainment.

The three verses beginning with "At the foot of a tree" were spoken while he was dwelling in the Kapotakandara cave, at a time when he was struck by a *yakkha*, in order to demonstrate his own state of being unperturbed through the power of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
In that context, "shaven-headed" (*muṇḍa*) does not mean one whose hair has been cut off.
“Clad in the outer robe” (*saṅghāṭipāruta*) means sitting after having put on the *saṅghāṭi*. Some also read: “well-clad in the *saṅghāṭi*.
“The elder supreme in wisdom” means that having become an elder, he is supreme in wisdom; the meaning is that he is the best among disciples in wisdom.

“He meditates” (*jhāyati*) means he meditates by means of contemplation upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and contemplation upon characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*); the meaning is that he dwells frequently in the state of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

"He is possessed of it so long" means that when he was struck on the head by the *yakkha*, at that very moment he entered the fruit-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) of the fourth jhāna, which is free from applied thought (*avitakka*), and was thus possessed of and endowed with noble silence. For the word "is" (*hoti*) here is used in the present tense to express a past state.

"He does not tremble like a mountain": a bhikkhu whose all defilements have been shattered through the destruction of delusion is like a mountain made of rock; he is immovable and well-established, and does not tremble before anything such as the desirable and so forth—the meaning is that he remains unshaken in every circumstance.
Then one day, while the Elder was absent-minded and the corner of his lower robe was hanging down, a certain novice said, "Venerable Sir, the lower robe should be worn evenly all around.
Hearing this, as if receiving it with his head, saying, "It is well said by you,
my good man," he stepped back a short distance at once, adjusted his lower robe so that it was even all around, and [said], "For those like me..."
Showing that "this too is indeed a fault," he spoke the verse beginning with "Of one who is stainless" (*anaṅgaṇassa*).
Then, demonstrating his own equanimity toward both death and life, he spoke two verses beginning with "I do not rejoice" (*nābhinandāmi*).
Subsequently, while preaching the Dhamma to others, he spoke two verses beginning with "By both of these" (*ubhayena midaṃ*). Therein, "by both" means:
"In both" means "at both times. The letter *m* in *midanti* is a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*).
This is indeed death; there is such a thing as death, and no such thing as non-death. To the question "At which two times?", he says:
"Either later or earlier"—that is, death is simply death, whether it occurs later in middle age at the time of being worn out by old age, or earlier in youth.
It is exclusively so. Therefore, practice the right way; fulfill the right practice; do not perish by practicing wrongly;
do not experience the great suffering in the states of misery. "Do not let the opportune moment pass you by" means: may this ninth moment, which is free from the eight non-moments, not elude you.
Then one day, seeing the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika and proclaiming his virtues, he spoke three verses beginning with “Peaceful.

Therein, having already stated the meaning by way of general description as “he shakes off,” he now speaks the verse beginning with “He has shaken off” (*appāsī*) in relation specifically to the Elder.
In that context, *appāsī* means “he has just now shaken off. *Anāyāso*...

"Unassailable" means being free from the suffering of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Serene and untroubled" means that because of the absence of lack of faith and so forth, his mind is perfectly serene, and because of the state of having untroubled intentions, he is untroubled.
The verse beginning with "One should not trust" refers to the sons of the Vajjis who remained there after placing their trust in Devadatta and finding pleasure in his view.
[These words] were spoken with reference [to this]. In that context, "one should not place trust" means one should not be over-familiar, nor should one believe; such is the meaning.
"Among some" means among certain worldlings (*puthujjana*) whose essential nature is unstable.
"In this way" means just as you placed your trust, thinking, "Devadatta is practicing rightly. "Among householders" means among laypeople. "Even though they have been good" means...
Because the state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is unstable— like a gourd placed on the back of a donkey or like a wooden stake driven into a heap of chaff—
therefore some who were initially good and remained so later become bad.
Just as Devadatta was formerly endowed with virtue and attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), yet later became obsessed by gain and honor.
Now, having lost his excellence, he has become one bound for the states of misery, like a crow with its wings clipped.

Therefore, such a person should not be trusted as "good" merely upon first sight. However, some who were initially not good due to a lack of association with virtuous friends later indeed become good through association with the virtuous;
therefore, regarding those like Devadatta, who are counterfeits of the good, [one should not trust them] as "good."
The meaning is: "one should not place trust.

Having stated the verse beginning with "Sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) to show that those in whom the mental defilements (*cittupakkilesa*), such as sensual desire and the rest, have not departed are unwholesome (*asādhu*), while those in whom they have departed are wholesome (*sādhu*), [the author] now states [the following] to show the characteristic of a truly good person (*sādhulakkhaṇa*) as it reaches its highest excellence through its unique qualities.
The two verses beginning with “yassa sakkariyamānassa” were spoken [first].

Then, in order to demonstrate that [state] as having reached its highest excellence in an uncommon way, the Teacher spoke the verses beginning with “mahāsamuddo,” illustrating both himself and others.
Therein, “mahāsamuddo” refers to this great ocean; “mahāpathavī” is the great earth; “selo pabbato” is a rocky mountain; and from the divisions such as the eastern direction...
And the wind endures what is desirable and undesirable by virtue of its own insentience, not through the power of reflection;
but as for that supreme state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) in which the Teacher stands— having attained Arahantship, being equal toward all things such as the desirable and remaining unshaken—
it is for the sake of that excellent liberation of the Teacher, the liberation of the fruit of the highest attainment, that these great oceans and so forth serve as similes.
The meaning is that they do not match even by way of comparison; they do not approach it even by a fraction.

"A follower of the wheel" means one who follows the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Teacher. "An Elder" (thera) means one who is an elder by virtue of possessing the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those beyond training (asekha).
"One of great knowledge" (mahāñāṇī) means one of great wisdom. "Concentrated" (samāhita) means [concentrated] by means of access concentration and absorption concentration.

And he was composed through supreme concentration. “Equal to earth, water, fire, and air” means that in the encounter with desirable and other objects, by virtue of his lack of perturbation, his mode of being is similar to that of earth, water, fire, and air. Therefore it is said: “He is neither delighted nor offended.

“Attained the perfection of wisdom” means having reached the limit, the furthest boundary, of disciple-knowledge. “Of great intelligence” means having attained the state of being vast, broad, swift, sharp, and penetrative.

He is endowed with great intelligence and wisdom (*mahatiyā buddhiyā paññāya*). "Great-minded" (*mahāmāti*) means he is endowed with a great grasp of method (*nayaggāha*) known as the discernment of the underlying principles of phenomena (*dhammanvaya*).

For he has attained, in their entirety and without exception, all those classifications of wisdom—whether fourfold, sixteenfold, forty-fourfold, or seventy-sevenfold; it is because of this that he possesses great wisdom (*mahāpaññatā*).
Moreover, by virtue of his divine qualities, this Great Elder deserves to be called preeminently "of great intelligence.
As the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is wise; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has great wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has broad wisdom;
bhikkhus, Sāriputta has joyous wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has swift wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has sharp wisdom..."

“Monks, Sāriputta is wise; monks, Sāriputta possesses penetrative wisdom,” and so forth. Herein, this is the exposition of the distinctions among the states of being wise and so on. One is “wise” by virtue of these four reasons:

skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*), skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*), skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*).
This is the textual passage for showing the distinctions among such qualities as “great wisdom” and so on:
“What is great wisdom? It is called ‘great wisdom’ because it grasps great meanings; it is called ‘great wisdom’ because it grasps great phenomena (dhammas);
it is called ‘great wisdom’ because it grasps great linguistic expressions (niruttiyo); it is called ‘great wisdom’ because it grasps great inspired insights (paṭibhānāni);
it is called ‘great wisdom’ because it grasps the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha); [it is called ‘great wisdom’] because it grasps the great aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).”
She is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great aggregate of wisdom; she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great aggregate of liberation;
she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;

she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great [distinctions between] the possible and the impossible; she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great meditative abidings and attainments.
