She is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps [the truths]; she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great Noble Truths;
she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great foundations of mindfulness; she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great right efforts;
she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great bases of psychic power; she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great faculties.
She is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps great powers; she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great factors of enlightenment;
she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great Noble Path; she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great fruits of recluseship;
she is called "of great wisdom" because she grasps the great direct knowledges; [she is called "of great wisdom"] because she grasps the great ultimate goal, Nibbāna.
She grasps [it]—thus she is one of great wisdom. What is wide wisdom?
Knowledge proceeds with respect to various and diverse aggregates; thus it is wide wisdom. Knowledge proceeds with respect to various and diverse elements;
thus it is wide wisdom. Knowledge proceeds with respect to various and diverse bases; thus it is wide wisdom. Knowledge proceeds with respect to various and diverse dependent originations...
Knowledge proceeds, thus it is "vast wisdom" (*puthupaññā*); knowledge proceeds regarding various and diverse emptinesses and non-apprehensions, thus it is "vast wisdom";
knowledge proceeds regarding various and diverse meanings, thus it is "vast wisdom"; knowledge proceeds regarding various and diverse phenomena, thus it is "vast wisdom";
knowledge proceeds regarding various and diverse etymologies, thus it is "vast wisdom"; [knowledge proceeds] regarding various and diverse ingenuities...
Knowledge occurs, thus it is wide wisdom; knowledge occurs regarding the various and diverse aggregates of virtue, thus it is wide wisdom;

knowledge occurs regarding the various and diverse aggregates of concentration, thus it is wide wisdom; knowledge occurs regarding the various and diverse aggregates of wisdom, thus it is wide wisdom;
knowledge occurs regarding the various and diverse aggregates of liberation, thus it is wide wisdom.
Wisdom that operates regarding the various and diverse aggregates of the knowledge and vision of liberation is "wide wisdom" (puthupaññā);
wisdom that operates regarding various and diverse points and non-points is "wide wisdom"; wisdom that operates regarding various and diverse abidings and attainments is "wide wisdom";
wisdom that operates regarding the various and diverse noble truths is "wide wisdom"; wisdom regarding the various and diverse foundations of mindfulness is... [wide wisdom].

It occurs widely, thus it is wide wisdom; knowledge occurs regarding the various and manifold right efforts, thus it is wide wisdom; knowledge occurs regarding the various and manifold bases of psychic power, thus it is wide wisdom;
knowledge occurs regarding the various and manifold faculties, thus it is wide wisdom; knowledge occurs regarding the various and manifold powers, thus it is wide wisdom;
knowledge occurs regarding the various and manifold factors of enlightenment, thus it is wide wisdom.
Wisdom that operates regarding the various and diverse noble paths is "wide wisdom" (puthupaññā);
wisdom that operates regarding the various and diverse fruits of recluseship is "wide wisdom"; wisdom that operates regarding the various and diverse direct knowledges (abhiññā) is "wide wisdom";
and wisdom that operates regarding the ultimate truth of Nibbāna, having transcended the states shared by worldlings (puthujjana), is "wide wisdom."
“What is wisdom accompanied by joy (*hāsapaññā*)? Here, someone who is full of joy, full of rapture, full of contentment, and full of gladness fulfills the precepts;
thus it is wisdom accompanied by joy. Being full of joy... [and so on] ...being full of gladness, one fulfills restraint of the sense faculties;
thus it is wisdom accompanied by joy. Being full of joy... [and so on] ...being full of gladness, one fulfills moderation in eating; thus it is wisdom accompanied by joy.”
"One who abounds in laughter... [and] abounds in gladness fulfills the practice of wakefulness; this is 'laughter-wisdom' (hāsapaññā). One who abounds in laughter...

[and] abounds in gladness fulfills the aggregate of virtue... [and] the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation... [and so on]... penetrates them. One fulfills the dwellings and attainments."
To penetrate the noble truths; to develop the foundations of mindfulness; to develop the right efforts; to develop the bases of psychic power;
to develop the faculties; to develop the powers; to develop the factors of enlightenment; to develop the noble path...
[and so on] ...to realize the fruits of recluseship—this is wisdom of laughter. One who abounds in laughter, abounds in joy, and abounds in contentment.
Wisdom of laughter (*hāsapannā*) is that by which one who is abundant in gladness (*pāmojja*) penetrates the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Wisdom of laughter is that by which one who is abundant in joy, abundant in rapture, abundant in contentment, and abundant in gladness realizes the ultimate goal, Nibbāna.
“What is wisdom of speed (*javanapannā*)? Whatever form there is—past, future, or present... [as before] ...whether far or near...”
Or, the wisdom that swiftly impels [the mind] toward all form as impermanent is "impelling wisdom" (javanapaññā);
the wisdom that swiftly impels toward it as suffering is "impelling wisdom"; the wisdom that swiftly impels toward it as non-self is "impelling wisdom. Whatever feeling there may be... and so on ...
whatever consciousness there may be—past, future, or present... and so on ... the wisdom that swiftly impels toward all consciousness as impermanent is "impelling wisdom."
It swiftly impels [the mind] toward suffering: this is impulsive wisdom. It swiftly impels [the mind] toward non-self: this is impulsive wisdom. Regarding the eye... and so on...
up to aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, it swiftly impels [the mind] toward impermanence:
this is impulsive wisdom; it swiftly impels [the mind] toward suffering: this is impulsive wisdom; it swiftly impels [the mind] toward non-self: this is impulsive wisdom.

“Having weighed, scrutinized, and analyzed form—past, future, and present—as impermanent in the sense of destruction, as suffering in the sense of terror, and as non-self in the sense of corelessness;
having made it manifest, one swiftly courses toward the cessation of form, which is Nibbāna: this is ‘swift wisdom’ (javanapaññā).
… [The same applies to] feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness … the eye … [and so on] … up to aging-and-death—past, future, and present.”

Having weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that "the impermanent is in the sense of destruction, the painful is in the sense of terror, and the non-self is in the sense of corelessness," one swiftly speeds toward Nibbāna, the cessation of aging and death; thus it is "speeding wisdom" (*javanapaññā*).
"Form—past, future, or present—is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, and subject to destruction."
Having weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that [form] is subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, one swiftly impels toward the cessation of form;
thus it is "impelling wisdom" (*javanapaññā*). Feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness... the eye...
and so on, up to... aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.

Having weighed, scrutinized, discerned, and made manifest that [all things] are subject to decay, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, one swiftly speeds toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death; this is "swift wisdom" (javanapaññā).
What is "sharp wisdom" (tikkhapaññā)? It is sharp wisdom because it swiftly cuts off defilements; for example, when a thought of sensual desire has arisen...
One does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes to vanish [an arisen thought of ill will]; thus one has sharp wisdom.
One does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes to vanish an arisen thought of ill will; thus one has sharp wisdom.
One does not tolerate an arisen thought of cruelty... and so on... one does not tolerate whatever evil, unwholesome states arise.
She abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes to cease [unwholesome states]; thus she is one of sharp wisdom. She does not tolerate arisen lust;
she abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease; thus she is one of sharp wisdom. [Likewise] arisen hatred...
arisen delusion... arisen anger... arisen resentment... slander... spite... envy... and avarice.

She does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and eliminates deceit... guile... obstinacy... hostility... conceit... arrogance... intoxication... negligence... all defilements... all misconduct... all volitional formations...
[and so on] ...all kamma leading to existence; thus she is one of sharp wisdom. In a single sitting, she attains the four noble paths.
The four fruits of asceticism, the four analytical knowledges, and the six direct knowledges have been attained, realized, touched, and verified by wisdom—this is sharp wisdom.
What is penetrative wisdom? Here, someone is full of urgency and full of trepidation toward all conditioned phenomena.
Abounding in longing, abounding in discontent, and abounding in lack of delight, one who looks outward finds no pleasure in all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
Because it pierces and shatters the mass of greed never before pierced or shattered, it is "penetrating wisdom" (*nibbedhika-paññā*);
because it pierces and shatters the mass of hatred never before pierced or shattered, it is "penetrating wisdom."
“Penetrating wisdom is so called because it penetrates and shatters the mass of delusion never before penetrated and never before shattered;
it penetrates and shatters anger… [and so on] … resentment… [and so on] … all kamma leading to existence that has never before been penetrated and never before shattered.”
Thus, because he was endowed with great wisdom (paññā) according to the divisions as described above, he is called "one of great intelligence" (mahābuddhi).
Furthermore, this elder’s possession of great wisdom should also be understood by way of his insight into phenomena according to their sequence (anupadadhammavipassanā). For it has been said:
"Monks, Sāriputta practiced insight into phenomena according to their sequence for half a month. This, monks, was Sāriputta’s practice of insight into phenomena according to their sequence."
“Here, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures... Sāriputta enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
And as for those states in the first jhāna—namely, applied thought... and one-pointedness of mind;
contact, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—these states are defined by him one by one in successive order.”
Those phenomena arise for him known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
He understands thus: "Indeed, in this way my phenomena come into being having not been, and having been, they vanish.
Toward those phenomena, he is without approach, without departure, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated from that which is delimited by the sphere of perception.
He dwells with his mind [thus]. He understands: "There is a further escape. Through frequent practice of that, it truly exists for him.
"Furthermore, monks, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought... [Sāriputta] enters and dwells in the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna.
[He enters and dwells in] the base of infinite space... the base of infinite consciousness..."
The base of nothingness... having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Mindful, he emerges from that attainment;
having emerged from that attainment with mindfulness, he contemplates those states which are past, ceased, and changed, thinking: "Thus indeed were my states..."
“They come into being without having been sacrificed, and having been sacrificed, they pass away.

Toward these phenomena, he dwells without approach, without departure, unattached, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries. He understands: “There is a further escape.
Through frequent cultivation of this, there is indeed for him the state of its existence.

“Furthermore, monks, Sāriputta, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
Mindful, he emerges from that attainment; having emerged from that attainment, being mindful, he reflects upon it.”
Regarding those phenomena that have passed away, ceased, and changed, he contemplates them thus: "Indeed, these phenomena of mine, having not been, come to be;

having been, they vanish. Toward those phenomena, he dwells without approach, without departure, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind for which no boundary has been set. He thinks: "There is no further escape beyond this."
He understands it. Through frequent practice of that, there comes to be for him the realization of non-existence.
"Monks, if one were speaking rightly, one might say of him: 'He has reached mastery, he has reached perfection in noble virtue;
he has reached mastery, he has reached perfection in noble concentration; he has reached mastery, he has reached perfection in..."
“‘One who has attained mastery and reached perfection in noble wisdom and noble liberation’—
it is of Sāriputta alone that one could rightly say this.
Thus, because he was endowed with such great intelligence, which had attained the state of vastness, breadth, speed, swiftness, and penetrative sharpness.
"Thera" means one of great intelligence. His realization of the underlying principles of the Dhamma (*dhammanvaya*) should be illustrated by the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*;
for in that sutta, the Elder’s grasp of the method is said to be equal to the knowledge of omniscience.

"Not dull, yet appearing as if dull" means that while he was in every respect not dull due to having reached the pinnacle of wisdom among disciples, he made himself appear as if ignorant through his supreme fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*).

Having acted thus, he always moves—that is, he constantly dwells—like one dull in vision, resembling a fool, yet extinguished and cooled due to the absence of the fever of the defilements (kilesa-pariḷāha).
The verse beginning with "Pariciṇṇo" was spoken by the Elder while manifesting that his own task was accomplished; its meaning is exactly as stated above.

"Exert yourselves without negligence"—this, moreover, was spoken by way of giving exhortation to the monks who had assembled at the time of his own final Nibbāna. Its meaning is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāriputta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ānanda.
The verses beginning with "By backbiting and by anger" are those of the Venerable Ānanda Thera. What is their origin?
This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara as the half-brother of the Teacher;
his name was Sumanas. His father, however, was named King Ānanda. To his own son...
When Prince Sumanakumāra reached maturity, the King gave him the city of Bhoganagara, located two hundred yojanas from Haṃsavatī.

From time to time, he would come and see both himself and his father. At that time, the King personally and respectfully attended upon the Teacher and the Saṅgha of one hundred thousand bhikkhus; he did not allow others to attend to them.
At that time, the border regions were in revolt. Without reporting the state of the revolt to the king, the prince himself pacified it.
Hearing of this, the king was delighted in heart; he summoned his son and said, "My dear son, I grant you a boon;
choose a boon. The prince replied, "I wish to live for three months while attending upon the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
"I wish to make it fruitful," he said. "That cannot be done; ask for something else. "Your Majesty, there are no two kinds of talk among the kṣatriyas;
give me this very thing, for I have no need for anything else. "If the Teacher permits it, it shall be given.
He went to the monastery, thinking, "I will know the Teacher's mind."
At that time, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, had entered the fragrant chamber.
[The man] approached the monks and said, "Venerable sirs, I have come to see the Blessed One; please show me the Blessed One.
The monks said, "There is an elder named Sumana who is the Teacher's attendant; go to him."
So he went into the presence of the Elder, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, please show me the Teacher.
Then the Elder, even as the prince was looking on, sank into the earth and approached the Teacher.
He said, "Venerable sir, the prince has come to see you. "In that case, bhikkhu, prepare a seat outside," [the Teacher replied].

The Elder, while the youth was still watching, took the Buddha’s seat, vanished within the Fragrant Chamber, appeared outside in the monastery courtyard, and prepared a seat in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber.
When the youth saw this, he conceived the thought: "How great indeed is this monk!"
The Blessed One, having emerged from the fragrant chamber, sat down on the prepared seat.
The prince, having paid homage to the Teacher and exchanged greetings, said: "Venerable sir, this elder is, I believe, dear to you in the Dispensation. "Yes, prince, he is dear.
"By doing what, venerable sir, does he become dear? "By performing meritorious deeds such as giving and the like."
“Blessed One, I too wish to become as beloved in the future Buddha-sāsana as this elder is. The Teacher, having granted him the meal for the army camp, said:
“Venerable sir, on the seventh day, I received from my father a boon that you should be cared for by me for three months;
please accept my invitation for the three-month rains retreat. The Blessed One replied, “There is...”
Having reflected, "Is there any purpose in going there? and seeing that there was, he said, "Young man, the Tathāgatas take delight in empty dwellings.
The prince replied, "Understood, Blessed One; understood, Sugata.
Venerable sir, I shall go on ahead and have a monastery built; when I have sent word, please come with a hundred thousand bhikkhus."

Having obtained his promise, he went into the presence of his father and said, "Your Majesty, I have received a promise from the Blessed One; when I have sent for him, you should dispatch the Blessed One.
Having paid homage to his father, he departed and traveled a journey of one hundred and twenty *yojanas*, constructing a monastery every *yojana* along the way.
Upon arriving, he searched for a site for a monastery in his own city, [and found it] at Sobhana.
Having seen the park belonging to the householder Nāma, he purchased it for one hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and after spending another hundred thousand, he had a monastery constructed there.
Having built a fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) for the Blessed One and huts, caves, and pavilions for the other monks to serve as places for staying by night and day,
and having completed the surrounding wall and the gateway tower, he went into the presence of his father.
He sent word, saying, "My task is finished; please send the Teacher.
After the King had fed the Blessed One, he said, "The Blessed One, Suman’s task is finished; he awaits your arrival.
The Blessed One, surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, proceeded along, staying at monasteries every yojana.
Hearing that "the Teacher is coming," the prince went out to meet him for a league.

Honoring him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he led him into a monastery built at a cost of one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] in the beautiful park named Sobhana, which he had purchased for one hundred thousand. Then he said:
"Purchased by me for a hundred thousand, Built for me at a cost of a hundred thousand; ... [he offered it to the Blessed One]."
“The garden named Sobhana—accept it, O Great Sage.

He offered it to him. On the day of entering the rains retreat, having distributed a great almsgiving and instructed his wife, children, ministers, and officials regarding their respective duties, saying, “You should continue to give alms in this very manner,” he himself [entrusted the matter] to the Elder Sumana.
Dwelling right near the Teacher’s residence and attending upon him for three months, he entered a village as the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) drew near.

Having distributed a great almsgiving for seven days, on the seventh day he placed his three robes at the feet of the Teacher and the hundred thousand bhikkhus, and having paid homage, said: "Venerable Sir, that which was given by me for seven days from the camp-site donation..."
"From this point on, the merit I have performed was not for the sake of attaining heavenly rebirths and the like;
rather, may I become the attendant of a future Buddha, just as this Elder Sumana.
Having made this aspiration, the Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, gave his prediction and departed.
During that appearance of a Buddha, he performed meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand years; thereafter,
having accumulated further sublime meritorious actions in various successive births, he wandered among gods and humans until, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa,
he made an offering by giving his upper robe to a certain elder who was walking for alms, in order to receive his bowl.
Having been reborn again in heaven and passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī.
There, having seen eight paccekabuddhas and having fed them, he had eight leaf-huts constructed in his own Maṅgala Garden.
For their use as seats, he prepared eight thrones made of all kinds of gems along with gemstone pedestals, and he attended upon them for ten thousand years.
He performed these deeds in manifest states.
However, while performing meritorious deeds here and there throughout a hundred thousand kalpas, he was reborn together with our Bodhisatta in the Tusita heaven;
passing away from there, he was reborn in the home of King Amitodana. Of him, all...
Because he was born bringing joy to his kinsmen, he was given the name Ānanda.
Gradually reaching maturity, having gone forth and attained supreme enlightenment, and having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, the Blessed One first went to Kapilavatthu.
When the Blessed One departed from there, Bhaddiya and others went forth to join his retinue.

Having gone forth together and received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta before long and was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, for twenty years after the Blessed One’s first awakening, there were no fixed personal attendants.
At one time Nāgasamāla went about taking his bowl and robes; at another time it was Nāgita; at another time Upavāna; at another time Sunakkhatta;
at another time the novice Cunda; at another time Sāgata; and at another time Meghiya.
For the most part, they did not please the Teacher’s mind. Then, on a certain day, the Blessed One was seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the courtyard of the Gandhakuṭī.
Seated surrounded by the community of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old;
some monks, when told by me, 'Go by this path,' go by another;
some place my bowl and robe on the ground. Know the monk who is my constant attendant. Having heard that, the monks...
A sense of spiritual urgency arose in him. Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said:
"Venerable sir, I shall attend upon you. The Blessed One declined his offer.
By this same means, all the great disciples, beginning with Mahāmoggallāna, rose up, each saying: "I shall attend upon you; I shall attend upon you."
With the exception of the Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One rejected them as well. But he remained silent.
Then the monks said to him, "Friend, you too should request the position of the Teacher’s attendant. "What kind of position is it that is obtained by requesting?
If it is pleasing to you, the Teacher himself will speak," [he replied]. Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, no..."
“Ānanda must be urged by others; once he has understood for himself, he will attend upon me,” he said.
Then the monks said, “Arise, friend Ānanda, and request the Teacher’s position as attendant.
The Elder rose and said, “Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One does not give me the fine robe he has obtained for himself, [I shall not accept it].”
“I will serve the Blessed One in this way: I will not give him choice almsfood; I will not allow him to dwell in the same fragrant chamber; and having accepted an invitation, I will not go [to it].
He said this for the purpose of clearing himself from reproach, thinking, “What burden is there in serving the Teacher when one gains such virtues?
And these four refusals were made: “If, Bhante, ...”
"The Blessed One will go to the invitation accepted by me. If I am able to see those who have come from various other regions at that very time;
if, whenever doubt arises in me, I am able to approach the Blessed One at that very moment;
and if the Blessed One would speak the Dhamma again to me regarding what was taught in his absence—then indeed I [shall serve] the Blessed One."

“I shall attend upon him. Thinking, “Even for this much he does not receive favor from the Teacher,” and for the sake of clearing away reproach as well as for the fulfillment of the perfection of being the Dharma-treasurer, he took these eight boons—namely, these four requests—and became a constant attendant.
For the sake of that very position, [he had fulfilled] a hundred thousand eons.

He attained the fruit of the perfections (pāramī). From the day he obtained the position of attendant, he served the One of Ten Powers with various duties, such as providing two kinds of water, three kinds of tooth-sticks, massaging the hands and feet, rubbing the back, and sweeping the Gandhakuṭi and its courtyard;
and while serving, he would think: "At this particular time, it is fitting for the Teacher to receive such-and-such."
Thinking, "It is proper to do this," he remained in the Teacher's presence for part of the day; then, during the night, taking a large torch,
he walked nine times around the Gandhakūṭi courtyard so that, when the Teacher called him,
he could give a prompt reply and dispel sloth and torpor.
Then the Teacher, while seated in the Jeta Grove in the midst of the assembly of noble ones,
praised him in many ways and established him in the foremost position among the monks who are learned, mindful, possessed of wisdom, endowed with fortitude, and devoted attendants. Thus,
having been placed by the Teacher in these five categories as being foremost, he was endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities.

This Great Elder, the guardian of the Teacher’s treasury of Dhamma, while still a trainee (*sekha*), was—after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna—exhorted by the monks in the manner described above and moved by a deity, [to think]: "The communal recitation of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgīti*) must now indeed be performed;
yet it is not fitting that I, being a trainee with duties still to be fulfilled, [should do so] alongside the elders who are beyond training (*asekha*)."
Thinking, "I shall go to the assembly to recite the Dhamma together," he was filled with zeal;
yet, although he applied himself to insight meditation for much of the night, he could not attain a balance of energy while walking on the meditation path.
Entering the monastery and sitting down on his bed, as he desired to lie down, he turned his body over. Before his head had even reached the pillow—
As soon as his feet were released from the ground, in that very interval, his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging, and he became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Emerging from the gate of the monastery, Padumuttara, the Great Sage;”
Raining down the rain of the Deathless, he brought peace to the great multitude.
"A hundred thousand wise ones, possessing the six direct knowledges and great psychic power,
attend upon the Perfectly Awakened One like a shadow that never departs."
“Mounted upon the back of an elephant, with the most excellent white parasol held over me,
I beheld one of beautiful form, and a sense of rapture arose within me.
Descending from the elephant’s back, I approached that bull among men.”
“I held a parasol made of jewels over the Best of Buddhas.
Knowing my intention, the Great Sage Padumuttara set aside that matter and spoke these verses:
“I shall now praise him who carried the parasol adorned with golden ornaments; listen as I speak.
Having departed from here, this person shall dwell in the Tusita heaven.”
He will experience prosperity, honored by celestial nymphs.
Thirty-four times he will exercise sovereignty over the gods;
as a commander of forces, he will dwell upon the earth for eight hundred [years].
“Eighty-eight times he will be a wheel-turning monarch;
he will exercise extensive sovereignty over the earth.
After a hundred thousand aeons, born into the Okkāka clan...”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
He will be a kinsman and relative of the Sakyan banner of the clan;
one named Ānanda by name will be the attendant of the Great Sage.”
“Ardent and wise, skilled in the many branches of knowledge,
humble in conduct and free from arrogance— he shall become a master of all that is to be learned.
With his self dedicated to striving, he will be peaceful and free from acquisitions.”
“Having fully understood all taints, one will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
There are forest-dwelling elephants, tuskers sixty years of age,
mighty lords with temples split in three, with tusks like plow-poles, and of noble breed.”
“Even those many hundreds of thousands, wise and possessed of great psychic power—all of them were not equal to the aspiration of that Naga of a Buddha.
I pay homage to my predecessors: to those of the past, to those of the middle period, and to those of the future.”
With a serene mind and joyful heart, I attended upon the Supreme Buddha.
"Ardent, wise, clearly comprehending, and mindful,
I attained the fruit of stream-entry, becoming skilled in the stages of training."
“The deed that I performed one hundred thousand aeons ago, for that I have reached this plane, established immovably in the True Dhamma.
Welcome indeed has come to me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”
Having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges, he entered the Saṅgīti-maṇḍapa and, while rehearsing the Dhamma,
collected together the verses spoken on various occasions for the purpose of exhorting the bhikkhus and for illustrating his own practice;
then, at the time of the recitation of the Khuddaka Nikāya, he included them in the Thera-gāthā during the formal rehearsal.
“A wise person should not form friendship with one who is divisive, angry, miserly, or who delights in ostentation; for association with a wicked man is evil.
But one should associate with one who has faith, who is virtuous, wise, and learned.”
A wise person should form friendship; association with a superior, a true man, is auspicious.
Behold this painted image, a heap of diseased limbs assembled together—afflicted, full of many thoughts, and lacking any lasting stability.
“Behold this form, fashioned by art, with its jewel and earring;
covered with skin and flesh, it shines together with garments.
The feet are dyed with red lac, and the face is smeared with cosmetic powder.”
Enough for the delusion of the fool, but not for one who seeks the further shore.
"The hair is arranged in eight patterns, the eyes are anointed with collyrium;
enough for the delusion of the fool, but not for one who seeks the further shore."
“Like a fresh collyrium box, this putrid body is adorned;
it is enough to delude the fool, but not the seeker of the further shore.
The hunter has set his snare, yet the deer did not enter the trap.”
“Having eaten the bait, we shall go, while the deer-trappers wail:
‘The snare for the deer is cut; the deer did not enter the net.
Having eaten the bait, we shall go, while the deer-hunters grieve.”
“Learned and eloquent, an attendant of the Buddha;
With the burden laid down and detached, Gotama makes his bed.
One whose taints are destroyed, detached, beyond all bonds, perfectly quenched.”
He bears his final body, having gone beyond birth and death.
“In that upon which the qualities of the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, are established—
the path leading to Nibbāna— there stands this Gotama.”
“From the Buddha I received eighty-two thousand [teachings], and two thousand from the monks;
thus eighty-four thousand teachings have been set forth for me.
This man of little learning grows old like an ox.”
His flesh increases, but his wisdom does not increase. "One who,
though learned, looks down upon the unlearned because of his learning—
such a person appears to me just like a blind man carrying a lamp."
“One should attend upon one who is learned and not let what has been heard be lost;
that is the root of the holy life, therefore one should be a bearer of the Dhamma.
One who knows what precedes and what follows, who knows the meaning, and is skilled in grammar and words,”
He grasps what has been well-grasped and examines its meaning.
Through patience he becomes zealous; having exerted himself, he weighs it.
At the proper time he strives, being well-composed within.
“One who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, wise, a disciple of the Buddha—
one who desires the discernment of the Dhamma should associate with such a person as this.
One who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, a guardian of the treasure of the Great Seer.”
The one with great learning is worthy of honor by the whole world.
Delighting in the Dhamma, rejoicing in the Dhamma, reflecting upon the Dhamma,
and recollecting the Dhamma, a bhikkhu does not fall away from the true Dhamma.
“He who is weighed down by stinginess regarding the body, who fails to exert himself when there is decline, and who is greedy for physical comfort—how can there be peace for such a recluse?
All directions are not clear to me; the teachings do not manifest to me.”
When one has gone to a spiritual friend, it appears like darkness [dispelled].
For one whose companion has passed away and whose teacher has gone before,
there is no such friend as mindfulness directed to the body.
“Those who were ancient and have passed away do not agree with me in their newness.
Today I meditate all alone, like a bird that has entered its nest.
Many people from various kingdoms have come forward to see me.”
"Do not stop the listeners; let them see me at this time.
To those who have come from various kingdoms, diverse and many, desiring a vision, the Teacher grants access; the Visionary One does not forbid them."
“For twenty-five years, while I was still a trainee, no perception of sensual desire arose in me; behold the excellence of the Dhamma!
For twenty-five years, while I was still a trainee...”
No perception of fault arose; behold the excellence of the Dhamma!
For twenty-five years I attended upon the Blessed One with loving bodily action, like a shadow that never departs.
“For twenty-five years I attended upon the Blessed One with loving verbal action, never departing from him like a shadow.
For twenty-five years I attended upon the Blessed One.”
“Through a mental action imbued with loving-kindness, like a shadow that never departs,
I walked behind the Buddha as he paced back and forth;
while the Dhamma was being taught, knowledge arose within me.”
“I still have duties to perform; I am a trainee who has not yet attained his heart’s goal, while the Teacher who was compassionate toward us has entered final Nibbāna.
That was truly terrifying; that was truly hair-raising.”
When the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with every excellent quality, has attained final Nibbāna:
Ānanda— learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, the treasury-keeper of the Great Seer,
the eye of the entire world— has also attained final Nibbāna.
“Learned and a bearer of the Dhamma, the treasury-guardian of the Great Seer;
the eye of the entire world, dispelling darkness in the gloom.
That sage who possesses insight, mindfulness, and fortitude—”
The Elder Ānanda, the upholder of the True Dharma, a treasury of jewels, declared:
“I have served the Teacher; the Buddha’s dispensation has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; there is now no further becoming.”
He spoke these verses.

Regarding them, the first two verses beginning with "By malicious speech" (*pisuṇena ca*) were spoken for the purpose of admonishing the group-of-six monks (*chabbaggiya*), whom he saw associating with the monks who were partisans of Devadatta.
In that context, "by malicious speech" (*pisuṇena*) means by malicious [tongue] (*pisuṇāya*).

By speech. For a person engaged in that [speech] is called "slanderous," just as a cloth associated with the quality of blue is called "blue. "By the angry" means by one whose nature is to be prone to anger.
"By the miserly" because of the occurrence of stinginess (*macchariya*), which is characterized by the concealment of one's own prosperity.
"By those delighting in destruction" means by those who desire the destruction, ruin, or loss of beings; or alternatively, by those who delight in what is distinct (*vibhūta*).
"Bhāvo" means division; this was said with reference specifically to those on Devadatta’s side.

For they, by causing a schism among many people who were practicing rightly through their exposition of the five points, acted for the great harm of the multitude, being characterized by stubbornness, stinginess, and other forms of avarice toward the Teacher due to their alienation from him.
"Sakhitaṃ" means one should not form friendship, association, or intimacy [with them].
For what reason? Association with a wicked person, meeting with a base and evil individual, is low and contemptible.
For those who fall into following his example, it brings about nothing but the characteristics of a fool, such as ill-thought-out intentions and so forth;
how much more so for one who actually carries out his words. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, whatever fears arise..."
“All those things arise from the fool, not from the wise,” and so forth.

To show with whom association should be made, it is said: “By one who has faith,” and so on. Therein, “by one who has faith” means by one endowed with faith in kamma and its fruit, as well as faith in the Triple Gem. “By one who is kindly” means by one whose nature is loving.

"Endowed with virtue" (sīlasampannena). "Possessing wisdom" (paññavata) means being endowed with wisdom by way of the wisdom that penetrates and understands the arising and passing away [of phenomena].
"Learned" (bahussuta) means being learned through the fulfillment of both scriptural learning (pariyatti) and penetration (paṭivedha).

"Blessed" (bhaddo): the intention is that association with such a virtuous person is blessed, beautiful, and auspicious, as it brings about welfare consisting of various types, such as those pertaining to the present life (diṭṭhadhammika).

The seven verses beginning with "Passa cittakataṃ" were spoken for the purpose of generating a sense of revulsion toward the body in the laywoman named Uttarā, who had conceived sensual thoughts upon seeing her own physical beauty.
Some also say they were spoken for the purpose of giving advice to those whose minds were distracted by seeing the courtesan Ambapālī. Their meaning has already been explained above.
The two verses beginning with "Bahussuto cittakathī" (Learned and eloquent) were spoken by the Elder as an inspired utterance (*udāna*) after he had attained *arahatta*.
In that context, "paricārako" means an attendant. "He makes his bed" is said because he lay down immediately upon attaining *arahatta*;
for the Elder, having spent most of the night walking in meditation (*caṅkama*), entered his cell to allow his body to cool.
Having entered, while sitting on the couch and with his feet still off the ground, and before his head had reached the pillow, he attained *arahantship* in that interval and lay down.

"One whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*) means one whose four taints are completely exhausted; for that very reason, he is "disjoined from the four bonds" (*visaṃyutta*). Because he has transcended attachment to passion and the like, he is "beyond attachment" (*saṅgātīta*). Because the fever of all defilements has been entirely stilled, the meaning is that he is "well-extinguished" (*sunibbuto*), having become cool.
"Upon which the teachings are established"—this verse was spoken by the Great Brahmā, whose taints were exhausted, with reference to the Elder.
For when the recitation of the Dhamma had been convened, certain monks spoke concerning the Elder, saying, "One monk emits a foul odor.
Then, having attained Arahatship, the Elder [opened] the door of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave for the sake of granting the Saṅgha the gift of harmony.

The Great Brahmā of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa-mahābrahmā) arrived, and by manifesting his state of one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), he spoke the verse beginning with “In whom the teachings are established,” putting those bhikkhus to shame.

Its meaning is as follows: the teachings (dhammā) of the Buddha, the Blessed One—namely, the teachings of realization and the teachings of scripture—were both attained and proclaimed by him alone. That particular person in whom they are established is this [Buddha].

By clan he was Gotama; as the Dharma-treasurer, because he had attained *nibbāna* with residue remaining (*saupādisesa*), he now stood firm on the path leading to *nibbāna* without residue remaining (*anupādisesa*). He was thus a partial counterpart to him.
Then one day, a brahmin named Gopakamoggallāna asked the Elder: "Are you very learned? [The Elder replied: "In comparison to the Buddha..."
“Are you well-known in the Dispensation? How many teachings have been spoken by your Teacher that you have retained?
Giving his reply to him, the Elder spoke this verse beginning with “Dvāsīti. In this context, the construction is “dvāsīti sahassāni” (eighty-two thousand).
“Gaṇhinṃ buddhato” means that from the Fully Enlightened One, I received eighty-two thousand aggregates of Dhamma from the presence of the Teacher.
"Attained" is the meaning. "Two thousand from the monks" means I received two thousand sections of the Dhamma from the monks;
I acquired them from the presence of monks such as the Dhammasenāpati and others.
"Eighty-four thousand" means, when those two are combined, eighty-four thousand plus four thousand. "Those teachings which were proclaimed by me."
"These aggregates of Dhamma, which have been described according to their measure, are familiar to me, mastered by me, and revolve upon the tip of my tongue.
Then, on one occasion, having gone forth in the Dispensation, the Elder saw a certain person who was not devoted either to the task of insight (vipassanā) or to the task of study (gantha).
Seeing the danger in the absence of great learning, he spoke the verse beginning with "By little learning," thereby making known that peril. In this regard:
"Of little learning": he is one who has not learned even one or two [discourses], or perhaps as few as one or two suttas, among the fifty or the sections;
thus he is of little learning. However, having mastered a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and applying himself to it, he is indeed one of great learning.
"He grows old like an ox": just as an ox, while growing old, continues to grow in size...
It does not grow for the sake of mother, father, or other relatives; rather, it simply decays uselessly.

In the same way, this person also does not perform the duties toward a preceptor, nor the duties toward a teacher, nor the duties toward newcomers and so forth, nor does he apply himself to meditation;
he simply decays uselessly. His flesh grows like that of an ox.
Just as the flesh of one who has been abandoned in the forest— because he is incapable of carrying burdens such as plowing—
grows as he wanders about, eats, and drinks however he may, even though he is left to himself; in the same way, for this person as well, who has been left by his preceptor and others,
and who nourishes his body by obtaining the four requisites through reliance on the Saṅgha and performing such things as purging with emetics.
His flesh increases, and he wanders about having become a person of stout body. As for his wisdom—both mundane and supramundane—not even a single finger’s breadth of it increases.
The intention is that, just as creepers and the like grow in the forest, his craving and the ninefold conceit increase by depending upon his six sense-doors.
The verse beginning with "Bahussuto" was spoken concerning a certain bhikkhu who, relying on his own great learning (*bāhusacca*), looked down upon others.
In this context, "on account of what has been heard" (*sutenā*) means by reason of hearing, that is, for the sake of one's own great learning.

"He looks down upon" (*atimaññati*) means he thinks beyond [his measure], exalting himself and disparaging another. "In the same way" (*tatheva*) refers to how a blind man, in the darkness, [seeks] a lamp of oil...
While maintaining it, one brings benefit only to others through the gift of light, not to oneself; likewise,
a person who has heard much through mastery of the scriptures but does not apply that learning to fulfill their own welfare is like a blind man who,
by giving the light of knowledge, brings benefit only to others and not to themselves— such a person appears to me like a blind man carrying a lamp.
Now, showing the benefits of great learning (*bāhusacca*), he spoke this verse beginning with "the learned" (*bahussuta*). Therein, *upāseyya* means one should attend upon.
*Sutañca na vināsaye* means that having attended upon the learned, one should not let what has been heard perish;
one should not cause it to waste away, but should increase it through memorization, mastery, inquiry, and mental attention. *Taṃ mūlaṃ brahmacariyassa*: because...
Having attended upon one who is learned, that which has been acquired— the learning consisting of mastery of the scriptures— is the root and the primary cause for the holy life of the path.
Therefore, being a bearer of the Dhamma, and standing at the head of the bases of liberation,
one should first become a bearer of the Dhamma through mastery in order to retain the Dhamma as it has been heard.
Now, in order to show the purpose that must be accomplished through great learning in the scriptures (*pariyatti-bāhusacca*), it is said:

“One who knows what precedes and what follows,” and so forth. In this context, one who knows both what precedes (*pubba*) and what follows (*apara*) is called “one who knows what precedes and what follows” (*pubbāparaññū*).

For even if the prior portion of a certain verse is not understood, or if the prior portion is understood but the subsequent portion is not, [the meaning is established] by means of the prior portion for this subsequent portion, or...
One who knows that "this latter portion must have been preceded by this former portion" is called one who knows the sequence of before and after (*pubbāparaññū*).
One who knows the meaning of each respective teaching, such as the benefit for oneself (*attattha*) and so forth, is called one who knows the meaning (*atthaññū*).

"Skilled in etymological analysis" (*niruttipadakovida*) means one who is proficient in the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), namely, in etymology (*nirutti*) and in the remaining three categories. "And he grasps what has been well-grasped" means:
By that very state of expertise, having thoroughly mastered the Dhamma both in meaning and in phrasing, he grasps it.

"He examines the meaning" means that he examines the meaning of the Dhamma as it was heard and as it was learned; he reflects upon it with the mind, thinking: "Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom; these are material and immaterial phenomena."

"Through patience, he becomes desirous": when those phenomena have been examined by the mind, having brought about acceptance through the contemplation of views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*), he becomes desirous—that is, one in whom desire has arisen—regarding the application of insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*) by way of the discernment of form (*rūpapariggaha*) and so forth.
Being thus disposed, while performing the work of insight, he exerts himself and scrutinizes by way of seeing the various conditions of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Having exerted effort and applied the three characteristics thereafter, he weighs it, considering that name-and-form as "impermanent," "suffering," and "non-self";
thus he scrutinizes and contemplates it through insight. At the appropriate time, he strives, being well-composed within;
thus, while seeing in this way, he strives by means of exertion and so forth for the mind at times when it must be exerted, and while striving—
And he should become well-concentrated through insight-concentration and path-concentration upon the internal object of focus within his own range,
and should abandon the defilements that are the causes of non-concentration. Since all these qualities belong to one who attends upon a disciple of the Buddha who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma,
and possessed of wisdom, therefore, with reference to the unconditioned Dhamma among [the truths] such as suffering...

Because its function is distinguished by full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth, one who desires the knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-ñāṇa*), which is termed "phenomenal consciousness" (*dhamma-viññāṇa*), should associate with such a friend of virtue as described above;
that is to say, he should follow, serve, and attend upon him—this is the meaning.
Thus, showing his worthiness of honor due to his great helpfulness, the author spoke the verse beginning with "the learned" (*bahussuto*). Its meaning is as follows:
One who has heard much—the discourses, verses, and so forth—is called *bahussuta*.
One who retains that very Dhamma of the teaching without letting it perish, like lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel, is called *dhammadhara*.

For that very reason, one who guards the treasure of the Dhamma, the jewel of the Dhamma, which belongs to the Blessed One, the Great Sage, is called *kosārakkha*. Because, through his equal vision, [he protects] the world including its devas...
“Having become the eye, therefore the eye is to be honored and revered by the whole world.
Thus, in order to show that one who is learned is worthy of honor by many people, the word “learned” is stated once more as a conclusion.
Showing that even after obtaining such a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), it is only for the doer that there is no decline, and not for the non-doer, [the text continues]:
He spoke the verse beginning with “one who delights in the Dhamma. Therein, the Dhamma of serenity and insight is a “delight” (ārāma) in the sense of being a place of dwelling;
one who takes pleasure and finds delight in that very Dhamma is “one who delights in the Dhamma” (dhammarata).
By repeatedly reflecting upon that same Dhamma, the meaning is that he contemplates and attends to the Dhamma while recollecting it. They recollect that very same Dhamma.
"Recalling. "The true Dhamma": such a bhikkhu does not fall away from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttaradhammā*);
the meaning is that there is never any decline for him from those.
Then, one day, in order to inspire the bhikkhu named Kosallāya—who was not free from lust for the body, was indolent, and lacked energy—he [the Buddha] stirred him.

He spoke the verse beginning, “*Kāyamaccheragaruno*. Therein, “*kāyamaccheragaruno*” refers to one who is heavy with stinginess regarding the body—one who is full of bodily rigidity, possesses attachment to the body, and wanders about without performing even that which ought to be done for his teachers and preceptors by means of the body.
“*Hiyyamāne*” means while one’s own body and life are wasting away moment by moment. “*Anuṭṭhaheti*” [refers to] not practicing the precepts and so forth.
One would not exert the energy of striving for the sake of fulfillment. "Greedy for bodily comfort" means one who has fallen into attachment solely to the pleasure of his own body.
"How can there be a monk’s well-being?"—for such a person, how can there be a state of ease through the life of a recluse?
The meaning is that a state of comfort does not exist for him.
The verses beginning with "Na pakkhanti" were spoken by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, after he had heard of the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the Venerable [Mahākassapa].
Therein, "all directions do not appear" means that all directions, distinguished as the east and so forth, do not appear;
the sense is that he was disoriented regarding the directions. "Dhammas do not occur to my mind" refers to those teachings which, though previously well-mastered...
"Even though the teachings (pariyattidhammā) are now being carefully attended to, they do not appear clearly to me. 'When the Good Friend has passed away' means:
when the General of the Dhamma—who was the Good Friend of the world including the devas—has entered Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna).
'It appears as darkness' means: the entire world appears like darkness, despite every means."
"Abbhatītasahāyassa" means one whose companions have departed; the meaning is "one who is devoid of virtuous friends.
"Atītagatasatthuno" means one for whom the Teacher has passed away and entered *nibbāna*; the meaning is "when the Teacher has attained final *parinibbāna*.
Just as the cultivation of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) brings absolute welfare to the practitioner, so too does such [mindfulness] [bring welfare].

The intention is this: for a person who is without a protector (*anātha*), there is no other friend that brings about absolute welfare; however, for one who has a protector (*sanātha*), even other forms of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) bring about welfare.
"Ancient" (*purāṇa*) means those of old; he speaks with reference to virtuous friends such as Sāriputta and others. "By the new" (*navehi*) means by those who are junior. Not...
“My mind does not agree with them; they do not please my mind”—this is the meaning. “Today I meditate alone”:
today, being separated from those who are senior, I am alone and meditate; I am devoted to jhāna. “Like one who has approached his nest”:
like a bird that has approached its nest during the rainy season. There is also a reading, “vāsupeto,” which means “one who has gone to his dwelling.”
"‘Come for the sake of seeing’—this verse was spoken by the Teacher. Its meaning is as follows:
‘Ānanda, do not prevent the many people from various foreign lands who have come for the sake of seeing me; let them approach me. Why?
Because they are hearers of the Dhamma; let them see me, for this is the very occasion for seeing.’”
Having heard that, the Elder spoke another verse beginning with “To those who have come for a visit.

For the sake of establishing the connection, the preceding verse is placed here. By this very verse, he demonstrates the fulfillment of the meaning of the phrase: “If I should receive [the opportunity] to show [them] immediately upon their arrival from other regions.”
The twenty-five stanzas beginning with "For twenty-five years" were spoken to demonstrate his status as the foremost attendant.

Indeed, because he was devoted to the practice of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and intent on attending upon the Teacher, even though the perceptions of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*) and so forth had not been completely eradicated by the Path, they did not arise in the Elder;
furthermore, his bodily, verbal, and mental actions were at all times preceded by loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward the Teacher and permeated by loving-kindness.
...there were. Therein, "twenty-five years" means twenty-five years.

"While I was one who has become a trainee" means while I was established in the fruit of stream-entry on the plane of training. "Perceptions of sensual desire" means perceptions accompanied by sensual desire did not arise;
and here, by the statement regarding the non-arising of perceptions of sensual desire and so forth, he demonstrates the purity of his own disposition (*āsaya*) through "loving-kindness..."

By the passage beginning with “by bodily action,” etc., [he shows] purity of application. Therein, loving bodily action should be understood as performing services and duties for the Teacher, such as by decorating the Perfumed Chamber; loving verbal action as announcing the time for the preaching of the Dhamma, and so forth;
and loving mental action as attending upon the Teacher when he has gone into seclusion, bringing to mind considerations that promote his welfare.
“Mental action. “Knowledge arose in me” refers to his own attainment of the stage of a trainee (*sekha*).

“I have work yet to be done” is a verse spoken by him while overcome with grief after entering the circular pavilion (*maṇḍalamāḷa*) and leaning against the monkey-head pillar at the time of the Teacher’s final passing away (*parinibbāna*).
In that context, “I have work yet to be done” refers to [the tasks] such as the full comprehension of suffering.
"I have duties to perform; I am one who still has work to do. "One who has not attained his heart's desire" means one who has not yet realized the fruit [of Arhatship].
"And the Parinibbāna of the Teacher" means that the Parinibbāna of my Teacher has presented itself before me. "He who was compassionate toward us" refers to the Teacher who was my benefactor.

"Then there was that which was terrifying" is the verse spoken out of a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) upon seeing the earthquake, the sounding of the divine drums, and other such portents at the time of the Teacher’s Parinibbāna.
The three verses beginning with "Bahussuto" were placed there by the compilers of the collection (saṅgītikārā) in order to praise the Elder. In that context:
"Possessed of insight" (gatimanto) means endowed with an incomparable course of knowledge; "possessed of mindfulness" (satimanto) means endowed with supreme mindfulness and discretion;
"possessed of fortitude" (dhitimanto) means endowed with an attainment of fortitude capable of uniquely grasping both the phrasing and the meaning.
For this elder, standing on a single spot, grasps sixty thousand words exactly according to the method taught by the Teacher;
and what has been grasped never perishes at any time, like lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel.
He is endowed with wisdom preceded by mindfulness capable of retaining the phrasing without error, and with mindfulness preceded by wisdom capable of retaining the meaning.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “This is the foremost, monks, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are learned,” and so forth.
Likewise, the General of the Dhamma said: “The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning,” and so forth. He is a “mine of jewels” because he is a source of the jewel of the True Dhamma.
The verse beginning with “He has served [the Teacher]” was spoken by the Elder at the time of his final Nibbāna; its meaning is exactly as stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ānanda is finished.
The commentary on the Tiṃsanipāta (The Section of Thirty) is finished.
18. The Cattālīsanipāta (The Section of Forty).
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākassapa The verses beginning with "Not surrounded by a retinue," etc., belong to the venerable Elder Mahākassapa.
What is his origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there was a man named Vedeha in the city of Haṃsavatī, possessing a wealth of eight hundred million.

He was a householder. Being a lay follower who cherished the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, while living his life in this way, he one day on the Uposatha day ate a fine meal early in the morning. Having resolved upon the Uposatha precepts and taking perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he went to the monastery.
There, having honored and paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side.
At that moment, the Teacher placed the Elder Mahānisabha as the third disciple among his monks, saying:
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the monks who are exponents of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), namely Nisabha.

Having heard this, the lay devotee was filled with faith. At the conclusion of the Dhamma discourse, when the great multitude had risen and departed, he paid homage to the Teacher and said: “Tomorrow...”
“Please accept my almsfood,” he invited them. “The community of monks is large, lay follower.
“How many, venerable sir? “Six million eight hundred thousand monks. “Venerable sir, please accept my almsfood without leaving even a single novice behind in the monastery.
The Teacher consented. Knowing that the Teacher had consented, the lay follower—

Having returned home, he prepared a great almsgiving and on the following day announced the time for the Teacher’s arrival. The Teacher, taking his bowl and robe and surrounded by the community of monks, went to the lay follower’s house;

having sat upon the prepared seat, he performed the meal distribution, receiving the rice-gruel and other offerings at the conclusion of the water-offering ceremony. The lay follower also sat down near the Teacher.
In the meantime, while wandering for alms, the Elder Mahānisabha entered that very street.
Seeing him, the lay follower rose, went forward, paid homage to the Elder, and said, "Venerable sir, please give me your bowl. The Elder gave him his bowl.
"Venerable sir, please enter right here; the Teacher is sitting in the house as well. "That will not do, lay follower," he replied.
So he took the elder’s bowl, filled it with almsfood, and gave it to him.

Then, having followed the elder back and returned, he sat down near the Teacher and said: "Venerable sir, when it was said that even the Teacher would not wish to enter when told 'the Teacher is sitting at home,' the Elder Mahānisabha did not wish to enter either;
is there perhaps someone who possesses qualities exceeding yours? And for the Buddhas...
There is no such thing as stinginess regarding praise; therefore, the Teacher said this:
"Lay follower, we sit in our homes waiting for alms, but that bhikkhu does not sit in such a way while looking for alms.
We dwell in lodgings within the village, but he dwells only in the forest. We dwell under cover, but he dwells only in the open air."
The Blessed One, as if filling the great ocean, recounted his virtues, saying, "Such and such are his qualities.
The lay follower, who was already like a lamp burning naturally, became even more deeply inspired—like a lamp drenched with oil—and thought: "What need have I for any other attainment?
In the future, in the presence of a certain Buddha, I shall strive for the sake of being foremost among those who preach the ascetic practices (dhuta)."
“I shall make an aspiration. Having again invited the Teacher, he gave a great almsgiving for seven days according to that same procedure.

On the seventh day, having given three robes to the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he prostrated at the Teacher’s feet and spoke thus: “Venerable Sir, whatever merit I have gained while giving alms for these seven days...”
Loving-kindness in bodily action, loving-kindness in verbal action, and loving-kindness in mental action are established;
by this, I do not aspire to any other divine success— whether the success of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā— but rather that this karma of mine may, in the future,
lead to the attainment of the position reached by the Elder Mahānisabha in the presence of a certain Buddha.
"May he have the right to the preeminence among those who bear the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas).
The Teacher, observing whether this great position sought by him would be fulfilled or not, saw that it would indeed be fulfilled and said:
"A pleasing position you have sought. In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise."
“You shall be his third disciple, the Elder named Mahākassapa,” he prophesied.
Having heard this, the lay follower thought, “There are no two kinds of words from the Buddhas,” and on the following day, he regarded that prosperity as something already attained.
He gave gifts for as long as he lived, undertook and guarded the precepts, and performed various kinds of wholesome deeds.
Having done so, he passed away and was reborn in heaven.
From that time forth, experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, ninety-one aeons ago,
when the Sammasambuddha Vipassi was dwelling in the Khema Migadāya near the city of Bandhumatī, [he] passed away from the world of the gods and [was reborn] in a certain...
He was reborn into a family of very aged brahmins. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī preached the Dhamma every seventh year, which caused a great commotion.
Deities throughout the entire Jambudīpa announced, "The Teacher will preach the Dhamma.
The brahmin heard this report, and he had only a single lower garment.
It was the same for the brahmin woman. However, the cloak worn by both of them was one and the same. Consequently, he became known throughout the entire city as the "Brahmin with a Single Garment.

Whenever there was an assembly of brahmins for some business, he would leave his wife at home and go himself, wearing that garment. When there was an assembly of brahmin women, he would remain at home himself.
The brahmin woman, having put on that cloth, was going along. On that day, however, the brahmin said to the brahmin woman:
"Madam, will you listen to the Dhamma at night or during the day? She replied to the brahmin, "We women by nature are unable to listen at night;
we shall listen during the day," and leaving him at home, she put on that cloth and [went] with the female lay disciples.
Having gone together during the day, she paid homage to the Teacher and sat to one side; having heard the Dhamma, she returned together with the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*).
Then the brahmin left his wife at home, put on that garment, and went to the monastery.
At that time, the Teacher was seated upon the decorated Dhamma-throne in the midst of the assembly, holding a fan of peacock feathers, [and looking toward] the celestial Ganges.
As if pouring down, as if churning the ocean with Mount Sineru as the churning-stick, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma.
As the brahmin sat at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, in that very first watch of the night, five-colored rapture arose, filling his entire body.
He gathered up his wrapped garment, thinking, "I shall give it to the One of Ten Powers."
He thought. Then, as it were displaying a thousand dangers, stinginess arose within him.
He thought, "The brahmin woman and I have only this one garment; we have no other covering, and it is impossible to go outside without being clothed.
Thus, he was entirely unwilling to give it away. Then, when the first watch had passed, during the middle watch as well—
In that very way, rapture arose. Having thought in that same manner, he likewise remained unwilling to give it.
Then, when the middle watch had passed and during the last watch as well, rapture arose in him just as before.
At that time, thinking, "Whether it be this or that, I shall know later," he folded the cloth and placed it at the feet of the Teacher. Then, having crossed his left hand over [his lap]...
Having clapped his right hand three times, he cried out three times, "Victory is mine! Victory is mine!
At that moment, King Bandhumā was sitting behind the Dhamma-seat within the curtain, listening to the Dhamma.
Now, the sound "Victory is mine" was unpleasant to a king; so he sent a man, saying, "Go, [find out] this..."
"Ask him what he says. Having gone there and being questioned by him, [the man] said:
"It is no marvel that the rest of them, having mounted elephant-vehicles and the like, and taking up swords, shields, and so forth, conquer the enemy army.
But I, like one who crushes the head of a rogue ox coming from behind with a club and drives it away, have crushed the mind of stinginess and [taken] the cloth that was wrapped around [my neck]."
"I gave it to the One Endowed with the Ten Powers; thus has my stinginess been conquered," he said. That man returned and reported the matter to the king.
The king said, "We, sirs, did not know what was appropriate for the One Endowed with the Ten Powers;
the brahmin knew. He sent a pair of garments. Seeing them, the brahmin thought, "While I sat here in silence..."
Without first giving anything himself, he gave [the cloth] to one who was speaking of the Teacher’s virtues.

But thinking, "What use have I for that which has arisen dependent upon the Teacher’s virtues?", he gave even that pair of cloths to the One Endowed with the Ten Powers alone. The king also, having asked, "What was done by the brahmin?
and having heard, "He too gave that pair of cloths to the Tathāgata alone," [gave] other [cloths] as well.
He sent two pairs of garments, and the brahmin gave those away as well. The king sent four more, and in this manner he continued until he had sent thirty-two pairs of garments.

Then the brahmin thought, "This is like taking what has been increased again and again," and so he took two pairs for himself—one for himself and one for his wife—and gave the remaining thirty pairs to the Tathāgata alone.
From that time on, he became one who inspired the Teacher’s confidence.

Then one day, seeing him listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher during a cold season, the king gave him a red woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand pieces—something he himself had worn—and said: "From now on, listen to the Dhamma while wearing this."
Thinking, "What is the use of this blanket being brought to this putrid body?

he went and made it a canopy over the Tathāgata’s bed inside the Fragrant Chamber. Then one day, the king went to the monastery early in the morning and sat down in the presence of the Teacher within the Fragrant Chamber. At that time, the six-colored rays of the Buddha...
They struck against the blanket, and the blanket shone exceedingly. Looking up and recognizing it, the king said:
"Venerable sir, this is our blanket; it was given by us to a single-robed brahmin. "Great King, you honored the brahmin, and the brahmin has honored us.
The king, becoming confident that "the brahmin understood what was appropriate, whereas we did not," was filled with faith.

Having grouped together all those things that were beneficial to human beings into sets of eight, he gave a gift known as the "All-Eight" (*sabbaṭṭhaka*) and appointed him to the position of court chaplain.
He, too, thinking, "Eight times eight makes sixty-four," had sixty-four daily meal-tickets (*salākabhatta*) assigned for himself;
having given alms for as long as he lived and guarded his virtue, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in heaven.
Passing away from there, in this same eon, he was reborn in Benares in the household of a householder during the interval between two Buddhas, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana and the Daśabala Kassapa.
Having grown up and living the life of a householder, one day he went for a walk in the forest. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was on the bank of a river...
While he was engaged in sewing robes, as the wind did not blow favorably, he began to fold them up and set them aside.

Seeing this, [the man] asked, "Venerable sir, why are you setting them aside after folding them? "The wind does not blow favorably," he replied. "Venerable sir, work with this," he said, giving him an upper robe, and made this aspiration:
"May there never be any deficiency for me in whatever place I am reborn."
While his wife was quarreling with his sister, the Paccekabuddha entered for alms.
Then the sister, having given alms-food to the Paccekabuddha, made a wish concerning his wife:
"May one avoid such a fool even from a distance of a hundred leagues. Standing on the courtyard of the house, she heard this.
Saying, "Let him not eat the food given by this woman," she took the bowl, threw away the alms-food, filled it with mud, and gave it back.

Seeing this, the other said: "Foolish girl! You may revile me or strike me as you please, but it is not right to throw away the food from the bowl of one who has fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable aeons and give him mud instead."

He said: Then his wife’s reflection arose. She said, "Wait, venerable sir," and having discarded the *kalala* (fertilized egg), she washed the bowl, rubbed it with fragrant powder, and filled it with choice food and the four sweets.
Having placed it upon the *paccavekkhaṇa*-butter—which was shining like the interior of a lotus—she placed it in the hand of the Paccekabuddha.
“Just as this alms-food has become luminous, so may my body become luminous,” he made this aspiration.
Having offered his thanks, the Paccekabuddha soared into the sky.
Those husband and wife also performed wholesome deeds for the duration of their lives, were reborn in heaven, and after passing away from there, the lay follower—
In the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the son of a merchant possessing eighty million in wealth;
she too was reborn as the daughter of a merchant of equal means. When he had reached maturity, they brought that very merchant’s daughter to him as his wife.
However, due to the power of an evil deed whose result had previously been undesirable, as soon as she entered her husband's family home—
Within the palace grounds, her entire body became foul-smelling, like an opened latrine.
When the merchant’s son asked, “Whose scent is this? and heard it was that of the merchant’s daughter, he cried out, “Take her away! Take her away!
and sent her back to her family home by the very same route she had been brought. By that same process of being sent back, she was turned away at seven different places.
And at that time, Kassapa the Great, the Bull of Men, attained final Nibbāna.
For him, they began to construct a stupa one *yojana* in height, using bricks of red gold worth a hundred thousand [pieces] each, with solid foundations.
While that stupa was being built, that merchant’s daughter thought: “I have been turned back from seven places; what is the use of my life? Thus she...
Having had her jewelry and ornaments broken up, she had a golden brick made—one cubit long, one span wide, and four finger-breadths high.
Then, taking lumps of yellow orpiment and realgar and carrying eight handfuls of blue lotuses, she went to the site where the stupa was to be built.
At that moment, a row of bricks came along, having already encircled [the site].
The brickwork was short by one brick. The merchant’s daughter said to the mason, “Place this brick here.

He replied, “Mother, you have come at a fortunate time; you place it yourself. She climbed up, mixed oil with a lump of yellow orpiment and red arsenic, and having fixed the brick with that adhesive, she made an offering over it with eight handfuls of blue lotuses.

Having paid homage and made the aspiration, “In every place where I am reborn, may the fragrance of sandalwood issue from my body and the fragrance of blue lotuses from my mouth,” she paid homage to the cetiya,
circumambulated it, and departed.
At that very moment, regarding that merchant’s son to whom she had first been led to his house—
When he was present, the thought arose in him: "A festival has been proclaimed even in the city.
He said to his attendants, "There is the daughter of the treasurer who was brought here on that occasion; where is she? "She is at her father's house, sir," they replied.
"Bring her here; we shall enjoy the festival," he said. They went, paid homage to her, and stood waiting. When she asked them, "Why have you come, dear ones? they [replied]:
They reported the matter: "Dear ones, I have worshipped the Cetiya with my jewelry; I have no ornaments left.
They went and informed the merchant's son: "Bring her here; she will receive the adornments. They brought her.
As soon as she entered the house, the entire dwelling was filled with the fragrance of sandalwood and blue lotuses.

The merchant’s son asked her: “First your body emitted a foul odor, but now sandalwood fragrance emanates from your body and the scent of blue lotuses from your mouth. What is this? She related the deed she had committed from the very beginning.
The merchant’s son, gaining confidence that “the teaching of the Buddha is indeed leading to liberation,” [gave] a yojana’s distance...
Having draped the Golden Cetiya with a woolen cloak, he adorned it here and there with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels, each twelve cubits in length.
Having lived there for the duration of his lifespan and been reborn in heaven, he passed away from there and was born at a place one *yojana* from Bārāṇasī.
He was reborn in the family of a certain minister, while a merchant’s daughter, having passed away from the world of the gods, was reborn as the eldest daughter in the royal household.
When they had reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the prince resided.
He said to his mother, "Mother, give me a garment; I shall play at the festival. She brought out a washed cloth...
She gave it to him. He said, "Mother, this is too coarse. She brought out another and gave it to him, but he rejected that as well.
Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, in a house such as ours where we were born, there is no merit sufficient for us to obtain anything finer than this.
"In that case, Mother, I shall go to a place where it can be obtained. "Son, today itself I shall [send you] to the city of Bārāṇasī..."
“I wish to obtain the kingdom as well. Having paid homage to his mother, he said, “I am going, Mother. “Go, dear son,” she replied.
For it was her thought: “Where will he go? He will sit here or there within this very house.
But he, departing according to the course of his merit, went to Bārāṇasī and sat with his head [resting] upon the auspicious stone slab in the park.
Having put on [the garment], he lay down. It was now the seventh day since the death of the King of Bārāṇasī.
After the ministers had performed the funeral rites for the king, they sat in the royal courtyard and deliberated:
