"The king has only one daughter and no son; a kingdom without a king perishes. Who shall be the king? "You be it! You be it! they said.
They said. The chaplain said: "It is not proper to look about much; let us release the Phussa-chariot.

Having yoked four horses the color of white water-lilies, and having placed the fivefold royal insignia and the white parasol upon the chariot itself, they released the chariot and had musical instruments played behind it. The chariot—
Having exited through the eastern gate, he set out toward the park. Some said, "He is going toward the park out of habit;
let us turn him back. The chaplain said, "Do not turn him back. The chariot, having circumambulated the prince, stood ready for him to mount.
The chaplain, having pulled back the corner of his upper garment, was looking at the soles of the prince's feet.
“Let this island be; he is worthy to rule over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands,” he said.
Then, saying, “Play the musical instruments again! Play them again! he had the instruments played three times.
Then the prince opened his mouth, looked out, and asked, “For what purpose have you come? “O Lord, for you...”
“He shall attain the kingship. “Where is the king? “He has passed away to the world of the gods, sir. “How many days have elapsed?
“Today is the seventh day, sir. “Has he no son or daughter? “There is a daughter, Your Majesty, but no son.
“I shall take over the kingship. They immediately had a consecration pavilion constructed and [adorned] the princess with all her ornaments.

Having adorned him and brought him to the pleasure garden, they performed the prince’s consecration. Then, when his consecration was completed, they presented him with a garment worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
He asked, "What is this, dear sirs? "It is a lower garment for you, Your Majesty. "Is it not too thick, dear sirs?
"There is nothing finer than this among the garments used by humans, Your Majesty. "For you..."
“Does your king wear clothing such as this? “Yes, Your Majesty,” they replied. “I do not think your king is a man of merit;
bring a golden pitcher! We shall obtain the cloth. They brought the golden pitcher.
He rose up, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, took water in his hand, and sprinkled it toward the eastern direction. At that very moment, the solid earth...
Having broken [the water], eight wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) sprang up. Again, taking up water, he sprinkled it in the four directions—south, west, and north—and so on;
having done so eight times in every direction, thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees sprang up.
He, having dressed himself in one divine cloth and draped another over his shoulder, [said to] King Nanda:
"Let the women who weave threads in the conquered territory not weave threads," he said, and having ordered that the drum be beaten accordingly,
he raised his parasol, adorned and ready, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, entered the city, ascended the palace,
and enjoyed great prosperity.
As time passed in this way, one day the queen, seeing the king’s great prosperity, showed an expression of compassion, saying, "Oh, what asceticism!
When asked, "What is this, O Queen? she replied, "Your majesty, your prosperity is indeed very great. In the past, having faith in the Buddhas, you performed wholesome deeds;
now, however, you do not perform the wholesome acts that serve as a provision for the future."
“To whom shall we give? There are none who possess virtue. “Your Majesty, Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants;
you should simply prepare the alms-giving, and I shall find the Arahants,” she said. On the following day, the king had the alms-giving prepared at the eastern gate.
Early in the morning, the queen, having undertaken the observance precepts (uposathaṅga), lay down on her chest upon the upper terrace of the palace, facing eastward.
"If there be any Arahants in this direction, let them come tomorrow and receive alms from us," she said.
There were no Arahants in that direction, so they gave that honor to the poor beggars.
On the following day, having prepared an offering at the southern gate, she acted in the same manner; on the next day, at the western gate; and [on the next day] at the northern gate.

On the day of the preparation, however, while the queen was likewise inviting them, Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha—the eldest of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were living in the Himālaya mountains, sons of Padumavatī—addressed his younger brothers:
“Sirs, King Nanda is inviting you; please accept his invitation. Having accepted, on the following day...
Having washed their faces at the Anotatta Lake, they came through the air and descended at the northern gate.
When people saw them, they went and reported to the king, "Your Majesty, five hundred paccekabuddhas have arrived.
The king, together with his queen, went out, paid homage, took their bowls, and having brought the paccekabuddhas up to the palace, he gave them alms there.

Having given [these gifts], at the conclusion of the meal, the king and the queen prostrated themselves at the feet of the Elder of the Saṅgha and the youngest member of the Saṅgha respectively, and made this request:
“May the noble ones not be distressed for lack of requisites; may we not diminish in merit.
Grant us your promise to dwell here for as long as we live. Having thus obtained their promise, he constructed five hundred leaf-huts and five hundred walking-paths in the royal park.
Having prepared dwelling places in every respect, they had them inhabited there.
As time passed in this way, the king’s border region rose in revolt.
He instructed his queen, saying, “I am going to suppress the border region; do not neglect the Paccekabuddhas,” and then he departed. Even before he had returned, the Paccekabuddhas—

The life-formations were exhausted. Having sported in the play of jhāna throughout the three watches of the night, the Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, at the rising of the dawn, grasped his support-board and, while still standing, attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue. By this same method, all the others did likewise;
thus they all passed away. On the following day, the queen smeared the place where the Paccekabuddhas had sat with green clay.
Having had flowers strewn and incense offered, she sat waiting for their arrival;
seeing no sign of them coming, she sent a man, saying: "Go, dear sir, find out whether the noble ladies are unwell in any way.
He went, opened the door of Mahāpaduma’s leaf-hut, and not seeing them there, [proceeded to] the walkway.
Having gone there, he saw [the Elder] standing leaning against a support-board; after paying homage, he said, "It is time, Bhante.

[The Elder replied,] "What will a body that has attained final Nibbāna say? He is likely sleeping. Having approached and touched the back of the feet with his hand, and having recognized the state of final Nibbāna by both the coolness and the rigidity of the feet, he went into the presence of the second [Elder].
Having thus learned that all three had attained final Nibbāna, he went to the royal palace. When asked, "Where are the Paccekabuddhas, dear father?
he replied, "They have attained final Nibbāna, Your Majesty. The Queen, weeping and wailing, came out and went there with the citizens;
she had the funeral rites performed for the Paccekabuddhas and [collected] their relics.
Having taken it, he established it as a shrine.
When the king returned after having pacified the border regions, he went out to meet the queen who had come to welcome him and asked:
"My lady, did you not neglect the Paccekabuddhas? Are the noble ones free from illness? "They have passed away, O King," she replied. The king thought: "Even for such as these..."
“The death of the wise has occurred; where can there be liberation for us?
Without going to the city, he entered the pleasure grove, summoned his eldest son, handed over the kingdom to him, and himself went forth into the ascetic life.
The queen, thinking, “Now that he has gone forth, what shall I do? likewise went forth right there in the pleasure grove.
Having developed the two jhānas, they passed away from there and were reborn in the Brahmā world.
While they were dwelling right there, our Teacher appeared in the world and, having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, eventually entered Rājagaha.
While the Teacher was residing there, this young Brahmin Pippali lived in the Brahmin village of Mahātittha in the Magadha kingdom.

He was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of the brahmin Kapila. This Bhaddā Kāpilānī was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of a brahmin of the Kosiya clan in the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom.
As they grew up in due course, when the twenty-first year of the young man Pippali and the sixteenth year of Bhaddā had arrived, their parents—
Looking at their son, they pressured him intensely, saying, "Dear son, you have reached maturity; you must establish the family lineage.
The young man said, "Do not speak such words within my hearing.
I will look after you as long as you live; after your passing, I shall go forth and enter the religious life."
After some days had passed, they spoke to him again. He likewise refused.
From then on, they continued to speak to him incessantly.
The young man, thinking, "I shall persuade my mother," gave a thousand gold *nikkhas* of refined gold and provided her with all her desires.

Having had a golden image of a woman fashioned by goldsmiths, and at the conclusion of the work such as its polishing and finishing, he had her dressed in that red cloth, adorned with beautiful flowers and various ornaments, and then summoned his mother, saying:
"Mother, if I can obtain such an object as this, I shall remain living in the house; if not, [I shall go forth]."
“I shall not remain here. The wise brahmin woman thought: “My son is meritorious, a giver of gifts, and one who has made a firm resolve;
he did not perform his merit alone. Surely those who have performed merit together with him will be like golden figures.
Having summoned eight brahmins and satisfied them with all their desires, she [prepared] a golden figure.
Having placed him upon the chariot, he dispatched them, saying: "Go, dear ones;
wherever you see a girl of a family equal to ours in birth, lineage, and wealth, take this very golden image as a gift and return.
Thinking, "This is indeed our business," they set out, and after considering, "Where shall we go? they headed toward the Madda kingdom.
“Let us go to the Madda kingdom,” they said, and so they went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom.
There, having placed that golden image at a bathing ford, they sat down to one side.
Then Bhaddā’s nurse, having bathed Bhaddā, adorned her, and seated her in the bedchamber, went herself to the water-ford to bathe. There—
Seeing that golden image, he struck it on the back, asking, "Who is this ill-mannered woman standing here?
Realizing it was a golden image and forming the perception, "This is my noble daughter," he said, "But she is not even like the one who received my noble daughter's lower garment.
Then those men surrounded him and said, "One such as this..."
They asked, "Who is she? [He replied,] "What is she? Compared to this golden image, my noble daughter is a hundredfold, a thousandfold more beautiful.
Even while sitting in a twelve-cubit chamber, she has no need for a lamp;
by the radiance of her own body, she dispels the darkness. Saying, "In that case, let us go," they took that hunchbacked woman and the golden image.
Having placed him upon a chariot, they stood at the door of the brahmin of the Kosiya clan and announced his arrival.
The brahmin, having offered a hospitable greeting, asked, "From where have you come? "From the house of the brahmin Kapila in the village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha," they replied.
"For what reason have you come? "For this specific reason. "Excellent! he said.
“Father, our brahmin is of equal birth, lineage, and wealth; I shall give him my daughter,” he said, and took the gift.
They sent a message to the brahmin Kapila, saying, “The girl has been found; do what must be done.
Having heard that message, they informed the young man Pippali, “It seems the girl has been found. The young man thought, “I—”
"I thought, 'They will obtain [these things],' yet these people say, 'We have already obtained them. Though I have no desire for them, I shall send a letter.
Having gone into seclusion, he wrote a letter: "Bhaddā, may you obtain a household life befitting your own birth, lineage, and wealth;
as for me, I shall go forth and renounce the world. Do not later feel regret. Bhaddā too, thinking, "It is said that such-and-such a person..."
Having heard, "He wishes to give me [in marriage]," she thought, "I shall send a letter," and in private she wrote a letter:
"May my noble son obtain a household life befitting his own birth, lineage, and wealth; as for me, I shall go forth into the religious life. Do not later feel regret.
Both letters met on the road. "Whose letter is this? "It is from Pippali-māṇava."
"Sent by Bhaddā. "To whom does this belong? "It was sent by Bhaddā to the young man Pippali.
When this was said, they both read the letter, and saying, "Look at the work of these children," they tore it up and discarded it in the forest.
Then, having written another letter of equal value, they sent it back and forth. Thus, the letters of the boy and the girl were alike devoid of any worldly honor.
The meeting of the two took place against their own will.
On that very day, the young Brahmin Pippali had a flower garland woven, and Bhaddā did so as well.
After they had both finished their evening meal, they placed those garlands in the middle of the bed, thinking, "We shall go to sleep. Then the young man lay down on the right side of the bed.
"Ascend. Bhaddā climbed up on the left side and said, "We shall know that passion has arisen in whichever side the flowers wither;

this flower-garland must not be allowed to touch [the other side]. However, out of fear of physical contact with one another's bodies, they spent the entire three watches of the night without descending into sleep, though during the day they did not even so much as smile.
There was none. Unattached to worldly pleasures, they did not manage the household while their parents were still living;

however, when they had passed away, they began to do so. Great was the youth’s prosperity—it was necessary to obtain as much as twelve measures of Magadha gold dust, enough to cover his body once it had been rubbed down and discarded on a single day. These were bound by machinery...
There were sixty great reservoirs, a twelve-yojana agricultural estate, fourteen villages equal in size to Anurādhapura,
fourteen elephant divisions, fourteen cavalry divisions, and fourteen chariot divisions. One day,
having mounted a decorated horse and surrounded by a great multitude, he went to the agricultural estate and stood at the edge of the field.
Standing where the ground had been turned up by the ploughs, he saw crows and other birds picking out and eating earthworms and other small creatures.
He asked, “Father, what are these eating? “Earthworms, Master. “To whom does the evil committed by these belong?
“To you, Master. He thought: “If the evil committed by these belongs to me, then...”
“What will eighty-seven crores of wealth do for me? What will twelve leagues of agricultural estates do? What will the reservoirs equipped with water-wheels do?
What will fourteen villages do? Having handed all this over to Bhaddā Kāpilānī, I shall go forth from the household life into homelessness.
At that moment, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, having had three jars of sesame seeds spread out in the inner courtyard by her nurses...
Surrounded [by her attendants], she sat down; seeing crows eating sesame seeds, she asked, "Mother, what are these eating?
"Seeds, noble lady. "Who would incur demerit for this? "You, noble lady. She thought:
"It is right that I should receive four cubits of cloth and a measure of boiled rice; yet, if by such a small amount as this, so many people..."
“Whatever unwholesome deed I have committed cannot be lifted from the cycle of existence even in a thousand lifetimes.
As soon as the noble son arrives, I shall hand over everything to him, depart, and go forth into homelessness.
When the young man arrived, he bathed, ascended the palace, and sat upon a magnificent couch. Then, for that wheel-turning monarch—
They prepared suitable food. After both had eaten and the attendants had departed, they sat down in a secluded and comfortable place.
Then the young man said to Bhaddā: "Bhaddā, when you came to this house, how much wealth did you bring with you?
"Fifty-five thousand carts, noble sir. "All of that, and whatever else is here—"
“In my home, there is wealth consisting of seven hundred and eighty million [coins], as well as various things such as reservoirs equipped with mechanical devices;
all of this I entrust to you alone. “But where are you going, noble lady? “I shall go forth into the religious life.
“Noble lady, I too have been sitting here waiting for your very arrival. I, too, shall go forth.”
To them, the three realms of existence appeared like a hut of burning leaves.
Having had garments dyed with astringent juices brought from the market, as well as clay bowls, they shaved one another's hair, saying,
"Our going forth is for the sake of those who are Arhats in the world," and having gone forth, they placed their bowls in bags and slung them over their shoulders.
They descended from the palace. Among the household slaves and laborers, no one recognized them.
Then, as they departed from the brahmin village and proceeded through the gate of the slave village, the inhabitants of the slave village recognized them by their deportment and gestures.
Weeping, they fell at their feet and said, "Noble sirs, why do you treat us like orphans?"
“Friends, we have gone forth thinking, ‘The three realms of existence are like a thatched hut on fire.
If we were to set even one among you free, it would not suffice for even a hundred years. You yourselves should wash your own heads and live as free men.
Having said this, they departed while those [others] were still weeping.
As the Elder was walking ahead, he turned back and looked, thinking: "This Bhaddā Kāpilānī, the most precious woman in all of Jambudīpa, is following behind me.
It is possible that someone might think, 'Even these who have gone forth cannot exist without each other; they are acting unbecomingly,' and thus some person might fall into evil."
"Having defiled my mind, he might fill the realms of misery; it is fitting for me to go on while abandoning him," he thought and resolved.
As he was walking ahead, he saw a forked path and stood at its head.
Bhaddā also arrived, paid homage, and stood there. Then he said to her, "Bhaddā, such a woman as you coming behind me..."
Seeing this, he thought, "Even though they have gone forth, these people are unable to be without women;
if the great multitude, with minds corrupted toward us, were to fill the states of misery, it would be a tragedy. He said, "At this fork in the road, you take one path, and I shall go by the other.
[The other replied,] "Yes, noble sir, for those who have gone forth, women are an impediment; 'even having gone forth, they cannot be without them'—this is what we..."
“They will show their hostility; you take one path, we shall go without you.

Having thus circumambulated him three times to the right and prostrated at four places with the five-fold salutation, he raised his hands in a brilliant añjali formed by the joining of ten fingers and said, “The friendship cultivated over the course of a hundred thousand aeons is broken this day.”
“You are of a right-hand birth; a right-hand path is suitable for you. We are women, of a left-hand birth;
a left-hand path is suitable for us. Having said this, they paid homage and set out on their respective paths.
At the moment they had split apart, this great earth thought: “Although I am capable of supporting the world-system and Mount Sineru, I am not capable of supporting your virtues.”
Crying out as if saying, "I cannot," she trembled; a sound like a thunderclap occurred in the sky, and the Cakkavāḷa and Sineru mountains roared.

Sitting in his fragrant chamber within the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana, the Perfectly Enlightened One heard the sound of the earth’s trembling and, reflecting on it with the thought, "Why is the earth shaking?
he perceived: "The young Brahmin Pippali and Bhaddā Kāpilānī [are seeking me]..."

“Having renounced immeasurable prosperity for the sake of the goal, they have gone forth. At this place of their separation, this earthquake has occurred through the power of the virtues of both [the Buddha and the two disciples].
It is fitting that I too should show them favor.
Having thus spoken, he emerged from the Gandhakuṭī, took his own bowl and robes, and without informing even one of the eighty great elders, traveled three gāvutas along the road.
Having gone out to meet him between Rājagaha and Nālandā, he sat down cross-legged at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree.
But instead of sitting like some other refuse-rag wearer, he assumed the appearance of a Buddha and sat down, emitting the eighty cubits-thick rays of a Buddha’s splendor.
Thus, at that moment, [the ground] was covered with canopies of leaves as large as cartwheels and gabled houses.

The Buddha’s rays, spreading and streaming forth from here and there, made that forest region one mass of light, as if creating the moment when a thousand moons and a thousand suns have risen together.

With the splendor of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the forest shone like the sky filled with a multitude of stars, or like water filled with fully blossomed lotuses and water-lilies. Of the Nigrodha tree...
Its trunk was white, its leaves were blue, and its fruits were red. On that day, however, the Nigrodha tree with its hundred branches appeared as if it were the color of gold.
The Elder Mahākassapa thought, "This one will be our Teacher; it is for his sake that I have gone forth."
Starting from the spot where he had seen [the Buddha], he went along bowing down again and again; having paid homage at three places, he said:
"Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am his disciple. Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am his disciple. Then the Blessed One said to him:
"Kassapa, if you were to perform this act of prostration upon the great earth, even she would not be able to sustain it."
"He could not. The homage you have rendered me, knowing such greatness of virtue in the Tathāgata, cannot move even a single hair on my body.
Sit down, Kassapa; I shall give you the inheritance. Then the Blessed One conferred the full ordination upon him with three exhortations.
Having done so, he departed from the foot of the Bahuputtaka Nyagrodha tree and [addressed] the Elder...
Having made Mahākassapa his attendant, he set out on the road.
The Teacher’s body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, while Mahākassapa’s body was embellished with the seven marks of a Great Man;
he followed step by step behind the Teacher like a great golden ship following in its wake. After traveling a short distance along the road, the Teacher [left the path].
Having approached, he showed the manner of sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
The Elder, perceiving that "the Teacher wishes to sit," folded his own worn-out rag-robe (pilotika-saṅghāṭi) into four layers and spread it out.
The Teacher sat there and, while smoothing the robe with his hand, said: "This [seat] of yours, Kassapa, is indeed soft."
“a robe made of rags from a dust-heap,” he said. The Elder, understanding, “The Teacher speaks of the softness of my robe;
he must wish to wear it,” replied, “Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One wear the robe.
“What will you wear, Kassapa? “I shall wear what I receive as your undergarment, Venerable Sir. “But what, then, will you—”
“Kassapa, will you be able to wear this rag-robe worn out by use?
For on the very day I took up this rag-robe, the great earth shook to its watery boundaries. This robe worn out by the use of the Buddhas cannot be worn by one of meager virtue;
it can only be worn by one who is capable, one who is able to fulfill the practice, and one who is a true wearer of rags.”
"It is proper to keep it," he said, and exchanged robes with the Elder.
Having thus exchanged their robes, the Blessed One put on the robe worn by the Elder, and the Elder put on the Teacher's robe.
At that moment, even this great earth, though insentient, thought: "Venerable sir, you have performed a difficult task."
"There has never been before a robe worn by myself given to a disciple;
I am unable to sustain your virtue," she said, as it were, and the earth shook, bounded by the waters.
The Elder, too, thinking, "I have now obtained the robe used by the Buddhas; what further remains for me to do? remained free from pride.
Having undertaken the thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) in the very presence of the Buddhas, he remained an ordinary person (puthujjana) for only seven days;
on the eighth day, together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Of Padumuttara, the Blessed One, the World-Chief, the Neutral One;”
When the Protector of the World had passed into Nibbāna, people performed offerings to the Teacher.
With uplifted hearts, the multitude was joyful and exceedingly glad;
as they were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, rapture arose within me.
“Having gathered my kinsmen and friends, I spoke these words:
‘The Great Hero has attained final Nibbāna; come, let us pay him honor.
Having agreed, saying ‘So be it,’ they gave rise to even greater joy in me.”
“In the presence of the Buddha, the Lord of the World, we shall perform an accumulation of merit.
Having fashioned a well-made offering, rising a hundred cubits high and spread over one and a half cubits,
a celestial palace shall ascend into the sky.”
“Having constructed a pavilion there, adorned with rows of palm trees,
and having gladdened his own heart, he worshipped the most excellent shrine.
Blazing like a mass of fire, it was like a *kiṃsuka* tree in full bloom.”
Like a celestial pillar in the sky, it illuminated the four quarters.
Having brought my mind to confidence therein and performed much wholesome merit,
and recollecting my former deeds, I was reborn among the Thirty-three gods.
“Established upon a divine vehicle drawn by a thousand horses,
my palace rose up on seven stories, towering high.
There were thousands of gabled chambers, all made entirely of gold.”
Blazing with their own splendor, they illuminate all directions.
"There were also other turrets made of ruby at that time;
they too shone with radiance throughout the four directions."
“Produced by meritorious deeds, these well-constructed gabled houses shine, made of jewels,
throughout the ten directions on every side.
As they were shining thus, a vast radiance arose.”
“I overcome all the gods; this is the fruit of meritorious deeds.
Sixty thousand eons ago, I was a kshatriya named Ubbiddha;
having conquered the four quarters, I dwelt upon the earth.”
“Likewise, during the Bhaddaka aeon,
thirty times I was a wheel-turning monarch of great power, delighted by my own deeds.
Endowed with the seven treasures, I was the lord over the four continents.”
There too, my palace rose up like Indra’s staff.
Twenty-four *yojanas* in length and twelve in width was the delightful city named Ramaṇa, with its strong walls and gate-towers.
“Five hundred [yojanas] in length, and half of that in width;
crowded with throngs of people, like the city of the Thirty-three.
Just as twenty-five needles might be thrust into a needle-case...”
They strike one another; it is crowded and adorned.
"Even so is my city, thronged with elephants and chariots;
always crowded with people, a delightful and supreme city."
“Having eaten and drunk there, I returned again to the state of a deva.
In my final existence, there was for me a perfection of lineage;
born into a family of brahmins, I was a treasury of great jewels.”
“Having abandoned eighty crores of gold, I went forth.
‘The four analytical knowledges... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, Kassapa approaches families like the moon, keeping his body withdrawn.”

Having praised him with such words as, "With a mind withdrawn, ever-new among families, free from arrogance," the Blessed One later, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, placed him in the foremost position among those who uphold the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who speak of the ascetic practices, namely Mahākassapa. By way of extolling his delight in solitude...
Giving exhortation to the bhikkhus and making manifest his own practice, he said:
"One should not wander about preceded by a group; one becomes dejected, and concentration is hard to find.
The gathering of various people is painful; seeing this, one should not take pleasure in a group."
“The sage should not go forth among families; if he is dissatisfied, concentration is hard to attain.
Being anxious and greedy for flavors, he neglects that goal which brings happiness.
For they have declared that this salutation and worship among families is indeed a mire.”
The subtle arrow is difficult to extract; honor is hard for a base man to relinquish.
"Having descended from my lodging, I entered the city for alms;
seeing a leper eating, I attended upon him with great care."
“Then, with a hand that was raw, he offered me a morsel of food;
as he was dropping the morsel, his finger was cut off right there.
Leaning against the base of a wall, I ate that morsel.”
Whether eating or having finished eating, no loathing arises in me.
My food is alms gathered from house to house; my medicine is fermented urine;
my lodging is at the foot of a tree; and my robe is made of discarded rags.
Having fully realized these, that person is indeed one who dwells in all four directions.
Where some are distressed while ascending the mountain peak,
there the heir of the Buddha remains clearly comprehending and mindful.
Supported by the power of his psychic attainments, Kassapa ascends.
Having returned from his alms round, Kassapa has climbed the mountain;
free from clinging, he meditates, having abandoned fear and terror.
“Having returned from his almsround, Kassapa ascended the mountain;
free from clinging, he meditates, extinguished while others are burning.
Having returned from his almsround, Kassapa ascended the mountain...”
He meditates without clinging, having done what was to be done and being free from taints.
“The delightful mountain slopes, spread with garlands of kareri flowers,
beautiful and resounding with the cries of elephants— those crags bring me joy.”
“Blue-black in hue and beautiful, cool with water and bearing pure [snow],
covered with *indagopaka* insects— those mountains delight me.
Resembling the peaks of blue-black clouds, they have the appearance of excellent gabled houses.”
“Those mountains, delightful and charming with the trumpeting of elephants,
bring me joy. Those mountains, their lovely slopes bathed by rain,
frequented by seers, and resounded by peacocks, bring me joy.”
“Enough for me, who am intent on meditation and resolute;
enough for me, a bhikkhu who desires the goal and is resolute.
Enough for me, a bhikkhu who desires comfort and is resolute.”
Enough for me, who am desirous of yoga, resolute, and poised.
Like *umā* flowers, covering the sky like clouds,
and strewn with flocks of various birds— those mountains delight me.
“Untrodden by householders, frequented by herds of deer,
and filled with various flocks of birds— those mountains delight me.
With clear waters and broad rocks, they are inhabited by *gonaṅgula* deer.”
“Those mountains, covered with ambu-sevala moss,
delight me. Such is my delight as I correctly contemplate the Dhamma with a one-pointed mind, that it does not equal even the pleasure found in a fivefold musical ensemble.”
“One should not perform much work; one should avoid busy people and not exert oneself.
For he who is eager and greedy for flavors neglects the goal that brings happiness.
One should not perform much work; one should avoid what is not conducive to one’s own welfare.”
The body suffers and is exhausted; being afflicted, he finds no tranquility.
Merely by striking his lips together, he does not even see himself;
with neck held stiff, he wanders about, thinking, "I am better."
“The fool, though inferior, considers himself superior to one who is truly superior;
the wise do not praise that man whose mind is arrogant.
But he who thinks ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am not superior’—”
Whether inferior, equal, or superior, he does not waver in his various stations.
"If a wise person praises one who possesses wisdom, who is such as that, well-composed in virtues, and devoted to mental tranquility— "
“He in whom no reverence for his fellow-celibates is found Is far removed from the True Dhamma, just as the earth is from the sky.
But those in whom moral shame and fear of wrongdoing are always properly established...”
Their holy life has been fulfilled; for them, rebirth is exhausted.
A monk who is agitated and restless, though clothed in rag-robes, does not shine because of them—just as a monkey in a lion’s skin.
“Unagitated and unflustered, prudent and with senses restrained,
he shines in his rag-robe like a lion in the mountain caves.
These many gods, possessed of psychic power and renown,”
Ten thousand devas, all of them belonging to the Brahma-realm,
stood with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the Hero, the General of the Dhamma, the great meditator, the concentrated Sāriputta.
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
We do not fully comprehend that upon which you rely for your meditation.
Truly wonderful is the Buddhas’ own domain; it is profound.”
"We did not know that we had come together for the hair-parting ceremony.
Upon seeing Sāriputta, who was worthy of worship and honored by the hosts of gods, Kappina then broke into a smile.
“Within the entire field of a Buddha, setting aside the Great Sage himself, I am preeminent in the ascetic qualities (dhuta-guṇa); no one equal to me is found.
The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.”
The heavy burden has been laid down; there is now no further becoming.
Gotama is unstained by robes, bedding, or food;
he is immeasurable, like a stainless *mūlāla* flower.
“Inclined toward renunciation through water, escaped from the three realms of existence— this great sage,
whose neck is the foundations of mindfulness, whose hands are faith, whose head is wisdom,
and who possesses great knowledge, always wanders in peace.”
He spoke these verses. Therein, the first three verses were spoken by way of exhortation upon seeing monks who were overly socializing with groups and families.
Among them, "one should not walk about preceded by a group" means that one should not walk or dwell surrounded and preceded by groups of monks.
Why? Because one who maintains a group becomes dispirited, and concentration is difficult to attain due to the arising of suffering.
When he assists with recitation, exhortation, and instruction, he becomes dejected and his mind becomes disturbed due to the failure of those being instructed to practice as directed;
consequently, for one who fails to attain one-pointedness through such social contact, concentration is difficult to obtain.
For such a person, even access-concentration does not succeed, let alone the other. This is what is meant by "association with various people."
The gathering of people who have diverse inclinations and diverse tastes by means of soft foods, snacks, and so forth—this is called "painful," meaning it is difficult and arduous.
"Having seen thus" means having seen in this way the manifold dangers in the gathering of a group, having observed them with the eye of wisdom.
One should not delight in a group, nor take pleasure in living in a group, nor desire it.
"A sage should not resort to families" means that one who has gone forth in this teaching should not approach families such as those of the kshatriyas and so forth.
Why is that? Because the mind becomes distracted and concentration is difficult to attain.

Being eager and intent upon visiting families, he becomes greedy for and falls into attachment for the sweet flavors and other delicacies obtainable among families, and thus becomes preoccupied with the various duties and obligations arising therein.

"Engaging in practice by oneself": "He abandons the goal that brings happiness" means that he abandons, relinquishes, and does not devote himself to that goal—consisting of the purification of virtue and so forth—which brings the happiness of the path, fruit, and Nibbāna for oneself.
The third verse has already been explained above.

The four verses beginning with "Having descended from the lodging" are spoken by way of giving exhortation to the bhikkhus, showing through the example of his own contentment with the requisites how a bhikkhu should practice.
Therein, "having descended from the lodging" is said because the lodging was on a mountain. "They attend upon him respectfully" refers to that leper.
Desiring to attain noble prosperity, and being in need of alms, I approached with reverence a family that gave choice food and stood there, like a man of great ambition.

"By the putrid" means by that which is putrefied due to the presence of leprosy reaching the bones. And here, "a finger was cut off" means that his finger was severed and fell into this bowl along with the food.
"Near the base of the wall": having sat near such a house wall for the purpose of inspiring confidence in that man, I ate—that is, consumed—a mouthful of food.
However, this practice of the Elder should be understood as occurring before the training rule had been promulgated.
This was because of the excellence of his noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*), by which he perceived even what is repulsive as if it were not repulsive, through the perception of non-repulsiveness.
As the elder was swallowing it, no loathing arose; however, for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), such things being eaten would cause the intestines to come out.
Therefore he said: "Whether eating or having eaten, no loathing exists in me.
*Uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa* means alms-food to be taken by standing up and remaining at the door of others' houses; [it is so called because] of the strength of one's legs.
The meaning is: alms-food obtained by going from house to house. "Putrid urine" refers to things such as harīṭaka fruit that have been soaked in cow's urine.
"He who delights in these" means that monk who, having delighted in these four requisites—beginning with the *uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa*—by means of the final term, partakes of them.
"He indeed is a man of the four quarters" means that such a person is, in every respect, one who is fit for the four directions, beginning with the east.
The meaning is that he is non-obstructive in some places and is able to dwell in any direction whatsoever.

Then, when people said to the Elder during his old age, "Venerable sir, how is it that you, while such old age is prevailing, climb the mountain day after day?", he spoke the four verses beginning with "Where some... (Yattha eke).
He spoke thus. In that context, "where" (*yattha*) means in the final stage of life. "Some" (*eke*) means certain individuals.

"Are distressed" (*vihaññanti*) means they undergo mental affliction due to physical exhaustion. "A mass of rock" (*siluccaya*) means a mountain. "There" (*tattha*) refers even to that time when one is worn out by old age.

By the phrase "clearly comprehending and mindful" (*sampajāno paṭissato*), he shows the absence of mental distress; by the phrase "steadfast through the power of psychic potency" (*iddhibalenupatthaddho*), he shows the absence of physical distress.
Because the defilements that are the causes of fear have been utterly eradicated, he has abandoned fear and terror.

"While [beings] were burning" means while beings were being consumed by the eleven fires, beginning with the fire of passion (*rāgaggi*). Being extinguished and cooled through the absence of the fever of defilement (*saṃkilesa-pariḷāha*), he was at peace.
Again, people asked: "Venerable sir, why do you dwell only in the forest and on mountains even in your old age? Are not these places such as Veḷuvana [suitable]?"

When it was said, "The monasteries are delightful," he spoke these twelve verses beginning with "Spreading with rows of *kareri* trees" to show that for him, the forest and the mountains alone were delightful.
Therein, "spreading with rows of *kareri* trees" means covered by lines of *varuṇa* trees;
some also say it means "covered with black-colored flowers. "Resounding with the cries of elephants" refers to the qualities such as the echoing calls of elephants roaming their feeding grounds.
They were awakened by the thunders;
they were drenched by the great cloud that poured down rain. "With delightful surfaces" means that their surfaces became beautiful due to the removal of dust, dirt, leaves, weeds, and so forth.
They are called "mountains" (*naga*) because they do not go to other regions, and "rocks" (*sela*) because they are composed of stone.
And the mountains received their names. "Resounded by peacocks" means resounded with sweet voices. "Alam" means fit or capable.

This same method should be applied to such phrases as "to one desiring to meditate" and "to one desiring welfare. "Bhikkhu" refers to one whose defilements have been broken; this is connected with the word "me" (to me).

"Equal to the umā flower" means resembling the *umā* blossom because of its dark-blue hue. "Covered by clouds from the sky" means that for that very reason, it is covered by black clouds like the clouds in the autumn sky; the meaning is that it is blue-colored.

“Uncluttered” means unconfused and unobstructed. Even for one surrounded by music endowed with the five factors—such as the *ātata* and so forth—there is no such delight as that which belongs to one whose mind is unified, whose mind is concentrated, and who correctly practices insight (*vipassanā*) into material and immaterial phenomena as impermanent and so forth. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Whenever one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates,
one gains rapture and gladness— that is the deathless for one who understands.
These two verses, beginning with “Kamma is the most important,” were spoken as an exhortation to those monks who delight in worldly activity and are greedy for requisites.
It has been said. In that context, "one should not have much work done" means that, being fond of work, one should not cause much work to be done nor undertake it;
however, the repair of broken or dilapidated parts is indeed permitted by the Teacher.

"One should avoid people" means one should avoid people who are unwholesome friends. "One should not exert oneself" means one should not make an effort by way of procuring requisites, forming groups, and so forth.
“*Anattaneyyametan’ti means that this—beginning with the undertaking of new building works—is not conducive to one’s own welfare; this is the meaning.

He states the reason for this: ‘The body suffers, it becomes exhausted. For one who is intent on new building works and wanders here and there, because of the lack of bodily comfort and so forth, he falls into hardship, becomes exhausted, and undergoes fatigue; and by that...”

Afflicted by physical exhaustion, that person does not find tranquility nor attain mental concentration due to the absence of practices such as the purification of the physical basis (*vatthuvisada*) and self-reliance (*attaneyya*).
The two verses beginning with "By merely striking the lips... are spoken by way of censuring one who is devoted to learning alone and who fancies himself wise; thereafter—
The latter two [verses] are spoken by way of praise for the wise person.
In that context, "by the mere movement of the lips" means by the mere turning of the lips in the form of recitation; the meaning is: by the mere act of reciting the Buddha’s word.
"He does not even see himself" means that, due to a lack of knowledge of what is beneficial, he does not understand the truth that is directly evident to himself, as it truly is.
The meaning is that one does not delimit the proper measure. "He wanders with neck held stiff" means that, being stiffened by conceit—thinking, "I am learned, mindful, and wise;
there is no one else like me"—he wanders with neck held stiff, like one who has swallowed an iron pin, showing no respect even toward those worthy of honor. He thinks, "I am superior."
"He thinks, 'I alone am better, I am supreme.

Regarding the phrase "The fool, being inferior, thinks himself superior": this means that while he is actually inferior and lowly, the fool—being dull-witted—treats himself as equal to another who is superior and excellent, and by virtue of his very foolishness, he conceives of himself in that way.

"The wise do not praise that": the wise, the learned, do not praise such a fool—a man whose mind is stiffened by arrogance due to a state of over-exertion; they do not praise him at all, but rather only censure him.
As for the wise person who thinks "I am superior," or who, out of a sense of equality with those inferior to himself, thinks "I am not... [inferior].
Not giving rise to even the slightest conceit such as “I am better,” he does not waver on account of anyone among the nine divisions of the ninefold types of conceit.
“Possessed of wisdom” means possessed of the wisdom of the supreme fruit; “such-like” (tādi) because he has attained the state of such-likeness (*tādibhāva*) toward the desirable and so forth;
“well-composed in virtue” because he is firmly established in the virtues of the Asekha-fruits; and [he is so] by way of the attainment of the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) of Arhatship.

"One devoted to mental tranquility" means that wise ones—the Buddhas and others—praise, extol, and honor such a person who has entirely abandoned conceit and whose taints are destroyed; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, having seen a certain monk who was difficult to speak with, he spoke the two verses beginning with "He toward whom his fellow-celibates... while elucidating the danger of being difficult to speak with and the benefit of being easy to speak with. These [verses] have already had their meaning explained.

Again, seeing a certain monk who was agitated and arrogant, he spoke two verses beginning with “An agitated, fickle monk,” thereby distinguishing the fault in being agitated and the virtue in not being agitated.
Therein, “like a monkey in a lion’s skin” means like a monkey covered by a lion’s skin; that monk, being possessed of such faults as agitation, [is like that].
One does not shine with the rag-robe, the banner of the Noble Ones, due to the absence of noble qualities.
To show who it is that does shine, the words "unagitated" and so forth were spoken.
These five verses beginning with "These many... are [spoken by] the deities of Brahma’s retinue as they pay homage to the Venerable Sāriputta.
This was said as a sign of the manifestation of a smile by the Venerable Kappina upon seeing them.

In that context, the word "these" (*ete*) is used because they were directly perceived. The word "many" (*sambahulā*) is used because of their great number; having delimited that great number, he says, "ten thousand deities.
"Deities" (*devā*) refers to deities by birth. Distinguishing their status as deities from others, he says: "All of them..."
He said, “The Brahmakāyika devas. Because they are endowed with great personal power of rebirth, great divine majesty, and a full retinue, he therefore said, “Possessing psychic power and renowned.
In response to the question, “Who indeed is your general? he replied by way of explanation: “The Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me...”
By saying, "Sāriputta follows after the Unsurpassed One," the Blessed One has authorized the Venerable Elder Sāriputta’s status as the General of the Dhamma;
thus he said: "To the heroic Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, the great meditator, the concentrated one.
In this context, "heroic" means possessed of valor through the crushing of the Māras of the defilements and so forth, and of great prowess.

"Great meditators" (*mahājhāyī*) means those who meditate greatly by reaching the pinnacle of the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*) and so forth. For that very reason, they are "composed" (*samāhita*) by way of having utterly destroyed all distraction.
"They pay homage" (*namassantā*) means they stand paying homage with their hands joined in reverence at their heads.

"Whatever it is depending upon" (*yampi nissāya*)—the Brahmās spoke thus because of their status as worldlings (*puthujjana*), thinking, "We do not know what object (*ārammaṇa*) he is depending upon or taking as a basis while he meditates."
“Accheraṃ vata” means “how wonderful indeed. “Of the Buddhas” refers to those who have awakened to the Four Noble Truths.
“The domain is profound” means it is supremely deep, exceedingly difficult to see, hard for ordinary persons to comprehend, not shared with them, and outside their sphere.
Now, in order to show the reason for its profundity, the passage beginning with “ye mayam” was spoken. In that context, “vālavedhisamāgatā” means:

The meaning is: "We who have come here, capable like archers who pierce a single hair, to penetrate even the most subtle object, though we have investigated, do not perceive it; indeed, profound is the domain of the Buddhas.
"That [was] likewise by the hosts of gods" means that Sāriputta, who was worthy of worship by the world including the gods, was [honored] at that time by those belonging to the Brahma-hosts.
Seeing him thus honored, the Venerable Mahākappina smiled, thinking:
"This is a domain for disciples where even the Brahmās, esteemed by the world, have no sphere of influence.
Then the Elder spoke this verse beginning with "As far as the Buddha-field extends," roaring a lion's roar concerning himself.
In that context, "in the Buddha-field" refers to the field of his authority (*āṇākhetta*).

"Setting aside the Great Sage" means excluding the Perfectly Enlightened One. For the Blessed Buddhas have indeed reached the highest pinnacle among all beings even by virtue of their ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*);
however, with minds impelled by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they observe such great benefit for beings and [choose] dwelling in village lodgings and so forth.

"To follow after" means that it becomes contrary to this or that ascetic quality (*dhutadhamma*). "In the ascetic virtues" (*dhutaguṇe*) refers to the qualities expected through the virtue of shaking off the defilements, such as being a forest-dweller and so forth.
Alternatively, this locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. The intended meaning is: "There is no one equal to me;
how much less anyone superior. For it was for this reason that this Elder was established in the foremost position therein.
In the verse beginning with “Not in robes,” the meaning already stated—“having set aside the Great Sage”—is made even more evident.

The fruit of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is non-adherence to craving regarding robes and the other requisites. Therein, the construction is: “not by the staining of craving when a robe has been obtained.
“On a bed” means on a lodging. “Gotama” is an address to the Blessed One by way of his clan. “Immeasurable” is because of the absence of defilements that would establish a measure.
And because of his immeasurable qualities, he is unfathomable. "Like a stainless *muḷāla* flower in the water":
just as a spotless, dust-free lotus is not smeared by water, so too the Blessed One Gotama is not smeared by the stain of craving and the like—this is the meaning.
Inclined toward renunciation, inclined toward going forth, and for that very reason, escaped from the three states of existence, he is free from the three realms of becoming.
"Released" means dissociated.

By showing those factors that constitute his limbs—namely, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth—through which he became untainted in whatever situation and inclined solely toward renunciation due to the perfection of their cultivation, the author spoke the concluding verse beginning with "necked with the foundations of mindfulness. In this context, it refers to a mass of virtues.

Because it serves as the foundation for wisdom (*paññā*), which is the head (*uttamaṅga*), mindfulness-establishment (*satipaṭṭhāna*) is its neck; thus, he is "necked by mindfulness-establishment" (*satipaṭṭhānagīva*).
Because faith (*saddhā*) is his hand for grasping blameless qualities (*anavajjadhamma*), he is "handed by faith" (*saddhāhattha*).

Because wisdom is the head of the body of virtues due to its being the supreme limb, he is "headed by wisdom" (*paññāsīsa*). [He is so called] because of the great attainment, the great range of objects, and the great majesty.
Because he possesses great strength and possesses the great knowledge known as omniscience (*sabbaññuta*), he is a "Great-Knower" (*mahāñāṇī*).
He always, at all times, dwells extinguished and cooled. Here, the sutta passage, “Well-concentrated... [the elephant]... the Nāga,” should be cited.
As for that which has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning, it follows the same method explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākassapa is finished.
The commentary on the Forty-Four-Verse Section (Cattālīsanipāta) is finished.
19. The Fifty-Verse Section (Paññāsanipāta).
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tālapuṭa.
The verses beginning with “kadā nu kho” (When indeed... belong to the Venerable Elder Tālapuṭa. What is his origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences...
During this dispensation of a Buddha, having been reborn in a certain family of actors in Rājagaha and reaching maturity,
he attained proficiency in dance performances appropriate to his lineage and became a world-renowned master of actors throughout all of Jambudīpa.
Accompanied by a retinue of five hundred women and with great theatrical splendor, he performed at festivals in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, receiving immense honor and hospitality.

Having obtained [permission], while wandering he came to Rājagaha; after putting on a performance for the city-dwellers and receiving honor and respect, because his knowledge had reached maturity, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
Having paid homage and sat down to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I have heard this from the actors of old, the teachers of former teachers, as they were speaking:"

“If that actor who, in the midst of the stage and in the midst of the assembly, makes people laugh and delight with truth and falsehood, is reborn after the breakup of the body, after death, in the company of the Laughing Devas—what does the Blessed One say about this?
Then the Blessed One refused him three times, saying, “Do not ask me this. When questioned for the fourth time:
He said: “Headman, these beings are already bound by the fetter of lust, the fetter of hatred, and the fetter of delusion by their very nature.

If one further provides them with things that provoke lust, hatred, and delusion, and through negligence [causes them to act], then at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in hell. But if he holds such a view as this: ‘That actor who, in the midst of the stage...’”
‘In the midst of an assembly, one who entertains and delights people with truth and falsehood will, after the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of the laughing devas.
This is his wrong view. And for one with wrong view, one of two destinations must be expected:
either hell or the animal realm. Having heard this, Tālapuṭa...
The village headman wept. "Village headman, did I not forbid you beforehand, saying, 'Do not ask me this'?
"Venerable sir, I am not weeping because of what the Blessed One has said regarding the future destiny of actors.
Rather, venerable sir, I am weeping because I have been deceived by the actors of old, my teachers and their teachers, who said: 'An actor [provides] a theatrical performance for the multitude.'"

“Having shown [this], he is reborn in a happy destination. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth, and upon receiving full ordination, applied himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā). In no long time, he attained arahantship.
But having attained arahantship, he reflected on the manner in which, prior to his attainment of arahantship, he had restrained his own mind.
Right attention arose; in order to demonstrate that by analyzing it in many ways, he said:
"When indeed shall I dwell alone, without a companion, in mountain caves?
Clearly seeing all states of existence as impermanent—when indeed will this come to pass for me?"
“When indeed shall I, a sage wearing tattered robes, clad in saffron garments, free from possessiveness and without longing,
dwell happily in the forest, having destroyed passion, hatred, and likewise delusion? When shall I [abandon] this body—
impermanent, a nest of death and disease, and afflicted by death and old age?”
“Practicing insight, free from fear, dwelling in solitude in the forest—when indeed will that time come?

When indeed, having taken up the sharp sword made of wisdom, shall I cut down that creeper of craving—which gives rise to fear, brings suffering, and follows after manifold forms—and dwell as its master? When indeed will that time come?”
“When shall I suddenly seize the sword of the seers, made of wisdom and possessing soaring power, and swiftly shatter Māra along with his host? When indeed will that happen at the lion-throne?
When indeed, in assemblies of the virtuous, shall I be seen by those who revere the Dhamma and are established in equanimity?”
When will that time come when, seeing things as they truly are and having conquered the sense faculties, I shall apply myself to the effort?
“When indeed will weariness, hunger, thirst, wind, heat, or insects and reptiles no longer afflict me while I am seeking my goal in the mountain fastness? When will that time come?”
“When indeed shall I go, with mind composed and mindful, to that which was realized by the Great Seer—the four truths so difficult to see? When indeed, through wisdom, will that come to pass for me?
When indeed, regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—however immeasurable they may be...”
"Engaged in tranquility, I shall see this burning state with wisdom: when will this happen for me?
When indeed, having been addressed with harsh words, shall I not become dejected because of that;
and likewise, even when praised, shall I not be elated because of that—when will this happen for me?"
“When indeed shall I weigh these things equally— logs, grass, and creepers, as well as these immeasurable phenomena,
both internal and external? When indeed shall the rain-cloud of the monsoon season,
with its fresh waters, drench me and my robes in the forest?”
"When will it be that I shall hear the cry of the crested peacock, the winged bird dwelling in the mountain caves, as he calls out upon the path frequented by the seers while it rains?
When, having heard his song in the forest, shall I rise up for the sake of attaining the Deathless and reflect upon it? When will that time be?"
“When indeed, by my psychic power, shall I fly unimpeded over the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Sarassatī, Pātāla, Khitta, and Vaḷavāmukha? When indeed will that terrifying feat come to pass?
When indeed, like a snake moving without attachment, shall I shatter my desire for the strands of sensual pleasure?”
“Extinguishing all signs of beauty, absorbed in meditation—when indeed will that be?
Like a poor man oppressed by his creditors who has found a hidden treasure, when indeed will I be joyful, having attained the teaching of the Great Sage? When indeed will that be?”
“For many years I have entreated you, Citta; enough now of this lack of respect for you.
Now that I have gone forth as a renunciant, for what reason do you not apply your mind [to me]?
Surely I, Citta, was entreated by you regarding the birds with variegated plumage in Giribbaja.”
Roaring with a sound like that of a great elephant, they shall delight you as you meditate in the forest.
“Having abandoned family, friends, beloved kinsmen, the pleasures of play, and the strands of sensual desire in the world—
having come here after relinquishing all these— you still do not find satisfaction in me, O mind.”
“This was for me alone, not for others; what is the use of lamenting at the time of donning armor?
Seeing that all this is unstable, I went forth seeking the state of the Deathless.
He who speaks with perfect consistency, the supreme among bipeds, the great physician, the charioteer of men to be tamed—”
“The mind is restless, like a monkey; it is very difficult to restrain for one who has not yet abandoned passion.
For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and enchanting, wherein foolish worldlings are bound.
Seeking renewed existence, they desire suffering; led by their own minds, they are cast down into hell.”
“In this forest resounding with the cries of peacocks and herons, dwell surrounded by leopards and tigers.
Abandon all longing for the body; do not fail me! Thus, O mind, you have exhorted me in the past.
Cultivate the meditative absorptions and the spiritual faculties, the powers, and the development of the factors of enlightenment and concentration.”
“Touch the three true insights within the Buddha’s teaching—thus you urged me on, O mind, in the past.
‘Cultivate the path leading to the attainment of the Deathless, the path that leads to deliverance and results in the destruction of all suffering;
the Eightfold Path that purifies all defilements—thus you urged me on, O mind, in the past.’”
“Contemplate the aggregates wisely as suffering, and abandon that from which suffering arises.
Make an end of suffering right here; thus indeed did you formerly direct me, O mind.
Contemplate wisely: ‘It is impermanent, it is suffering,’ and ‘It is empty, it is non-self, it is a calamity, it is a destroyer.’”
“Restrain the mind’s discursive thoughts,” so you used to urge me, O mind, in the past.
“Shaven-headed and disfigured, come under a curse, beg from house to house with an alms-bowl in hand;
apply yourself to the words of the Teacher, the Great Sage,” so you used to urge me, O mind, in the past.
“Wandering through the streets with yourself well-restrained, your mind unattached to families and sensual pleasures—
just like the moon on the night of the full moon— you used to direct me thus, O Citta, in the past.
‘Become a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a charnel-ground dweller, and a wearer of rag-robes.’”
“Be one who never lies down to sleep, always delighting in the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga); thus you used to urge me on, O mind, in the past.

Just as one who, having planted trees, desires to cut down that very tree at its root once it has borne fruit—so do you act toward this mind, when you urge me toward what is impermanent and unstable.”
“Formless, far-reaching, and wandering alone—your word I shall not heed here now.
For sensual pleasures are painful, bitter, and full of great fear; with my mind intent only on Nibbāna, I shall wander.
Neither out of ill fortune nor out of shamelessness,”
Not for the sake of wealth, nor from distant longing,
nor for the sake of livelihood did I go forth; rather,
O mind, my promise was made to you.
“Fewness of wishes is praised by the noble ones; it is the abandoning of malice and the stilling of suffering.
Thus indeed you directed me at that time, O mind, but now you are going toward what was practiced in the past.
Craving and ignorance, the pleasant and the unpleasant, beautiful forms, and pleasant feelings—”
"Delightful sensual pleasures have been vomited up; I cannot bear to swallow back what has been vomited.
'In every respect, O mind, you have done as I commanded; through many births, provoked by anger, you have wandered on.
Born from within yourself, yet out of gratitude for what was done for you, you have long transmigrated through suffering.'"
“O mind, you alone make us a brahmin; you make us a kshatriya, a king, or a lord.
At one time we become vaiśyas or śūdras, and even by your power alone we attain the state of gods.
It is because of you that we become asuras; rooted in you, we become denizens of hell.”
Furthermore, at times you have even been born among the animals, or perhaps as a hungry ghost, solely through the force of your own actions.
"Will you not deceive me again and again, showing yourself like a recurring actor?
You entice me like one who is mad, even though my mind has never failed you."
“In former times this mind wandered on its journey wherever it wished, wherever it desired, and in whatever way it pleased.
Today I shall restrain it with systematic wisdom, just as one seizes a rutting elephant by the trunk.
And the Teacher has determined for me that this world is impermanent, unstable, and devoid of essence.”
“O mind, leap forward into the teaching of the Victor; carry me across the great flood so difficult to cross.
“O mind, you are not as you were before; I am no longer able to return under your control.
I have gone forth into the teaching of the Great Sage; those like me do not remain subject to destruction.”
“Mountains, oceans, rivers, and the earth, the four quarters, the intermediate directions, below and above—all these conditioned states of existence are impermanent and afflicted.
Where will you go, O mind, that you might find happiness? What will you do with me, O mind, who am so devoted to patience?
You are not sufficient for me, O mind, as one who must follow your lead.”
“Never touch a double-mouthed skin-bag; fie on it, full of flowing streams of new filth!

Rather, you shall take delight there, having entered a cave-dwelling in a mountain slope—naturally beautiful, frequented by boars and deer, with its forest canopy sprinkled by fresh rainwater in the monsoon.”
“Birds with azure necks, beautiful crests, and lovely eyes, with wings and feathers of pure hue,
uttering sweet and melodious songs like the sound of thunder— these shall delight you as you meditate in the forest.
When the rain has fallen and the grass is four inches high, and the grove is in full bloom like a mass of clouds;”
“In the forest, I shall lie down like a tree; to me, that ground will become as soft as cotton.
I shall prepare it just as a master does, yet even with what is obtained there, let it suffice for me.
I shall not prepare it with such unremitting effort as one who has thoroughly beaten out a cat’s skin.”
“I shall train him just as a lord [trains a horse], so that even by what is obtained [thereby] it will be enough for me.
By means of energy, I will bring him under my control, like a skilled handler of the goad controls an intoxicated elephant.
For with you, well-tamed, steadfast, and straight, I shall proceed like a master of horsemanship with a horse.”
I am able to enter upon the auspicious path, always frequented by those who guard their minds.
"I shall bind you with force to the object, as one binds an elephant to a pillar with a strong rope;
thus well-guarded by mindfulness and well-cultivated, you shall become independent of all states of existence."
“Having cut off that which follows the wrong path with wisdom, having restrained it with effort and established it on the right path;
having seen both the arising and the passing away of things, you shall become an heir to the teachers of the highest word.
My mind, which was held under the sway of the four perversions, you have led around like a village circle.”
“Surely you serve the Great Sage, the compassionate one who cuts through the fetters and bonds.
“As a wild deer in a beautiful forest, I shall delight in that mountain—lovely, with its rain-cloud-crowned peaks.
There, on that undisturbed mountain, I shall find joy; O mind, you will undoubtedly reach the beyond.”
“Those men and women who live according to your will and under your influence enjoy whatever happiness there may be;
they are ignorant and subject to the power of Māra.”
“O Disciple, your mind delights in existence.
In this context, “kadā nu” means “when indeed? “Pabbatakandarāsu” means in mountains and in caves, or in the caves of a mountain.
“Ekākiyo” means alone. “Addutiyo” means free from craving; for craving is indeed called the “companion” of a person.
“Vipassanti viharissāmi”: they will dwell contemplating all existence as impermanent. The construction is:

when will they dwell contemplating every kind of existence—the division of existence into sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth—as “impermanent in the sense of having been and then ceasing to be”?

This is merely an illustration; for according to the statement, “What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self,” the other two characteristics [suffering and non-self] are also implied.
"It should be understood as 'already stated. 'When will this thought of mine come to pass? means: when indeed will this reflection of mine reach its culmination?
When indeed will it attain its peak? Here, *taṃ nū* is merely an expletive particle (*nipātamattaṃ*).
This is the summary of the meaning here: when indeed shall I, like a great elephant, [break] the bond of the chain?"
"Having severed the bonds of household life and gone forth, I shall dwell alone in mountain caves, cultivating physical seclusion;
without a companion and indifferent to all things, I shall practice insight into the impermanence and other characteristics of all conditioned phenomena.

"Wearing tattered robes" means wearing clothes that are worn out; this is stated with the addition of the letter *na* for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukha*). [The robes are] those whose value, touch, color, and integrity have been destroyed by being cut with a knife.

The meaning is: "wearing a rag-robe. A *muni* is one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*). One who is "without 'mine'" (*amama*) is so because of the absence of the sense of "mine" regarding either a family or a group.
One who is "without hope" (*nirāsa*) is so because of the absence of longing for any object whatsoever.

Having slain [the defilements], happy, and gone to the forest—having utterly eradicated defilements such as lust by means of the Noble Path, he dwells happily in the great forest through the bliss of the path and the bliss of the fruit.
When indeed shall I dwell [thus]?
"The nest of the disease of death" means it has become a nesting place for both death and disease. "This body" refers to this body comprised of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
For even these five aggregates—[as it is said]: "Bhikkhus, for a person immersed in ignorance and followed by craving... [are like a nest].
In such passages as "this very body is external name-and-form," it is called "the body.

"Afflicted by death and old age" means oppressed by both death and aging; the meaning is: "While I am practicing insight, I am free from fear through the abandoning of the causes of fear—when will that state come to pass?
"The producer of fear" refers to that which serves as the cause for the arising of the twenty-five great fears, both physical and mental.

And it is "bringing suffering" because it brings about all the suffering of saṃsāra. "The creeper of craving that follows after manifold [objects]" means that it follows after or stretches toward manifold objects, or indeed toward existence itself;
thus it is the creeper designated as craving. "Consisting of wisdom" means consisting of the wisdom of the Path;
it is a well-sharpened sword-blade held by the hand of faith, which is gripped by the strength of energy.
The construction is as follows: having grasped [the sword] and severed [the bonds], the reflection, "When indeed shall I dwell [in peace]?"—when will that come to pass?

"With fierce energy" means possessing sharp energy due to its keenness through serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). "The weapon of the seers" means it has become the weapon of the seers—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*).

"They shall swiftly shatter Māra together with his army" means they shall shatter Māra, along with the army of the defilements (*kilesa*), including the Māra of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra-māra*) and so forth.
"I shall break it suddenly and very quickly. "In the lion-throne" means on a firm seat; the meaning is the *aparājita-pallaṅka*.
"He has been seen in assemblies of the virtuous" means: because he is devoted to reverence for the Dhamma, by those who are reverent of the Dhamma;

by those who have attained the characteristic of being "such-like" (*tādi*); by those who see things as they truly are through unerring vision; and by those with conquered faculties, because they have conquered their faculties solely by means of the Noble Path.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "When will that reflection of mine come to pass, which I have thought while meeting with the Buddhas and other holy ones—'When indeed shall I be seen as one striving in exertion?
In this manner, the grammatical connection (*padayojanā*) is to be understood in all instances;
we shall, however, explain only the meaning of the words (*padatthamatta*).
*Tandī* means laziness. *Khudā* means hunger. *Kīṭasarīsapā* means insects as well as reptiles. *Na bādhayissantī* means they will not afflict me;
the intention is that because pleasure, pain, joy, and grief have been warded off by the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), they will not cause me distress.
*Giribbaje* means in a mountain cave. *Atthatthī* means one who is intent upon the goal known as one's own true welfare (*sadattha*).

"That which was known by the Great Sage" means that the Four Truths—which were known and penetrated by the Great Sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through his self-born knowledge—those four truths are very difficult to see for those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit.

"I shall go" means that with a mind concentrated by the meditative absorption of the Path, mindful through right mindfulness, and by means of the wisdom of the Noble Path, I shall penetrate and attain them; this is the meaning.
"Forms" (*rūpa*) refers to forms cognizable by the eye. "Immeasurable" (*amita*) means immeasurable by knowledge; the meaning is that they are undelimited and not fully understood.
"Tangible objects" (*phusitabba*) refers to tangibles. "Phenomena" (*dhamma*) refers to phenomena cognizable by the mind.

Alternatively, "immeasurable" refers to forms divided into many varieties by way of blue and so forth, sounds by way of the sound of a drum and so forth, tastes by way of roots and so forth, and tangibles by way of hardness, softness, and so forth.

The meaning is: "and by way of pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as the various distinctions such as sound and the rest. "From being ablaze" means from the state of being set on fire by the eleven fires.
"Endowed with tranquility" means possessed of the concentrations of jhāna, insight, and the path.
"I shall see with wisdom" means I shall perceive with the wisdom of the path accompanied by the wisdom of insight.

"Spoken with harsh words" means struck by ill-spoken speech. "The sign from that" refers to the cause of abusive language. "I shall not be dejected" means I shall not become sorrowful. "Then" (*atha*) means then. "Praised" means commended by someone.
"Sticks" (*kaṭṭha*) refers to logs of wood. "Grass" refers to bundles of grass. "These" refers to these five aggregates included within my own continuity.
"And immeasurable phenomena" refers to material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) immeasurable by any other aggregate of faculties.

Therefore he said: “Both internal and external. “One should weigh them equally” means that one should examine them all as being exactly the same by way of their impermanence and so forth, and by way of similes such as their lack of essence.
“Traveling on the path traversed by the sages” refers to the path of serenity and insight correctly set forth by the great seers, beginning with the Buddha.
"Moving about" means proceeding. During the rainy season, the dark cloud, with its fresh rainwater from the monsoon, shows his own reflection upon thinking while in the open air:
"When indeed will it rain upon me in the forest, wetting me with my robe?
"Of the crested peacock, the twice-born bird in the forest"—this refers to its being born twice, namely from the mother's womb and from the eggshell.
When, in the forest, amidst the mountain recesses, he hears the cry— the *kekā* sound— of the peacock (*mayūra*), the crest-born (*sikhā-sambhava*) *śikhaṇḍin*,
having observed the proper time and arisen from his bed for the sake of attaining the Deathless, that is, for the realization of *nibbāna*. When it is said "he reflects" (*saṃcintaye*),
the meaning is that he should attend to existence as impermanent and so forth, and thus practice insight (*vipassana*).
The construction is: "When indeed might one cross, without being stuck, by means of supernormal power consisting of meditation, these great rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarassatī?
Regarding "Pātālakhittaṃ baḷavāmukhañca": it is called *pātāla* because it is sufficient (*alaṃ*) for falling (*pāta*).

That very thing is the "thrown" (*khitta*), meaning it remained fixed in that manner at the time of the earth's formation; thus it is *pātālakhitta*. It is divided into [regions] measuring hundreds of *yojanas* and so forth.
The coastal regions within the earth of the ocean are places where various beings such as *nāgas* dwell, while others remain entirely empty.
"The mouth of Bālavā" refers to a great whirlpool-mouth in the great ocean;
for when the gates of the Great Hell are opened, a massive mass of fire issues forth from them, extending for many hundreds of *yojanas* in length and breadth toward that very place.
It burns the region of the ocean below; when that is burnt, the water above whirls around and falls down with a great roar. Therein lies the designation "the mouth of Bālavā.
Thus, one who is unimpeded by psychic power (*iddhi*) might wonder: "When indeed shall I cross over that terrifying and fearsome mouth of Bālavā cast into the abyss?"
"Parivitakkitaṃ" means: "When indeed will it be? When indeed, having produced supernatural power consisting of meditation (bhāvanāmaya), shall I exercise such power?
"Nāgo va asaṅgacārī padāleti" means:
just as a rutting elephant, having broken a firm pillar and an iron chain...
Having shattered [all attachments], moving without clinging, having entered the forest alone and without a companion, he wanders according to his own inclination;
even so, when shall I— having cast off the sign of all beauty, having discarded it without remainder, and not being under the sway of sensual desire—
