be devoted and intent upon jhāna, and thereby properly shatter, cut, and abandon desire for the strands of sensual pleasure?
"When will that which I have been contemplating ever come to pass?"—
like a poor man oppressed by debt who, having failed to repay what he owed,
becomes distressed by his debt and harassed by his creditors, yet eventually finds and acquires a hidden treasure.
Just as one who, having cleared his debt and living in comfort, would be satisfied, so too I have reflected:
"When indeed shall I, having abandoned sensual desire— which is like a debt— and having attained the Buddha’s teaching,
which is like a treasure-store filled with jewels such as gems and gold due to its being replete with the Noble Ones' wealth, become satisfied?"— that is to say, when will this come to pass?

Having thus shown the course of his own thoughts as they occurred by way of renunciation prior to his going forth, he now spoke the verses beginning with "For many years," demonstrating the ways in which, after having gone forth, he admonished himself and thereby attained realization.
Therein, "For many years you were entreated by me: 'Is enough for you this life in a house? refers to that.
"Enough, it is sufficient for you, O mind, that you have lived in the midst of the household for many years, bound by various sufferings.
Indeed, was I not entreated by you for this very thing over many years?
Now that I have gone forth as a renunciant—having been made to go forth by such exertion on your part—for what reason [do you trouble me]?"
"O mind, you do not apply yourself; having abandoned serenity and insight, you direct yourself toward base indolence"—this is the meaning.
"Was I not entreated by you, O mind?"—O mind, was I not indeed entreated, I think, by you?
If I was entreated, why do you now not practice in accordance with that? This is the intention [of the verse]. By the words beginning with "In Giribbaja," etc.,...
He displays a form as if he were begging. "Birds with variegated plumage" means peacocks, possessing many-colored tail-feathers and wings.
"Roaring with a sound like the thundering of clouds" means they have the habit of crying out intensely due to the cause of the thundering sound of the clouds.
"They will delight you in the forest, O meditator"—will not those peacocks delight you, who are devoted to meditation, in that forest?
This shows that he was requested by her.

“In the family” means within the circle of the family. “Having come to this” means having come to this forest place or to the state of renunciation (*pabbajjā*). “Furthermore, O Citta, you do not please me” means that even though you remain following me, you will not satisfy me.
“This belongs to me alone, for you do not belong to others” means, O Citta, this [mind] belongs to me alone; therefore, you do not belong to others.

But as for you, having acted like others, what is the purpose of this lamentation after you have declared your inclination toward fighting the Māra of the defilements at the time of donning the armor of meditation? The intention is: "I will not allow you to speak otherwise from now on.
"Beholding all this as unstable" means that because one sees that "this mind and all other conditioned phenomena of the three planes..."
"Unsteady and unsettled"—thus observing with the eye of wisdom, he went forth from his home and from sensual pleasures, seeking and searching for the deathless state, Nibbāna.
Therefore, the intention is: "O mind, without following after [sensual objects], I shall pursue only the search for Nibbāna.

The construction is as follows: the one who speaks what is well-reasoned, the speaker of well-spoken words, the supreme among bipeds, the Great Physician, the Charioteer of men to be tamed, said that the mind of one not free from lust is difficult to restrain, unsteady, and like a monkey—just like a wild monkey in the forest.

"Where ordinary people who lack knowledge are stuck"—meaning those who are stuck to, or bound by, both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*), those blind ordinary people, through that craving for sensual pleasures, desire rebirth and thus seek nothing but suffering.
And being led by their own minds into hell, they are cast down; being slaves to their minds, they perform karma that leads to hell.
This shows that one must restrain the mind alone; for having been cast out from well-being and happiness, one is led to hell by one’s own mind and not otherwise.

Furthermore, intending to restrain the mind itself, he said: "Resounding with peacocks and herons," and so forth. Therein, "resounding with peacocks and herons" means it is filled with the cries of crested peacocks and cranes.
They dwell there surrounded by leopards and tigers because they abide in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāritā*).
Living in the forest, preceded and surrounded by such animals as these, he speaks of the cultivation of emptiness (*suññabhāva*) by this means.
"He abandons regard for the body entirely; he abandons it being completely indifferent to the body"—by this he speaks of self-exertion (*pahitatta*).
"Do not fail"—do not fail this ninth moment, which is so very difficult to obtain. Thus indeed, O mind, in the past...
"You urge me on"—the meaning is that you, O mind, thus exhorted me toward right practice prior to my going forth.
"Develop" means produce and increase. "Jhānas" refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first.

"Faculties" refers to the five faculties beginning with faith. "Powers" refers to those same five as powers. "Development of the factors of enlightenment and concentration" [refers to the seven bojjhaṅgas and samādhi].
The seven factors of enlightenment and the four developments of concentration; and the three true knowledges, namely the three knowledges beginning with the knowledge of past lives.

Touch—attain—these while established in the teaching of the Buddha, the instruction of the Perfectly Enlightened One. "Leading out" means bringing about an exit from the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

"Plunging into the destruction of all suffering" means plunging into the deathless, having Nibbāna as its foundation and Nibbāna as its object. "Purifying all defilements" means the complete cleansing of the stains of all mental corruptions.
“Khandhā” refers to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*). “View thoroughly with wisdom” means:

view correctly by means of the appropriate method and way through insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) in various ways, such as [seeing them] as a disease, as an abscess, as a dart, as misfortune, as an affliction, and so forth. “Abandon that” means:
abandon, utterly sever, that craving which is the origin of suffering. “Right here” means: in this very selfhood (*attabhāva*).
"Impermanent": see it as impermanent because it has an end, because it is subject to cessation, because it is temporary, and because it is the negation of permanence.
"Suffering": see it as suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away, because it is fearful, because it is painful, and because it is the negation of pleasure.
"Empty": [see it as empty] because it lacks mastery, because it is ownerless, because it is without essence, and because it is the negation of a self.

It is empty; for that very reason, it is non-self (*anattā*). The construction is as follows: "one who sees clearly" (*vipassī*) [sees] it as "misery" (*agha*) because it is to be censured, and as "slaughter" (*vadha*) because it does not bring about growth or freedom from affliction.

"Restrain the mind's wanderings" means: for one who perceives the mind's wanderings, restrain—that is, repeatedly suppress—the eighteen mental wanderings based on the household life, such as the mental application of joy (*somanassupavicāra*), and so forth.
“Shaven-headed” (*muṇḍo*) means one who has attained the state of being shaven, having had his hair and beard shaved off.

“Ugly” (*virūpo*) means that by virtue of that shaven state, due to the growth of body hair and the wearing of tattered, torn saffron robes, he has become ugly and has reached a state of disfigurement.

“Has come upon a curse” (*abhisāpam āgato*) means he has encountered the curse to be uttered by the Noble Ones, namely: “He wanders about as a beggar, with bowl in hand. For this has been said: “This is a curse...”
“Monks, you wander about the world like a beggar with bowl in hand. Therefore he said: “Like one with a bowl in hand, beg for alms among families.
“Apply yourself to the Teacher’s word” means: exert yourself and devote yourself to the instruction of the Fully Enlightened One.
“Well-restrained” means: perfectly restrained by body, speech, and mind. They wander through the streets for the purpose of begging for alms.

"Moving among specific desires": the construction is that he moves like the moon on a full-moon night free from blemish—meaning, like the moon, he moves with a lovely appearance among families that are always new [to him].
"Always delighting in the ascetic virtues" means he is constantly devoted to the qualities of purification (*dhuta-guṇa*). "You make this mind like that" means you make it similar to that [moon].
Just as some man, desiring fruits, might plant fruit trees and then, before obtaining any fruit from them, wish to cut them down at the root— O mind,
you act in this way or in a manner similar to that. "That you would employ me, who am impermanent and fickle"—
this refers to having urged me toward the going-forth, and then, after I had gone forth and traveled the path, [denying] the fruit of the going-forth.
"Impermanent" means you engage [it] in the mouth of *saṃsāra*, causing it to proceed by way of binding.
They are "formless" (*arūpa*) because of the absence of form; for the mind has no such configuration or differentiation of colors such as blue and so forth.
Therefore it is said they are "formless. It is "far-reaching" (*dūraṅgama*) because of its proceeding to distant places. Even though the mind is not even the size of a spider's thread—

There is no such thing as "going" toward the eastern or other directions; rather, it is called "far-reaching" (*dūraṅgama*) because it apprehends an object situated at a distance. It is "solitary" (*ekacāri*) because it proceeds by way of moving alone;
for not even two or three minds are capable of arising together, but only a single mind arises within a single continuum.
When that has ceased, another arises as a single entity; therefore, it moves alone.

"I will not do your bidding now"—even though previously I followed under your control, from this moment on, having received the Teacher's instruction, I shall no longer be subject to the mind [of defilement].
Why is that? For sensual pleasures are painful, bitter, and fraught with great danger.
These sensual pleasures were painful even in the past, and they will have bitter fruit in the future as well;

being pursued by great fear through various forms such as self-reproach, they are truly terrifying. "I shall wander with my mind directed toward Nibbāna alone; therefore, I shall dwell with my heart set directly upon Nibbāna.

Demonstrating this very state of being directed toward Nibbāna, he said, "Not through ill fortune," and so forth. Therein, the construction is: "Not through ill fortune"—that is, due to misfortune or lack of glory—I did not depart from home.
"Ahirikkatāya" means by way of shamelessness, acting like one who engages in play according to what is blameworthy.
"Cittahetu" means being under the sway of the mind, like a person whose mind is unstable—sometimes being a Nigaṇṭha, sometimes a Paribbājaka, and so forth.

"Dūrakantāya" means through the state of having become distrustful after first showing friendship toward kings and others, and then betraying them. "Ājīvahetu" means for the sake of livelihood, caused by the need for a living.
"Having made this offering, out of fear for my livelihood, I neither went forth nor did I renounce the world.

By saying, "And what promise was made by you to me, Citta? he shows: "Citta, has not the promise been made by me thus: 'From the time of going forth, I shall no longer act under your control, but rather I shall act under my own control'?"
"Fewness of wishes is praised by the virtuous" means that it is commended by the Buddha and others as "excellent indeed is the state of being entirely free from desire for the requisites.

Likewise, the abandonment of malice—the relinquishing of the smearing over of the virtues of others—and the subsiding of all suffering, its pacification and extinction, are praised by the virtuous. Thus, O Citta, you exhorted me at that time.
“Friend, you should establish yourself in those virtues”—thus, Citta, you then exhorted me.
Now you depart; having now abandoned me, you are pursuing your own former habits, such as great desire (mahicchatā) and the like.
What is this?—this is the intended meaning.
With reference to this meaning, it was said: "You go to what was practiced in the past. To demonstrate that, it was said: "Craving and ignorance," and so forth.
Therein, "craving" refers to craving for the conditions; "ignorance" refers to the ignorance that conceals the danger in those very same conditions.
"The dear and the non-dear" refers both to the state of endearment consisting of affection for children, wife, and so on, as well as [attachment] to secluded lodgings and to wholesome states.
The state of being unpleasant, known as dissatisfaction, involves both attraction and aversion.
"Beautiful forms" refers to beautiful forms both internal and external. "Pleasant feelings" refers to pleasant feelings arising in dependence upon desirable objects.
"Delightful strands of sensual pleasure" refers to the remaining portions of the sensual realm that are mind-pleasing. "Vomited" means cast out from that which was dependent upon them.
"Vomited" means by way of suppression, abandoning, and relinquishing of desire and lust (*chandarāga*).
"I am not able to vomit back what has been vomited"—thus he says that he is unable to swallow back again those things already discarded; they have simply been relinquished.
"In all places" means in all states of existence (*bhava*), in all modes of birth (*yoni*), in all destinations (*gati*), and in all stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*). *Vaco* (speech).
"‘What was said by me,’ friend mind, means: ‘Your word has been carried out by me. And while doing so, ‘in many births you were not provoked’ means:
moreover, in numerous births you were not provoked by me; nor were you ever treated with contempt.
Nevertheless, although you arose within—having come into being inside me—because of your ingratitude, long wandering in suffering was caused by you."
"In the beginningless suffering of saṃsāra that has been produced, I have wandered and roamed for a very long time.

Now, in order to show in detail—by way of the distinctions of rebirth and the distinctions of destinations—the meaning briefly stated as 'you have wandered for a long time in suffering,' he said, 'You yourself... In this context, "rājadasī" means you were a king.
The letter *da* functions as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). The construction is: "At times we become Vaiśyas and Śūdras through your very agency (*vāhasā*).
Or, "Even our state of being gods (*devattanaṃ*)—that too you alone, O mind, bring about for us.
The term *vāhasā* means by way of being the cause. "Through your very cause" means by way of your being the cause. "Rooted in you" means having you as its condition.

"Surely you will betray me again and again"—meaning, "O mind, just as in the past throughout infinite births you, appearing as a friend but being an enemy, have betrayed me again and again, I think you will betray me now in the same way;
therefore, I shall not give you the opportunity to roam about as before. It is like one who is constantly being led on a leash.

They display themselves repeatedly, as if showing a mind worthy of being followed, like one who deceives a man worthy of following and produces a follower; thus they show various states of existence again and again.
"You entice me as if I were a madman" means that, sporting with me as if I were a madman, you display various things intended to allure.
"You entice me. "O mind, even though you have failed me," means: "O mind, what indeed have you failed me?
Tell me that"—this is the intended meaning.
"This mind before" means: this so-called mind, previously, through passion and so forth toward objects such as forms and the like, by which...
He desired according to his inclination; wherever desire arose for him, by its power he wandered wherever he wished and as he pleased.
And wandering thus as he liked, he traveled on his journey for a long time according to his pleasure.

Today, like a skilled elephant trainer known as a master of the hook, I have used systematic attention (yonisomanasikāra) as a hook, just as one would with an elephant whose rut has burst and who is intoxicated.
"I shall restrain him; I shall not allow him to transgress.
And my Teacher has resolved upon this world: "My Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has resolved upon this entire world of the aggregates (khandha) by means of his knowledge.
How so? By way of impermanence in the sense of non-existence after having been; and by way of the absence of anything whatsoever that is permanent or stable."
“Because of its non-existence, because of its instability, and because of the absence of any essence such as happiness—it is without core.

Leap into me, O mind, into the Conqueror’s teaching! Therefore, in order to practice according to reality, O mind, leap into and enter into my teaching, the teaching of the Conqueror, the Blessed One.
There is also a reading, “pakkhandimaṃ,” meaning: “Leap into this world with wisdom into the Conqueror’s teaching.”
"Carry me across as it truly is; leaping forth and proceeding by way of the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa), carry me across the great, most difficult-to-cross flood of saṃsāra.
This, O mind, is not as it was before"—O mind, this house of the personal existence (attabhāva) is ancient.
The meaning is: "It is not as it was for you. Why? Because of the words, "I am no longer fit to be brought back under your control," which means:

"Now I am no longer suitable to be turned back into your power. Since I have gone forth into the teaching of the Blessed One, the Great Sage, from the very moment of my going forth, those called *samaṇas* like me are no longer subject to destruction; the meaning is that they become *samaṇas* in the absolute sense.
"Mountains" refers to all mountains, such as Sineru, Himavanta, and so forth.

"Oceans" refers to the eastern ocean and others, as well as the cold oceans and so forth, but not every body of water. "Rivers" refers to all rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others. "The earth" is the ground.

"The four directions" refers to the four directions distinguished as east and so forth. "The intermediate directions" refers to the four directions starting from the southeast (east-south) and so forth.
Anudiśā means "the intermediate directions. *Adho* means "below," as far as the wind-element that supports the waters. *Divā* means "the heavenly worlds.
By the inclusion of the term "day" (*divā*), one refers here to the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) existing within those realms.

"All three existences are impermanent and afflicted" means that all three existences—the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth—are both impermanent and afflicted (*upadduta*), oppressed by birth and other such things, as well as by the defilements (*kleśa*) of lust and so on; there is nothing here [that is otherwise].
"There is indeed a place of safety; since that does not exist [here], where, O mind, will you go to find happiness?
Therefore, seek the escape from this"—this is the intended meaning.
"O mind, what will you do to me, who am steadfast, devoted to steadfastness, and established in the highest state of firmness?"
The meaning is: "Then you will not be able to move me even slightly. Therefore he said: "It is not enough for you, O mind, to be one who follows your own whims.
Now, making that same point more explicit, he said: "Never touch a bellows with both ends open; fie on it, full of the nine streams! Therein, *bhasta* means a bellows. *Ubhatomukha* means...
A cesspool with openings on both sides. One should never touch it even with a single foot;
indeed, one should not touch it at all—that which is full of various kinds of impurity, a flowing stream of filth from nine orifices like a wound.
"Fie upon that latrine!"—let there be condemnation of it.

Having thus exhorted the mind by means of twenty-eight verses through the method of restraint, he now spoke the verse beginning with “frequented by boars and deer” (*varāha-eṇeyya-vigāḷha-sevite*) while encouraging him by describing the place of seclusion and so forth.

Therein, “frequented by boars and deer” (*varāha-eṇeyya-vigāḷha-sevite*) means frequented after having been entered by both boars and deer. “On a ridge and a peak” (*pabbhāra-kuṭṭe*) means on a sloping place and on a mountain summit.
*Pakateva sundare*: naturally beautiful, inherently pleasing and charming.
Alternatively, the reading is *pakativasundhare*, meaning "in a naturally excellent region. *Navambunā pāvusasittakānane*:

in a forest recently sprinkled by the rainwater fallen from clouds during the rainy season (*pāvusa*). *Tahiṃ guhāgehagato ramissasi*: there, having entered the abode of the cave, you will find delight. In that...
Having entered a dwelling known as a cave within the mountain forest, you will delight in the joy of meditation.
"They will delight you" means that those peacocks and other creatures, by evoking the perception of a forest, will bring you pleasure.
"When it has rained, O Deva" refers to when the clouds have poured forth rain. "In grass four finger-breadths high" means that by that very falling of dew and water, there [is grass] there.
There, when the grass has grown four finger-breadths long, resembling a blanket of deep red hue;
when the forest is in full bloom like a dark cloud—meaning, when it has blossomed perfectly in a grove that resembles a rain-cloud;
and in the midst of the mountains—meaning, within the mountain ranges—I shall lie down like a tree branch, like a tree, being without possessions. That [bed] will be soft for me.
"That grass mat will be like cotton—soft and pleasant to the touch; my bed shall be like cotton, resembling a cotton-down mattress.
I will act in such a way that I am like a lord," as some powerful person [acts] toward his own obedient slaves and so forth.
“Citta, you bring [the mind] under your control; I too, Citta, will act in such a way that I shall indeed bring it under my own control.
How so? ‘Whatever is obtained, let that suffice for me’—regarding the four requisites, whatever kind or sort is obtained, let that be sufficient and adequate for me.
By this, he shows that because some beings here [act] on account of the arising of craving...
"Others follow under the sway of the mind, but I, avoiding the arising of craving from afar and making the mind like a slave, keep it under my own control.
"I shall not let you go, O mind, as one who is untiring, just as a well-beaten cat’s skin [is not released from its case]"—this is said for the purpose of avoiding the arising of craving in the mind.
Again, he touches upon that mind, just as another person would.

Just as someone, through the application of right effort and diligent cultivation, makes their own mind capable of work and fit for action, so too shall I, O mind, bring you—made capable of work and fit for action—under my control. How so?
Like a cat’s skin that has been well-beaten; "naiti" is merely a particle. Just as [a cat’s skin] that has been thoroughly beaten...
Just as a cat’s skin, when treated with oil, becomes fit for work, capable of labor, and easy to handle, so shall I treat you.
By means of energy, O mind, they will bring you under my control; therefore, O mind, by your own energy, generate the power of meditation and thereby bring yourself under my control.
Just as one skilled in handling an elephant brings a rutting elephant under control with a goad.
Just as a skilled elephant trainer, holding the goad, brings a rutting elephant under his control by the power of his own training—such is the meaning.

"By you, well-tamed and established"—here *hī* is a mere particle; O mind, by you who are well-tamed through the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), and for that very reason established because you have correctly entered the path of insight.

"By means of a horse that is straight, just like a trainer of horses": just as a trainer of horses, a driver of horses to be tamed, is able to set out from an unsafe place toward a land of safety by means of a well-tamed, straight horse—one whose gait is not crooked—so too am I able to set out upon the path.
"Peaceful" (*siva*): it is peaceful because of the absence of the defilements (*kilesa*) which produce the state of non-peace.
"By those who guard their own minds"— meaning by the Buddhas and others whose nature is to protect their own minds—
I am able, I am capable, to practice and to attain the Noble Path which has been cultivated at all times.
"I shall bind it to the object with force, like an elephant to a post with a strong rope"— just as a trainer of elephants [binds his charge].
"Just as one binds a great elephant to a hitching post with a strong, firm rope, so too, O mind,
shall I bind you to the object of the meditation subject by the power of development. 'That [mind] of mine will be well-guarded and well-developed by mindfulness'—
thus, O mind, having become well-guarded and well-developed by my mindfulness, you shall roam independent of all states of existence through the power of developing the Noble Path."
In all states of existence, such as the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava) and others, you will become independent of the bases for craving and the like.
Having severed those who follow by-deviant paths with wisdom— meaning, having seen the arising of the sense-bases (āyatana-samudaya), which leads one onto wrong paths, exactly as they are—

you [should apply yourself] to the restraint of the faculties, which is the counter-dependence against the outflowing and the agitation of the defilements that cause one to go astray by means of that very arising.
Having severed [the defilements] by means of the wisdom of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna-paññā*), one creates an obstruction by way of cutting off the stream [of consciousness].
"Restraining by means of yoga" means having restrained them through the power of dispelling [defilements] by means of yoga, which is designated as the cultivation of insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*).
"Establishing on the path" means having established them in the course of insight (*vipassanā-vīthi*) and having made them firm. But when insight has been brought to its culmination by the Path...

When you strike [the bell], then by means of the wisdom of the Path, through the demonstration that "whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation," you will see, without delusion, the dissolution and the emergence of the entire collection of sense-bases;
thus the meaning is: "you will become an heir and a legitimate son of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the foremost teacher in the world including the devas."

"Under the sway of the four perversions": established under the influence of these four perversions—perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the foul as beautiful, suffering as happiness, and the non-self as self—it follows along.
"O mind, you lead me around like a village circle," he says: "O mind, you drag me about like a village boy, here and there."
"You drag [me] along. Indeed, do you not serve the Great Sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is compassionate and the cutter of the ten bonds known as the fetters?
By saying, "You avoid such a person of great power from afar, yet you marry off an ascetic like me according to your whim," he praises the Teacher with a hint of lack of faith.
"Just as a deer," means: just as a deer delights in a forest that is well-variegated and undisturbed by trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth, being free and independent;

[and] "the delightful mountain garlanded with rain-clouds" means: because it is endowed on all sides during the rainy season with garlands of land and water flowers, it is like a garland of clouds (*abbhamālinī*); and it is "delightful" (*rammaṃ*) due to its seclusion from people and its beauty.
"Having obtained a mountain, I shall delight there on that peak"—this means, "O mind, you will undoubtedly and entirely come to ruin;
you will remain amidst the calamities of *saṃsāra*.
By saying, "those who act according to your desire and under your influence," he speaks of all ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) by way of their commonality with the mind.

The meaning of this is as follows: O mind, those men and women who abide by your will, your power, and your preference, and who experience or will experience that happiness dependent on the household life—they are the ignorant, the blind fools, subject to the power of Māra, habitually following the sway of the defilement-Māra and others, delighting in existence because they take pleasure only in the existence of sense-desires and so forth; such are your disciples who follow your instructions.
"But we are disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One; we do not act under your control.

Thus the Elder, having analyzed in various ways the appropriate attention that had previously arisen within him—which functioned as a restraint of the mind—delivered a discourse on the Dhamma by way of exhorting the monks standing nearby.
Furthermore, whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning from time to time is already clear in meaning because it follows the method explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Tālapuṭa is finished.
The commentary on the Fifty-Verse Section (Paññāsa-nipāta) is finished.
20. The Saṭṭhinipāta (The Chapter of Sixty) 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna In the Saṭṭhinipāta, the verses beginning with “Āraññiko” are the verses of the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna. What is their origin?
The account of his life has already been told in the *Dhammasenāpati-vatthu*.

For on the seventh day after his ordination, while the Elder was practicing the ascetic life near the village of Kallavāla in the kingdom of Magadha, when sloth and torpor had overcome him, the Teacher addressed him:
"Moggallāna, Moggallāna, do not, O Brahmin, be negligent regarding noble silence," and so forth.
Aroused by a sense of spiritual urgency, he dispelled sloth and torpor and, while listening to the meditation subject on the elements as taught by the Blessed One, increased his insight.
Proceeding through the three higher paths in succession, at the moment of the supreme fruit, he reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,
dwelt in the Himalayas, honored by hosts of gods. At that time,
I was a king of the nāgas named Varuṇa.”
“I can assume any form at will, dwelling in the great ocean.
Having left the assembly and its company, I set up musical instruments;
then, surrounding the Perfectly Enlightened One, the celestial nymphs played.”
While musical instruments were being played, the gods struck their own instruments;
hearing the sound of both, the Buddha also awakened.
Having invited the Fully Awakened One, I returned to my own abode.
Having prepared a seat, I announced the time:
"Surrounded by a thousand who have destroyed the taints, the Leader of the World,
illuminating all directions, has come to my abode."
“When the Great Hero, the God of Gods, the Bull among men,
had sat down together with the community of monks, I then gratified him with food and drink.
The Great Hero, the Self-Existent One, the Supreme Person, expressed his appreciation.”
Sitting in the community of bhikkhus, he spoke these verses:
“He who honored the Saṅgha and the Buddha, the Leader of the World,
by that clarity of mind he will go to the world of the devas.”
“Seventy-seven times he will exercise sovereignty over the gods;
he will dwell upon the earth exercising sovereignty over the land for eight hundred times.
And fifty-five times he will become a wheel-turning monarch.”
"Incalculable enjoyments shall arise for him for that long.
'In an immeasurable eon from now, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a teacher in the world.'"
“Having passed away from hell, he will go to the human state;
known by the name Kolita, he will become a kinsman of Brahmā.
Later, having gone forth into homelessness, urged on by the root of his wholesome merit,”
“He will be the second disciple of the Blessed One Gotama.
Ardent in energy, resolute, having reached the perfection of psychic power,
and having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.”
“Relying upon evil friends, fallen under the power of sensual lust,
with a corrupted mind I killed both my mother and my father.
Whichever womb I was reborn in— whether in hell or among humans— ”
“Possessed of evil karma, I am dying with my head split open.
‘This is my last [birth]; my final existence is now unfolding.
Even here, at this time of death, it shall be thus for me.’”
“Devoted to solitude, delighting in the cultivation of concentration,
having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
Even the earth, though very deep, thick, and difficult to shake— ”
Having reached the perfection of psychic power, I could shake [the earth] with my left big toe.
"I do not perceive any conceit of 'I am'; no pride exists in me.
Even toward a novice, I maintain a mind of reverence."
“In an immeasurable aeon from now, the deed that I performed—by that [merit] I have reached this ground;
I have attained the destruction of the taints.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Later on, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher, assigning his disciples to the foremost positions according to their respective virtues, placed him at the head for his possession of supernormal powers, saying:
"Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who possess supernormal powers, this one is the foremost, namely Mahāmoggallāna.
Thus he was established as the foremost for his supernormal power. By that very [act]...

These verses were spoken here and there by that Great Elder—who had been designated as foremost by the Teacher and had reached the pinnacle of the perfections of a disciple—on account of various specific signs.
At the time of the Council, they were compiled by the Dhamma-recorders thus:
“Forest-dwellers, alms-collectors, delighting in what comes into their bowls from gleanings;”
“With our minds well-composed within, let us shatter the army of Death.
Dwelling in the forest, subsisting on alms, delighting in what has come into our bowls from gleaned food,
let us shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.”
“Dwelling at the foot of trees, constant in practice, delighting in what comes into the alms-bowl;
with minds well-composed within, may we shatter the army of Death.
Dwelling at the foot of trees, constant in practice, delighting in what comes into the alms-bowl.”
We shall shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes off a reed-hut.
“Alas for that foul-smelling, putrid thing, once cherished as ‘mine’— this skeleton-cottage bound together with flesh and sinews!”
“Your body has nine streams, it is foul-smelling and obstructed;
the bhikkhu avoids it, just as one who desires purity avoids excrement.
If people knew you thus, just as I know you, [they would avoid you].”
One should avoid it from afar, just as a rain-cloud avoids a place of dung.
"It is even so, O Great Hero, just as you, O ascetic, have spoken;
herein some sink down, like an old ox in the mud."
“Whoever might think to dye the sky with turmeric,
or even with some other pigment, would only experience frustration.
So too is the mind that is well-composed within, which is equal to space.”
"Do not, O evil-minded one, attack me, like a bird attacking a mass of fire!
Behold this body fashioned by the mind, a heap of sores piled together—
afflicted, full of many thoughts, and lacking any permanent stability."
“Behold this form fashioned by art, with its gem and earring;
the bone wrapped in skin shines together with the garments.
The feet are painted with red lac, and the face is smeared with cosmetic powder.”
It is enough to delude the fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
The hair is fashioned into eight-lobed curls, the eyes are anointed with collyrium;
This is enough to delude the fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
“Like a fresh collyrium box, this putrid body is adorned;
it is enough to delude the fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
The hunter set the snare, but the deer did not enter the trap.”
“Having eaten the bait, we go, while the deer-trappers lament.
‘The snare is cut for the deer; the deer has not entered the net.
Having eaten the bait, we go, while the deer-hunters grieve.”
“At that time there was horror; at that time there was hair-raising terror, when Sāriputta, endowed with manifold qualities, had passed away.
‘Impermanent indeed are conditioned things, subject to arising and passing away…’”
Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is blissful.
“They penetrate that which is subtle, as one might [strike] a hair-tip with an arrow—those who see the five aggregates as alien and not as self.”
“Those who see conditioned phenomena as other and not as self have pierced through with precision,
like an arrow through the tip of a hair.
Like one struck by a spear, or as if his head were on fire,”
For the abandoning of sensual lust, let the mindful bhikkhu wander forth.
Like one struck by a spear, or as if his head were on fire,
for the abandoning of the lust for existence, let the mindful bhikkhu wander forth.
“Challenged by the one of developed self, who bears his final body,
I caused the Palace of Migāra’s Mother to tremble with my big toe.
This was not undertaken out of laxity, nor was it done with little strength.”
Nibbāna is to be realized, the liberation from all fetters.
"And this young bhikkhu is a supreme person;
having conquered Māra together with his mount, he bears his final body."
“Lightning flashes illuminate the cleft between Mount Vebhāra and Mount Paṇḍava;
there, in the mountain cleft, meditates the son of the Peerless Tathāgata.
Peaceful and restrained, the Sage dwells in remote lodgings.”
The heir of the Best of Buddhas, saluted by Brahmā:
“The Sage who is peaceful and restrained, who dwells in remote lodgings—
Salute Kassapa, O Brahmin, the heir of the Best of Buddhas.”
“Even if one were to pass through a hundred births among all the brahmin castes,
as a learned scholar (*sottiya*) perfected in the Vedas, again and again among human beings—
even if one were a reciter who had mastered the three Vedas— ”
This [offering] is not worth even a sixteenth part of the homage paid to him who,
before the morning meal, attained the eight liberations in forward and reverse order, and then went forth for alms.
“O Brahmin, do not dig up your own root; eat such a bhikkhu.
Place your mind in full confidence in the Tathāgata, the Arahat;
quickly worship him with palms joined, lest your head split apart.”
“He does not see the true Dhamma, being led by the cycle of rebirth;
he runs along the downward path, the crooked way, the wrong road.
Like a worm smeared with filth, he is infatuated with conditioned phenomena.”
“Submerged in gain and honor, empty Poṭṭhila goes away.
But look at this Sāriputta approaching, so beautiful to behold—
liberated in both ways, inwardly well-composed.”
“Visalla, who has destroyed all fetters, the possessor of the three knowledges, the conqueror of death, the one worthy of offerings among humans, the unsurpassed field of merit. 1187.
These many gods are possessed of psychic power and renown.”
Ten thousand deities, all of them Brahmapurohitas, stand with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to Moggallāna:
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!”
“Since your taints are exhausted, you are worthy of offerings, O Blessed One.
Honored by the god among men, you have arisen as the conqueror of death;
like a lotus by water, you are not defiled by conditioned things.”
“That bhikkhu who, in a single moment, has realized the world in its thousandfold extent, including the Brahma-world, and who dwells in mastery over the powers of psychic potency,
the passing away and rebirth of beings, and the knowledge of the times— he beholds the deities.
Sāriputta alone is supreme in wisdom, in virtue, and in tranquility.”
Even a bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore may reach this much at most:
“In an instant I can manifest a hundred thousand million bodies;
I am skilled in transformations and have attained mastery over psychic power.”
“Having reached mastery and perfection in concentration and true knowledge, Moggallāna by clan, in the teaching of the Unattached One;
wise and with faculties composed, he has utterly severed his bonds, just as an elephant [shakes off] a rotten creeper.
‘The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.
“What was that hell like where the immoral one was cooked,
having offended against the disciple Vidhura and the brahmin Kakusandha?
There were a hundred iron spikes, and all experienced individual sensations.”
Such was the hell that existed where the unvirtuous were cooked for having harmed the disciple Vidhura and the brahmin Kakusandha.
"The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, who fully understands this..."
"By attacking such a bhikkhu, O Kaṇha, you shall undergo suffering.
'In the middle of the lake stand celestial mansions that endure for an eon—
brilliant like beryl, beautiful, radiant, and luminous.'"
There, celestial nymphs of various diverse forms dance.
"He who fully understands this... [as before] ...O Kaṇha, you shall experience suffering.
He who was indeed exhorted by the Buddha while the Saṅgha of monks looked on...
He shook the Palace of Migāra’s Mother with his big toe.
“Whoever knows this... [as above] ...O Kaṇha, you shall experience suffering.
He who shook the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe... [as above] ...O Kaṇha, you shall experience suffering.
Supported by the power of his psychic success (*iddhi*), he caused the deities to tremble:
"He who fully understands this... [and so forth] ...O Kaṇha, you shall encounter suffering.
He who questions Sakka in the Vejayanta Palace—
"Friend, do you know the destruction of craving and liberation?
When asked this question, Sakka answered it exactly as it is:
'He who fully understands this... [as before] ...O Kaṇha, you shall undergo suffering.'"
“O Brahmin, you who stand in the Sudhamma assembly and question Brahmā—
even today, friend, that view of yours remains the same as it was before.
Do you see him, radiant, transcending even the world of Brahmā?”
“Brahmā, being questioned, answered his question exactly as it was:
‘My dear sir, that view which I previously held is no longer my view.
I see one who has transcended [the world], radiant in the Brahma-world.’”
“Thus today I shall speak falsely: ‘I am eternal, I am permanent.
He who fully understands this... [and so on] ...O Kaṇha, you shall encounter suffering.
He who has touched the peak of Mount Neru with liberation;
The forest belongs to the people of Pubbavideha and those men who dwell upon the earth.
“O Bhikkhu, disciple of the Buddha, whoever understands this—
by attacking such a Bhikkhu, O Kaṇha, you shall incur suffering.”
“Fire does not think, ‘I shall burn the fool’;
it is the fool who, having approached the blazing fire, is consumed by it.
In the very same way, Māra, you have approached the Tathāgata.”
"You will burn yourself, O fool, like one who touches fire.
"Māra has produced demerit by attacking the Tathāgata.
What do you think, O Evil One? Does my evil not ripen?"
“By your own doing, O End-maker, evil is heaped up for a long time.
Mara, be weary of the Buddha; do not place your hope in the monks.
Thus did the monk rebuke Mara in the Bhesakaḷā Grove.
"Then that dejected yakkha vanished right there.
Thus indeed did the Elder Venerable Mahāmoggallāna speak these verses.
Having been compiled in this sequence, they were thus established as a partial collection.
In this context, the four verses beginning with “forest-dwellers” (āraññikā) were spoken by way of giving exhortation to the bhikkhus.
“Forest-dwellers” means those who, having rejected dwellings within the village boundary, are forest-dwellers by undertaking the forest-dweller’s ascetic practice (dhutaṅga).

“Alms-food eaters” means those who, having rejected communal meals, are alms-food eaters by undertaking the alms-gathering ascetic practice; [those who subsist] on alms-food obtained from house to house...
"Those who subsist on what is brought to them": they delight in what has come into their alms-bowls through the practice of begging;
they are delighted by and content with that alone. "We shall shatter the army of Death":

because it acts as an ally in producing harm, we shall utterly destroy the stream of defilements which constitutes the army of King Māra. "Well-composed within": regarding the internal objects of the sphere of activity.
"Having become well-concentrated"—by this he states the means for its destruction.
"Dhunāma" means we shall shake off, we shall demolish.
"Sātatikā" refers to those who act with constancy, whose energy is continuously applied to meditation.
The four verses beginning with “In a hut made of a skeleton” were spoken as an exhortation to a courtesan who had approached to seduce him.
Therein, “in a hut made of a skeleton” means in a hut constructed from a chain of bones. “Stitched together with sinews” means sewn all over with nine hundred sinews.
In the forest, huts are built by erecting wooden poles and binding them together with creepers and the like.
[He] shows that [these things] are made, whereas you, however, are constructed by binding together with the most loathsome skeleton and the most loathsome sinews;
thus, they are exceedingly loathsome and repulsive. "Fie upon you, O full one, foul-smelling!"—this means:
fie upon you who are full and complete with various kinds of impurities such as hair and body hair, and for that very reason, foul-smelling. This is an expression of reproach (*dhīkāra*).
"Let it be. To say, "I shall claim this as mine," regarding that which is a danger arising from the putridity upon this foul-smelling mass—

this undertaking, which is impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive— is to exercise a sense of ownership toward such a body, which is like the limbs of dogs, jackals, and worms in another place.
"Like a bag of dung" means like a bag filled with excrement. "Bound with skin" means bound with skin, [a body] whose foulness is concealed by a mere covering of hide.

"A female ogress with goiters on her chest" means one who possesses two goiters situated upon her breast, resembling a *piśāca* (ogress) due to her terrifying nature and because she brings about misfortune.
"Those which flow at all times" refers to the nine streams, the nine openings of wounds, which flow constantly, day and night.
They flow; they drip with impurity.
They obstruct—that is, they become an obstruction to right practice. "Bhikkhu" means one who sees the fear in *saṃsāra*, or one whose defilements are broken;
thus, avoiding [impurity] from afar, he does not form attachment (*mamatta*). "And just as one desiring cleanliness [avoids] filth"—the word *ca* here is merely a particle.
Just as one of pure birth, desiring purity, having bathed including his head, would see filth and avoid it from afar—
so too is the meaning of "the monk. If people knew this body,
known as the "body," to be a heap of impurities exactly as I know it, [they would treat it with the same revulsion].
"I know this as it truly is; may the great multitude know it likewise, and may they avoid it from afar.
Just as one of pure birth would avoid a place of filth during the rainy season when it is constantly drenched in impurity, so too [the wise] avoid him.
However, because he does not know it as it truly is, he is submerged therein and does not lift his head—this is the intended meaning.

When the elder had thus analyzed the defects of the body, that courtesan, her face bowed with shame, established a sense of reverence toward the elder and said the verse, "So it is, O Great Hero," and having paid homage to the elder, she stood there. In this context, *ettha c'eka* means:
even though this body has such an evident and repulsive nature, some beings sink into despair due to the strength of their attachment.
They fall into [misfortune]. The meaning is that, like an old ox in the mud, or like a weak bullock fallen into the depths of a great quagmire, they encounter only ruin.
Furthermore, the Elder, showing that for one such as me this kind of practice is useless and brings only distress, says: "In the sky," and so forth.

He spoke two verses. Their meaning is as follows: If a person should imagine that he could dye the sky with turmeric or some other kind of dye, his effort would result only in frustration, bringing about mental distress, just like an endeavor directed toward what is not its proper object.
"That mind is equal to space" means: this mind of mine is equal to space because it does not cling to anything whatsoever within.
"Very well-composed"—therefore, do not approach me with a wicked mind. This means: "Do not approach one like me, who am submerged in sensual desires, with a base mind, a lowly mind.
"Like a moth approaching a mass of fire": just as a moth (*pakkhimā*) that approaches a mass of fire meets only with misfortune, so too is this for you; thus he shows it.

The seven verses beginning with "Passa cittakataṃ" were spoken as an exhortation to those monks whose minds had become perverted upon seeing that same courtesan. Having heard this, the courtesan became abashed and fled by the very path she had come.

The four verses beginning with "Tadāsī" were spoken concerning the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. Therein, "endowed with manifold aspects" means perfected in various modes such as the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara) and so forth.
"They penetrate what is subtle for you" means those yogis penetrate what is exceedingly subtle. How so?

"Just as a hair-tip pierced by an arrow": the meaning is that it is like piercing with the flash of a lightning bolt a single tip of a hair split into a hundred parts within the blinding darkness of night.
"Who, then, are they? he says: "Those who see the five aggregates as 'other' and not as 'self'.
In this context, "as other" means as non-self; for this is a demonstration of the rejection of the grasping after a self.

Therefore he said, "And not as self. By this, he has stated the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) regarding the truth of suffering by way of the Noble Path that has emerged from [the view of] non-self;
however, it should be understood that because of the inseparable connection with that [realization], the easy penetration of the other realizations is also thereby stated. Some, however, say:
"The five aggregates of clinging are called 'others' because they do not act for one's benefit..."
Regarding the phrase “seeing from another,” they say that by this [expression], everything has been correctly stated in particular. *Paccabyādhiṃsu* means they penetrated [the truth].
“As if struck by a spear” refers to the first verse spoken concerning the Elder Tissa; the second [verse] concerns the Elder Vaḍḍhamāna. Their meanings have already been explained above.

The verse beginning “Charged by one whose self is developed” (*codito bhāvitattena*) was spoken with reference to the *Pāsādakampana-sutta*. In that context, the phrase “by one whose self is developed, a bearer of his final body” (*bhāvitattena sarīrantimadhārinā*) speaks of the Blessed One.
The two verses beginning with "Not by slack effort" (*nāyam sithilam ārabbhā*) were spoken concerning a young bhikkhu named Vedana who was deficient in energy.
In this context, "slackly" (*sithilam*) means having made one's effort lax, that is, without exerting energy.

"By little strength" (*appena thāmasā*) means that this Nibbāna is not to be attained by a small amount of the power of energy; rather, it must be reached only by the great energy of the fourfold right striving (*sammappadhāna*). This is the meaning.

The two verses beginning with *Vivaram anupabhaṇtī* were spoken concerning his own state of seclusion (*viveka*). Therein, "honored by Brahmā" means he was praised and worshipped by Mahābrahmā and by the world together with its devas, who stood facing him.

The five verses beginning with *Upasantaṃ uparataṃ* concern a brāhmaṇa of wrong view, the nephew of the Elder Sāriputta, who, upon seeing the Elder Mahākassapa entering Rājagaha for alms, looked at him and thought, "I have seen a person of ill omen."

Having seen him, out of compassion for him—thinking, "May this brahmin not perish"—and for the sake of countering the disparagement of the Noble Ones, he spoke thus, urging him on by saying, "Pay homage to the elder.
In that context, "he would go through a hundred births" means he might undergo a hundred successive births. "A *sottiya*" means one born into the *sottiya* caste.
"Endowed with the *Veda*" means endowed with knowledge. "Of this one" refers to the elder. This, then, is the meaning here.
The summary of the meaning: That person who might approach, in successive order, the unadulterated lineages of the hundred Brahmin clans that have arisen again and again,
and who has attained proficiency in the branches of Brahminical knowledge (*vijjā*), being one who has mastered the three Vedas while fulfilling the duties of a Brahmin—
for such a person, this practice of the branches of knowledge and so forth belongs to the Elder Mahākassapa.
It does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit consisting of homage; indeed, the merit consisting of homage is far greater than that.
"The eight liberations" refers to the eight liberations beginning with the meditative absorptions (jhanas) of the form realm.

For the form-sphere jhanas, when attained through the process of development (bhāvanā), proceed by way of being thoroughly liberated from opposing states and by way of delighting in their objects without attachment.
They are called "liberations" (vimokkha) by way of dependence. However, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is so called precisely because it is liberated from opposing states.
In this context, however, only the meditative absorptions (jhāna) are to be understood. As for "in direct order" and "in reverse order":

starting from the first jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the direct order; starting from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the first jhāna is the reverse order.
In reverse order. "Before the meal" means precisely before the duty of eating. "He touched" means he attained various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) characterized by manifold manifestations.
"Then he went for alms" means: having emerged from that attainment, or after having entered that attainment, he now goes for alms;
this is said with reference to the Elder’s practice as it occurred on that very day.
But the Elder continued to behave in that very same way day after day.

"Do not attack such a monk" means: do not attack such a monk—one who has awakened following the Buddhas, whose great taints are exhausted, and whose virtues have been described even partially by terms such as "one who is a month [in seniority]"; do not harm yourself, O Brahmin, by attacking him. Thus it was said, O Brahmin.
Do not destroy yourself; do not uproot your own wholesome qualities by slandering the Noble Ones.
"Be well-disposed in mind" means: gladden your heart with the thought, "Oh, how truly excellent is this ascetic!

"May your head not split asunder" means: may your head not shatter into seven pieces because of the offense you have committed against him. Therefore, for the sake of making amends to him, act quickly.
With palms joined in reverence, he paid homage. Having heard this, the brahmin became afraid, agitated, and his hair stood on end; he immediately asked the elder for forgiveness.
The two verses beginning with "He does not see" were spoken by way of a reproach upon seeing the bhikkhu named Poṭṭhila practicing wrongly and engaging in a wrong livelihood.
Therein, "He does not see the True Dhamma" refers to this bhikkhu Poṭṭhila. Of those who are virtuous...

He does not see the Dhamma of the Buddhas and others—the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Why? Because he is led by the round of existence (*saṃsāra*), being preceded by the ignorance and other fetters that bind one to *saṃsāra*;

because he is destined for rebirth in the states of misery; because he follows a downward course, tending toward the lower realms; because he pursues a crooked path due to his adherence to deceit and fraud;
and because he wanders along and revolves within a wrong path, which is a false way of livelihood.
"Like a worm in filth": like a dung-worm, he is smeared all over with filth;

he is infatuated with and has fallen headlong into conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) mixed with the impurity of the defilements (kilesa). "Plunged into gain and honor": he is thoroughly and deeply submerged in gain and honor by way of craving (taṇhā).
"He goes empty, like Poṭṭhila": because of the absence of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), he is empty and lacks essence.
Having made the offering, the bhikkhu Poṭṭhila departs and proceeds.
The two verses beginning with "And seeing this... were spoken by one praising the Venerable Sāriputta.

Therein, "And seeing this" refers to the Venerable Elder Sāriputta; having seen him, with a mind full of serene confidence, he addresses his own heart. "Sudassana" (well-seen) [is the name of the village].

It is "beautiful to behold" because of the fulfillment of the aggregates of virtue (sīlakkhandha) of those beyond training (asekha) and the fulfillment of the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections (sāvakapāramīñāṇa).
It is "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāga-vimutta) because it is liberated from both sides:

from the form-body (rūpakāya) by means of the formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti), and from the name-body (nāmakāya) by means of the Path, through the respective stages of suppression and eradication by those very [attainments and the Path].
The meaning is "liberated. One should see him as "thornless" due to the complete absence of the thorns of passion and the like;

as "one whose bonds are destroyed" because of the thorough exhaustion of the yokes of sensual desire and so forth; as "possessed of the three knowledges" (tevijja) because of the attainment of the perfectly pure triple knowledge;
and as "the destroyer of death" (maccuhāyin) because of having shattered King Māra—such is the construction of the sentence.
These verses beginning with "Ete sambahulā" were spoken by the Venerable Elder Sāriputta while praising the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
In this context, "honored by men and gods" means honored with the highest honor by both humans and deities.
"Arisen as the conqueror of death" means having arisen in the world, he stands having overcome death. Alternatively, "honored by Naradeva" [is explained as follows].
He has arisen through the noble birth, having the Perfectly Enlightened One as his cause.
For the Perfectly Enlightened One, first being a human by means of karma, later became through noble birth the supreme deity, the god beyond gods;
therefore, he is called "the god among men" (*naradeva*). Honored by that Blessed One, the god among men, he has arisen by way of praise for one who has overcome death.

Having arisen in the world, being overcome by death yet the conqueror of death, he is not defiled by the smear of craving and views regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), just as a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) is not defiled by water;
the meaning is that he is independent of anything whatsoever. "Of whom" means by whom.
"For a moment" means for a brief duration of time. "A thousandfold" means of a thousand kinds. "The world" refers to the world of space (*okāsaloka*).

This is the meaning here: by that venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who possessed great psychic power (*mahiddhika*), the thousandfold world-system (*sahassilokadhātu*)—including its Brahmās, being like the Great Brahmā himself—was correctly known in a single moment;
he had direct knowledge through his mastery of the powers of adverting the mind and so forth, and he was skilled in the passing away and rebirth of beings.
"He sees them at the proper time" means that at the appropriate time, he sees the deities with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
The verse beginning with "Sāriputto" was spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna while proclaiming his own virtues.

Therein, the summary meaning of the verse "Sāriputto" is as follows: that bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore—having reached the limit, the pinnacle—by means of wisdom (*paññā*), that is, the perfection of wisdom; by means of virtue (*sīla*), that is, the attainment of virtue; and by means of tranquility (*upasama*), that is, the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*).
Sāriputta had reached the highest excellence among disciples in qualities such as wisdom. He had indeed reached the highest excellence in wisdom and virtue;

he was the very limit, the ultimate, and there was nothing superior to him. However, the Elder spoke thus in order to show that while Sāriputta was supreme in wisdom, he himself was supreme in concentration. For this very reason, he said, "Of a hundred thousand times ten million," and so forth.
In that regard, "he creates in an instant" means he would be capable of creating a hundred thousand million bodies in just an instant;

there is no burden for me in creating them. "Skilled in transformations, I have mastery over psychic power" means that I have not only attained mastery over mental-transformations, but have reached mastery over all forms of psychic power as well.

"Having reached the perfection of mastery in concentration and true knowledge": you have attained the ultimate limit of perfection through mastery over concentrations such as those with applied and sustained thought, as well as over true knowledges such as the knowledge of past lives.
In the teaching of that Teacher who is free from dependence on craving and other such bonds, you have reached the highest excellence by means of the aforementioned qualities.
You are "wise" (*dhīra*) because of your possession of fortitude; you are "Moggallāna" because your lineage is Moggallāna.

"Because his faculties were well-established, he possessed concentrated faculties; just as a noble elephant easily cuts through a binding of rotten creepers, so too did he utterly sever the entire bond of the defilements.
As for the verses beginning with "What was that hell like?", they were spoken by one who was threatening Māra after he had entered a storehouse and then emerged from it.
[The verses] were spoken by the Elder. Regarding that: "of what kind" means of what sort.
"Where the Dussī" means in which hell there is a Māra named "Dussī. "He was roasted" means he was roasted by the fires of hell.
"The disciple Vidhura" refers to the chief disciple of the Blessed One Kakusandha named Vidhura. "Having assailed" means having struck or afflicted. And "the brahmin Kakusandha."
The meaning is that he assailed the Perfectly Enlightened One. A stone hurled by Māra after being aimed at the Prince and released toward the Blessed One fell upon the Elder’s head.
"A hundred iron spikes arose" means that, it is said, for those reborn in that hell, their physical form was three gavutas in height; this was also the case for Dussīmāra.

He became exactly like that. Then the hell-wardens, taking up seven iron spikes each as large as the trunk of a palmyra tree—blazing, fiercely flaming, and glowing with fire—thought, "While standing in this very place, you committed evil by thinking it in your heart," and as if grinding lime in a lime-vat, they ground his heart to pieces;
then fifty men [attacked him] toward his feet.
Fifty people go along, striking with their heads directed forward;
as they go in this manner, having reached both ends in five hundred years, they turn back again and reach the center of the heart in another five hundred years.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "There were a hundred iron spikes. "All [the beings] experience individual sensations" means that they themselves produce distinct sensations.
It is said that this sensation is more painful than the sensation of the Great Hell (mahāniraya).

Just as the seven days of convalescence after drinking oil are more painful than the seven days of treatment, so too is the sensation upon emerging from the Ussada hell more painful than the suffering of the Great Hell.
Regarding the phrase "such was the hell," at this point the Niraya Sutta (Devadūta Sutta) should be cited to illustrate the hell.

"He who understands this" means he who, possessing great supernormal powers (*mahābhijñā*), understands this fruit of karma directly and face-to-face, as if looking at an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of his hand.
"The bhikkhu, a disciple of the Buddha" means a bhikkhu whose defilements are destroyed, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"O dark one, you shall undergo suffering" means [suffering] through entirely black, evil states.
Because you have come into contact with them, O Māra, you will experience suffering.
Regarding the phrase "in the midst of the rays": it is said that palaces produced by making the water in the middle of the great ocean their foundation endure for an eon (*kappa*).
Therefore he said, "the palaces endure for an eon. Their color is like that of beryl.
Their flames shine like bundles of reeds burning on a mountain peak; therefore, they are exceedingly radiant and possessed of splendor.
Thus he said: "Lustrous with the color of beryl, possessing rays, and radiant.
"Many of various colors" means that many celestial nymphs (accharā), possessing diverse colors such as blue and so forth, dance there in those celestial mansions (vimāna).

"He who directly knows this" means he who knows this celestial mansion (*vimāna*) by making its site manifest before his eyes. Indeed, this meaning is to be illustrated by the *Vimānavatthu* and *Petavatthu*.
"Urged by the Buddha" means urged and dispatched by the Perfectly Enlightened One. "While the great community of monks was looking on" means while the vast assembly of monks was watching.
"He made the Migāramātupāsāda shake with his big toe" [occurred] at the Eastern Monastery (*Pubbārāma*).
I shook with my big toe the Great Palace, built by the great female lay devotee Visākhā and adorned with a thousand chambers.
For on one occasion, while the Blessed One was staying in the aforementioned palace at the Eastern Monastery,
a number of junior monks sitting in the upper story began to engage in frivolous talk, paying no heed even to the Teacher.
Having heard that, the Blessed One, wishing to stir them up and make them fit vessels for his own teaching of the Dhamma, addressed the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna:
"Moggallāna, do you see these new bhikkhus intent on worldly talk?
Having heard this, the Elder, perceiving the Teacher's intention, attained the fourth jhāna based on the water-kasina as its object, which serves as a foundation for direct knowledge (abhiññā).
Having entered and emerged from that attainment, he resolved: "Let there be water in the place where the palace stands.
He struck the pinnacle at the top of the palace with his big toe; the palace tilted and stood on one side.
He struck it again, and it stood on the other side. Terrified and agitated by the fear that the palace might collapse, those monks departed from there.
They stood near the Blessed One. The Teacher, having observed their inclinations, taught the Dhamma.

Having heard it, some among them were established in the fruit of stream-entry, some in the fruit of once-returning, some in the fruit of non-returning, and some were established in the fruit of arhatship.
This matter is to be illustrated by the Pāsādakampana Sutta.
"Vejayantapāsāda": that Vejayanta Palace in the Tāvatiṃsa realm is a thousand yojanas in height, adorned with many thousands of turrets and gabled chambers.
It is named "Vejayanta" because it arose while Sakka, lord of the gods, was victorious after defeating the asuras in the battle between the devas and asuras and stood in the midst of the city;
referring to this, he says "Vejayantapāsāda."

For this Elder also caused him to tremble with his big toe. On one occasion, while the Blessed One was dwelling at the Eastern Park, Sakka, the king of the gods, approached him and asked about liberation through the destruction of craving.
The Blessed One answered him. Having heard this, Sakka was uplifted and joyful; he paid homage, circumambulated the Blessed One to the right, and returned to his own celestial realm.
He had departed. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thought:
“This Sakka approached the Blessed One and asked such a profound question concerning Nibbāna, and the Blessed One answered the question;
did he depart having understood it, or rather without understanding it? Suppose I were to go to the world of the devas and find out the truth of the matter.”
Thereupon, having gone to the realm of the Thirty-three, he questioned Sakka, the lord of the devas, regarding that matter.

Sakka, being intoxicated by his divine prosperity, became distracted. In order to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency in him, the Elder caused the Vejayanta Palace to tremble with his big toe. Thus it was said:
“He who, established in the power of his psychic potency, shook the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe and caused the deities to tremble”—
this meaning should be illustrated by the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta. The manner in which it was shaken has already been described above.
"He questioned Sakka" refers specifically to the elder’s inquiry regarding liberation through the destruction of craving as previously described.
Therefore it was said: "Friend, do you know [the nature] of liberation through the destruction of craving?

"Sakka answered him" means that when the elder caused the palace to tremble, Sakka—his heart being moved with spiritual urgency, having abandoned negligence and applied wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*)—gave his reply.
This was said with reference to the fact that the question had been answered. For at that time he spoke according to the very method taught by the Teacher.

Therefore it is said: "When asked the question, [he spoke] as it truly is. Therein, "he questioned Sakka" means that the Elder Moggallāna questioned Sakka, the king of the gods, regarding the fact that the liberation through the destruction of craving had been correctly grasped by him as taught by the Teacher.
He asked. For this is a present-tense verb used in the sense of the past. "Do you know, friend? means, "Friend, do you indeed know? What do you know?

He asked, "What do you know regarding the liberation through the destruction of craving?"—that is, he asked whether you know it in the same way that the Teacher has taught you the liberations consisting of the destruction of craving. Alternatively, "regarding the liberation through the destruction of craving" refers to his inquiry about the teaching of the *Taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta*.
"Brahmānanti" means [addressing] Mahābrahmā. "Sudhammāyaṃ ṭhito sabhaṃ" means standing in the Sudhamma assembly hall.
Now, this Sudhamma assembly hall exists in the Brahma-world, not in the Tāvatiṃsa realm; indeed, there is no heavenly world devoid of the Sudhamma assembly hall.
"Even today, friend, that same view remains which was previously yours"—this refers to having approached this Brahma-world.
"There is no ascetic or brahmin capable [of refuting you]; has that view which you held prior to the Teacher’s arrival here not vanished even now?
"Do you see it shining forth in the Brahma-world? [He replied:
"I see it transcending [into] the Brahma-world, as he is surrounded by disciples such as Mahākappina and Mahākassapa."
The meaning is: "Do you see the radiance of the Blessed One, who is seated after having entered the fire-element concentration, together with his disciples?
For on one occasion, the Blessed One, having assembled and sat down in the Sudhamma Hall in the Brahma-world, thought:
"Is there perhaps any ascetic or brahmin of such great psychic power that he would be able to come here?"
Knowing the mind of the Brahmā as he was thinking, [Mahāmoggallāna] went there and sat in the air above the Brahmā’s head;
entering the fire-element and emitting radiance, he considered the arrival of Mahāmoggallāna and the others.
Simultaneously with that thought, they too went there, paid homage to the Teacher, and, understanding the Teacher’s intention, entered the fire-element.
Sitting in the various directions and emitting a radiance, the entire Brahma-world became one mass of light.
Knowing that the Brahma’s mind was ready, the Teacher taught the Dhamma that reveals the Four Noble Truths.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many thousands of Brahmas were established in the paths and fruits; with reference to this, he exhorted him, saying: "Even today..."
"Friend, that is the view," he said, and spoke this verse. This meaning, however, should be illustrated by the *Baka-brahma Sutta*. For it is said there:
"On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Now at that time, a certain Brahmā had such an evil speculative view arisen as this:"
“There is no ascetic or brahmin who could come here. Then the Blessed One,
knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of that Brahmā,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, vanished from Jeta’s Grove and appeared there.
He appeared in the Brahma-world. Then the Blessed One sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahmā, having entered the fire-element attainment.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: "Where is the Blessed One dwelling at present?"

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw the Blessed One seated cross-legged in the upper story of that Brahmā’s abode, having attained the fire-element meditation. Having seen him,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, [he vanished from the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta and appeared before the Blessed One].
In this very way, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he appeared in that Brahma world. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna,
having attained the fire-element, sat cross-legged in the upper story of that Brahma’s palace, leaning toward the eastern direction and lower than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: “Where is the Blessed One dwelling now?

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Mahākassapa saw the Blessed One seated cross-legged in the upper story of that Brahmā’s palace, having entered the fire-element meditation. Having seen him, just as...
Just as a strong man... [as previously described] ...even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he appeared in that Brahma-world.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, leaning toward the southern direction, sat cross-legged in the upper atmosphere above that Brahma, having attained the fire-element concentration, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākappina: “Where is the Blessed One dwelling now?

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Mahākappina saw the Blessed One seated cross-legged in the upper story of that Brahmā’s palace, having entered the fire-element concentration. Having seen him, just as if...
Just as a strong man... [as previously described] ...even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he reappeared in that Brahma-world.

Then the Venerable Mahākappina, leaning toward the western direction, sat cross-legged in the upper atmosphere above that Brahmā, having attained the fire-element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Where is the Blessed One dwelling now?

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Anuruddha saw the Blessed One seated cross-legged in the upper story of that Brahmā’s palace, having attained the fire-element meditation (*tejodhātu-samāpatti*). Having seen him, just as...
Just as a strong man might... [as previously described] ...even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he reappeared in that Brahma-world.

Then the Venerable Anuruddha, leaning toward the northern direction, sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahma, having attained the fire-element, at a lower level than the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...
He addressed that Brahmā with a verse:
“Friend, even today you still hold that same view which you held before;
do you see [us] passing beyond, shining brightly in the Brahma-world?”
“Sir, that view which I formerly held is no longer mine.
I see one who is transcending, radiant in the Brahma-world.
How then could I today maintain: ‘I am eternal, I am permanent’?”
Then the Blessed One, having inspired that Brahmā with a sense of urgency, just as a strong man might...
[as before] ...even so, vanishing from that Brahma-world, he reappeared in Jeta’s Grove. Then that Brahmā addressed a certain member of his assembly:
“Come, dear sir, go to where the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is; having approached him, [speak thus].”

“Please say this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: ‘Is it true, dear Moggallāna, that there are other disciples of that Blessed One who possess such great supernormal power and such great majesty as you, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha?
“Very well, dear sir,” that member of Brahmā’s assembly replied to that Brahmā.
He approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and, having approached him, said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
"Is there, dear Moggallāna, any other disciples of that Blessed One who possess such great psychic power and such great majesty as you, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha? Then...
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed that member of Brahmā’s assembly with a verse:

“Many are the Buddha’s disciples: those possessed of the threefold knowledge, those who have attained supernormal powers, those skilled in discerning the minds of others, and the Arhats whose taints are destroyed.”
