Then that member of Brahmā’s assembly, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s words,
approached that Brahmā and said to him: “Venerable sir,
the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna says this:”
“Possessing the threefold knowledge and attained to psychic powers, skilled in the penetration of others’ minds, these many disciples of the Buddha are arahants whose taints are destroyed.
This is what that member of Brahmā’s assembly said. And that Brahmā, being pleased, rejoiced in the words of that member of Brahmā’s assembly.
With reference to this, it was said: "This matter, however, should be illustrated by the *Baka-brahma-sutta*.
By the term "the peak of Mount Mahāmeru," he refers to the entire king of mountains, Sineru, using the word for its summit as a designation for the whole.

"He touched with liberation" means that he touched it through higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) based on the liberation of meditative absorption (*jhāna-vimokkha*). "The forest" refers to Jambudīpa; for it is...
Because of its abundance of forests, it is called "vana" (forest). Therefore he said, "the lord of Jambusaṇḍa. Regarding "of the Pubbavidehas":
this refers to the region of Pubbavideha; the meaning is "Pubbavideha. And as for those humans who dwell upon the earth:
these so-called "earth-dwelling humans" are the people of Aparagoyāna and Uttarakuru. Indeed, because they lack houses, they are called "earth-dwellers."
The connection is: "He touched all the edges. This meaning, however, can be illustrated by the taming of Nanda and Upananda:

"Once, it is said, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please accept almsfood at my home tomorrow with five hundred bhikkhus,' and then departed."
On that same day, as the Blessed One was surveying the ten-thousandfold world system at the time of dawn, the Naga king named Nandopananda came within the range of his vision.
The Blessed One, reflecting—“This Naga king has come within the range of my vision;
what might happen?”—perceived the underlying potential for taking refuge.
Having seen him, he reflected: "This man holds wrong view and has little faith in the Three Jewels; who indeed might liberate him from this wrong view?
While thus reflecting, he saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, having attended to his bodily needs, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda,..."
"Announce to the five hundred bhikkhus: 'The Tathāgata is going on a journey to the celestial realm.

On that very day, they prepared Nandopananda’s drinking hall. There, seated upon a celestial jewel-couch with a divine white parasol being held over him, surrounded by the three kinds of theatrical performances and the assembly of nāgas, he [was served] from celestial vessels.
He was sitting there, watching for the proper time to offer food and drink.
Then the Blessed One, acting so that the Naga king would see him, set out toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven together with five hundred bhikkhus, passing directly over the top of his palace.
Now at that time, the Naga king Nandopananda held such an evil view as this:
The thought arose in him: "Indeed, these shaven-headed ascetics enter and exit the abode of the Tāvatiṃsa devas above our realm;
from now on, I will no longer allow them to pass while scattering the dust from their feet upon my head.
Having risen and gone to the foot of Sineru, he [assumed] that state of existence.
Having left Sineru and encircled it seven times with his coils, he spread his hood over it;
then, catching the Tāvatiṃsa heaven beneath his hood, he made himself invisible.
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to the Blessed One: “Formerly, Bhante, in this place...”
Standing here, I saw Sineru; I saw the terraces of Sineru; I saw the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; I saw the Vejayanta Palace;
and I saw the banner atop the Vejayanta Palace. But what, Bhante, is the cause and what is the reason that now I see neither Sineru... nor the banner atop the Vejayanta Palace?
“Do you see him? “I do, Bhante. “Rāṭṭhapāla, this Nāga king named Nandopananda is angry with you;
he has encircled Sineru seven times with his coils, covered it above with his hood, and stands there having created darkness.
“I shall tame him, Bhante. But the Blessed One did not grant him permission. Then the Venerable Bhaddiya—
"Venerable Rāhula!"—at these words, all the bhikkhus rose up in succession. But the Blessed One did not grant permission.
At the end, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, "Venerable Sir, I shall subdue him. "Subdue him, Moggallāna," the Blessed One granted permission.
The Elder, casting off his own form, manifested himself in the great appearance of a royal nāga.
Having surrounded Nandopananda fourteen times with his coils, he placed his own hood upon the head of the other’s hood and pressed him down together with Mount Sineru. The Naga king emitted smoke;
the Elder thought, “Smoke exists not only in your body, but in mine as well,” and he too emitted smoke. The Naga king’s smoke did not distress the Elder.
However, the Elder’s smoke vexed the Nāga king. Thereupon the Nāga king blazed up.
The Elder also blazed up, thinking, “Fire exists not only in your body; it exists in mine as well.
The Nāga king’s heat did not vex the Elder, but the Elder’s heat vexed the Nāga king. The Nāga king thought, “This man is crushing me with Mount Sineru...”
Thinking, "He both smokes and blazes," he asked in return, "Sir, who are you?
"Nanda, I am Moggallāna. "Venerable sir, remain in your own state as a monk.
Thereupon, the Elder abandoned that form and entered through his right ear-canal and emerged from his left ear-canal.
He emerged; having entered through the left ear-canal, he emerged from the right ear-canal.
Likewise, having entered through the right nostril, he emerged from the left nostril; having entered through the left nostril, he emerged from the right nostril.
Then the Naga king opened his mouth. The Elder entered through the mouth and [traversed] within the belly from the east to the west.
And he paced up and down. The Blessed One said, “Moggallāna, pay attention; this is a nāga of great psychic power.
The Elder replied, “Venerable sir, my four bases of psychic power have been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken.
Let alone Nandopananda, Venerable sir; I could handle nāga kings equal to Nandopananda.”
“‘I could tame even a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand,’ he said.
The Nāga king thought: “While entering, he was not seen by me; now, at the time of his departure, I shall seize him between my fangs and crush him like a sesame seed!
Having thought this, he said: “Come out, venerable sir! Do not [enter] into my belly.”
"He has been harassing me as I walked back and forth," he said. The Elder went out and stood outside.
When the Naga king saw him, thinking, "This is he," he released a blast of breath from his nostrils. The Elder entered the fourth jhāna;
not even a single pore of his body could the wind move. [The Buddha said: "It is said that the remaining monks were able to perform all the miracles from the beginning."
"However, having reached this place, they will not be able to attain [jhāna] so quickly," thinking thus, the Blessed One did not permit them to subdue the Naga king.
[The Naga king thought: "I was unable to move even a single hair-pore of this ascetic with the wind from my nostrils; he possesses great psychic power."
"He is indeed a recluse," he thought. The Elder, casting off his own form and manifesting the shape of a garuḍa, pursued the Naga king while displaying a garuḍa-gale.
The Naga king, in turn, cast off that form and manifested the appearance of a young brahmin;
saying, "Venerable sir, I go for refuge to you," he bowed at the Elder's feet.
The Elder thought, “The Teacher has arrived; come, let us go,” and having tamed the Naga king and rendered him harmless, he took him and went into the presence of the Blessed One.
The Naga king, having paid homage to the Blessed One, said, “Venerable Sir, I go for refuge to you.
The Blessed One, saying, “May you be happy, O Naga king,” surrounded by the community of monks, departed.
He went to the residence of Anāthapiṇḍika.
Anāthapiṇḍika asked, "Venerable sir, why have you arrived so late? [Moggallāna replied,] "A battle took place between Moggallāna and Nandopananda.
"But whose victory was it, venerable sir, and whose defeat? "It was Moggallāna’s victory."
“Nanda’s defeat. Anāthapiṇḍika said, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal for seven days in succession;
for seven days I shall perform an offering of honor for the Elder.

Having said this, he performed a great offering of honor for five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Buddha for seven days. Therefore it was said: “It should be illustrated by the taming of Nanda and Upananda.”
"He who fully understands this" means he knows this aforementioned liberation by way of making contact with it.
Fire does not think, "I am burning the fool," nor does fire intend in such a way;
nor does it make an effort or exertion for the purpose of burning. Rather, the fool himself [thinks], "This is a slow-witted person," as if toward that which is blazing without even flickering.
Just as one is burned by approaching a fire, even so, Māra, we do not wish to burn you nor do we wish to harm you;
rather, by attacking the noble disciple— who is like a mass of fire because of his having come forth in such a way— you will burn yourself,
and you shall not be released from the suffering of that burning.
"He generates demerit" means he acquires demerit. "My evil does not ripen"—thinking "my evil does not ripen," why, O Māra, do you think thus?
This is not so. "The evil of one who acts accumulates for you": for one who acts, evil certainly accumulates for a long time, for a long duration, to his disadvantage and suffering.
"O Māra, be disenchanted with the Buddha": be disenchanted with the Buddha who has awakened to the Four Truths, and with the disciples of the Buddha.
“Having become disillusioned with the work of others, do not harbor hope for a monk”—that is, do not harbor the hope, “I shall oppose or harass the monks.
“Thus” means in this way. “He rebuked Māra”: the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna [said], “Māra, be disillusioned... do not harbor hope for a monk.
“In the Bhesakaḷā Grove” means in the forest of that name. “From that” means because of that rebuke. “That spirit was dejected” refers to Māra.
Becoming dejected, he vanished right there, in that very place, and went out of sight.

And this verse was placed [in the canon] at the time of the Dhamma-saṅgāyana. As for whatever here has not been analyzed in terms of its meaning from time to time, that is self-evident because it follows the method already stated below.

Thus this Great Elder, having terrified Māra and performed a service for sentient beings—unshared with other disciples—by means of his travels among the gods and his journeys through the hells, attained final Nibbāna at the end of his lifespan.
And while attaining final Nibbāna, he made a vow at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassi; from that time forth, in various successive births, he performed sublime meritorious deeds.
Although he stood at the pinnacle of the perfections of a disciple, due to a fragment of karma arising from an evil deed committed in the past, he was harassed by thieves incited by the sectarians;
having undergone no small amount of physical suffering, he attained final nibbāna.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest in the World,
the Bull among Men, dwelt in the Himalayas, honored by the hosts of gods.
Then the Blessed One, the Conqueror, having descended from there, wandered on his journey.”
Out of compassion for the group of seven, he approached Bārāṇasī.
Surrounded by a thousand monks whose taints were exhausted, the Leader of the World,
the Great Sage, shone forth, illuminating all directions.
“Then, having been a householder, urged on by my friend Sarada of great psychic power, I approached the Teacher.
Having approached the Sambuddha and invited the Tathāgata, I— ”
Honoring the Great Sage, he led him to his own dwelling:
“I then gratified with food and drink the Great Hero, the God of Gods, the Bull among Men,
together with the community of monks as he stood there.”
“The Great Hero, the Self-Existent One, the Supreme Person,
having sat down with the community of monks, spoke these verses in approval:
‘Since he honored the Saṅgha and the Buddha, the Leader of the World;’”
By that confidence of heart, he will go to the world of the gods.
For seventy-seven times he will exercise sovereignty over the devas;
for one hundred and eight times he will rule the earth and dwell upon the land.
“Fifty-five times he will become a wheel-turning monarch;
during that time, incalculable riches will arise for him.
In an immeasurable eon from now, he will be born in the lineage of Okkāka.”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
Having passed away from hell, he will go to human status;
known by the name Kolita, he will become a kinsman of Brahmā.”
“Thus, having gone forth later on, urged by the root of merit,
he will become the second disciple of the Blessed One Gotama.
Ardent in energy and resolute, he will reach the perfection of psychic power.”
Having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
Relying on evil friends, fallen under the power of sensual lust,
I, with a corrupt mind, even killed my mother and my father.
“Whichever womb I am reborn in—whether in hell or among humans—because I am possessed of evil karma, I die with my head split asunder.
This is my final birth; my last existence is now unfolding.”
Even here, such will be my state at the time of death:
Devoted to seclusion, delighting in the cultivation of concentration,
having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
“Having reached the perfection of supernormal power, I could shake even the very deep, thick, and unassailable earth with my left thumb.
I perceive no ‘I-am’ conceit; pride does not exist within me.”
"From the time I was a novice, I have maintained a mind of reverence toward my teachers.
Because of the karma I performed throughout immeasurable eons since then,
I have now reached this stage and attained the destruction of the taints."
“The four analytical knowledges... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is finished.
The commentary on the Sixty-Verse Section is finished.
21. Mahānipāta 1.
Vaṅgīsa Thera-gāthā-vaṇṇanā:
The verses of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa Thera, beginning with "O, that I have indeed emerged from the sevenfold [world] while still existing," etc.
What was his origin? It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn into a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī.

Having gone to the monastery and heard the Dhamma in the same manner as before, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those possessed of ready wit (*paṭibhānavantānaṃ*).
Having performed a service for the Teacher, he made this aspiration: "In the future, may I also [be foremost] among those possessed of ready wit."
Having made the aspiration, "May I become the foremost," he was prophesied by the Teacher. Having practiced wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a brahmin family;
named Vaṅgīsa, while learning the three Vedas, he pleased his teacher and, having mastered the art of dissecting a corpse's head, [became known as] Chavasīsamanta.
Having struck with his fingernail, he knew, "This being has been reborn in such-and-such a womb.
The brahmins, realizing, "This is our means of livelihood," took Vaṅgīsa, seated him in a covered carriage, and traveled through villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
At the end of three years, Vaṅgīsa also had the heads of those who had died brought to him.

Having struck [the ground] with his fingernail and said, "This being has been reborn in such-and-such a womb," he would summon various people for the sake of cutting through the doubts of the great multitude and have each of them declare their own destiny. Because of this, the great multitude placed great confidence in him.
Relying on that, he received from the hands of the great multitude even hundreds or thousands [of coins]. Thus did the brahmins take up the case of Vaṅgīsa.
Having wandered about according to their pleasure, they returned once more to Sāvatthī. Having heard of the Teacher’s virtues, Vaṅgīsa desired to approach the Teacher.
The brahmins, however, dissuaded him, saying, "The ascetic Gotama will ensnare you with his magic.
Disregarding their words, Vaṅgīsa went into the presence of the Teacher; after exchanging pleasant greetings, he sat down to one side.
The Teacher asked him: "Vaṅgīsa, do you know any craft? "Yes, Master Gotama, I know the so-called 'Chavasīsamanta' (the art of the human head).
By means of it, even for those who have died three years ago, I can determine the place where they were reborn by tapping their heads with my fingernail.
The Teacher showed him one head that had been reborn in hell, another among humans, and another—
Among the gods, he showed him the head of one who had attained final Nibbāna. Having first struck that head, he said, "Master Gotama, this being has been reborn in hell.
"Excellent, Vaṅgīsa; you have seen well. Where has this being been reborn? he asked.
"In the human world," [he replied]. "And where is this one? "In the world of the gods. Thus it was for all three.
He described the place where [the Buddha] was reborn. But when he struck the head of the one who had attained final Nibbāna with his fingernail, he could see neither its end nor its limit.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Are you unable, Vaṅgīsa? [Vaṅgīsa replied,] "I am merely examining it.
Although he turned it over again and again and struck it, how could one who follows the external mantras know the destination of one whose taints are exhausted?
Then sweat broke out from his head. Feeling ashamed, he stood silent.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Are you weary, Vaṅgīsa? "Yes, Master Gotama; I am unable to know the origin of this [sweat];
if you know it, please tell me. "Vaṅgīsa, I know this as well, and I know even more than this," he said, and then—
“He who fully understands the passing away of beings and their rebirth,
who is unattached, well-gone, and awakened— him I call a brahmin.
Whose destination neither gods, nor gandharvas, nor humans know...”
“He who has destroyed the taints, the Arahant—him I call a brahmin.

He spoke these two verses. Vaṅgīsa, showing his reverence, said, “In that case, Master Gotama, give me that knowledge,” and sat down in the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher said, “We shall give it to one who shares our same religious mark. Vaṅgīsa—
Thinking, “Whatever must be done, it is right for me to take up this mantra,” he said to the brahmins:

“Do not worry about me when I go forth; once I have mastered the mantra, I shall become the foremost in all Jambudīpa, and by that, it will surely be beneficial for you as well. Having approached the Teacher for the sake of the mantra, he went forth.
He made his request. At that time, the Elder Nigrodhakappa was standing near the Blessed One, and the Blessed One commanded him:
"Nigrodhakappa, ordain this man. By the Teacher's command, he ordained him.
Then the Teacher said to him, "First, learn the protective charms," and gave him the meditation subject of the thirty-two parts of the body and the meditation subject of insight.
He explained it. While reciting the thirty-two marks, he established insight meditation.
The brahmins approached Vaṅgīsa and asked, "Sir Vaṅgīsa, what craft have you learned in the presence of the ascetic Gotama?
He replied, "What is the use of learning a craft? Go away; I have no business with you."
The brahmins said, "Now even you have fallen under the sway of the ascetic Gotama, enticed by his magic;
what can we possibly do in your presence? and they departed by the very same path they had come. The Elder Vaṅgīsa, having increased his insight (vipassanā), realized Arhatship.
Thus it is stated in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the eye-seer regarding all phenomena,
arose as a Guide one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.
Just like waves in the ocean, or stars in the sky,”
Thus was his teaching inscribed by the Arahants:
“Honored by gods, asuras, nāgas, and humans,
the Supreme Victor stood in the midst of the people, crowded with recluses and brahmins.”
“Illuminating the world with his radiance, the Victor who has reached the end of the world awakens the lotuses of those to be trained with his word.
Endowed with the four forms of self-confidence, he is the Supreme among Men.”
Having abandoned fear and agitation, having attained security and being confident,
the Chief of the World claims for himself the pre-eminent place of the bull, the entire stage of a Buddha,
and there is no one anywhere who can challenge him.
“For that Tathāgata who roars the fearless lion’s roar,
no opponent is found— whether a god, a human, or a Brahmā.
Teaching the sublime Dhamma, he brings across the world together with its gods.”
He sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, confident among the assemblies.
Having extolled his many virtues— the foremost of those possessed of inspired eloquence and highly esteemed by the virtuous— he placed him at the head of that list.
“At that time, in Haṃsavatī, I was a brahmin held in high esteem;
I was born as one who knew all the Vedas, a master of speech, a vanquisher of debaters.
Having approached that Great Hero and heard his teaching of the Dhamma,”
I obtained the supreme joy, delighting in the virtues of the disciple.
Having invited the Sugata, the delighter of the world, together with the Saṅgha,
and having fed them for seven days, I then covered them with fine cloths.
“Bowing my head at his feet, having been granted leave and with palms joined, I stood to one side, joyful, and praised the Supreme Victor:
‘Homage to you, crusher of opponents! Homage to you, best of seers!’”
Homage to you, supreme among all the world; homage to you, who grant fearlessness.
Homage to you, crusher of Māra; homage to you, destroyer of wrong views.
Homage to you, giver of peace and happiness; homage to you, who provide refuge.
“You are the protector of the protectorless, the giver of fearlessness to those who are afraid,
the resting place for the weary, and the refuge for those seeking refuge.
Having thus extolled the Fully Enlightened One, who possesses great virtues, with these and other such words...
“I shall attain the destination of that bhikkhu, the subduer of disputants.
Then the Blessed One, possessed of infinite eloquence, said:
“He who for seven days fed the Buddha together with his thousand disciples...”
“With his own hands, full of faith, he proclaimed my virtues:
‘This monk aspires to the status of a crusher of opponents.
In a future time, you shall attain that heart’s desire.”
Having experienced no small measure of prosperity among gods and humans:
"In a hundred thousand aeons from now, one born of the Okkāka clan,
known by the name Gotama as his lineage, will become a Teacher in the world."
“He will be an heir to the Dhamma, a true-born son fashioned by the Dhamma;
he will be a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Vaṅgīsa.
Having heard this, being filled with joy, he then [served] the Conqueror for as long as life lasted.
With a mind of loving-kindness, I attended upon the Tathāgata with various offerings.
By that well-performed deed and through my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned this human body, I went to the Tusita heaven.
“In this my final existence, I was born into a brahmin family;
when I was born again, I was seven years old.
I became a knower of all the Vedas and skilled in the science of debate.”
An eloquent speaker, a master of discourse,
who crushes the arguments of opponents: “Born in Vaṅga,
thus ‘Vaṅgīsa,’ or ‘Lord in Speech’— this was my name, approved by the world.”
“When I had reached the age of discretion and stood in the prime of youth,
I then saw the great Sāriputta in delightful Rājagaha.
As he wandered for alms with bowl in hand, perfectly self-controlled,”
"With steady eyes, speaking measuredly, looking only a yoke’s length ahead—
seeing him, I was struck with wonder and spoke these verse-words,
which were worthy of me and like a cluster of *kaṇikāra* flowers."
“He pointed out to me the Teacher, the Fully Awakened One, the Leader of the World;
then that wise hero spoke further to me:
‘Having made [yourself] fit for the supreme word concerning dispassion, which is difficult to see—’”
Satisfied by those various manifestations, that Neutral One said to me:
"Bowing my head at his feet, I said, 'Please ordain me.
Then that one of great wisdom led me to the Best of Buddhas."
“Bowing my head at the Teacher’s feet, I sat down in his presence.
‘Do you know anything, Vaṅgīsa? the Best of Speakers asked me.
To him I replied, ‘I know something of craft.’”
“Even if it were made of lead, purified by the forest,
and twelve years old— if you are able, recite it by means of your special knowledge.
When he replied, “I agree,” he showed him three heads.
When I was reborn among the hell-beings and the gods, I recited [the teachings].
Then the Leader showed his head even to one whose taints were exhausted;
thereupon, with my burden cast off, I requested the going-forth.
“Having gone forth, I was familiarizing myself here and there with the Sugata;
therefore, you, who are skilled in poetry, rebuke me here, O monks.
Then, for the sake of testing me, the Buddha, the Leader, said:”
“But these verses are for logicians; they occur to you spontaneously.
‘I am not a master of poetic composition, O Hero; they occur to me spontaneously.
Therefore, Vaṅgīsa, from this moment on, speak in praise of me spontaneously.’”
“Then I praised the Hero, the best of seers, with verses.
Instantly pleased with me, the Conqueror placed me at the foremost rank.
With my brilliant wit, I used to look down upon others.”
Touched by that, I was moved with spiritual urgency and attained arahantship.
"There exists no one else who is the foremost among those possessed of inspired eloquence, such as this monk Vaṅgīsa; thus you should remember him, O monks."
“An action performed a hundred thousand eons ago has shown its fruit to me here;
like an arrow released from a bow, it has completely liberated me.
My defilements have been incinerated, and all states of existence have been uprooted.”
Like a snake that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
"How welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Best of Buddhas!
The three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled."
“The four analytical knowledges, and these eight liberations;
the six direct knowledges have been realized—the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.
Having become an arahant, as the elder was going into the presence of the Teacher, from the moment he came within the range of his vision, by means of the moon...

Praising the Teacher with hundreds of verses by comparing Him to the sun, the sky, the great ocean, Sineru the king of mountains, the lion the king of beasts, and the noble elephant, he approached while extolling the Teacher in this manner.
Therefore, the Teacher, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, placed him in the foremost position among those possessed of ready wit. Then, by the Elder—
These were spoken both before and after the attainment of Arahatship, having approached various states of mind. They were also spoken by the Elder Ānanda and others in reference to the Elder:
"Alas, while I was still living at home, I have now gone forth from the household life into homelessness..."
Thoughts run wild; these are the audacious ones of the dark side.
"Like sons of high-born nobles, great archers, well-trained and firm-bowed, a thousand of them might surround one from all sides, never fleeing."
“Even if even more women than this were to come,
they would not disturb me, for I am firmly established in the Dhamma.
For I have heard this from the witness, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.”
“The path leading to Nibbāna— therein my mind delights.
‘If you, O Evil One, approach me while I am dwelling thus,
I shall deal with Death in such a way that you will not even see my path.’”
“Having abandoned both aversion and delight, and all thoughts connected with the household life;
let him not harbor any mental thicket anywhere—he is a monk who is free from the thicket and free from obstruction.
Whatever here exists on earth or in the sky, whatever form has come to be, whether hidden or manifest;”
“All that is impermanent decays; having understood this, the wise live accordingly.
People are attached to acquisitions—what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
Here, O unshaken one, dispel desire! The sage who is not stained by these things is called ‘one who has crossed over.’”
“Then those sixty who were possessed of thought and settled in the unrighteousness of worldlings—
yet that bhikkhu did not join any faction anywhere, nor was he one to grasp at what is blameworthy.
Dabba was long-established in concentration, free from deceit, prudent, and without envy.”
The Sage has attained the state of peace; depending on that, he has attained final Nibbāna and awaits his time.
“Abandon conceit, Gotama, and abandon the path of conceit without remainder;
for you were long immersed in the path of conceit and have been full of remorse for a long time.”
“Defiled by hypocrisy, people smitten by pride fall into hell;
smitten by pride and reborn in hell, these people grieve for a long time.
For the bhikkhu who has conquered the path and practices rightly never grieves.”
He experiences fame and happiness; they call him a "seer of Dhamma" because of that very state.

Therefore, one who is here free from harshness, striving with diligence, pure after abandoning the hindrances, having abandoned conceit without remainder, a peaceful sage, becomes a maker of the end through clear knowledge.
“I am burning with sensual lust; my mind is consumed by fire.
Please tell me, out of compassion, O Gotama, how to extinguish it.
“Because of a perversion of perception, your mind is consumed by fire.”
Avoid signs associated with beauty that incite passion.
Develop a mind focused on the foul, one-pointed and well-concentrated.
Let mindfulness directed toward the body be present, and be full of disenchantment.
“Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit;
then, through the full comprehension of conceit, you shall wander at peace.
One should speak only those words by which one does not burn oneself.”
And that which does not harm others—that indeed is well-spoken speech.
One should speak only pleasant words, those words that are welcomed;
one should speak what is pleasing to others, without taking up any evil.
“Truth indeed is the deathless word; this is the eternal Dhamma.
In truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma, the virtuous say the noble ones are firmly established.
Whatever word the Buddha speaks for the attainment of Nibbāna, which is security...”
For the making an end of suffering— that indeed is the supreme of speeches.
“Profound in wisdom, intelligent, skilled in what is the path and what is not the path,
Sāriputta of great wisdom teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.”
“He teaches in brief and speaks in detail;
his voice is like that of a sālika bird, and his eloquence wells up.
As he teaches this, they listen to his sweet voice.”
With voices charming in their essence,
worthy of being heard, and melodious, the bhikkhus, uplifted in mind and joyful, lend their ears. "Today,
on the fifteenth day of the purification, five hundred bhikkhus have assembled."
The seers, free from distress, have severed the fetters and bonds and exhausted all further becoming.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, surrounded by his ministers,
traverses this earth bounded by the ocean on every side.
“Thus do the disciples—possessors of the threefold knowledge and conquerors of death—wait upon the unsurpassed Caravan-Leader who has won the battle.
All are the sons of the Blessed One; here no ‘stranger’ is to be found.”
I pay homage to the Kinsman of the Sun, the slayer of the arrow of craving.
More than a thousand bhikkhus attend upon the Sugata as he teaches the stainless Dhamma— Nirvana, free from fear from any quarter.
“They hear the stainless Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One;
truly the Buddha shines forth, seated at the head of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The Blessed One is named ‘Nāga,’ the seventh among the seers.”
Having become like a great cloud, you rain down upon your disciples.
“Emerging from the monastery during the day, out of a desire to see the Teacher,
the disciple Vaṅgisa pays homage at your feet, O Great Hero.”
“Having overcome Māra’s path of snares and having broken through the bolts,
behold him who effects release from bondage, like one who has divided a raw hide into its parts.
For the sake of crossing over the flood, he has proclaimed the path in its many varieties.”
And in that deathless state thus proclaimed, those who see the Dhamma stand firm and unshakable.
Having penetrated it as the light-maker, he saw the transcendence of all stations;
having known and realized it, he taught this supreme state to the tenfold world.
“When the Dhamma has been so well-taught, who that understands the Dhamma would be negligent?
Therefore, in the teaching of that Blessed One, one should always train respectfully with heedfulness.
The Elder Koṇḍañña, who awakened after the Buddha, was one of fierce exertion.”
He is a frequent attainer of pleasant dwellings and of seclusions.
"Whatever can be attained by a disciple who acts according to the Teacher's instruction—
all that has been attained by him as he trains with diligence."
“Of great power, possessing the threefold knowledge, skilled in discerning the minds of others—
Koṇḍañña, the heir of the Buddha, pays homage at the feet of the Teacher.
Seated on the side of the mountain, the Sage who has gone beyond suffering.”
His disciples, possessors of the threefold knowledge who have abandoned death,
attend upon him. Moggallāna, of great psychic power, surveys them with his mind,
searching their hearts as they are fully liberated and free from acquisitions.
“Thus do they attend upon Gotama, the Sage who has reached the further shore of suffering, endowed with all qualities, perfected in manifold ways.
Like the moon in a cloudless sky, or like the sun free from stain, he shines forth.”
In this way too, O Aṅgīrasa, you, the Great Sage, outshine the entire world with your glory.
“Formerly we wandered from village to village and city to city, intoxicated by poetry.
Then we saw the Perfectly Awakened One, who has gone beyond all phenomena.”
“Thus the Sage, who has gone beyond suffering, taught me the Dhamma.
Having heard the Dhamma, we gained confidence, and faith arose within us.
Having heard his words regarding the aggregates and the sense-bases...”
Having understood the elements, I went forth into the homeless life.
"Truly, for the benefit of many do Tathāgatas arise—
for those women and men who act according to the teaching."
“Truly, it was for their sake that the Sage attained enlightenment—
for the monks and the nuns who have seen the path to certainty.
Well-expounded by the Visionary One, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.”
The Four Noble Truths, out of compassion for living beings:
suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering,
and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.
“Thus have these been spoken by him; I have seen them exactly as they are.
My own goal has been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Buddha.”
Among well-classified phenomena, I have attained that which is supreme:
"I have reached perfection in direct knowledge; the faculty of hearing is purified;
I am possessed of the three knowledges, have attained the supernormal powers, and am skilled in discerning the minds of others."
“I ask the Teacher of peerless wisdom, who cuts through doubts even in this very life:
A bhikkhu well-known and renowned, whose self was fully extinguished, passed away at Aggāḷava.
‘Nigrodhakappa’ was the name given to him by you, O Blessed One, for that brahmin.”
Thus, seeking liberation, he practiced paying homage to him, having aroused energy and seeing the Dhamma firmly.
“O Sakka, we all also wish to know that disciple of yours, O All-Seeing One!
Our ears are poised to hear; you are our teacher, you are unsurpassed.”
“Cut off our doubt; speak this to us, O one of vast wisdom, who has attained final Nibbāna!
Speak to us from the midst, O All-Seeing One, like Sakka among the gods with his thousand eyes.
Whatever fetters there are here, paths of delusion, sides of ignorance, and grounds for doubt—”
Having reached the Tathāgata, they no longer exist, for he is the supreme eye among men.
For if a man never dispels his defilements as the wind disperses clouds from the sky,
then the entire world would be shrouded in darkness for him, and even luminous bodies would not shine.
“The wise become makers of light; O Hero, I consider them to be exactly so.
We have approached the All-Seeing One who knows all things; reveal the *kappa* among our assemblies.
Swiftly utter your lovely, lovely voice; like a swan, raise it and warble gently.”
With well-articulated and clear enunciation, all of you listen with focused minds:
“I shall teach the Dhamma to the pure one who has completely cast off birth and death without remainder, having mastered them.
For ordinary people act according to their own desires, whereas Tathāgatas act according to what is reckoned right.”
“Perfect is this exposition of yours, well-grasped by you of straight wisdom.
This is my final salutation with palms joined; do not delude me, O you of knowing and peerless wisdom!
Having understood the noble Dhamma from beginning to end, do not delude me, O you of knowing and peerless energy!”
“Just as one tormented by the heat longs for water in the summer heat, I long for your voice; rain down what has been heard!
‘Whatever purpose Kappāyana pursued while practicing the holy life—was it not in vain?
Did he attain Nibbāna, or did he have a residue remaining? We wish to hear how he was liberated.’”
“He has cut off craving here for name-and-form,” said the Blessed One,
“the stream of Kaṇha that had lain dormant for a long time.
He has crossed over birth and death without remainder,” so spoke the Blessed One, the Best of the Five.
“Having heard this, I have confidence in your words, O best of seers;
my question was indeed not in vain, for the brahmin has not deceived me.
As he speaks, so he acts—he was a disciple of the Buddha.”
He has cut through the net of Death, that strong snare spread by the Deceiver.
"The Blessed One, the one who acts rightly, has seen the beginning of clinging;
indeed, he has transcended the realms of existence, the realm of Death so difficult to cross."
“I pay homage to that God of Gods, your son, O Best of Bipeds;
to the Great Hero who has followed in your footsteps, a true Naga born from the breast of a Naga.
These verses were compiled together and included in the Canon at the time of the Council. Therein, [the words] “Indeed, I have gone forth... [are spoken].

The five verses beginning with "Tranquil" (*santaṃ*) were spoken by the Venerable Vaṅgīsa when, having been newly ordained not long ago, he entered a monastery and saw many women adorned and prepared for decoration; overcome by lust, he spoke these words to dispel it.
Therein, "While I am tranquil, having gone forth from home to homelessness" means having departed from the household life to the homeless state.
"While I am one who has gone forth"—"thoughts" refers to evil thoughts such as sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so on.
"They run toward me" means they approach my mind. "Impudent" means those who are unrestrained and possessed of impudence; they are shameless because they do not consider:
"This man has gone out from his home and gone forth; it is not right to harass him. "From the black side" means from the dark side.
The meaning is "of lowly status. The word "these" refers to those who are personally known to him.
People who live by impure livelihoods and are accompanied by retinues are called "Ugga" because of their fierce deeds; their sons are "Uggaputta.
"Mahissāsa" means great archers. "Sikkhitā" means those who have mastered their craft after twelve years of training in a teacher's household.
“Daḷhadhammino” means those with strong bows. A “strong bow” is said to have a strength of two thousand [paccabaddha]. As for the phrase “a strength of two thousand”:
when it is strung, if one holds the handle and raises it into the air from the ground to the height of an arrow’s length, the weight of the bowstring—made of iron, lead, and so forth—is released.
“They would scatter all around” means they would shoot arrows in every direction.
If one asks, "How many? he says, "A thousand who do not flee. This refers to about a thousand others with faces [turned toward the enemy] in battle.

What is meant is this: even if there were a thousand well-trained, skilled, noble sons of high rank, possessing firm bows and great archery, who had never suffered defeat in battle, and who, being vigilant, stood all around leaning against a pillar—nevertheless...

They might rain down. Even when surrounded on all sides by thousands of such arrows, a well-trained man, taking up his staff, would cause all those arrows not to fall upon his own body and instead drop them at his feet.
In that situation, there is no single archer who could shoot two arrows simultaneously. But as for women, by way of the object of beauty and so forth—
"Five by five they hurl arrows together; thus they hurl them.
"More than these"—more women than these [already mentioned] destroy themselves by means of their feminine gestures, laughter, and so forth.

"For this I have heard from an eyewitness"—I have heard this directly from [the Buddha's] presence. "The path leading to Nibbāna"—this is stated with a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
It is said; the meaning is "the path leading to Nibbāna," which is stated with reference to insight (vipassanā).
In that context, "my mind delights therein" means that my consciousness delights in that path of insight.
"And while I am dwelling thus" refers to dwelling in this way through both the cultivation of the meditative absorption on impermanence and foulness, and the cultivation of insight.
"Me dwelling"—this refers to the speaker. "Pāpimā" (the Evil One) is an address to the *kilesamāra* (the Māra of defilements). "I shall thus bring about his death;
you shall not even see my path"—the construction is: "I shall bring about his end in such a way that you do not even perceive the path I have taken.
The five verses beginning with "And discontent" (*aratiñca*) were spoken by him while dispelling the discontent and other states that had arisen within his own continuum.
In this context, "discontent" (*arati*) refers to weariness with superior wholesome states and secluded dwellings. "Delight" (*rati*) refers to delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure.

"Having abandoned" (*pahāya*) means having relinquished. "And all thoughts based on the household life" means having completely abandoned all wrong thoughts connected with the household life, such as thoughts concerning children, wife, and relatives, including thoughts about kin.
"One should not create a thicket anywhere" (*vanathaṃ na kareyya kuhiñci*)—means one should not create a mental thicket or obstruction regarding anything whatsoever.
One should not form craving toward any object whatsoever, whether internal or external.
One who is free from craving in every respect, and for that very reason free from attachment due to the absence of any delight (*nandi*) anywhere—that one is called a *bhikkhu*.
This is because he truly perceives the terror of *saṃsāra* and has shattered the defilements (*kilesa*). This is the meaning.
"Whatever here on earth or in the air, whatever form exists hidden in the world"—whatever here is on the earth, dependent on the ground;
or in the air, situated in the sky, dependent on the world of the gods; whatever form exists, whatever kind of form, having the nature of being affected by change (*ruppaṇa-sabhāva*);
hidden in the world, mundane, included within the three realms of existence, conditioned—*all that decays, all is impermanent*.
"All that is overcome by aging; therefore it is impermanent, therefore it is suffering, and therefore it is non-self"—thus he spoke of the application of the three characteristics.
This, they say, was the Elder’s "Great Insight" (*mahāvipassanā*).

"Thus, having fully understood, they wander as liberated"—thus, having fully understood and thoroughly penetrated by means of the wisdom of the path accompanied by the wisdom of insight, they are liberated because their personal existence has been fully comprehended.
The wise ones move about and dwell [thus].
"In the acquisitions" (upadhīsu) means among the aggregates as acquisitions and so forth. "Fools" (jana) refers to blind worldlings. "Attached" (gadhitāse) means those whose minds are bound.
For here, specifically showing that desire for the acquisitions consisting of the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa-upadhi) must be removed, he says: "In what is seen, heard, and touched..."
"And in the mute as well. "Seen and heard" means both what is seen and what is heard; the meaning is "in visible forms and sounds.
"Resistance" refers to tangible objects that cause impact. "In the mute" refers to the remaining mute objects, meaning "in odors and flavors.
In the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, it is stated: "By the term 'resistance,' odors and flavors are included; by the term 'mute,' the objective field of the tangible is included. Here...
"Dispel desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure"—dispel sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) regarding these five objects of sense, which are divided into the seen and so forth;
being thus, you will be unshaken and free from conceptual proliferation (*avikappa*) in all respects.

"The sage whom they call 'one who does not smear' here"—for those wise ones call him a "sage" (*muni*) because he stands in the state of sagehood (*moneyya-dhamma*), as he is not smeared by the stain of craving (*taṇhā*) toward these strands of sensual pleasure.

They say: "Now, as for the phrase 'supported by sixty' (*saṭṭhisitā*), some—intending that this is the reading of the text—explain the meaning as 'supported by objects consisting of sixty phenomena' (*saṭṭhidhammārammaṇanissitā*).
However, the actual text reads: 'The sixty-eight with applied thought are supported [by views]' (*aṭṭhasaṭṭhisitā savitakkā*).
For indeed, a slight deficiency or excess does not affect the count. Thus, 'supported by sixty-eight' means wrong thoughts associated with the sixty-two types of views (*dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigata*)."

Some say there is a specific purpose [for this]. Since the proponents of wrong views have adopted the conviction that the realms of beings do not exist, the phrase "then sixty are with applied thought" is stated by way of those other than them, setting aside the doctrine of fortuitous origination.

For just as one is called a "bhikkhu" due to the absence of the stain of craving (*taṇhā-lepa*), so too is it said to show that [the view-holders] are free from the stain of views (*diṭṭhi-lepa*); thus, "then sixty are with applied thought," and so forth, was spoken.

"Unrighteousnesses are settled in the state of the worldling": those wrong thoughts, however, by way of grasping at permanence and so forth, are unrighteous—having departed from what is righteous—and are settled, firmly adhered to, within the state of the worldling among the blind and foolish. "And for one who has entered a faction, nowhere at all":
wherever in any matter he has entered a faction of wrong views such as eternalism and so forth, being a holder of that [view].

And it would not exist for him. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, having cited the line, “Then sixty thoughts accompanied by applied thought, many unrighteous thoughts, are settled among the people,” it is stated:
“Then many unrighteous thoughts based on the six objects are settled among the people.
Likewise, regarding the phrase “and nowhere for one who has entered a faction,” [it means] nowhere at all by virtue of those [thoughts].

And it is said: "He should not fall into the category of the defilements. Furthermore, "that monk is not one who grasps what is gross" means that he should not be one who, because he is corrupted by defilements, is exceedingly gross, nor one whose habit is to grasp gross false doctrines;
such a person is called a "monk."
A sage (*dabbha*) is one of a sage-like nature, a wise man. "Long-established in concentration" means he has been concentrated for a long time.
"Ungreedy" means free from hypocrisy, not crafty, and not deceitful. "Discerning" means subtle and skillful. "Without longing" means free from craving.
"He attained the state of peace" means he realized *nibbāna*. He is a sage (*muni*) because he is endowed with the qualities of a sage. "Parinibbuted" means [he is so] by way of making it his object.
"Depending on Nibbāna, he has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining.
"He waits for the time" means that now he awaits the time for the sake of Nibbāna without residue. The intended meaning is: "There is nothing further to be done by him;
he has perfected himself so that he will become such as this."
The four verses beginning with "Abandon conceit" were spoken by him while dispelling the pride arising within himself, based on his excellence of inspired eloquence.
Therein, "abandon conceit" means: relinquish the ninefold conceit, such as the conceit of superiority (*seyya-māna*) and so forth.
"Gotama": he addresses himself as belonging to the Gotama clan because he is a disciple of the Blessed One of the Gotama clan. "The path of conceit" (*mānapatha*).

Abandon—meaning, give up entirely—birth and so forth, which serve as the basis for conceit and are enveloped by improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), through the abandoning of the defilements bound to them. "In the path of conceit he is infatuated" means he has fallen into a swoon (*muccha*) regarding the object that is the ground for conceit.
"Becoming remorseful for a long time" refers to the period after this moment of indulgence in the path of conceit has passed.
He would have attained *arahatta* even earlier; thus he became remorseful, thinking, "I am ruined.

One who is "smeared with malice" (*makkhī*) is so called because they are defiled by malice—the characteristic of which is the smearing over of others' virtues—having exalted themselves through pride (*sūra*) and the like, and having disparaged others.
For as a person smears over the virtues of others to whatever extent, to that same extent...
"One heaps up one's own virtues" means one rejects them. "Struck down by pride" means one whose virtues have been destroyed by pride.
"Falling into hell" means being reborn in hell.
"Conqueror of the path" means one who has conquered the defilements by means of the path. "Fame and happiness" means both the praise of the wise and physical and mental happiness.
"Experiences" means he attains. "A seer of phenomena"—the wise call him such because he has practiced rightly and perceives phenomena as they truly are, according to their actual state (*tathatā*).
"Without harshness" means free from the five mental obstructions (*cetokhila*). "Diligent" means endowed with the energy of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*). "Purified" means...
With a mind purified by the departure of the clouds known as the hindrances, having abandoned all nine kinds of conceit without remainder through the supreme path,

he— being one who has stilled [the defilements] and is a maker of the end of true knowledge— instructs himself: "I have reached the culmination of the threefold true knowledge, with my afflictions entirely stilled."
Then one day, having been invited by a certain high minister of the king,
the Venerable Ānanda went to his house in the morning and sat down on a prepared seat, with the Venerable Vaṅgīsa as his attendant monk. Then, in that house,
women adorned with all their ornaments approached the Elder, paid homage, and asked a question.

They questioned him and listened to the Dhamma. Then, because the Venerable Vaṅgīsa had recently gone forth and was unable to grasp a suitable object of meditation, lust arose for him toward an unsuitable object.
That faithful son of good family, thinking, "If this lust of mine increases, it will destroy my welfare both in this life and in the life to come," remained exactly as he was sitting.
Revealing his own state of affairs, the elder spoke the verse beginning with “By sensual lust.
Therein, although the feverish heat of the defilement of passion afflicts the body as well, it is stated that it afflicts the mind for a longer duration;
thus, after saying “I am burning with sensual lust,” he said, “my mind is burning. “Extinguishing” refers to the cause for extinguishing passion, namely, the feverish heat of passion.
The meaning is: "Give instruction capable of extinguishing [the defilements].
The verse beginning with "Through a perversion of perception" was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda when he was so requested.

"Perversion" (*vipariyesa*) means through a distortion, that is, through a perverted grasping which occurs by taking the beautiful in what is unattractive. "Sign" (*nimitta*) means a sign that gives rise to defilements.
"Parivajjehi" means "go forth. Regarding "the beautiful associated with lust":

while avoiding the beautiful that serves as an object for the increase of lust, one should avoid it by means of the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) and, in all cases, by means of the perception of non-delight (*anabhiratisaññā*). Therefore, showing both of these, he said, "By means of the perception of foulness," and so forth.
In this context, "by means of the foul" means by means of the contemplation of the foul (*asubhānupassanā*). "Develop a one-pointed mind, well-concentrated" means:
having made your own mind one-pointed through the absence of distraction and well-concentrated—fixed and absorbed—upon the objects of meditation, develop your contemplation of the foul;

I shall explain it so that it may be easy for you to perform. "May mindfulness directed to the body be established in you" means: the cultivation of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) previously mentioned has been developed by you.
The meaning is: "May it be cultivated. "Be full of disenchantment" means: be full of penetration regarding the entire personal existence (*attabhāva*). "And cultivate the signless" means:
by removing the signs of permanence and so forth, specifically the contemplation of impermanence is called the "signless";
cultivating that, one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) through the attainment of the supreme path in the sequence of the paths.
"Cut it off. "The realization regarding conceit" means both the realization through the vision of conceit and the realization through its abandonment.
"Peaceful" means that you will move about and dwell in complete tranquility due to the subsiding of passion and the other defilements.
These four verses beginning with "That very speech... were spoken by the Blessed One when he was filled with joy upon the teaching of the Subhāsita Sutta.
These were spoken by the Elder while extolling the Blessed One in his presence.
"By which one does not torment oneself" means that by whatever speech acting as a cause, one would not torment or afflict oneself with remorse.
"And does not harm others" means that one does not injure others by causing dissension among them. "That indeed is well-spoken speech" means that such speech is, in every respect, well-spoken.
The construction is: "Therefore, one should speak only that speech. With this verse, he praises the Blessed One by way of non-slanderous speech (*apisuṇavācā*).
"Welcomed" (*paṭinanditā*) means welcomed because it is pleasing to the face; it is beloved and accepted by those who hear it both now and in the future.
"Taking up nothing" (*yaṃ anādāya*) refers to that speech which, when spoken, does not involve evil, unpleasant, or undesirable harsh words toward others.
Without taking up—that is, without grasping—the sweetness of either the meaning or the phrasing, he speaks only what is dear.

"He should speak only such pleasant speech" is said by way of praising him for his pleasant speech. "Immortal" means that, by virtue of its excellence, it is like the deathless (amata). For this has been said: "Truth is indeed the most excellent of flavors."
Or it is "immortal" because it has the deathless Nibbāna as its condition. "This Dhamma is ancient":
this which is called true speech is the ancient Dhamma, the conduct, the tradition. For this indeed was the practice of the ancients, that they did not speak untruth.
Therefore he said: "The virtuous say that they are established in truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma. Therein, because of being established in truth...
Thus, it should be understood that they are established in their own welfare and the welfare of others; and because they are established in welfare, they are established in the Dhamma.
Or rather, this is a qualification of "truth": they are established in truth. Of what kind?
In welfare and in the Dhamma—that is, in that which is not devoid of welfare for others, and thus does not obstruct welfare.
"Because it does not depart from the Dhamma, it accomplishes the goal that is the Dhamma and truly in accordance with the Dhamma. With this verse, he praised [the teaching] by way of truthful speech.
"Secure" means fearless and free from calamity. If one asks for what reason, it is because it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna and the making of an end to suffering;
since it brings about the Nibbāna of the defilements and conduces to the making of an end to the suffering of the round of existence, it is therefore called "secure."

The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, because he proclaims the path of security for the sake of the two elements of Nibbāna—either for the attainment of Nibbāna or for the making of an end to suffering—the Buddha speaks words that are secure.
"That indeed is the supreme among words": the meaning here should be understood as that speech being the best of all speeches.
By way of this verse, it is spoken as an expression of wisdom (*mantā*).
Praising the Blessed One, he brings the hymn of praise to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
The three verses beginning with "Deep in wisdom" (gambhīrapañño) are spoken by way of extolling the Venerable Sāriputta Thera.
In that context, "deep in wisdom" means being endowed with subtle wisdom that operates regarding the profound aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth.
He is one of profound wisdom (*gambhīrapañña*). Because he is endowed with the wisdom of the nutriment of the Dhamma (*dhammoja-paññā*) known as intelligence (*medhā*), he is wise (*medhāvī*).

Because of his expertise regarding what is the path and what is not the path—knowing, "This is the path to an unhappy destination, this is the path to a happy destination, and this is the path to Nibbāna"—he is skilled in the path and the non-path (*maggāmaggakovida*).
By virtue of his wisdom, which has reached the pinnacle of the great knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*)...
"Of great wisdom": he teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus by correctly distinguishing between engagement and withdrawal.
To show the manner in which that teaching proceeds, it is said, "even in brief," and so forth.
Therein, "even in brief" means: "Friends, there are these four noble truths. Which four? Suffering..."
“The noble truth... [and so on] ...These, friends, are the four noble truths; therefore, friends, the application ‘This is suffering’ should be practiced.
Thus he teaches in brief. Then, analyzing those very same truths by way of the method beginning with, “And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering?
Birth is suffering,” and so forth, he speaks in detail. This is also the case in the teachings on the aggregates and other categories.
The same method applies here. "Like the cry of a myna bird":
just as when a myna bird, having tasted a sweet mango fruit, flaps its wings and utters a sweet sound, so too is the Elder’s voice sweet as he preaches the Dhamma.
For the speech of the General of the Dhamma is unimpeded by bile or other humors.
A sound issues forth like that of a bronze bowl struck with a wooden mallet.
"Inspiration arises" means that when there is a desire to speak, an infinite inspiration arises one after another, like waves from the ocean.
"Of him" refers to the General of the Dhamma. "To him" refers to [the Buddha] while teaching the Dhamma. "They listen" means: "What the Elder is telling us."
Thinking, “We shall hear this,” they listen with a sense of reverence. "Sweet" means desirable. "Enchanting" means lovely.
"Worthy of being heard" means pleasant to the ear. "Melodious" means smooth and captivating. "With uplifted minds" means having minds uplifted and not dejected by way of rapture and joy.
"Rejoicing" means delighted and endowed with gladness. "They incline" means they apply their minds toward understanding.
While attending [to the Buddha], they bring forth their ears.

The four verses beginning with "Today is the fifteenth" were spoken by one who, having seen the Teacher seated surrounded by the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the time of the teaching of the Pavāraṇā Sutta, was paying him homage.
Therein, regarding "the fifteenth": for at the time when the Blessed One was at the Pubbārāma...
Having sat down and taught the Dhamma appropriate to the time and occasion to the assembled company at the evening hour,
he bathed his limbs at the water cistern, put on his lower garment and upper robe, arranged his great Sugata-cloak over one shoulder,
and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared against the central pillar of Migāra’s Mother’s palace, surrounded on all sides.
Having looked upon the community of monks seated there, he sat on that very day of the Uposatha, the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony;
the meaning is that it was the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. "For the sake of purity" means for the purpose of purification, for the Pavāraṇā of purification.
"Five hundred monks had assembled" means that approximately five hundred monks were seated surrounding the Teacher.
And they have come together by way of their respective inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*). And they are "cutters of the bonds of the fetters" (*saṃyojanabandhanacchida*);
that is, having cut off the defilements (*kilesa*) known as fetters which act as the bonds for the continuity of existence (*santāna*), they abide [in that state].

For that very reason, they are "seers free from distress, whose renewed existence is exhausted" (*anīghā khīṇapunabbhavā isī*): they are "free from suffering" because of the absence of the suffering of defilements; and they are "seers" (*isi*) because of their state of seeking (*esita*) the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those beyond training (*asekha*).
“Victorious in battle” means that he has conquered the battle of the defilements (*kilesa*), and because he has vanquished the power of Māra, he is one who has won the battle.
“Charioteer of the caravan”: having mounted beings who are to be trained upon the chariot of the Noble Eightfold Path, he leads them and delivers them from the wilderness of *saṃsāra*;
thus the Blessed One is the Charioteer of the Caravan. Therefore Brahmā Sahampati said: “Arise, O Hero, victorious in battle, Charioteer of the Caravan!”
The construction is as follows: disciples attend upon that unsurpassed caravan leader, the Teacher— disciples who possess the threefold knowledge and have overcome death—
and surrounded by such disciples, he wanders all around on a tour of the countryside, like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by his ministers.

*Palāpa* means empty and devoid of internal essence; the meaning is "one who lacks virtue. "I revere the Kinsman of the Sun" means he says, "I revere the Teacher, the Kinsman of the Sun, the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.

The four verses beginning with *Parosahassaṃ* were spoken by one praising the Blessed One as he was teaching the Dhamma to the bhikkhus with a discourse connected to Nibbāna. Therein, *parosahassaṃ* means more than a thousand.
This was said with reference to twelve thousand five hundred bhikkhus. "Fearless from all sides" (*akutobhaya*): in Nibbāna there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever;
and for one who has attained Nibbāna, there is likewise no fear from any quarter—thus Nibbāna is called "fearless from all sides.
Because the Blessed One is called a "Nāga" by virtue of the reasons stated in the passage beginning with "He commits no offense," the Blessed One bears the name Nāga.

"Isīnaṃ isisattamo" means the supreme seer among the seers—namely, the disciples, the paccekabuddhas, and the [worldly] seers—or the seventh seer counting from the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Vipassī. "Mahāmeghova" means being like a great cloud that covers the four continents.

"Divā vihārā" means from his place of solitary retreat. "Sāvako te, mahāvīra, pāde vandati vaṅgīso"—this was said by the Elder, having attained arahantship, as he proclaimed his own special achievement.

The four verses beginning with "Ummaggapathaṃ" were spoken by the Blessed One when he asked Vaṅgīsa, "Vaṅgīsa, were these verses previously reflected upon by you, or did they occur to you spontaneously? Vaṅgīsa showed that they had occurred to him spontaneously.
But why did the Blessed One speak to him in this way? It is said that a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha: "The Elder Vaṅgīsa..."
"One who has abandoned his learning performs no work through recitation, nor through interrogation, nor through wise attention;
he wanders about composing verses and fashioning strings of words. Then the Blessed One, thinking, "These monks do not know the excellence of Vaṅgīsa’s inspired eloquence;
I shall make them know his excellence of inspired eloquence," [spoke].
“Why indeed, Vaṅgīsa? and so forth—with these words he asks. “The path of the ummaggas” means the many paths by which defilements arise;
for it is called a “path” because it is the way leading to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
“Having split the bolts” means that you wander having broken the five bolts, such as lust and the rest. “Behold him!”—behold the Buddha who wanders thus, having both overcome and severed them.
"Behold" means: "one who effects the release from bonds," that is, one who effects liberation from bondage. "Independent" means not dependent [on anything else].

"Having analyzed by way of parts" means having made the Dhamma to be analyzed according to its divisions, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). There is also a reading *pavibhajja*. The meaning is:
having analyzed and analyzed the Dhamma in various ways according to its divisions, such as the summaries (*uddesa*), he teaches the Dhamma.
"Of the flood" means of the four floods, beginning with the flood of sensual desire (*kāma*).

"In many ways" means manifold by way of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth, or of various kinds by way of the thirty-eight meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). He "proclaimed" or spoke of the path that brings the Deathless.
"And in that Deathless proclaimed" means in that Deathless which brings the Deathless, proclaimed by him. "Seers of Dhamma" means those who have seen the Dhamma.
"Standing unshakable" means being established as something that cannot be moved by anything. "Piercing through" means having pierced through.
"Of all standpoints" (*sabbaṭṭhitīnaṃ*) means of all bases for views or stations of consciousness.

"He saw the transcendence" means he saw Nibbāna, which is the state of transcendence. "The supreme Dhamma" (*aggaṃ dhammaṃ*) means the highest Dhamma. Alternatively, the reading is *agge*, meaning "the first. "Of ten directions" (*dasaddhānaṃ*).
The meaning is that he taught the foremost Dhamma to the group of five, or that he taught it from the beginning, which is the foremost.

Therefore—meaning because one who knows "this Dhamma is well-taught" should not be negligent—one should train accordingly; that is, one should train in the three trainings according to the sequence of insight and the sequence of the path.
The three verses beginning with "Enlightened by the Buddha" (Buddhānubuddho) are spoken in praise of the Venerable Aññāta-Koṇḍañña Thera.

Thus it was said. In that context, "awakened after the Buddhas" (*buddhānubuddha*) means awakened following the Buddhas. For the Buddhas first awakened to the Four Truths, and afterwards the Elder [Sāriputta] was the very first;
therefore he is called "awakened after the Buddhas. He is an "elder" (*thera*) because he is endowed with the steadfast aggregates of virtue and so forth;
the meaning is that his nature is unshakable. "One of intense exertion" (*tibbanikkama*) means one who possesses firm energy. Regarding "of the pleasant dwellings" (*sukhavihārānaṃ*):
"Of dwellings in happiness in this very life": of the three kinds of seclusion (*viveka*). "Of all that":
whatever is to be attained by a disciple, all of that has been attained by him. "Training with diligence": training while being diligent.

"One possessing the three knowledges, skilled in reading the minds of others": he mentions four of the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*); even though the other two are not mentioned, [they are understood].
The Elder, however, was one possessed of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña).

Because these verses were spoken by one who, having seen the Elder after he had come from the Chaddanta Lake in the Himālayas and had shown the highest reverence to the Blessed One, and having praised the Elder in the presence of the Blessed One with a mind full of faith upon seeing him prostrating, it is said:
"Koṇḍañña, the heir of the Buddha, pays homage at the feet of the Teacher."
While the Blessed One was staying on the Black Rock together with five hundred bhikkhus— all of whom were arahants— the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, searching the minds of those bhikkhus,
perceived their liberation through the fruit of arahantship. Seeing this, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Blessed One and the elders with these three verses beginning with "Nagassa passe."
He spoke. Therein, "on the slope of the mountain" means on the black rock on the slope of Mount Isigili. "Seated" means sitting.

"With his mind" means with his own knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*). "Searching their minds" means searching the minds of those bhikkhus whose taints were exhausted. "He traverses" means he delimits them in succession.
Thus, [he praises] the perfection of the Teacher, described as "the Sage who has gone beyond suffering, endowed with all limbs."
And by the phrase “possessing the threefold knowledge, having abandoned death,” he is endowed with the excellence of the disciples; thus, he is complete and possessed of all these factors.
For, by this term “Muni,” the Teacher’s awakening to the entire range of knowable things through that which is termed “wisdom” (mona) is expressed;

thereby, the inclusion of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and so forth, is effected by means of his unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). Thus, he demonstrates his perfection in wisdom.

By the phrase "those who have gone beyond suffering," the perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*) is shown. Through both of these, the Teacher’s perfections such as majesty (*ānubhāva*) are demonstrated.
By the two phrases "possessors of the three knowledges" and "those who have abandoned death," the excellence of the Teacher and his disciples is shown;

for, by illustrating the disciples’ attainment of knowledge (*ñāṇasampatti*) and their realization of the element of Nibbāna (*nibbānadhātu*), the perfection of both the Teacher and his disciples is revealed. Thus, the aforementioned meaning—
To make it more clear, it is said: “They wait upon Gotama, the Sage who has gone beyond suffering, endowed with manifold qualities.
Therein, “endowed with manifold qualities” means endowed with many modes; the sense is that he is possessed of numerous qualities of various kinds.
The verse beginning with “Just as the moon... was spoken by the Blessed One while he was at the Gaggarā lotus pond on the outskirts of the city of Campā, together with a great community of monks.
Having seen him surrounded by many thousands of gods and nāgas, shining with his own beauty and glory, they—
filled with joy and uttering words of praise— spoke thus. In that context, [he was like] the moon in a cloudless sky,
just as at the time of autumn when it is free from clouds and other defilements such as mist that resemble clouds.
"The full moon shines in the liberated sky;

like the sun free from stain"—just as the sun, the maker of light, shines when it is free from stains such as clouds through their disappearance, so too, O Aṅgīrasa, you, the Great Sage, the Blessed One, who possess radiance with the splendor streaming forth from your limbs, outshine the world including the devas by surpassing it with your own glory. Thus you shine.

The ten verses beginning with "Kāveyyamattā" were spoken by [the Elder] after he had attained Arahantship, reflecting upon his own practice and elucidating the virtues of both the Teacher and himself.
Therein, "Kāveyyamattā" means those who are intoxicated, proud, esteemed, or possessed of the arising of virtue by means of *kāveyya*, that is, the composition of poetry. "Addasāma" means "we saw."
"Truly it has arisen for us": truly, the Three Jewels have arisen for our benefit.
"The word": a discourse on the Dhamma connected with truth. "The aggregates, the bases, and the elements":
the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements. At this point, a discussion of the aggregates and so forth should be related. That...
Since these have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, they should be understood according to the method stated therein.
"Having known" means having understood through preliminary knowledge (*pubbabhāga-ñāṇa*) by way of the analysis of form and so forth, and by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Those who carry out the teaching" refers to those beings who are followers of the Tathāgatas' instruction; for their great benefit indeed do the Tathāgatas arise.

"Those who have seen the way to certainty" (*niyāmagataddasa*) means that "the way to certainty" (*niyāmagata*) is simply certainty itself; those monks and nuns who have seen—that is, attained—the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
For their sake, indeed, the Sage, the Blessed One, attained enlightenment (*bodhi*), which is to say, perfect self-enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*); such is the construction of the verse.
"Well-taught" (*sudesita*) means well-expounded both in brief and in detail, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*). "By the Visionary One" (*cakkhumatā*)—
By means of the five eyes, the Visionary One [has seen them].

Those things which are to be practiced by those desiring their own welfare, which produce the state of an Ariya, or which belong to the Ariya—the Blessed One—are called the *Ariyasaccas* (Noble Truths). "Suffering," and so forth, is the demonstration of the actual nature of these Noble Truths.
At this point, a discourse on the Noble Truths should be given; it has been explained in detail in all its aspects in the *Visuddhimagga*.
In this regard, they should be understood according to the method already stated. Thus, these are "such" (*tathā*):
these noble truths of suffering and so forth are thus—meaning they are non-false and non-otherwise in their mode of being as suffering and so on. "They have been seen by me just as they were spoken":

just as they were spoken by the Teacher, so have they been seen by me, because they have been penetrated by the knowledge of the Noble Path; such is the case for them. This is one's own goal (*sadattha*).
I have attained arahantship; it has been realized by me. Furthermore, I have fulfilled the instruction and guidance of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
"Svāgatam vata me āsi" means "a truly happy arrival indeed was mine. "Mama buddhassa santike" means "in the presence and nearness of my Buddha, the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One."

"Attained perfection in the higher knowledges" (*abhiññāpāramippatto*) means he has reached the limit and the pinnacle of all six higher knowledges. To explain the very meaning stated by this phrase, it is said: "The faculty of hearing was purified," and so forth.
The twelve verses beginning with "I ask the Teacher" were spoken by him while inquiring about the state of final nibbāna of his own preceptor.
For at the time of the Venerable Elder Nigrodhakappa’s final nibbāna, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was not present in person.
He had previously seen his [the preceptor’s] hand-twitching and so forth;

for, due to the influence of past impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*), even those whose taints are destroyed may still have such occurrences, just as the Venerable Pilindavaccha was addressed with the term "outcaste" (*vasala*).
Therefore, having given rise to the thought, "Has my preceptor attained final Nibbāna, or has he not?", he questioned the Teacher.
Therefore it was said: "It was spoken by one who was asking about the state of the preceptor’s final passing away.

In that context, "the Teacher" refers to the one who instructs those to be trained regarding matters pertaining to the present life and so forth. "Of unsurpassed wisdom": *oma* means limited, inferior, or base;
"not of limited wisdom" is *anomapañña*, meaning one of great wisdom. "In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in direct experience, in this very world.
"Selfhood" (*attabhāva*) is the meaning. "Of doubts" (*vicikicchānaṃ*) means of such kinds of uncertainties or discursive thoughts;
he is their "cutter. "At Aggāḷava" means in the monastery known as the Aggāḷava Cetiya. "Renowned" (*ñāta*) means well-known. "Illustrious" (*yasassī*) means endowed with gain and honor.
"One who has attained final peace" (*abhinibbutatta*) means one whose nature is tranquil and whose mind is not burning with affliction.
“Made by you”: because he was seated at the foot of a banyan tree (*nigrodha*) possessed of such shade, the name “Nigrodhakappa” (Banyan-like) was given by you;
thus he speaks according to how he himself perceived him.
However, the Blessed One does not address him as such merely because of his sitting there, but also because he had attained *arahantship* there. “Of the brahmin.”
He speaks with reference to his birth; it is said that he went forth from a prominent brahmin family.
"I wandered paying homage" means he lived while paying homage. "Seeking liberation" means established in *nibbāna*.
