"One who sees the firm Dhamma" is an address to the Blessed One; for *nibbāna* is the "firm Dhamma" in the sense of being unshakable, and the Blessed One both saw it and showed it.
"Sakka" is an address to the Blessed One himself by his family name. "We too, all" is said by him, including the entire assembly without exception, while indicating himself as well.
"Samantacakkhu" is an address to the Blessed One himself by means of his omniscient knowledge.
"Samavaṭṭhitā" means properly established, standing with focused attention. "No" means "to us. "Savanāya" means for the hearing of this...
The answer to the question is for the purpose of hearing. "With the ear" means with the ear-element (*sotadhātu*). "You are our teacher;
you are unsurpassed"—this he says by way of words of praise.
"Cut off our doubt" refers to that reflection which is a counterfeit of doubt; it is [the cutting off] of unwholesome doubt.
But the Elder was free from doubt. "Tell me this," means: tell me this very thing.
Since you were requested by us, saying, "O Sakka, we too all wish to know that disciple," [the Buddha said: "O Brahmin of vast wisdom, perceive that he has attained final Nibbāna.
Having understood that he had attained final Nibbāna, the Blessed One of great wisdom spoke right in the midst [of the assembly].
"Speak in a language that we all may understand so that we all may know.
The phrase "Sakka, the thousand-eyed one among the gods," however, is merely words of praise. Furthermore, the intended meaning here is this:
just as Sakka, the thousand-eyed one, speaks words that are respectfully received by the gods in their midst, so too may you speak words that are respectfully received by us in our midst.
Reciting this verse, "Ye kecī," he speaks in order to generate a desire to praise the Blessed One. Its meaning is as follows:

whatever fetters there are, such as covetousness and the rest, because delusion (*moha*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*) cannot be abandoned so long as they remain uneliminated, they are called "paths of delusion," "sides of ignorance," and "bases of doubt. All of these [refer to] the Tathāgata.
Having reached [this state], they are shattered by the power of the Tathāgata’s teaching and perish. Why is that?
Because this is the supreme eye for humans; since the Tathāgata, by dispelling all fetters and generating the eye of wisdom, is said to be the supreme eye for humans.
Reciting this verse, "No ce hi jātū," he speaks while generating a desire to say something further. In this context, *jātu* is an emphatic particle.
*Puriso* refers to the Blessed One. *Jotimanto* refers to Sāriputta and others, who are endowed with the light of wisdom (*paññājoti*).
This is what is meant: if the Blessed One, like a wind from the east or other directions, [dispels] the clouds of ignorance through the force of his teaching...
One should destroy the defilements; for otherwise, just as the world covered by clouds becomes shrouded in darkness, so too the entire world, enveloped by ignorance, would be in darkness.
Furthermore, even those such as Sāriputta and others who now appear radiant would not speak or illuminate [the truth].
And he spoke this verse, "The wise," in the same manner as before. Its meaning is as follows: The wise, those men of wisdom, become makers of light;
they produce the light of *paññā* (insight). Therefore, O Hero, endowed with the vigor of striving, I consider you, the Blessed One, to be likewise wise;
indeed, I consider you to be a maker of light. We too [are] seekers of insight regarding all phenomena.
"Knowing that the Blessed One sees things as they truly are, we have approached him. Therefore, reveal the *kappa* among our assemblies;
even though you are already *parinibbūta*, reveal and make manifest the *nigrodhakappa*.
He spoke this verse, "Quickly," in the same manner as before. Its meaning is: "O Blessed One, quickly utter your voice."
Speak words that are lovely, lovely, without delay—words that are lovely and heart-captivating.

Just as a golden swan, while seeking its feeding ground, sees a grove of *jātassara* reeds and, stretching out its neck and fluttering its wings, cries out with a lovely voice, slow and unhurried, joyful and delighted; even so, you too, slowly...
"Chirp with this one of the marks of a Great Man, with this well-modulated, well-prepared, resonant voice!
We shall all, being upright and with undistracted minds, listen to your chirping.

"Having abandoned birth and death"—this too he said in the same manner as before. In that context, "not remaining" (*na sissati*) means "without remainder" (*aseso*); that which is without remainder is "the remainderless" (*asesaṃ*).
It is meant that birth and death have been abandoned without remainder, as in the case of those who have entered the stream (sotāpanna) and so forth.
"Having restrained" means having bound [the mind]. "The cleanser" (dhona) refers to one who has shaken off all evil. "I shall speak" means I shall cause the Dhamma to be told.

"There is no acting according to one's own will among ordinary people" (puthujjana) means that the three types of persons—ordinary people (puthujjana), those in training (sekkha), and so forth—do not possess the power to act according to their own whims; they do not know whatever they might wish to know.
They are unable to speak [of them]. However, the phrase "those who can enumerate the Tathāgatas" implies that those who investigate the Tathāgatas possess actions preceded by wisdom;
thus, whatever they wish to know or to speak about, they are indeed able to do so.
Now, in order to clarify that ability to enumerate, he recited the verse beginning with "perfect in exposition. Its meaning is as follows:

For thus has the Blessed One spoken and set forth for you—whose wisdom is upright and whose wisdom is directed straightly because it is unimpeded in all respects—a perfectly articulated and accomplished explanation:
"The minister Santati will rise to the height of seventy palm trees and attain final Nibbāna; the Sakyan Suppabuddha will enter the earth on the seventh day."
Having thus correctly grasped what was well-learned and seen without error, he again extended his hands in salutation with even greater devotion and said:
"This final salutation is well-offered. This means that yet another salutation has been offered with even greater excellence.
"May you not delude us, knowing; may you not delude us by remaining silent, for you know its destination"—thus he addressed him as one of "unfathomable wisdom" (anomapañña).
He addresses the Blessed One.
Furthermore, by means of this verse beginning with "paroparaṃ," he speaks while requesting non-delusion once again through another method.

In that context, "paroparaṃ" refers to the beautiful and the ugly, or the distant and the near, according to the distinction between the supramundane and the mundane. "Ariyadhammaṃ" [means] the noble Dhamma.
The Dhamma of the Four Truths. "Having known" means having penetrated. "Knowing all" means knowing every dhamma that is to be known.
"I long for your word": just as a person exhausted and parched by heat during the summer season longs for water, even so do I long for your word.
"Rain down what has been heard": rain down, pour forth, release, and set in motion that which is called "the heard," namely, the sphere of sound.
There is also a textual reading, *sutassa vassā*. The meaning is: "it rains upon" (*vassati*) the rain of the sound-base (*saddāyatana*) of the kind already described.
Now, demonstrating what kind of speech he desires, he spoke the verse beginning with "yadatthikam.
In that context, "Kappāyano" is said by way of honorific reference to Kappa himself. "As one liberated" means: "What [is there] in the Nibbāna-element without residue?"
"Is it as one beyond training (asekkha), or rather as one with a residue remaining (saupādisesa), or as one still in training (sekkha)? Thus he asks. The rest here is self-evident.
Having been thus requested by means of these twelve verses, the Blessed One, answering him, said: "He has cut off," and so forth.
Therein, "He has cut off craving for name-and-form here" (thus the Blessed One said)—the stream of darkness that had lain dormant for a long time.

In this name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), craving—divided into categories such as sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) and so forth—has lain dormant (*anusayita*) for a long time in the sense of being unabandoned;

it is also called the "stream" of Māra, who is named Kaṇha (the Black One). Kappāyana cut off that craving in this name-and-form, which is the stream of Kaṇha, released [from the past], and lying dormant for a long time.
"Thus said the Blessed One"—this, however, is the statement of the compilers of the collection. He crossed over birth.
"Having cut off that craving without remainder, he has crossed over birth and death entirely and attained parinibbāna without residue (anupādisesa)"—this is what is shown.
"Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Best of the Five": when asked by the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, the Blessed One spoke thus;
he is the best among those possessing the five faculties beginning with faith, which are not shared by others, or he is the best by way of his eyes. Alternatively, "the Best of the Five" means:
"Excellent, supreme, and preeminent by way of the five aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue, or by way of the five perfections beginning with the perfection of causes"—
this is also a statement of the compilers of the Council.
When this had been said, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, his mind rejoicing in the Blessed One’s words, recited the verses beginning with "Having heard this."

He said: Regarding that, in the first verse, "he did not deceive me" means that because he has attained final Nibbāna (*parinibbuto*), he did not deceive or mislead me who desired to know his state of having attained final Nibbāna. The rest is self-evident.
In the second verse, because he dwelt looking toward liberation (*mutyapekho*), it was said with reference to him: "As he spoke, so he acted."
“He was a disciple of the Buddha. “The snare of Death” refers to Māra’s snare of craving, which is spread throughout the cycle of existence in the three realms (*tebhumakavaṭṭa*).
“Of the deceitful one” means of him who possesses much deceit. Some read “*tathā māyāvino*”;
for them, the intended meaning is: “of him who approached the Blessed One many times with various deceits.”
In the third verse, "the beginning" (ādi) refers to the root cause. "Of clinging" (upādānassa) means of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).

The cycle of existence is called "clinging" (upādāna) in the sense that it is to be clung to by firm kamma and defilements. With the eye of knowledge, he saw the beginning of that clinging—the causes consisting of ignorance, craving, and so forth.
He speaks with the intention: "It is fitting to say, 'The Blessed One is capable (kappo kappiyo).'"
"Accagā vata" means "he has indeed transcended. "Maccudheyyaṃ" (the realm of death) means that death dwells here;
thus it is the realm of death—the cycle of existence consisting of the three planes which is so difficult to cross. Having become aware of this, he says, "He has indeed transcended.
Now, with a mind full of confidence toward the Teacher and his own preceptor, manifesting that state of confidence, he says: "That God of Gods."
He spoke the concluding verse. Therein, "I pay homage to that God of Gods":

he is the God of Gods because he is the supreme deity among all those who are gods by convention (*sammutideva*), gods by birth (*upapattideva*), and gods by purity (*visuddhideva*). I pay homage to that Blessed One, the Supreme among Bipeds.

Not only him alone, but also [those] born after you (*anujāta*) through being produced in accordance with the Dhamma following your perfect enlightenment (*saccābhisambodhi*), and through the victory over Māra.
I pay homage to the Great Hero because of his great heroism; to the Nāga in the sense of being one who has come [to the Dhamma], and so forth;
and to the son born from your own breast (*orasa-putta*) and to him who is like a banyan tree (*nigrodha-kappa*).
Thus, these two hundred and sixty-four great elders, beginning with Subhūti and ending with Vaṅgīsa, are here in this text.
Having ascended, they are all of one kind by virtue of being disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One;

likewise, they are of one kind by virtue of being those beyond training (*asekha*), by having the cross-bar lifted, by having the enclosures broken down, by having the thorns pulled out, by being without bolts, by having the banner lowered, by having the burden laid down, by being detached, and by having completed their residence in the ten noble abodes (*ariyavāsa*). For it is thus that they are.
They have abandoned five factors, are endowed with six factors, possess a single guard, have four foundations,
have shaken off individual truths, have thoroughly given up searching, have untroubled intentions, have tranquil bodily formations, and are well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom.
In this manner, they are of one kind.
There are two kinds of those ordained by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhubhāvena*): those ordained by the "Come, monk" formula and those not ordained by the "Come, monk" formula.
Among them, there were the five bhikkhus of the group beginning with Aññā-Koṇḍañña;
the thera Yasa; his four companions—Vimala, Subāhu, Puṇṇaji, and Gavampati; and fifty-five others who were also his companions, making thirty... [in total].
The Bhaddavaggiyas, the thousand former matted-hair ascetics headed by Uruvelakassapa, the two chief disciples,
the one hundred and twenty-five wanderers who were their followers, and the thera Aṅgulimāla the robber—
altogether they number three thousand and fifty. Therefore, this is said:
“Seven hundred and one thousand, and another fifty;
these elders of great wisdom, all of whom were ordained by the ‘Come, monk’ formula.
And not only these, but there are many others as well. For example, the brahmin Sela—his...
There were three hundred brahmins who had become his pupils; Mahākappina and the thousand men who formed his retinue;
ten thousand men from Kapilavatthu sent by King Suddhodana; and sixteen thousand people, including Ajita and others, who had become pupils of the brahmin Mahābāvari.
Apart from those mentioned thus, there were no others [ordained] by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhubhāva*).

Regarding full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is obtained through these four modes: full ordination by going for refuge, full ordination by receiving instruction, full ordination by answering questions, and full ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*).

For instance, when the elders first came to the state of "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*), the Blessed One permitted their full ordination through the three goings for refuge alone, just as he had permitted their going forth (*pabbajjā*).
This is the formal admission through going for refuge. Furthermore:

"Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Strong shame and dread of wrongdoing shall be established in me toward elders, juniors, and those of middle standing. Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself. Therefore...

“Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will listen to it all, making it my bone, attending to it, applying my whole mind, and lending an ear.
In this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘Accompanied by joy...’”
“‘And may mindfulness directed to the body not abandon me’—in this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself.
By accepting this instruction, the Elder Mahākassapa’s admission to the higher ordination (*upasampadā*) was authorized; this is what is called “ordination by acceptance of instruction.
Furthermore, while walking back and forth in the Eastern Monastery, the Blessed One said: “Sopāka, the perception of a bloated corpse is indeed a perception of form (*rūpasaññā*).”

When questions concerning the bases of foulness were asked— such as, "Are these states different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they identical in meaning and only different in phrasing?"—
and when the seven-year-old novice Sopāka approached the Blessed One and replied, "Whether it be called 'the perception of a bloated corpse' or 'perception of form,' O Blessed One,
these states are identical in meaning; only the phrasing is different," and so forth.
“Having reconciled these questions with this omniscient knowledge, they have been answered”—thus, with a mind thus inclined, the Blessed One granted the admission to the order.

This is what is called the admission to the order by way of answering questions (*pañhābyākaraṇūpasampadā*). The admission to the order by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is indeed well known.
Just as there are two kinds of admission—by the formula “Come, monk” (*ehibhikkhu*) and not by the formula “Come, monk”—so too...

They are also twofold according to the distinction between those who are in the presence [of the Teacher] and those who are not in his presence. Those who were born into noble birth during the Teacher’s lifetime—such as Aññā-Koṇḍañña and others—are called "disciples in his presence.

However, those who attained distinction after the Blessed One’s final nibbāna are [disciples] despite the fact that the Teacher’s Dhamma-body was directly present to them, because of the Teacher’s physical body.
Because they have not been personally witnessed, they are called "disciples in absentia.

Likewise, there are those liberated both ways and those liberated by wisdom; however, it should be understood that only those liberated both ways are mentioned here in the text. For this is stated in the *Apadāna*:
"These eight liberations have been realized, along with the six direct knowledges."

Likewise, there is a distinction between those with *apadāna* and those without *apadāna*. For those who have an *apadāna*—reckoned as the *sāvakapāramitā* (perfection of disciples)—which was performed by way of meritorious deeds under previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, Pacceka Buddhas, or disciples of Buddhas, they are "with *apadāna*," such as the elders (theras) recorded in the *Apadāna-pāḷi*.
But those for whom that does not exist are "without *apadāna*."
But can the full and perfect realization of the Truths possibly occur entirely without the perfection of prior causes?

It cannot occur. For there is no attainment of the Noble Path for one who lacks the perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya*), because that [Path] is by nature extremely difficult to perform and difficult to realize.
As it has been said: "What do you think, monks, which is more difficult to do or more difficult to realize..."
"...or," and so forth. If this is so, why was it said: "But those for whom that does not exist are 'without a foothold' (anapadānā)"?
This should not be understood as meaning "those who are entirely devoid of the excellence of a decisive support (upanissaya) are without a foothold," because such persons are not intended here.
Rather, those for whom there is no foothold that has reached the highest excellence are here called "without a foothold."
It is not said that they are entirely devoid of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

For these beings, seeing the majesty of the Buddhas—the expansion of their inconceivable and marvelous qualities manifested upon the arising of a Buddha—gain faith in the Teacher because he inspires confidence in every respect throughout the world of the four measures.
Likewise, through hearing the true Dhamma and by witnessing the right practice of the disciples, [they gain faith].
Sometimes they acquire faith in the true Dhamma by witnessing the resolution of mind toward perfect enlightenment made by great Bodhisattvas, and by receiving instruction and advice from them.
Having acquired faith therein, even though they perceive the dangers in saṃsāra and the benefits in nibbāna,
because of their great defilement (raja), they do not achieve the security from bondage, and thus from time to time—

They indeed plant the wholesome seed that is the necessary condition for turning away from the round within their own continuum, because of the great extent of their reliance upon true persons. Therefore he said:
“If we should fail in the teaching of this Lord of the World, In a future age, we shall stand face to face with him.”
"Just as people crossing a river, having missed a convenient ford,
take hold of a lower ford and cross over the great river—
so too, if we all were to release this Conqueror, [we would likewise cross over]."
"In a future time, we shall be present before him"—

it cannot be said that a wholesome state of mind generated with such a resolve directed toward the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*) does not serve as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the attainment of liberation after an interval of four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons; this is even more so when the service is performed by way of aspiration.
Having been thus established, these [disciples] are of two kinds.
They are of three types: the Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka), the Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka), and the Ordinary Disciples (Pakatisāvaka).
Among them were the Venerable Aññā-Koṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, Assaji, Nālaka, Yasa, Vimala, Subāhu, Puṇṇaji, Gavampati, and Uruvelakassapa.
Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana,
Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākapphiṇa, Mahācunda, Anuruddha, Kāṅkṣārevata, Ānanda, Nandaka, Bhagu, Nanda, Kimbila, Bhaddiya,
Rāhula, Sīvalī, Upāli, Dabba, Upasena, and Khadiravaniya Revata.
Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, Puṇṇa of Sunāparanta, Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, Soṇa Koḷivisa, Rādha, Subhūti, Aṅgulimāla,
Vakkali, Kāḷudāyī, Mahāudāyī, Pilindavaccha, Sobhita,
Kumārakassapa, Raṭṭhapāla, Vaṅgīsa, Sabhiya, Sela, Upavāna, Meghiya, Sāgata, Nāgita, and Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya.
Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja, Mahāpanthaka, Cūḷapanthaka, Bākula, Kuṇḍadhāna, Dārucīriya, Yasojja, Ajita,
Tissa-Metteyya, Puṇṇaka, Mettagū, Dhotaka, Upasīva, Nanda, Hemaka, Todeyya, Kappa,
Jatukaṇṇī, Bhadrāvudha, Udaya, Posāla, Mogharāja, and Piṅgiya— these are known as the eighty great disciples.
But why are those very elders called "great disciples" (mahāsāvaka)?
Because of the greatness of their initial resolve (abhinīhāra). For even the two chief disciples (aggasāvaka) are included among the great disciples.

Although they stand in the foremost position among disciples due to their attainment of the supreme state through reaching the pinnacle of the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), they are nevertheless called "great disciples" by virtue of the commonality of the greatness of their resolve.
These are so called. The others, however, possess a far more distinguished great resolve than ordinary disciples (*pakatisāvaka*).

For they made their aspiration during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Precisely because of that, they are masters of the superknowledges (*abhiññā*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), and possess the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) in abundance.
Granted, all Arahants alike, having accomplished the purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) and the other stages, have minds established in the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are, and having exhausted the defilements without remainder through the sequence of the path,
they become established in the highest fruit. Nevertheless, just as there is certainly a desired distinction between one who has attained vision and one liberated by faith,

and between one liberated in both ways and one liberated by wisdom— due to the difference in their prior-stage development— so too is there a distinction here due to the greatness of the initial aspiration and the greatness of previous practice.

Because they have produced a preeminent distinction of qualities within their own mental continuums, these disciples are "great" by virtue of their qualities such as morality; thus, they are called *mahāsāvakas* (Great Disciples).

Furthermore, among those very disciples, there are those who, through the diligent application of a specific effort directed toward that end—which serves as the cause for the production of an extraordinary function in right view and right concentration, which are the foremost and principal factors among the qualities conducive to enlightenment—are [distinguished].
Having been continuously concentrated for a long time through right practice, they attained the highest perfection in wisdom and concentration respectively;
thus, by virtue of their preeminence in all qualities, they stood at the summit of all disciples.

Although Sāriputta and Moggallāna were Great Disciples, they stood at the head of all disciples because they had reached the pinnacle of disciple-perfection and because of the greatness of their original resolve (*abhinīhāra*).
And because of the greatness of their prior application (*pubbayoga*), they are called "chief disciples" (*aggasāvaka*).

However, those noble disciples who are neither like the chief disciples nor like the great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*), but rather number in the hundreds and thousands, are "ordinary disciples" (*pakatisāvaka*).
Those included here in the text, however, are limited in number, as they are selected by way of verses. Nevertheless, even among the great disciples—
Some of these have not been included here in the Pāḷi.
Thus, these three types are each threefold according to the divisions of the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha) and so forth, and they are also threefold by way of the attainment of liberation.
For these three liberations are: the void liberation (suññata-vimokkha), the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha), and the desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha).
And those liberations are to be attained by means of the three contemplations, beginning with emptiness, such as the contemplation of impermanence.
For initially, there is an application of insight to impermanence and so forth by way of any one aspect.
But when the emergence of the path occurs through the insight leading to emergence which comprehends formations under the aspect of impermanence, then that insight—
Even though the signs of passion and so forth have been eradicated, she does not relinquish the sign of formations;
thus, failing to obtain the name "signless" in the ultimate sense, she is unable to bestow the name "signless" upon her own path.
Although the signless liberation is not explicitly mentioned in the Abhidhamma, it is obtained in the Suttanta through the eradication of the signs of passion and the rest.
“Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit;
then, through the full comprehension of conceit, you shall wander at peace.
By such passages, the cultivation of the signless liberation through insight and the state of the unsurpassed signless liberation are described.

When the emergence of the path occurs through insight that comprehends formations as suffering, then that insight receives the name "wishless" (*appaṇihita*) by way of the total eradication of longing for sensual desire and so forth;

thus it is called the wishless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*). And the path immediately following that is the wishless liberation. However, when the insight leading to emergence— [...]* *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

When one emerges from the path by means of contemplating [the aggregates] in their aspect of non-self (*anattākāra*), then insight receives the name "emptiness" (*suññata*) through the eradication of the view of self;
thus it is called the "emptiness liberation" (*suññatavimokkha*). And the path immediately following that is also called the emptiness liberation.
Among these three liberations, which constitute the supreme path, some of these elders [attain] by means of the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*).

Some [attain] by means of the liberation of the signless, some by the liberation of the desireless, and some by the liberation of the void. Therefore it was said: "They are threefold according to the division of the signless liberation and so forth;
they are also threefold according to the attainment of liberation.

They are fourfold according to the analysis of the way of practice (*paṭipadā*). For there are four ways of practice: the painful way with sluggish direct knowledge, [the painful way with swift direct knowledge, the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge, and the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge].
The painful practice with quick direct knowledge, the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge, and the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Therein,
among the applications of insight through the door of form and so forth, one who applies insight by way of the door of form,
having discerned the four great elements, discerns derived form and discerns the formless— that is, both form and the formless— [is described as follows].

However, for one who, while discerning [the aggregates], succeeds in discerning them only with difficulty, pain, and exhaustion, there is what is called the "painful way of practice" (dukkha-paṭipadā).

For one who has discerned both the material and immaterial, but whose insight is sluggish due to a delay in the manifestation of the path during the period of preparatory insight (vipassanā-parivāsa), there is what is called "slow direct knowledge" (dandhābhiññā).
Furthermore, for one who, having discerned the material and immaterial, is defining name-and-form (nāmarūpa) with difficulty...
One who defines [name-and-form] with difficulty and weariness, and who, having defined name-and-form,
dwells in the probationary period of insight and is only able to arouse the Path after a long time— for him too, this is called the "difficult practice with sluggish direct knowledge.
Another, having defined name-and-form, grasps the conditions with pain, difficulty, and weariness.

When one dwells in the probationary period of insight after having discerned the conditions, and only after a long time does one arouse the Path—this is called the "difficult practice with sluggish direct knowledge.

Another, having discerned the conditions and penetrating the characteristics, penetrates them with pain, difficulty, and exhaustion; yet, having penetrated the characteristics, he dwells in the probationary period of insight...
When one develops the path slowly during the spring season, this is likewise called "the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge.
Another person, having penetrated the characteristics [of the three marks], while insight-knowledge is sharp, keen, clear, and flowing, suppresses the craving for insight that has arisen;
yet he does so with difficulty, with hardship, and with exhaustion, and having suppressed that craving—

When one dwelling in the probationary period of insight (vipassanā-parivāsa) arouses the path only after a long time, this is called the "difficult way with sluggish direct knowledge" (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā).
Among the aforementioned ways of practice, when there is swiftness in the manifestation of the path, it is the "difficult way with quick direct knowledge" (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā);
however, when those ways of practice are accomplished without difficulty, yet there is slowness in the manifestation of the path, [it is the easy way with sluggish direct knowledge].

Furthermore, by way of swiftness and sequence, one should understand the "pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge" (*sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*) and the "pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge" (*sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā*).
Through these four modes of practice, the fourfold nature of the elders who have attained the supreme path should be understood;
for there is no attainment of the Noble Path without these modes of practice. Thus, in the Abhidhamma it is said: "In which..."

The Noble Path is analyzed together with its modes of progress (*paṭipadā*) in such passages as: "At this time, one develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation, conducive to dispersal...
[etc. ...which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge. Therefore it is said: "It is fourfold by way of the analysis of its modes of progress.
It is fivefold by way of the analysis of the predominance of the faculties (*indriya*). Although there is a commonality among them in the realization of the Truths (*saccābhisambodha*), some elders—
Some were preeminent in faith, such as the Elder Vakkali; some were preeminent in energy, such as the Elders Mahāsoṇa and Koḷivīsa;
some were preeminent in mindfulness, such as the Elder Sobhita; some were preeminent in concentration, such as the Elder Cūḷapanthaka;
and some were preeminent in wisdom, such as the Elder Ānanda. For he was indeed possessed of such a state of being.

And he is praised for possessing skill in the meaning (*atthakosalla*) and so forth; furthermore, this classification is stated according to the specific qualities found in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).
However, at the moment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*), it is accepted that all the other faculties (*indriya*) also possess a single nature.

Likewise, there are five types: those who have reached perfection (*pāramippatta*), those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidāppatta*), those with the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*), those with the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*), and those who practice bare insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
For among his disciples, some have reached the pinnacle of disciple-perfection, such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna;

others have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) by way of these four analytical knowledges: the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
Some are "possessed of the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiññā*) by way of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) such as the knowledge of the modes of psychic power;
some are "possessed of the three true insights" (*tevijjā*) by way of the three types of clear vision (*vijjā*) such as the knowledge of past lives.

However, those who, having established insight while remaining in mere momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*), have attained the supreme path—these [are included] from the beginning and intermittently through the factor of jhāna born of concentration within the interior of insight.
Because they lack the attainment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), insight is "dry" for them; thus they are called "dry-insight practitioners" (*sukkhavipassaka*).
This classification was stated after examining the commonality among disciples. However, no dry-insight practitioners appear at all here in the text. For this very reason it was said:
"The four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and these eight liberations (*vimokkha*)."
"The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished," and so forth.
Thus, it is fivefold by way of the attainment of the perfections and so on.
It is sixfold by way of the signless and so on, such as "one liberated through the signless" and others.

There are two types: those whose burden is faith (*saddhādhura*) and those whose burden is wisdom (*paññādhura*). Likewise, there are those liberated through the desireless (*appaṇihita-vimutta*) and those liberated through wisdom (*paññā-vimutta*). Thus, by way of liberation through the signless (*animitta-vimutta*) and so forth, and according to the classification of liberation by way of synonyms, there are seven types.

For there are four who, having made each one of the four formless attainments (*arūpa-samāpatti*) a basis, have begun insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*; and [those who] have emerged from cessation (*nirodha*)...

There are five who have attained *arahantship*. There are two who are liberated both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*); and there are two who are liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*) according to whether they belong to the class of those whose burden is faith (*saddhādhura*) or those whose burden is wisdom (*paññādhura*).
Thus, they are sevenfold by way of the classification of liberation.

They are eightfold by way of the classification of the burden and the path of practice. For he who goes forth by means of the painful path of practice (*dukkha-paṭipadā*) with sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*), [is one type].

That [Arahantship] is twofold by way of the burden of faith and the burden of wisdom; likewise for the remaining modes of practice (*paṭipadā*). Thus, it is eightfold through the classification of burdens and modes of practice.

It is ninefold by way of the classification of deliverance (*vimutti*): five who are liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), two who are liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*), and the two Chief Disciples who have attained perfection in both liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) and liberation by wisdom.
Thus it is ninefold. It is tenfold by way of deliverance alone: having made each of the four formless-sphere jhānas a basis (*pādaka*), [one attains] Arahantship.

The four who have attained [the fruits], and the dry-insight practitioner—these five are liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*); together with those previously mentioned who are liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), there are thus ten types according to the classification of liberation.
When these are divided according to the aforementioned classification of the "burdens" (*dhura*), they become twenty.

When divided according to the classification of the "ways of practice" (*paṭipadā*), they become forty. Furthermore, when divided by way of the classification of the ways of practice and the classification of the burdens...
When further divided, they become eighty. Then, when divided according to the distinctions of emptiness, liberation, and so forth, they become two hundred and forty.
Furthermore, when divided by way of the predominance of the faculties (*indriya*), they become one thousand two hundred and twenty.
Thus, among those noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) established in the paths and fruits, who are analyzed into many divisions according to their own qualities—those [who...]

They also clarify their own progress in practice and so forth. Those who uttered verses such as "My hut is covered" by way of *udāna* and the like have been included here under the heading of "verses. Therefore he said: "Like lions roaring...
having touched the deathless state. Thus should the incidental discussion (*pakiṇṇakakathā*) herein be understood.
